title: How could Great Britain look under proportional representation? See the results for your area | Electoral reform | The Guardian
description: These visualisations from exclusive polling modelling show how the UK parliament could change under different voting systems
Author: Antonio Voce
Headline: These visualisations from exclusive polling modelling show how the UK parliament could change under different voting systems
Content: Composite: The GuardianView image in fullscreenComposite: The GuardianElectoral reformHow could Great Britain look under proportional representation? See the results for your areaThese visualisations from exclusive polling modelling show how the UK parliament could change under different voting systemsAntonio VoceandAshley KirkWed 30 Sep 2026 08.45 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 16.00 EDTShareNew analysis produced exclusively for the Guardian reveals how different voting systems would return significantly different seat totals in the UK parliament, based on recent polling.While the current first past the post (FPTP) system could leaveLabourshort of a majority with 250 seats, the modelling shows how proportional systems would be likely to reduce the number of seats given to the leading party – and give the UK a more finely balanced parliament that better represents the votes people cast.The prime minister, Andy Burnham, has announced a new national commission on electoral reform aimed at changing the electoral system,a plan supported bymore than 100 Labour MPsas well as parties such as the Liberal Democrats, the Greens, the SNP and Plaid Cymru. Electoral reform has enjoyedincreased public support in recent years.Theresearch conducted by More in Commonsuggests that, under proportional systems such as single transferable vote or regional party list, the UK could end up being governed by a minority government – or aprogressive allianceof parties.How proportional systems could change the mapProportional representation (PR) aims to produce a parliament that more closely reflects how people voted, allowing voters to back their preferred party without worrying about tactical voting. It often makes it harder for a single party to win a majority and is more likely to result in coalition governments.Alongside the current first past the post system, More in Common modelled three different PR systems for the Guardian: regional party list, single transferable vote (STV) and additional member system (AMS).The More in Common research shows that no single party would achieve a majority according to their projected polling, regardless of which system is used.The current FPTP system would come the closest, giving Labour 39% of the seats off just 26% of the vote – still short of a majority. The party would most likely need the support of the Lib Dems and the SNP to form a majority government.The proportional systems would not give Labour such a boost: regional party list is estimated to give the party 26% of seats off 26% of the vote; AMS would give it 26% of the seats off 29% of the vote; and STV would give it 27% of the seats off 28% of the vote.Under each of these systems, either a progressive coalition of parties – a combination of Labour, the Lib Dems, the Greens, the SNP orPlaid Cymru– or a Reform-Conservative-Restore coalition would be the only paths to forming a government. Even then, several scenarios would lead to a minority government in a finely balanced parliament.While the leading Labour party would lose the largest proportion of seats under the proportional systems, smaller parties would be the biggest winners.The Green party would win only three seats under FPTP under current polling, but more than 50 seats in all three PR systems that we’re modelling – 9% of the seats on offer, more closely matching their vote share. Likewise, the far-rightRestore Britainparty would surge above 30 seats in each of the PR systems, compared with winning just one seat under FPTP.Charlie Buckley, a senior research associate at More in Common, said: “With [Nigel] Farage’s [Reform UK] party having lost some momentum and Andy Burnham being – for now – a more popular prime minister, it’s Labour who would reap the benefits from our current electoral system.“Despite only being four points ahead of the Tories, our model shows Labour winning double the number of seats under first past the post, while a proportional system would give us a parliament which better reflects the close three-horse race we now have between Labour, Reform and theConservatives.”Burnham said in his conference speech that Labour shouldn’t “open the door” to a “divisive government” that could win power on “less than 30% of the vote”.The proportional systems were more likely to remove the regional dominance of any one party. InLondon, Labour is estimated to gain 69% of seats under FPTP. This number would drop dramatically under PR, to 37% in the party list system and 42% under AMS.Reform and the Greens would be the biggest beneficiaries in the capital: while Reform would win one seat and the Greens nothing under FPTP, they’d collectively win 18 seats – nearly a quarter of London’s seats on offer – under the party list system.The same disparity can be seen in the east of England, with the poll-leaders there, Reform, gaining 43% of the seats under FPTP but falling to 29% under both the party list and AMS systems.How would your local representation change?Use the postcode search below to see how your local representation would change under each system. Under systems that use regional vote counts to produce more proportional results, you would have regional representatives in place of – or in addition to – constituency ones.What is wrong with first past the post?The most recent polling in Britain, as well as recentelections, show an unprecedented fragmentation of the political system. Labour leads on an average of 26%, with Reform second on 23% and the Conservatives third on 20%. The Greens and the Lib Dems are each polling at 10%.This is based on an average of the last 10 polls, with Labour enjoying a slim lead in the national polls since the party chose Burnham as its new leader and prime minister.With three parties clustered closely together in the polls, the FPTP system means small shifts in vote share could producehighly volatile and sometimes counterintuitive seat projections, as marginal changes in local contests are amplified into large swings in parliamentary representation.Chart showing UK poll averagesIn the last general election,Labour won 411of 650 seats with just 34% of the vote.Areport from the Electoral Reform Societymodelled the 2024 vote under different voting systems. Only first past the post gave Labour a majority, with all proportional systems giving smaller parties more representation and leading to a hung parliament.There have been renewed calls for proportional representation. In his conference speech, Burnham said: “We will contest the next election with a manifesto commitment to change the electoral system so that everyone’s vote counts and everyone’s voice is heard.”Farage has alsopreviously called for electoral reform, calling the current system “outdated” and “not fit for purpose”, but has gone quiet on the subject since Reform went on to lead the polls – until Burnham’s Labour retook a slim lead.Could the voting system change?Experts say any attempt to introduce proportional representation for Westminster elections would be likely to face strong pressure for a referendum, given its significance as a constitutional change and the precedent set by the2011 referendum on the alternative vote system (AV).The referendum saw voters decisively reject AV, showing the difficulty of winning public support for electoral reform. Experts warn that any future move to proportional representation could face similar challenges, as voters are familiar with first past the post and may be reluctant to replace a system they already understand.Buckley said: “The real winners with a PR system would be on the edges of the political spectrum. The Greens would go from a handful of MPs to a sizeable bloc, while Restore Britain would arrive in parliament in numbers, potentially giving these smaller parties a kingmaker role in the formation of coalitions.“So the prospect of forming a workable majority – already a dubious one in our current electoral system – looks even more complicated under a proportional one. Regardless of the system in place, our fragmented politics would make any election in Britain a challenge for those seeking to enter and control government, and the idea of a ‘commanding majority’ is out of reach for all the major parties right now.”When More in Commonconducted similar modelling in July, Reform was leading in the polls, and they found the proportional systems would equally not give Reform the same seats boost that FPTP would. The researchers said then that it was difficult to predict how voters might adjust their own behaviour under a new system.Darren Hughes, the chief executive of the Electoral Reform Society, told the Guardian: “The prime minister’s pledge for a new commission to look at electoral reform is an important step in the right direction. This needs to be an independent and trusted process that focuses on making sure parliament properly reflects the way the country voted.“There is a growing problem with our democracy in that parliament is looking less and less like the way people voted. The last general election saw the biggest mismatch in British history between the votes people cast and the seats parties won.“This is largely due to the fact that our outdated two-party voting system can’t cope with the multiparty politics we now have, and is throwing up increasingly distorted and unstable results.“Simply put, bringing in a system of proportional representation would mean parliament better reflects how the country voted by making sure seats match votes.”MethodologyLatest polling and seat distribution figures were provided by More In Common (MIC). Alternative electoral system modelling is based on MIC and Guardian assumptions about constituency boundaries.Party list uses 11 regions – the nine official English regions plus Scotland and Wales – with variable seat totals. AMS uses a combination of the eleven regions and 631 existing first past the post constituencies. STV uses 52 subregional constituencies – composed of the current FPTP constituencies – of variable size depending on aggregate population.Northern Ireland and the Commons speaker’s seat of Chorley are excluded from the modelling. This results in 631 total modelled seats for FPTP, STV and party list systems, and in 1,052 seats for AMS.The exact details, shown as seat totals, boundaries and regional groupings, are based on assumptions on how the new proportional systems could work, and in reality, these totals and exact workings would vary should another voting system be adopted.

title: Building of the Pep supremacy is an era that will be defined by sham-ball | Manchester City | The Guardian
description: Guardiola’s success at Manchester City was underpinned by financial cheating. Now he can only double down on his adherence to the owners
Author: Barney Ronay
Headline: Guardiola’s success at Manchester City was underpinned by financial cheating. Now he can only double down on his adherence to the owners
Content: Pep Guardiola lifts the Premier League at Brighton in 2019 but all his successes at Manchester City are now tainted by the guilty verdicts.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPep Guardiola lifts the Premier League at Brighton in 2019 but all his successes at Manchester City are now tainted by the guilty verdicts.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianManchester CityBuilding of the Pep supremacy is an era that will be defined by sham-ballGuardiola’s success at Manchester City was underpinned by financial cheating. Now he can only double down on his adherence to the ownersBarney RonayWed 30 Sep 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Do you know the question that you are asking me? Today, do you honestly think it is my job to make this kind of question happen …” Cut to the long, painful pause. Chuck in a deep, shaming stare, eyes that have suddenly become death rays of betrayal and disgust andPep Guardiolahimself transformed from a man cheerfully toasting his own FA Cup final victory to a grizzled chief detective addressing a room full of convicted perverts.Guardiola had the wind entirely at his back at this point, sitting in the Wembley press room an hour afterManchester City’s 6-0 defeat of Watford in May 2019. Success drowns out every other noise in football. To be good is also to begood, noble, virtuous. History is written by the domestic treble winners. Right up until the moment it isn’t.Rival clubs feel relegating Manchester City to Championship would not be enoughRead moreThe question in question was asked by Rob Harris of the Associated Press. It was basically this: information is now in the public domain that suggestsRoberto Mancini received a second salary from Abu Dhabiwhen he was City manager. Mancini was one of Guardiola’s immediate predecessors. So had he, Pep, ever received two salaries?Even as Harris was asking this he was interrupted by City’s press officer, saying: “We’re not going here,we’re really just not going there.” A simple “no” would have done the job. Instead the exchange ended with another beautifully executed mad-dog stare from Guardiola; not angry, just sad and disappointed. But also, let’s be honest, really angry as well.Fast forward to this week and a clip has been doing the rounds of the same Rob Harris, now of Sky News, and still the same perky, questing figure. Harris is approaching Ferran Soriano this time, Pep’s key man through that era, and asking the same entirely legitimate things, with a very different outcome. “The Premier League maintains you cheated for nearly a decade … is all this success, as the Premier League says, based on sham contracts?”There is no glare in return now, no outrage, no flushed moral high ground. “Thank you, thank you,” Soriano mutters, with the look of a man caught shoplifting a Twix at the local primary school fete, followed by a mute, fumbling exit.Sunlight. Scrutiny. Awkward questions from awkward people. It turns out these are still the best disinfectant. Just as it turns out “the question” was the only one worth asking in that room in 2019. Not that anyone agreed at the time. Predictably enough the comments on social media were about scum, bias, the press as a national embarrassment. Even other journalists held a perfumed kerchief to their noses, suggesting this was all a non-issue because, er, the club had just won a treble.It turns out the exact opposite was true. It was entirely the right moment to ask this question. That Cup final win came at the end of the main period of shammery. It was in many ways its unholy coronation. There was an industrial-scale embarrassment in that room. But it wasn’t the person asking the questions.View image in fullscreenThe sports correspondent Rob Harris confronts Manchester City’s chief executive, Ferran Soriano, in Copenhagen.Photograph: Sky NewsThere is an obvious problem with the City story at this stage. It’s just too big. There is too much to say, an entire Dickensian multiverse interlayered with oddities and moments of jaw-drop. This is not, repeat not, a media story. And yet it kind of is a media story. After all, it was media scrutiny and the efforts of the hacker Rui Pinto that first winkled it out. As such, Harris deserves his moment of grace, living proof that it’s culturally vital to keep on asking questions, the same Rob Harris I have seen grilling Vladimir Putin about corruption on the hoof in Zurich, and also walking into a pillar at the World Cup in São Paulo while running off with his laptop to ask someone else something else, a man so deeply locked into the news cycle even reinforced stadium infrastructure doesn’t register.It is also worth mentioning at moments like this Nick Harris, AKA Sporting Intelligence, who has kept going at this story relentlessly despite an unusual degree of abuse, harassment and threats, and who has every right to feel vindicated, part of a world where we can still hold power to account, where a cat can look at a king. But for now the real object of interest in this exchange is, of course, the person on the other end of it. Welcome to the stage once again Pep Guardiola, the public face of the club for the past decade.What did Pep know? This is more than just football legacy chat. It relates to pretty much everything here, the true nature of the club, of elite football itself, and more basic things like truth, spectacle and human nature. Is believing the assurances of others any kind of defence, given Guardiola was in the perfect position to ask questions of his own? Is any kind of deniability plausible here?Andy Burnham admits to ‘concern’ if Manchester City lose their owners after guilty verdictsRead moreThe other significant statement from Guardiola in that time came after City’s two-year ban from theChampions Leaguefor a serious breach of Uefa’s financial fair play rules wasoverturned by the court of arbitration for sport. “We didn’t break the rules. We played the same rules as all the clubs in the Premier League,” was Guardiola’s conclusion, which seemed pretty silly at the time, given time-barring of offences was key to that decision. How does it look now?To this day Guardiola’s stance remains slavish adherence to the promises of his paymasters, as evidenced by his first statement on the matter on Wednesday. Guardiola sayshe will be getting through the current unpleasantnesswith the club and its fans, sticking together as always. But were you together, really? Because City’s fans have some urgent questions of their own now. The majority believed what they were told, and put their faith in the “irrefutable body of evidence” schtick. That ring binder of truth really is going to have to do a lot of instant high-speed kung fu when it finally comes screeching into the appeal room on its trail bike. Not to mention explaining where it’s been over the past three years of information exchange.Guardiola will face his own questions too, and on a level that will hurt him. The coach who only stays for three or four years stretched this out to a full decade at a club where 80% of that time was spent under a cloud of sham contracts and casual hubris. Through all this he had a deeply personal relationship with his chair, Khaldoon al-Mubarak. The pair of them are seen whispering tenderly in the recent Prime documentary, in which Guardiola is presented as the most genuine and heartfelt of truth-seekers, a lone castaway on Integrity Island, Jedi-like in a tailored hoodie, eyes brimming with tears as he talks feelings and eternal truths, like a dad in the pub on Christmas Eve.View image in fullscreenKevin De Bruyne joined Manchester City from Wolfsburg for £51m in 2015.Photograph: Ash Allen/EPAIn his farewell hagiographies, Guardiola was routinely described as the greatest modern manager. He invented the Messi role for Messi. He reimagined the basic texture of the sport in this country. If this guy isn’t good, nobody’s good. On the other hand, the only logical conclusion on the facts as they stand is that all his City trophies were won with the benefit of concerted macro-cheating.During the period embraced by the charges, City’s net spend on transfers was, according to Transfermarkt, almost £400m more than Manchester United in second place, and five times as much as Liverpool and Arsenal. From 2016 to 2018, the key period in building the Pep supremacy, they massively outspent every other team. After which they won the league on the final day or by a single point three times. There were little things throughout, like digging out an extra £25m for Kevin De Bruyne, stretching those fine details in your direction. How is it possible not to see that success as unrelated to stolen margins? This is an era that will now be defined by sham-ball, trophies hoisted with a hand behind your back and a thumb on the scale.Pep can only double down now and ride this to the end. His life’s work, his vast and all-consuming reputation is at stake. “We will get through this together,” he says in Wednesday’s statement. Well, you have no choice now, Pep. Wherever that destination might be.There are others who must now enter the matrix of who knew what. Soriano, subject of the second Harris grilling, is utterly bound up in this. He’s there right at the start, speaking to us in the leaked emails published by Der Spiegel. “We will need to fight this,” Soriano writes in one leaked memo, “and do it in a way that is not visible.” Hmm. How’s that part working out?Soriano’s own pre-City past has already been sliced and diced by those who wish to see a pattern. For the record, and as a basic statement of fact, he was at Barcelona during the period when the alleged, unproved, time-barred refereeing scandal happened, but not implicated or punished. He was at Air Spain when it collapsed, but cleared of any wrongdoing. And now he’s been at City in the period of inflated income that has, in effect, left the club dangling over the edge of a cliff. It is certainly an unfortunate chain of coincidence.‘Throw your medals in the bin,’ Roy Keane tells Manchester City playersRead moreOthers who will be asked what they knew, or not asked because he’s not going to speak to you, include the owner, Sheikh Mansour. This has an added element. It speaks to the ultimate test, some way down the line, of fitness to run a football club. How is it possible to spend so much family money on this thing, to dole out what are in effect government contracts, and not know the actual process here?But let’s face it, we all knew really. Weren’t the sham dealings obvious? It was there even in the absence of furious statements of support from the independent directors at First Abu Dhabi Bank, Etihad Airways, Experience Abu Dhabi, Emirates Palace Hotel in Abu Dhabi, Aldar Properties of Abu Dhabi, Masdar Energy of Abu Dhabi, e& telecoms of Abu Dhabi. Come on, chaps. Stand up for the investment. No word either from Dude Wipes, the club’s official male-oriented toilet-paper partner. Although who knows, we may now be entering full Dude Wipes territory.We knew about the sportswashing aspect, knew that City was a soft-power vehicle for the state of Abu Dhabi, which has a record of alleged – and of course denied – human rights abuses and so on. And of course City’s fans must have known this too, or felt it on some level. It was there cooked into the blueprint, the sense of something brutally high-end but strangely cold.JG Ballard coined the phrase “the death of affect” to describe the institutionalising of public feeling, rage and triumph commodified as a spectator event. Some champion teams have a strut. City’s basic vibe was always closer to an unceasing V-sign. Perhaps there was even a buried unease here. No one really enjoys being treated as a glove puppet, even when it is done gently and with a hand held discreetly under the desk. On which note, Pep? Any other questions now? Is this a good time?Explore more on these topicsManchester CityPep GuardiolafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Winter review – Richard Armitage’s new cop drama is as ferociously watchable as it is daft | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: Sometimes you want prestige drama that roils with nuance and complexity. And sometimes you want Armitage shouting in a cagoule
Author: Sarah Dempster
Headline: Sometimes you want prestige drama that roils with nuance and complexity. And sometimes you want Armitage shouting in a cagoule
Content: Richard Armitage as forensic pathologist Ethan Winter.Photograph: Eagle Eye DramaView image in fullscreenRichard Armitage as forensic pathologist Ethan Winter.Photograph: Eagle Eye DramaTV reviewTelevision & radioReviewWinter review – Richard Armitage’s new cop drama is as ferociously watchable as it is daftSometimes you want prestige drama that roils with nuance and complexity. And sometimes you want Armitage shouting in a cagouleSarah DempsterWed 30 Sep 2026 17.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 17.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDr Ethan Winter is a maverick, a wildcard, a lone wolf who won’t play by the rules. “Winter!” gasps DI Lauren Bell as the muscular outsider bursts into a police interrogation room and proceeds to subject a tremulous pensioner to the full force of his waxed cagoule. “You can’t do this!” But he can do this. And he will do this. Why? Because he’s Dr Ethan Winter, dammit, one of the greatest forensic pathologists of his generation; a bearded genius whose approach to obstacles is as uncompromising as his approach to tremulous pensioners.And yet. Dr Ethan Winter is troubled. We know this because Winter – the new six-part ITV police procedural that shares his starkly unseasonable surname – keeps cutting to scenes in which our protagonist paces silently around his fashionably underlit Bristol flat while scowling into the middle distance. Has he misplaced the keys to his vintage sports car? No, they’re over there, next to the gruesome autopsy photos he keeps on the kitchen table in the hope they’ll prompt visitors to ask what made him want to be a forensic doctor (“I became a forensic doctor …to mend sores”). Could it be, then, that the source of his malaise is … complicated? That it could in fact have something to do with the murder, a decade ago, of his fiancee – a case which, though ostensibly closed, continues to raise enough questions to provide the series with its narrative backbone? While leaving sufficient time in each episode for the agitated hunk to solve a new, self-contained crime? It’s certainly possible!Dr Ethan Winter is played by Richard Armitage, in accordance with the scriptures. His presence here (in his sixth – sixth! – TV thriller since 2021) serves as a seal of quality, or at least an assurance that the ensuing brooding will be accompanied by a) gratuitous demonstrations of upper-body strength, and b) a voice like a Twix melting in a bra fire.Anyway, the body of a young woman has been found in a freezer lorry so it’s time for some plot. Prickly DI Bell (Annabel Scholey), who has recently moved to Bristol after a mysteriously self-curtailed career with the Met (“It’s a long story”), suspects a local recidivist. Bejumpered sidekick DS Ellis Daldry (a wonderfully rumpled turn from Jamie Kenna) knows better. Best leave the solving stuff to our perturbed hero, he tells her. “Ethan can,” after all, “read a body like other people read a book.” And he can. If by reading a body you mean slowly circling a cadaver while huskily whispering things like “hello, stranger” and “fly eggs”. Still, it seems to work, and soon we’re bounding after him as he tears excitedly through the woods, nostrils flapping at the prospect of another crime scene at which he can be a maverick.“Can you smell that?” he gasps. We cannot. Tell us more, corpse man. “FAECES,” he bellows, hurtling towards a disused well like a cannonball in a Barbour. “ROTTING MEAT … IT’S A DEAD BODY!”View image in fullscreenArmitage with Annabel Scholey as DI Lauren Bell.Photograph: Eagle Eye DramaAt this point, there is a strong chance you’re thinking, “This sounds like an absolutely terrible TV programme.” And you would be absolutely correct. But only partially. The script may be a thing of string and glue but the dead fiancee stuff is gripping and Winter’s production values are uncommonly high; the direction, soundtrack and lighting (so many burnished brass sconces!) conspiring to paint Bristol as a glowering storm cloud of polo-necked pain and longing. Based on long-running French thriller Balthazar, the aesthetic here shares a similar, ’ow you say, narked grandeur.The upshot? It’s a potboiler in a belted trenchcoat. Silent Witness saying “bof” while eating an onion. And yet even the many, many ridiculous bits work, folded as they are into a soufflé that is as ferociously watchable as it is unnecessarily expensive.The fact of the matter is this: sometimes you want prestige drama that roils with nuance and complexity. And sometimes you want Richard Armitage shouting, “FAECES!” while sprinting through Bristol in a cagoule. Let us give thanks.Winter aired on ITV1 and is on ITVX nowExplore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV reviewTelevisionreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Do parents make the politician? Find out on the Today programme’s psychotherapy couch | John Crace | The Guardian
description: Dad’s the word for Andy Burnham, so maybe all party leaders should be seen afresh through a Freudian lens
Author: John Crace
Headline: Dad’s the word for Andy Burnham, so maybe all party leaders should be seen afresh through a Freudian lens
Content: The prime minister, Andy Burnham, told the Labour party conference he wanted to build the country his late father had hoped to see.Photograph: Phil Noble/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe prime minister, Andy Burnham, told the Labour party conference he wanted to build the country his late father had hoped to see.Photograph: Phil Noble/ReutersThe politics sketchAndy BurnhamDo parents make the politician? Find out on the Today programme’s psychotherapy couchJohn CraceDad’s the word for Andy Burnham, so maybe all party leaders should be seen afresh through a Freudian lensWed 30 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 16.15 EDTShareIs this the sketch my father would have wanted? Not something I have previously given much thought to. He died 15 years before I even started this job. But my guess is that it is. He was the loveliest of men who only ever wanted for me what I wanted for me. He was stupidly proud of even my most forgettable successes. I still see him in my dreams, cheering me on. He’d almost certainly be embarrassed, but secretly pleased, to find himself in the first paragraph.But that’s enough about my father issues. Time now to talk about Andy Burnham’s. In his emotional and gamechanging leader’s speech on Tuesday – I can’t tell you how refreshing it is to have a politician other than Nigel Farage say exactly what he thinks and believes – Andy told us he wanted to build the country his father would have wanted. It was almost a debt of honour. Burnham was very precise. This was not his vision. This wasn’t the country he wanted to build. It was the one his dad had wanted. Andy was merely a conduit, channelling Roy, whodied earlier this month.So come Wednesday morning, on the traditional post-speech media round, the BBC’sNick Robinsonhad clearly designated himself a latter-day Sigmund Freud for Burnham’s Today programme interview. You get the picture: Andy on the couch, Nick sitting just behind his right shoulder, firmly out of view. Never let the therapist get in the way of the subconscious. Only Robinson can’t take the silences. Some analysts pride themselves on a 50-minute session where nothing is said. That’s when the real psychotherapeutic work gets done. Apparently. A nice earner if you can get it.There was no time to bother with the niceties. Nick specialises more in speed therapy. Done and dusted inside 20 minutes. From nought to catharsis. There was no “How are you feeling? Is there anything you need to talk about today?” Instead, he cut straight to the chase. And why not? Everyone knows that all patients are merely mainlining their parents. Everything can be traced back to childhood.Andy clearly doesn’t hold with the Philip Larkin “They fuck you up” doctrine. He only got good stuff from his dad. Or maybe the good stuff is all that he cares to remember. Siggy Robbo missed a trick there. Surely your father would be telling you not to be so nostalgic, he said, but Burnham was adamant. Roy would have stuck to his roots of quiet patriotism. Nick tried another tack. The funeral was taking place on Friday. Was he on an emotional rollercoaster? Andy conceded that he could be. But rollercoasters were his happy place.View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham and Lucy Powell, the education secretary, join in a chorus of The Red Flag and Jerusalem at the end of this year’s Labour party conference on Wednesday.Photograph: Victoria Jones/ShutterstockThis could be habit-forming. Maybe it’s an approach we should take with all our party leaders. Rather than seeing them as players on a global stage with the capacity to make our lives infinitely worse, we should be more understanding. Treat them as patients in need of treatment. After all, you’ve surely got to be a dangerously unbalanced narcissist to even imagine you can run a country. Desire for office should act as a disqualification on health grounds. Some politicians would probably get an automatic upgrade from narcissist to sociopath. Donald Trump and Boris Johnson come immediately to mind.Think also of Keir Starmer, Nigel Farage and Kemi Badenoch. Keir clearly hada tricky relationship with his dad. One where there was a lot that went unsaid. So maybe we shouldn’t blame him for never being able to articulate what he felt. Then there’s Nige. Has he inherited a hatred for all immigrants, or is he reacting against his parents? Maybe they took in refugees and forced the seven-year-old Nige to play with them against his will. And where did he get his pathological need for money, no matter how questionable the source? Did his parents squander his inheritance on gifts to charity? As for Kemi, where to start? I’ve never seen a politician so full of loathing. Could that be down to a Larkin-like childhood?With the therapy over, Siggy briefly turned to the substance of the speech. All the big-ticket policies were for after the next election. What was going to happen in the next three years? Andy shrugged. He was a straight-talking guy. There wasn’t much he could do. Energy bills were going up faster than he could offer rebates. He couldn’t stop the wars around the world. The cost of debt was out of his hands. The Tories could say they would cut welfare, but nothing much would change. We needed to be patient. Things would get better. Just so long asLabourwon in 2029.Social care, the triple lock, Brexit and electoral reform. These were the real engines that would transform the country and reconnect voters with politics. Instruments of trust. How that would happen would be for others to decide. Single market, customs union, rejoin. All were on the table. Let’s just hope the far right haven’t taken over the EU by the time it happens. A national care service. Not ideal – some people would still lose their homes – but better than what was currently on offer. Just don’t forget: Andy was merely a channel of peace. In a rare turnabout, Nick thanked Burnham for the therapy session. The bank transfer would follow.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOver in the main hall, the conference proper was dying on its arse. You could hear the exhibition stands being dismantled as Yvette Cooper, Lucy Powell and others made the last few speeches to polite applause. We ended as all Labour conferences ended – with renditions of The Red Flag and Jerusalem – and then it was a dash for the exits. Not that there was a scrum. Most people had already left.But it was always going to be this way when the main event had taken place the previous afternoon. This had been theAndy Burnhamshow. And delegates couldn’t have been happier. The Labour party had rediscovered its soul. Its belief. A leader who could go toe-to-toe with the other parties. Maybe this was also the sketch that Andy Burnham’s father would have wanted.Explore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamThe politics sketchLabour conference 2026LabourNick RobinsonNigel FarageKemi BadenochcommentShareReuse this content

title: Energy bills: what to do as prices head for £2,000 a year, from switching deals to insulating | Energy bills | The Guardian
description: The price cap is to soar for about 20 million households in Great Britain from January, but there are ways to save
Author: Zoe Wood
Headline: The price cap is to soar for about 20 million households in Great Britain from January, but there are ways to save
Content: Household energy bills in Great Britain are predicted to reach £1,999 a year for the typical household from January.Photograph: Simon Dack/AlamyView image in fullscreenHousehold energy bills in Great Britain are predicted to reach £1,999 a year for the typical household from January.Photograph: Simon Dack/AlamyEnergy billsExplainerEnergy bills: what to do as prices head for £2,000 a year, from switching deals to insulatingThe price cap is to soar for about 20 million households in Great Britain from January, but there are ways to saveEnergy bills in Great Britain forecast to jump by £276 a year from JanuaryZoe WoodWed 30 Sep 2026 11.44 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 16.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHousehold energy prices are set to soar in January, with a typical bill forecast tojump by £276to the equivalent of nearly £2,000 year.It is a worrying outlook but there are practical steps you can take to mitigate the predicted price shock.Fixed energy deals“Switching energy tariff to a well-priced fixed deal is the biggest lever households on the price cap can pull to bring their costs down right now,” says Richard Neudegg, the director of regulation at Uswitch.About 20 million households in England, Scotland and Wales are on variable tariffs set by Ofgem’s price cap, which increases by 4% from Thursday, equivalent to taking the typical annual dual-fuel bill up by £60 to £1,723.The cap is due to rise 16% further to £1,999 in January, according to thelatest forecastfrom the consultancy Cornwall Insight. “The cheapest deal on the market is currently £324 less than this,” says Neudegg.The number of cap-beating deals has been steadily declining in recent weeks but there are still 34 deals below the January forecast, with some cheaper than October’s rates. At the moment the cheapest is Fuse Energy’s 12-month fix at £1,675, beating the October price cap by £48, and potentially January’s by as much as £324.Check your boiler and hot water settingsCombi boilers work best when they heat radiators to 60C or below. But in many homes the “flow temperature” is often set much too high at 70C- 80C. It only takes a few minutes to turn it down and this alone could save you about £60 a year. With some people reluctant to fiddle with their boiler settings, the charity Nesta has a step-by-stepguide on its website.Combi boilers allow users also to control the temperature of hot water supplied to taps and showers. Reducing the hot water temperature to 42C reduces the amount of fuel needed to heat the water and doing this could shave 2% off your gas bill, it suggests.Block draughts ... then turn down the thermostatView image in fullscreenTurning down the thermostat by 1C could save about £120 a year.Photograph: RossHelen editorial/AlamyInstalling inexpensive draught-proofing strips around windows and doors is a quick and easy DIY job that could shave £25 a year off your energy bill.You can buy foam, metal or plastic draught strips, or brush seals for sash windows, cut them to size and attach around opening casements. Use a thicker option for doors. Flues can be plugged easily with a chimney balloon or a draught excluder.Curtains are another easy way of reducing draughts and retaining heat. You could invest in some heavy-duty thermal-lined curtains, or alternatively buy a thermal lining for your existing ones.According to the World Health Organization, the lowest comfortable temperature for most people is between 18C and 21C so if you’re warm enough, try turning your thermostat down by 1C – this could save you about £120 a year, according to the Energy Saving Trust.Turn down radiatorsIf you have thermostatic radiator valves (TRVs), the dial that controls how much hot water enters the radiator it is attached to, you will be able to adjust the temperature separately in each room. TRVs usually have a scale from 0 to 6, where 0 is off and 6 is fully open.TheEnergySaving Trust recommends putting it on the lowest setting that keeps the room at a comfortable temperature, which could be 3 or 4 for rooms you use the most and 2 or 3 for others. Managing the temperature this way can save a household about £40 a year.Insulate your hot water tank and pipesMost modern hot water tanks have plenty of insulation, but an older tank might have only a small amount. Adding an 80mm jacket to a tank with 25mm foam built-in can save homeowners in Great Britain about £45 a year, it says. The jackets cost about £20 and are widely available from DIY retailers.Insulating (or lagging) pipes helps keep in the heat and prevent damage during cold winter months. There are several different types of material used for lagging but the most popular is polyethylene foam mainly because of how affordable and easy it is to install.Insulate your loft (and walls)View image in fullscreenInsulating a loft is a job many homeowners can do themselves after watching an online tutorial.Photograph: DWImages/AlamyHomes can lose about 25% of their heat through an uninsulated roof. Many already have some loft insulation but topping it up can help retain more heat. If your current setup is about 120mm thick, increasing it to the 270mm (the minimum recommendation for new builds) could save you in the region of £20 a year.There are plenty of online tutorials showing you how to do this yourself. DIY stores sell rolls of mineral wool insulation, with a roll of standard “top-up” insulation £27 at Wickes, for example.Most homes built between 1920 and 1990 were constructed with uninsulated cavity walls, and the Energy Saving Trust estimates adding cavity wall insulation (where an installer injects insulation material from the outside) could save £200 a year.Get a heat pumpIf your boiler needs replacing it might be time to explore a green alternative. The government’s boiler upgrade scheme offers grants of £7,500 to help homeowners in England and Wales with the cost of installing an air-to-water or ground-to-water heat pump system.Households not connected to the gas grid qualify for an additional £1,500 in support, increasing the grant to £9,000. If you live in Scotland, you may be able to get aninterest-free loan or a grantto make your home more energy efficient.When it comes to bills, the Energy Saving Trust says the biggest saving comes in homes that switch to a dedicated heat pump energy tariff and add other green technologies such as solar panels.The tariff is vital because heat pumps run on electricity, which is generally more expensive per unit than gas. On a standard tariff, this can lead to substantial energy bills, negating some of the efficiency benefits. Heat pump users moving on to a time-of-use tariff can saveabout £330 a yearcompared with sitting on a flat-rate tariff, the trust says. This rises to about £800 with extras such as solar, although these add to the upfront costs.Explore more on these topicsEnergy billsHousehold billsConsumer affairsEnergy industryEnergy efficiencyHeat pumpsexplainersShareReuse this content

title: Udder madness: why are highland cows suddenly everywhere? | Homes | The Guardian
description: This shaggy beast is now plastered across everything from mugs to hot water bottles. Or you can sit on her, wrap yourself in her, wipe your feet on her …
Author: Lucy Knight
Headline: This shaggy beast is now plastered across everything from mugs to hot water bottles. Or you can sit on her, wrap yourself in her, wipe your feet on her …
Content: A kind of live, laugh, love sign for the 2020s?Photograph: ShaoChen Yang/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA kind of live, laugh, love sign for the 2020s?Photograph: ShaoChen Yang/Getty ImagesHomesUdder madness: why are highland cows suddenly everywhere?This shaggy beast is now plastered across everything from mugs to hot water bottles. Or you can sit on her, wrap yourself in her, wipe your feet on her …Lucy KnightWed 30 Sep 2026 08.24 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 08.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePicture this: you get home from work, wipe your feet on your doormat, which has a picture of a highland cow on it, sniff the flowers growing from your highland cow-shaped plant pot, then step inside, hang your coat on one of your highland-cow-themed hooks and put some water on to boil in your highland cow kettle. When the tea is ready, you drink it from one of your highland cow mugs, plucked from a highland cow mug tree, discarding the teabag in a highland cow-emblazoned pedal bin. Oops, you’ve spilled a drop, but not to worry – there’s a fresh roll of kitchen roll waiting for you in between the resin cow-butt and cow-head of its highland cow-shaped holder.You then carry the tea to your living room, and place it (atop a highland cow coaster, of course) on your coffee table, which has been carved into the shape of a highland cow, before taking a seat in an accent chair made to resemble a highland cow’s head. If you get cold, you can always wrap yourself in a hooded throw, designed to make the wearer look like a highland cow, or reach for your dressing gown-wearing highland cow hot-water bottle.View image in fullscreen‘Here to bring a smile to every season’ … Hamish the Highland Cow kettle and toaster.Photograph: Emilia Holden/NextEvery one of these products is available fromNext, which stocks so many highland-cow-themed products that it has created its own character, Hamish the Highland Cow, who is apparently “here to bring a smile to every season” and “make everyday moments special”. A search for “highland cow” on the clothes and homeware shop’s website yields 589 results, including Hamish pyjamas, toothbrush holders and wall art.Next certainly isn’t the only shop to have gone all-in on Scottish-cattle-themed products: from Asda’s highland cow in a pumpkin ornament to Wilko’s highland cow-printed washing-up brush, they seem to be everywhere. On a recent visit to Pets at Home I even spotted a highland cow dog toy.View image in fullscreenMooed awakening … a highland cow dog toy.Photograph: Pets at HomeClearly there’s a demand for such products: “I love anything highland cow,” writes one reviewer of Next’s highland cow glass chopping board, thanking the retailer for introducing a wider range of highland-cow-themed products. “How gorgeous is this?” comments another highland cow fan on TikTok, showing off Next’s highland cow crockery.Home and garden shop the Range, which sells highland-cow-themed products such as bedding, lamps and kitchenware, saw an 88% increase in searches for highland cow products in August. “There’s a rise in the number of customers looking for decor that feels personal and the highland cow offers just that,” says a spokesperson for the company. “Instantly recognisable,” they add, it has “a strong connection to British heritage and countryside living, bringing a sense of warmth and calm into a space”.Kate Hewitt, DIY content creator and former contestant on Interior Design Masters, first noticed the highland cow trend last autumn, and says it’s now “appearing more and more”. She thinks its popularity is part of a wider shift towards a “cosy, country, vintage-style look,” with lots of people wanting “an antique-y, cosy cottage home”.View image in fullscreenGeneral ‘cosiness’ … a highland cow chopping board.Photograph: Dan Avery/NextShe thinks the appeal of highland cattle in particular is largely “because they are cute” and, unless you live in Scotland, something a bit unusual: “You don’t see them every day.” The brown and orange hues and the general “cosiness” of highland cattle decor fit the “autumnal” interior design that has become more popular in recent years – it is not uncommon to see influencers on Instagram changing elements of their home design to match the seasons.‘I organised my spices – and feel happy every time I cook!’ 12 readers on their most rewarding tiny accomplishmentsRead moreWhile the aesthetic doesn’t necessarily match Hewitt’s taste, she says: “Some of the prints I’ve seen are actually quite beautiful.” She could see herself incorporating the odd highland cow cushion into a space – though she “wouldn’t decorate a whole room in it”.That said, Hewitt says her mother has bought “loads” of highland cow items for her house. “She loves it and it makes her smile,” she says. “That’s what it’s all about, isn’t it?”“Iwould never buy it but my mum loves it” is a common response when I chat to friends and colleagues about the trend. It strikes me ashun-cultureadjacent (most directly reflected in Next’s ornament of a highland cow ironing while drinking prosecco), a kind of live, laugh, love sign for the 2020s.Chances are, even if you are too cool for highland cow decor, you’ll have someone in your life who loves it. So best to beat the Christmas shopping rush and get your hands on a highland cow nativity scene now.Explore more on these topicsHomesNextInteriorsAnimalsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: No 10 gathering evidence on public support for UK rejoining EU | Brexit | The Guardian
description: Senior Downing Street officials reach out to thinktanks and pollsters as they look to test backing for reversing Brexit
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: Senior Downing Street officials reach out to thinktanks and pollsters as they look to test backing for reversing Brexit
Content: Andy Burnham said he would lay out ‘the different options for Britain’s long-term relationship with our European partners’.Photograph: Susannah Ireland/ReutersView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham said he would lay out ‘the different options for Britain’s long-term relationship with our European partners’.Photograph: Susannah Ireland/ReutersBrexitNo 10 gathering evidence on public support for UK rejoining EUSenior Downing Street officials reach out to thinktanks and pollsters as they look to test backing for reversing BrexitKiran StaceyandLisa O’CarrollWed 30 Sep 2026 14.33 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSenior Downing Street officials have been reaching out to thinktanks and pollsters as they look to test public support for the UK rejoining the EU.Aides toAndy Burnhamhave been talking to EU experts in a range of organisations about how the public would view a promise to rejoin, as momentum builds behind including such a pledge in the next Labour manifesto.Some in No 10 are keen to promise thatLabourwould at least negotiate over re-entry to the bloc, something Burnham has previously said he wants to see happen “in his lifetime”. Others are nervous, however, that making such a promise could revive the flagging political fortunes of Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader.Burnham used hisfirst Labour conference speechas leader to announce a review ofthe optionsfor Britain’s relationship with Europe, and added on Wednesday that these options should include rejoining entirely.The prime minister told delegates on Tuesday: “Brexit has done more harm than good. So I will take the opportunity around the [UK-EU] summit to lay out to you, to lay out to the country, what I believe are the different options for Britain’s long-term relationship with our European partners.”View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham announced a review of the options for Britain’s relationship with Europe in his speech at the Labour party conference.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianOn Wednesday he clarified that this wouldinclude an optionto rejoin – something ruled out by his predecessor Keir Starmer.Burnham told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme: “We could stay as we are. That’s definitely an option, if people think this is the right place to stay. We could look at what [the former Conservative chancellor] George Osbornehas said about a customs union, we could look at what the Liberal Democratssaid at their conferenceabout the single market, or we couldgo all the way.”Andy Burnham wants to review the UK’s relationship with the EU. What are the options?Read moreBurnham’s comments sparked joy among pro-EU campaigners, who argue that rejoining is the best way to boost UK growth rates – and outrage from political opponents.Alex Burghart, the Conservative deputy leader, said: “Labour cannot blame a democratic vote from over a decade ago for the consequences of their own economic decisions.”The Guardian has learned that Burnham’s comments are part of a wider effort by No 10 to test consensus over rejoining, with a view to possibly including such a promise in the next manifesto.Officials have been in talks with several prominent thinktanks and pollsters, who have been working on projects to flesh out arguments over rejoining and test public opinion.Last week, the Tony Blair Institutereleased a paperarguing that Burnham should seek talks with Brussels over becoming a member once more but should only do so if Europe relaxed its regulations in sectors including energy and technology.On the same day, the pro-EU campaign group Best for Britain released a megapoll conducted by YouGov suggesting Labour could more than double its seat total if it went into the next election promising to rejoin.Over the coming weeks, the influential Institute for Public Policy Research will release a paper calling for the country to rejoin, while Think Labour has also been looking into how difficult it would be to do so.Some in Downing Street are buoyed up by polling which shows that promising to re-enter the bloc does little to boost support for Reform. They also point out that Farage attacked the prime minister’s speech for the promise to change the pensions triple lock, rather than his comments about Europe.View image in fullscreenPro-EU campaigners argue that rejoining is the best way to boost UK growth rates.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/Zuma Press/ShutterstockThe Guardian has been told that some at the top of government wanted the prime minister to use this week’s speech to promise to begin work on rejoining after the next election, rather than carrying out a review.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn the end, such an option was ruled out because the party was already bracing itself for a fight over pensions and did not want to give succour to Farage while he faces accusations about millions of pounds’ worth of donations to his party.No 10 said the prime minister did not ever consider making such a promise in the speech and that it was not included in any draft of it.Some believe it would be difficult to persuade Brussels, which has engaged in multiple rounds of talks about Britain’s relationship with the EU, to embark on negotiations over re-accession.But in a major boost to supporters of rejoining, Emmanuel Macron on Wednesdaywelcomed Burnham’s comments. “Welcome back,” the French president said in English at a press conference in Madrid on Wednesday.He continued in French: “If the British want to come back and if the prime minister is moving in that direction, I think that is very good news, both for his country and for the Europeans.”An EU spokesperson said: “The UK is a close and valued partner of theEuropean Union. It is for the UK government to set out how it wishes to develop its relationship with the EU going forward. We remain open to engaging on the options it may put forward.”Burnham’s willingness to look at all options seems to have been accompanied by fresh engagement on the EU’s Made in Europe legislation, which threatens to lock UK goodsout of certain supply chainson the continent.No 10 has sought to have British manufacturers classified as European for the purposes of that legislation, with officials threatening to delay an EU-UK summit until London receives signals that there could be an accommodation.Since Burnham’s speech, however, there is now talk of holding the summit on 20 November.One EU diplomat said it was necessary to get Starmer’s old reset agenda concluded before talks of “a real reset” could begin, confirming support for a UK-EU summit as early as possible.A second diplomat said there was “a good feeling” that Burnham was now looking at all options and seeking a consensus, “something Brussels has wanted to see”.Explore more on these topicsBrexitForeign policyAndy BurnhamLabourEuropean UnionEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Whoever is hearing me, we need help’: how flight 1073 survived its 17,000ft plunge | Israel | The Guardian
description: On morning service from Dubai to Tel Aviv, 150 passengers witnessed a horrific cockpit assault and a daring rescue
Author: Oliver Holmes
Headline: On morning service from Dubai to Tel Aviv, 150 passengers witnessed a horrific cockpit assault and a daring rescue
Content: Passengers arrive at Ben Gurion airport in Israel via a second flight from Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, where their original flight FZ 1073 was forced to make an emergency landing.Photograph: Ariel Schalit/APView image in fullscreenPassengers arrive at Ben Gurion airport in Israel via a second flight from Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, where their original flight FZ 1073 was forced to make an emergency landing.Photograph: Ariel Schalit/APIsrael‘Whoever is hearing me, we need help’: how flight 1073 survived its 17,000ft plungeOn morning service from Dubai to Tel Aviv, 150 passengers witnessed a horrific cockpit assault and a daring rescuePilot who stabbed co-pilot on Israel-bound plane may have tried to crash it, says NetanyahuOliver HolmesWed 30 Sep 2026 13.47 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 16.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs flight FZ 1073 soared west over the waters of the Gulf towardsIsrael, its passengers may have bemoaned a 20-minute delay at takeoff. For a low-cost airline route, flydubai’s daily service to Tel Aviv is usually convenient and reliable. The nonstop flight takes about three and a half hours and departs early enough from Dubai that it usually lands at Ben Gurion airport at about 9am local time.That was not the case for Wednesday’s catastrophic flight. The passenger jet never made it to its scheduled destination. Instead, it dropped thousands of feet in seconds before limping down to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia – perhaps miraculously, since photos suggested a large part of the tail of the aircraft was missing.Flight path mapPassengers evacuated, some covered in blood, with stories to share of a pilot-on-pilot stabbing, and footage posted online from inside the fuselage showed the aftermath of violence.In one video, two men lie on the floor with breathing masks on their faces as passengers stand over them in the cramped gangway. One wears a white shirt soaked red with blood, and the distinctive pilot stripes on his shoulders. He appears almost unresponsive. The other man blinks slowly, with blood smeared on the wall next to him. A person off camera appears to encourage the injured man to remain conscious: “No sleep,” he says.7:37Mid-air panic as pilot attacked on Israel-bound flight - The LatestMore footage, apparently from a seat further back, shows passengers screaming and weeping in distress as the Boeing 737 Max shakes. Israeli media reported that the plane was carrying about 150 Israeli passengers.Accounts from the airline, passenger testimony, flight trackers and Israeli officials describe a series of horrific events starting about two and a half hours after takeoff.The flight tracking website Flightradar24 recorded the aircraft abruptly descending from its cruising altitude of about 34,000ft to 17,000ft in less than two minutes. Investigators will look at whether such a sudden and ferocious movement was the reason for damage to the aircraft’s rudder.Flight altitude graphicMinutes later, the plane sent out a series of emergency transponder signals in the form of “squawk codes”. These four-digit codes are normally used by pilots to broadcast their position but can be used in an emergency situation, even if pilots are in radio contact with air traffic control.Aircraft trackers at Flightradar24 said the flydubai plane transmitted emergency and hijack signals. The aircraft made an erratic circle close to the Jordanian border before turning around and heading south.In one video, a passenger with blood dripping from an open wound on his head pleads for assistance and says the jet is descending into Saudi Arabia. “Whoever is hearing me, we need help,” the man says in Hebrew. “We are in the Tabuk area of Saudi Arabia, which we don’t know. All the passengers are OK except for the pilot. We need help.”Passenger on the plane appeals for helpWhat was happening during these critical minutes is still being investigated, but early unconfirmed reports pointed to a cockpit fight, followed by passengers storming up the aisle, and then either one or more pilots who were travelling as passengers wresting control of the plane to avert a disaster.The Israeli newspaper Haaretz cited a passenger as saying that the plane lost control and began to dive.Dalia Shpigel was quoted as saying that “suddenly there were terrible screams throughout the plane” before “three to five guys burst into the cockpit” and subdued the alleged assailant and began treating an injured pilot.“We realised that the situation was stabilising and continued the flight. Gradually, information began to emerge about what had happened in the cockpit,” Shpigel told Haaretz.Chaos onboard flydubai flight to Tel Aviv after pilots altercationHer fellow passenger Miryam Shira Ohayon said the “co-pilot tried to murder the pilot and basically carry out a suicide attack on the plane”.Speaking to reporters via speakerphone held up by her mother, who was waiting at Ben Gurion airport, she said the plane “was really on the way to crashing, and it was simply the resourcefulness of many people who took control of the co-pilot and neutralised him”.“There was also a doctor who gave first aid, and people who treated both of them … but the bigger fear was really a crash, which is exactly what he was trying to do,” she said.The Emirati carrier, in a statement later on Wednesday, said the aircraft was “successfully secured by on-duty flydubai crew travelling on the flight”, who diverted and landed the aircraft safely at Tabuk airport. Airlines often move pilots around different airports as passengers, and it is possible it was these pilots who sent the emergency codes.One passenger, Almog Itali, was quoted by the BBC as saying that one of the pilots onboard who stabilised the plane was British. “There were two spare pilots who were supposed to operate the next flight,” he said. “The relief pilots are European, one of them British, who entered [the cockpit] and pulled the aircraft up, pulled the yoke, stabilised the plane and landed us in Saudi Arabia.”1:19Mother of passenger on Israel-bound flight describes incident – videoStanislav Bukhman, the head of risk at Osprey Flight Solutions, an aviation security firm based in the UK, said investigators were likely to focus on a few key areas, including how pilots were vetted, and crew screening at the departure airport.On how the flight deck might have been accessed, he said cabin crew could request entry to the cockpit using an emergency access code. “This exists for situations where the pilots are incapacitated. There is a safeguard built in, though. If the pilots are conscious and operating normally, they can deny that request and keep the door locked. This is designed to protect the flight deck in a hijacking or hostage situation,” he said.What we know so far about alleged stabbing of pilot by co-pilot on flight to IsraelRead more“At this stage there isn’t enough information to say how the flight deck on FZ 1073 was accessed. The door may have been opened by the captain, who reportedly resisted the co-pilot’s attempt to take control, or by cabin crew using the emergency procedure.”The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, announced that one of the pilots had planned to crash and kill its mostly Israeli passengers, who stopped a “major disaster” with their actions. The alleged assailant was arrested after the plane landed, Netanyahu ‌said.“During the flight, as they approached the country, one of the pilots stabbed the other pilot and apparently tried to crash the plane with everyone onboard,” Netanyahu said in a video message, calling the passengers “heroes”. All the passengers were accounted for and safe.Flydubai, however, said an “altercation” occurred in the flight deck of flight FZ 1073, and it warned against drawing conclusions about the motive.“At this early stage, the underlying reasons and motives behind this event are unknown and remain subject to a formal investigation,” a flydubai spokesperson said in a statement. “We urge all parties to refrain from premature speculation while authorities gather the facts.”Agence France-Presse contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsIsraelAir transportMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Strong indications’ that Iran played role in RAF Fairford incident, says Burnham | UK news | The Guardian
description: PM also defends decision to release suspects on bail and expresses ‘complete confidence’ in security services
Author: Peter Walker
Headline: PM also defends decision to release suspects on bail and expresses ‘complete confidence’ in security services
Content: Police officers guarding an area near RAF Fairford on TuesdayPhotograph: Toby Shepheard/ReutersView image in fullscreenPolice officers guarding an area near RAF Fairford on TuesdayPhotograph: Toby Shepheard/ReutersUK news‘Strong indications’ that Iran played role in RAF Fairford incident, says BurnhamPM also defends decision to release suspects on bail and expresses ‘complete confidence’ in security servicesPeter WalkerSenior political correspondentWed 30 Sep 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere are “strong indications” that Iran played a role in events in which five men were arrested near RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire as part of a terror investigation, Andy Burnham has said.Speaking to the media at the end of the Labour party conference in Liverpool, Burnham said he could not give any more details amid a police investigation, but that Iran was believed to be involved.On Tuesday, Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state,said Washington believed“a foreign actor” was involved in the events on Sunday night at the airbase, which has been used by US planes for missions against Iran.In an interview with BBC News, Burnham said: “There are strong indications that Iran played a part in what happened over the weekend at RAF Fairford, but of course it remains an ongoing, complex, and serious police investigation.“And of course, we are working closely with our colleagues in the United States of America. So it’s ongoing.”Noting that he had held a meeting of the government’s Cobra emergency committee while in Liverpool, Burnham said: “We are on top of it in every possible way imaginable.”He added: “We will say more in due course, but we can confirm our belief that we believe Iran to have played a part.”Asked why he believed this, Burnham replied: “Well I can’t go into all of those details, but obviously I wouldn’t say it lightly.”In a separate interview with Sky News, Burnham was asked if he needed to recall parliament, which is in recess for the party conference season. He replied: “At this stage there is not an urgent need to do that, but should that arise, of course, I wouldn’t hesitate.”The five men, all in their 20s and from London, were arrested in the Gloucestershire countryside near the airbase after a local woman driving home saw a series of vans and men in masks, and called police.They were first arrested on explosives charges and then later for preparing acts of terrorism. All five were released on police bail on Monday after an examination of what was found in the vans, and searches of addresses linked to them across London.On Tuesday the Guardian reported increasing confidence of an Iranian link to the weekend’s events.The decision to release the men has prompted criticism from the Trump administration, with Rubio saying he was “disturbed” by it.Questioned by the BBC about US criticism of the bail decision, Burnham said this had happened only with very strict conditions.He said: “I think people need to understand that when it says released, that isn’t as people might think. It’s obviously with the strictest possible bail conditions. We’ve been talking to counterparts in the United States all week to explain what is happening here, how things are being done. I have complete confidence in the way British security services are handling this.”Itemerged on Tuesdaythat one of the five men arrested called the police to report the incident.The local woman who also phoned police subsequently told newspapers that she was alarmed the men had been allowed to get so close to the airbase without apparently being noticed.However, UK officials and Wes Streeting, the UK defence secretary,have indicatedthat security services were aware in advance of what was happening.A statement from Britain’s head of counter-terrorism police hinted that officers swooped on the rural location for several reasons.Assistant commissioner Laurence Taylor said: “A police response was activated in the early hours of Sunday morning due to a range of information received, including a call from a member of the public about several vehicles acting suspiciously close to RAF Fairford.”Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Drumcree standoff continues after Orange Order says it will ‘not surrender’ to proposed deal | Northern Ireland | The Guardian
description: Unionists spurn NI secretary’s attempt to resolve impasse after nationalists block controversial Garvaghy Road march
Author: Lisa O’Carroll
Headline: Unionists spurn NI secretary’s attempt to resolve impasse after nationalists block controversial Garvaghy Road march
Content: Orange Order legal adviser Jamie Bryson addresses an event in Portadown on Wednesday.Photograph: Mark Marlow/PAView image in fullscreenOrange Order legal adviser Jamie Bryson addresses an event in Portadown on Wednesday.Photograph: Mark Marlow/PANorthern IrelandDrumcree standoff continues after Orange Order says it will ‘not surrender’ to proposed dealUnionists spurn NI secretary’s attempt to resolve impasse after nationalists block controversial Garvaghy Road marchLisa O’CarrollSenior correspondentWed 30 Sep 2026 17.31 EDTFirst published on Wed 30 Sep 2026 14.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTalks to end the Drumcree parade dispute are on a knife-edge after Jamie Bryson, the legal adviser of the Orange Order, said it would “not surrender” to a deal proposed by theNorthern Irelandsecretary, Chris Bryant.With echoes of the former Democratic Unionist leader Ian Paisley’s “no surrender” mantra of the 1980s, Bryson told supporters in Portadown that Bryant could keep his deal.He said he had the authority of the Orange Order’s district master to say: “The Portadown District will not surrender the fundamental principle, not now, not last week, not next week, not ever – ever.”Bryson said the Portadown Orangemen would not “sell out” even if they were offered £20m.Government sources said they expected talks to continue on Thursday and possibly into Friday.Earlier today, Bryant said an end to the dispute was “tantalisingly close”, as the Garvaghy Road Residents’ Coalition signalled it would accept a document setting out a resolution if the Orange Order also did so.Breandán Mac Cionnaith, the leader of the nationalist group, said on Wednesday afternoon that he had been through the document drawn up by Bryant and his team.“Obviously, I can’t divulge what is in it,” he said after a meeting with Bryant. “But if it’s accepted by the Orange Order, it will be accepted by us.”Butafter a second meeting with Bryant on Wednesday evening, Bryson rubbished the residents’ leader’s words.“Do not be panicked by Breandán Mac Cionnaith coming out and saying there is a document on the table. The document can stay on the table because it won’t be accepted by the Portadown District.”Earlier in the day, Bryant urged parties to “search deep in their souls for another chunk of compromise” to break the deadlock, after meeting with both sides at Hillsborough Castle, just outside Belfast.On Tuesday, Mac Cionnaith had described mediation over the dispute as“dead in the water”.View image in fullscreenNorthern Ireland’s first minister, Michelle O’Neill, met Drumcree residents on Wednesday.Photograph: Mark Marlow/PABryant said on Wednesday: “I would just appeal to everybody – including the wider community, not just the people I have been meeting in the room – that people are going to have to search deep in their souls for another chunk of compromise if we’re going to get to a successful long-term resolution of the situation.”He added that he and his team were “working flat-out to try and get to a successful resolution, and I think that is tantalisingly close if everybody can just go that extra mile”.Politicians and others had warned that any parade down Garvaghy Road risked returning NorthernIrelandto the bleak days of the Troubles.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut on Sundaya court of appeal overturned a high court injunctionbanning the Orange Order from processing through the mainly nationalist area, leading to a four-day standoff that has heightened sectarian tensions.Attempts to march down Garvaghy Road were blocked by protesters, and a small group of Orange Order members has remained at Drumcree church, the starting point of the parade, vowing not to leave until the parade goes ahead.Jon Boutcher, the chief constable of Northern Ireland’s police force, said the protest stopping the parade was unlawful, and that a major criminal investigation into the blockade was under way. He warned that mob rule must not be allowed to win, and that he would continue to seek a way to facilitate the Orange Order march.The first minister of Northern Ireland, Michelle O’Neill, visited Garvaghy Road on Wednesday, despite accusations by unionist leaders that she had broken the law by supporting protesters when she went there on Sunday.Asked if she had broken the law, O’Neill said: “I accept that I made a choice, a choice to stand with the residents of the Garvaghy Road. It is a choice I will continue to make.“This is very clearly a community which feels under siege, a community that has been put in reverse and retraumatised in terms of what happened 28 years ago.”The parade was given the go-ahead by the Northern Ireland Parades Commission on Friday, ending a 28-year ban on the Orange Order marching in Garvaghy Road. At a special sitting of the high court the next day, Justice Patricia Smyth issued an order temporarily suspending the parade, but that was overturned on appeal in the small hours of Sunday morning.Critics of the Parades Commission’s decision included the taoiseach, Micheál Martin, who called it “incomprehensible and wrong”, given that the march promptedsome of the most serious violenceseen in Northern Ireland in the late 1990s – includingthe murders of three children– and nearly derailed the 1998 peace process.On Tuesday, the Garvaghy Road Residents’ Coalition lodged a fresh legal challenge against the march, this time arguing the Parades Commission had “materially misdirected itself” by using historical police assessments over the risk of violence as opposed to a future-looking risk assessment.Explore more on these topicsNorthern IrelandNorthern Irish politicsIrelandChris BryantShareReuse this content

title: Andy Burnham admits to ‘concern’ if Manchester City lose their owners after guilty verdicts | Manchester City | The Guardian
description: The primer minister said: ‘City have been a huge partner in building modern Manchester,’ while the Independent Football Regulator said it is monitoring the case
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: The primer minister said: ‘City have been a huge partner in building modern Manchester,’ while the Independent Football Regulator said it is monitoring the case
Content: Andy Burnham has thanked the City Football Group for investment in Manchester.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham has thanked the City Football Group for investment in Manchester.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianManchester CityAndy Burnham admits to ‘concern’ if Manchester City lose their owners after guilty verdictsClub ‘a huge partner in building modern Manchester’Independent Football Regulator monitoring caseMatt HughesWed 30 Sep 2026 14.31 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham has said he would be “really concerned” to lose Manchester City’s owners as a result of the club being found guilty of more than 100 breaches of Premier League rules.On the day that the Independent Football Regulator confirmed it has powers to investigate the suitability of the Abu Dhabi United Group to own an English club afterthe damning judgment of an independent commissionregarding £900m of sham contracts, the prime minister praised City’s owners for their investment of billions of pounds into Manchester.Manchester City could be forced to pay Premier League up to £50m in legal costsRead more“I would be really concerned to lose them,” Burnham said. “They’ve been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester, and the building of Manchester City into the global force that it is.“I do actually thank the City Football Group and the wider ownership for the money that they didn’t just put into the Etihad [Stadium] and the campus around it but also into the city.”Burnham insisted he would not get involved in the Premier League’s disciplinary process, despite the potential impact that punishing City could have on the UK-Abu Dhabi trading relationship, which is worth around £30bn a year.Despite this, Burnham appeared to express some sympathy for City’s plight by referring to his previous involvement in campaigning on behalf of Everton, who in 2023were docked six pointsby the Premier League for breaching profitability and sustainability rules.“I can’t intervene more in the process,” he said. “It would be wrong for me to do that. It would be wrong, I think, to jump to a conclusion before having really studied all of the detail. But obviously it’s ongoing, and because it’s still contested by Manchester City then I think it’s right that I don’t say much more.“Everton was in this position a few years ago and you might remember that I fought for Everton in that situation. I still hold the view very firmly that they weren’t fairly treated in that process.
