I remember people proclaiming Everton guilty at the time and, with hindsight, I think more people would say that wasn’t fair the way that was handled.”In a statement released earlier on Wednesday the IFR chief executive, David Kogan, confirmed the regulator is monitoring the City case and could take action. “The independent commission’s decision raises serious issues,” Kogan said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“The IFR has powers to assess the suitability of owners, directors and executives and we will use these powers where appropriate, in the interests of protecting the sustainability, honesty and integrity of English football where there is clear evidence of wrongdoing by individuals.“This includes taking account of findings made by the leagues. However, as the proceedings remain ongoing between Manchester City and the Premier League we will await further developments.”Explore more on these topicsManchester CityAndy BurnhamPremier LeagueFinancesBusinessnewsShareReuse this content

title: Hegseth confirms plan to cut 20% of US top military brass and rails at ‘beardos, weirdos and wimps’ | US military | The Guardian
description: Amid latest extraordinary attack on diversity, US defense secretary also suggests military is retaining service personnel at ‘record’ rates
Author: Shrai Popat
Headline: Amid latest extraordinary attack on diversity, US defense secretary also suggests military is retaining service personnel at ‘record’ rates
Content: The secretary of defense, Pete Hegseth, gestures after giving a State of the Force address at Marine Corps Base Quantico in Virginia on Wednesday.Photograph: Alex Wong/Pool Getty Images North America/APView image in fullscreenThe secretary of defense, Pete Hegseth, gestures after giving a State of the Force address at Marine Corps Base Quantico in Virginia on Wednesday.Photograph: Alex Wong/Pool Getty Images North America/APUS militaryHegseth confirms plan to cut 20% of US top military brass and rails at ‘beardos, weirdos and wimps’Amid latest extraordinary attack on diversity, US defense secretary also suggests military is retaining service personnel at ‘record’ ratesSend us your questions about how the Iran war will affect US voters in the midtermsShrai Popatin Washington andAriana Baioin New York CityWed 30 Sep 2026 17.20 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 21.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US defense secretary,Pete Hegseth, has confirmed plans to cut 20% of generals and admirals and declared “no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps” would be tolerated inside the country’s military.Delivering his latest extraordinary attack on diversity, and dismissing reports of low morale within the US armed forces as “false claims”, Hegseth also suggested they were retaining service personnel at “record” rates.The defense secretary pointed to those onboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, following concern over mental health and supply issues on the aircraft carrier, which was deployed for almost nine months. About “80% of the force” onboard was retained, he said.Pete Hegseth appoints Elon Musk to US taskforce on future of warfareRead moreAddressing lower-ranking troops at the Marine Corps Base on Wednesday, Hegseth boasted about the anti-diversity policies in the Pentagon pushed by Donald Trump’s administration.“The only focus, as you know, in your formations should be training, readiness, accountability, discipline and lethality,” Hegseth said. “And when you pursue those things, you don’t have to walk on eggshells … the complainers, the ideologues and the poor performers are no longer in the driver’s seat.”He added: “But it’s worth saying again, so the fake news understands it. We are no longer the woke department or the weak department. Simple translation of that: no fatties, no trannies, no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps, no radicals. Just warriors.”Generals “who clung to the woke department, or seemed to think civilian control of the military is simply a suggestion, well, they no longer work here”, Hegseth said.Eight US navy personnel assigned to the Lincoln attempted suicide since the start of their lengthy deployment as part of the US war on Iran,it emerged last week.Hegseth appeared to reference the carrier while attacking the media on Wednesday, insisting there are “disingenuous headlines about deployment lengths, patently false claims of low troop morale, or flat-out propaganda, as if it’s written by our adversaries”.The crew of the Lincoln, which was at sea for 286 days,disembarkedon 1 September in a Thai resort city. The crew had been scheduled to wrap their deployment in May, but it was extended amid Trump’s war on Iran.During his speech in Quantico, Virginia, the defense secretary announced several new initiatives, including a a new Pentagon project which will see Elon Musk, Palmer Luckey – a top Trump donor and ally – and Newt Gingrich, the former US House speaker, work with the department to study the “future of warfare”.The Guardian previouslyreportedon how Luckey’s company, Anduril Inudstries, a major defense technology company, has received billions in government contracts over the last year.Hegseth also took aim at Ivy League universities and liberal arts colleges during his speech – which Trump has targeted routinely since he returned to office. The defense secretary branded the institutions as “DEI-worshipping woke factories”. Notably, Hegseth is a graduate of Harvard and Princeton Universities – both members of the Ivy League.Hegseth said the Pentagon would now partner with other institutions as part of its educational pipeline. Some of these schools, such as Liberty University and Hillsdale College, are known for conservative values.Others joining the partnership are Louisiana State University, Mississippi University and Tuskegee University.Explore more on these topicsUS militaryPete HegsethUS politicsTrump administrationUS-Israel war on IranUS foreign policyRepublicansnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Hugely exciting’ finds on tiny Scottish island shed light on spread of Christianity | Archaeology | The Guardian
description: Community-funded archaeological excavations of ‘really important’ sixth-century monastery also rewrite story of Lismore
Author: Esther Addley
Headline: Community-funded archaeological excavations of ‘really important’ sixth-century monastery also rewrite story of Lismore
Content: Islanders and volunteers have been digging in the early medieval cemetery, where they have discovered the earlier buildings, burial grounds and other finds.Photograph: Robert HayView image in fullscreenIslanders and volunteers have been digging in the early medieval cemetery, where they have discovered the earlier buildings, burial grounds and other finds.Photograph: Robert HayArchaeology‘Hugely exciting’ finds on tiny Scottish island shed light on spread of ChristianityCommunity-funded archaeological excavations of ‘really important’ sixth-century monastery also rewrite story of LismoreEsther AddleyWed 30 Sep 2026 19.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTo the residents of the Scottish island of Lismore, population 190, history is never very far away. The tiny island near Oban in Argyll has no row of shops or even a pub – if islanders want to meet for a coffee, the only place to do so is in the livelyGaelic heritage centrethat records the many centuries of community life on the island.This quiet place, documentary evidence records, was home to a monastic settlement in the sixth century AD, when missionaries from Ireland were first moving into northern Britain to spreadChristianity. But apart from a few fragments of an early carved cross, there was almost nothing to see from this period of history.A group of local people from the island’s historical society were determined to look a bit harder, however. After scraping together funding from grants, donations and legacies of locals and a crowdfunding campaign, they commissioned a professional archaeologist, Dr Clare Ellis of ArgyllArchaeology, to lead a group of islanders and other volunteers in an excavation on the site of a much later medieval cathedral.View image in fullscreenThe site contains extensive burial grounds, decorated stonework and early buildings.Photograph: Robert HayTheir “hugely exciting” findings have not only rewritten the story of the island but cast new light on the spread of Christianity in the period, according to archaeologists. What the islanders discovered were extensive burial grounds, decorated stonework and early buildings – all the features belonging to a major sixth-century monastery, comparable to the much better known site of Iona a little to the south-west.In addition, the excavations uncovered rare evidence of slightly later high-status craftworking, including huge numbers of crucibles which had been used to cast gold and silver. The finds have shown that rather than being a small island church in an overlooked backwater, the monastery of Lios Mór, founded bySaint Mo Luóc or Moluag, was a high-ranking site of international importance, experts say.To Robert Hay, a retired plant scientist who moved to the island in 2001 and who coordinated the fundraising and volunteer efforts, the experience was thrilling. “We were [excavating] in this really unfavourable, boggy area. To be digging out the best small crucibles ever found inScotland– it’s extraordinary,” he said.View image in fullscreenA crucible freshly out of the soil.Photograph: Robert Hay“The most exciting moment for me was when they were doing the post-excavation analysis and they found that they had been melting gold, copper, silver, and they were making jewellery on our little island in the seventh century.”While plenty of islanders have an idle interest in its history, a “dynamic minority” of mostly older people had mustered the volunteers and funds to carry out the digs, said Hay. Raising the low five-figure sum needed to pay for it all had been “just a business of getting down to it and organising and so on”, he said. “It was actually a lot easier than what my previous job used to be.”Gordon Noble, a professor of archaeology at the University of Aberdeen, said the finds were highly significant. “We know about sites like Iona having these very famous monastic sites from this early medieval world. But apart from the association with Moluag and a piece of sculpture from this site, we knew practically nothing really about Lismore. So it was hugely exciting to see the results emerging through the local group’s work with Clare [Ellis] … This was clearly a really important early Christian establishment.”View image in fullscreenNewly identified early-medieval sculpture fragments from Lios Mòr.Photograph: Gordon NobleWhile professional archaeologists often worked with local people, Noble said, “it’s not always the community themselves coming up with the ideas. Here, it was very much a bottom-up approach of the heritage society coming up with a plan, working with professionals – and lo and behold, what a great series of discoveries they’ve made at the site.”Hay said he hoped the finds would go some way to restoring the reputation of Moluag, who has long been overshadowed by the more celebrated Saint Columba, the founder of Iona and the subject of an influential ninth-century biography. “Unfortunately, Moluag never had a hagiographer, so his contribution to the evangelisation of Scotland has been very much underestimated,” he said. “So finding his monastic site and [the evidence of metalworking] – it’s all about recalibrating the situation. I think Moluag had a very big impact on the evangelising of Scotland, but unfortunately, he didn’t get his PR right.”The results of the community excavations will bepublished in the forthcoming edition of Antiquity.Explore more on these topicsArchaeologyScotlandHeritageChristianityReligionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Patrick Radden Keefe’s bestseller London Falling shortlisted for Baillie Gifford prize | Books | The Guardian
description: The acclaimed American journalist, who won the nonfiction prize in 2021, is shortlisted alongside Andrea Wulf and Matthew Sweet
Author: Emma Loffhagen
Headline: The acclaimed American journalist, who won the nonfiction prize in 2021, is shortlisted alongside Andrea Wulf and Matthew Sweet
Content: The 2026 Baillie Gifford prize shortlisted books.Photograph: Baillie Gifford prize /Preference StudiosView image in fullscreenThe 2026 Baillie Gifford prize shortlisted books.Photograph: Baillie Gifford prize /Preference StudiosBooksPatrick Radden Keefe’s bestseller London Falling shortlisted for Baillie Gifford prizeThe acclaimed American journalist, who won the nonfiction prize in 2021, is shortlisted alongside Andrea Wulf and Matthew SweetEmma LoffhagenWed 30 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFormer Baillie Gifford winner Patrick Radden Keefe is among the authors shortlisted for the 2026 prize, this time with his book on London’s criminal underbelly.The six-strong shortlist spans literary biography, ancient history, true crime and international reportage, withJames Baldwin, Barbara Cartland and Alexander the Great among its subjects.Keefe, whowon the prize in 2021for his book Empire of Pain, is this time selected for London Falling. This book tells the story of the death of Zac Brettler, a British teenager who fell from a luxury London apartment after pretending to be the son of a wealthy Russian oligarch, described as “a scrupulously researched work of narrative nonfiction” and “grimly absorbing from start to finish” in Ian Thomson’sGuardian review.Keefe is joined by Andrea Wulf – who was previously longlisted in 2008 – along with Nicholas Boggs, Matthew Sweet, Edmund Richardson and Anand Gopal. The winner, announced on 4 November, will receive £50,000.Wulf has been recognised for a second time with The Traveller, which traces the life of George Forster, an 18th-century naturalist and explorer who joined Captain Cook’s second voyage around the world as a teenager.Matthew Sweet’s The Great Dictator explores the life of the prolific romance novelist Barbara Cartland, who famously dictated the 723 novels she authored, against the backdrop of the changing sexual and social politics of her era. Ina Guardian review, Kathryn Hughes wrote: “Sweet pays his subject the compliment of absolute seriousness, regarding her as a cultural phenomenon whose extraordinary life, stretching the entire 20th century, deserves deep study.”Edmund Richardson made the shortlist for his book Alexander, which charts the life of Alexander the Great. Meanwhile, Nicholas Boggs’ biography, Baldwin, reflects on the friendships, romances and creative relationships that influenced the writer’s work. Ralf Webb praised Boggs’s “exhaustive” research inhis Guardian review, enabling the author to “meticulously re-stage Baldwin’s life in something like biographic ultra-high-definition”.The final book on the shortlist, Anand Gopal’s Days of Love and Rage, examines the Syrian civil war through the experiences of residents of Manbij, a city in the country’s north.Chair of judges Kirsty Lang said the books offer “something for everyone”. “It is an eclectic list united by stories of people navigating a world full of conflict as well as hope,” she said. “At a time when many of us are trying to make sense of a complex and frightening world, nonfiction can help us find our way through.”The shortlist was drawn from alonglist of 13 books, including Murder in Paris ’68 by Edward Chisholm, The Nord Stream Conspiracy by Bojan Pancevski, Ukrainian Lessons by Charlotte Higgins, Redwood by Ben Macintyre, Hotel Exile by Jane Rogoyska, Never Say War by Åsne Seierstad and Stay Alive by Ian Buruma. The books were selected from more than 350 eligible titles published between 1 November 2025 and 31 October 2026.Alongside Lang, the judges include novelist Elif Shafak, Waterstones head of books Bea Carvalho, writer and cultural historian Tiffany Jenkins, Spectator literary editor Sam Leith, and editor and reporter Ravi Mattu.The prize was founded in 1999 as the Samuel Johnson prize, and has been sponsored by investment management firm Baillie Gifford since 2016. The firm has faced criticism over its investments in fossil fuels and companies with links to Israel. In 2024, campaign group Fossil Free Booksorganised boycottsof literary festivals sponsored by Baillie Gifford.Last year’s prize was won by Australian writer Helen Garner for her collected diaries,How to End a Story.Explore more on these topicsBooksBaillie Gifford prize for nonfictionJames BaldwinHistory booksBiography booksAutobiography and memoirnewsShareReuse this content

title: Floating scarecrows: how Cornish fishers are stopping seabirds drowning in their nets | Fishing | The Guardian
description: Simple deterrents can slash the number of razorbills and guillemots being trapped underwater, two-year study shows
Author: Patrick Barkham
Headline: Simple deterrents can slash the number of razorbills and guillemots being trapped underwater, two-year study shows
Content: Cornish fishing vessels were used to test the deterrent effect of the towed ‘scarecrow’ buoy.Photograph: Nina Constable MediaView image in fullscreenCornish fishing vessels were used to test the deterrent effect of the towed ‘scarecrow’ buoy.Photograph: Nina Constable MediaFishingFloating scarecrows: how Cornish fishers are stopping seabirds drowning in their netsSimple deterrents can slash the number of razorbills and guillemots being trapped underwater, two-year study showsPatrick BarkhamWed 30 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 19.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBird-shaped kites and a floating scarecrow are being tested to try to stop endangered seabirds drowning in fishing nets.Every year an estimated 95,000 diving birds, including razorbills and guillemots, are accidentally caught in nets off European coasts.But simple deterrents tested by Cornish fishers and devised by scientists and the RSPB have been shown to reduce the toll by about two-thirds.The scarecrow – or more properly a looming-eyes buoy – has a spinning head with two large eyes that scare diving birds away from gillnets, walls of netting which hang vertically beneath the surface.The LEB was tested alongside a commercially availablescarybird kite.View image in fullscreenThe buoy cut the chance of seabirds being caught in gillnets by 59%. Kites achieved a 71% figure.Photograph: Nina Constable MediaTen Cornish fishers andFishtek Marine, which created the LEB, fitted cameras to boats to monitor the effect of the devices on seabird behaviour.The results of the two-year trial, which was analysed by scientists from the University of Exeter and published in the journalConservation Letters, showed that the chance of seabirds being caught in gillnets fell by 59% using LEBs and by 71% using kites.The research revealed that inCornwallmost seabirds were caught in winter, which will help target the use of the devices by season.Tom Horton, lead author of the University of Exeter research, said: “This study provides some of the strongest evidence to date that simple, practical deterrents can substantially reduce seabird bycatch in gillnet fisheries.“By also identifying when and where bycatch risk is highest, we now have a clear opportunity to target mitigation measures where they can deliver the greatest conservation benefit for vulnerable seabird populations and encourage sustainable fishing practices.”Yann Rouxel, bycatch programme manager at the RSPB, said: “After over a decade of research into gillnet bycatch and its solutions, it’s great to see this work moving towards real-world implementation.“The performance of the LEB and kite, as evidenced in this study, is a major milestone in the effort to reduce seabird bycatch without impeding gillnet fishers while at sea.”Explore more on these topicsFishingFishing industryBirdsCornwallMarine lifeWildlifenewsShareReuse this content

title: From Childline to changing TV for ever: Esther Rantzen’s revolutionary life | Television | The Guardian
description: Be it her pioneering approach to consumer injustice or her extraordinary tackling of systemic social issues, the broadcaster was at the forefront of what television could be
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: Be it her pioneering approach to consumer injustice or her extraordinary tackling of systemic social issues, the broadcaster was at the forefront of what television could be
Content: Esther Rantzen at her home in Hampstead, 1989.Photograph: Karen Robinson/The ObserverView image in fullscreenEsther Rantzen at her home in Hampstead, 1989.Photograph: Karen Robinson/The ObserverTelevisionFrom Childline to changing TV for ever: Esther Rantzen’s revolutionary lifeBe it her pioneering approach to consumer injustice or her extraordinary tackling of systemic social issues, the broadcaster was at the forefront of what television could beEsther Rantzen, TV presenter and Childline founder, dies aged 86Esther Rantzen: from That’s Life! to Childline – in picturesZoe WilliamsWed 30 Sep 2026 15.01 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 16.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEsther Rantzen’s early CV reads like a chronicle of the world working as the 1960s thought it should. A smart young woman, privately educated in north London from the age of 10 (the Rantzens had previously lived in New York), then at Somerville College, Oxford, she started on the bottom rung and had exactly the right mixture of graft and luck. Having trained as a radio studio manager, she got her first TV production job as a researcher for BBC-3, Ned Sherrin’s satirical show in the mid-60s. From there, she went to Braden’s Week, a magazine show hosted by Bernard Braden, a serendipitous connection for two reasons – first, he put his researchers on screen, then he decided to return to his native Canada. From there, That’s Life! was born, with Rantzen as the main presenter. It was 1973, and it was conceived as a new, revamped Braden’s Week. In reality, it was nothing like it.That’s Life! ebbed and flowed over its 21 years, but at its various peaks, it would draw in audiences of more than 22 million. It definitely became more searching and serious as it went on, but even from the start, it would have bizarre and audacious gear changes, from an item about funny-shaped vegetables to another on lethal patio doors without skipping a beat. That is not to cast shade on the lighter material: there was a dog called Prince thatcould say “sausages”, and a generation of us have not been able to eat sausages without saying “sausages” in Prince’s voiceat least oncesince. It was delightful to watch partly because there was so much texture to the studio audience’s laughter: there’s one part affection for the dog, one part affection for the owner, five parts,dude, your dog is not saying “Anthony”,and then this wild overflow of excitement when the Yorkie says something that definitely sounds like “sausages”. Then, wham, the next story would be a toddler with life-changing injuries from a poorly surfaced playground, then Victoria Wood would come on and be funny.View image in fullscreenEsther Rantzen filming That’s Life! in 1983.Photograph: Radio Times/Getty ImagesIt shouldn’t have worked, since surely audiences either wanted to be amused or have their heartstrings tugged, or be mobilised in outrage: how could they cope with the emotional maelstrom of all those things at once? Yet it did work, partly because it was a different era: mainstream culturewas extremely macabrein the 1970s and 1980s. Kids were always being electrocuted in public information videos, there was a kind of glee to it.These huge audiences, bombarded with consumer injustices, large and small, forced change at incredible speed. Seatbelts were made mandatory for children as a result of That’s Life!; schools nationwide brought in anti-bullying policies after Rantzen’s campaign inspired by the tragic death of Katharine Bamber, who took her own life as a teenager in the early 1990s.As the impact of her investigations became more and more extraordinary, Rantzen’s focus turned to issues that were more serious and systemic; fewer dodgy door-to-door salesmen and kitchen appliances that might give you an electric shock, more stark and in-depth stories on organ donation, maternity care and stillbirth, mental health problems or the dark side of food manufacturing. She became the person who lifted the lid on the tragedies nobody talked about, and it was in that spirit that Childwatch was conceived: a one-off special in 1986, in which survivors of childhood abuse talked of their experiences. The immediate consequence was Childline, Britain’s first anonymous helpline for children who were being abused.View image in fullscreenRantzen with her husband, Desmond Wilcox, in 1986.Photograph: United News/Popperfoto/Getty ImagesThe BBC didn’t have a clue about what it was about to unleash. This show was heartbreaking, as people in their 20s and 30s shared, often for the first time, their accounts of what they had endured in childhood. But it also revealed that the country simply didn’t know how to have this conversation. The Childwatch set was dominated by a gigantic cake, as if the stark subject matter could be leavened by the trappings of light entertainment. What do people want when they have just said a terribly sad thing? Well, cake, obviously. For 48 hours after the show, the professionally staffed phone lines weren’t operational, and calls were being taken by the production team, who were overwhelmed, not just by the numbers but by the urgency and gravity of what they were hearing – young kids in mortal fear, asking for help. Quite soon, better news stories began to surface, as the project was professionalised and the police and other agencies began to get involved, but at the outset it was necessary and stunningly naive, in the way that pioneering work probably is by definition.More than 30 years on,far too little progresshas been made on child abuse, but two things stand out: first, that nothing will change until victims of abuse have someone to tell who won’t stonewall them; second, that Rantzen understood that instinctively, at a time when so many relevant institutions were making it their business not to.It was as a result of a call to Childline that Rantzen subsequently uncovered the “nest of paedophiles” at Crookham Court boarding school. It resulted in three criminal convictions and a growing awareness of the predatory nature of abusers – that it was the result of active strategy, not tragic happenstance, to find them concentrated in boarding schools and children’s homes. Again, this is taking decades to resolve, but once more Rantzen was at the frontier.Widowed in 2000 when her husband, Desmond Wilcox, died, she also campaigned on palliative care and spoke movingly about the pain of bereavement. In 2013, The Silver Line was launched nationally, to address loneliness and isolation in old age. Having been awarded a CBE for services to children in 2006, Rantzen was made a dame in 2015, in recognition of both Childline and the Silver Line. Her legacy is complicated by the fact that our approach has changed; so many of the subjects she broached seem glaringly ill-suited to the breezy magazine TV format she favoured. But her groundbreaking approach to making television raises a question: without her interventions, would that change have come about?Explore more on these topicsTelevisionEsther RantzenfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Of course I’m the underdog’: the British former spin doctor trying to turn California red | Steve Hilton | The Guardian
description: Steve Hilton’s long-shot campaign for governor is courting Golden state voters with unapologetically populist message
Author: Andrew Gumbel
Headline: Steve Hilton’s long-shot campaign for governor is courting Golden state voters with unapologetically populist message
Content: ‘People are out of the habit of voting Republican. Still, I see a narrow but real path to victory,’ Steve Hilton says.Composite: The Guardian/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘People are out of the habit of voting Republican. Still, I see a narrow but real path to victory,’ Steve Hilton says.Composite: The Guardian/Getty ImagesSteve Hilton‘Of course I’m the underdog’: the British former spin doctor trying to turn California redSteve Hilton’s long-shot campaign for governor is courting Golden state voters with unapologetically populist messageAndrew Gumbelin Los AngelesWed 30 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 21.43 EDTShareSteve Hilton stands almost no chance of becomingCalifornia’s next governor, but that isn’t stopping him from campaigning as though he was just one step away from pulling off the impossible.The former Downing Street political adviser and Fox News host refuses to be daunted by the rancid political environment for Republican candidates this year, or byopinion pollsthat tell him he is lagging20 percentage points or morebehind his Democratic rival, Xavier Becerra.Instead, as he barnstorms the state in an effort to rally the Republican faithful and win over as many Democrats and independents as he can find, he is following a full-throated people-versus-the-powerful script and pumping out what he hopes will be crowd-pleasing policy proposals as fast as he can come up with them.Abolish the department of motor vehicles, he suggested a couple of weeks ago. Cut the price of gas to $3 a gallon. Start a new business school in working-class East Los Angeles. Set up a competition among California’s 58 counties to build 10 brand-new cities from the ground up.Many of these ideas dovetail with the argument Hilton has made from the day he started running, that California has been driven to the brink of ruin by 16 years of Democratic party control over every statewide office. “Enough is enough,” as his campaign slogan says.But they also mark a return to his roots as a prolific and occasionally unpredictable political ideas man, known during his time working for the British Conservative party for spitting out proposals while wandering barefoot through the corridors of power.‘Un-pigeonhole-able’?Policy has been one of the few throughlines in Hilton’s unconventional political journey from one side of the Atlantic to the other. He’s been a restaurant owner and business consultant as well as a senior adviser in the coalition government led by David Cameron in the 2010s. He came to California largely because his wife, Rachel Whetstone, established herself as a big tech public relations guru in Silicon Valley.For many years, Whetstone was considered thepower in the couple, while he wrote a couple of policy books – about “positive populism” and putting a human face on government – and used his connections in the conservative movement to land his Fox News show. Seizing the chance to try to resuscitate a largely moribund California Republican party came only much later.Hilton prides himself on being “un-pigeonhole-able” and thinks of his campaign style as some combination of three startlingly different recent presidential candidates – Bernie Sanders, for his unwavering commitment to lift up struggling people; the Kentucky senator Rand Paul, for his fondness for libertarian free-market solutions; and John Kasich, the former governor of Ohio, for his “happy warrior” campaigning style.View image in fullscreenSteve Hilton talks to attendees during a town hall in Modesto, California, on 26 August 2026 in an effort to connect with farmer’s about their concerns for the upcoming governor’s race.Photograph: Los Angeles Times/Getty ImagesMany of his ideas come straight out of the Republican playbook, accounting for the mistrust he inspires in many Democratic voters. He wants to set up a California version of Doge, Elon Musk’s so-called department of government efficiency that took a hatchet to federal agencies in the opening months of Trump’s second presidency. He wants to kill several environmental regulations, including a plan to introduce more energy-efficient vehicle tires over the next decade. (Hilton calls theenergy commissionerwho came up with the idea a “tire-rant”).He also wants to cancel big, expensive public works projects starting with the long-delayedhigh-speed trainfrom San Francisco to Los Angeles, which Hilton, in common with other Republicans, calls “the bullshit train to nowhere”.Many of his other proposals, though, are harder to define: a plan to eliminate state taxes on the first $150,000 of income, which echoes similar proposals from some of Becerra’s more progressive Democratic primary challengers; the business school plan, which would offer free tuition to lower-income students; or a plan to turn the highway patrol into a full-fledged statewide police investigation force “liberated” from the DMV that currently finances it.Still, Hilton is a savvy and appealing communicator, with a keen understanding of what frustrates and infuriates ordinary Californians. He acknowledges that his more outlandish ideas are unlikely to win this or any other election. But he believes they tell voters he is a pragmatic, independent thinker who, in an age of extremes and polarized political discourse, can talk to anyone, negotiate with anyone, and can entertain any good idea as long as it makes people’s lives easier and lifts the burden of government inefficiency and bloat.He knows that California voters of all political persuasions are frustrated by the daily struggle of keeping up with soaring food and gas prices and looking for solutions to an array of social ills from homelessness to dwindling access to healthcare. It’s a big part of the reason why he led the polls for much of the primary campaign and ended up a close second behind Becerra in a crowded field.“I’m not ideological,” he likes to say. “I’m not tribal.”The ‘T’ problemA major problem for him, though, is that he belongs to a party in thrall to “the president whose name begins with T”, as Hilton calls him – a leader whose name is particularly toxic in California, where registered Democrats outnumber Republicans by a two-to-one margin, and, this year, is dragging down Republican candidates across the country.That has greatly complicated his quest to convince Californians that, by shrinking the size of the state government and slashing what he sees as over-burdensome regulations on small businesses, he can make the state more affordable for ordinary people. However encouraging it was to win close to 25% of the primary vote in June, building up another 25% of the vote in the general election has proven daunting.And Hilton knows it. “Of course I’m the underdog,” he said. “Of course it’s an uphill battle. People are out of the habit of voting Republican. Still, I see a narrow but real path to victory. I see winning.”View image in fullscreenSteve Hilton reacts during his campaign watch party in Huntington Beach, California, on 2 June 2026.Photograph: Mike Blake/ReutersOften, Hilton finds himself walking a fine line between indulging California’s Trump diehards, a vital part of his base, and broadening his appeal. He has made clear he doesn’t wantDonald Trumpor any other national Republican figure to campaign for him. He hasdistanced himselffrom Trump’s complaints of a “rigged system” and sees no need to restrict mail-in voting. But he has talked in the past of being friends with half of Trump’s cabinet and earned Trump’s endorsement during the primary, making it difficult to put much distance between himself and the man in the Oval Office.When facing crowds of the Republican faithful, as he did during the primaries and continues to do at town halls up and down the state, his non-tribal bona fides are quickly tested by supporters eager to talk about Democrats stealing elections, conspiring to take away gun rights, and unjustly prosecuting insurrectionists who attacked the US Capitol on January 6, 2021.At a recent event in San Gabriel, in the eastern Los Angeles suburbs, Hilton did nothing to discourage such talk. Rather, he milked several applause lines by promising to be a champion for such supporters once he was in office. “I’ve never said anything I don’t believe,” he explained in an interview shortly before the event. “I just don’t say everything that I believe.”Away from the Maga faithful, Hilton has made the case that California’s problems have far more to do with the Democrats than with the occupant of the Oval Office. “You don’t have to like Trump. You don’t have to become a Republican,” he wrote in an unusualfull-page advertisementthat ran in the Los Angeles Times and the San Francisco Chronicle in July. “You just have to ask yourself: does it make sense to vote the same way and expect a different result?”View image in fullscreenSteve Hilton attends a discussion with film and television industry workers in Manhattan Beach, California, on 15 September 2026.Photograph: Jae C Hong/APOn the campaign trail, Hilton likes to point out that California sees more people moving to other states each year than it receives in new residents.This trendgoes back to Schwarzenegger’s governorship, and has not, in most years, led to an overall decline in the state population because international migrants have made up the shortfall. Still, Hilton has woven it into his stump speech. “In the time Gavin Newsom has been governor, millions have moved out of the greatest state in the greatest nation on earth. That’s a terrible indictment,” he says. “Are they fleeing Trump? I don’t think so. Most of them are fleeing to states run by Republicans.”The voters Hilton hopes will be most open to such lines of argument are those he sees suffering most acutely from California’s affordability crisis – working-class, non-college educated, many of them Latino. From the early days of his primary campaign, he has sat down with small groups and listened to them talking about the tax and regulatory burdens on their businesses, or the high cost of running a car or truck, or the struggle to find high-quality public schools in non-affluent parts of the state.Such small-scale campaigning goes against received wisdom in California, where consultants of both parties have traditionally relied on television and internet advertising in the belief that a state of 39 million people is too big to reach any other way. Still, Hilton is betting that by talking to voters who don’t normally get to interact with candidates, he can spread the word that he is personable, willing to listen, and eager to help improve people’s lives.A race to the finishHilton knows his idiosyncratic mix of styles exposes him to mockery, if not actual satire – his shoot-from-the-hip policy ideas were memorablyparodiedon the British TV show The Thick of It. He recalled, for example, an episode of his Fox News show when he insisted on promoting the distinctly un-Republican virtues of home nursing visits to promote perinatal health. “It was a low-rated segment,” he said.But Hilton also has faith in his ability to connect to voters – the British accent probably helps – and his talent for a pithy phrase. He can be devastating, for example, when talking about Becerra, who he calls an “empty suit” embodying the very worst of Democratic party complacency.“The level of disrespect for the process is actually shocking,” Hilton said. “Clearly he assumes he’s just going to coast to victory on the back of the Democratic machine … We keep inviting him to engage with us in different ways, but he keeps citing schedule conflicts. What are these conflicts? He’s not scheduling anything.”View image in fullscreenA supporter of the Republican California gubernatorial candidate wears a ‘Team Trump’ hat at Hilton’s election night event in Huntington Beach, California, on 2 June 2026.Photograph: Patrick T Fallon/AFP/Getty ImagesBecerra did eventually agree to one debate with Hilton, set for Wednesday. In response to Hilton’s criticisms, Becerra spokesperson Jonathan Underland said: “Steve is desperate to land his dream job as a talking head on the Fox propaganda network. That’s why he can’t stop saying Xavier Becerra’s name.”It remains to be seen if the debate can shake some of the Becerra camp’s confidence, but for now Hilton is on track to do worse than Gavin Newsom’s barely remembered Republican challenger from 2022, Brian Dahle, who lost by 18 points. A recent poll from the Public Policy Institute of California showed even independents favoring Becerra by close to a 20-point margin.View image in fullscreenHilton sports a California flag jacket at his primary night event.Photograph: Mario Tama/Getty ImagesHilton, though, is refusing to let these numbers bother him as the race enters its final frenetic stretch and his campaign stops become shorter and more intense. On a recent Saturday, Hilton dropped into an Orthodox synagogue in Beverly Hills, where he sported a tallit and a kipa to address a congregation of Iranian Jews for a brisk 10 minutes. On his next stop, 35 miles to the east, he poured exactly one beer and served up one table’s worth of taco plates at a family-owned Mexican restaurant in the foothills of the San Gabriel mountains.He has learned to spit out his message in small bites, asking a group of tattooed truckers at the Mexican restaurant how they would like it if their annual vehicle registration fee was capped at $73 (part of his DMV abolition plan), then telling a gaggle of Republican women in stars-and-stripes shirts that they needed to copy Democratic get-out-the-vote techniques instead of complaining about the other side cheating.“This election is not about who you hate in Washington,” Hilton pleaded in his Trump-distancing ad in July, “it’s about what you love here.” His supporters keep telling him he has to win because their livelihoods depend on it. But, so far, the wider California electorate believes the race is indeed about who they hate in Washington – and nothing Hilton does or says seems to be changing their minds.

title: Who’s your Uber driver on the phone to? Welcome to the long, long diaspora phone call | Life and style | The Guardian
description: For those employed in arduous solitary work such as cab driving, a marathon phone call is the perfect place to navigate the dislocations of immigrant life
Author: Nesrine Malik
Headline: For those employed in arduous solitary work such as cab driving, a marathon phone call is the perfect place to navigate the dislocations of immigrant life
Content: ‘Shooting the breeze’ … long distance conversations aid decompression.Illustration: Joe Plimmer/Guardian Pictures/Getty/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘Shooting the breeze’ … long distance conversations aid decompression.Illustration: Joe Plimmer/Guardian Pictures/Getty/ShutterstockThe Long WaveLife and styleWho’s your Uber driver on the phone to? Welcome to the long, long diaspora phone callFor those employed in arduous solitary work such as cab driving, a marathon phone call is the perfect place to navigate the dislocations of immigrant lifeDon’t get The Long Wave delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereNesrine MalikWed 30 Sep 2026 09.19 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 09.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe question of the week is: “who are Uber drivers always talking to on the phone?” It’s one that regularly surfaces on Reddit threads and social media and even, on a couple of occasions, in the office. It’s not my question (I know who they are talking to), but I think the fact that many people are so baffled by it tells us a lot about the separate worlds we occupy.View image in fullscreenLong distance … seemingly aimless phone calls can mean so much to loved ones across continents.Photograph: Maskot/AlamyWhen you get a cab on a ride-hailing app, the chances that your driver will be on the phone is high. The conversation is almost always quiet, containing pauses so long that it often seems they are actually no longer on a call. But then comes a rejoinder, a laugh, an interjection, and the marathon continues.For anyone of an immigrant background, the question of who they are talking to is absolutely no mystery. They are talking to us; their siblings, parents, cousins and friends. Sometimes the person on the end of the line is back home, other times they are in a western city also navigating the dislocations of immigrant life. The long phone call is a regular feature of diaspora lives, and even more so for those employed in long, solitary work such as cab driving. These conversations are about nothing and everything.What are they talking about?View image in fullscreenKeeping close … the conversations that help the diaspora stay close to family, and home.Photograph: 10’000 Hours/Getty ImagesThis is not an exhaustive list, but based on the calls I constantly field from friends and family, the content I receive in a follow-up call, and familiar themes from chats with drivers in Arabic (which I sometimes get drawn into), the subjects are remarkably consistent. The range includes family gossip, wedding updates, complaints about the cost of living in the west, advice on navigating complex immigration systems, extremely detailed health updates, and political analysis of whatever crisis is unfolding. These conversations can broadly be sorted into one of two categories: “serious technical resolution of a problem” or “shooting the breeze”.In my experience, these beast mode long phone calls are between someone on a long shift, commute or drive, and a mother cooking in the kitchen. There is a languorous quality to the call. Time and conversational convention shift to accommodate long silences without explanation, as one person or the other breaks away to get on with something – dismount or park or blitz something in the food processor. Because the point is not the actual chat. It is a broadly phatic – that is to say language used for bonding – form of communication, an exercise in yearning and homesickness. It helps us bridge a gap between long distances and absences, and simulate a proximity that is so deeply longed for.Why talk all through the working day?View image in fullscreenLong distance … when physical socialisation is impossible, the phone does the work.Photograph: Sergey Strelkov/Getty ImagesThe interminable phone call is an immigrant’s lifeline, now made cheap and stable by voice over IP (the ability to make calls on an internet connection). But it is also a feature of broader cultural and economic patterns. Western time is personal, individual, literally “me time”, something that is violated if demanded without permission. This time is parcelled out necessarily for decompression, for work, for leisure. In other cultures, time is social and public.In Sudan, for example, there is no such thing as calling ahead before a visit. Your home is a drop-in destination from about 11am onwards. A neighbour will pop in for a chat, a relative will be driving home and swing by, and if there are children in the household, their own social lives mean you just never know how many people you are cooking for. The corner shop is a lifeline of last minute provision as numbers swell unexpectedly. If you are an introvert, good luck.When that physical socialisation is impossible, the phone does the work. Certain conditions make the visit and the call possible. Homes where there is often a homemaker to receive, or work that does not require strict, in-office professional deportment and execution. Highly structured working environments and fast-paced modern lives mean that entire societies are firmly post-casual-phone-call. In these contexts, I find myself so wary of ambushing or alarming people with a call that I send a clear warning beforehand. No, there is nothing to worry about, and are you sure this is a good time to speak? Absolutely no worries if not.But it is also a mindset, which you can lose over time. I find myself becoming increasingly post-phone call outside work, constantly thinking to myself that I will ring a relative back when I have the time. Generally, I prefer to message or voice note, conscious that when I return the call, it absolutely will not be a quick and efficient catch up. But, in truth, I do have the time, I have just assimilated the same rigid notions of downtime and non-urgent phone calls as an incursion. Fundamentally, this is an extremely capitalist notion of time as purely a function of work, where even if you are not working, you are “re-charging” in anticipation of more work.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe Long WaveNesrine Malik, Micha Frazer-Carroll and the team guide you through the biggest Black stories from around the worldEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionReclaiming the lost art of the ambling phone callView image in fullscreenA lost art … the case for bringing back the long, meandering phone call.Photograph: Maskot/Getty ImagesThe fact that the long driver call is such a bewildering anomaly is a meeting of those two worlds. In one, a passenger cannot fathom that you might have so much to say to someone over the phone, because everyone you love or want to see is generally within your immediate social reach, and because it is unfathomable to dedicate so much of your precious bandwidth to seemingly aimless conversation. In another, loved ones are in a different country or sprawl all over the world, and without their constant companionship life is just alienation and monotonous work.But I suspect there is more to the lost art of the phone call in certain societies than just the pressures of modernity. In contemporary life, there are so many ways to feel like you are in touch and in conversation when you are not. So many ways to feel part of some slipstream of humanity, when in fact we are scrolling, meme-ing, seeing news from friends and strangers alike via story updates, while not exchanging anything meaningful or even uttering a single word. Those in exile are acutely aware of alienation, and reach out to remedy it. But for those in their home countries, loneliness still lurks in ways harder to recognise. A phone call is honestly less time consuming and more replenishing than anything else we use our devices for.Tap inDo you have long, aimless phone calls? How do you think your preferred mode of communication connects to your culture? Share your thoughts by replying to this, or emailing us atthelongwave@theguardian.comand we may include your response in a future issue.Diaspora discussesLast week, we explored Britain’s fraught relationship with its historical role in enslavement. You shared your thoughts on the publication of theRegister of British Slave Tradersand therecords of enslaved people, and mounting calls for recognition and reparations.double quotation markI started to search online for my enslaved ancestors for the first time and discovered that decades of British secrecy means I have no written records of my ancestors to start with. No names no approximate births or death dates. This legacy means I have a family left not literate enough to document their history. Ancient family members that don’t speak English. People who make up their new own names because their family names derived from the slavers. It’s great that we have this info but I wish there was more help in finding the people we want to know about.Michelle B, based in Stroud, UKdouble quotation markThe stories that a country tells itself make a huge difference. Kudos to Germany for making sure that the blot on their journey is never forgotten among their own. Former colonial powers would do well to teach history accurately – otherwise they risk forgetting the past rather than learning from it, and helping to correct the damage that was done while they enriched themselves for generations.David P.A. Mullings, based in the US and Jamaica• To receive the complete version of The Long Wave in your inbox every Wednesday,please subscribe here.Explore more on these topicsLife and styleThe Long WaveAfricaCaribbeanRemittancesFamilyMobile phonesnewslettersShareReuse this content

title: How Europe’s housing crisis is fuelling a new movement | World news | The Guardian
description: As soaring rents and house prices across Europe​ feed into the political discourse, campaigners believe they have a rare opportunity to force housing to the top of the agenda
Author: Ashifa Kassam
Headline: As soaring rents and house prices across Europe​ feed into the political discourse, campaigners believe they have a rare opportunity to force housing to the top of the agenda
Content: People from all walks of Madrid have gathered to protest policies which affect everyone.Photograph: Rodrigo Jimenez/EPAView image in fullscreenPeople from all walks of Madrid have gathered to protest policies which affect everyone.Photograph: Rodrigo Jimenez/EPAThis Is EuropeWorld newsHow Europe’s housing crisis is fuelling a new movementAs soaring rents and house prices across Europe​ feed into the political discourse, campaigners believe they have a rare opportunity to force housing to the top of the agendaDon’t get This Is Europe delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereAshifa Kassamin MadridWed 30 Sep 2026 10.45 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 11.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was billed as one of the largestreal-estate eventsin Europe, attracting as many as 15,000 people ranging from investment firms to developers. But as the District trade show and summit got under way last week in Madrid, housing campaigners from 140 organisations across the globe turned up, intent on holding their own “counter-summit” to push back against the idea of housing as a financial asset.Many of the campaigners arrived in the Spanish capital as Maricarmen Abascal, an 87-year-old woman who uses a wheelchair,was being evictedfrom the apartment where she had lived for seven decades. Asanger over the evictiongave way to days of protests andan encampmentin the heart of Madrid,the presenceof campaigners from Italy to Ireland was a poignant reminder of the global dimension of the crisis.The eviction underscored how brutal access to housing had become for so many around the world, said Teresa Mamede, a housing campaigner from Lisbon who travelled to Madrid for the counter-summit.“Nobody among us is safe from having this happen to them.”The Guardian has long reported on the depth of thehousing crisis across Europe. Within the EU, prices soared by 53% between 2010 and 2024, according to Eurostat, while rents increased 25% over the same period.Not all countries have been hit equally; while Viennaremains a bright spotfor its ample stock of public housing that has tempered rental costs, Estonia has seen rentssurge 208% in the same time period, while Ireland and Hungary have seen increases of more than 100%.Some of the soaring costs can be chalked up to the “ever-intensifying social experiment” playing out in Europe, research fellow Tim Whitenoted last year,as officials see whether the machinations of finance capitalism can deliver on the fundamental need for housing. “The evidence now seems overwhelming: no.”Instead, vulnerable people and minorities have beendisproportionately affectedby the market’s shortcomings, while others warn that the crisis could drive voters into the arms of the far right. “We cannot remain stuck in the rhetoric of defending democracy, inclusive societies and equal opportunities if people’s standard of living is getting worse,” Jaume Collboni, the mayor of Barcelona,told me last year.Voters in Berlin, however, recently opted for another path. In a city where rents had climbed nearly 70% in the past decade, a quarter of voters backed the leftwing party Die Linke in this month’s state elections, making it Berlin’s strongest party. The strategy behind their success was far from rocket science,said Guardian Europe columnist Fatma Aydemir. “Because, more than any other party in this campaign, Die Linke made this issue [of housing] unmistakably its own: the question of who gets to live in Berlin, and at what price.”‘This is just getting started’View image in fullscreenProtesters in Madrid demand political action to stop evictions and alleviate the housing crisis.Photograph: Susana Vera/ReutersSome have sought shared solutions to the shared crisis. At the Madrid counter-summit, campaigners launched a pan-European alliance to demand indefinite rental contracts and rent control across the continent.Earlier this month, dozens of organisations launched the European Citizens’ Initiative,calling on people to sign their petitionfor EU-level measures to protect tenants, curb speculation and convert empty buildings into homes. “In every European country, in every major survey, and across all age groups, housing emerges as the number one concern of citizens,”the initiative notes. “We see and feel it every day: workers who can no longer afford the city they build, young people who cannot leave their parents’ home, tenants pushed out of their neighbourhoods after renovation, empty buildings while people sleep on the street.”InSpain, where the days-long encampment in Madrid has led to similar camps in cities such as Barcelona, Seville and Palma de Mallorca, the protests have already begun to have an impact.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMaricarmen, the evicted octogenarian, will beallowed to returnto her apartment, it was confirmed on Tuesday. Her rent will remain around the €500 a month she had paid for years – significantly less than the €2,650 the investment firm that owns her apartmenthad initially demanded.This week the Spanish government also said it had approved two housing decrees that include reforms such as a ban on evictions until 2030, and the regulation of temporary lettings and lettings by room. But these measures will now have to win approval in the country’s fractured parliament.What exactly comes next for the housing movement that has gripped Spain in recent days is anyone’s guess. With the spectre of general elections looming and the Socialist-led coalition scrambling to shore up its base of progressive voters, campaigners have spotted a singular opportunity to tackle an issue that Spaniards have long ranked as one of the country’s biggest problems.“The coming days will be crucial,” the Madrid Tenants’ Union said on Tuesday as it called for further protests this weekend. “A historic window of opportunity has opened to reverse decades of the commodification of housing. That is why we need to step up the pressure.”Or, as the Málaga Tenants’ Union put it in an online post: “This is just getting started.”To receive the complete version of This Is Europe in your inbox every Wednesday,please subscribe here.Explore more on these topicsWorld newsThis Is EuropeEuropeHousingCommunitiesProtestSpainnewslettersShareReuse this content

title: Exposed bras and unitards: why are people wearing underwear on the outside? | Fashion | The Guardian
description: From crystal balconettes on the catwalk to mankinis on the parkrun, showing off your undies seems to be all the rage
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: From crystal balconettes on the catwalk to mankinis on the parkrun, showing off your undies seems to be all the rage
Content: The bra-as-top has been creeping up on us for some time … Fendi’s 2027 spring/summer collection.Photograph: Pixelformula/SIPA/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe bra-as-top has been creeping up on us for some time … Fendi’s 2027 spring/summer collection.Photograph: Pixelformula/SIPA/ShutterstockPass notesFashionExposed bras and unitards: why are people wearing underwear on the outside?From crystal balconettes on the catwalk to mankinis on the parkrun, showing off your undies seems to be all the rageWed 30 Sep 2026 13.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleName:Underwear.Age:The first loincloths date from about 7,000 years ago.Appearance:Increasing.You mean people are increasingly wearing underwear?No, they’re increasingly wearing it on the outside.This is what happens when you let educational standards slip.They’re wearing it on the outside on purpose.Why?Fashion. In recent shows Fendi had models striding the catwalk wearingskirts with matching bras.What about their tops? Did they match as well?The braswerethe tops.I don’t know much about designer fashion, but this is a category mistake: the bra is a foundation garment.Nevertheless, the bra-as-top hasbecome an established trend. It’s been creeping up on us for some time, with glimpses of bra beneath unbuttoned shirts.And the shirt has finally been removed from the equation?Not always: at Erdem’s London fashion show, crystal bras were worn over the top of shirts.I suppose if I had a bra made of jewels, I’d want to wear it on the outside.All kinds of bras are being reimagined as outerwear: tube bras, bandage bras, bralettes …Bras for women who don’t need bras, you mean.Meanwhile, unitards are becoming popular for men.They are not.They are: the single-piece “speedsuit” favoured by some elite athletes has started to work its way down to the amateur runner.If wearing a mankini can help you win a race, it’s probably worth cramming yourself into one.The thing is, while speedsuits may enhance performance to some degree at a professional level, they’re not going to do much to improve your parkrun time.Somen are just wearing them because they like the way they feel?Or the way they look. “You have to have some level of audacity to wear one,” an amateur marathon runner told theWall Street Journal. “And I think I have that audacity.”The audacity to wear underwear in the street.He probably doesn’t see it that way.If walking around in their smalls makes people feel modern, who am I to judge?Actually the underwear as outerwear idea hasbeen with us for quite a while– corsetry was a popular fashion trope in the 1990s, as were slip dresses.I suppose we have superheroes to thank for all this.While it’s true that Superman and others wore their pants on the outside, there is no evidence to suggest it ever caught on with the wider public.Do say:“There is nothing new in fashion – let’s not forget that the ubiquitous T-shirt was once considered underwear.”Don’t say:“It’s eight o’clock and the Uber is here! Why aren’t you dressed yet?”Explore more on these topicsFashionPass notesUnderwearUnderwear for menfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Electoral reform could be a gamble too far for Burnham – but so far he’s on a winning streak | Zoe Williams | The Guardian
description: Though proportional representation poses risks for Labour, it’s a change that feels necessary for today’s volatile politics, says Guardian columnist Zoe Williams
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: Though proportional representation poses risks for Labour, it’s a change that feels necessary for today’s volatile politics, says Guardian columnist Zoe Williams
Content: Andy Burnham at the Labour party conference in Liverpool on 30 September 2026.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPAView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham at the Labour party conference in Liverpool on 30 September 2026.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPAOpinionElectoral reformElectoral reform could be a gamble too far for Burnham – but so far he’s on a winning streakZoe WilliamsThough proportional representation poses risks for Labour, it’s a change that feels necessary for today’s volatile politicsWed 30 Sep 2026 10.55 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 13.13 EDTShareAnumber of people have admitted to tears during Andy Burnham’s Labour partyconference speech, and most of them mean when he talked about his father, who died very recently. But then there were a few (not me) who welled up when he announced a commission onelectoral reform. It was just the sheer shock of it: that we may finally have a prime minister who will follow through on his own long-held beliefs and remain loyal to his long-term support base, even if it makes him avoidable enemies and, medium-term, destroys Labour’s only-trodden path to victory. It felt a bit like slipping through time, and I couldn’t even tell you to when (definitely not the 1990s).Burnham’s support for proportional representation has always been extremely unusual for a Labour politician. To this day, he ascribes that to his experience of winning an election as mayor of Greater Manchester on a supplementary votes system, where people get to choose a first- and second-preference candidate. He said thatcampaigning under that system“finally aligned the conversation on the door with what people want from politics, which is about problem-solving first and foremost, not about point-scoring”. He went a bit further this morning, asking Nick Robinson on the Today programme: “Can we really watch a party with less than 30% walk into Downing Street?”Plainly, he was talking about the spectre of a Reform government, and it’s that very context that makes this already difficult constitutional conversation even more vexed. Back in May, the all-party parliamentary group for fair elections held a meeting to discuss theaftermath of the local elections. It feels like a long time ago, and furthermore, so different in atmosphere as to be irrelevant to the prime minister, but 2020s politics are defined by their switchblade turns. In the matter of constitutional reform, the overriding priority has to be to build a system that’s fair across a range of imaginable scenarios, not just the one in front of you.The locals delivered great results for Reform, and satisfactory ones for the Liberal Democrats, which reflected the realities of a first-past-the-post (FPTP) system – first, it rewards the winner, and second, it rewards geographical concentration. Labour walked away from the 2024 general election with 63% of the seats on 34% of the votes, thelargest overrepresentation ever. The Greens have spent years commanding the fervent support of a geographically diffuse but not insignificant minority, with almost nothing to show for it in parliamentary terms.The distortions of FPTP have been well-known for years, but historically they were only ever discussed in terms of the barrier to entry they presented to insurgent parties, and the democratic deficit they constituted to any voter who didn’t live in a marginal seat, which is to say the majority of voters. So the counter-arguments were that, for all its flaws, by keeping out insurgents, the traditional voting system kept out extremists: and who wouldn’t sacrifice a little bit (or a huge amount) of democracy, for the sake of steadiness?Stability was the first myth to fall, when it transpired, over the past 10 years, that you can keep on returning one of two main parties as reliably as you like, and they will have no problem confecting so much intra-party turmoil that you might as well have voted for the Monster Raving Loony party. The efficacy of FPTP in keeping out extremists, meanwhile, was – like a stock market bubble – true until it wasn’t. Once politics has fragmented, the system rewards short bursts of popularity with potentially very long periods of power. That has a toxic effect on the supposedly sober heads of the political centre who, once they see extreme, often bigoted, positions pay off in the polls, steer straight towards them. The best prophylactic against extremism is not a gamified voting system but some political backbone. Undoubtedly in response to all that, public attitudes to proportional representation have changed enormously, hitting an all-time high of60% support last year. In 2011 it was27%.To return to that meeting in May, there was one more finding from the local elections: once you start to lose, under FPTP, you lose calamitously. So the obvious solution, to a room full of already fully committed constitutional reformer MPs, was for the next prime minister to change the system, right? Psephologists John Curtice and Prof Tim Bale sounded the warning: you can’t change the rules just because you’re losing. The point was so self-evident, from such trusted sources, that all the air seemed to leave the room. But four months on,Labouris ahead in the polls, Reform’s support is tailing off and seems to have further to fall. Far more importantly, this week Burnham showed himself prepared to have a thorny, inconvenient debate that wouldn’t necessarily even serve his political interests, and even if it did, would certainly disperse his power, because he believes in his cause and does so persuasively. So he doesn’t look like he’s losing.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionZoe Williams is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsElectoral reformOpinionAndy BurnhamLabourFirst past the postProportional representationLabour conference 2026Constitutional reformcommentShareReuse this content

title: Government must stop dithering over energy bill support for the vulnerable | Energy bills | The Guardian
description: Ministers should introduce a properly targeted social tariff rather than tinker with the warm homes discount
Author: Nils Pratley
Headline: Ministers should introduce a properly targeted social tariff rather than tinker with the warm homes discount
Content: Virtually everyone agrees the current warm homes discount is inadequate.Photograph: Solarisys/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenVirtually everyone agrees the current warm homes discount is inadequate.Photograph: Solarisys/ShutterstockEnergy billsGovernment must stop dithering over energy bill support for the vulnerableNils PratleyMinisters should introduce a properly targeted social tariff rather than tinker with the warm homes discountEnergy bills forecast to jump by £276 a year from JanuaryWhat to do as prices head for £2,000 a yearWed 30 Sep 2026 13.04 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 20.41 EDTShareAfter the hopeful good vibes in Liverpool, here comes a reminder of what is coming this winter: a mighty new year shock in energy bills, hitting the poorest hardest, that the government looks unprepared for.From the quarterly price cap level of £1,723 that will apply from Thursday for an average dual-fuel household, take your pick from a range of forecasts for the first three months of 2027. The energy consultancy Cornwall Insightsays £1,999. The big supplier EDFthinks £2,076. Split the difference and we’re talking about an 18% quarter-on-quarter rise in the unit rate at the worst time of the year, the months of peak consumption.Everybody knows the immediate reason – soaring gas prices – but the government cannot claim to be surprised by events. The threat of a prolonged price spike has been present ever since Donald Trump’s Middle East misadventure became more than a one-week affair.Energy bills: what to do as prices head for £2,000 a year, from switching deals to insulatingRead moreThe government, it’s true, has fiddled at the margin. Rachel Reeves, when chancellor, took a chunk of green levies into general taxation from April. Andy Burnham cut VAT on electricity from 5% to zero for six months, starting on Thursday, in one of his “breathing space” measures. But what is missing from the government’s response is properly targeted help for the most vulnerable.There is the warm homes discount scheme – worth £150,used by 5.5m low-income householdslast year and paid for by all bill payers – but virtually everybody agrees it is inadequate for the bills on the way and misses swathes of households who would fall within a better definition of “vulnerable”, such as those with high energy needs for health reasons.The consensus answer, promoted by various thinktanks, charities, regulators and energy companies for years, is a well-designed flexible social tariff or discount scheme.Here, for example, was the chief executive of Ofgemas long ago as February 2023after the gas price spike caused by Russia’s war on Ukraine: “We think that, with bills continuing to be so high, there is a case for examining with urgency the feasibility of a social tariff for customers in the most vulnerable situations.”Three winters later, it is hard to spot signs of urgency on the part of successive governments. Nobody pretends a social tariff is easy to design. At heart, it’s a data exercise that would have to take in household income (as opposed to information on individual incomes held by HMRC), health records and energy consumption. Cliff-edge judgments would have to be made. Perfection would be impossible.But the result would surely be better than what will come this winter, which will probably be John Healey upping the level of the warm homes discount in next month’s budget because it’s the only lever available to him.In addition, Healey could conceivably remove VAT from gas as well as electricity (though that would run against the national electrification agenda). Or,as urged by 120 organisationsa fortnight ago, he could take more of the “hidden taxes” of energy transition into taxation (there are excellent reasons to do so, though all will look expensive from his point of view).skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMiatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, seems to recognise the mess she has inherited. She could hardly miss it now that unpaid consumer debts in the energy system are projected to reach a colossal£7bn by the end of this year. “There is a question that needs to be answered … we have to think about the costs and how we recover it in the most fair way,” she told this site’sPolitics Weekly podcastthis week.Yes, that is indeed the question, and it’s encouraging that Fahnbulleh is not parroting her predecessor’s dreamy line about “£300 off bills by 2030”, because everybody can also see that“stubbornly high”– EDF’s projection for bills for the end of the decade – is more realistic. Higher “non-commodity” costs are coming down the track even when the gas price falls.But it does not sound as if the government is even close to settling on a joined-up model for bill support for the most vulnerable that could serve for this winter and future winters. It’ll be the usual last-minute scramble for ideas and higher levels of fuel poverty than needs to be the case. The multi-year dithering is inexcusable.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: I have a new favourite medical drama – and now I want to have a nasty accident in Pittsburgh | Adrian Chiles | The Guardian
description: The Pitt is on a different level – it’s not so much like watching drama as being in one, writes Adrian Chiles
Author: Adrian Chiles
Headline: The Pitt is on a different level – it’s not so much like watching drama as being in one, writes Adrian Chiles
Content: Top team … Perlah (Amielynn Abellera), Dr Langdon (Patrick Ball) and Dr Garcia (Alexandra Metz) in The Pitt.Photograph: Warrick Page/HBO MaxView image in fullscreenTop team … Perlah (Amielynn Abellera), Dr Langdon (Patrick Ball) and Dr Garcia (Alexandra Metz) in The Pitt.Photograph: Warrick Page/HBO MaxOpinionThe PittI have a new favourite medical drama – and now I want to have a nasty accident in PittsburghAdrian ChilesThe Pitt is on a different level – it’s not so much like watching drama as being in oneWed 30 Sep 2026 12.20 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 13.43 EDTShareIdo like a TV doctor. I’m not talking about proper doctors who sit on studio sofas dispensing wisdom. I’ve nothing against them – why, I worked with Dr Hilary Jones on ITV and he was a very nice chap – but it’s to fictional doctors I want to entrust my care.I’ve not always felt this way. Either the standard of fictional TV medics has improved or, more likely, I’m losing the plot. It’s a relatively recent thing. I never watched ER, for some reason, and I find Casualty to be quite entertaining without ever fantasising about being rushed into Holby City hospital for emergency treatment. As for being treated by the staff ofGrey’s Anatomy, that would be fine, but the constant playing of pop songs at key moments would get on my nerves. Nurse Jackie? Jackie Peyton and Dr O’Hara are a compelling nurse-doctor pairing, but too unhinged for me to take the risk with them. Shame, but I’ve got to be sensible.There’s only one place I want to take my accident-and-emergency requirements. Be it a mere ankle sprain or a full-on life-threatener, to Pittsburgh is where I’ll be heading.The Pitt, on HBO, is on a different level.It’s not so much like watching drama as being in one. I feel so close to the doctors, from the trainees to the top dog, that first and foremost I want to be friends with them. Although, understanding the need to keep our doctor-patient relationships professional, I appreciate this won’t be possible.It’s in their capacity as doctors I want to engage with them. If I had a nasty accident in Pittsburgh – I haven’t ruled out going there to try to make this happen – and I woke up in that emergency room, I’d be absolutely made up. Seriously, even knowing they are actors and not doctors, I’d be very happy to have their medical attention. Perhaps not for actual surgery – that would be silly – but for general diagnosis and a bit of stitching or some such, bring it on.I’ve given some thought as to my top picks. Naturally, it depends on the nature of my emergency, but at my bedside I’d go for Frank Langdon. Not everyone’s cup of tea, but he has bags of experience and he’s dealing very bravely with his drug-dependency problem. Alongside him I’d want Cassie McKay: no nonsense, but compassionate with it. And I would, of course, be hoping against hope that my case was complex or nasty enough to warrant them calling out for Dr Robbie to come over and have a look. No further intervention would be necessary. Two minutes with him would see me rise from my bed and walk away, right as rain.Inside The Pitt: the stunning, smash-hit medical drama from the team behind ERRead moreAs for my primary-care needs, geographically challenging though it would be, as it’s 3,600 miles away, my GP would be on the Cornish coast. There’s no one for me but Doc Martin’s Dr Martin Ellingham. I’ve only recently come across this classic, thanks to my mum, whom I gently mocked when I found her watching it. One episode and I was hooked.I had it down as chocolate-box fluff, but there’s more to it than that. The doctor is engagingly misanthropic and some of the storylines and themes are decidedly dark. I went back to the beginning and I am binge-watching all 79 episodes. I love it so much that I interviewed its creator, Dominic Minghella. While he was naturally pleased at my enthusiasm, I got the sense that even he thought I might be going a little over the top.But Martin Clunes’ Dr Ellingham is exactly what I want from a GP. Enough of the kindly, understanding family doctor guff; I want someone skilled, but also impatient, abrupt, direct and unpardonably rude. Just give it to me straight. And if Doc Martin can’t help, he can pack me off to Pittsburgh to do the rest.Adrian Chiles is a broadcaster, writer and Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
