title: I heard one thing loud and clear in Andy Burnham’s landmark speech: the left has won the arguments | Owen Jones | The Guardian
description: The PM’s stated trajectory is a rebuke to past Tory and Labour governments. The challenge now is to make his project progressive in word and deed, says Guardian columnist Owen Jones
Author: Owen Jones
Headline: The PM’s stated trajectory is a rebuke to past Tory and Labour governments. The challenge now is to make his project progressive in word and deed, says Guardian columnist Owen Jones
Content: Andy Burnham at the Labour party conference in Liverpool, 29 September 2026.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham at the Labour party conference in Liverpool, 29 September 2026.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesOpinionAndy BurnhamI heard one thing loud and clear in Andy Burnham’s landmark speech: the left has won the argumentsOwen JonesThe PM’s stated trajectory is a rebuke to past Tory and Labour governments. The challenge now is to make his project progressive in word and deedWed 30 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 08.18 EDTShareAs Andy Burnham delivered hisconference speechto the Labour faithful yesterday, it was hard not to recall Jeremy Corbyn’s words after the party’s shattering 2019 election defeat. “I am proud that on austerity, on corporate power, on inequality and the climate emergency,” hewrotefor this publication, “we have won the arguments and rewritten the terms of political debate.” Given Boris Johnson’s 80-seat majority, widespread mockery ensued.But when it comes to rhetoric, who can now deny that the left has won the argument? ALabourprime minister has declared that “Britain has been on the wrong path for a long time”, listing five villains: “Deindustrialisation, deregulation, privatisation, austerity, Brexit.” His speech was infused with class politics, as he condemned a society “run for vested interests, not in the public interest, with power held in too few hands”.When he committed to break with the “flawed thinking of the last 40 years”, he lumped together Conservative and Labour governments. He has already repeatedly labelled the culprit:neoliberalism. This has long been the received wisdom of the left: that as Clement Attlee’s postwar government established a social-democratic consensus that the Tories upheld for a generation, so Margaret Thatcher bequeathed a settlement that New Labour maintained.These beliefs were condemned to the fringes of Labour, even though Tony Blair himselfeventually confessed: “I always thought my job was to build on some of the things she had done rather than reverse them.” Any mention of neoliberalism was a sure way of provoking an eye-roll from a mainstream politician or commentator. We were denied any debate about an economic system based on extraction rather than investment; an economy based on financialisation rather than making things. Corbynism was an insurgency against all of this – until it crashed on the shores of Brexit.Add to this the new foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, telling those who opposed Israel’s genocide and were infuriated by Labour’s position on Gaza: “You were right.” We should add, too, the disastrous past wars backed by Labour: Iraq, Afghanistan and Libya.The left should feel vindicated by the political shift taking place. We were right – at home and abroad. We were mocked, demonised and marginalised for making these arguments. Now most of the left’s worldview is embraced by the Labour top brass. This happened after Keir Starmer’s faction based their entire project on defining themselves against the left. As the Labour activistAli Milani– who was part of Burnham’s team – told me, that strategy nearly brought about the party’s destruction.Burnham only became prime minister because Labour’s leftwing voters rebelled – by defecting en masse to Zack Polanski’s Green party in the Gorton and Denton byelection, then in local elections in England, Scotland and Wales. That is clearly understood by Burnham’s team, or they would not be so confidently doubling down on their new strategy.But winning the argument on a rhetorical level is not the same as substance. Burnham is clearly shifting towards state intervention. That’s taking the form ofGreat British Grid, a new publicly owned network body, and he condemned privatised water as “a symbol of what has gone wrong with Britain”.The shift in this direction actually began under the last Conservative government. Did Liz Truss not commit to asubsidy for energy billsworth tens of billions of pounds? What of Rishi Sunakbeing forcedto bring railways into public ownership? Starmerism expanded the semi-nationalisation of the railway and foundedGreat British Energy. Neoliberalism has exhausted itself and governments are being forced to abandon its tenets, whether they want to or not.But full public ownership of water seems far off, with “public control” acting as a rather flexible label. Burnham has committed to a large-scale building of new council homes and preventing them from being flogged off through right to buy. Yet he hasalready backtrackedon a pledge to spend the government’s entire £39bn affordable homes programme on council and social housing.Crucially, he remains committed to the suffocating fiscal rules that block the investment Britain’s crumbling infrastructure and starved services need, especially given there remains no promise to hike taxes on the well-to-do.While committing to a national care service is extremely welcome, scrapping the triple lock on pensions is not. Britain still spends significantly less on pensions than other major European countries such as Germany, France and Spain, and about two million pensioners languish in poverty.Burnham has a battle plan, with social care the flagship. Risks lie ahead, but Labour now travels in hope | Polly ToynbeeRead moreConsider, too, that the Labour parliamentary benches were stuffed with candidates deemed loyal to the Starmer project. The rightwing factionalists who ran the party may currently be sulking on the fringes, but do not underestimate their capacity to inflict damage.A key difference between Burnhamism and what came before may well be expressed by what Miliband told activists attending a Labour fringe event organised by the soft-left pressure group Mainstream. “Too often in the past, we thought that kicking some of our supporters would do us political credit,” he said, “and we were absolutely wrong.” Offending people “in the progressive community”, he admitted, was sometimes done “deliberately”.Because of pressure from the streets and the ballot box, Labour has shifted its rhetoric. The substance is a bit more complicated. Where Starmerism defined itself against the left, could this new government be pushed in a more progressive direction? That question has not yet been answered. But the left should indeed feel emboldened. The winds are shifting in our direction.Owen Jones is a Guardian columnist. His latest book, The Fall of the West: How They Really Lost It, is published on 1 October. title: Heavy metal is about uplifting the downtrodden. So why is alleged abuse by Marilyn Manson so easily forgotten? | Marilyn Manson | The Guardian
description: Slipknot sharing their stage with a man accused of wrongdoing by more than a dozen women is the antithesis of everything the genre should stand for, even if he denies it
Author: Matt Mills
Headline: Slipknot sharing their stage with a man accused of wrongdoing by more than a dozen women is the antithesis of everything the genre should stand for, even if he denies it
Content: Marilyn Manson.Photograph: Steve C Mitchell/EPAView image in fullscreenMarilyn Manson.Photograph: Steve C Mitchell/EPAMarilyn MansonHeavy metal is about uplifting the downtrodden. So why is alleged abuse by Marilyn Manson so easily forgotten?Matt MillsSlipknot sharing their stage with a man accused of wrongdoing by more than a dozen women is the antithesis of everything the genre should stand for, even if he denies itWed 30 Sep 2026 08.53 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 08.54 EDTShareIhave so many fond memories of my first heavy metal festival. It was Download 2012, and I was 15 years old. Metallica headlined, playing their landmark Black album in full for its 30th anniversary, and it was my first exposure to one of my future favourite bands, Trivium. But just as important as the music I heard that day was the sense of acceptance I felt when I was there. Outside of that field, my shaggy hair and my penchant for noisy riffs were looked down upon; inside, everybody looked like me. It seemed like some kind of paradise, and I went home feeling empowered.I’m far from the only person who’s had an experience like this. It’s easy to dig up interviews with everyone from Metallica’s James Hetfield to Judas Priest singer and gay icon Rob Halford about how heavy music champions the misfit – or at least it’s supposed to.This week, Marilyn Manson was confirmed to support Slipknot in front of 90,000 people at Wembley Stadium next July. He was booked despitethe wave of sexual misconduct allegationslevelled against him, plusa lawsuit from his former assistantalleging physical, emotional and psychological abuse that’s set to go to trial in November 2027. (The singer denies any wrongdoing, and in2025 a four-year investigation into his alleged crimes was droppedwith no charges filed.) If metal is supposed to uplift the downtrodden, then putting a man accused of wrongdoing by more than a dozen women on one of Europe’s biggest stages feels like the antithesis of everything the genre stands for.double quotation markMetal has never felt more fractured or unwelcoming, its inclusive messaging never more hollowManson, whose real name is Brian Hugh Warner, retreated from the public eye afterthe start of the allegations against him in 2021, but he returned in 2024 with a new record deal and a string of high-profile tour dates. He’s far from the only allegedly problematic figure to have recently made a successful musical comeback. Chris Brown, who in 2009pleaded guilty to felony assault of his ex-girlfriend Rihanna, andYe(formerly Kanye West), who made a string of antisemitic statements in 2022, are playing massive venues. Earlier this month,the Guardian published an op-edabout Queen of the Stone Age frontman Josh Homme’s cosy image rehabilitation after he kicked a female photographer and his ex-wife accused him of domestic abuse.Metal, with its long-established identity as a dangerous and anti-mainstream force, appears to be particularly lenient with this kind of figure. The news of Manson touring with Slipknot came three months after Pantera supported Metallica on their second night at the 62,500-capacity London Stadium. In 2016, Pantera singer Phil Anselmo faced widespread backlash for raising his hand andscreaming “white power!” onstageat a charity concert. He eventually apologised, but in 2017 gavean interviewwhere he called some of his detractors “phonies”. None of it stopped his band from reuniting to much celebration in 2022. In November, Nuclear Blast Records, the same label to which Manson signed in 2024, will release a new album by Anselmo’s other group, Down.In February, As I Lay Dying are poised to release a new album. The band split in 2014 after its sole constant member, singerTim Lambesis, was sentenced to six years in prison for soliciting the murder of his ex-wife. Then, in 2024, everyone bar Lambesis quit the band, and somedisturbing videosurfaced online where he’s seen flipping a table that another ex-wife was sitting at. (The former couple have each accused the other of abuse.) As I Lay Dying’s latest single, aptly entitled Polarized, has amassed 560,000 YouTube views in two weeks regardless.Those figures are wildly outdone by US metalcore band Falling in Reverse’s track Joseph: currently one of the hottest songs in metal, boasting 20m YouTube views in two weeks, boosted by guest spots from Slipknot’s Corey Taylor and System of a Down’s Serj Tankian. This is after frontman Ronnie Radke became a lightning rod for controversy, having made a number of transphobic comments on social media, and contorted the backlash into part of his image: the cover of the band’s 2024 album Popular Monster bears his mugshot after a 2012 arrest for domestic assault. (The charge was dismissed in court in 2014.)As far as pushback against these artists goes, the most consistent voices have been the disappointed fans on social media, who have dominated the announcement of the Slipknot/Manson tour to the point that theBBCandNMEhave reported on it. However, in previous instances, these disaffected cries have been drowned out by ticket sales: Manson’s tour of the UK in February 2025 completely sold out. Even more disheartening has been seeing other artists play along. Arena-fillers Five Finger Death Punch attempted to launch a Manson rehabilitation narrative ahead of their summer 2024 tour together, guitarist Zoltan Bathory saying it was OK because Manson is now “clean and sober”. Lamb of God toured with Pantera in 2023 and 2024: singer Randy Blythe apparently didn’t see any irony in doing this, then in 2025 called Elon Musk a “fucking asshole” for raising his hand in a similar manner to Anselmo’s gesture.Queens of the Stone Age’s Josh Homme kicked a woman and his ex-wife alleged domestic abuse. Why the cosy makeover?Read moreOf course, metal has never entirely been the post-judgmental utopia I experienced at 15: there has long been a drought of female representation and hate has found pockets in underground subcultures such as the Nationalist Socialist Black Metal scene. But in 2026 – with some of its biggest artists being accused of heinous acts against vulnerable people, only to return as popular as before, possibly more – the genre has never felt more fractured or unwelcoming, its inclusive messaging never more hollow. If I were to walk into my first metal festival today, see Falling in Reverse orMarilyn Mansonplay to thousands of fans, then go home and look at their histories, there’s a very strong chance I’d never go to a second.Explore more on these topicsMarilyn MansonMetalSlipknotcommentShareReuse this content

title: Bill Gates thinks AI could kill a billion people – but can we trust his judgment after Epstein? | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: He knows a thing or two about tech, but what to make of the views of a man who met Jeffrey Epstein 30 times and couldn’t see what a monster he was?
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: He knows a thing or two about tech, but what to make of the views of a man who met Jeffrey Epstein 30 times and couldn’t see what a monster he was?
Content: Bill Gates at the World Economic Forum in January this year.Photograph: Denis Balibouse/ReutersView image in fullscreenBill Gates at the World Economic Forum in January this year.Photograph: Denis Balibouse/ReutersOpinionBill GatesBill Gates thinks AI could kill a billion people – but can we trust his judgment after Epstein?Arwa MahdawiHe knows a thing or two about tech, but what to make of the views of a man who met Jeffrey Epstein 30 times and couldn’t see what a monster he was?Wed 30 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTShareThe Bill Gates rehabilitation tour is in full swing. After having his carefully cultivated image tarnished by the revelation ofhis connection to Jeffrey Epstein, Gates lay low for a while. Now, however, the Microsoft co-founder is once again thrusting himself into the public consciousness, this time with adire warning about AI. If left unchecked, AI could cause “a billion deaths”, Gates declared in an interview with NBC on Sunday.Perhaps I should be terrified by this announcement from a man who, for all his sins, knows a thing or two about technology. But I’m sick of hearing about the hypothetical dangers of AI when the technology is being usedto kill people today.Gates may not be directly involvedin Microsoft any more, but, rather than making prophecies about the future, I’d love to hear what he thinks aboutthe company’s rolein the AI-enabled destruction of Gaza.Another thing I’d like to hear Gates explain is why he reckons anyone should trust his judgment about anything, considering he met with Epstein on several occasions after being introduced to him in 2011. To be clear: that’s three years after the financier pleaded guilty to charges including solicitation of prostitution from a minor. Gates, who has not been accused of involvement in Epstein’s crimes,has saidhe recalled “being aware that Epstein had faced prior legal issues”, but didn’t understand the extent of them. Two minutes of Googling (or Binging) could havemade it clearthe man was bad news.The oversight is particularly strange because Gates is obsessed with his public image. His team have a custom-size mannequin on which they test his outfits. The goal,per the Wall Street Journal, is “to depict someone calm and approachable, like Mister Rogers”. Not someone who cavorts with a sex offender.Ignorance isn’t Gates’ only excuse. He has alsosaid that Epstein“knew a lot of very rich people and [claimed he] could get them to give money to global health”. It seemsthe 17th richestman in the world didn’t know any wealthy people he could hit up for donations himself and, for the sake of the world’s health, had to lean on a dodgy financier whose funds were obtainedin mysterious ways.I’m not accusing Gates of anything nefarious. But, if we are to take his Epstein excuses at face value, I’m accusing him of being a fool. If we can’t trust his judgment about a man like Epstein, I’m not sure we should trust his proclamations about the future of humanity.Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Things are changing behind the scenes, so you must decide: do you want human civil servants or AI bots? | The civil servant | The Guardian
description: Rapidly expanding AI use within the government is numbing departments to its profound threats. And try arguing with a faceless digital bureaucrat, warns a British civil servant
Author: The civil servant
Headline: Rapidly expanding AI use within the government is numbing departments to its profound threats. And try arguing with a faceless digital bureaucrat, warns a British civil servant
Content: Protesters on Whitehall demand the government pause its AI use, London, 16 September 2026.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenProtesters on Whitehall demand the government pause its AI use, London, 16 September 2026.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesOpinionUK newsThings are changing behind the scenes, so you must decide: do you want human civil servants or AI bots?The civil servantRapidly expanding AI use within the government is numbing departments to its profound threats. And try arguing with a faceless digital bureaucratWed 30 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 12.27 EDTShareAnother day, another apocalyptic warning about the likelihood that rampantly uncontrollable artificial intelligence will solve all of our problems, including the problem of being alive.Hot on the heels of disgruntled Anthropic researchersannouncing the end of civilisationby 2030, we’ve now had the portentously namedHugging Face incident, as well as the Australian government’s grim discovery of a rogue AI’sattackon its Medicare website. Swarms of experts are nowfalling over each otherto warn us that much, much worse is on the way.Thank God, then, that PM Uncle Andy has thrust Britain on to the bleeding edge of the fight against the rise of the self-improving machines. Except he hasn’t. Not really.Yes, Burnham went to the United Nations and riskedenraging the Orange Onewith talk of Britain’s prospects of leading the drawing-up of international rules for AI. Slightly awkwardly, however, one of Burnham’s first acts after sweeping into office wasto abolishthe Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT), the very department that had been leading work on AI safety. It’s a move that the Institute for Government warns will cause “real harm” and which former government AI adviser Matt Clifford has said “wastes time and energy that’s desperately needed for the actual substance”.Isn’t there something gloriously British about all this? Having failed thus far to regulate the technology effectively at home, we are going to world-beatingly coordinate its regulation everywhere else. Whatever it is, it doesn’t quite feel like the response of a state gripped by existential urgency.But perhaps that is because all of us – government ministers included – have already become desensitised to the risk of AImageddon. You can get used to anything. Sure, if one industry insider inadvertently leaks the news that scientists building a new technology believe it might kill everyone, a spot of existential panic is to be expected. But if you ram these tidings down our collective throat every couple of weeks, eventually the prospect of mass extinction acquires the urgency of that bowel cancer screening kit you’ve been meaning to send back to the doctor.Civil servants understand this aspect of human nature only too well. Like the prospect of the galloping climate crisis, we too are simultaneously terrified by AI and utterly bored by it. The extraordinary becomes familiar; the familiar becomes an item on a civil service risk register, after which the real fear is that someone will arrange a Teams call to talk about it.AI could kill all humans in next decade, warn experts: but how seriously should we take them?Read moreThemedian age of civil servants, remember, is 43 years, so many have already witnessed enough technological revolutions to choke a chatbot. Which means that, like me, there’s a large faction of the workforce that remembers the replacement of fax machines by email, and their first introduction toClippy, that damnably moronic AI ancestor office assistant whose principal stab at sentience was appearing uninvited to chirp: “It looks like you’re writing a letter. Would you like help?”So it’s entirely possible that civil servants of my vintage might not yet have been compassionately euthanised by the time government departments such as the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) or HMRC contain more AI agents than carbon-based officials.It may sound melodramatic, but that’s where we are headed. Ministers – convinced that harnessing AI will help keep Reform at bay by offering the tantalising possibility of slashing civil service jobs – have calmly and robotically emoted their concerns about the machines jumping their guardrails, while enthusiastically searching for things to give them. That’s amid civil service union concerns that the government is moving too quickly, citing theFabian Society’s research findingthat only 29% of those surveyed said they had been consulted about AI tools in their workplace.They’re right to be worried. Before DSIT was deleted, its permanent secretary, Emran Mian,reportedly had plansfor AI to eventually replace almost every departing civil servant in his department rather than replacing them with humans. Elsewhere, the DWP has beenbusily experimenting with AIacross the welfare state, directing its machine-learning systems to identify supposedly high-risk universal credit claims. And in response to “serious concerns” about transparency and the handling of personal data, the DWP has been careful to insist that humans retain the final decision and that AI does not determine entitlement.Is this just practical common sense, or the kind of world-beating complacency thatsome have pointed outis an echo of the government’s response to the climate emergency? Either way, the reassurances given by AI minister Kanishka Narayan to theparliamentary business and trade committeesound increasingly hollow after the spate of recent AI rampages.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCivil servants – especially those in public-facing government departments – are acutely aware that saying “a human remains in the loop” is not the same thing as saying “a human remains in charge”.This really, truly, matters, because the commodity on which every government ultimately runs is not data, or productivity, or even money. It is trust, including the trust that – while below theOECD average– the British public still has in the civil service, and which, according to thepublic accounts committee, is being jeopardised by inadequate transparency and weak standards on AI.We already have a national catchphrase for what happens when human discretion – and the accountability that comes with it – disappears. Little Britain’s “computer says no” still resonates – thanks in part to the haunting legacy of the Post Office’sHorizon scandal. Everyone recognises the terror of the human being behind the desk surrendering responsibility to a system whose conclusion can’t be questioned because nobody in the room understands how the hell it got there.And that may be the real warning from Whitehall. Not that killer robots are about to lock the doors and announce the abolition of humanity. But that long before then, governments might quietly surrender thousands of small human judgments to a swarm of digital bureaucrats because doing so is cheaper, quicker and can be passed off in a ministerial speech as “transformation”. It will not feel like that to the public.The author works for the UK civil serviceExplore more on these topicsUK newsOpinionCivil serviceAI (artificial intelligence)Technology policycommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on Lula v the Bolsonaros: the decision of Brazilian voters will affect us all | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Sunday’s general election is too close to call, with the incumbent president facing the son of the man who attempted a coup against him
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Sunday’s general election is too close to call, with the incumbent president facing the son of the man who attempted a coup against him
Content: Flávio Bolsonaro campaigning in São Paulo on 28 Sepptember 2026.Photograph: Allison Sales/APView image in fullscreenFlávio Bolsonaro campaigning in São Paulo on 28 Sepptember 2026.Photograph: Allison Sales/APOpinionBrazilThe Guardian view on Lula v the Bolsonaros: the decision of Brazilian voters will affect us allEditorialSunday’s general election is too close to call, with the incumbent president facing the son of the man who attempted a coup against himWed 30 Sep 2026 13.37 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 18.41 EDTShareSunday’s election in Brazil could hardly be a clearer-cut choice – nor a closer call. President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, known as Lula, isneck and neckin the polls with Flávio Bolsonaro, the son and champion of the jailed far-right former president Jair. Mr Bolsonaro senior is serving a 27-year sentence forplotting a coupto “annihilate” democracy after losing the last election.Brazil is Latin America’s largest democracy, but military dictatorship is in its recent past. Mr Bolsonaro wants to free his father and those who rioted in his support in 2023. The senator has campaigned as a less crass and temperamental version of his father, but he is no less extreme. For many on both sides, this is a vote against a man they detest more than an endorsement of their own candidate. Most votersdisapprove of bothmen.Initially, pundits predicted victory for the leftwing incumbent. Some feel that at 80 he is too old to begin a fourth term, though he remains energetic. His social programmes are extensive, but frustration at Brazil’s enduring failure to match its economic record to its potential may hobble him, especially with growth slowing. Violent crime remains a top issue.View image in fullscreenPresident Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.Photograph: Adriano Machado/ReutersThen came the Banco Master financial scandal, which has snowballed into a corruption case spanning Brazilian politics and the judiciary. First, Flávio Bolsonarowas caught on tapeasking the failed bank’s playboy owner, Daniel Vorcaro, for almost $27m to make a film about his father. He denies wrongdoing.Then compromising messages between Mr Vorcaro and the supreme court judge who led the prosecution of the ex-presidentwere revealed. The allegations fed the perception that politicians are all dirty, and bolstered the unfounded far-right claim that Mr Bolsonaro Sr was stitched up. His son has also papered over a damaging public rift with his stepmother Michelle – an influential figure, key to the evangelical support he needs.Mr Bolsonaro Jr has said he will abide by the election’s result. But the Bolsonaros have spent years working toundermine trustin internationally respected Brazil’s electronic voting system. A narrow first-round victory for Lula would probably be contested. With other candidates on the right, Mr Bolsonaro Jr would also have an advantage in a second-round vote. He has talked up theprospect of privatisationand cuts to public spending and taxes if he wins. He has pledged to pack the supreme court with anti‑abortion conservative judges, who would also be critical to future election disputes. He has vowed to introduce the kind of aggressive anti-crime drive that has trampled human rights elsewhere.President Donald Trump and Marco Rubio, his secretary of state, will be further emboldened in their “Donroe doctrine” of aggressive intervention in the western hemisphere if Mr Bolsonaro Jr is victorious.US meddlingin this election has often backfired – high tariffs on Brazil have allowed Lula to run as the patriot defending the country against foreign interference. But it is no less disturbing.Mr Trump’s more ruthless and reckless second term also offers an alarming vision of how another Bolsonaro presidency might look. The first showed historic levels of deforestation in the Amazon as well as a surge in illegal resource extraction and the invasion of Indigenous people’s lands. Those fell sharply once Lulareturned to power. A Bolsonaro presidency would be bad for women, the poor and minorities. Democracy would probably be its first, local victim. But the climate would surely be another – with consequences for us all.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on falling pupil numbers: a chance to improve opportunities for young people | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Empty classrooms are a sign of falling fertility and high living costs. But they should also free up more resources to spend on young people
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Empty classrooms are a sign of falling fertility and high living costs. But they should also free up more resources to spend on young people
Content: ‘Fewer schools make areas less attractive to families, particularly in rural places where alternatives may be miles away.’Photograph: Nathan Stirk/GettyView image in fullscreen‘Fewer schools make areas less attractive to families, particularly in rural places where alternatives may be miles away.’Photograph: Nathan Stirk/GettyOpinionSchoolsThe Guardian view on falling pupil numbers: a chance to improve opportunities for young peopleEditorialEmpty classrooms are a sign of falling fertility and high living costs. But they should also free up more resources to spend on young peopleWed 30 Sep 2026 13.36 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 18.41 EDTShareSchool closures are an alarming symptom of Britain’s shrinking birthrate. Several factors have contributed to falling enrolment, but the most significant is that people are havingfewer children. Declining pupil numbers could be an excuse to free up spending for anageing population. Instead, the government should see this as an opportunity to improve the quality of provision for young people.The fall has been most acute in inner London, where90 schools have shut since 2021. In Southwark, where the number of children born each year has dropped bymore than a thirdsince 2010, eight primary schools haveclosedin the past six years. As London’s councils have observed, high living costs are pricing families out of the centre and dissuading people from having children. It is no surprise that Islington and Westminster, two of the most expensive places to live in Britain, also have among the lowest fertility rates in England and Wales.Declining enrolment shapes the quality of education that schools can provide. They receive funding for each child they enrol, which is currently£7,000 per primary-age pupilin England. Schools with fewer pupils are forced to make their funding stretch further,cutting teachers, merging classes, and losing extracurricular activities. Official forecasts have previouslyoverestimatedthe future number of young people, making it harder for local authorities to plan. They have not been helped by the promotion of free schools, which have created asurplus of school places, or the expansion of academies, which decide their own admissions and can entice pupils away to neighbouring areas. The government has recently given local authoritiesgreater powersto object to academy expansion, which should help them plan more effectively.The Treasury may be tempted to recycle savings from falling pupil numbers towards rising demand for health and social care. Over the past seven years, for example, as primary school pupil numbers in Englandfell by 5%, the number of teachers and classes shrank by 4%. But treating this development as a justification for cutting spending on education would be a mistake. Lucy Powell, the education secretary, haspromisedexpanded enrichment activities and earlier intervention for children with special educational needs. Falling pupil numbers offer an opportunity to deliver these ambitions, provided the government retains the resources to do so. The gap between private school fees and state school spending per pupil hasmore than doubledover the past decade, and spending more on state school pupils would help narrow this inequality.The closure of a school shapes an area. “Without this school it’s all just tourists, isn’t it?” one parentrecently saidof Soho’s last remaining primary school, which is at risk of imminent closure. Fewer schools make areas less attractive to families, particularly in rural places where alternatives may be miles away. Yet if people continue havingfewer children, more schools will probably have to close. In some cases, this may be unavoidable.Schools that have large numbers of unfilled places tend to perform worse on average, but closing them won’t necessarily improve results. Local authorities, which haveexcelled at selling off public assets, should be required to keep hold of shuttered schools. Empty classrooms could berepurposed as youth clubs, turned over to nurseries, or transformed into Sure Start centres. The focus should be on managing resources to improve education and opportunities for young people in an increasingly old society.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: A proportional representation voting system could spell disaster for Labour | Electoral reform | The Guardian
description: Letter: Gian Lorenzo Spisso says his knowledge of Italian voting systems and British politics leads him to the view that first past the post is the lesser of two evils
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Gian Lorenzo Spisso says his knowledge of Italian voting systems and British politics leads him to the view that first past the post is the lesser of two evils
Content: ‘I come from Italy, where I have seen the proportional systems at work. They drive a wedge between MPs and their constituents.’Photograph: Vickie Flores/EPAView image in fullscreen‘I come from Italy, where I have seen the proportional systems at work. They drive a wedge between MPs and their constituents.’Photograph: Vickie Flores/EPAElectoral reformLettersA proportional representation voting system could spell disaster for LabourGian Lorenzo Spissosays his knowledge of Italian voting systems and British politics leads him to the view that first past the post is the lesser of two evilsWed 30 Sep 2026 12.53 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 13.00 EDTShareReading that Andy Burnham wants to push electoral reform forward and move the UK towards proportional representation (Report, 29 September), I found myself shouting at the screen.I come fromItaly, where I have seen proportional systems at work. They drive a wedge between MPs and their constituents. They reward tribalism (yes, even more than here). They leave large parts of the electorate hostage to the whims of tiny parties, and force parties into ragtag coalitions that produce unstable, ineffective governments. And for all that, people do not seem to feel any better represented.Having lived in the UK since 2014 and watched its parties with an outsider’s eyes, I still see first past the post as the lesser of two evils.Brexit exposed a complete lack of leadership in David Cameron’s Conservative party, and it was an act of unprecedented self-harm that we are all still paying for, quite literally. But it also showed that parties outside the big two can exert enough pressure to force the party in power to adapt and, alas, to listen to voters.Labour, meanwhile, has reinvented itself remarkably: from Ed Miliband’s soft left to Jeremy Corbyn’s more radical programme, and back again when that proved ineffective. Would a major party put itself through so much self-scrutiny without the incentives of first past the post? Or would it have split into several streams, perhaps more representative but far less effective, squandering its history as so many parties of the Italian left have done?As a settled-status resident who expects to become a citizen this year, and is hoping to vote for Labour at the next general election, I can only say: please don’t do this.Gian Lorenzo SpissoBristolHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Andy Burnham’s social care plans could be much more radical | Labour | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to the Labour leader’s conference speech and plans for changes to social care and the state pension triple lock
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to the Labour leader’s conference speech and plans for changes to social care and the state pension triple lock
Content: Andy Burnham at the Labour conference, 29 September 2026.Photograph: Gary Roberts/SOPA Images/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham at the Labour conference, 29 September 2026.Photograph: Gary Roberts/SOPA Images/ShutterstockLabourLettersAndy Burnham’s social care plans could be much more radicalReaders respond to the Labour leader’s conference speech and plans for changes to social care and the state pension triple lockWed 30 Sep 2026 12.53 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 13.00 EDTShareIn the aftermath of Andy Burnham’sspeech to the Labour conference, media discussions are focusing on how to define social care and estimate its cost (How will Burnham’s national care service work – and how will it be funded?, 29 September).Most arguments assume that any new system will look like the existing one, with services outsourced to large companies, using contracts without scope for innovation, with rigidly defined targets, often delivered using poorly rewarded, precariously employed migrant workers.The reality is that many of the services needed by elderly and incapacitated people – such as cleaning, meal preparation, transport to medical appointments, household repairs and personal services such as podiatry, hair care, physiotherapy, counselling or therapeutic massage – are also required by others and are already freely available in local markets.The trouble is that they are most often supplied by online platforms such as Uber, Deliveroo or Housekeep with no commercial incentive to address social need.One solution would be to set up local platforms that supply these services to anyone, regardless of age or disability. If these platforms made sure that all staff were suitably trained, qualified and security-checked, and their vehicles suitably adapted, they could be attractive to all local residents, whose commercial use of them would help subsidise their costs. Social care recipients could be provided with access to them using a voucher system that would be much cheaper than setting up such services from scratch or bundling them in with huge outsourcing contracts.With suitable public oversight, using platform technology for public good would also bring other benefits to the local economy. Services would be better for all. Workers could upgrade their skills and gain job security. And, instead of being siphoned off to tax havens, any profits could remain, as Burnham might put it, “in every postcode”.Ursula HuwsLondonAndy Burnham’s commitment to a national care service brings welcome clarity to a debate that has too often avoided difficult choices. But before deciding how to pay for care, we must answer a prior question: what should people be able to count on?Reports that the proposed service may follow Scotland’s model of free personal care raise an important distinction. Removing charges for help with washing, dressing and eating could make a substantial difference. But social care is about much more than these tasks. When we in the coalition government developedthe Care Act,we placed wellbeing at its heart. Its purpose extends to dignity, independence, relationships, participation and people’s control over their own lives.There is a risk that defining a national care service primarily through free personal care narrows our understanding of what social care is for. The two need not be in conflict. Free personal care could form part of a wider national guarantee, grounded in the Care Act’s wellbeing principle and applying to people across adulthood.TheCasey commissionhas an important opportunity to help establish that wider promise. The question is whether the new service will simply change what people pay, or also strengthen the care and support that they can rely on to live their lives.Paul BurstowFormer minister of state for care services, 2010-12Andy Burnham’s decision that proposals for social care reform will not happen until after the next election is the latest instalment in almost two-decade saga of delays.Since a Labour government firstcommitted to social care reformin 2007, we have seen a succession of unfulfilled promises: the discarded Personal Care at Home Act 2010, David Cameron’s part-implemented Care Act 2014, Theresa May’s failed 2017 proposals, and Boris Johnson’s 2019 pledge on the steps of Downing Street to fix social care – delayed under Rishi Sunak, then scrapped by Rachel Reeves in 2024.In the years since this saga of broken promises began, both of my parents were diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease. One of them survives, and our family continues to wait for any meaningful help.Families living through the reality of the social care crisis do not have the luxury of waiting for another election cycle. Mr Burnham needs to get a move on.Dr Ruth CharlesSwavesey, CambridgeshireAs a 69-year-old in receipt of 20 years’ teacher’s pension and a full state pension, I say by all means take money from pensioners. Scrap national insurance (a retrogressive tax) and increase income tax. Scrap all age-related tax benefits/exemptions. But please don’t hit the triple lock until the state pension reaches parity with most European states (Will pensioners be poorer as a result of Burnham scrapping the triple lock?, 29 September). It is mainly women who rely solely on this inadequate pension, and many of them live alone in rented accommodation. They are the last people who should be asked to make sacrifices.Sarah JamesMonmouthAs an 86-year-old, I’m sure I am not alone in having anxiety about paying for a care home if the need arises, and am delighted that Andy Burnham is determined to sort out the system at last. While the triple-lock pension increases are very welcome, I’d happily accept their change into simply keeping up with prices as a trade-off for never having to worry about paying for social care.Michael MillerSheffieldHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Unfair method of splitting pensions can add to the pain of divorce | Divorce | The Guardian
description: Letters: Richard Nobbs draws attention to fundamental flaw in way pension assets are split on divorce and calls on Labour to act
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Richard Nobbs draws attention to fundamental flaw in way pension assets are split on divorce and calls on Labour to act
Content: ‘A fundamental flaw in the legal process compounds unfairness and is both unnecessary and easily rectified.’Photograph: Kobus Louw/GettyView image in fullscreen‘A fundamental flaw in the legal process compounds unfairness and is both unnecessary and easily rectified.’Photograph: Kobus Louw/GettyDivorceLettersUnfair method of splitting pensions can add to the pain of divorceRichard Nobbsdraws attention to fundamental flaw in way pension assets are split on divorce and calls on Labour to actWed 30 Sep 2026 12.53 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 12.55 EDTShareYour article on the impact of the escalating cost of living on divorce settlements (Unhappy couples staying put due to cost of living crisis, say divorce lawyers, 23 September) provides a timely reminder of the financial inequities facing many separating couples.As a pensions expert, I have regularly encountered a particular imbalance in the splitting of pension assets on divorce. Although the lastLabourgovernment enabled pension savings to be taken into account in divorce settlements, there remains, 25 years on, an inherent unfairness in the way many such arrangements are implemented.Where one partner (usually the husband) has built up valuable pension entitlements through a defined benefit pension, the allocation of those assets on divorce is often based on an equivalent cash value at the point of divorce, known as “external sharing”.In thousands of such cases, especially those involving private sector pensions, this leads to the undervaluing of pension assets transferred – usually to the wife and, in some cases, by many thousands of pounds.Divorce is a traumatic enough experience. This fundamental flaw in the legal process compounds unfairness and is both unnecessary and easily rectified. The government should address this urgently to avoid sleepwalking into another pensions scandal.Richard NobbsExcalibur ActuariesHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Is this how Andy Burnham sees the future of work? | Andy Burnham | The Guardian
description: Brief letters: Parental influence | Public investment | Capital gains tax on property profits | A degree of success? | Oxygen of publicity
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Brief letters: Parental influence | Public investment | Capital gains tax on property profits | A degree of success? | Oxygen of publicity
Content: Andy Burnham hugs his parents Eileen and Roy in 2016.Photograph: Peter Byrne/PAView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham hugs his parents Eileen and Roy in 2016.Photograph: Peter Byrne/PABrief lettersAndy BurnhamLettersIs this how Andy Burnham sees the future of work?Parental influence | Public investment | Capital gains tax on property profits | A degree of success? | Oxygen of publicityWed 30 Sep 2026 12.53 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 13.00 EDTShareKeir Starmer reminded us often that his father was a toolmaker, a skilled occupation. In his Labour partyconference speech, Andy Burnham referenced his parents, Eileen and his late father Roy. He did not mention that Roy was a telecoms engineer, also a skilled job, and one that was and is fully unionised, with decent terms and conditions. Perhaps the PM sees in that not just the past but also the future of work.Keith FlettTottenham, LondonAndy Burnham’s belief that investment in public spending will save money in the longer term is a positive-sum calculus targeted at improving the quality of life. After all, if private capital can generate profit from privatised utilities and services, then by the same token public spending can direct funding to benefit the common good.Austen LynchGarstang, LancashireNow that Andy Burnham has grasped the nettle of the pension triple lock, perhaps he will have the courage to wade into the nettlebed to end the exemption from capital gains tax of the enormous gains from the sale of private residences.Maurice Henry CollierSolihull, West MidlandsAndy Burnham’s speech to the Labour party conference was a masterclass in political oratory. Burnham has a degree in English literature. I wonder if the two things are perhaps related. I think young people should be told.Glyn TurtonBaildon, West YorkshireThanks to Andy for a wonderful speech. I enjoyed that he denied those attention-hungry politicians the oxygen of publicity they seek.Jude CarrLondonHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: ‘I like him as a No 9’: Bellingham a striking alternative for England, says Tuchel | England | The Guardian
description: Thomas Tuchel’s hunt for alternatives to Harry Kane has led to him identifying Jude Bellingham as an option at No 9 for England
Author: Jacob Steinberg
Headline: Thomas Tuchel’s hunt for alternatives to Harry Kane has led to him identifying Jude Bellingham as an option at No 9 for England
Content: Jude Bellingham wore the captain’s armband after coming off the bench against Czechia.Photograph: Martin Divisek/EPAView image in fullscreenJude Bellingham wore the captain’s armband after coming off the bench against Czechia.Photograph: Martin Divisek/EPAEngland‘I like him as a No 9’: Bellingham a striking alternative for England, says TuchelHead coach sees Real Madrid man as an option up frontKane praises Alexander-Arnold’s impact and work rateJacob SteinbergWed 30 Sep 2026 14.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 16.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThomas Tuchel’s hunt for alternatives to Harry Kane has led to him identifying Jude Bellingham as an option at No 9 for England. Kane continued his remarkable scoring record in the2-0 win against Czechiain the Nations League on Tuesday, moving to 87 goals in 123 international appearances with a late strike in Prague, but he has little cover up front.There is no prospect yet of Tuchel having to consider life without Kane. TheEnglandhead coach backed the 33-year-old striker to last another decade at the highest level, tipped him to reach a century of international goals soon, and said England cannot expect to produce a replica of their greatest forward. However, there is concern over whether England have enough depth in attack.Alexander-Arnold proves his worth to England with trademark assist against Czechia | Jacob SteinbergRead moreOllie Watkins and Ivan Toney have been overlooked for this camp. Dominic Calvert-Lewin, who came on for Kane during thedefeat by Spainon Saturday, is 29 and has four goals in 13 caps. Liam Delap, the 23-year-old Nottingham Forest forward, is yet to earn a senior call-up and it was noted that Bellingham led the line after coming on for Kane in the closing stages against Czechia.“You will not get anotherHarry Kane, first of all,” Tuchel said. “We look for different solutions. We finished the game with Jude as a No 9. There will be someone else but it will not be Harry or a copy of Harry. We will find a solution when it comes to it but maybe not me. It might be another 10 years.”Bellingham wore the captain’s armband after coming off the bench in Prague on Tuesday. “I like him as a [No] 9,” Tuchel said. “Then he can contribute to both sides and overloads the sides and doesn’t affect so much of the balance. We found a bit of a new role for him in the last match, as a central [No] 10, so he can go to both sides and it is more of a 4-2-3-1 than a 4-3-3 to have Harry and Jude closer together and to give them a chance to overload both sides.“We are working on that. Jude in general should always be able to go through the last line and be able to end up in the box. He is a natural goalscorer and has the hunger to be on the scoreboard. He wants to have the decisive action so it makes not a huge difference if he plays as a [No] 9 or a [No] 10.”England moved second inNations LeagueGroup A3 after seeing off Czechia, who were reduced to 10 men midway through the first half. Anthony Gordon opened the scoring and Kane finished well late on.“The ball falls down and you see Harry taking the shot and that is exactly the player you want it to drop down to,” Tuchel said. “He does it in every single match. The highest level of finishing.”Tuchel was the manager who took Kane to Bayern Munich in 2023. Uli Hoeness, Bayern’s honorary president, has since said the former Tottenham striker is the club’s greatest signing. “That is so beautiful as it tells me everyone can see his true value and his personality,” Tuchel said. “It is not easy to change and to come to Bayern Munich when you win, win, win and it is a big club. You are under the spotlight and he won everyone over.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEngland’s next assignment is a trip to Rijeka to face Croatia on Saturday. It remains to be seen if Tuchel sticks with Trent Alexander-Arnold after the right-back marked his first international appearance since June 2025 by creating Gordon’s goal.“Trent’s outstanding,” Kane said. “The delivery, the passing range, the crossing but also today defensively he was outstanding. He’s a fantastic player. Trent just has to keep his head down, keep working hard. He’s been great in camp so far. He’s showing to the boss that he wants to be here.”Explore more on these topicsEnglandThomas TuchelJude BellinghamHarry KaneNations LeaguenewsShareReuse this content

title: Hampton’s heroics preserve WCL point for Chelsea on Bompastor’s OL Lyonnes return | Women's Champions League | The Guardian
description: Hannah Hampton made a crucial late save to ensure Chelsea left OL Lyonnes with a 0-0 draw on Sonia Bompastor’s return to her former club
Author: Tom Garry
Headline: Hannah Hampton made a crucial late save to ensure Chelsea left OL Lyonnes with a 0-0 draw on Sonia Bompastor’s return to her former club
Content: Hannah Hampton at full stretch to deny Ada Hegerberg late on.Photograph: Olivier Chassignole/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenHannah Hampton at full stretch to deny Ada Hegerberg late on.Photograph: Olivier Chassignole/AFP/Getty ImagesWomen's Champions LeagueHampton’s heroics preserve WCL point for Chelsea on Bompastor’s OL Lyonnes returnTom Garryat Groupama StadiumWed 30 Sep 2026 17.11 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 19.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere were plenty of encouraging signs for Chelsea as they claimed a valuable point in the Champions League on their head coach Sonia Bompastor’s return to face her former teamOL Lyonnes.The goalless draw was a slow-burner but concluded with a flurry of late action where both teams missed chances to steal the points. However a draw felt fair on a night when Chelsea’s double pivot of Keira Walsh and Lexi Potter in midfield continued to flourish, three days after they similarly impressed inSunday’s victory over Arsenal.Leah Williamson blunder gifts Paris FC a point as Arsenal’s struggles continueRead moreOL Lyonnes had scored eight times in their first fixture in the league phase, away against the Swiss side Servette, but Chelsea looked comfortable for large periods and Bompastor said: “I’m really proud of my team, being able to not concede here. We are happy also with the ball, the way we performed, we were able to exploit different spaces. The only thing that was missing was the goal.”The French side had scored at least seven times in all four matches they had played in all competitions this season. Given that formidable form and the confidence in the hosts’ front line, Chelsea were grateful to Hannah Hampton for her sharp save from Salma Paralluelo on 20 minutes, and similarly glad to see Melchie Dumornay’s powerful effort fizz just wide of a post a few minutes later.Chelsea had the majority of the ball, however. Potter, buoyed by the receipt of her first senior England call-up on Tuesday, gave as good as she got in the physical battle in midfield and generally appeared at home on this stage, at the record eight-time European champions, which will have been pleasing for Sarina Wiegman. The 20-year-old, alongside her compatriot Walsh, helped Chelsea maintain an element of control.Unlike Chelsea, who played a fiery derby against Arsenal in England, the top French sides were able to rest at the weekend, in between the first two European fixtures, as the French league helps its sides stay fresh for the Champions League. Other French top-tier sides played in the League Cup instead. It was therefore reasonable to assume that Lyonnes might look the stronger as this contest went on. That was true to a degree, as Chelsea – missing Katie McCabe through illness – tired slightly late on.Quick GuideWCL roundup: Barcelona win big againShowBarcelonacontinued their emphatic start to their title defence by brushing asideRoma6-0 in the Italian capital. Caroline Graham Hansen got Barça off the mark in Rome inside 20 minutes. A Shukurat Oladipo own goal put them two up before the break and Clàudia Pina (pictured) made the points safe just after, before Graham Hansen and Pina both got their second goals and Ewa Pajor put the cherry on the cake late on.Bayern Munich, who gave up a two-goal lead last week to draw with Manchester City, were in danger of behind held again atBenfica, but won 3-0 thanks to three goals from in the last 16 minutes from Klara Bühl, Pernille Harder and Franziska Kett.JuventusdownedHäcken3-0 in Sweden to make up for  last Tuesday’s defeat by Benfica. The Spanish World Cup winner Alba Redondo scored again, making it three goals in as many games and seven in 12 in all competitions since joining from Real Madrid.AFPPhotograph: Domenico Cippitelli/Shutterstock EditorialWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.It was Chelsea, however, who started the second period the brighter. They thought they deserved a penalty when Tarciane took out Sjoeke Nüsken at the far post, just as the Chelsea midfielder looked certain to score, but after a check on the monitor, the referee concluded that Lucy Bronze had been interfering with play from an offside position as the ball was crossed. Tarciane was booked for her challenge, nonetheless.Bompastor, who won this competition as a player and a manager with Lyonnes, brought on Lauren James to give her side a different forward dynamic with just over half an hour remaining, while Lyonnes introduced a former Ballon d’Or winner in Ada Hegerberg, but neither side looked likely to break the deadlock until much later, as the off-the-ball qualities of both teams appeared to cancel each other out. A cautious approach, from Chelsea in particular, was understandable; this was, by a significant distance, the toughest-looking fixture of their league-phase matches, against last season’s runners-up.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenChelsea’s Lexi Potter impressed on the big stage after her first England call-up.Photograph: Alexandre Dimou/ReutersLyonnes, owned by the London City Lionesses and Washington Spirit owner, Michele Kang, have high ambitions to win this title this term. They thought they had scored on 72 minutes, when Paralluelo struck a low shot into the bottom corner, but the offside flag was raised.Just a few minutes later, a moment of real controversy arose, as Chelsea were awarded a penalty for a foul by Damaris Egurrola on James. After a video review, the decision was overturned with the referee appearing to conclude that James had made contact with Egurrola rather than the other way around. The Lyonnes midfielder, though, looked very fortunate to escape, having mistimed her tackle and also missed the ball completely. Chelsea were exasperated. Bompastor said later that she felt it was a “clear penalty”.James had Chelsea’s best chance late on but her close-range strike was blocked by Mala Grohs in goal, before Hampton saved superbly from Hegerberg at the other end, as the match finally came to life in the very late stages and Maika Hamano dragged a shot wide deep into stoppage time. But Chelsea will be satisfied with this point.Explore more on these topicsWomen's Champions LeagueOL LyonnesChelsea WomenWomen's footballmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Like father, like son: Sinfields take diverging paths on road to Grand Final | Rugby league | The Guardian
description: Kevin’s ultramarathon challenge ends in time for kick-off at Old Trafford as son Jack vies for first title with Wakefield
Author: Aaron Bower
Headline: Kevin’s ultramarathon challenge ends in time for kick-off at Old Trafford as son Jack vies for first title with Wakefield
Content: Kevin Sinfield passes through Wakefield during his ultramarathon challenge on Wednesday.Photograph: Allan McKenzie/SWpix.com/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenKevin Sinfield passes through Wakefield during his ultramarathon challenge on Wednesday.Photograph: Allan McKenzie/SWpix.com/ShutterstockRugby leagueLike father, like son: Sinfields take diverging paths on road to Grand FinalKevin’s ultramarathon challenge ends in time for kick-off at Old Trafford as son Jack vies for first title with WakefieldAaron Bowerin WakefieldWed 30 Sep 2026 13.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 16.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere are few families with more stories to tell when it comes to theSuper LeagueGrand Final than the Sinfields but, even by their lofty standards, this week will take some beating.Leeds has been the epicentre of that story for more than 20 years but this week the focus has moved 10 miles down the road to Wakefield.Wakefield stun Wigan and storm into their first Super League Grand FinalRead moreJack will fulfil a childhood dream by playing at Old Trafford for the first time on Saturday, whenWakefield Trinityattempt to win their maiden Super League title. Unsurprisingly his father, Kevin, will be there – but in circumstances that make this story all the more remarkable.Sinfield Sr is in the midst of his seventh and final fundraising challenge to support those living with motor neurone disease, which will conclude at Old Trafford on Saturday and passed through Wakefield on Wednesday.He will finish the last leg of his seventh ultramarathon in seven days at the Grand Final and will carry the match ball into the stadium for Wakefield’s showdown with Warrington Wolves. Waiting for him on the pitch will be his son, who first attended the event shortly after he was born, when Kevin played in the 2004 final forLeeds Rhinos.Jack has been in the stands for all eight of his father’s Grand Final appearances but, this weekend, the roles will be reversed. “When he planned this last challenge and for it to finish at Old Trafford, I don’t think even he could have imagined that I would be playing in it,” the 22-year-old says with a smile. “So it’s worked out pretty well, right?”Just as Kevin will no doubt be beaming with pride at his son’s upcoming debut in a Grand Final, Jack unsurprisingly possesses similar emotions when asked about his dad’s incredible fundraising efforts, which continued from Wakefield’s stadium on Wednesday morning, with a message of good luck delivered to the Trinity squad.View image in fullscreenKevin’s 22-year-old son, Jack Sinfield (centre) has helped Wakefield reach the Super League final.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PA“It was really nice to see him this morning before he set off,” the half‑back said on Wednesday. “I’ve missed him a lot when he’s been away because I’m still living at home, so it’s really weird around the house without him! I’m hoping I’ll see him on Thursday when he goes past home and he runs up near our neck of the woods. But I’m so proud of him.”Jack holds as his favourite rugby memory the 2015 Grand Final, Kevin’s final match as a player which ended with victory andLeeds winning the treble. “I’ve got that picture on my phone still,” he says when reflecting on a family photo from that game. “It was a pretty special moment – hopefully there’s a chance to have another picture this weekend.”His exposure to the biggest game of the season began much earlier than that, though. “My first ever rugby league game was the 2004 final when I was three weeks old. I have been to every single one of the Grand Finals my dad has played in but the last one really stands out in 2015 for all the right reasons.”But this is where their respective stories begin to diverge. While Kevin won everything there was to win as a Leeds player, Jack’s career has taken a different path. Unable to force his way into the first-team picture at the Rhinos after coming through the academy, he made the decision to look elsewhere last winter.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenJack Sinfield left his father’s former club Leeds Rhinos to join Wakefield last year.Photograph: Alex Whitehead/SWpix.com/ShutterstockHis lifelong affiliation with the Rhinos over, Sinfield Jr made the decision to move across West Yorkshire and sign with Wakefield. Sold by their vision of a club determined to step out of the significant shadows of their past, Jack may have been forgiven for wanting to do the same, with the pressure of being Sir Kevin Sinfield’s son at Headingley ominous.But he has blossomed away from that pressure and has played a key role in taking Wakefield to within one win of a first league title in almost 60 years. Just as his father helped deliver a first league title to Leeds in over 30 years in 2004 and begin an era of success, Jack now has the chance to do the same in his own way.“It’s been a dream of mine to go there one day and emulate him and win one. As soon as I spoke to the club, I knew I wanted to come here. They’re growing, they’re hungry to go and win things and so am I.”And as they both head for their most memorable venue, albeit in very differing ways, on Saturday, will there be too much contact between father and son? “I’ve spoken to him a little bit but obviously he’s just been really tired,” Jack says. “Hopefully we can celebrate together after … I just hope he gets a shower first.”Explore more on these topicsRugby leagueSuper LeagueWakefield TrinityLeeds RhinosfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Quips, slights and a surprise twist: Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury come face to face | Boxing | The Guardian
description: Anthony Joshua revealed he is speaking to Tyson Fury’s uncle Peter ahead of their fight in December as the pair shared some back-and-forth at a press conference in London
Author: Donald McRae
Headline: Anthony Joshua revealed he is speaking to Tyson Fury’s uncle Peter ahead of their fight in December as the pair shared some back-and-forth at a press conference in London
Content: Tyson Fury (left) and Anthony Joshua meet at a press conference in London.Photograph: John Sibley/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenTyson Fury (left) and Anthony Joshua meet at a press conference in London.Photograph: John Sibley/Action Images/ReutersBoxingQuips, slights and a surprise twist: Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury come face to faceJoshua reveals he is speaking to Peter Fury on trainingFury vows to ‘blast him out’ at London press conferenceDonald McRaeWed 30 Sep 2026 15.15 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnthony Joshua has revealed that he is in contact with Tyson Fury’s uncle Peter, in a surprise twist to the buildup between the two former world champion heavyweightswho will finally meet in the ring in Cardiffin December.Peter Fury trained Tyson when he shocked Wladimir Klitschko towin his first world heavyweight title, in 2015. The uncle and nephew fell out soon afterwards, apparently over a financial dispute, and have not spoken in many years.Fury v Joshua fight confirmed for December at Cardiff’s Principality StadiumRead more“I speak to Peter Fury,” Joshua said before the fight’s first press conference on Wednesday evening in London. “He’s willing to help me as well. Yeah, I’ll speak to him [before I fight Tyson Fury].”Asked if he can learn more about Fury from his uncle, Joshua said: “Not about Fury but about our training and how I can approach the fight. This is where I can improve. Everybody’s going to tell me how to win. But the most important person to listen to is myself at this point in my career.”Joshua said he last spoke to Peter Fury about a month ago. “I speak to Matty Harris [the British heavyweight whom Fury Sr trains] quite a lot. Matty Harris comes down for some sparring. That’s how it all comes about. Through Matty and Peter.”Ben Davison will train Joshua for the fight and he, too, has also worked previously with Fury. Davison helped Fury to return to boxing in 2018, after the fighter had been out of the ring with drink and drug problems for three years following his defeat of Klitschko.Fury seemed initially taken aback when he was told that Davison will be in Joshua’s corner. In seemingly genuine surprise, Fury asked: “Is it confirmed? Is he gonna have him?” He paused and then turned to Frank Warren, who has promoted him for years and said, in deadpan style: “That’s deflating, isn’t it, Frank? It is deflating.”Fury soon made clear that his last comment was a joke: “Don’t forget I left Ben Davison to go with SugarHill [Steward] because he wasn’t good enough and this is the same Ben Davison whoAnthony Joshualeft because he wasn’t good enough.”View image in fullscreenPeter Fury (left) trained Tyson Fury when he shocked Wladimir Klitschko in 2015.Photograph: Lee Smith/ReutersAfter Joshua was dropped numerous times andthen stopped by Daniel Duboisin September 2024, he switched from Davison to work with Oleksandr Usyk’s team. Fury, who was in a cheerful mood, said: “When he got knocked out by Dubois it was the same Ben Davison who everyone said: ‘Oh, he’s this, he’s that …’ Now they’re going back to him?“So that gives me encouragement. That gives me happiness. [Joshua] will probably go out there, get told to throw a jab and throw an uppercut and get himself chinned.”Joshua stressed that “it wasn’t so much going to Ben and Peter because they have worked with Fury before”, saying: “The reason why I went with Ben is because he and his team pinpoint things. [Against Dubois] there are things I could have done better so I won’t put all that blame on Ben.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“What I’ve got to do is take control of my fight with Fury, but also add their touch. And with these two powerhouses coming together, I think it will be a match made in heaven. Ben and his team are very good at pinpointing certain things leading up to a fight that I can execute and exploit. I believe that they will get me that one step closer to landing the perfect punch to pin Fury to the ground.”At the press conference Joshua called for a minute’s silence, which was impeccably observed, when he rememberedthe close friends he had lostover the past 10 months. Unexpectedly, Fury then spoke respectfully about Joshua as they shared the stage. But Fury did insist that: “I’m going to blast him out. I’m going to catch him and when I do it’s going to be curtains.”Joshua smiled, saying: “I don’t expect anything else from this man than him saying he’s going to render me unconscious.” He then laughed when Fury quipped: “This man is built like an Adonis, I’m built like a blancmange.”Fury turned to Joshua and said: “I hope after this fight we can have a pint of Guinness together.” Joshua paused and then said: “I don’t know if I can trust you.”But the traditional face-off between the two men passed peacefully and calmly, for both fighters know that none of the intrigue and wisecracks will matter when the first bell rings and they leave their corners to face each other and fight.Explore more on these topicsBoxingAnthony JoshuaTyson FurynewsShareReuse this content

title: Leah Williamson blunder gifts Paris FC a point as Arsenal’s struggles continue | Women's Champions League | The Guardian
description: Arsenal threw away a 2-0 lead to draw 2-2 in their Women’s Champions League game at Paris FC, a mix-up between Leah Williamson and Misa Rodríguez costing them dearly
Author: Suzanne Wrack
Headline: Arsenal threw away a 2-0 lead to draw 2-2 in their Women’s Champions League game at Paris FC, a mix-up between Leah Williamson and Misa Rodríguez costing them dearly
Content: Maeline Mendy (centre) gets a handshake from Kaja Korosec after scoring Paris FC’s equaliser.Photograph: Catherine Steenkeste/ReutersView image in fullscreenMaeline Mendy (centre) gets a handshake from Kaja Korosec after scoring Paris FC’s equaliser.Photograph: Catherine Steenkeste/ReutersWomen's Champions LeagueLeah Williamson blunder gifts Paris FC a point as Arsenal’s struggles continueSuzanne WrackWed 30 Sep 2026 15.31 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 19.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRenée Slegers did not attend the post‑match press conference, the manager understood to have been too furious after Arsenal threw away a two-goal lead in their draw withParis FCon Wednesday night.The assistant coach Aaron D’Antino stepped in to speak to the media instead of Slegers, after a disastrous mix-up between the goalkeeper Misa Rodríguez and the centre-back Leah Williamson gifted Paris FC a penalty that Maeline Mendy converted to deny Arsenal all three points in the Champions League.Hampton’s heroics preserve WCL point for Chelsea on Bompastor’s OL Lyonnes returnRead more“The most frustrating part is how much we are working behind the scenes to try and turn this around, and it is just not going our way at the moment,” D’Antino said.Alessia Russo and Georgia Stanway had given the Gunners a two-goal lead but Clara Mateo pulled one back before Williamson handled the ball after the referee deemed play to have restarted from a goal-kick when Rodríguez passed it to her.D’Antino said: “If we’re looking at what we can control, it’s just passing the ball to Leah. From what I remember seeing, the ball was still rolling and she was moving it to Leah for her to take the goal-kicks as we normally do. So maybe the learning in that is how we get the ball to Leah, so we don’t put ourselves in that situation. But as far as we’re concerned, that’s not a penalty … we haven’t taken a goal-kick, there’s no advantage gained by Leah stopping the ball.”It has been a tough start to the season for Arsenal, who are up against it in the title race with only five points from their opening four games, and the closing stages of the match in Paris delivered another gut punch.Quick GuideWCL roundup: Barcelona win big againShowBarcelonacontinued their emphatic start to their title defence by brushing asideRoma6-0 in the Italian capital. Caroline Graham Hansen got Barça off the mark in Rome inside 20 minutes. A Shukurat Oladipo own goal put them two up before the break and Clàudia Pina (pictured) made the points safe just after, before Graham Hansen and Pina both got their second goals and Ewa Pajor put the cherry on the cake late on.Bayern Munich, who gave up a two-goal lead last week to draw with Manchester City, were in danger of behind held again atBenfica, but won 3-0 thanks to three goals from in the last 16 minutes from Klara Bühl, Pernille Harder and Franziska Kett.JuventusdownedHäcken3-0 in Sweden to make up for  last Tuesday’s defeat by Benfica. The Spanish World Cup winner Alba Redondo scored again, making it three goals in as many games and seven in 12 in all competitions since joining from Real Madrid.AFPPhotograph: Domenico Cippitelli/Shutterstock EditorialWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Paris FC had promised another tricky test, with teams that are happy to concede possession frustrating an Arsenal side that just cannot seem to find their way through low blocks. Chelsea hadread that script on Sunday: they were organised at the back and punished Arsenal’s profligacy and failure to make their early dominance count.At the Stade Jean-Bouin, which sits in the shadow of Paris Saint-Germain’s Parc des Princes, the story was familiar. As a result, it was less a wave of relief that swept through the pocket of travelling Arsenal fans and the players when their first goal went in and more a tsunami. It had looked as if Arsenal’s hesitancy had cost them a possible opening again when Stanway prodded the ball towards Russo but the England forward took several touches to create the space to shoot before firing her low effort in.With the home team forced to come out more, that it took only five minutes after the restart for Arsenal to double their lead was no surprise. It was a stylish finish from Stanway that gave Arsenal breathing space, the midfielder pushed Emily Fox’s cross forward a little with her chest before lashing a volley in from close range.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenGeorgia Stanway is embraced after scoring Arsenal’s second goal before their evening took a turn for the worse.Photograph: Catherine Steenkeste/ReutersHowever, only 22 minutes of comfort followed, before the team that inflicted a shock win on penalties to knock Arsenal out of qualifying in 2023 pulled the goal back that would test the Gunners’ resolve.It was a mix-up between the centre-backs Lotte Wubben-Moy and Williamson that delivered the goal. The pair both moved to close down Evelyne Viens and the Canadian forward slipped the ball wide to Clara Mateo who raced free, rounded Rodríguez and slotted into the empty net.Paris FC 2-2 Arsenal: Women’s Champions League – liveRead moreIt was tense as the clock ticked down. Paris posed a threat throughout, but the leveller followed the most calamitous of mistakes by Arsenal. Rodríguez collected the ball for a goal-kick, rolled it on to the pitch and then passed it to Williamson who bent and stopped the ball with her hand. The referee’s whistle went and she pointed to the spot, with Rodríguez deemed to have taken the goal-kick while Williamson clearly assumed she was being given the ball to take it. VAR did not intervene and Mendy converted from the spot, driving powerfully into the bottom corner.It was a bruising end to another bruising game for Arsenal, who really need some luck to go their way to lift the increasing pressure.
