Meanwhile, Slegers’s decision to avoid talking after the game will have only ramped that pressure up further ahead of a must-win game against league leaders Manchester City on Sunday.Explore more on these topicsWomen's Champions LeagueParis FCArsenal WomenWomen's footballmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Craig Bellamy urges Wales improvement but wary of Norway’s threat | Wales | The Guardian
description: Wales were ‘unrecognisable’ in defeat against Denmark, Craig Bellamy said, while Norway’s Kristoffer Ajer said Erling Haaland had been ‘exactly the same’ after the Manchester City verdict
Author: Ben Fisher
Headline: Wales were ‘unrecognisable’ in defeat against Denmark, Craig Bellamy said, while Norway’s Kristoffer Ajer said Erling Haaland had been ‘exactly the same’ after the Manchester City verdict
Content: Craig Bellamy took the blame for Wales’s 2-0 defeat against Denmark in Copenhagen.Photograph: Ulrik Pedersen/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenCraig Bellamy took the blame for Wales’s 2-0 defeat against Denmark in Copenhagen.Photograph: Ulrik Pedersen/NurPhoto/ShutterstockWalesCraig Bellamy urges Wales improvement but wary of Norway’s threatWales ‘unrecognisable’ in defeat against DenmarkHaaland ‘exactly the same’ after Manchester City verdictBen FisherWed 30 Sep 2026 13.11 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 17.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCraig Bellamy has said Wales must improve against Norway on Thursday after appearing unrecognisable in theirdefeat against Denmark, and highlighted their next opponents’ run to the World Cup quarter-finals as proof of their talent.Wales host Norway in Cardiff hoping to record their first win since last November and their first since promotion toNations LeagueA. “This team has been on a surge,” he said of Ståle Solbakken’s side. “They are progressing and they will keep going as well – they ain’t going away, especially with the youngsters they’ve got coming through. We’ve all been waiting [for them to flourish]. But it was coming and it’s come with a bang.”Denmark dominate Wales in Nations League to leave Bellamy ‘really hurting’Read moreBellamy said Norway having two teams in the Champions League – Bodø/Glimt and Viking – would have been a “miracle a number of years ago”. Addressing the Norwegian media at his pre-match press conference on Wednesday, Bellamy said: “I think you’re all sneakily hoping we don’t talk about you as much butthe World Cupexposes you. But I’m on to yous. I know what you’re up to and I know your younger age groups are getting even stronger.“Sander [Berge], [Martin] Ødegaard and [Erling] Haaland, they are really close friends and their three sons are all the same age, born within a few months of each other. They’re already preparing the next generation, so we’re all in trouble.”Addressing Wales’s 2-0 defeat in Copenhagen on Sunday, Bellamy said: “I didn’t recognise anything about us in the game and that was hard. We didn’t look clear in what we were doing, we were ‘in between’ and that comes from myself. I want us to improve as a team and I want to improve.”Meanwhile, the Brentford defender Kristoffer Ajer insisted Haaland has displayed the same personality as normal amid the noise surrounding Manchester City after the club were found guilty ofbreaching the Premier League’s financial rules across a nine-year period. “Ever since I met him he’s been a guy that brings a lot of energy and joy to the group and that’s the biggest compliment I always give Erling,” Ajer said.“When people ask about him, he hasn’t changed one bit since the first time I met him, even though he’s the biggest star on the planet right now. He’s been exactly the same the last few days as well, which is not a surprise for me.”Solbakken, Norway’s head coach for the past six years, said “everything’s fine” with Haaland, who has scored three goals in his past two matches, and played down the idea that the City verdict has been a distraction. “[He’s been] very good, scoring goals,” Solbakken said.“He missed one chance against Portugal that he usually doesn’t miss and that’s the only thing I can say negative, because he’s on fire.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBellamy said he did not expect Haaland to be bothered by his club’s situation at Cardiff City Stadium. The Wales head coach said: “I don’t think he’ll be distracted, the guy’s a machine. Have you seen his record at international level? He’s brilliant. If you love football, you have to appreciate him … You see certain moments in certain sports. Remember the Jonah Lomu factor [in rugby union]? We’re coming through the Haaland factor at this present moment.”Ødegaard is a doubt for the game on Thursday after a poor challenge by Bernardo Silva in the 2-1 defeat by Portugal on Sunday. “He will probably test himself a bit today,” Solbakken said of the Arsenal and Norway captain before training in the Welsh capital. “If he had no chance [of playing], he wouldn’t be here.”Explore more on these topicsWalesCraig BellamyErling HaalandNorwayManchester CityNations LeaguenewsShareReuse this content

title: Cristiano Ronaldo walks out on Portugal after being dropped from starting lineup | Cristiano Ronaldo | The Guardian
description: With Jorge Jesus, the Portugal coach, saying Cristiano Ronaldo would again be a substitute against Denmark, the 41-year-old has left the team’s training camp
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: With Jorge Jesus, the Portugal coach, saying Cristiano Ronaldo would again be a substitute against Denmark, the 41-year-old has left the team’s training camp
Content: Cristiano Ronaldo was left on the bench against Norway and was set to be a substitute once more against Denmark.Photograph: Johan Nilsson/TT/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenCristiano Ronaldo was left on the bench against Norway and was set to be a substitute once more against Denmark.Photograph: Johan Nilsson/TT/ShutterstockCristiano RonaldoCristiano Ronaldo walks out on Portugal after being dropped from starting lineupJorge Jesus earlier said captain would again be a subThe 41-year-old has trained alone in gym since weekendAgence France-PresseWed 30 Sep 2026 15.55 EDTFirst published on Wed 30 Sep 2026 10.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Portugal captain,Cristiano Ronaldo, announced on Wednesday that he had left the team’s training camp in Denmark after head coach Jorge Jesus told reporters that the iconic striker would not start their next match.Ronaldo had been due to train with his teammates at the Parken Stadium in Copenhagen on Wednesday but left abruptly after Jesus’s press conference. The veteran coach had said that Ronaldo, who spent the entire match on the bench against Norway on Sunday, would not start Thursday’sNations Leagueclash away to Denmark either.Nations League roundup: Lamine Yamal sinks Croatia in Spain’s World Cup homecomingRead more“Following the national team coach’s press conference, and after having a conversation with the Portuguese Football Federation president, I decided to leave the national team’s training camp,” Ronaldo wrote on Instagram. “In due course, I will tell the truth to all the Portuguese people about my reasons for leaving the national team, to which I have always been dedicated.“Now is time to wish good luck toPortugaland to all my teammates, without exception.”Jesus had insisted earlier that there was no rift between him and Ronaldo, although the 72-year-old did acknowledge that his captain had been disappointed to remain on the bench in the side’s Nations League win over Norway.Following the 2-1 victory in Oslo, Ronaldo went straight to the changing rooms without joining his teammates in acknowledging the Portuguese supporters in the stands. “There was no incident whatsoever,” Jesus told reporters.“Any player – and I was a player myself … when you spend 20 or 30 minutes warming up and then don’t get on … no one is happy about that,” Jesus said on Wednesday.The Portuguese coach added that he had told Ronaldo before the match that he would not be in the starting lineup, but that he might bring him on towards the end of the game.“Afterwards, as coach, I decided not to bring him on. It’s nothing to make a fuss about,” Jesus insisted. The former Benfica manager also explained that Ronaldo had not refused to train on Tuesday, as some Portuguese media outlets had suggested, but that he had had to do individual exercises for physical “mobility” and “strengthening”.Jesus had said that the five-time Ballon d’Or winner would train as normal on Wednesday. However, despite arriving at the stadium in the team bus, Ronaldo did not join his teammates on the pitch. Portuguese media shared a video of him leaving Parken alongside two members of the backroom staff just after Jesus’s press conference. Reports also said that Ronaldo’s private jet was heading to Copenhagen. Just before Ronaldo’s social media post, the Portuguese federation had released a brief statement merely confirming that the former Real Madrid, Manchester United and Juventus player had not trained.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJesus had said earlier that for the Denmark match he again intended to start the Milan striker Gonçalo Ramos, who scored the winner against Norway.“If everything goes according to plan, it will be Gonçalo who plays,” he said, before adding regarding Ronaldo: “If I need him, he’ll come on. If I don’t need him, he won’t.”At 41, Ronaldo announced this summer that this season would “probably [be] my last year in football”. He is Portugal’s leading goalscorer and most capped player, with 146 goals in 234 appearances.Explore more on these topicsCristiano RonaldoPortugalNations LeaguenewsShareReuse this content

title: Next Generation 2021: why slow and steady sometimes wins the race | Soccer | The Guardian
description: Our NextGen picks from five years ago show that breaking through early does not guarantee longevity or future success
Author: Marcus Christenson
Headline: Our NextGen picks from five years ago show that breaking through early does not guarantee longevity or future success
Content: (Left to right): Youssoufa Moukoko, Adrian Blake and Jack Hinshelwood.Composite: Guardian Pictures; Gonzales Photo/Alamy; Orange Pictures/Shutterstock; PAView image in fullscreen(Left to right): Youssoufa Moukoko, Adrian Blake and Jack Hinshelwood.Composite: Guardian Pictures; Gonzales Photo/Alamy; Orange Pictures/Shutterstock; PANext generationSoccerNext Generation 2021: why slow and steady sometimes wins the raceOur NextGen picks from five years ago show that breaking through early does not guarantee longevity or future successRead the full updates on our class of 2021hereandhereMarcus ChristensonWed 30 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 13.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 2021, as every year, we picked 80 players from around the world who had a chance of making it in world football –20 from the Premier Leagueand60 from the rest of the world– as part of ourNext Generation series.We then follow these talented boys on their journeys for five years. Often it is almost impossible to predict how they will get on (OK, when Sid Lowe sent overLamine Yamal in 2024we had an inkling he might do well).Five years ago we had an exciting array of young players on the list, most of them 17 years old but some 16, with one youngster from Brighton being profiled like this:double quotation markThe ball-playing central midfielder comes from a footballing family and academy staff believe his tactical awareness is born from growing up around the game. His father, Adam, played for Brighton and is now manager along the coast at Worthing FC, while Martin (his great uncle), Paul (his grandad), and Wally (his great grandad), all enjoyed careers as players.It was quite an understated entry, especially compared with this one in the world section:double quotation markThe youngest to play in the Bundesliga at 16 years and one day, youngest player to appear in the Champions League 17 days later, youngest goal scorer in Bundesliga 11 days after that and youngest player and youngest goal scorer for the Germany Under-21 team before he has turned 17.Borussia Dortmund’s Youssoufa Moukoko went on to play for Germany at the World Cup the following year, at the same time as Jack Hinshelwood was promoted to the Brighton Under-21s. Different trajectories, different pressures. Moukoko was already known around the world and tipped for a long career at the top. There was something completely carefree about his style, young Michael Owen-esque. Take a look at his early (and subsequent) goals in the Bundesligahere.Then life interfered. Moukoko sustained some injuries and struggled to make the Dortmund starting XI. To be fair, he also had some decent competition up front as Erling Haaland had arrived in 2020. Moukoko had a really good spell at the start of the 2022-23 season, after Haaland had joined Manchester City, but sustained an ankle ligament tear and never quite got his starting place back.These days Moukoko is playing in the Turkish top flight with Corum, on loan from Copenhagen, where he moved in 2025. His switch to the newly promoted Turkish top-flight side was low key with the club welcoming Moukoko to the “family” with a short statement. He is yet to start a game but his cameos off the bench have offered flashes of his quality – most notably marking his home debut with a sharp assist in a 3–0 win over Eyüpspor. His market value is €5m (£4m) reckons transfermarkt.com.Meanwhile, Hinshelwood has made 67 Premier League appearances and was included on Thomas Tuchel’s 55-man longlist for the 2026 World Cup. A frustrating ankle injury has hampered him at the start of this campaign but his star is rising and he has a market value of €28m (£24m). Not that Brighton are about to sell him.Neither player chose their path and whether they broke through early. They simply developed at a different pace. Hinshelwood was not ready to play top-flight football at 17; Moukoko was. Did the early exposure have a negative impact on Moukoko? It is impossible to say.Not that it has been straightforward for Hinshelwood either. It never is. His father, Adam,told Sky this yearthat “it is definitely not just a straight line”, saying: “There were lots of bumps and ups and downs along the way.” There was one moment when Hinshelwood, then with the under-15s, was set a challenge to play with an older age-group, and that arguably made him as a footballer. “It was a big catalyst for Jack,” Adam said. “He rolled up his sleeves and became a proper footballer.”Graphic with players’ senior capsOut of our 60 world talents, 24 have gone on to represent their countries. Moukoko stands on two caps, some distance behind players such as Julio Enciso and Gavi. Some have had to swap allegiances to play senior international football, such as Livano Comenencia, who started out with the Netherlands age-group teams but has more than 20 caps for Curaçao and played at this summer’s World Cup.From our Premier League picks in 2021 astonishingly few players are with the same club. Hinshelwood is one, Liverpool’s Kaide Gordon another, but that is it. The other 18 are playing around the globe, including in the US, Qatar and Hong Kong.Graphic showing number of players currently in each leagueThe 20 players have played a total of 145 top-flight games, not a bad tally, but Hinshelwood accounts for almost half of those. Adrian Blake, who was with Watford in 2021, has carved out a very successful career in the Netherlands, having joined Utrecht in 2023. But he too, struggled in the beginning. “It hasn’t been easy and a lots of ups and downs,”he told Football-oranje.com in 2025. “But now I am getting my rewards and showing why I made the right decision by moving here.”Top-flight games played by each playerBlake moved to the Netherlands when he was 17. It was a huge gamble for someone so young but he says he chose the Eredivisie “because it is a great league for young players”, offering opportunities that often do not exist in England. “For me it was a no-brainer,” he said.The 21-year-old has almost his whole career in front of him, as do Moukoko and Hinshelwood – and yet they have experienced so much already. What will the next five years bring?Explore more on these topicsFootballNext generationfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Esther Rantzen, TV presenter and Childline founder, dies aged 86 | Esther Rantzen | The Guardian
description: Rantzen announced lung cancer diagnosis in 2023 and became a vocal assisted-dying campaigner
Author: Alexi Duggins
Headline: Rantzen announced lung cancer diagnosis in 2023 and became a vocal assisted-dying campaigner
Content: Esther Rantzen at home in Wiltshire in 2021.Photograph: Millie Pilkington/The GuardianView image in fullscreenEsther Rantzen at home in Wiltshire in 2021.Photograph: Millie Pilkington/The GuardianEsther RantzenEsther Rantzen, TV presenter and Childline founder, dies aged 86Rantzen announced lung cancer diagnosis in 2023 and became a vocal assisted-dying campaignerFrom Childline to changing TV for ever: Esther Rantzen’s revolutionary lifeEsther Rantzen: from That’s Life! to Childline – in picturesAlexi DugginsandPriya BharadiaWed 30 Sep 2026 14.55 EDTFirst published on Wed 30 Sep 2026 14.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEsther Rantzen, the Bafta-winning TV presenter and founder of Childline, has died aged 86.In a statement, her family paid tribute to “the most wonderful mother” and “cherished grandmother”, whose “legacy of compassion and understanding will live on in her charities Childline and the Silverline, and through those of us who were lucky enough to love and be loved by her”.From Childline to changing TV for ever: Esther Rantzen’s revolutionary lifeRead more“We are grateful she is finally at rest with her beloved husband, Desmond Wilcox, but we will miss her immeasurably. She was our sunshine. We will always remember her endless capacity for joy, her ability to comfort every heartache, her beautiful way with words and her expert guidance in all things,” said her three children.Rantzen announced a diagnosis of stage four lung cancer in 2023, and becamea vocal campaigner to change the law around assisted dying. In September 2026, she announced she had to abandon plans to end her life in Swiss clinic Dignitas,due to being too physically frail.“Unfortunately, when I was strong enough to make the flight and go to Dignitas, my life was not unbearably painful; indeed, I was able to relax in my beloved cottage in the New Forest,” she said in a statement. “And by the time life did become unbearable, I was too physically fragile to make the journey and go through the Dignitas process.”“So even though I had spent the money and made the plans, I was not ready to end my life back then, and did not realise that would be my last chance.”The prime minister, Andy Burnham, said: “Very sad to hear that Dame Esther Rantzen has died. Through her decades of campaigning, including founding Childline and The Silver Line, she changed countless lives and gave a voice to people who often went unheard.“And I will always admire the characteristic courage and openness with which she spoke about her illness, making us all think about the difficult questions we face at the end of life. My thoughts are with her family and all who loved her.”Kim Leadbeater, the Labour MP who introduced a bill to legalise assisted dying, said: “Esther was a strong, warm and compassionate woman and a fighter to the end.“Her positivity and determination never to give in gave me strength, but more importantly helped all those others like her who were confronting a terminal illness to keep going in the knowledge that they were not alone.”Rantzen was born in Berkhamsted, Hertfordshire, in 1940 and began her career in 1963 as a BBC radio studio manager. Having moved into television as a researcher, she became a presenter in 1968, as part of the consumer affairs show Braden’s Week, before being appointed as the main host of its replacement programme, That’s Life!, in 1973.View image in fullscreenRantzen with the cast of That’s Life in 1987.Photograph: BBCPart magazine, part consumer show, with hard-hitting investigations and jokes, That’s Life! drew more than 20 million viewers at its peak – and ran for 21 years with Rantzen as anchor. After she successfully pitched an episode about child abuse to the then BBC controller Michael Grade, a set of phone lines was opened for 48 hours, which enabled children to call in and speak to social workers. The volume of responses led her to turn the service into a permanent fixture, launching the children’s charity Childline in 1986.Esther Rantzen: from That’s Life! to Childline – in picturesRead moreIn 1988, Rantzen created Hearts of Gold, a series focusing on people responsible for outstanding acts of kindness, and hosted her own BBC Two chatshow, Esther, from 1994, when That’s Life! came to an end, until 2002. Further TV projects included the consumer affairs show Old Dogs New Tricks, as well as competing in Strictly Come Dancing’s second series and the 2008 edition of the ITV reality show I’m a Celebrity … Get Me Out of Here! She received an OBE for services to broadcasting, Bafta’s Richard Dimbleby award for factual programming anda lifetime achievement prize at the Women in Film and Television awards.View image in fullscreenEsther Rantzen on the campaign trail in 2010 as a candidate for Luton South.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianHer wide-ranging charity work saw her act as a patron or vice-president of numerous organisations. In 2010, she launched the Silver Line – a free confidential helpline for older people, which led to her being made a dame for services to children and older people.In 2010, she stood as an independent candidate for Luton South in that year’s general election,coming fourth after winning 4.4% of the vote. She wrote numerous books, including a murder-mystery novel. In later years, she was a regular contributor to the One Show andhosted a podcast with her former That’s Life! colleague Adrian Mills.On Instagram, the television presenter Anna Williamson described Rantzen as “somebody truly iconic, who really cared, and who has left behind one hell of a legacy”.Fellow presenter Lorraine Kelly also paid tribute to Rantzen on social media for being a “pioneer and a force of nature – [who] helped so many people – funny, forthright and fabulous”.One of Rantzen’s former co-hosts of That’s Life!, Howard Leader, said: “Over the time that I was with her, through her fantastic generosity, she taught me how to be a journalist.“I think Esther’s skill was that she really understood how to use the platform she had to create an effect for, we hope ... the improvement of people in our country.”Her husband, Desmond Wilcox, whom she married in 1977, died in 2000. Rantzen is survived by their three children, Miriam, Rebecca and Joshua – as well as five grandchildren.Explore more on these topicsEsther RantzenTelevisionAssisted dyingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Israeli forces overwhelmed by violent settlers in ‘terrorist attack’ on Palestinian family | West Bank | The Guardian
description: Settler violence in West Bank makes everyday life ‘untenable’ for Palestinians, says ICRC after assault on family trying to return home in Jalud
Author: Emma Graham-Harrison
Headline: Settler violence in West Bank makes everyday life ‘untenable’ for Palestinians, says ICRC after assault on family trying to return home in Jalud
Content: Israeli settlers attacked the West Bank village of Jalud, south of Nablus, early on Tuesday.Photograph: Atef Safadi/EPAView image in fullscreenIsraeli settlers attacked the West Bank village of Jalud, south of Nablus, early on Tuesday.Photograph: Atef Safadi/EPAWest BankIsraeli forces overwhelmed by violent settlers in ‘terrorist attack’ on Palestinian familySettler violence in West Bank makes everyday life ‘untenable’ for Palestinians, says ICRC after assault on family trying to return home in JaludEmma Graham-Harrisonin JerusalemWed 30 Sep 2026 15.01 EDTFirst published on Wed 30 Sep 2026 10.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) has said Israeli settler violence in the West Bank has made everyday life for Palestinians “untenable”, as a mob attack on Palestinians trying to return home prompted one of Benjamin Netanyahu’s main rivals to warn of a campaign of settler terror.More than 100 militant settlers overwhelmed Israeli security forces early on Tuesday to attack a Palestinian family as they attempted to reclaim their homes which had been seized by settlers in theWest Bankvillage of Jalud. Three Israeli security officials were injured and houses were set on fire.The impotence of the Israeli military, the scale of the assault and the injuries inflicted on Israeli security officers by settlers prompted unusually harsh condemnation from Israeli politicians and commenters.Israel is facing unprecedented international pressure over surging violence in the occupied West Bank, where settler militants backed by cabinet ministers have accelerated acampaign of ethnic cleansingahead of Israel’s elections next month.Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, condemned the attacks in Jalud as a “moral stain”. Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief andNetanyahu’s leading challengerin the upcoming elections, called for action to halt a “campaign of terror and violence”.Deadlier attacks by Israeli settlers, including ones targeting Palestinian children, have drawn less attention inside Israel.“Palestinian rights or safety are not the concern, even for people who are in the opposition,” said Mairav Zonszein, a senior analyst on Israel-Palestine with International Crisis Group. “The settler violence is an issue [for them] because it’s making Israel look bad, and also the idea that the military is losing control.”View image in fullscreenA Palestinian family were attacked as they attempted to reclaim their homes which had been seized by settlers in Jalud.Photograph: Atef Safadi/EPAThe ICRC said attacks, settlement expansion and severe restrictions on movement were making everyday life untenable for Palestinian civilians, who Israel has a responsibility to protect under international law. .“The frequent and severe violence must be brought to an end,” said Julien Lerisson, the head of the ICRC’s delegation for Israel and Palestine. “What international humanitarian law says on the protection of private and public property, and on the population’s access to essential services, must be respected.”A graphic showing number of Palestinians killed in the West Bank by settlers or Israeli civiliansA bar on imports of settlement goods came into force in the Netherlands last week, the UK has announced plans foreven broader controlson trade and financing of settlements, and a similar bill will be introduced in the US legislature on Thursday.‘The settlers brought the violence’: the ethnic cleansing of a West Bank villageRead moreOn Tuesday, a Senate bill demanding a human rights report on Israel’s occupation of the West Bank wasnarrowly defeatedafter winning backing from all but one Democrat.“Tonight a disaster was averted, but the barrier has been broken,” the Israeli analyst Roy Sharon wrote on social media after the vote, warning that “anarchy in the West Bank” may cost Israel military aid from the US and its international legitimacy.A cartoon in Israel’s largest-circulation newspaper, Yedioth Ahronoth, on Wednesday showed two soldiers watching an arson attack on a Palestinian home. “They’re going to ruin my trip to Amsterdam,” one says to the other.More than 60 Palestinian communities in the occupied West Bank have been wiped off the map since October 2023 and 18 others have been partly displaced, according to the Israeli rights group B’Tselem. Nearly 5,000 people have been forced from their homes, almost half of them children.View image in fullscreenMahmod Tubasi, 60, and his wife, Aedah, 51, and their family had been forced out of their homes this summer by settler militants.Photograph: Ammar Awad/ReutersThe Tubasi family, whose homes were burned in Jalud, had been forced out this summer after a weeks-long siege by settler militants. Last week they secured a high court ruling ordering the Israeli state to evict settlers and secure their return.Late on Monday the Israeli military told the family that about 15 military police officers would escort them home immediately, Israel’s Haaretz newspaper reported. That was a small number given that Israel is celebrating the Sukkot holiday. The number of violent extremists in illegal settlements usually rises during festivals, and the force was outnumbered by a violent crowd within minutes of arriving.“To carry out an operation such as this, and during the holiday of Sukkot when the [settler] outposts are packed, is madness,” a security source said. The military had not informed national police and the Shin Bet domestic intelligence service of their plans, so they had no security backup.Settlers attacked a house when the Tubasi family arrived, forcing them to the roof, before the military decided to evacuate them in armoured military vehicles. The crowd then set the homes on fire, blocked roads and threw stones at Israeli security forces, injuring three personnel.The two houses “were damaged beyond description”, said Wael ​Tubasi. “They damaged everything – the doors, the tiles were removed, the stairs were removed. They smashed the bathrooms, doors and windows. They left nothing, everything was broken,” he told Reuters.View image in fullscreenThe Tubasi family’s homes were ‘damaged beyond description’, said Wael Tubasi. ‘Everything was broken.’Photograph: Ammar Awad/ReutersEarlier this year the former prime minister Ehud Olmertcalled forthe international criminal court to intervene to stop settler violence because the state had failed.Netanyahu condemned the “violent riots” and called for prosecution of the attackers, but defended the illegal settler movement. “The handful of rioters are not representative of the law-abiding settler public in Judea and Samaria,” the prime minister said, using an Israeli term for the occupied West Bank.A landmark 2024 ruling from the UN’s international court of justice found that the occupation violated international law, a position the British government has endorsed.An Israeli military spokesperson said two suspects had been detained, and called for action to tackle settler militants who targeted Israeli security forces.“The violence directed at soldiers while they were carrying out their duties crosses a clear red line and is unacceptable,” the spokesperson said. “There is no place for such incidents in the state of Israel, and they must not be allowed to become the norm. Such phenomena must be addressed at their root.”On Wednesday, some in Israel questioned whether the army and the state had the capacity to do that. “We have to look reality squarely in the eye: this was a terrorist attack and a failure by the Israeli defence establishment in its entirety,” Avi Ashkenazi wrote in the Maariv newspaper. “It is clear at this point that the real sovereign in Judea and Samaria are the extreme rightwing terrorist activists.”Explore more on these topicsWest BankPalestineIsraelInternational Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC)Middle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Catholic clergy sexually abused nearly 1,000 Massachusetts children over decades, report finds | Massachusetts | The Guardian
description: No new indictments from eight-year investigation as state attorney general says church knew about abuse
Author: Alba Asenjo Domínguez
Headline: No new indictments from eight-year investigation as state attorney general says church knew about abuse
Content: Andrea Joy Campbell, the Massachusetts attorney general.Photograph: Leah Millis/ReutersView image in fullscreenAndrea Joy Campbell, the Massachusetts attorney general.Photograph: Leah Millis/ReutersMassachusettsCatholic clergy sexually abused nearly 1,000 Massachusetts children over decades, report findsNo new indictments from eight-year investigation as state attorney general says church knew about abuseAlba Asenjo DomínguezWed 30 Sep 2026 15.53 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 16.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore than 270 Catholic clerics sexually abused nearly 1,000 children across threeMassachusettsdioceses over several decades, according to a report released by the state’s attorney general’s office on Wednesday.The eight-year-long investigation did not result in new indictments, the office said, claiming that some conduct identified was not a crime under Massachusetts law at the time it occurred, and that in other cases the applicable statute of limitations had expired.However, three cases were referred to different district attorney’s offices and one of those resulted in criminal charges. The majority of the abuse occurred before 2002.“The evidence gathered during this investigation also shows that, for decades, and especially before 2002, church officials in all three dioceses knew about the sexual abuse of children yet did not take effective action to prevent it or to examine the institutional failures of leadership that led to scores of children being victimized at the hands of abusive priests,” the report stated.The attorney general’s office said the report was “the first comparable public accounting of the institutional failures within the Fall River, Springfield and Worcester dioceses”.The abuses in thearchdiocese of Bostondrew international attention after the Boston Globe published its Pulitzer-winning coverage in 2002, and prompted other investigations around the world that found similar cases of sexual abuse.“I strongly urge the dioceses and the broader church to take these recommendations seriously and implement greater, meaningful changes to strengthen child protection and improve responses to allegations of abuse,” the Massachusetts attorney general, Andrea Joy Campbell, said at a press conference.“Behind every one of those numbers is a child whose safety was violated, a family that was changed forever and a survivor who carried that abuse for years, and in many cases decades. They continue to carry this trauma even today,” Campbell said.“I know many survivors have been waiting a long time to see these findings made public. I understand the frustration that comes with that wait. It is my hope that today is a meaningful step forward toward truth, accountability and healing that survivors deserve,” she added.Only one of the three dioceses responded to the report in a statement. “We will study the attorney general’s report to identify any additional improvements that can be made to respond to victims of past abuse and to continue to strengthen efforts to keep children safe,” said the diocese of Worcester in astatement.The diocese of Worcester did not apologise on Wednesday for its clerics’ behavior, but pointed to an apology by Bishop Robert J McManus, who wrote in 2022 that he was “profoundly sorry for the abuse of minors by priests” within his diocese.“I continue in my commitment with the help of many collaborators to do everything we can to ensure such abuse does not happen again,” he said at the time. The diocese of Worcester also highlighted that no charges were filed.Many of the individuals identified in the report are also deceased, the report said. “Any legal limitations do not diminish the seriousness of what this investigation found. The office believes that while criminal law cannot provide justice for all survivors today, the office still has a responsibility to tell the truth of what happened.”In the US, call or text theChildhelpabuse hotline on 800-422-4453 or visittheir websitefor more resources and to report child abuse or DM for help. For adult survivors of child abuse, help is available atascasupport.org. In the UK, theNSPCCoffers support to children on 0800 1111, and adults concerned about a child on 0808 800 5000. The National Association for People Abused in Childhood (Napac) offers support for adult survivors on 0808 801 0331. In Australia, children, young adults, parents and teachers can contact the Kids Helpline on 1800 55 1800, orBraveheartson 1800 272 831, and adult survivors can contactBlue Knot Foundationon 1300 657 380. Other sources of help can be found atChild Helplines InternationalExplore more on these topicsMassachusettsCatholicismReligionChristianitynewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘We want justice’: series of rapes trigger mass protests at Indian universities | Delhi | The Guardian
description: Women say nothing has changed since Delhi’s infamous Nirbhaya bus rape case 14 years ago
Author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen
Headline: Women say nothing has changed since Delhi’s infamous Nirbhaya bus rape case 14 years ago
Content: Student activists protest against alleged gang rapes.Photograph: Rajat Gupta/EPAView image in fullscreenStudent activists protest against alleged gang rapes.Photograph: Rajat Gupta/EPADelhi‘We want justice’: series of rapes trigger mass protests at Indian universitiesWomen say nothing has changed since Delhi’s infamous Nirbhaya bus rape case 14 years agoHannah Ellis-PetersenandAakash Hassanin DelhiWed 30 Sep 2026 11.56 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 16.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe posters, just like the women holding them, were taking no prisoners. “Girls don’t need curfews, rapists need consequences,” read one. “Lock your dicks rather than your women at home,” read another.As hundreds of women walked from the gates of their university campus into the streets ofDelhi– where sexual harassment, assault, catcalling and molestation are a constant, daily threat – they shouted together in a chorus of rage and defiance: “We want justice.”The fury that has erupted on India’s university campuses over the past week has been double-edged. The trigger was a series ofbrutal rapesthat have taken place in Delhi in recent weeks, including the alleged gang-rape of a 17-year-old in a public park close to Delhi University by three men who posed as police officers.From Jamui to Delhi, the burden of safety from sexual assault cannot fall on womenRead moreJust a week earlier, another 17-year-old was gang-raped and murdered in Delhi’s Swaroop Nagar neighbourhood after she went to meet friends. The accused allegedly raped her, stabbed her to death and dumped her body in a field, where it was discovered days later half eaten by dogs.Rapes of an 11-year-old and a six-year-old were reported in the same month. Last month, a 16-year-old was allegedly raped by a bus driver and conductor after she boarded a sleeper bus in Delhi.Women who have taken part in protests on Delhi university campuses have condemned these alleged violent rapes on minors as disgusting and unforgivable – but they have also been at pains to emphasise that they are not out of the ordinary.Fourteen years have passed since Delhi’s infamous Nirbhaya rape case, when a woman was gang-raped on a bus and died from her injuries. But while it provoked international outrage and a slew of legislation and government promises, women say nothing has changed; for them, India’s streets, particularly in Delhi, remain as unsafe as ever. According to statistics, a women is raped inIndiaevery 20 minutes – though the real scale is believed to be far worse due to chronic under-reporting.This week, the supreme court said the five successive rape cases “starkly underlined a systematic failure” and it could not help but “draw painful parallels to the Nirbhaya incident of 2012”.Vaishnavi Dhruw, 21, a history student at Delhi University, was among the female protesters at the “smash the patriarchy” protest march on Wednesday afternoon. “I don’t know a single woman who lives in this city and feels safe,” she said.View image in fullscreenStudents’ Federation of India (SFI) members protest over the alleged rape of a 17-year-old girl.Photograph: Rajat Gupta/EPAWhile some of the key demands of the protest have been better lighting and policing, Dhruw emphasised that for anything to change, the country required a deep societal shift where men no longer felt they had ownership over women’s bodies.“We are not marching for safety, we are here to protest for our freedom, for the most basic right to walk in our own streets,” she said. “Again and again, women are told to stay indoors, to not go out at night, to cover ourselves, to protect ourselves. When will society tell men in our country not to rape?”Much of the anger driving the protests has also been prompted by the response by the authorities to the rapes, which women say once again has only been to police their freedoms. Women in Delhi were told to stay out of parks at night, and classes were temporarily halted at one of Delhi’s most prestigious female colleges. Many hostels where female students stay impose strict curfews preventing them from going out at night.“Instead of going after criminals, you’re going to tell women to sit at home,” said Aranya Rathore, 25, a student at Delhi University. “A demand for more surveillance is not a solution. In fact, it’s going to curtail our freedom more.”Female students say a lot of their time is taken up by safety logistics – from wearing modest clothes to reorganising their days to ensure they do not travel alone or at night and always having a trackable live location on their phones. There is widespread awareness that should anything happen, the onus of blame – both within the family home and more widely in society – tends to fall on women. As one poster at Wednesday’s march pointed out, “no one ever asks what the rapist was wearing”.Yet despite their best efforts, many women said it was almost impossible to avoid harassment. Ananya Wig, a 26-year-old graduate of Delhi University and the founder of Her Huq, a gender equality initiative, said she had experienced harassment both around university campuses and in public spaces.She recounted an incident where a driver rolled down his car window and began masturbating as she and female friends got off a rickshaw and walked through the college gates. “This wasn’t at night, it was in the middle of the day,” she said. “I’ve always lived in Delhi and the city has not changed.”‘If you saw her body, you will never sleep again’: despair as India rape crisis growsRead moreThe protests have brought into focus a dilemma faced by many Indian women, who are being educated in greater numbers than any time in the country’s history and have better job opportunities than ever before, but still have to navigate the constant debilitating threats to their safety and the conservative pressures from their families.“I know so many girls, not just 10 years ago but even today, who end up choosing educational institutions and jobs and other employment opportunities depending on how close they are from their home,” said Wig. “Not on the basis of their marks, not on the basis of their aspirations, but simply, ‘OK, the shorter the distance is, the more likely it is that I will be safe’.”Many of the Delhi University students who took part in the marches said that sexual harassment had become prevalent on campus, and have demanded better accountability mechanisms for reporting assault. The university has not responded.Devyani Sarkar, 24, who is studying for a master’s in English, said: “Delhi University is one of the most prestigious universities in India right now but there are various cases of women being assaulted by professors, sometimes unfortunately also for grades. It’s despicable, but it’s also a living truth.”Many on the marches said it was no coincidence that they were taking place in the aftermath ofIndia’s “cockroach” movement, in which hundreds of thousands of young Gen Z Indians took to the streets over education reform.“My generation is not afraid to stand up and protest. We know that society has to change,” said 17-year-old Subhani. “The days of women being silent is over.”Explore more on these topicsDelhiIndiaRape and sexual assaultViolence against women and girlsProtestSouth and central AsianewsShareReuse this content

title: Wildlife arrives on time at rewilded chalk grasslands built along HS2 route | HS2 | The Guardian
description: The trains may be running late, but the Western Slopes project is already attracting birds and insects on lands around the high-speed railway
Author: Patrick Barkham
Headline: The trains may be running late, but the Western Slopes project is already attracting birds and insects on lands around the high-speed railway
Content: A chalk grassland meadow created by HS2.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA chalk grassland meadow created by HS2.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianHS2Wildlife arrives on time at rewilded chalk grasslands built along HS2 routeThe trains may be running late, but the Western Slopes project is already attracting birds and insects on lands around the high-speed railwayPatrick BarkhamWed 30 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 12.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe air is scented with the sweet tang of ladies bedstraw and made musical by skylark and blackcap song. An abundance of marbled white butterflies, small skippers and common blue damselflies dart over the flowering knapweed, yarrow and wild carrot.That the largest chalk grassland in the Chilterns is full of wildlife may not surprise you. But the fact that it is completely artificial, only four years old and has been built by the much-malignedHS2, may do.TheWestern Slopes“rewilding” project is due to open to the public next year on land beside the high-speed railway as it dives under the M25 and into a10-mile tunnel beneath the Chilterns. The trains may berunning late, but the wildlife has already arrived.View image in fullscreenA marbled white butterfly.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianA decade ago, this area was a vast wheatfield with precious little biodiversity. Today, as the construction effort winds down, more and more of the 127-hectare site is being turned into wildlife-rich grasslands, wet meadows, ponds and small woods.It is now one of the largest wildlife habitat creation projects in south-east England, and has already witnessed the arrival ofhedgehog clover, which hasn’t been recorded in Hertfordshire since 1878, alongside water voles, lesser emperor dragonflies and pyramidal orchids.The transformation began when Matt Hobbs, lead ecologist at Jacobs, was invited to take a look at the huge planned HS2 works around the south entrance to the Chilterns tunnel.“I asked the engineer: ‘What’s coming out of the tunnel?’ When he said ‘chalk’, it was like a lightbulb moment. I thought, I know what I’d like to do with that chalk,” said Hobbs, who hasdesigned and overseen the Western Slopes projectfor HS2.Chalk grassland is one of the most wildlife-rich habitats in southernEnglandbecause a wide range of wildflowers flourish on its thin, nutrient-poor alkaline soils, alongside an array of associated invertebrates, including rare moths and bees.View image in fullscreenMatt Hobbs.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianAccording to Hobbs, the valley slopes could have been expensively restored to arable land by HS2, as much of the land temporarily taken for the huge construction effort will be. “We saw the opportunity to do something different,” he said. “This project is unique. The whole landscape was predicated on what’s the best thing to do with the earthworks and soils. We’re not moving any soils or material off site. Any concrete waste from this site is crushed and used as aggregate under the grasslands.”Reusing 10m cubic metres of chalk, topsoil and subsoils from the construction effort in the immediate vicinity of the tunnel mouth has also drastically reduced CO2emissions, and the construction traffic that dumping it elsewhere would have entailed.According to HS2’s calculations, the wildlife grasslands here could sequester 7% of the carbon impact of the whole high-speed line’s construction, because grassland is much better at storing carbon than regularly-ploughed arable land, which releases carbon every time it is ploughed.Over the past four years, all the chalk excavated from the tunnel has been sculpted into rolling “downs” on the land above the Colne Valley, creating varying topsoils and a future mosaic of grassland, scrub, woodland and ponds and wet areas.View image in fullscreenTwo HS2 workers. Chalk grassland is one of the most wildlife-rich habitats in southern England.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianIt took the ecologists a bit of effort to retrain the digger drivers who were spreading the chalk over the site. Groundworks teams are trained to leave everything beautifully smooth and neat, whereas the ecologists were seeking topographical variation, with dips, hollows and “untidy” rough areas.The future vision is a “wood pasture” landscape, inspired by rewilding sites such as Knepp in West Sussex, where a mixture of scrub and wildflower glades are grazed by herbivores.Four cattle-grids have been installed on roads – believed to be the first in Hertfordshire – to enable free-roaming cattle to graze within four separate compartments.“They were really key to the project. We wanted to have that Knepp rewilding technique where you have cattle that can move anywhere they want within the site – it’s brilliant for soil health, soil carbon and dung beetles,” said Hobbs.View image in fullscreenA damselfly.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianLuke Craner, a senior landscape clerk of works for the HS2 contractor Align, said: “I’m really keen to get livestock grazing sooner rather than later so we can kickstart biological processes. We’ve already got a really good grassy sward establishing. We want natural regeneration to occur, because it’s always much more beneficial for wildlife. We’ve already got loads of hawthorn and quite a few oaks coming up. It’s already going out nicely.”HS2 to ‘rewild’ 127 hectares around its 10-mile Chilterns tunnelRead moreLater this summer, green hay from other calcareous grassland in the local area will be spread on the Western Slopes to bring in more invertebrates. As ant populations develop, rare butterflies including the Adonis, chalkhill and small blue are likely to arrive, with these species interacting with ant colonies. There is also a mammal shelf built into a culvert beneath the railway, enabling badgers, stoats and other mammals to safely cross the high-speed line.Some footpaths through the site are set to be opened up in the next 18 months, although the western portion of the site is likely to remain protected from public access to boost the ground-nesting birds – from skylarks to little ringed plover – that have quickly colonised the land.While HS2 is still under construction, the forthcoming track-building and electrics phase will require a much smaller construction footprint, enabling the nature areas to be expanded.At the bottom of the slopes, beside the River Colne, nearly five hectares of new wetlands have been established. These pretty ponds have been rapidly colonised by club-rush, water mint and sneezewort, as well as breeding reed warbler and lesser emperor dragonfly.View image in fullscreenLuke Craner.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The Guardian“We’ve definitely extended the population of kingfishers,” said Craner, who has also recorded new sightings of water vole on a tributary of the Colne. “Water voles are a massively declining species because of habitat loss – we’ve put in habitat that’s good for water voles. They’ve colonised it immediately.”What Craner has noticed is the changing soundscape. While the roar of the M25 and the clank of ongoing construction is never far away, in certain glades the human din is now overwhelmed by birdsong and insect hum.“We didn’t have this harmony last year and all of a sudden it’s never silent,” said Craner. “This is our hidden gem.”This article was amended on 30 September 2026. An earlier version said that the image of the damselfly was a dragonfly.Explore more on these topicsHS2Rail transportTransportRewildingEnglandfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Half a million trees to be planted in England in three years, says government | Trees and forests | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Environment secretary Angela Eagle to make pledge as part of efforts to protect against extreme weather
Author: Fiona Harvey
Headline: Exclusive: Environment secretary Angela Eagle to make pledge as part of efforts to protect against extreme weather
Content: Newly planted tree saplings in protective tubes in a field in north London. Under the plans, local groups will be given new funding for restoring natural landscapes.Photograph: Jack Jango/AlamyView image in fullscreenNewly planted tree saplings in protective tubes in a field in north London. Under the plans, local groups will be given new funding for restoring natural landscapes.Photograph: Jack Jango/AlamyTrees and forestsHalf a million trees to be planted in England in three years, says governmentExclusive: Environment secretary Angela Eagle to make pledge as part of efforts to protect against extreme weatherFiona HarveyEnvironment editorWed 30 Sep 2026 02.08 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 14.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHalf a million trees will be planted across England in the next three years to protect against extreme weather, the environment secretary,Angela Eagle, will pledge on Wednesday morning.Mayors, local authorities, charities and grassroots groups will be given new funding and responsibilities for restoring natural landscapes such as wetlands, river edges and meadows, which canprovide natural flood managementand reduce the damage done by droughts.The £79m package, to be set out in Eagle’s speech to the Labour party conference in Liverpool, will include £53m for tree-planting and £26m for “local nature recovery strategies”.This summer’s droughtshowed the urgent need for more trees, and more protection of natural landscapes, Eagle is to say. “In areas where nature has been allowed to flourish, the ground held more water, and the droughts were less severe,” she will tell the conference. “On streets where trees have been planted, the shade meant temperatures were lower. And when rain finally came, those same trees reduced the risk of floods. We all deserve access to the benefits that nature can bring.”Trees can reduce air temperatures by 4C in cities,making heatwaves more bearable, while a single mature tree can intercept 15,000 litres of water a year, reducing flood and water run-off risks during storms. They can also halve noise pollution and absorb air pollution, and provide habitats for wildlife in towns and cities.Echoing the localism agenda championed by Andy Burnham, Eagle will tell the Labour party conference the UK must combine a focus on local communities with the need to make the whole countrymore resilient to the increasingly intense impacts of the global climate crisis.She will say that putting decision-making in the hands of those who know their communities best is the most effective way to improve nature and strengthen the UK against a changing climate.Craig Bennett, the chief executive of The Wildlife Trusts, said the plans were “very encouraging”, and appeared to signal that Burnham would change the government’s direction on nature.“The mood could not be more different from Keir Starmer and Rachel Reeves, whopresented nature as a block to development,” he said. “This will be very welcome. For a long time local authorities have been trying to help nature but did not have the power, money or political support. The Burnham government seems to have realised that nature is crucial to the country’s future.”Rewilded land remains green amid drought-stricken English countryside, images showRead moreEngland has lost more than 90% of its wetlands over the last century. “We need to make Britain wet again,” said Bennett. “We could have tens of thousands of new wetlands.”Richard Benwell, the chief executive of the Wildlife and Countryside Link charity, said: “Investing in the critical nature infrastructure we need to protect businesses and communities makes good economic sense and good ecological sense, especially when investments are guided by locally agreed nature restoration plans. This is a good start towards Burnham’s promise of the government getting ahead of long-term challenges, recognising nature’s role in supporting our economy and adapting to climate change.“This should be followed by a commitment to rapidly scale up nature investment as part of the prime minister’s 10-year plan, funded by businesses who will benefit, and by making sure polluters pay.”The government has faced sharp criticism in recent days over the management of payments to farmers, intended to help them protect nature on their land. Last Tuesday, the Sustainable Farming Incentive was opened at 10am forapplications from farmers willing to undertake environmental improvementssuch as conserving wildlife habitats, growing trees and nurturing soil.But within six hours, the £253m pot wasexhausted and many farmers were left disappointed.Bennett said farmers needed support to play their role in nature protection and fostering resilience to the climate crisis. “We need to stop thinking about this as just a farming budget, but as a national security and natural resilience budget,” he said.Explore more on these topicsTrees and forestsAngela EagleClimate crisisnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK banks are Europe’s biggest coal financiers, report finds | Coal | The Guardian
description: Study says UK-based banks provided $8.3bn in coal financing in four years, with Barclays and HSBC leading rise
Author: Matthew Taylor
Headline: Study says UK-based banks provided $8.3bn in coal financing in four years, with Barclays and HSBC leading rise
Content: Urgewald tracked loans and underwriting from 744 commercial banks around the world to companies operating across the ‘coal value chain’.Photograph: Dan Himbrechts/AAPView image in fullscreenUrgewald tracked loans and underwriting from 744 commercial banks around the world to companies operating across the ‘coal value chain’.Photograph: Dan Himbrechts/AAPCoalUK banks are Europe’s biggest coal financiers, report findsStudy says UK-based banks provided $8.3bn in coal financing in four years, with Barclays and HSBC leading riseMatthew TaylorWed 30 Sep 2026 07.58 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 08.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUK banks are Europe’s biggest financial backers of the global coal industry, providing billions of pounds in funding for the climate-wrecking fossil fuel in the past four years, according to a report.The studyfound UK-based banks had provided $8.3bn (£6.2bn) in coal financing sinceCop26 in Glasgow in 2021, when global leaders pledged to “phase down” coal use. This compared with $4.9bn from German banks and $3.4bn from French banks over the same period.The sums provided by UK banks were largely driven byBarclaysand HSBC, which both increased their coal financing between 2022 and 2025 despite high-profile climate and net zero commitments, according to the research.It found Barclays’ coal financing increased by 34%, from approximately $1.2bn in 2022 to $1.6bn in 2025, while HSBC’s more than doubled from $200m to $414m.The research was carried out by Urgewald, a Germany-based environmental and human rights organisation. It tracked loans and underwriting from 744 commercial banks around the world to companies operating across the “coal value chain” – those organisations involved in every aspect of the industry, from mines and power generation to logistics, exploration and trading organisations.Heffa Schücking, the director of Urgewald, said: “Barclays and HSBC should explain why their financing is moving in the opposite direction to the rest of Europe.”A spokesperson for HSBC said the bank had committed to phasing out financing “for thermal coal-fired power and thermal coal mining” by 2030 in EU and OECD markets and by 2040 in other markets.They added: “These commitments support our ambition to align the financed emissions in our portfolio with net zero by 2050. As reported in our 2025 annual report and accounts, financed emissions from thermal coal mining fell by 94% between 2020 and 2024, while reported thermal coal financing exposures, calculated on the basis set out in our disclosures, fell from approximately $1bn to approximately $0.5bn over the same period.”A spokesperson for Barclays said many of the companies named in the report were “diversified energy or mining companies”. They said Barclays did not provide financing to companies that generated “more than 30% of revenues from thermal coal mining or power generation”.“Barclays is financing an energy sector in transition, providing finance to meet current energy needs and also financing the scaling of clean energy,” the spokesperson said. “Over the past three years we have facilitated more than $300bn of sustainable and transition finance, including billions to cleaner energy projects, and invested millions into climate tech.”Urgewald defended its definition of companies in the “coal value chain”, saying it was widely accepted by many financial institutions.Its report found that although some UK banks had reduced their coal financing, the overall financial flows from Britain-based banks to the “coal value chain” grew by 17% over the period. This compares with a 46% reduction overall from EU banks.Globally, Urgewald found that between 2022 and 2025 bank financing for coal remained broadly flat, averaging about $117bn a year, despite the commitment made at Cop26 in Glasgow.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHowever, researchers said the headline figure concealed a growing divide within the banking industry, with Chinese and US banks increasing their funding.The study found Chinese banks accounted for 62% of global coal financing, providing $289bn, an 8% rise over the four-year period. US banks provided $67bn, a rise of 23%, while Indonesian banks increased their coal financing by 64%, from $1.4bn in 2022 to $2.3bn.By contrast, banks in the EU, Taiwan, Malaysia and Thailand significantly reduced their coal financing.Schücking, welcomed the decrease, saying it showed that a clear coal policy could “disrupt the flow of money to the industry”.But she cautioned that this progress was “being swallowed up” by rising coal finance elsewhere. “Banks still funding coal cannot hide behind distant climate promises. They need policies that rule out new coal and bring their financing down now,” she said.Explore more on these topicsCoalFossil fuelsEnergyClimate crisisBankingHSBCBarclaysnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Beyond priceless’: how a halt to dredging saved the seas of Scotland’s Summer Isles | Scotland | The Guardian
description: Fish and shellfish populations were falling rapidly as scallop dredgers devastated the seabed, but local activists and small-scale fishers battled hard to protect their coastline
Author: Karen McVeigh
Headline: Fish and shellfish populations were falling rapidly as scallop dredgers devastated the seabed, but local activists and small-scale fishers battled hard to protect their coastline
Content: People in the Summer Isles hold a weekend-long Maerl and Herring festival to celebrate 10 years of a ban on dredging for scallops, which has sparked a dramatic revival of marine life.Photograph: Samuel James-Griffiths/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPeople in the Summer Isles hold a weekend-long Maerl and Herring festival to celebrate 10 years of a ban on dredging for scallops, which has sparked a dramatic revival of marine life.Photograph: Samuel James-Griffiths/The GuardianSeascape: the state of our oceansScotland‘Beyond priceless’: how a halt to dredging saved the seas of Scotland’s Summer IslesFish and shellfish populations were falling rapidly as scallop dredgers devastated the seabed, but local activists and small-scale fishers battled hard to protect their coastlineSupported byAbout this contentKaren McVeighWed 30 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 06.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleInside a bothy overlooking the Summer Isles, in the north-west ofScotland, the lilting tones of a traditional Gaelic duo fill a room full of musicians, storytellers, artists, local people and revellers, hung with fish-shaped lanterns and “Happy Birthday” signs.It’s no ordinary birthday. The people in the small cabin have come together, on a windy night in Achiltibuie, a string of coastal hamlets and villages north of Ullapool, to celebrate an important milestone in the community’s history: a hard-won battle to protect their waters from the ravages of scallop dredging.The coastline here, a metallic grey seen through the bothy’s windows, is dotted with beds of one of the UK’s most biodiverse and carbon-rich habitats, a 9,000-year-old pink seaweed called maerl, two of which are a mile long. This rare, fragile andthreatened seaweedproduces hard, chalky, coral-like skeletons that provide nurseries for scallops and fish.Now, 10 years after local people, divers, activists and creel fishers ran a successful campaign to have scallop dredging banned by law in a 600 sq km (150,000 acre) zone now designated a marine protected area (MPA), they say they have already witnessed a dramatic revival of marine life. The transformation of a seabed damaged by decades of dredging has allowed the recovery of scallop populations and ended the fractious territorialbattles between the industrial dredge fishing boatsand the smaller, more sustainable creel boats, local people say.View image in fullscreenHighland life moves at a sedate pace in Achiltibuie, looking out over Badentarbat Bay.Photograph: CW Images/AlamyView image in fullscreenHerring eggs on maerl. The rare seaweed site is 9,000 years old.Photograph: Chris Rickard/BHAThe community rowing club and nearby tour operators report increased sightings of whales, porpoises and dolphins. A large spawning ground for herring, once plentiful here but since overfished,has been spotted nearbyand in prawn and lobster creels, or pots, which are laid on the seabed.Diyanne Ross, 65, the local artist who made the lanterns, is part of theBlue Hope Alliance(BHA), a coalition of groups using citizen science to protect marine ecosystems in the north-west Highlands. She says the community’s achievements in protecting underwater habitats was the “most amazing thing to happen to the Summer Isles. It is an archipelago that is made in heaven for breeding fish.”View image in fullscreenOrfhlaith McDevitt, who runs Coigach Community rowing club.Photograph: Samuel James-Griffiths/The GuardianAs a child, Ross remembers going out to sea for “boxes” of haddock, ling, pollack and cod – before populations declined. But she has seen recent signs of recovery. “There is more variety of fish being caught here than before,” she says. – anglers are catching haddock and cod.”Outside on the pier, a hardy angler on holiday from Glasgow who has braved the wind to catch what he can, is rewarded by three fresh mackerel.View image in fullscreenLocal artist Diyanne Ross.Photograph: Samuel James-Griffiths/The GuardianThe recovery of scallop stocks, says Alasdair Hughson, a scallop diver, Scottish Creel Fishermen’s Federation (SCFF) chair and one of the BHA’s founders, has been “massive” and the seabed transformation like “night to day”. A decade ago, a boat supplying hand-dived scallops to his company, Keltic Seafare, would spend just two weeks in the Summer Isles.Hughson, whose firm supplies shellfish to UK restaurants, admits his business stands to gain from the dredge ban, but says hand-diving is more sustainable, a claim backed up byresearch from Open Seas. The marine conservation organisation found low-impact fishing methods, such as diving and creeling, are not only more sustainable than dredging or trawling but that more of the revenue generated stays in the local economy.Now, the Donna Marie creel boat, skippered by Ullapool-based Gary Lewis, runs to the Summer Isles almost all year. Lewis, who used to have to travel farther, to Skye and the Western Isles, before the dredge ban, says: “It’s not just the catch that’s improved, but the general health of the seabed.”Central to the weekend-long Maerl-Herring festival celebrations, which includes storytelling, artworks and film, is the public launch of a BHA report spanning a decade of citizen science studies.Jason Hall-Spencer, a professor of marine biology at Cyprus University of Technology, who wrote the report, says it shows the dredge ban in Wester Ross’s MPA, set up to protect the slow-growing maerl habitats and other marine features, has done its job. It has “protected the maerl to a massive extent” he says.View image in fullscreenAlasdair Hughson, scallop diver, SCFF chair and one of the founders of BHA.Photograph: Samuel James-Griffiths/The GuardianAuthor of theConservation Status of Maerl Habitats in north-west Scotland, partly funded by NatureScot, Hall-Spencer has carbon dated the maerl in the bay as 9,000 years old.“If scallop dredgers had spent the last 10 years going up and down here, the habitat would be obliterated,” he says. A single pass of heavy towed gear such as that used by scallop dredgerscan crush or bury up to 70% of maerl.“The seabed is now incredibly rich. Maerl is a very important habitat, chock full of bivalves which provide food for skates and rays.”Peter Drake, 73, a retired prawn fisherman from Polbain, a hamlet that is part of Achiltibuie, was part of Sea Change Wester Ross, a campaign group supported by SCFF, which grew into BHA. “It’s good to remember what we have achieved here” says Drake. “There’s already an improvement in fish populations, but it will take time.”Orfhlaith McDevitt, 25, who has lived here for two-and-a-half years and runs Coigach Community rowing club, says: “People from the club say they see more minke whales, dolphins and porpoises than they did 10 years ago.”Years before Ocean, David Attenborough’s documentary, sparked outrage by showingfootage of scallop dredgers bulldozingthe seabed, causing damage that could be seen from space, Sea Change and the SCFF compiled a body of evidence of the devastation scallop dredgers were doing to fishing grounds and seabeds in Wester Ross.View image in fullscreenSara Nason, in the bobble hat, chats to guests at the Maerl and Herring festival.Photograph: Samuel James-Griffiths/GuardianThe dossier was presented to Scottish ministers in parliament. In 2016,despite fierce opposition by the dredging lobby, scallop dredging was forbidden by law in the Wester Ross MPA, now the biggest protected area in the world for maerl. Prawn trawling is permitted in designated areas, while hand-diving for scallops and creel fishing by local boats under 150 gross tons, is also permitted.The maerl’s three-dimensional structure allows high levels of oxygen, essential to scallops, and emits a chemical that attracts them.But threats to the ecosystem remain: the BHA surveys, also highlighted damaged maerl in some locations – from illegal dredgers and from invasive algal growth that scientists believe could be caused by nutrients from salmon farms.Giving nature a say: why Scottish marine scientists appointed the ocean to their boardRead more“We know that salmon farms put more nutrients into the water,” says Sara Nason, a journalist and documentary maker who founded Sea Change, which later became the BHA and organised the Maerl-Herring festival.The BHA has now launched a three-year project with more than £153,000 of support from the National Lottery Heritage Fund and additional funding from members of the North & West District Salmon Fishery Board, to continue its work.Elsehere, the battle for Scotland’s sea rages on. The Scottish government,which was criticised in Juneby the independent watchdog Environmental Standards Scotland for not fulfilling its legal duty to restore and protect the seabed, haslaunched a public consultationon improving protections for marine habitats and species inside and outside the MPA network.Theresa Ross, who runs Achiltibuie Stores for the community of about 250 people living along this stretch of coastline, says the MPA is “fully supported” by local people as it “ensures fishing is more sustainable”.But for a rural coastal community, where the sea supports livelihoods and few jobs exist, there are competing concerns, she says.View image in fullscreenThe venue for the evening’s celebrations at the Maerl and Herring festival in Achiltibuie.Photograph: Samuel James-Griffiths/The Guardian“There are more people working on the fish farm here than fishermen,” says Ross, whose husband is one of about six fishers in the village, while her son is one of 10 working on the farms.“I support the status quo. But the fish farms are full-time jobs, guaranteed employment and well paid,” she says. “They are not weather dependent, like fishing.”Nevertheless, Nason is one of many who are delighted that the end to dredging has been such a success, describing the protection of the maerl beds as “beyond priceless … We’ve achieved recovery of the whole ecosystem.”Explore more on these topicsScotlandSeascape: the state of our oceansEndangered habitatsFishingShellfishMarine lifeConservationCoastlinesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Two million people in England unaware their properties are at risk of flooding | Flooding | The Guardian
description: Environment Agency warns residents of 6m at-risk properties to prepare for wet and windy three months ahead
Author: Matthew Taylor
Headline: Environment Agency warns residents of 6m at-risk properties to prepare for wet and windy three months ahead
Content: Flooding in Tewkesbury, Gloucestershire, in 2023. El Niño is one of several factors influencing the UK’s weather this year.Photograph: Ben Birchall/PAView image in fullscreenFlooding in Tewkesbury, Gloucestershire, in 2023. El Niño is one of several factors influencing the UK’s weather this year.Photograph: Ben Birchall/PAFloodingTwo million people in England unaware their properties are at risk of floodingEnvironment Agency warns residents of 6m at-risk properties to prepare for wet and windy three months aheadMatthew TaylorWed 30 Sep 2026 09.50 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 16.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore than two million people in England are unaware their properties are at risk of flooding, as the UK braces for a wet and stormy start to the winter, according to theEnvironment Agency.Experts say the next three months are more likely than usual to be wet and windy – due to a combination of large-scale weather patterns and the “subtle” impact of asupercharged El Niño– increasing the risk of flooding.However, the EA warned on Wednesday that people in a third of the six million properties most at risk of flooding are unaware of the threat they face.Caroline Douglass, the director for flood and coastal risk management at theEnvironment Agency,said: “We know with the 6m properties at risk [in England] … we know that one-third of people who are at risk don’t think they are at risk.”She urged people tocheck on the government websitewhether their properties were at risk, and to take measures to prepare.“We want the public to make sure they know what their risk is, so check on gov.uk. We need them to sign up for flood warnings … and if they are at risk, to have a flood plan so they know what they need to do.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOne in nine new homes in England built in areas of flood risk, study showsRead moreFloodingcaused havoc across the UK last yearand the Met Office said that, after a summer ofdroughts, extreme heat and wildfires, the UK was facing a wet and stormy start to winter.Will Lang, the chief meteorologist with the Met Office, said its three-month outlook indicated there was an increased likelihood that October, November and December would be wet and windy, adding there were early indications of drier, colder and calmer conditions later in the winter.“There is an increasing likelihood of it being wet overall, windier than normal and milder than usual as well,” said Lang.He said El Niño – which is bringingdevastation to other parts of the world– increased the likelihood of wetter and windier conditions in the UK but was only one of several factors influencing the UK’s weather. “This is just a subtle shift in the odds of it being wetter and windier,” he said. But he added that would lead to “a heightened potential for flooding”.The Met Office said that although flooding was likely in the months ahead, drought conditions would remain in large parts of the UK until reservoirs returned to their normal water levels, adding that would require above-average rainfall over the winter.Explore more on these topicsFloodingExtreme weatherHome insuranceInsurancePropertyClimate crisisEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: BBC removes article linking bare nails trend to ‘white supremacist standards of beauty’  | BBC | The Guardian
description: Corporation says story did not meet editorial standards after it attracts criticism from US and UK media
Author: Michael Savage
Headline: Corporation says story did not meet editorial standards after it attracts criticism from US and UK media
Content: BBC bosses concluded the article did not challenge quotes in the piece linking bare nails to white supremacy.Photograph: Posed by model; LaylaBird/GettyView image in fullscreenBBC bosses concluded the article did not challenge quotes in the piece linking bare nails to white supremacy.Photograph: Posed by model; LaylaBird/GettyBBCBBC removes article linking bare nails trend to ‘white supremacist standards of beauty’Corporation says story did not meet editorial standards after it attracts criticism from US and UK mediaMichael SavageMedia editorWed 30 Sep 2026 10.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleABBCarticle that included a claim that a trend for bare nails was linked to “white supremacist standards of beauty” has been permanently removed from its website, after editors concluded it did not meet the corporation’s editorial standards.The article, which first ran on the BBC’s website on 27 September, examined an apparent “viral craze” for bare rather than decorated nails. It said the trend had been flooding social media and fashion catwalks.It also covered criticisms of the trend, which suggested it could “stigmatise bold manicures”.
