The article noted that nail art had its roots in black, Latino and Asian communities.In an early section of the article, it quoted the beauty journalist Kristina Rodulfo as saying: “That trend really promotes blankness and this kind of sameness and erasure of culture and identity that is so important to black and brown communities.“They are often called elegant or tasteful and these are often usually euphemisms that perpetuate white supremacist standards of beauty.”Later in the piece, Rodulfo was quoted again as saying: “The examples are almost always white women or celebrities … [and] they’ll often conflate class and taste with that bareness.”View image in fullscreenThe article noted that nail art had its roots in black, Latino and Asian communities.Photograph: John Sibley/ReutersThe BBC initially removed the article from its website on Tuesday after the piece had attracted criticism from media outlets in the US, particularly on the political right. The corporation stated it had been removed “pending an editorial review”.However, the BBC has since confirmed that the article had been permanently removed. Bosses concluded there was no challenge in the piece to the quotes linking bare nails to white supremacy, or any context that such opinions would be seen as extreme.A Wall Street Journal piece stated the BBC article was “embarrassingly retrograde – displaying outdated intellectual fashion – in its attempt to locate offences against social justice in the decisions of individual women whether or not to paint their nails”.It stated: “When you see someone dressed for a costume party, you notice how conspicuous that person is. So it is with the BBC’s attempt to gin up outrage over the semiotics of nail polish.”The New York Post, part of Rupert Murdoch’s media stable, also ran an article criticising the piece, as did Fox News.An opinion piece in the Telegraph also attacked it. “I’ve had some rude awakenings in my time, but being told I’m a white supremacist before I’ve had my coffee? That’s got to be up there,”wrote Celia Walden, a feature writer.On its corrections and clarifications register, the BBC stated: “This article examined the trend of bare nails and what might be motivating it, hearing from a range of contributors as well as looking at the cultural significance of manicures. It was removed on 29 September pending an editorial review.“Following this review the article was permanently removed on the same day because it reported criticism of the bare nails trend without sufficient context or challenge and so did not meet our editorial standards.”The BBC has not revealed who made the decision to remove the article. However, the corporation’s deputy director general, Rhodri Talfan Davies, was appointed to the new role in order to catch potential editorial rows that plagued the leadership of the former director general, Tim Davie.Matt Brittin, who replaced Davie, was also keen to have a deputy for support on editorial matters, given his lack of television and editorial experience.The BBC is still the subject of legal action from Donald Trump over the wayan episode of Panoramaedited together two parts of a Trump speech. While the BBC apologised for the edit, it has always maintained the documentary did not defame the president.Explore more on these topicsBBCBeautyRaceNews websitesNewspapersNewspapers & magazinesnewsShareReuse this content

title: New UK gas and oil projects are a ‘no-brainer’, says EDF boss | Oil and gas companies | The Guardian
description: Developing North Sea fields does not contradict net zero goals, according to Simone Rossi
Author: Jillian Ambrose
Headline: Developing North Sea fields does not contradict net zero goals, according to Simone Rossi
Content: A demonstration outside the Labour conference in Liverpool against the Rosebank oil project. A decision on the development is expected in weeks.Photograph: Peter Byrne/PAView image in fullscreenA demonstration outside the Labour conference in Liverpool against the Rosebank oil project. A decision on the development is expected in weeks.Photograph: Peter Byrne/PAOil and gas companiesNew UK gas and oil projects are a ‘no-brainer’, says EDF bossDeveloping North Sea fields does not contradict net zero goals, according to Simone RossiJillian AmbroseEnergy correspondentWed 30 Sep 2026 12.24 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 16.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNew oil and gas projects are a “no-brainer” that pose “no contradiction” to the net zero agenda, according to the head ofEDF Energy.Simone Rossi has joined a string of renewables leaders in making the case for more North Sea production as the government prepares to decide on two projects there.He said ministers should give the Rosebank andJackdawfields the green light, while accelerating support for heat pumps and electric vehicles.“It will take decades to wean off from that dependency,” Rossi said in an interview with the BBC. “So while this is happening we should use the resources that we’ve got rather than importing them from afar. For me, it’s really a no-brainer. It is not in contradiction.”View image in fullscreenSimone Rossi, the chief executive of EDF Energy, says UK oil and gas projects have lower emissions than imports.Photograph: PA Images/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.New North Sea developments would help to create jobs and increase government tax receipts that could be used to support households struggling to pay energy bills, according to Rossi.He said locally produced fossil fuels had lower emissions than imports because they do not need to transported over long distances.“In the UK the only way we can reduce emissions is to genuinely reduce the usage of fossil fuels at the point of use,” he said. “Over time, the only solution is electricity.”The boss of EDFEnergy, which generates about a fifth of the UK’s low-carbon electricity, has become the latest high-profile advocate of climate action to also make a case for more North Sea production. Others include: Greg Jackson, the founder of Octopus Energy; Jürgen Maier, the former boss of GB Energy; and Tara Singh, the boss of RenewableUK.EDF Energy, which is owned by EDF of France, has about 8 gigawatts of low-carbon generation capacity in the UK, including eight nuclear power plants with a combined capacity of 6GW and 2GW of wind, solar and battery storage. It is building the much-delayed Hinkley Point C nuclear power station in Somerset.Politicians to have spoken out in favour of more North Sea production include: the former chancellor Rachel Reeves; the defence secretary, Wes Streeting; former ScottishLabourleader Anas Sarwar; Liberal Democrat leader and former energy secretary, Ed Davey; and the leaders of the largest trade unions.Support on the left aligns with theLabour party’s election manifesto, which ruled out granting exploration licences while still allowing for some new streams of North Sea oil and gas. This was provided they came from already licensed areas or fields adjacent to existing projects, which can use the same infrastructure.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMinisters have come under pressure from environmental groups as well as from Zack Polanski, the Green party leader in England and Wales, to deny final consent to Rosebank and Jackdaw aftera summer of heatwaves caused by the intensifying climate crisis, and increased volatility in oil and gas prices.Both projects already have licences – granted under the Conservative government – which means they could be given final approval without breaching the manifesto.Andy Burnham promised to take a“pragmatic approach”to the North Sea after Donald Trump used one of his first conversations with the new prime minister to urge him to “open up” more drilling.The government is expected to decide on Rosebank and Jackdaw within weeks. The decision wasreportedly delayeduntil after the 8 October Holborn and St Pancras byelection – in which Polanski plans to stand.The oil and gas proposals were put to the government earlier this year after a court ordered the developers to resubmit their applications with additional consideration for the climate impact of burning their fossil fuels.Explore more on these topicsOil and gas companiesEnergy industryEDF EnergyFossil fuelsClimate crisisLabourAndy BurnhamnewsShareReuse this content

title: Grenfell police hand files on 20 organisations and 54 people to CPS | Grenfell Tower fire | The Guardian
description: Met calls move ‘milestone’ moment that paves way for ‘very best possible evidence for charging decisions’
Author: Ben Quinn
Headline: Met calls move ‘milestone’ moment that paves way for ‘very best possible evidence for charging decisions’
Content: The fire on 14 June 2017 led to the deaths of 72 people and was found by a public inquiry to have been avoidable.Photograph: Ben Bauer/PAView image in fullscreenThe fire on 14 June 2017 led to the deaths of 72 people and was found by a public inquiry to have been avoidable.Photograph: Ben Bauer/PAGrenfell Tower fireGrenfell police hand files on 20 organisations and 54 people to CPSMet calls move ‘milestone’ moment that paves way for ‘very best possible evidence for charging decisions’Ben QuinnandPeter WalkerWed 30 Sep 2026 13.33 EDTFirst published on Wed 30 Sep 2026 09.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePolice investigating theGrenfell Tower firehave asked prosecutors to consider charges including manslaughter and fraud against a range of companies and individuals.TheMetropolitan policeannounced they had given prosecutors evidence relating to 20 companies and organisations and 54 individuals ahead of charging decisions, in what the force described as a “milestone moment”.Andy Burnham joined survivors’ groups in saying it had “taken too long”, but he pledged to support Grenfell families “to ensure they get the justice and accountability that they deserve”.Potential charges include corporate manslaughter, gross negligence manslaughter, health and safety offences, fraud and fraud-related offences and misconduct in public office.The housing secretary, Angela Rayner, said on Wednesday that the files passed to prosecutors by police included one relating to her department. The Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) would review whether the department, which police began investigating in 2023, had potentially breached the Health and Safety at Work Act.“I recognise the significance and gravity of this development, and we will respond with the appropriate and necessary diligence and care,” she said.The Guardian has learned that a leading prosecutor has been appointed to head any possible court cases.The fire in North Kensington, westLondon, on 14 June 2017, led to the deaths of 72 people and was found by a public inquiry to have been avoidable.It was the result of “decades of failure” by central government to stop the spread of combustible cladding, combined with the “systematic dishonesty” of multimillion-pound companies whose products spread the fire, a public inquiry found in 2024.The CPS has said charging decisions will be made before the 10th anniversary of the disaster, which falls on 14 June 2027.Kevin Southworth, a deputy assistant commissioner at the Met, said: “This is a milestone moment in the police investigation into this devastating tragedy which took the lives of 72 people.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDirector who oversaw Grenfell cost-cutting given senior council housing roleRead more“We appreciate, of course, it has taken nine years to get to this point. As we have said before, this is one of the most complex investigations ever undertaken by any UK law enforcement agency – the scale is truly enormous.“While we know this has had a significant impact on those waiting for answers, it has necessarily taken this long to ensure our investigation is meticulous and presents the very best possible evidence to the CPS for charging decisions.”Investigators have looked at the role of more than 15,000 people and 700 organisations as part of the inquiry, and have submitted 12,600 pages of evidence to the CPS.A total of 14,700 statements have been taken and more than 27,000 exhibits, including cladding, insulation, doors, windows and other parts of the building – down to screws, nuts and bolts – are stored in a secure warehouse.Scale replica parts of the tower are being built at a cost of £2m in anticipation of potential court proceedings.Grenfell United, which represents some bereaved families and survivors, said: “We expect the Met and the CPS to do everything in their power to make sure this case moves forward without further unnecessary delay. Our families have waited long enough.“We want those responsible to face justice. If people are found guilty of crimes that cost our loved ones their lives, we want to see them behind bars. Only then will people see that there are real consequences for what happened at Grenfell.”Burnham told Channel 5 News: “It has taken too long, but at least [the evidence] has been submitted. To be fair to the Metropolitan police, it has been a complex and wide-ranging investigation and they’ve had to do it in a forensic way, dealing with multiple, multiple organisations.”He cited the role of the Hillsborough law, which he was involved in campaigning for, and which imposes a duty of candour on public authorities to prevent cover-ups.“It’s intended to speed up situations like this so we can get the truth and justice much more quickly. And accountability, that’s the piece that’s often lacking. There must be accountability for Grenfell,” he said.Frank Ferguson, the head of the CPS’s special crime and counter-terrorism division, said the service remained confident that it would complete the process and make charging decisions before the 10th anniversary of the fire next year.Explore more on these topicsGrenfell Tower fireMetropolitan policeLondonEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Kristi Noem, former Trump homeland security chief, files for divorce | Kristi Noem | The Guardian
description: Noem cites irreconcilable differences in filing that comes after husband Bryon Noem involved in tabloid scandal
Author: Robert Tait
Headline: Noem cites irreconcilable differences in filing that comes after husband Bryon Noem involved in tabloid scandal
Content: Kristi Noem with her husband Bryon Noem, right, at a Senate judiciary committee hearing in Washington in March.Photograph: J Scott Applewhite/APView image in fullscreenKristi Noem with her husband Bryon Noem, right, at a Senate judiciary committee hearing in Washington in March.Photograph: J Scott Applewhite/APKristi NoemKristi Noem, former Trump homeland security chief, files for divorceNoem cites irreconcilable differences in filing that comes after husband Bryon Noem involved in tabloid scandalRobert Taitin WashingtonWed 30 Sep 2026 19.58 EDTFirst published on Wed 30 Sep 2026 16.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKristi Noem, who was fired by Donald Trump after a rumbustious stint as homeland security secretary, is divorcing her husband, Bryon Noem, after 34 years of marriage, citing “irreconcilable differences”.The divorce claim “for settlement purposes only” was disclosed in court records filed in Hamlin county,South Dakota, the state of which Noem was previously governor.The document was signed by Noem’s lawyer, Michael Sabers, on 6 April – just over a week afterthe Daily Mail published picturesof her husband wearing inflated fake breasts under a spandex shirt.At the time, Noem issued a statement saying she was “devastated” by the images, adding that “the family have been blindsided by this”.The papers were only filed in court this week, according tothe New York Times.Sabers confirmed Kristi Noem had filed for divorce and said she would reserve further comments for the legal process.Tim Bottum, Bryon Noem’s attorney, said his client was “saddened that the marriage is ending” and would welcome the opportunity to share his perspective if court proceedings were necessary.“Bryon’s priority is to protect the family and move forward as loving parents and grandparents,” Bottum said in a statement.The revelations came weeks after Noem had lost her job at the department of homeland security.The state of her marriage had already been subject of speculation amid rumors that she was in a relationship with her aide at the department, Corey Lewandowski.In a Capitol Hill on 4 March, a Democratic member of Congress asked her openly whether she had sexual relations with Lewandowski.Answering under oath, Noem – who was accompanied to the hearing by her husband – dismissed the question as “tabloid garbage” but did not say no.She was fired the following day after Trump was reportedly angered by her answers to questions about a taxpayer-funded publicity campaign that promoted Noem’s image. Noem told the committee that Trump had signed off on the spending.Noem was replaced by Markwayne Mullin as homeland security secretary after a controversial period that had included the shooting deaths of protesters Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis during an immigration enforcement surge. Noem came under intense criticism after calling Good and Pretti “domestic terrorists”.Noem, 54, married Bryon Noem, 56, in 1992. They have three adult children.Explore more on these topicsKristi NoemUS politicsSouth DakotaRepublicansnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ohio woman sues hospital for allegedly amputating wrong leg during surgery  | Ohio | The Guardian
description: Sharon Jacks, 74, alleges hospital removed left leg instead of her right during below-the-knee amputation in 2025
Author: Lucy Campbell
Headline: Sharon Jacks, 74, alleges hospital removed left leg instead of her right during below-the-knee amputation in 2025
Content: Marietta, Ohio, on 17 September 2026.Photograph: Carolyn Kaster/APView image in fullscreenMarietta, Ohio, on 17 September 2026.Photograph: Carolyn Kaster/APOhioOhio woman sues hospital for allegedly amputating wrong leg during surgerySharon Jacks, 74, alleges hospital removed left leg instead of her right during below-the-knee amputation in 2025Lucy CampbellWed 30 Sep 2026 17.47 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 17.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnOhiowoman is suing a hospital after doctors allegedly amputated the wrong leg during a scheduled operation last year.Sharon Jacks, 74, of Meigs county, alleged that she went to Selby general hospital in September 2025 to undergo a planned below-the-knee amputation of her right leg. Instead doctors removed her left leg during the procedure, according to the lawsuit, which was filed earlier this month in Washington county court in Marietta, where the hospital is based.Her attorney, Brad Layne, said the error ultimately left Jacks, an army veteran, a double amputee after doctors at another hospital in Ohio had to remove the correct leg four months later.According to the 32-page complaint, Jacks “suffered physical injury, permanent disability, pain and suffering, emotional distress, humiliation, loss of enjoyment of life, medical expenses and other damages”.Jacks and her husband named nine defendants in the lawsuit, including the hospital and Jacks’ medical and surgical teams, accusing them of gross negligence, battery and reckless conduct.“Defendants acted willfully, wantonly, recklessly, maliciously, and with conscious disregard for the substantial certainty of catastrophic injury,” the complaint alleged.The amputation of Jacks’ lower right leg was recommended as part of a treatment plan for a diagnosis of squamous cell carcinoma, a type of skin cancer, according to the lawsuit, and she “consented only to surgery involving her right lower extremity” and “never consented to amputation of her left lower extremity”.According to the complaint, medical records show that the surgical team conducted two “time-outs” before the procedure. In surgery, these pauses are supposed to be used to confirm the patient’s identity, the planned procedure and the correct surgical site. But “despite multiple opportunities … to identify and correct the error”, the team proceeded to amputate the wrong leg, it alleged.“The performance of surgery upon the wrong extremity constituted a complete failure of basic safety procedures,” the lawsuit said.In a statementto WBNS-TV, the hospital acknowledged that “this was an avoidable event, and that our expected operating room procedures were not followed.”The statement added: “Those involved were held accountable for their actions and are no longer in their positions.“We are saddened by what occurred, and our team continues to keep this patient and their family in our prayers.”The lawsuit seeks unspecified compensatory and punitive damages on behalf of Jacks.Explore more on these topicsOhioUS healthcareLaw (US)newsShareReuse this content

title: French court jails six men for manslaughter over mass drowning in Channel | France | The Guardian
description: Seven others found guilty of lesser charges in connection to incident in 2021 when inflatable dinghy sank killing at least 27 people with four more still missing
Author: Angelique Chrisafis
Headline: Seven others found guilty of lesser charges in connection to incident in 2021 when inflatable dinghy sank killing at least 27 people with four more still missing
Content: French police patrol the Slack dunes the day after 27 people died attempting to cross the Channel.Photograph: Pascal Rossignol/ReutersView image in fullscreenFrench police patrol the Slack dunes the day after 27 people died attempting to cross the Channel.Photograph: Pascal Rossignol/ReutersFranceFrench court jails six men for manslaughter over mass drowning in ChannelSeven others found guilty of lesser charges in connection to incident in 2021 when inflatable dinghy sank killing at least 27 people with four more still missingAngelique Chrisafisin ParisWed 30 Sep 2026 11.58 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 16.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA Paris court has jailed six ⁠men for manslaughter over the deaths of at least 27 people in theworst mass drowningon record from a small-boat crossing in the Channel.Seven other men were ⁠found guilty of lesser smuggling charges with varying degrees of seriousness, including facilitating illegal immigration as part of ⁠an organised gang and criminal conspiracy.Five years on, another four people are still missing.The court heard that the sinking of an inflatable dinghy in November 2021 was caused by “individuals driven by greed, with utter disregard for human life”.Prosecutors said the convicted men helped launch a “substandard small boat, uncertified, unfit for navigation on the open sea, overcrowded and lacking appropriate lifejackets”.Emmanuel Daoud, a lawyer for one victim’s family, called the proceedings a “trial of greed, cynicism and inhumanity”.Twenty-seven peoplewere confirmed dead when theirinflatable dinghy sankin the early hours of 24 November 2021. Four people remain unaccounted for.View image in fullscreenLawyers and relatives of victims arrive at court in Paris for the trial of the alleged smugglers.Photograph: Simon Wohlfahrt/AFP/Getty ImagesThe victims were mostly Iraqi Kurds, but also included people who were Afghan, Ethiopian, Iranian, Somali, Vietnamese and Egyptian. The youngest known victim was a seven-year-old girl. The confirmed dead included 15 men, seven women and two teenagers.Sentences for the six men found guilty of manslaughter ranged ‌from six to 10 years in prison. For others, sentences ranged from six months suspended to four ​years in prison. The court heard that the men were linked to Afghan and Iraqi-Kurdish smuggling networks ⁠that organised the migrants’ passage to Britain from camps near Grande-Synthe and Calais in northernFrance. One man was found innocent.According to testimony from the two survivors, the flimsy boat, which had attempted to cross one of the world’s busiest shipping lanes between the northern French coast and Kent in southern England began to deflate and take on water after several hours at sea.Passengers fell overboard and drowned one after another, despite making about a dozen desperate calls for help to French and British rescue services. Only two men survived.For the people onboard the sinking boat, despite several distress calls, it was nearly 12 hours after the first pleas for help before the dinghy was finally found by a French fishing vessel.A separate investigation is continuing in France into seven French military personnel – five members at a maritime rescue coordination centre, and two sailors onboard a patrol vessel. They have been under investigation since 2023 for failing to help a person in danger. They deny the allegations.Zana Mahmand Mohammed travelled from Erbil in Iraqi Kurdistan to address the court about his younger brother, Twana, 18, who drowned in the disaster but whose body has never been found.He said: “We’ve been waiting for our brother’s body for five years. I live with the uncertainty of ever finding out what happened. We lost a member of our family. He had a project for another future to live … ”The family had tried to dissuade Twana from leaving home, but he had wanted to find a job and develop his sporting success as a black belt in taekwondo and escape the violence and insecurity of his region.Mohammed said every time he read in the media about other small boats in difficulty, he relived the tragedy. “Destruction is being repeated,” he said.Explore more on these topicsFranceRefugeesImmigration and asylumMigrationEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Sweden must apologise for harm done to Sami people, says state-backed report | Sweden | The Guardian
description: Truth commission accuses country of failing Indigenous people, amid rising tensions over land rights
Author: Miranda Bryant
Headline: Truth commission accuses country of failing Indigenous people, amid rising tensions over land rights
Content: Sami children campaigning with the climate activist Greta Thunberg in Jokkmokk, Sweden, in 2020.Photograph: Naina Helen Jama/EPAView image in fullscreenSami children campaigning with the climate activist Greta Thunberg in Jokkmokk, Sweden, in 2020.Photograph: Naina Helen Jama/EPASwedenSweden must apologise for harm done to Sami people, says state-backed reportIndependent commission accuses country of failing Indigenous people, amid rising tensions over land rightsMiranda BryantNordic correspondentWed 30 Sep 2026 11.40 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 13.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn independent commission set up by the Swedish state has called on the country’s government to apologise for the “harm and injustice inflicted upon the Sami people” and to start a national process for “redress and reconciliation”.The Truth Commission for the Sami People also called for a special apology to be issued urgently to elderly Sami people who were forced as children to attendsegregated so-called “nomad school”and other boarding schools where they were “subjected to violations or abuse”.‘The same struggles as 100 years ago’: exhibition highlights lives of Sami people in SwedenRead moreThe commission’s report, published on Wednesday, is the outcome of a four-year investigation and hundreds of interviews with Sami people across Sweden. It was due to be presented to a government representative at a ceremony featuring readings from the text, but with no government yet in place after theelection earlier this month, it went instead to Parisa Liljestrand, the last government’s culture minister.The commission’s chair, Lena Nyberg, told her: “We hand over a big responsibility.” Liljestrand thanked the members of the commission and those who were interviewed for the report, saying it had been a “historic process”.There have been similar truth commissions into the treatment of Sami people – Europe’s only recognised Indigenous people – in Norway and Finland. Norway hasissued an official apologyand discussions in Finland are ongoing.The new report accusesSwedenof failing to meet its domestic and international human rights obligations and says that as a “direct consequence” of mistreatment, the Sami people today face “major challenges” in preserving and developing their culture.View image in fullscreenPlans to expand mining operations in Kiruna, Sweden, threaten traditional grazing lands used by Sami reindeer herders.Photograph: Johan Ylitalo/The GuardianIt coincides with rising anti-Sami rhetoric in Sweden, including from political leaders, amidclashes over landused for grazing by Sami reindeer herders for hundreds of years, which the state wants to mine for rare-earth minerals.The report says issues with the handling of Sami land rights in Sweden have been “reinforced and aggravated” by an ideology that Sami people are “an inferior people and therefore neither deserving of nor capable of exercising the same rights and responsibilities as other citizens”.It adds that the Swedish state has failed to implement theUnited Nations declaration on the rights of Indigenous peoples.The commission’s71-point call to actionrecommends an official apology for the harm and injustice inflicted upon the Sami people, as well as financial compensation and completing the process of ratifying the International Labour Organization’sconvention on Indigenous and tribal peoples.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt calls for the establishment of a national centre for redress and reconciliation, and for authorities to recognise that the Swedish nation was founded on lands belonging to two peoples – the Sámi and the Swedes – and that parts of the land have Sami names and are part of Sami cultural heritage.It also urges recognition that Sápmi, the region traditionally inhabited by the Sami people, extends across present national borders; an end to racial discrimination against Sami people; and better provision for children to learn Sami languages. It adds that the Swedish government must uphold the Sami people’s right to practise reindeer husbandry and other cultural practices on their traditional lands.The report concludes that the state, including the Swedish parliament, government and public authorities, and in some cases the Church of Sweden, must “bear responsibility” for policies and decisions that led to the violation of Sami rights.It says: “Accepting responsibility also requires the state to work towards providing redress for the harm inflicted on the Sami people and individual Sami, while pursuing policies that do not repeat these historical injustices.”Explore more on these topicsSwedenIndigenous peoplesEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: US trade regulator opens investigation into AI giants including Anthropic and OpenAI | Trump administration | The Guardian
description: FTC move is first official US enforcement ⁠action on rogue AI agents, following surge in incidents first reported in July
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: FTC move is first official US enforcement ⁠action on rogue AI agents, following surge in incidents first reported in July
Content: Dario Amodei, Anthropic CEO, at the White House in Washington DC on Tuesday.Photograph: Shawn Thew/EPAView image in fullscreenDario Amodei, Anthropic CEO, at the White House in Washington DC on Tuesday.Photograph: Shawn Thew/EPATrump administrationUS trade regulator opens investigation into AI giants including Anthropic and OpenAIFTC move is first official US enforcement ⁠action on rogue AI agents, following surge in incidents first reported in JulyReutersWed 30 Sep 2026 14.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US’s main trade regulator is conducting an industry-wide investigation ⁠intoAnthropic, OpenAI and other ⁠AI labs ​to uncover the potential dangers their technology poses to consumers.The investigation by the Federal Trade Commission is the first official US enforcement ⁠action that delves into rogue AI agents, following a surge in incidents first reported in July that have stoked fears among the public that uncontrolled AI could one day ⁠harm humans.The FTC plans to issue formal demands for information and compel testimony from executives at top ​AI developers, including Anthropic, OpenAI and the research ‌group Metr, according tomultiplereports.Anthropic and ‌OpenAI have used Metr to conduct independent investigations into security incidents involving their agentic AI technology.Anthropic, OpenAI and ‌Metr did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The New York Post first reported the news.Andrew Ferguson, the FTC chair, had concerns about the companies before AI agents developed by OpenAI hacked the open-source platform Hugging Face. The incident, in which OpenAI agents probed the AI coding hub for vulnerabilities before carrying out a large-scale attack, sparked global discussion of the issue.Ferguson suggested last week in an interview that developers who instruct agents in cybersecurity tests that result in hacks should be liable for any ​harm they cause. The US should look to existing laws before seeking to pass new ones regulating AI, Ferguson said at an event in Austin.The FTC has broad authority to sue companies over unfair or deceptive practices, and has used that authority in the past to take action against companies for failing to ⁠take reasonable measures to secure consumers’ data.Donald Trump met with top ​AI executives on Tuesday, where the ​companies agreed to establish voluntary standards.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTrump AI deal rebrands ‘artificial intelligence’ as ‘superintelligence’Read moreTrump has ​repeatedly called fears about AI a hoax as he seeks to prioritize US dominance ​in the technology over regulation. ‌At the same ​time, he has ​also said the government can use existing laws against AI companies for any harm they may cause.Explore more on these topicsTrump administrationOpenAIAnthropicAI (artificial intelligence)US politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK income growth revised upwards as markets hail ‘resilient’ economy  | Economics | The Guardian
description: Boost for John Healey before budget as GDP figure shows UK economy grew faster than first estimated in second quarter
Author: Phillip Inman
Headline: Boost for John Healey before budget as GDP figure shows UK economy grew faster than first estimated in second quarter
Content: The ONS said the Britain’s GDP rose by 0.5% in the second quarter.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/SOPA Images/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe ONS said the Britain’s GDP rose by 0.5% in the second quarter.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/SOPA Images/ShutterstockEconomicsUK income growth revised upwards as markets hail ‘resilient’ economyBoost for John Healey before budget as GDP figure shows UK economy grew faster than first estimated in second quarterBusiness live – latest updatesPhillip InmanWed 30 Sep 2026 10.13 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 16.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUK household income grew at a stronger pace than previously estimated during the first six months of the year, according to revisions of official data.The rise in income per head to 1.1% between January and June followed an increase in the level of economic growth that illustrated the resilience of the UK economy since the outbreak of hostilities in the Middle East more than seven months ago.The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said gross domestic product (GDP) increased by 0.5% rather than the previously estimated 0.4% in the April to June quarter, showing that the UK economy grew at the same pace as the US in the first six months of the year. The economy grew 0.6% in the first quarter.Economic growth in UK and US revised higher; diesel on brink of £2 a litre for first time – business liveRead moreAnalysts said a “Burnham bounce” in confidence could have been a factor, as the Makerfield byelection announced in May paved the way for the former mayor of Manchester to become prime minister.The ONS said households were also able to put some of the rise in incomes into savings accounts. The savings rate increased from 8.6% in the first three months to 8.8% in the three months to the end of June.Thomas Watts, a fund manager at the private bank Julius Baer, said the figures were “yet more positive news for the new administration” afterprevious data had shown the resilience of the UK economysince the start of theUS-Israel war on Iranin February.The upgrade is a boost for the chancellor, John Healey, as he prepares to give his first budget next month.The sharp increase in GDP per head in the first half of the year put the UK near the top of the G7 leader board, ahead of Germany, France and the US and just behind Canada, which topped the poll with a growth rate of 1.3% in the first and second quarters.Businesses also kept spending, especially on investment. The ONS said business investment increased by 1.8% in the second quarter and was estimated to be 5.2% higher compared with the same quarter a year ago.Kathleen Brooks, the research director at XTB, said the markets were in an “upbeat mood” after the revisions, which “suggest that the UK economy was resilient to the effects of the Iran war, the energy price surge and the rise in borrowing costs”.She said: “Stronger services growth and rising household spending boosted the figure. This is fairly typical of the UK economy, which is service based; the real surprise was the strength of business investment and an improvement in the trade figures, which showed a boost in exports.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCurrency markets reacted positively to the figures. Traders speculated that the UK’s strong growth rate may persuade the Bank of England that the economy is “running hot” and needs higher interest rates to calm it down, especially when inflation at 3.1% is above the central bank’s 2% target.Sterling hit a six-week high against the euro and edged higher against the US dollar, up 0.4% to a one-week high of $1.3292. Against the euro, sterling was at its highest since mid-August, with the euro down nearly 0.3% at 85.43p.UK government bond yields, which provide a measure of the interest rate paid on UK debt, eased on the stronger economic data and lower global oil prices.Two-year UK bond yields were down 0.05 of a percentage point at 4.86%, while 10-year UK bond yields were four basis points lower at 5.356% on Wednesday.Oil and gas prices have surged since the conflict first started. After a ceasefire in the summer, traders have lost confidence in efforts to secure a peace deal and sent Brent crude prices back above $100 a barrel, though they have eased in recent days.Explore more on these topicsEconomicsAndy BurnhamEconomic growth (GDP)newsShareReuse this content

title: Energy bills in Great Britain forecast to jump by £276 a year from January | Energy bills | The Guardian
description: Cap poised to rise by 16% to equivalent of £1,999 for dual-fuel bill, the biggest quarterly increase since January 2023
Author: Jillian Ambrose
Headline: Cap poised to rise by 16% to equivalent of £1,999 for dual-fuel bill, the biggest quarterly increase since January 2023
Content: The increase for the January to March quarter is well above Cornwall Insight’s previous prediction of a 9% rise.Photograph: NORRIE3699/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenThe increase for the January to March quarter is well above Cornwall Insight’s previous prediction of a 9% rise.Photograph: NORRIE3699/Getty Images/iStockphotoEnergy billsEnergy bills in Great Britain forecast to jump by £276 a year from JanuaryCap poised to rise by 16% to equivalent of £1,999 for dual-fuel bill, the biggest quarterly increase since January 2023What to do as prices head for £2,000 a yearJillian AmbroseEnergy correspondentWed 30 Sep 2026 02.17 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 12.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHousehold energy bills in Great Britain are predicted to reach almost £2,000 a year for the typical household from January as the impact of the Middle East war continues through the coldest months of winter.The government’s cap on energy prices is poised to jump by 16%, equivalent to adding £276 to the average annual dual-fuel bill to take it to £1,999, according to the leading forecaster Cornwall Insight.The latest blow to struggling households was published as millions braced for energy charges torise by 4% from Thursdayas the quarterly energy bill cap climbs to its highest level in three years this winter.What is Burnham’s GB Grid plan and could it bring down energy bills?Read moreThe consultancy’s January forecast increase is well above its previous prediction of a 9% rise, with analysts blaming the uptick on the recent rise in gas market prices to three-year highs.It would be the biggest quarterly jump since January 2023, when the energy crisis that followed the full-scale invasion of Ukraine the year before was at its height.Craig Lowrey, a principal consultant at Cornwall Insight, said: “These prices are going to hit households hard. January is already a difficult month for many, with cold weather and bank balances still recovering from Christmas, and now they face the biggest price cap rise we’ve seen in four years.”The chief executive of the supplier EDF Energy, Simone Rossi, said the UK was “walking into a second energy crisis”. Speaking to the BBC, he called for the government to do more to lower domestic bills after its six-month VAT holiday, which will save the typical home about £45 a year from Thursday.Andy Burnham said he would not call Rossi’s crisis warning an overstatement, telling BBC Radio 4’s Today programme that the rising cost of home energy, as well as pump prices, was “very difficult indeed”.In response to questions over whether the government would consider abandoning the planned fuel duty rise, the prime minister said “every possible measure” was being considered to ease energy costs, adding: “We’re looking at any measure that can give people breathing space, that can take the pressure off.”Cornwall’s latest forecast reignited calls for the government to offer targeted support to struggling households this winter. Simon Francis, a coordinator at the Energy Fuel Poverty Coalition, said the number of households in fuel poverty was set to rise again “at the most dangerous time of the year”.He said: “The chancellor has no choice but to act to provide increased targeted support to vulnerable households and plan to deliver wider universal help for people facing a sixth winter of high energy prices.“If ministers do nothing, millions will spend this winter in cold, damp homes, unable to cook a hot meal. People will get ill. Some will die. And every one of those avoidable cases will be on this chancellor’s watch.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGas prices in Europe have doubled in recent months as the continent prepares to enter the cooler months with gas storesat their lowest level in 13 yearsafter the US-Israel war on Iran triggered an increase in global market prices.Buyers have delayed refilling storage facilities after a cold end to last winter, and extra gas power generation during the summer heatwaves, depleted stocks while oil and gas exports from the Gulf remain severely disrupted by threats to tankers passing through the Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab straits.Cornwall Insight said storage levels of EU gas were now at their lowest September level for 15 years.The energy regulator for Great Britain,Ofgem, sets the government’s price cap. It will base January’s figure on wholesale prices between 19 August and 17 November, so the outlook could still change if market prices drop, but Cornwall Insight said an increase was “all but certain” given the rises so far this month.From this Thursday the cap rises to the equivalent to £1,723 a year for a typical home’s gas and electricity use. The unit cost of electricity will rise from 26.11p a kilowatt hour to 26.32p, while gas charges will rise from 7.33p to 7.97p. However, actual household bills will depend on how much each consumes.Explore more on these topicsEnergy billsEnergy industryOfgemUS-Israel war on IranGasHousehold billsUK cost of living crisisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Super-rich UK energy and food magnates’ wealth skyrockets amid global crises | The super-rich | The Guardian
description: Analysis has shown the costs of daily essentials soaring in recent years, thanks in part to climate shocks, wars and geopolitical tensions
Author: Damien Gayle
Headline: Analysis has shown the costs of daily essentials soaring in recent years, thanks in part to climate shocks, wars and geopolitical tensions
Content: François Perrodo, left, spends some of his personal fortune collecting and racing cars as a ‘gentleman driver’.Photograph: Paulo Maria/DPPI/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenFrançois Perrodo, left, spends some of his personal fortune collecting and racing cars as a ‘gentleman driver’.Photograph: Paulo Maria/DPPI/ShutterstockThe super-richSuper-rich UK energy and food magnates’ wealth skyrockets amid global crisesAnalysis has shown the costs of daily essentials soaring in recent years, thanks in part to climate shocks, wars and geopolitical tensionsDamien GayleWed 30 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrançois Perrodo is what is known in motorsport as a gentleman driver. In June, he raced at Le Mans, earning a podium place. At the end of August he was back behind the wheel at the Circuit de Spa-Francorchamps. This time he won.Gentleman drivers are wealthy individuals who fund their own participation. The FIA governing body caps costs to keep racing accessible to such enthusiasts. But forself-confessedpetrolhead Perrodo, it is well within his means.Perrodo is in charge of his family’s company, Perenco, one of Europe’s largest privately held oil and gas companies. Between this summer’s two big races,he was in the Democratic Republic of the Congopresenting a multibillion dollar oil investment plan to the president. In the past four years, his family’s wealth has increased by about £3bn. He is one of a number of UK-linked billionaires whose wealth has soared since 2022, when Russia’s invasion of Ukraine kicked off a global cost of living crisis.An analysis has found that families whose fortunes came from energy grew their wealth four times faster than their super-rich peers since 2022. Families whose fortunes came from food production increased their wealth three times faster.The Perrodo clan take the first place in a list of 15 super-rich UK-linked families who have seen their wealth soar from doing business in energy or food production. In all cases, the analysis found, increases in wealth came alongside increases in profit margins at businesses they owned.The rises in energy and food prices, caused by climate shocks, wars and geopolitical tensions, have driven a multiyear cost of living crisis. Energy prices have fallen back from their peaks, but in August 2026 gas priceswere 31% higherthan in January 2020, while electricity prices were 17% higher. Petrol is more volatile, but iscurrently about twice as expensiveas 2020.UK food prices roseby a total of 38.6% between November 2020 and November 2025.The research, commissioned by the antipoverty charity War on Want, found that households on the Sunday Times Rich List whose fortunes came primarily from energy saw their wealth increase by 20% between 2022 and 2026 – four times the list average. Households whose fortunes came primarily from food production enjoyed a wealth increase of 15%.Ben Tippet, an academic who researches wealth inequality at Kings College London, did the analysis based on his previous research categorising the sources of the wealth of households in the Rich List. He compiled a sub-list of 15 families who had made the most money from doing business in energy or food.The list includes household names such as the Warburton family, who have increased their wealth by £185m as the cost of bread has risen, and Iceland supermarket founder Malcolm Walker, whose fortune grew by £106m.Top of the list for food is Ranjit Singh Boparan, for whom the past decade has seen a stunning turnaround in his fortunes. In 2018, the “chicken king” wasforced to step downas chief executive of his family company, 2 Sisters Food Group (2SFG), after a food safety scandal. The analysis found that he and his wife, whose companies are said to produce a third of all poultry products eaten in the UK, had tripled their wealth since 2022, taking it to over £2bn.Perenco, which specialises in eking out the last drops from ageing oil wells, has been embroiled in a number of scandals. Four years ago,it sued the Peruvian governmentto try to block an Indigenous people’s reserve. Three years ago,there was an oil spill in Dorset– an accident that earned it a£6m fine. And two years ago documents revealed it wasfailing to plug its old North Sea wells.Perenco said it was a “recognised expert in the optimisation of mature fields” and that it takes human rights and environmental law obligations “very seriously”. It noted that it had withdrawn its claim against the Peruvian government after the country’s ministry of culture determined there were uncontacted Indigenous people in the area.Regarding the Dorset oil spill, Perenco said “very specific conditions in this pipeline” led to a spill of 200 barrels of reservoir fluid, which was about one-eighth crude oil and seven-eighths production fluid, including biocides. “Perenco UK have made changes to their processes and conducted extensive checks to confirm that these conditions are not present elsewhere,” the company said. And it added that it is “fully compliant with all relevant deadlines” for its North Sea wells “and strongly refutes any suggestion that it is not fulfilling its decommissioning obligations, or is in any way putting the integrity of assets at risk”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBoparan has committed to higher welfare and cuts to emissions at 2SFG’s farms. But chicken factory farming nonetheless places a heavy load on the environment: farming is the UK’slargest cause of river pollution, and chicken farms in particular have been accused of causing severe pollution in the rivers Wye and Severn.Boparan and 2SFG declined to comment. But the British Poultry Council insisted “chicken farms are not harming rivers”.“All manure is managed and accounted for with designated routes of use, and all under government-regulated environmental permitting schemes,” said Richard Griffiths, the council’s chief executive. “Chicken consumption is growing and we have a responsibility to produce it sustainably ... Chicken is not the only way forward, but it is the one that can deliver today, tomorrow, and the next day.”The research comes asLabour members and politicians meet in Liverpool for the party’s annual conferencewith the cost of living crisis a priority for Andy Burnham’s government. War on Want says that can only work if the government also takes steps to limit extreme wealth. It is calling for the government to establish £10m as the upper acceptable limit for wealth; to introduce an annual wealth tax on all assets over £10m; and to work with foreign governments to support extreme wealth taxation globally, including through the emerging UN Tax Convention.“The super-rich are profiting from the food and energy industries that fuel both the climate and cost-of-living crises,” said Nuri Syed Corser, a campaigner at War on Want.“Working-class people face soaring prices and worsening climate impacts – and the billionaires who own food and energy companies are profiting from this hardship. We need to tax the super-rich and use their extreme wealth to tackle the climate and cost-of-living crises.”Explore more on these topicsThe super-richEnergy industryFood & drink industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Scottish screen sector boom brings questions over jobs and overtourism | Scotland | The Guardian
description: The Traitors and big film shoots help boost economy but some highlight lack of opportunities for local talent
Author: Eve Livingston
Headline: The Traitors and big film shoots help boost economy but some highlight lack of opportunities for local talent
Content: The Traitors has had added £21.8m to the Scottish economy since 2022, according to the BBC.Photograph: BBC/PAView image in fullscreenThe Traitors has had added £21.8m to the Scottish economy since 2022, according to the BBC.Photograph: BBC/PAScotlandScottish screen sector boom brings questions over jobs and overtourismThe Traitors and big film shoots help boost economy but some highlight lack of opportunities for local talentEve LivingstonWed 30 Sep 2026 12.53 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 16.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleScotland’s striking Ardross Castle, the oldest star of The Celebrity Traitors, which kicks off on Thursday night, is just one of the stops on the Scottish tourist board’s “screen tourism” trail. From Outlander and The Odyssey filming in the Highlands and islands, to Glasgow city centre standing in for New York and Gotham City in the latest instalments of Indiana Jones and Batman respectively, film and TV is increasingly big business inScotland.The country’s screen sector,growing year on year, is projected to be worth £1bn to the economy by 2030. But while some have celebrated the upsides of a booming production sector, others highlight a lack of opportunities for Scottish talent and the challenges of excessive tourism in areas featured on screen.After last year’s Celebrity Traitors finale, theBBC announcedthat the show had added £21.8m to the Scottish economy since 2022 through employment, supply chain spend and screen tourism, where visitors travel specifically to see on-screen sites in real life.Butresearch last yearby Peter Strachan, a documentary film-maker and academic who set up the campaign group Standing Up For Scotland’s Screen Talent, found that only about 6% of production staff on series three of The Traitors were Scottish, despite the production counting towards Ofcom quotas stating that the BBC must use 8% of network hours and expenditure in Scotland.“This is the tip of the iceberg,” Strachan wrote at the time. “We have found many other supposedly Scottish productions are failing to create jobs for broadcast freelancers in Scotland.”The BBC reiterated thatThe Traitorswas a Scottish production, and Studio Lambert, which makes the show, said Scottish representation was increasing behind the scenes each year.View image in fullscreenSet dressers transforming a street in Glasgow into Gotham City for the Batgirl film shoot.Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PAEarlier this month, Strachanalso calledfor Sony Pictures to release a breakdown of the local crew hired in Glasgow for Spider-Man: Brand New Day, which filmed in the city in 2025.“Local hiring is not necessarily the same thing as employing Scotland’s established screen-sector workforce,” he said. “Someone can be locally hired to work on a film without normally working in film and television – a Glasgow carpenter brought in for a few weeks of set construction, for example.”David Smith, the interim executive director of Screen Scotland, the national body for the country’s film and TV industry, said Scotland had benefited from its growing screen sector, but that there had been a “consistent decline” in the number of shows commissioned by public service broadcasters from Scottish production companies.“We think this needs to change,” Smith said. “Ultimately, we want to see a sustainable mix of film and TV projects made across genres, broadcasts and platforms.”Even for those not directly involved in the industry, its effects are still being felt. Glenfinnan, in Lochaber in the Highlands, is home to only about 150 people – as well as a majestic viaduct made world-famous when it doubled as the Hogwarts Express railway bridge in the Harry Potter films. In the years since, the tiny hamlet has become so overrun with film tourists that Police Scotland last monthissued a warning to visitorsover dangerous parking and antisocial behaviour.View image in fullscreenGlenfinnan viaduct doubled as the Hogwarts Express railway bridge in the Harry Potter films.Photograph: JP Offord/Rex/ShutterstockGillian Shields, 54, lives in Inverness, close to the village of Culloden where the Clan Fraser stone has become a major tourist attraction for fans of historical fantasy series Outlander. In 2023, the site was temporarily closed after deterioration caused by excessive visitor numbers.“People here are welcoming, and most of the visitors are lovely and respectful,” she said. “We’re not trying to turn anyone away, it’s just we see more and more every single year and it’s a worry whether our beautiful area can keep up with it.”Culloden battlefield, which features heavily in Outlander, saw a43% increase in visitor numberslast year, according to data from Glasgow Caledonian University and the Association of Scottish Visitor Attractions.‘Scots are the kindest people on earth!’ Meet the Americans moving to ScotlandRead moreJenni Steele, the film and creative industries manager at VisitScotland, said the benefits of film tourism “are worth millions to the economy, bringing jobs and opportunities, and are felt long after the film or TV series is released”.But she said: “We know that success can bring with it challenges in certain locations. Film and TV fans will be drawn to them regardless. That’s why we work with partners and local bodies to understand the challenges so we can educate and inform visitors of where and when they should visit and encourage them to act responsibly and explore beyond the on-screen locations.”Many Scots, though, are in full support of the country’s booming screen sector. Matthew, 42, lives in Glasgow city centre and has watched on in recent years as the streets around his home have been transformed into everything from 1960s New York (Indiana Jones and the Dial of Destiny) to dystopian America (The Running Man) and Soviet-era Moscow (Tetris).“Some people moan about road closures and parking, but it’s great to see the city buzzing with excitement when a new show comes to town,” he said, noting that local residents he knew had been employed as extras, and nearby restaurants as on-set catering suppliers. “The city needs those jobs and that money – and, to be frank, a bit of fun and glamour never hurt a Glaswegian either.”Explore more on these topicsScotlandTelevision industryThe TraitorsOvertourismnewsShareReuse this content

title: Renoir and Love review – the happiest exhibition of the year? Pourquoi pas! | Pierre-Auguste Renoir | The Guardian
description: Grab your straw boater – and revel in these light-as-souffle masterpieces that celebrate life’s pleasures, from picnics to dances to frolics in the bushes
Author: Jonathan Jones
Headline: Grab your straw boater – and revel in these light-as-souffle masterpieces that celebrate life’s pleasures, from picnics to dances to frolics in the bushes
Content: A flickering fragile wonder … Dance at the Moulin de la Galette, 1876, by Pierre-Auguste Renoir.Photograph: © Musée d'Orsay, Dist. RMN-Grand Palais / Patrice SchmidtView image in fullscreenA flickering fragile wonder … Dance at the Moulin de la Galette, 1876, by Pierre-Auguste Renoir.Photograph: © Musée d'Orsay, Dist. RMN-Grand Palais / Patrice SchmidtPierre-Auguste RenoirReviewRenoir and Love review – the happiest exhibition of the year? Pourquoi pas!National Gallery, LondonGrab your straw boater – and revel in these light-as-souffle masterpieces that celebrate life’s pleasures, from picnics to dances to frolics in the bushesJonathan JonesWed 30 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 13.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘They knew how to enjoy themselves,” David Hockney once told me, gleefully pointing out the cigarette and cigar butts littering the ground under Renoir’s dancers. There are broken clay-pipes too beneath the swirling pink skirts and blue trousers of the couple in his tall, narrow 1883 canvas Dance at Bougival as they bring their faces close, placing their arms around each other and pirouetting in the soft, airy space Renoir makes you feel as well as see. It’s an outdoor afternoon dance enclosed by fluffy, lime-coloured trees. A couple sitting at a table get friendlier with each swig of beer.And oh, the lunches! Renoir seems to have invented the slow French lunch, relaxed and liquid, that launched a thousand bistro daydreams. In After the Luncheon, another one to delight Hockney, we see a white-clothed, open air table neatly arranged with porcelain coffee cups, carafes and glasses – and a woman sipping a liqueur while the bearded man she’s lunching with lights up, savouring the moment as his cigarette end glows fire-red against the pale blues, whites and silvers. The Lunch at the Restaurant Fournaise (The Rowers’ Lunch) lingers on the same climactic moment, one man lounging back in tobacco reverie while the lovers or about-to-be-lovers on the other side of the table chat soulfully.View image in fullscreenLove is everywhere you look … Dance at Bougival, 1883, by Pierre-Auguste Renoir.Photograph: © Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, Picture FundPierre-Auguste Renoir, who was born in 1841 and lived until 1919, saw the height and fall of the French bourgeois civilisation whose pleasures he so infectiously celebrates. His son, the film director Jean Renoir, revisits his father’s world with the sadness of hindsight in his screen recreation of an impressionist picnic,Partie de Campagne: there you know the happiness is fragile. But in Pierre-Auguste’s paintings, there’s no punishment. Nobody gets syphilis or drinks themselves to death, or drowns in the Seine. This is the happiest art exhibition of the year.Et pourquoi pas? Renoir, this perfect exhibition lays bare, is the most radical of the impressionists, which will come as a shock to anyone who sees him as the soppiest and most kitsch. Impressionism started as a pejorative label chucked at a loose group of artists in 1870s France who tried to capture modern life in motion. It is Renoir who most enthusiastically embraces this as a philosophy of life itself. He doesn’t just paint the changing light of the passing moment. He urges us to live in it.This ideal of enjoying life as it comes makes his masterpiece Dance at the Moulin de la Galette, lent by the Musée d’Orsay, as grand as a history painting and as light as a souffle. As hosts of people take pleasure in each other’s company in this open air hangout in Montmartre, their flirtations, longings and consolations are caught in a dappled, mobile dance of golden light and cool shadow. The light is so ethereally pervasive it turns the crowded canvas into a flickering fragile wonder, a brief moment of revelation that you might have, sitting in this crowd silently for a second and seeing a blue-and-white dress, a straw boater, a woman’s sensitive face as she puts an arm around her friend, a young man’s open admiration as he looks at her.The exhibition is called Renoir and Love, and love is everywhere you look. On a rainy street under the canopy of umbrellas, a man looks dotingly on a woman who appears lost in her own daydream. In what seems at first a simple painting of a boatyard by the Seine, View of Bougival, we actually get to spy on a lovers’ tryst: the woman lowers her parasol, letting her dog play in the sun, as she converses deeply with her beloved.View image in fullscreenPerhaps she’s married … The Promenade, 1870, by Pierre-Auguste Renoir.Photograph: The J. Paul Getty Museum, Los Angeles, CaliforniaIt’s not all heterosexuality either. The curators cite a story by Maupassant to suggest that The Skiff, in which one woman rows another on the glittering, hallucinogenic, light-kissed water, may be a lesbian scene. Who knows? But there is no question that Renoir, like Maupassant and Zola, sees women as autonomous characters. In Place Clichy he focuses so exclusively on the flushed face of a woman in a furry coat and hat about to cross the road that the crowd behind her become blurred. It’s a cinematic close up from before the age of film – no wonder his son went into the movies.Renoir paints the moment but he is also a storyteller. Almost every lunch, rowing party and stroll in the park feels like a languid set-up for what will follow. Couples, or solitary women, in theatre boxes as the show is about to start fascinate him. Parks too are stages. The Promenade was painted in 1876 but recreates the 18th-century love scenes of Watteau as a man leads a well-dressed woman by the hand into the bushes. She looks uncertain. Perhaps she’s married. Or perhaps here is the menace Renoir usually doesn’t see.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toArt WeeklyYour weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitionsEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRenoir can strike some as a soft touch, especially when you compare him with the tough, ironic realism of Manet. He also went off later in his career. The National Gallery acknowledges this by including his anti-impressionist, nude indulgenceThe Great Bathers. The work’s fun in its way – but it’s the early Renoir who shines here as a truly great modern artist. Let’s remember the good times. Be happy, be in love,mes amis.AtNational Gallery, London, from 3 OctoberExplore more on these topicsPierre-Auguste RenoirArtPaintingExhibitionsNational GalleryreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Verity review – Dakota Johnson leaves teethmarks as she goes back to Fifty Shades erotic thriller territory | Movies | The Guardian
description: Anne Hathaway and Josh Hartnett co-star in this unconvincing mystery about a struggling writer who is asked to ghostwrite for a bestselling author
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Anne Hathaway and Josh Hartnett co-star in this unconvincing mystery about a struggling writer who is asked to ghostwrite for a bestselling author
Content: Power couple … Anne Hathaway (Verity Crawford) and Josh Hartnett (Jeremy Crawford) in Verity.Photograph: Amazon Content Services LLC/PAView image in fullscreenPower couple … Anne Hathaway (Verity Crawford) and Josh Hartnett (Jeremy Crawford) in Verity.Photograph: Amazon Content Services LLC/PAMoviesReviewVerity review – Dakota Johnson leaves teethmarks as she goes back to Fifty Shades erotic thriller territoryAnne Hathaway and Josh Hartnett co-star in this unconvincing mystery about a struggling writer who is asked to ghostwrite for a bestselling authorPeter BradshawWed 30 Sep 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 09.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe nation is crying out for a really enjoyable erotic mystery-thriller, a taste potentially at least as strong as the cosy-crime fetish currently dominating our every waking moment. The success of Paul Feig’s naughty-but-not-nice movie The Housemaid proves it. We are thirsting for a sexy encounter with a dishy yet maybe problematic nice-guy husband; we are pining for a damaged and dangerous beautiful wife; we are longing to identify with a vulnerable yet gutsy young person who finds herself in the middle of their creepy scenario and we are yearning to spend some time in a secluded luxury lakeside villa of gigantic modernist proportions down whose night-time corridors we can tremblingly tiptoe. So here is a drama, adapted by screenwriter Nick Antosca from the novel by Colleen Hoover, in which someone has such excitingly transgressive sex that they leave teeth marks on the headboard. During this film, audiences may be leaving teeth marks in the seatback in front of them. Or the back of someone’s head. But not in a good way.Dakota Johnson goes back into “Fifty Shades” ingenue-cute territory as Lowen, a struggling writer mysteriously approached by a legal team working for Verity Crawford, played by Anne Hathaway, a mega-bestselling author whose recent indisposition means that she is unable to finish her hugely lucrative novel series. Crawford’s people ask Lowen if she might be willing, in exchange for several shedloads of money, secretly to ghostwrite the rest of Crawford’s darkly saucy page-turners. Lowen agrees, largely because she is strangely drawn to Verity’s handsome, sensitive husband Jeremy, played by Josh Hartnett. She has to go and stay in their gorgeous Vermont home where she is upset to find that Verity is now immobile, using a wheelchair, and cannot speak. And she is even more upset to discover a certain manuscript by Verity which hints at a terrifying situation of which the world has no clue.So far, so silly and so entertaining, surely? There are cheeky hints of Daphne du Maurier and Brian De Palma that promise a good time. But we are entitled to wonder why Lowen doesn’t ask someone, anyone, how exactly Verity came to be in this unhappy situation. Perhaps she might be tempted to ask the sinister nurse (Irina Dvorovenko) but this character soon simply and bafflingly disappears. After a sensational opening sequence, the film gradually unwinds, and the entirety of the third act disintegrates into a shower of small substandard plot points that don’t convince. The narrative structure seems to rest on Lowen finding not one but two manuscripts, and we are finally asked to accept a lamely unresolved situation as something fascinatingly ambiguous. This needed a new draft.Verity is out on 1 October in Australia and on 2 October in the UK and USExplore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsSexDakota JohnsonAnne HathawayFilm adaptationsCrime filmsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: SKF advert review – let’s hope this dull AI Greta Garbo is not the future | Greta Garbo | The Guardian
description: Swedish-American actor exhumed for bizarre, humourless 99 seconds that give us another reason to resent AI
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Swedish-American actor exhumed for bizarre, humourless 99 seconds that give us another reason to resent AI
Content: ‘This Garbo is a bizarre soignée figure, a Stepford robo-star, a Hallmark-greeting-card parody.’Illustration: SKFView image in fullscreen‘This Garbo is a bizarre soignée figure, a Stepford robo-star, a Hallmark-greeting-card parody.’Illustration: SKFGreta GarboReviewSKF advert review – let’s hope this dull AI Greta Garbo is not the futureSwedish-American actor exhumed for bizarre, humourless 99 seconds that give us another reason to resent AIPeter BradshawWed 30 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 02.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePoorGreta Garbo.Perhaps, in life, she thought her final indignity would be the Peter Cook and Dudley Moore TV sketch from 1970, showing Pete as the legendary recluse standing on the back of a flatbed truck as it rumbles through the crowded city streets, shouting at everyone through a megaphone: “I vant to be alone!”Reanimated AI Greta Garbo stars again … in a ball-bearing advertRead moreBut now, 36 years after her death in 1990, there is something worse. As if to give us yet another reason to fear and resent AI, this technology has exhumed Garbo and brought her to a state of bland, mediocre undeadness for a bizarre 99-second TV ad from the Swedish ball-bearings company Svenska Kullagerfabriken (SKF), in which the screen legend, dressed in a silk blouse and stylish slacks, key-lit like a movie star, at first in dreamy profile-silhouette and then standing by a stool and prefacing her script by saying movie-type things like “Are we rolling?”, drones out her appreciation for this very boring industrial product. At the end, we get an odd, stilted sort of joke about her well-known yearning for solitude.There is a reason for it. In 1921, the 15-year-old future screen icon, then known as Greta Gustafsson, really did briefly appear in a promotional film for SKF. (This appears to have been an offshoot for the women’s clothing commercials she was doing at the time for Stockholm’s PUB department store, which got her into the movies.)The AI Greta Garbo is a bizarre soignée figure, a Stepford robo-star, a Hallmark-greeting-card parody of the icy hauteur, distraite sensuality and deadpan comedy that Garbo projected in life. The AI Garbo is like the classiest ever presenter of a TV shopping channel, purring her way through a dull and humourless script that seeks to create a brand synergy between the frictionless ball-bearings manufactured by SKF and what the company imagines to be Garbo’s own all-important smoothness. But Garbo’s impact rested on something other than smoothness. “One of my first films was for SKF and now I’m back for my last,” AI Greta remarks.Her last? Well, this film is supposedly derived not from any of Garbo’s own movie appearances, but reportedly from images and pictures that exist elsewhere. This perhaps means that SKF need not negotiate with any of the corporate movie studios – who might be rather chary of people making free with Garbo’s image, which is part of their copyright-protected IP – but only with Garbo’s distant relatives, who might well be more amenable. And they say that they are not averse to the idea of licensing the AI Greta Garbo for other movies. We need Mrs Merton to ask what first attracted them to that idea. Perhaps Humphrey Bogart, Gary Cooper and Rita Hayworth also have distant great-great-great nephews and nieces who can be induced to greenlight similar projects.Let’s hope this dull AI Garbo is not the way of the future. Guardrails were never more badly needed.Explore more on these topicsGreta GarboAI (artificial intelligence)SwedenTelevisionreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Cotton Queen review – mystery, matriarchs and magic in pioneering Sudanese debut | Movies | The Guardian
description: Suzannah Mirghani’s first feature contains a powerful performance by Rabha Mohamed Mahmoud as a village’s elder woman and tackles the long shadow of British imperialism and women’s rights
Author: Cath Clarke
Headline: Suzannah Mirghani’s first feature contains a powerful performance by Rabha Mohamed Mahmoud as a village’s elder woman and tackles the long shadow of British imperialism and women’s rights
Content: Can she shape her own future? … Rabha Mohamed Mahmoud as Al-Sit and Mihad Murtada as Nafisa in Cotton Queen.Photograph: Frida MarzoukView image in fullscreenCan she shape her own future? … Rabha Mohamed Mahmoud as Al-Sit and Mihad Murtada as Nafisa in Cotton Queen.Photograph: Frida MarzoukMoviesReviewCotton Queen review – mystery, matriarchs and magic in pioneering Sudanese debutSuzannah Mirghani’s first feature contains a powerful performance by Rabha Mohamed Mahmoud as a village’s elder woman and tackles the long shadow of British imperialism and women’s rightsCath ClarkeWed 30 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 06.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Idecide my past,” says a village matriarch in this intriguingly political and poetic drama from Suzannah Mirghani, making her feature debut – and with it becoming the first Sudanese woman to direct a feature. (She was forced to cancel the original shoot in Sudan whenwar broke out in 2023, moving production to Egypt.) It’s a film with things to say about the long shadow of the British empire, neocolonialism, women’s rights and female genital mutilation. But it mostly says it all without undermining its sense of mystery and shivers of magic realism.We’re in present daySudan, where village elder Al-Sit (Rabha Mohamed Mahmoud) is an iron-willed woman not to be messed with. Everyone knows the story of how as a young girl she ran the British out of town; small children in the village gleefully tell the story of how she slaughtered every single last one of them. Can it possibly be true? The trauma of her past is at the centre of the film, and Mahmoud’s witchy performance, fierce and powerful, is utterly compelling.Al-Sit is arranging the marriage of her beloved 15-year-old granddaughter Nafisa (Mihad Murtada). But Nafisa’s mother has another husband in mind – businessman Nadir (Hassan Kasala), who is of Sudanese heritage, but grew up abroad. He arrives in the village to flog farmers genetically modified cotton seeds manufactured by a multinational – and there is perhaps a sense here of history repeating itself, international interests trying to control local resources.Poetry-writing Nafisa is appalled by both husband options. She has a teenage crush on a sweet kid who grows onions. But while fault lines are set for a showdown, the film is not really about who she should marry, but her ability to shape her own future. It’s not perfect, and its tonal shifts don’t always work, but you’re unlikely to see another film like it this year.Cotton Queen is in UK and Irish cinemas from 2 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsSudanColonialismAfricaMiddle East and north AfricaWomen's rights and gender equalityreviewsShareReuse this content

title: On the Equality of All Things by Carlo Rovelli review – a physicist’s guide to life, the universe and everything | Science and nature books | The Guardian
description: Near-mystical musings from a scientist who believes we are on the brink of a revolution in understanding ourselves
Author: Farrah Jarral
Headline: Near-mystical musings from a scientist who believes we are on the brink of a revolution in understanding ourselves
Content: The Milky Way above the Grand Canyon of Thailand.Photograph: Suchart Kuathan/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Milky Way above the Grand Canyon of Thailand.Photograph: Suchart Kuathan/Getty ImagesBook of the dayScience and nature booksReviewOn the Equality of All Things by Carlo Rovelli review – a physicist’s guide to life, the universe and everythingNear-mystical musings from a scientist who believes we are on the brink of a revolution in understanding ourselvesFarrah JarralWed 30 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 12.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUnder the letter “B” in the index at the back of Carlo Rovelli’s latest book you will find Francis Bacon, bats, behaviourism, Henri Bergson, and the big bang.
