This intriguing little miscellany reflects the sweeping ambition of what is perhaps Rovelli’s most overtly philosophical work to date.Rovelli, who directs a quantum gravity research group in Marseille, has written several books on physics for the general reader, including the global bestseller Seven Brief Lessons on Physics.His latest is an attempt to integrate principles and theories from the discipline into a broaderWeltanschauung: one of the essential unity of all things, and the profoundly relational and perspectival nature of the universe. “Electrons and minds, stones and laws, judgments and galaxies do not essentially differ in nature from one another,” he writes. “They are notions that illuminate each other.”If this sounds familiar, that’s because it is. Rovelli echoes concepts that have been around for millennia in ancient thought, including Hinduism and Buddhism, from whose sacred texts he quotes. But what sets him apart from the countless other modern writers, dreamers and thinkers who preach the oneness of it all is that he grounds his ideas in scientific theory rather than theology or new age conjecture.double quotation markIt’s enough to give you vertigo, and Rovelli admits itOn the Equality of All Things is a slender volume holding an extraordinary density of ideas. Translator Simon Carnell, himself a poet, maintains the clarity and concision we have come to expect from Rovelli’s writing. In six chapters, or “lessons”, Rovelli lays out the philosophical significance of what he believes is a major scientific revolution, happening right now. The first lesson refers to his theory of relational quantum mechanics to ask us to abandon the notion that the world is made up of things with fixed properties. Rather, physical systems have propertiesrelativeto other physical systems. Also, everything’s moving, all the time, and there’s no fixed point around which we are in motion.The second lesson takes aim at the idea of linearity. Rovelli urges us to accept circularity and question the need to identify the ultimate foundation of things, when in fact, it’s turtles all the way down. The lessons continue. The world is not made up of things at all, butprocesses.“Even a stone is a process”, and so are we. Time itself is mutable and passes at different speeds in different places. Our knowledge of anything can only ever be partial.It’s enough to give you vertigo, and Rovelli admits it. “The resulting image of reality is haunting. Every fact is only a fact relative to something else, and even the fact that a fact is relative to something else is itself relative. There is no ground floor.” Yet, in contrast to the bleakness that can shroud such unflinching scientific accounts of the universe, Rovelli’s telling validates our messy, subjective human experiences. “None of this prevents us from describing the world from one perspective. Ours.” But the physics tells us that our perspectives are just that, and that there may be others.On the Equality of All Things takes its place as part of a blossoming movement that asks us to see the world as a set of interconnected relationships. As such, it sits alongside the work of mycologist Merlin Sheldrake, botanist Robin Wall Kimmerer, physiologist Denis Noble and nature writer Robert Macfarlane. Rovelli’s emphasis on perspective and relationality in physics echoes similar intellectual turns in social anthropology, ecology and biology that invite us to stop thinking about the world as something we stand without, and instead take our rightful placewithinit. Distancing himself from the more hubristic elements of the Enlightenment – an emphasis on certainty, linearity, and overconfidence in the imperfect instrument that is Reason – Rovelli asks us to embrace “the nimble lightness of circularity, complexity, ambiguity, metaphors, emotions, the acceptance of uncertainty and change”.His refusal to denigrate human culture as being inferior to or incompatible with hard science is refreshing. He observes wryly that the term “consciousness” has superseded the word “soul” because it is perceived to be more scientific, even though it is just as nebulous. Provided we understand that physical processes underlie everything, Rovelli sees no reason why we may not “calmly speak of the soul and emotions just as we speak of tables even if tables are collections of atoms”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFor all Rovelli is a gifted communicator, some of the science in this book required a level of intellectual scaffolding that, alas, my rusty physics A-level did not provide. At his explanation of loop quantum gravity, my brain started to creak and let off steam. Yet, even if you don’t have the foggiest idea what the granularity of spacetime means, engaging with this book as an internally coherent work of philosophy and literature is rewarding enough. And Rovelli’s conclusion is powerful: we are physical systems dancing among other physical systems, and the world “is our blood brother”. We’re at home, among family. Perhaps it’s time we honoured that kinship.On the Equality of All Things: Physics and Philosophy by Carlo Rovelli is published by Allen Lane (£20). title: Dèy by Edwidge Danticat review – motherhood and trauma in Miami  | Books | The Guardian
description: The first novel in over a decade from the acclaimed Haitian-American author lacks the power of earlier works
Author: Sukhdev Sandhu
Headline: The first novel in over a decade from the acclaimed Haitian-American author lacks the power of earlier works
Content: Edwidge Danticat.Photograph: Slaven Vlašić/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenEdwidge Danticat.Photograph: Slaven Vlašić/Getty ImagesBooksReviewDèy by Edwidge Danticat review – motherhood and trauma in MiamiThe first novel in over a decade from the acclaimed Haitian-American author lacks the power of earlier worksSukhdev SandhuWed 30 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDèy, Edwidge Danticat’s first novel in over a decade, begins with a bang. Magnolia, the daughter of Haitian parents now shopping for a birthday present for her own daughter, hears gunfire, maybe bombs, in a Miami mall. A killer is on the loose – a young man high on hate, the author of online screeds about how “our country is under attack”, obsessed by cane toads who’ve been coming in from the Amazon basin. As she scrambles to the floor of a restaurant called Oasis, surrounded by dozens of diners playing dead, a man asks, “Is this a mass grave?”Things have always been tough for Magnolia. Her mother chases pigeons by day, sleepwalks at night, is on and off lithium. Her father worked for many years as a bus driver in Brooklyn, saving every cent so he could buy a nice retirement home back in Haiti. She was brought up by an “aunt” whose family had been killed by goons employed by Haiti’s dictator-in-chief Papa Doc Duvalier. Later she gets to college, where “school was my refuge”.Magnolia makes it out of the mall alive but finds herself rattled. Why can’t she tell the father of her child about what she witnessed? She doesn’t confide in her work colleagues either. At a pool party she almost has a seizure when a friend playfully sprays her with a water gun. Is this trauma? She has often felt brittle – finding a photo of herself in her early 20s, when she was a new mother, she says her eyes “look like headlights in a staring contest with a deer” – but now the ground beneath her feet feels especially shaky.Her anxieties – about her daughter’s future, her parents’ health – keep mounting.double quotation markDanticat, a sometime travel writer, is at her most appealing in her commemorations of Miami’s Little HaitiViolence in Dèy isn’t confined to the mall. It runs through the news stories about Ramallah and Yemen and Congo that Magnolia follows. The reports she hears of daily life in Haiti, where gangs abduct young girls, torch homes, storm schools and even churches, prompt fears for the home her father has worked so hard to build. Then, both in the background and in everyone’s face, there is the US president himself, with his poisonous thought-blurts about Haitians eating dogs and coming from a “shithole” country.Danticat, a sometime travel writer, is at her most appealing in her commemorations of Miami’s Little Haiti, a weathered world full of bakeries and barbershops, churches and religious stores, beauticians whose clientele watch Nollywood movies and read old copies of Ebony. But these hubs are being priced out by fusion restaurants and pilates studios. Magnolia works in property and is an agent of the displacements she and her colleagues bemoan.Magnolia’s job attunes her not just to the economics but to the poetics of place. Her ears prick up when someone describes Haiti as “down there” or, in the case of her boss, “‘over there’, as though she were looking at its distant shores from the upper deck of a cruise ship”. A short but powerful chapter is devoted to the backstory of a Haitian security guard who was killed at the mall: after the 2010 earthquake he moved to Brazil to build stadiums for the 2016 Olympics, then on to Chile and Colombia, before braving swamps and mountains to get to the US/ Mexico border and low-paid jobs loading trucks, allowing him to send money to his siblings back home.These peripheral characters are more vivid than Magnolia herself, who remains a wan, disassociated narrator throughout. Her language is sometimes academic (she describes her own daughter as “a liminal creature”), sometimes straight from a lifestyle magazine (“flaxen-tressed Black woman”). Motifs are spelled out for hard-of-hearing readers (“houses have always fascinated me, not only as physical structures, but as ideas, stories”) or in the manner of reading-group prompts (“We don’t always choose where we call home. Sometimes it’s others who decide”). The churn in her head – the violence that terrifies her – emerges in the tamest, most gentrified prose imaginable.In the end, Dèy, which is set in 2018, reads like a tribute to 1990s postcolonial fiction. There are nods to the spectral (“I was sure my mother was a ghost”), riffs on “sympathetic pain” and “somatic knowledge” (“My period came for the first time on another September 11”), too much dining-table diplomacy. “Visual clutter bothers me,” admits Magnolia at one point; this novel – so tasteful, so scented – could do with more noise, smears, life.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. title: How Zach Cregger’s Resident Evil stands out from all other game adaptations | Games | The Guardian
description: There’s no Leon, Claire or Ada Wong in Cregger’s adaptation. Instead, it re-creates something more fundamental – the strange, terrifying experience of actually playing the game
Author: Keith Stuart
Headline: There’s no Leon, Claire or Ada Wong in Cregger’s adaptation. Instead, it re-creates something more fundamental – the strange, terrifying experience of actually playing the game
Content: Director Zach Cregger (right) with actor Austin Abrams on the set the new Resident Evil film.Photograph: Dušan Martinček/CTMGView image in fullscreenDirector Zach Cregger (right) with actor Austin Abrams on the set the new Resident Evil film.Photograph: Dušan Martinček/CTMGPushing Buttons newsletterGamesHow Zach Cregger’s Resident Evil stands out from all other game adaptationsThere’s no Leon, Claire or Ada Wong in Cregger’s adaptation. Instead, it re-creates something more fundamental – the strange, terrifying experience of actually playing the gameDon’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereKeith StuartWed 30 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 10.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’ve been surprised by the number ofResident Evilfans complaining on social media about Zach Cregger’s cinematic adaptation of the survival horror series. “It’s not arealResident Evil movie,” they’ve claimed. Were we watching the same film? Certainly, it doesn’t feature any of the familiar heroes – there’s no Leon, no Claire, no Ada Wong – and there’s a distinct lack of recognisable antagonists and well-known locations. Despite all of this, Cregger’s interpretation is one of the most accurate and interesting video game films ever made.On the surface, it’s about a zombifying virus that gets accidentally released in Raccoon City by the Umbrella Corporation. These are, of course, the foundations of the Resi mythos. More interestingly, Cregger seeks to replicate and explore the structural and narrative conventions of the series. In the film, the player character, hapless courier Bryan Hodukavich, is thrust into a viral outbreak, with no weapons and no idea what’s going on. He is then submerged into an uncanny shadow world of escalating peril and body horror. The film takes us through a series of locations dragged straight from the games – an abandoned farmhouse, a road tunnel crammed with abandoned cars, a hospital andthe obligatory sewer level. As he progresses, Bryan finds increasingly powerful weapons, from a handgun to an assault rifle – but he is always short on ammo. And there are typewriters in at least two scenes!Bryan’s understanding of the world is shaped, as in any Resident Evil game, through found footage (voice recordings, emails etc) and via short, enigmatic interchanges with non-player characters. There’s a sequence in the road tunnel where a recently infected young girl says to Bryan: “My mom bit me, I don’t know where she went.” This is a classic Resident Evil exchange: in one terse sentence she gives us narrative informationandan implied threat – the mother could be lurking anywhere nearby, waiting to pounce …Aware perhaps of online discourse, Creggerreleased a videoexplaining his vision for the movie, and how he has sought to reflect not just the fictitious universe of the games, but also the experience of playing them – that sense of quickly moving through a world of endlessly evolving horror. It’s also been interesting to see theories emerge about Bryan’s role as a sort of NPC precursor to a true lead character, leaving the hints, tips and ammo behind for someone capable to pick up.View image in fullscreenOmnipresent merchant … Resident Evil.Photograph: CapcomI always thought thatthe subsidiary non-playable characters in the early Resident Evil titles had the most interesting stories: affable old Barry Burton from the first game, cowardly helicopter pilot Brad Vickers fromResi 3,Resident Evil 4’s omnipresent merchant. “I’m interested in vulnerable characters, in normal human beings,” series creator Shinji Mikamionce told me. “The horror experience is most scary when the player really isn’t sure whether their character is going to live or die – death and survival need to be on a constant see-saw. If there’s a situation where you’re not 100% sure that you can avoid or defeat the enemies, if you feel maybe there’s a chance you’ll make it – that’s where horror lies.” Bryan Hodukavich lives in that space for the whole film.Cregger’s Resident Evil should perhaps be put alongside Kane Parsons’sBackroomsand Genki Kawamura’sExit 8as a movie that is as much an exploration of video game mechanics as it is any sort of translation. These movies make us feel like players, trapped in an unfamiliar nightmare world with its own rules, characters and temporal conventions, which we have to gradually unpeel. Cinema has always deconstructed other media, whether that’s the theatre (Les Enfants du Paradis, The Producers) or superhero comics (Unbreakable, Logan), and it’s fascinating to see video games having the same sort of scrutiny. This is, after all, the most self-reflexive medium – the audience is spectator and participant, the world is naturalistic yet necessarily artificial, with its yellow-painted walls (see:Keza’s newsletter just last week), and its indestructible barriers (to stop a player wandering out of the rendered environment).So yes, this is definitely a Resident Evil movie – it’s just that the camera pans away from Claire as she blasts another zombie, or Leon as he makes a daft wisecrack. Instead, it takes us just around the corner, to where the huddling masses of Raccoon City await their destiny, with maybe three bullets, two lines of dialogue and a voice recorder.What to playView image in fullscreenRagdoll-physics gore-fest … Happy Wheels is now available on Steam.Photograph: Jim Bonacci/Fancy ForceFirst appearing as a browser-based game back in 2010, the ragdoll-physics gore-festHappy Wheelsis now on Steam – and it’s just as ridiculous as ever. Your aim is to make it across an obstacle-laden landscape in whatever vehicle you’re given without falling into a chasm or being chainsawed in half, or stabbed or eaten. There are dozens of levels but you can also design your own and share them with the community. I’m not surprised the Steam version has been wishlisted by 750,000 players. This kind of hilarious, awkward, experimental game thrived in the Flash era of the noughties and it’s lovely to see a classic example return in all its blood-drenched, clipart-esque glory.Available on:PCEstimated playtime:Several laughable hoursWhat to readView image in fullscreenMicrosoft and Sony have filed for ad and monetisation patents, respectively.Photograph: Lucy Nicholson/ReutersIt’s been weird to watch Microsoft and Sony seemingly trying to find yet more ways to antagonise gamers after concerns over mass redundancies and the death of physical media. Two weeks ago, the gaming site Respawn FirstdiscoveredaMicrosoft patentto serve ads to Xbox players during down times in games, perhaps while loading a level or after a boss battle. Not to be outdone, Sony hasfiled a US patentfor technology allowing players to tap their phone or credit card on a PlayStation controller to pay for digital goods. Call me cynical, but perhaps more convenient advertising and monetisation models are not the best way to win back hearts and minds.Naughty Dog studio head Neil Druckmannhas revealedthat there are twoLast of Usprojects on the go, expanding on the canon of the first two games. Both are in the very early stages of development, and it’s not even known if they are games – they could include a new TV series, movie or graphic novel.Looking for somewhere nice to visit?Minecraftis getting itsfirst new dimension in 15 years,a particularly lush world named The Sift, filled with pastel-hued meadows, multicolour lakes and bunny-like mobs. It arrives in Minecraft Dungeons II this month, and will be in the main editions of the game next year.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat to clickAce Combat 8: Wings of Theve – brilliant aerial combat game fulfils the Top Gun fantasy | ★★★★★Playing video games with my 22-year-old son has brought me to tearsMeet the real-life Pokémon professors, the unsung heroes of competitive monster-battling‘Mum, where did my Robux go?’ :The Roblox scam targeting childrenQuestion BlockView image in fullscreenExtremely relaxing … Unpacking, a relaxing tidying game.Photograph: Witch BeamA cosy question fromSimon, via email:“Last year I ended up spending a lot of time supporting mydad during a roughpatch with this health, and this led to me playing a lot of Animal Crossing: Pocket Camp Complete on my iPhone. I havefound it really soothing during a challenging year but I’ve pretty much exhausted it.[Someone] recommended [playing] Stardew Valley but it doesn’t feel especially suited to playing on a relatively small mobile, nor my limited free time. Any suggestions? Hopefully nothing involving micro transactions?”Smartphone games can be an amazing tonic during tough times – I’m glad they helped you through them. If you’ve not playedUnpackingyet, it’s an extremely relaxing narrative tidying game with lots of subtle emotional touches. I also like the gentle platforming adventureSpiritfarerabout shepherding spirits to the afterlife. If you’re looking for more of an Animal Crossing vibe, there’sWilderness: Meadowfell, a lush exploration game set in a procedurally generated landscape, or try one of the classics from Japanese developer, Kairosoft, such as theGame Dev StoryorJumbo Airport Story. If you can stomach a couple of suggestions with very noninvasive in-app purchases My Leisure Time and Animal Restaurant, have been recommended to me as great life sims with bags of character.If you have a question for Question Block – or anything else to say about the newsletter – hit reply or email us atpushingbuttons@theguardian.com.Explore more on these topicsGamesPushing Buttons newsletterResident EvilAction gamesFilm adaptationsHorror filmsZombiesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Explosions of colour, cold war paranoia and hyper-erotic intimacy: five free shows to see | Art and design | The Guardian
description: In a new series, we review the best art exhibitions currently showing in commercial galleries, where entrance is free
Author: Eddy Frankel
Headline: In a new series, we review the best art exhibitions currently showing in commercial galleries, where entrance is free
Content: A bit of a squeeze … La DS (Cornaline) by Gabriel Orozco showing  at White Cube Bermondsey.Photograph: Matthew Chattle/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenA bit of a squeeze … La DS (Cornaline) by Gabriel Orozco showing  at White Cube Bermondsey.Photograph: Matthew Chattle/ShutterstockEddy Frankel's gallery crawlArt and designExplosions of colour, cold war paranoia and hyper-erotic intimacy: five free shows to seeIn a new series, we review the best art exhibitions currently showing in commercial galleries, where entrance is freeEddy FrankelWed 30 Sep 2026 10.29 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 11.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGabriel Orozco: Chronotopic★★★☆☆Walking into Gabriel Orozco’s show is like waking up with a headache and trying to piece together whatever the hell you did last night. Everything in the Mexican conceptualist’s exhibition is splintered, disjointed, a history you can’t make sense of.There’s a round of applause as you walk in, but the ovation morphs into the sound of rain. There are recognisable things here – cars, a football, cigarettes – but they don’t make sense. They’re suspended mid-air, broken into pieces, flipped upside down. An old Citroën has been split in half and glued back together too small, too narrow. There are kids’ toys and games, ceiling fans twirling with rolls of toilet paper attached to their blades, tree branches that have sprouted cigarette butts.So many artists deal with the idea of memory and the passing of time, but few manage to capture the slipperiness of it all like Gabriel Orozco. The whole show feels as if it’s about history, but stripped of its big names and important dates, leaving behind a bunch of fragmented memories instead.It’s all a bit too ephemeral, dense and self-satisfied, as if he can’t stop patting himself on the back for being so clever. But that doesn’t mean it isn’t good, it’s just odd, discomfiting art that makes you feel you’re about to forget your pin number.White Cube Bermondsey, London, until 8 NovemberMary Ramsden: The Feeling of What Happens★★★★★View image in fullscreenInstallation view of Mary Ramsden: The Feeling of What Happens.Photograph: Photo by Ben Westoby / Fine Art Documentation. Courtesy the artist and Pilar Corrias, LondonI like colour as much as the next guy, unless the next guy is Mary Ramsden, and then I might be beat. What you see first in the Yorkshire-based artist’s huge new abstracts is big washy swathes of colour, one canvas all neon pink and green lost in a haze of deep purple, another all mauve and lilac in a vastness of blue. They’re explosive bursts of hue and tone, totally mesmerising, abstraction at its abstractest.But look more, look longer, are those flower petals? Shafts of daylight through slats in a window? Everything is being constantly pulled between abstraction and reality, each work vacillating between still life and colourfield experimentation.Years ago Ramsden was painting love hearts over and over, as if she was abstracting her teenage diaries. Then she did the same thing to interior scenes of living rooms and furniture. Now nature has crept its way in. She says these works are all about the limits of consciousness and perception. Yeah, maybe, but what makes this show so good is its total, obsessive, overwhelming dedication to colour.Pilar Corrias, London, until 7 NovemberMartine Syms: Knot Eye★★★☆☆View image in fullscreenStill from RW-LO, 2026 by Martine Syms .Photograph: © Martine Syms. Courtesy the Artist, Sadie Coles HQ, Hoffman Donahue and Sprüth MagersI asked the ether – AKA people who follow me on social media – if anyone could explain what the hell Martine Syms’ show at Sadie Coles HQ is about, and someone replied “it’s about Martine Syms”. Which is as good an answer as any. The LA-based artist’s work is about brand Syms – literally, there’s a concept store of Syms merch, books and candles on the ground floor. But it’s about that idea in a wider societal sense too, about how we’re all brands: personalities constructed for display, amalgams of fiction, memory, capitalism and pop culture.There are two films upstairs. In the newest piece, three people at an afterparty talk about DMT and interdimensional travel, one starts tripping while the others fall asleep. Reality and fantasy crash together and never really get pulled apart.The other film follows a teenager who’s obsessed with an early 2000s reality star, an obsession that makes it impossible to distinguish a real person from the character they portray.None of it is brilliantly acted or scripted, but somehow it still sends you out into the street with a head full of questions. Syms lives in a world where the lines between who we are, who society wants us to be, and who we present to the world, are all being constantly blurred.Sadie Coles HQ, London, until 7 NovemberColin Self: Unseen★★★☆☆View image in fullscreenDetail from 365: A journey in that direction, 2000–2026  by Colin Self.Photograph: Courtesy the artist and Frith Street Gallery, London All works © the artist, DACS 2026If you had a penny for every exhibition that rediscovers some long-lost pop art innovator 60 years after they first nicked imagery from ads or cartoons, you’d have a ton of pennies. But Colin Self is worth adding to the purse.What sets Self apart from the other pop artists of his generation is an overwhelming atmosphere of paranoia and dread. While the rest of them were tackling ideas of consumerism and fame, Self was dealing with the aftermath of the second world war, the looming threat of nuclear annihilation in the cold war, and shivering with fear.A grinning face hangs by a thread as a Nazi bomb flies past in one work; a dog bares its teeth in front of a battery of missiles in another; he sculpts a war plane out of nails and fake leopard fur, he creates a portrait of a man made up of saws, knives, springs and tools. It’s atomic terror in a newly mechanised society that’s perpetually on the verge of self-annihilation. These early works are brilliant, pop art with all the fun and colour replaced by abject horror.Self is still at it, still making work at 85. Newer landscape paintings show his native East Anglia as a bleak old place filled with broken caravans and bomb craters. None of the more recent stuff here is brilliant, but it’s all still marked by that terror and dread.Frith Street Gallery, London, until 7 NovemberSomaya Critchlow: Pastels★★★★☆View image in fullscreenFigure in Front of Window, 2026, by Somaya Critchlow.Photograph: Courtesy of the artist and Maximillian William, LondonCritchlow’s erotic portraits have always been marked by a palpable sense of threat. The young English painter’s coquettish, 70s soft-focus nudes locked eyes with the viewer aggressively, confrontationally, as if they were on the verge of punching your lights out or throttling you with their negligees. But in this exhibition – her first since showing atDulwich Picture Gallerylast year – you don’t have to fear for your life.Instead, in these tiny, ultra-intimate pastels, Critchlow is luxuriating in form. These are unabashed celebrations of sensuality, nudity and eroticism. They’re still confident and confrontational figures, but you feel as if Critchlow is enjoying herself a bit more, letting things be sensual for their own sake, without being weighed down by anger and revenge. I miss the implication of violence, but they’re still really good, hyper-erotic, intimate images. They could also just be lulling you into a sense of false security – so watch your back.Maximillian William, London, until 14 NovemberExplore more on these topicsArt and designEddy Frankel's gallery crawlPaintingInstallationArtDulwich Picture GalleryfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Pussycat Dolls review – Nicole Scherzinger’s star power dominates fraught reunion | Music | The Guardian
description: First announced in 2019 and now launching with just three of the original lineup, the Dolls whip up a whirlwind of hair-flipping and put on a decent spectacle
Author: Alim Kheraj
Headline: First announced in 2019 and now launching with just three of the original lineup, the Dolls whip up a whirlwind of hair-flipping and put on a decent spectacle
Content: Back in formation … the Pussycat Dolls perform at Utilita Arena, Birmingham.Photograph: Jason Sheldon/Junction10/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenBack in formation … the Pussycat Dolls perform at Utilita Arena, Birmingham.Photograph: Jason Sheldon/Junction10/ShutterstockMusicReviewThe Pussycat Dolls review – Nicole Scherzinger’s star power dominates fraught reunionUtilita Arena, BirminghamFirst announced in 2019 and now launching with just three of the original lineup, the Dolls whip up a whirlwind of hair-flipping and put on a decent spectacleAlim KherajWed 30 Sep 2026 08.08 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 13.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe road to the Pussycat Dolls’ comeback tour has been fraught. Originally announced in 2019 with all but one of the group’s original members on board, the pandemic and then a legal dispute, led to its cancellation. After a few years of silence, three members –Nicole Scherzinger, Ashley Roberts and Kimberly Wyatt – shared plans for a 53-date world tour as a trio. Poor ticket sales nixed the US leg, though, while Maga-supporting former member Jessica Sutta alleged she was left out of the reunion because she was viewed as “a liability” (the group did not comment).Does a girlband ostensibly created as a dance troupe work as a trio? While Scherzinger’s voice pushed them into pop stardom – they scored six UK Top 3 hits in their initial 2005-09 run – their appeal was largely the fierce group choreography. On stage in Birmingham, they give it their best go. The nearly two-hour show is a whirlwind of hair-flipping, booty-shaking and synchronised strutting. Throughout When I Grow Up, Beep and I Don’t Need a Man, Scherzinger is still on lead vocals, predictably so after her recent Tony award-winning run on Broadway in Sunset Blvd. Roberts and Wyatt are given some time to shine, though: their solos amid the clacking pots-and-pans percussion of Wait a Minute feel pointed, as if to say that, yes, their mics are on.View image in fullscreenEntertaining, uneven … the Pussycat Dolls.Photograph: Jason Sheldon/Junction10/ShutterstockEach member also gets their own solo section to varying degrees of success. Wyatt’s involves a DJ set, while Roberts, showing off her dancing skills, is more restrained. Scherzinger gets the most airtime, beginning with a vocally impressive version of Sunset Blvd’s As If We Never Said Goodbye complete with X Factor-style cascading pyrotechnics, before her white gown is unwound like toilet paper for a breathless joyride through her solo material. Thundering Eurodance ballad Don’t Hold Your Breath and the cacophonous EDM of Wet are particular highlights.Pussycat dolls star Ashley Roberts looks back: ‘We had to be resilient – if your toe breaks, you still do the show’Read moreIt’s all very entertaining, but uneven, with Roberts and Wyatt struggling against Scherzinger’s imperious star power. With more members, this inequality may not have mattered, and in the final act – especially during honking 2020 single React and the slinky Buttons, which features a dance break by students from Wyatt’s dance academy – the scales seem to just about level out. Whether this imbalance is sustainable remains unknown, but it works for tonight’s spectacle, at least.ThePussycat Dollsplay Leeds First Direct Bank Arena, 2 October; then touring UK until 13 OctoberThis article was amended on 30 September 2026. Owing to a misunderstanding, an earlier version referred to Kimberly Wyatt playing a “faux DJ set”; to clarify, this was a live performance and not a recording.Explore more on these topicsMusicNicole ScherzingerPussycat DollsPop and rocklive music reviewsShareReuse this content

title: All at Sea review – faked death of ‘canoe man’ inspires waves of intrigue | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Fictionalising the true story of John Darwin, Alison Carr’s gripping two-hander follows the unexpected consequences of its antihero’s bid to escape debts
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: Fictionalising the true story of John Darwin, Alison Carr’s gripping two-hander follows the unexpected consequences of its antihero’s bid to escape debts
Content: Fleurs du mal … Phil Corbitt in All at Sea at Live theatre, Newcastle.Photograph: Von Fox PromotionsView image in fullscreenFleurs du mal … Phil Corbitt in All at Sea at Live theatre, Newcastle.Photograph: Von Fox PromotionsTheatreReviewAll at Sea review – faked death of ‘canoe man’ inspires waves of intrigueLive theatre, NewcastleFictionalising the true story of John Darwin, Alison Carr’s gripping two-hander follows the unexpected consequences of its antihero’s bid to escape debtsMark FisherWed 30 Sep 2026 08.53 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 08.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt sounds like a good plan. With credit cards maxed out, Colin Wilson will set off in his canoe and never come back. Once he is presumed dead, his wife, Deborah, will claim the life insurance. Pension and mortgage payouts will follow. Meanwhile, Colin will go into hiding until they can make a fresh start.View image in fullscreenA marriage capsized … Sarah Belcher and Phil Corbitt in All at Sea.Photograph: Von Fox PromotionsInspired by the true story of“canoe man” John Darwin, Alison Carr’s two-hander looks as though it will head into the sitcom territory ofCan You Keep a Secret?Like that BBC comedy, in which Mark Heap does a bad job at hiding, All at Sea considers the hurdles of staying out of sight. Where to go if someone comes around? What if the phone rings and you accidentally answer? How to stay sane?But unlike that show, Carr plays it for drama, not laughs. The further we go into Maria Crocker’s production, the more the challenges are not just practical but psychological. At first, this is primarily to do with Colin’s life in limbo. Played by Phil Corbitt, he is the captain relegated to the subs bench, at once controlling and ineffectual. It drives him to distraction.But the real intrigue is what happens to Deborah. Played by Sarah Belcher, she remains engaged with the world. Having gone through the motions of grieving, she finds herself living an emotionally independent life. It is as if Colin really were dead.While nothing changes in the prison of their home – in a functional if too literal design by Hannah Sibai – things continue to evolve for Deborah: the people she meets, the clothes she wears, the self-worth she feels. Slowly, subtly, the man she loved looks ever more patronising, jealously keeping her in check.Corbitt and Belcher are excellent at the push-pull of contradictory emotions, their troubling chemistry making the play’s grisly conclusion feel necessary.AtLive theatre, Newcastle, until 10 October and atStephen Joseph theatre, Scarborough, 16–31 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTheatreStephen Joseph theatreJohn Darwin canoe disappearancereviewsShareReuse this content

title: The secret lives of men who read romance books: ‘My life is full of love, so I’m drawn to them’ | Romance books | The Guardian
description: It’s often assumed straight men are not interested in romantic fiction – but many are sharing their passion in forums online
Author: Amandas Ong
Headline: It’s often assumed straight men are not interested in romantic fiction – but many are sharing their passion in forums online
Content: The bromantasy boom: why are so many men secretly obsessed with romance novels?Illustration: Laurie Avon/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe bromantasy boom: why are so many men secretly obsessed with romance novels?Illustration: Laurie Avon/The GuardianRomance booksThe secret lives of men who read romance books: ‘My life is full of love, so I’m drawn to them’It’s often assumed straight men are not interested in romantic fiction – but many are sharing their passion in forums onlineAmandas OngWed 30 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter a tiring day as a school maintenance worker, 28-year-old Paul loves nothing more than unwinding with a good romance novel – ideally one with a fantasy or horror element to it. He reads five or six a month – most recently Love Bytes, about an 8ft-tall werewolf woman who runs an extremely successful AI company and falls in love with a handsome ballroom instructor.Paul got into romance fiction via what he calls its “more traditional” side – such as the Regency romance series Bridgerton. He is partially sighted, so he mostly reads on his Kindle, where he can adjust the font size. In the first Bridgerton novel, “Simon, the main character, has a speech impediment that he has to work through,” says Paul. “I’m more attached to that one. Typically, I don’t come across disabled protagonists that much.”He doesn’t talk to anyone about his love of romance novels, communicating only with other users of a Discord channel called Romance for Men. “I was on a separate Reddit thread for book recommendations and someone asked if there’s romance out there for men,” he says. “And half of the comments were just, ‘Oh, you mean porn?’”View image in fullscreenThe Bridgerton TV series is based on the Regency romance novels.Photograph: NetflixStraight men like Paul who read and write romance are largely invisible to the wider world. Women are the genre’s main audience, followed by queer romance, which is a well documented success. The fifth volume of Alice Oseman’s Heartstopper – about the friendship between two teenage boys blossoming into love – is the UK’s fastest-selling graphic novel and a hit Netflix show, while novelists such as Alexis Hall are widely read and critically acclaimed. But in this corner of publishing, straight men are rarely seen and usually stigmatised.At Mills & Boon, the best known publisher of romantic fiction, men account for only 4% of sales, according to an editorial director, whileless than 2%of the UK’s Romantic Novelists’ Association is male. Almost nothing is known about how many men read romantic fiction, and why.For those I spoke to, however, reading romance is more than just entertainment. It offers a kind of liberation, allowing them to feel deeply, imagine being desired, and accept parts of themselves that conventional masculinity has little room for. Many would only speak anonymously, worried about being misunderstood or mocked.Before books, Paul’s path into romance began with role-playing video games in his teens: “You have some non-playable characters who are your companions, and you can build romantic relationships with them as you go along.” He gravitated towards playing aggressive male characters rallying different factions to war, realising later that the diplomatic approach worked better. The appeal of these characters was that they were so different from him. “I’m downright afraid of conflicts, and if there’s an argument, I just want to hide,” he says.In 2015, Paul learned that Stephenie Meyer, author of the vampire romance Twilight, had released a gender-flipped version of the book. “As a teenager, it was so cool to just hate on Twilight. But I read it anyway, and there’s a moment where Edythe, the vampire, tells the male protagonist that she is tired of trying to stay away from him. That’s when it hit. There’s a fantasy aspect in being wanted that badly.” Today, he seeks out novels known to fans as romance for men (RFM), such as Charlotte’s Reject by KR Treadway, which features a female character who’s “kind of scary”. “With women’s romance, it’s always the man being the aggressor,” he says. “Reading men’s romance is often the opposite, and it made me realise I’m fine being the way I am. I’m able to accept myself more, because I’ve seen that this is a possible dynamic in romantic relationships.”View image in fullscreenMen account for only 4% of sales of Mills & Boon books.Photograph: AlamyAndrew’s entry into romance was a deliberate experiment. The 31-year-old, who works in tech, is a huge lover of sci-fi and fantasy who considers himself “on the feminist side of the world”. He couldn’t look past the reality that the bulk of the dialogue in his favourite books was written by men and between men. “I just got really bored,” he says.Wandering around a bookshop three years ago, he made it his mission to pick up a book by a female author, and found Rebecca Yarros’ Fourth Wing, about the dragon-riding, lightning-wielding Violet Sorrengail. “I had very little context and just bought it. I didn’t know what romance or romantasy was,” he says. “It was refreshing to see things from the perspective of a female protagonist. I’d also never read a fantasy book that had so much in it about romance and sex.”Since then, Andrew has sought out other romantasy writers, from Penn Cole to Carissa Broadbent and Sarah J Maas. And he has introduced his wife to the genre. “She has a women’s book club, and they were all very sceptical in general, and then they all got hooked on it,” he says.Romantasy is not “grim” in the way that pornography is, Andrew says, but he would still blush at publicly buying books that are “substantially about sex”. “I like the anonymity of reading it on my phone or on Kindle, as opposed to a physical book on the tube,” he says. Still, he wonders if the genre’s constant idealisation of sex comes with a cost. “Every time they do it, it’s the best thing that’s ever happened to them. I can imagine there being some subtle toxic element to it, because real-life sex could be a bit of a letdown.”View image in fullscreenIt is not known how many men read romantic fiction.Photograph: Kosijerphotography/Getty ImagesAli, 54, a former investment banker, had his “first dedicated exposure to romance” 40-odd years ago. His younger sister had a subscription to the now defunct teen magazine Jackie, and as a teenager he used to read its romance photo-strips. “They were all boy-meets-girl stories,” he remembers. Another publication that stuck with him was Judy Blume’s Forever, a book so candid in its treatment of teenage sex that it has been targeted by censors since it was published in 1975. Later, as a student journalist at Oxford, Ali had the chance to interview Barbara Cartland, the undisputed queen of paperback romances. “It’s not a momentous event that changed my life,” he says, “but it’s quite funny to think about now.”A voracious reader, from contemporary historical romance writers such as Tessa Dare and Evie Dunmore to Jane Austen and Daphne du Maurier, Ali is not bothered by criticism that the genre is formulaic. Even Shakespeare, he points out, tells you upfront if a play you’ll be watching is a tragedy or comedy; the latter “will end with a wedding, probably more than one”. “Formulas are a blessing and a curse. The curse is when it’s done badly, and everyone yawns,” he says. “But when done right, there are huge payoffs – the dark moments, the happy endings.”Although Ali is happy to talk about romance “all day long”, he observes that other readers – male and female – might feel the need to lie about what they read to look good. He points to a market research phenomenon: “Everyone says they listen to Radio 3 or 4, but actually they all listen to Radio 2, right? And I think this insecurity is a genuine problem.”After studying creative writing at Kingston University in his 40s, Ali is now in two writers’ groups, where he’s notably the only person writing romance. He’s since written a series of three historical romance novels, all set in Mayfair in the late Victorian era. The first will be published soon, under the pen name Ali Murphy – combining his name and his wife’s birth name. “I chose it as a gender-neutral name,” he says. “I’m not trying to mislead people. But I don’t want anyone to pick up the book and say, oh God, it’s a bloke writing romance.”While Ali and Andrew prefer more mainstream romance, Paul and many other men are fans of a lesser-known strand of the genre. RFM is mostly self-published and sold digitally. It has a significant following: more than 10,000 weekly visitors to its dedicated Reddit, and a thriving Discord community where book recommendations are exchanged and discussed.Fans caution against any single definition of what RFM is, but agree that some patterns recur. It is typically written from the perspective of an ordinary man whose love interest is an unusually powerful woman – a straightforward inversion of narrative conventions in mainstream romance, where the heroine is expected to be relatable and the hero mythologised. Many readers indicate that the central crisis in RFM is often external to the couple’s relationship, such as a war or a shared enemy, rather than emerging from misunderstandings or jealousy between the two leads. There’s also a long-running argument about “harem” fiction, where one man is paired with several women. Some consider it the genre’s biggest success, while others don’t think it’s romance at all.Thirty-three-year-old Jonny Rogers works in finance. He reads copiously, has finished 90 books this year, and loves everything from Dostoevsky to the popular RFM series Would You Love a Monster Girl?, which he finished in six days. Two-thirds of what he reads is romance, most of it RFM.“I watched Titanic when I was about 11 and it really moved me,” he says. “I know it’s a little corny, but I just loved the idea of meeting someone and falling in love the way Jack and Rose did.” Wanting more of that feeling on the page, Jonny stumbled upon The Rosie Project, Graeme Simsion’s novel about an awkward, probably autistic man’s search for love. “I think there may have been some kinship there,” he says, explaining that he suspects he’s on the spectrum himself but is undiagnosed. Years later, a friend recommended Sarah J Maas’s A Court of Thorns and Roses. He read it in a week, then found his way to the RFM Reddit.View image in fullscreen‘I just loved the idea of falling in love the way Jack and Rose did.’Photograph: Photo Credit: Merie Weismiller Wallace/20th Century Fox/AllstarWhat keeps him riveted isn’t the fantastical trappings – spaceship battles, magic-wielding warrior women – so much as what’s underneath. “I just love following along with two people who fall in love with each other,” he says. “It’s the most human thing in the world, and it’s really magical.” He’s drawn to books with strongly written female leads, and insists a well written romance can be enjoyed by anyone.His girlfriend encouraged him to expand a short writing experiment into something longer. This became Daniel’s Dilemma, a novel about a young man falling for his best friend’s mother, warmly received by the RFM community. He chose the pen name Jonny Rogers not out of shame, he says, but caution: the book contains some explicit content, and “I don’t want my grandma or parents to buy my book and know I wrote that scene”. When he read his girlfriend a date scene between the two leads, she asked him: “That’s so romantic. How come you’re never that romantic with me?”Jonny’s close male friends know about his foray into writing. “None of them have actually bought it,” he says with a laugh. “I think when I told them, they were picturing erotica.” Although he’s never been bullied or insulted for enjoying romance, it’s not information that he volunteers outside his inner circle.One of RFM’s often-recommended authors is DH Willison, 58. He’s known for his Tales of Arvia series, set in a fantasy world where dragons and other creatures are central characters rather than obstacles for humans to conquer, and where unconventional pairings, such as a harpy and an incompetent adventurer, are ubiquitous.Willison feels he’s found more resistance among fellow writers than readers. At one writers’ group, someone mentioned finding an old pulp romance novel and gleefully picking it apart line by line as proof of the poor quality of romance stories, he recalls. In another writing group, he was told that a “real” romance requires the male and female leads to conform to certain rigid roles, down to genre conventions such as the “age gap” trope, which is assumed by default to mean an older man. The opposite is known as a “reverse age gap”. Willison thinks the distinction is “kind of silly”. This sort of gendered thinking, he adds, is self-fulfilling when extended to marketing: “I think romance is for everyone, but if you’re writing and selling with only women in mind, then you end up appealing only to women.”The other, more upmarket end of the romance spectrum mostly leaves sex off the page, together with the more obvious conventions. Mike Gayle and Bobby Palmer write at this more literary end, and publish under their own names.Gayle, 55, has been writing about love and relationships since his 1998 debut My Legendary Girlfriend, about a young man struggling to recover from heartbreak. He won the Romantic Novelists’ Association’s outstanding achievement award in2021, becoming the first man to do so, joining names including Jilly Cooper and Joanna Trollope. “I know of female readers who find it a breath of fresh air to read about love from a man’s perspective,” he says. “The more we’re exposed to different perspectives, the more we see we can both be right.”View image in fullscreen‘True romance is about staying together and making it work’ … Mike Gayle.Photograph: Hodder & StoughtonOver the years, Gayle has become more interested in writing about what happens after couples get together, rather than the lead-up – which is what most romances focus on. “It’s much sexier to write about the getting together,” he says. “But true romance is about staying together and making it work.” His writing has evolved in line with his personal life. “I was in my 20s, and kind of obsessed with finding ‘the one’. Now that I’ve seen relationships go by the wayside and taken for granted, I wanted to write about something deeper and more substantial.”Gayle’s next novel, Not Quite Myself, will be published in 2027. It’s co-written with his wife, Claire, and explores the lives of a couple who find themselves body-swapped after their youngest son goes to university. “It’s interesting to look at that stage of life where the only thing really keeping the couple together as a unit is the fact that they’ve got kids in the house,” he says. “How do you begin seeing your partner as a separate person again, from a fresh perspective?”Where Gayle now writes about what happens after the happy ending, Palmer, 33, is upending expectations around how romantic stories are told with his recently published third novel, Main Characters. It’s narrated entirely by the people around the central couple – but not the couple themselves – so that their relationship stays, as he puts it, “this kind of beautiful, private thing”, where readers never learn directly what the leads think or feel about each other.It’s also – in a departure from his previous books – being marketed as romance in the UK, with a bright pink cover. He’s noticed already that fewer men are getting in touch about it than with his other work.It’s their loss, of course, though not every man needs romantic fiction to teach them anything. Jonny, for his part, doesn’t think it has shaped him. “I’ve had a life filled with love,” he says. “Rather than romantic novels shaping my life, it’s actually that my life has been so full of love that I’m drawn to them.”Some names have been changedDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: ‘The Savage Skulls were the most dangerous gang in the Bronx’: Jean-Pierre Laffont’s best photograph | Art and design | The Guardian
description: ‘I’d read stories about gangs killing drug-pushers who targeted young people. Police would find their bodies at the bottom of five-storey buildings. I didn’t want to go looking for them alone’
Author: Chris Broughton
Headline: ‘I’d read stories about gangs killing drug-pushers who targeted young people. Police would find their bodies at the bottom of five-storey buildings. I didn’t want to go looking for them alone’
Content: ‘If you want just to look at our life, you’re welcome’ … New York street gang Savage Skulls by Jean-Pierre Laffont, 1972.Photograph: Jean-Pierre LaffontView image in fullscreen‘If you want just to look at our life, you’re welcome’ … New York street gang Savage Skulls by Jean-Pierre Laffont, 1972.Photograph: Jean-Pierre LaffontMy best shotArt and design‘The Savage Skulls were the most dangerous gang in the Bronx’: Jean-Pierre Laffont’s best photograph‘I’d read stories about gangs killing drug-pushers who targeted young people. Police would find their bodies at the bottom of five-storey buildings. I didn’t want to go looking for them alone’Interview byChris BroughtonWed 30 Sep 2026 10.41 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 16.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe late 1960s and most of the 1970s were a difficult time forNew York. I’d moved there from France in 1965 with a reporter friend and a plan to start a little agency, but soon found myself working alone. It could be a dangerous city, especially at night, but I enjoyed taking pictures of everyday life around me. In 1969, I became the first foreign correspondent for the Paris-based Gamma Agency, but always insisted on working on personal projects rather than assignments.Reading the New York Times in 1972, I would see stories about gangs in the Bronx that were killing drug-pushers who targeted young people in the area. The police would find their bodies on the kerb at the bottom of five-storey buildings they’d been thrown off. The gangs included the Savage Nomads and the Dirty Dozen, but the one I was most interested in was the most dangerous: the Savage Skulls.I didn’t want to go looking for them alone, so I drove with a French cameraman friend to Fox Street in the Hunts Point neighbourhood. As soon as we spotted members of the gang on the sidewalk, we stopped and wound down the window and they immediately came over wanting to know who we were. When they realised we were French and didn’t want to interview them, they said: “If you want just to look at our life, you’re welcome.” We spent that afternoon with them, then I came back alone the following day.double quotation markI didn’t meet their chief because he was in hospital having taken a bullet to the abdomenThe gang showed me their territory: the basement where they had their club, played music and kept a lot of their weapons, and the sidewalks where Savage Skulls tags appeared on walls, doors and trash cans. They also spent a lot of time on a nearby basketball court. They didn’t actually play basketball – they just fought all the time, play-fighting, like little cats.While on the court with them, I said: “OK, I’ll take a picture of you.” They immediately went over to the fence and got into the formation you see in the picture. I didn’t ask them to do that: it was completely spontaneous. They were keen to show off the sleeveless denim vests they wore, with a skull and crossbones painted on the back. You can see here how young they were. I think the youngest member I photographed was 13 and none of them were much older than 20. The photograph reminds me of a scene from West Side Story, but I don’t think members of the Savage Skulls ever left the Bronx.When I told the police about my project, they warned me they couldn’t offer any protection, but while I was with the gang one time they stopped a patrol car and I took a picture of them having a friendly chat with the officers inside. The members were mostly Puerto Rican and spoke Spanish to one another, so we communicated in broken English. I hardly spoke English then, so I think they considered me a fellow outsider. We had an easy connection and they seemed very relaxed, even exchanging guns in front of me. I didn’t meet their chief during the few days I spent with them because he was in hospital at the time, having taken a bullet to the abdomen.Last year, a woman called to ask if I remembered a photograph I’d taken of some of the gang members walking down the street, side by side, and if I recalled one of the people in it being a woman. When I told her I remembered the picture and the woman very well, she said: “That was my mother, and she died yesterday.” She asked for a copy, saying this was the only picture of her mother that she knew.As it happened, her mother appeared in a few more of my pictures from the time, including this one, where you can see her in front of the fence. I sent some big prints for the funeral. It was a very moving moment for me, because it made me realise that life goes on. Those kids I photographed in 1972 weren’t kids any more.Jean-Pierre Laffont: Rebels with a Causeis published by Damiani.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sam MatamorosJean-Pierre Laffont’s CVBorn:French Algeria, 1935.High point:Being made a Knight of the Order of the Legion of Honour for 60 years at the service of photojournalism in 2023.Top tip:My way of working is over, and the profession of photojournalist is being rewritten; it is up to young photojournalists to rewrite it. Yet there are essential things that define the profession and I have a few pieces of advice: go to museums, look at the work of the great photographers who inspire you, research the stories you want to cover, be observant, humble and curious – and don’t forget that you are doing the most beautiful job in the world. This profession is more important than ever and still makes people dream.Explore more on these topicsArt and designMy best shotGangsPhotographyYoung peopleSocial historyNew YorkfeaturesShareReuse this content
