title: Van Gogh goes on display before sale of ‘almost mythical’ private collection | Vincent van Gogh | The Guardian
description: Châtaigniers en fleurs, valued at $180m, to be auctioned along with 11 other works by likes of Cézanne and Monet
Author: Kim Willsher
Headline: Châtaigniers en fleurs, valued at $180m, to be auctioned along with 11 other works by likes of Cézanne and Monet
Content: Châtaigniers en fleurs was painted in May 1890 shortly after Van Gogh arrived in Auvers-sur-Oise. It and the other works have not been seen in public in decades.Photograph: Sotheby's New York/Blaquier-Arrieta collectionView image in fullscreenChâtaigniers en fleurs was painted in May 1890 shortly after Van Gogh arrived in Auvers-sur-Oise. It and the other works have not been seen in public in decades.Photograph: Sotheby's New York/Blaquier-Arrieta collectionVincent van GoghVan Gogh goes on display before sale of ‘almost mythical’ private collectionChâtaigniers en fleurs, valued at $180m, to be auctioned along with 11 other works by likes of Cézanne and MonetKim Willsherin ParisWed 30 Sep 2026 06.11 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 16.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor more than 50 years it was held in a private art collection with an “almost mythical status” that was likened to a miniature version of Paris’s Musée d’Orsay.But on Wednesday a painting byVincent van Goghcreated during the last two months of his life has gone on display before it is put up for auction with a value of $180m (£136m).Châtaigniers en fleurs (Chestnut Trees in Flower) was painted in May 1890 shortly after Van Gogh arrived in the French village of Auvers-sur-Oise. He died just weeks later.Most Van Gogh works from this period now hang in the world’s leading museums – but Châtaigniers en fleurs is one of 12 impressionist and modern masterpieces from the collection of the Argentinian collector Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier, who died in 2020.View image in fullscreenFleurs dans une coupe by Paul Gauguin is among the 12 works up for sale.Photograph: Sotheby’s New York/Blaquier-Arrieta collectionPhilip Hook, a former director of impressionist and modern art at the auction house Sotheby’s and a regular expert on BBC One’s Antiques Roadshow, said the opening of the collection to buyers was a “historic moment”.“For decades the Blaquier-Arrieta collection has been the stuff of legend: whispered about, kept from public view, it has attained an almost mythical status in the art world,” he said.“One of the last great private collections of impressionist and post-impressionist art, it was formed when major examples by the great names were still within reach.”View image in fullscreenPaul Cézanne’s Arlequin is valued at $150m.Photograph: Sotheby’s New York/Blaquier-Arrieta collectionThe Sotheby’s auction will also include Paul Cézanne’s Harlequin, painted in the late 19th century and valued at $150m.They will be sold along with 10 other significant works by Camille Pissarro, Pierre-Auguste Renoir, Edgar Degas, Claude Monet, Paul Gauguin, Alfred Sisley, André Derain, Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec and Maurice de Vlaminck.All 12 paintings, which are expected to fetch more than $450m in total, have gone on display at Sotheby’s in London on Wednesday for two days before being flown to Taipei, then Hong Kong and Paris before the auction on 18 November in New York.View image in fullscreenClaude Monet’s Le Jardin des Tuileries.Photograph: Sotheby’s New York/Blaquier-Arrieta collectionVan Gogh painted at least four major works featuring chestnut trees in Auvers-sur-Oise during a period of optimism and energy after his discharge from a psychiatric hospital at Saint-Rémy-de-Provence. After his death in July 1890, Châtaigniers en fleurs passed to his brother, Theo. A subsequent owner was George Gard “Buddy” DeSylva, the US songwriter and film producer who co-founded Capitol Records.It is one of only eight paintings Van Gogh produced in Auvers that are in private hands.View image in fullscreenAndré Derain’s Bâteaux au port de Collioure was painted in 1905.Photograph: Sotheby’s New York/Blaquier-Arrieta collectionSimon Shaw, a senior art adviser at Sotheby’s, said the collection felt “like a small museum – a miniature Musée d’Orsay, now opening its doors for the very first time”.Explore more on these topicsVincent van GoghPaintingArtnewsShareReuse this content

title: Jess Cartner-Morley on fashion: now is the perfect time to flash some lace | Fashion | The Guardian
description: What you need to lift your autumn wardrobe is something flimsy, flirty and unconventional
Author: Jess Cartner-Morley
Headline: What you need to lift your autumn wardrobe is something flimsy, flirty and unconventional
Content: Video: David Newby/The Guardian. Styling: Melanie WilkinsonGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Jess Cartner-Morley on fashionFashionJess Cartner-Morley on fashion: now is the perfect time to flash some laceWhat you need to lift your autumn wardrobe is something flimsy, flirty and unconventionalJess Cartner-MorleyWed 30 Sep 2026 10.28 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 13.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt this time of year, my job is mostly banging on about jumpers. Season of mists and mellow fruitfulness and merino sweaters, as Keats would surely have written had he been on Substack. Cosiness is next to godliness.I can worship at the altar of cashmere with the best of them. I can extol the virtues of a sweater in tones normally reserved for fine wines and newborn babies. But today I have a rather different proposition for your autumn wardrobe. The best fillip for your shoulder-season style is not a thick layer, but the opposite. What you need to lift your look right now is something flimsy, flirty, with an edging of lace. A sorbet-coloured lace-edged tank top that is virtually a camisole. A slinky black slip skirt with a lace hem. Something with a frill, that has the thrill of lingerie.Not on its own, obviously, or you will catch your death. You are going to wear your lacy little whatnot and then you are going to partly cover it up by wearing something on top, and this isthe whole point.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: David Newby/The GuardianLet me explain. Lace is beautiful, and rich in romance and storytelling – it is the stuff of weddings and funerals, after all. But it is also about sex. And sex appeal is key to what is excellent about lace. This is self-evidently useful if you are dressing for a date. But here’s the funny thing: oddly, it is also true if you are dressing for a meeting. Not because you are trying to get off with your colleagues (none of my business, obviously, but people are touchy about that kind of thing these days, so maybe don’t?) but because lace reminds people of lingerie, which reminds them of skin, which reminds them that you are a human being. And reminding other people that you are a human being with flesh and blood and feelings is surely helpful in almost any interaction.double quotation markSlip a lacy camisole under a jacket and you get a wink to the knicker drawer without putting it all out thereIn summer, when you aren’t wearing very much, lace can be a bit too straight-up saucy. No slut-shaming here; it’s just that I think many of us would like our vibe to land somewhere a little more subtle. Which is why this time of year, when you can slip a lace-edged camisole under a light jacket, or team a lace-trim skirt with a chunky sweater, is the best time to wear lace. You get a wink to the knicker drawer without putting it all out there.Miuccia Prada is the queen of this. At Miu Miu’s autumn show, amid the sensible coats and pencil skirts, there were peachy little camisoles and filmy dresses with scalloped underlayers. None of it felt especially come-hither. The lace was decently chaperoned by its accoutrements. Worn with proper skirts, coats and gloves, it looked less like undressing than an intriguing chink in the armour.At Saint Laurent in Paris, barely there lace skirts were balanced by teddy-bear plush faux-fur jackets. At Khaite in New York, flutters of lace came spliced with leather jackets or trousers. This sort of mismatch makes lace sing. Lace with more lace is lingerie; lace with something that looks capable of surviving a motorcycle accident is an outfit. Alexa Chung has long understood that a bit of lace becomes infinitely cooler when you put a buttoned-up cardigan on top.Jess Cartner-Morley on fashion: this sweltering summer, I finally stopped giving a tuckRead moreThe key phrase here isa bit of lace. We are not going full Miss Havisham. You don’t want to look as though there’s a wedding cake waiting for you in the next room. A couple of centimetres peeking from beneath a jumper is plenty. If you’re wearing a deep V-neck sweater, a lace-trimmed bra that accidentally-on-purpose is just visible at the neckline can be excellent. The point is the contrast: wool and skin, sensible and suggestive, covered-up with a wink to being the opposite. Knitwear will get its flowers soon enough, when it is too cold for leaving buttons undone. But in these last moments before the sun disappears till March, let a bit of lace shine. Keats had beauty and truth. I’ll settle for cashmere and a glimpse of a fancy bra.Styling: Melanie Wilkinson. Model: Moli at Milk. Styling assistant: Charlotte Gornall. Hair and makeup: Sophie Higginson usingDavines and Dr Sam’sSkincare.Necklace, £119, Daisy.Jacket, £55, Marks & Spencer.Top, £55.99,andbag, £29.99, bothMango.Skirt, £260, Essentiel Antwerp.Shoes, £140, VagabondExplore more on these topicsFashionJess Cartner-Morley on fashionWomenfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The best dehumidifiers: 14 favourites to beat damp and cut bills, tested | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Fed up with condensation, mould and musty smells? A dehumidifier could help – plus, they’re a cheaper way to dry laundry compared with tumble dryers
Author: Caramel Quin
Headline: Fed up with condensation, mould and musty smells? A dehumidifier could help – plus, they’re a cheaper way to dry laundry compared with tumble dryers
Content: View image in fullscreenGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterLife and styleReviewThe best dehumidifiers: 14 favourites to beat damp and cut bills, testedFed up with condensation, mould and musty smells? A dehumidifier could help – plus, they’re a cheaper way to dry laundry compared with tumble dryersThe best electric blankets and heated throws, tested by our expertCaramel QuinWed 30 Sep 2026 10.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou don’t have to live in the American deep south to feel the effects of humidity. At home, just breathing makes the air more humid, let alone cooking or showering.And when it gets too humid, it’s bad for our health as well as our homes. In fact, the two are connected: humidity lets mould and dust mites flourish – and they, in turn, can trigger asthma and allergies.Dehumidifiers can make your indoor environment more comfortable by reducing the amount of moisture in the air. Because of this, they’re also a great laundry-drying hack. I use mine to dry clothes fast, and for a fraction of the cost of tumble drying.Not sure if you need one? You can buy a hygrometer cheaply –the one I used for testing cost less than £10– to check your home’s relative humidity and make an informed decision. Should you opt to buy one, do your research at reputable sources (like, hint, the Filter). Researching this piece, I was shocked to learn thatcustomers had been dupedinto buying very basic dehumidifiers for well over the odds.At a glanceBest dehumidifier overallEbac4650e£309.99 at EbacBest budget dehumidifierVonHausSmart dehumidifier with laundry mode£144.99 at AmazonBest combined dehumidifier and air purifierDevolaPlatinum hybrid DVHA20L£161.99 at DevolaBest dehumidifier for drying laundryDuuxBora Smart£279.99 at DuuxBest quiet dehumidifierMeacoDryArete Two£299 at John LewisBest compact dehumidifierDevolaDVH12L£135.99 at DevolaWhy you should trust meI’m an award-winning consumer technology journalist with decades of experience testing electrical appliances; I’ve been reviewing gadgets for almost 30 years. I live in a terrace house with a lovely number of children and far too many pets, so there’s lots of laundry: I use a dehumidifier to dry clothes. I’ve also been known to use one for speedy DIY, drying plaster and paint faster.How I testedView image in fullscreenEach dehumidifier’s performance, energy consumption and noise levels were recorded.Photograph: Caramel Quin/The GuardianI selected 14 dehumidifiers from leading brands to test, then set them up and used them, each for several days. I used a power meter to measure how much electricity (and therefore money and carbon) they use. Using the Sound Meter app, I measured the noise from 1m away in decibels (dB) on multiple occasions – the figures featured here are all the ones that I measured at home, in consistent conditions, so they often differ from manufacturers’ official figures, which are measured in lab conditions but in inconsistent ways. More subjectively, I paid attention to the quality of the sound – was it annoying, gurgly, hard to ignore, easy to fall asleep to? And I measured each dehumidifier’s size.To measure the room’s humidity while testing, I used a digital hygrometer held 1m away (though humidity would be roughly the same elsewhere in the room), and a thermometer to check the temperature. Dehumidifiers fill a tank with water they have extracted from the air, so one measure of how good a job they’ve done is to measure how much water is in there – which I did, using a jug.Because conditions vary from moment to moment and room to room, it was impossible to test each one in precisely the same conditions. As such, I’ve only mentioned the results of these not-so-scientific tests when they stood out.After testing, any dehumidifiers that weren’t collected by manufacturers were donated toFurnishing Futures, a charity that fully furnishes the empty social housing in which women and children are placed after surviving domestic abuse.The best dehumidifiers in 2026View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Caramel Quin/The GuardianBest dehumidifier overall:Ebac 4650eEbac4650efrom£309.99£309.99 at Ebac£329 at ArgosWhat we loveBritish-made, long warranty, and great performanceWhat we don’t loveThere’s no window to see how full the water tank isView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Caramel Quin/The Guardian£309.99 at Ebac£329 at ArgosThis is the priciest dehumidifier on test, but it’s worth the money. It’s large but luggable, with a single deep handle on the rear that makes it easy to carry and an integrated cable tidy on the back that’s great when you want to store it.Why we love itI like the design. For example, a flap at the front opens to reveal a black water tank that’s easy to empty, with water coming out of just one hole (most water tanks are messier).The small display is colourful, and there’s a good range of modes, including laundry. A smart control feature remembers your home’s humidity levels and kicks in only when the levels start to rise: in a home that doesn’t have major damp problems, this will save a lot of electricity. It can be controlled via an app, and it also comes with an activated carbon filter for removing unwanted smells.Performance was good, bringing relative humidity down by 4% in a short time, and its capacity and smart controls make it a great all-rounder. You can simply leave it switched on and trust it to manage your home’s humidity levels without wasting electricity. The Ebac’s sound was inoffensive, too: I could definitely sleep with it on. It’s pretty energy efficient, and it’s made in north-east England, so its carbon footprint is lower than some other models. It also comes with a four-year warranty if bought directly from the brand.It’s a shame that …there’s no window to inspect the fill level.Dimensions:34 x 27 x 54cm (WDH)Dailyextraction rate:18lTank capacity:3.5lPeak power use on test:180WAverage noise level on top setting:10dBTarget humidity range:35-80%Laundry setting?YesRunning costs:5p/hourEbac4650efrom£309.99£309.99 at Ebac£329 at ArgosWhat we loveBritish-made, long warranty, and great performanceWhat we don’t loveThere’s no window to see how full the water tank isBest budget dehumidifier:VonHaus smart dehumidifier with laundry modeVonHausSmart dehumidifier with laundry modefrom£144.99£144.99 at VonHaus£144.99 at AmazonWhat we loveGreat value, quiet and app controlWhat we don’t loveThe air filtration is basicView image in fullscreen£144.99 at VonHaus£144.99 at AmazonAt the time of writing, a discount brings this dehumidifier’s price down to less than £150. Even at full price, though, it’s a bargain.Why we love itAlongside a laundry mode, a sleep mode brings down volume levels from an already quiet 15dB to 10dB by slowing the fan speed, and it turns off the screen so the lights won’t disturb you.Other modes include auto, which turns the machine off when it reaches the target relative humidity, and continuous, which means it won’t turn off until the tank is full. An app lets you control it from your phone or with Google Home or Amazon Alexa. Simple coloured lights on the front give a visual indicator of what mode it’s in.It’s a great all-rounder for the price. On test, it started cutting humidity levels within minutes, and over a couple of hours, it brought relative humidity down by at least 5%, pulling 450ml of water out of the air. It’s good for drying laundry and tackling damp – the only corner cut, when compared with pricier models, is Hepa air filtration.If you’re not sure whether or not to invest in a dehumidifier, this is a good buy for the price.It’s a shame that …it only has a washable dust filter, not Hepa air purification, even though there looks to be enough room for a larger filter.Dimensions:31 x 24 x 49cm (WDH)Dailyextraction rate:20lTank capacity:4.5lPeak power use on test:290WAverage noise level on top setting:15dBTarget humidity range:30-80%Laundry setting?YesRunning costs:8p/hourVonHausSmart dehumidifier with laundry modefrom£144.99£144.99 at VonHaus£144.99 at AmazonWhat we loveGreat value, quiet and app controlWhat we don’t loveThe air filtration is basicBest combined dehumidifier and air purifier:Devola Platinum hybrid DVHA20LDevolaPlatinum hybrid DVHA20Lfrom£161.99£161.99 at Devola£161.99 at Aircon CentreWhat we loveGood value for a model that features Hepa air filtrationWhat we don’t loveThe added cost of replacement filtersView image in fullscreen£161.99 at Devola£161.99 at Aircon CentreKill two birds with one stone with this new hybrid model that promises cleaner as well as drier air. It comes with a Hepa filter (for filtering the air), an ioniser (for pulling dust out of the air) and an ultraviolet lamp (for killing germs).Why we love itSeveral models on test come with Hepa filters, but what sets this model apart is that it measures air quality too: simply press a button to get a traffic light measure of PM2.5 particles (green, blue or red light, depending on your air quality). Air pollution is a silent killer, andindoor air quality can be worse than outdoor, so filtering these fine particles is a brilliant idea if you don’t already have an air purifier.Dehumidifier modes include laundry and night (quieter at 20dB), and the flap on the top is motorised, so it opens automatically and can be set to “swing” to circulate air.It was great being able to see the air quality improve, as well as the humidity. I found the Devola to be well designed, too: the water tank is accessed from the side and its handle doubles as a visual level indicator. And I found the tank easy to empty without making a mess.It’s a shame that …it’s not quieter.Hepa filterswill need replacing periodically, too (Devola suggests every six months, so budget about £15 a year).Dimensions:36 x 27 x 57cm (WDH)Dailyextraction rate:20lTank capacity:2.9lPeak power use on test:330WAverage noise level on top setting:30dBTarget humidity range:40-80%Laundry setting?YesRunning costs:9p/hourDevolaPlatinum hybrid DVHA20Lfrom£161.99£161.99 at Devola£161.99 at Aircon CentreWhat we loveGood value for a model that features Hepa air filtrationWhat we don’t loveThe added cost of replacement filtersFor more, read our guide to thebest air purifiersBest dehumidifier for drying laundry:Duux Bora SmartDuuxBora Smartfrom£279.99£279.99 at Duux£299 at AOWhat we loveQuiet and uses an eco-friendly refrigerantWhat we don’t loveNo Hepa air purificationView image in fullscreen£279.99 at Duux£299 at AOThis is a good-looking dehumidifier, with clean lines. The water drawer at the front has a useful visual indicator, so you can see at a glance how full it is. It features wifi and app control so that you can set schedules, and an activated carbon filter works to remove odours, gases and smoke.Why we love itI loved the four-hour laundry mode: it reduced relative humidity by 5% in the first five minutes, swiftly drying clothes. And you’ll be able to sleep nearby, since the Duux is Quiet Mark certified for its ultra-quiet operation. The night mode turns off the lights, although I had to turn down the fan speed myself – and in my tests it then reached an impressively low average of below 10dB, much quieter than the manufacturer’s claims. It sounds like a fan with a little bit of fridge sound thrown in, but quieter.I also like that it uses the environmentally friendlyR290 refrigerant, which has a lowglobal warming potential (GWP). In fact, its GWP is only triple that of carbon dioxide, while some refrigerants have a GWP that’s hundreds of times that of CO2 (andsome refrigerants now banned from salehave GWPs of thousands).It’s a shame that …it doesn’t offer Hepa air purification at this price.Dimensions:32 x 24 x 51cm (WDH)Dailyextraction rate:20lTank capacity:4lPeak power use on test:270WAverage noise level on top setting:20dBTarget humidity range:30-80%Laundry setting?YesRunning costs:7p/hourDuuxBora Smartfrom£279.99£279.99 at Duux£299 at AOWhat we loveQuiet and uses an eco-friendly refrigerantWhat we don’t loveNo Hepa air purificationBest quiet dehumidifier:MeacoDry Arete TwoMeacoDryArete Twofrom£299£299 at John Lewis£299.99 at MeacoWhat we loveImpressively quiet, Hepa filtration, app and a long warrantyWhat we don’t loveThe added cost of replacement filtersView image in fullscreen£299 at John Lewis£299.99 at MeacoYou’d expect the successor to the popularArete Oneto be impressive, and this doesn’t disappoint. It’s not just a dehumidifier – it also purifies the air, thanks to the included dust and medical-grade H13 Hepa filters.Why we love itThe Arete Two can be controlled via a smartphone app or voice control via Google Home or Amazon Alexa. Modes include continuous, smart (which aims for a middle-of-the-road 55% humidity) and laundry. The louvre on top opens manually and can be directed at your washing.Its display is slightly unusual: rather than a number, it shows a sliding scale of humidity levels, giving you a clear visual indication of the current humidity and your target. The interface is intuitive, however, and there aren’t too many buttons.The five-year warranty is the longest I’ve seen for a dehumidifier. But most of all, I was impressed by the quiet. The average noise was just 5dB, and this dropped to 4dB (considerably quieter than the manufacturer’s claimed noise level) in night mode. You can honestly forget that it’s on.It also has some thoughtful features. For example, if you leave it plugged in but not switched on, it will say “wet” on screen to alert you when it detects a relative humidity of 70% plus.You can also choose your type of air filtration when you buy refills (£39.99 for a pack of three). You can even add Google Home and Amazon Alexa voice controls. I could use my phone as a remote control from anywhere in the home to check on progress – rare for a dehumidifier at this price.It didn’t make the final cut because …the machine was loud at times (although the sleep setting averaged 17dB).Dimensions:34 x 24 x 57cm (WDH);dailyextraction rate:20l;tank capacity:6.5l;peak power use on test:395W;average noise level on top setting:20dB;target humidity range:30-80%;laundry setting?Yes;running costs:10p/hourBlack+DeckerBXEH60014GBfrom£174£174 at AO£186 at AmazonWhat we loveIt displays the precise humidity, and it has app controlWhat we don’t loveHigher running costs and loud at timesWhat you need to knowWhat is relative humidity?Relative humidity is the percentage of water vapour in the air compared with the maximum that the air can hold.Warm air can hold more water vapour than cold air. So if the amount of water in the air stays the same but the temperature drops, relative humidity increases.When relative humidity hits 100%, the air is fully saturated, and water condenses on surfaces, like how dew condenses on cool morning grass.What humidity should I aim for?All the dehumidifiers tested here measure the relative humidity (a percentage) and let you set a target.If the air is too humid, it feels muggy, and it’s hard for sweat to cool you on a hot day. If the air is too dry, it can lead to problems such as dry eyes and throats.For your health and your home, the ideal relative humidity is 40-60% in summer and 30-50% in winter.Do I need a dehumidifier?You may benefit from a dehumidifier if you have damp and mould problems. Humidity helps mould and dust mites flourish – and they, in turn, can trigger asthma and allergies.Another benefit is drying laundry fast. Use a dehumidifier to pull moisture out of the air, then clothes in the room dry much faster and without causing damp problems such as condensation on windows or walls.Dehumidifiers are also good for specific uses, such as drying paint or plaster faster, or helping a room dry out after flooding.If in doubt, usea cheap hygrometerto check your home’s relative humidity and make an informed decision.What are the different types of dehumidifier?Most of the dehumidifiers tested here arecompressor dehumidifiers, so they work a bit like a fridge, compressing and then expanding a refrigerant to cool a metal coil. Water from the air then condenses on the coil and drains off into a water tank. These are usually the best style of dehumidifier for the home.Don’t throw away the plastic tube if you find one in the box. Some models come with a drain hose – so you can constantly dry rather than stopping when the tank is full. Other models let you add a hose if you need it (but most people don’t use them, which is why they’re not always included).I tested onedesiccant dehumidifier. These excel in cold environments, such as garages, cellars and outbuildings. This is because they work by using moisture-absorbing materials that don’t rely on temperature to remove humidity. However, they use more electricity to do so. They don’t require refills (none of the units featured here needs refills for dehumidification – the only ongoing cost apart from electricity is that some have Hepa air filters that need replacing every three to six months).Peltier dehumidifiersare small and quiet, but they’re not very effective, and they use more energy, so we haven’t featured any in this roundup.What size dehumidifier do I need?The larger (20l a day) models tested here are good for larger homes and open-plan spaces. You can put them somewhere central to tackle humidity in the whole home.The smaller (12l a day) models are very popular and better for smaller homes or single tasks, such as drying laundry. However, if you have persistent damp problems, then it could be worth sizing up.You can add a hose to most dehumidifiers if you want to keep them in constant use without having to empty the tank.How much does a dehumidifier cost to run?I measured each dehumidifier’s power use on the top setting, in watts (W). Electricity costs are in kilowatt hours (kWh). For example, if you’re running a 200W dehumidifier for four hours, it would use 800Wh or 0.8kWh.The energy price cap for 1 October to 31 December 2026 is 26.32p a kWh. Multiply this by the last figure, and you’ll discover it costs about 21p to run the dehumidifier for four hours.This compares favourably with a tumble dryer.One load in a traditional model uses about 4.5kWh (£1.18), although an energy-saving heat pump model uses half that. Either way, it’s much cheaper to run a dehumidifier than either type of tumble dryer.What’s a laundry mode?Many dehumidifiers have a laundry mode that aims for a low relative humidity of 35%, with a timer that turns off automatically, typically aftersix hours.To dry laundry effectively, hang it in a room, turn on the dehumidifier and close the doors. That way, it’s drying the air (and speeding the laundry drying) without having to dry moist air that comes in from the outside world.How to clean your dehumidifierEmpty the water tank after each use, or when it’s full. Regular cleaning mainly involves dusting the unit and cleaning the air filters. Dust filters can usually be vacuumed and washed, while paper Hepa filters need replacing. How often depends on use: about three months for continuous use, six months for average use, or annually if you only run it occasionally. Smart models should track usage and alert you when the filter needs changing.If you use your dehumidifier mainly in the winter, then give it a thorough clean before storing it away.Start by running the unit on fan-only mode to dry the interior; if it doesn’t have one, set it to its highest humidity setting. Clean the unit and filters, then wash and disinfect the tank with a 50/50 mix of white vinegar and water to help prevent mould. Finally, leave everything to air-dry for at least 24 hours, ensuring it’s completely dry before reassembling and packing it away for the summer.How often should you empty your dehumidifier?A dehumidifier will stop working when its water tank is full, usually signalled by a flashing light, beep or app alert. But it’s good practice to empty the tank regularly rather than wait for this to happen.I mainly use a dehumidifier to dry laundry, which takes two to three hours and costs far less than tumble drying (see “How much does a dehumidifier cost to run?”).I simply turn it off when the clothes feel dry and empty the tank, or set the timer if I’m going out. Some models also have a dedicated laundry mode that switches off automatically.If you run a dehumidifier continuously, don’t aim for the driest air possible. Ideally, indoor relative humidity should be 40-60% in summer and 30-50% in winter. How often you need to empty the tank depends on the humidity, how much you use it, and tank capacity. A larger tank means you’ll have to empty it less often.Can dehumidifiers also cool rooms down?No. If anything, a dehumidifier makes a room a little bit warmer while it’s running. However, humid air makes sweat evaporate less effectively, so reducing humidity can help youfeelcooler on a warm day.This isn’t the case on a cold day, when high humidity can make you feel colder. That is because water vapour conducts heat away from the skin more efficiently than dry air. So getting the relative humidity right year-round improves comfort.For more, read the Filter’s guides:The best heated airers, testedThe best electric heatersThe best electric blankets to keep you toasty for lessCaramel Quin is a journalist specialising in consumer technology. She prides herself on real-world testing and plain language. Her pet hates are jargon, pointless products and overcomplicated instruction manuals. title: How to turn gherkin brine into a savoury ice-cream – recipe | Food | The Guardian
description: This sweet-and-sour combo is possibly one of the quirkiest flavours out there – epic served with waffles and bacon, it’s one for true pickle fanatics
Author: Tom Hunt
Headline: This sweet-and-sour combo is possibly one of the quirkiest flavours out there – epic served with waffles and bacon, it’s one for true pickle fanatics
Content: Tom Hunt's pickled cucumber and vodka ice-cream.Photograph: Tom Hunt/The GuardianView image in fullscreenTom Hunt's pickled cucumber and vodka ice-cream.Photograph: Tom Hunt/The GuardianWaste notFoodHow to turn gherkin brine into a savoury ice-cream – recipeThis sweet-and-sour combo is possibly one of the quirkiest flavours out there – epic served with waffles and bacon, it’s one for true pickle fanaticsTom HuntWed 30 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhile researching gherkins for aFood Filter columnlast year, I came acrossKühne’s recipe for pickled cucumber ice-creamand couldn’t resist. Niche, I know, but I’ll bet there are a lot of gherkin fanatics out there who’d be willing to give it a go. If not, the cocktail I’ve used as inspiration might well suffice. The pickleback is made with pickle juice and a spirit such as whisky, tequila or, my favourite, vodka, and that same punchy, sweet-and-sour combination comes together to make possibly the quirkiest ice-cream flavour you ever come across. Delicious in a cone and topped with a gherkin, and out of this world when served with waffles, bacon and maple syrup.Pickled cucumber and vodka ice-creamThis is one for the true gherkin fanatic, with a wild and funky flavour that tricks the mind with a rollercoaster of unexpected tastes. It’s sweet and dilly, but also tart and sour, with a lingering complexity from all the spices used to make the pickles. Fortified with a classic, creamy custard base, it’s best served with savoury waffles.1 egg70g sugar100ml milk250ml double cream10g dill, finely chopped10ml pickle juice20ml vodka(or rum, tequila or whisky)4 ice-cream cones, to serve4 pickles, to serveIn a bowl, whisk the egg, sugar, milk and cream until well combined, then pour into a thick saucepan and cook, stirring continuously, over a very low heat until the custard thickens enough to coat the back of the spoon. (Take care not to let it catch on the bottom, but, if it does, don’t fret: simply pour the custard through a fine sieve without scraping the bottom of the pan.) Take off the heat, stir in the dill and pickle juice, then stir in the vodka.Blend smooth, then churn in an ice-cream machine or transfer to an airtight container and freeze for at least five hours, stirring every 30 minutes to break up any ice crystals. Serve at once, or, if serving the next day or thereafter, pop the ice-cream in the fridge for 30-45 minutes (or leave it out at room temperature for 15 minutes) to soften. Serve in cones and topped with a gherkin.Explore more on these topicsFoodWaste notFood wasteIce-cream and sorbetSpiritsPickling, fermenting and preservingVegetablesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: From Malaysian chicken to Caribbean crab: four global curry recipes  | Indian food and drink | The Guardian
description: A Japanese fusion-fuelled garlic mushroom doria, an aromatic Malay chicken and squash curry, a rich Rajasthani papad ki sabji, and a Caribbean curry crab with roasted corn and dumplings
Author: Tim Anderson
Headline: A Japanese fusion-fuelled garlic mushroom doria, an aromatic Malay chicken and squash curry, a rich Rajasthani papad ki sabji, and a Caribbean curry crab with roasted corn and dumplings
Content: Mandy Yin’s chicken and squash curry.Photograph: Photography: Laura Edwards/The Guardian. Food styling: Joss Herd. Prop styling: Tabitha Hawkins.View image in fullscreenMandy Yin’s chicken and squash curry.Photograph: Photography: Laura Edwards/The Guardian. Food styling: Joss Herd. Prop styling: Tabitha Hawkins.Indian food and drinkFrom Malaysian chicken to Caribbean crab: four global curry recipesA Japanese fusion-fuelled garlic mushroomdoria,an aromatic Malay chicken and squash curry, a rich Rajasthanipapad ki sabji,and a Caribbean curry crab with roasted corn and dumplingsTim Anderson,Maunika Gowardhan,.Mandy Yin, Keshia SakarahWed 30 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 08.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMandy Yin’s chicken and squash curry (pictured top)Curry runs through Malaysia’s veins; it’s in every kitchen and at every food stall, whether run by Malays, Chinese or Indians. We tend to cook curries using either a wet spice paste (rempah) straight from the morning market, or a good curry powder – every household keeps a pack ofAdabiorBaba’sin the cupboard as a fallback; we have no shame in this at all. Only when you’ve got time on your hands, or you’re cooking to impress, do you build arempahfrom scratch.My favourite curries come from the Mamak Tamil Muslim cooks behind Malaysia’s all-nightkopitiams, who make the bestroti canaigoing. Go for the roti and the meat curries alongside, washed down withteh tarik– strong black tea sweetened with condensed milk, pulled until it froths.In my cookbook Simply Malaysian, I included my take on Dad’s Mamak lamb and potato curry. He starts with a whole leg, which he bones and trims himself, a heavy hand of curry powder, then the aromatics Malaysians callempat sekawan(the four friends): star anise, cassia, cloves, cardamom. Here, I’ve swapped the lamb for chicken thighs on the bone – they’re cheaper, quicker and what most of us reach for on a weeknight – and the potatoes for butternut squash. Pumpkins and gourds are a staple of Malay cooking, and are most at home in a coconut gravy, though they rarely share a pot with meat. So, squash takes the potatoes’ place and earns its keep, holding its shape and drinking up the sauce.A word on the meat. In Malaysia we cook it in the curry it’s going to be served in – not seared or simmered separately and folded in at the end – so the two season each other the whole way. And we cook it on the bone, always: bone-in gives a richer, glossier sauce than any fillet will. Like all curries, this eats even better the next day, once the flavours have settled. If you’re not eating it straight away, reduce the cooking time in the penultimate step to 10 minutes (to allow the squash to finish cooking when reheating it). Any leftover sauce eaten with rice and a fried egg or two is one of life’s simple pleasures.Prep15 minCook45 minServes4-61 medium onion,peeled and roughly chopped4 garlic cloves,peeled1 inch (2½cm) piece ginger,peeled and roughly chopped5 tbsp vegetable or peanut oil¾ tbsp table salt4 tbsp Adabi meat curry powder –alternatively, combine 1 tbsp chilli powder, 1 tbsp ground coriander, 1 tbsp ground turmeric, 1 tsp finely ground black pepper and 2 tsp ground cumin½ tsp chilli powder1 star anise4 cloves1 stick cassia bark,or ½ cinnamon stick2 green cardamom pods,lightly bashed with a pestle to crack the skin1kg skinless, bone-in chicken thighs200gtinned chopped tomatoes,or fresh tomatoes, roughly chopped1butternut squash,or part of a pumpkin, peeled, deseeded and cut into 3cm x 2cm chunks (approximately 800-850g)200ml coconut milk30g bunchcoriander,finely chopped stalks and all (optional)Emiko Davies’ Japanese curry rice (kare raisu) – recipeRead moreFinely chop the onion, garlic and ginger in a food processor. Heat the oil in a large, non-stick wok/saucepan or a deep casserole dish over a medium heat, then add the onion-garlic mix and salt, and stir-fry for five minutes, until softened.Turn the heat down to medium-low, then add the curry powder, chilli powder, star anise, cloves, cassia and cardamom, and stir-fry for two minutes. Add a splash of water if the spices start to catch on the bottom of the pan.Add the chicken thighs and turn them through the paste, until every piece is coated. Pour in 200ml water and the tomatoes, stir, then bring up to a boil. Lower the heat to medium-low, cover and simmer for 15 minutes, turning the thighs and stirring every five minutes.Add the squash/pumpkin and coconut milk, then cover and bring back to a boil over a medium heat. Check in every few minutes to see whether it has come up to a boil, and give it a stir. Take your time, as the chicken and squash slowly release their juices into the sauce, so you end up with enough liquid to keep almost everything submerged.Once boiling, lower the heat to medium-low and cook, uncovered, for 15 minutes, stirring every few minutes and nudging the squash carefully back under the sauce. Turn the heat off, stir through the coriander and serve with plenty of rice.Simply Malaysian by Mandy Yin is published by Quadrille at £27. To order a copy for £24.30, visitguardianbookshop.comKeshia Sakarah’s curry crab, roasted corn and cassava dumplingsView image in fullscreenWhen most people think of curry, they probably don’t think of the Caribbean, yet many of our dishes incorporate spices in a variety of ways. While they aren’t native or indigenous ingredients, they are now very much part of daily life.They were introduced to the region by the indentured labourers from the Indian subcontinent. Their use of spices in this new part of the world transformed the cuisine in many ways, using ground spices to flavour slow-cooked meat and fish, or toasting whole ones in oil to finish vegetables, and brought about a brand-new cooking style.I’ve eaten curry throughout my life, and thinking of my love for it unearths many fond memories: when I’m at Notting Hill carnival, I have to support my favourite food stands off Kensal Road. And then there are my many visits to the Caribbean. Experiencing curry on different islands, in a variety of ways, always piques my curiosity; it speaks to the cultural layers of the region and how the Caribbean really is a microcosm of the many communities that make up the world. In Guadeloupe, I triedcolombo– a classic French Caribbean curry (usually chicken or fish), which incorporates toasted, ground rice into the spices and lots of lime juice into the sauce. Unlike the curries of the anglophone islands (Jamaica, Antigua, Grenada, for example), it is more acidic and paler in complexion, yet still served with rice and beans. In Trinidad, home to one of the largest Indo-Caribbean communities, curry is a staple, originally found mostly in homes, but now also in roti shops across the island. Some of the best are in central Trinidad, where generations of Indian communities have settled for generations.Prep10 minRest30 minCook55 minServes4For the cassava dumplings125g cassava flour125g plain flour1⅛tsp fine sea salt,plus extra for cooking the dumplings½tsp baking powder1 tbsp olive pomace or rapeseed oil, plus extra for cooking the dumplings180ml cold waterFor the green seasoning2 spring onions6 garlic cloves,peeled5cm piece ginger15g flat-leaf parsley,leaves and stalks30g coriander,leaves and stalks75ml cold water1 lime,juiced2tbsp rapeseed oilFor the curry base2 fresh corn cobs3tbsp ghee or rapeseed oil2tbsp curry powder2tsp ground turmeric4tsp garam masala oramchar masala1 scotch bonnet,pierced600ml good-quality coconut milk290gwhite crab meatCombine all the ingredients for the cassava dumplings in a bowl, then knead to form a soft dough; set aside to rest for 30 minutes.Blend all the green seasoning ingredients apart from the oil in a blender until almost smooth, then transfer to a jar and stir in the oil.Roast the corn cobs over an open flame or under a hot grill, turning occasionally, until charred all over; set aside to cool. Once cool enough to handle, slice off the kernels and set aside, discarding the husks.For the curry base, heat the ghee/oil in a pan set over a medium heat. Add the spices and toast lightly for 30 seconds to a minute. Add 200ml cold water and gently boil for three to four minutes, then add two tablespoons of the green seasoning, the scotch bonnet and half the grilled corn, and mix well.Tip in the coconut milk, increase the heat until lightly boiling, then reduce to a simmer and cook for 10-12 minutes, until the sauce looks smooth and emulsified.Meanwhile, divide the dumpling dough into 32 equal pieces, then roll into balls. Place them spaced out on a tray, dusting with a little extra flour if they’re sticky. Cover with a tea towel and set aside.Bring a pan of water to the boil, then add a teaspoon of salt and a teaspoon of oil. Once boiling, cook the dumplings in batches for eight to 10 minutes, or until they float. Remove from the pan with a slotted spoon to a bowl of cold water (they will cook further in the curry later).To finish the curry, give the pan another stir – it should have reduced and thickened slightly. Remove the scotch bonnet and discard, then pour the curry into a blender and blitz smooth. Pass through a sieve, then return the liquid to the pan.Put over a medium-high heat, add the cooked dumplings, then reduce to a low simmer and cook foreight to 10 minutes, until the dumplings are soft and have absorbed some of the colour from the curry. Remove from the heat and gently fold in the crab meat, ensuring it doesn’t break up. Finish with the remaining grilled corn and a few more drops of the green seasoning, then serve.Caribe by Keshia Sakarah is published by Hardie Grant at £30. To order a copy for £27, visitguardianbookshop.comTim Anderson’s garlic mushroom currydoria(Japanese rice gratin)View image in fullscreenTim Anderson’s garlic mushroom curry doria (Japanese rice gratin).Japan’s currydoria– also known as yaki-curry, or baked curry – is one of my all-time favourite blank-slate meal formats. It is essentially a rice gratin, containing plump grains of Japanese short-grain rice smothered in smooth Japanese curry sauce, all tucked under a luxurious duvet of molten cheese. In other words, a masterclass in comfort cookery.Because its core elements are so amenably mellow in terms of flavour, the curry doria format works with just about any veg or protein you like, or whatever’s in season. But I like to lean into its heartiness with rich, meaty ingredients, such as the mushrooms and greens I’ve used here, along with a liberal dose of garlic and butter, inspired by old-school baked mushroom starters.Prep10 minCook45 minServes4Butter,as needed4 portions cooked Japanese rice (300g uncooked)400g mushrooms –I love oyster mushrooms, but use any you like4 garlic clovesSalt and black pepper100g mustard greens or chard,coarsely chopped1 pack (around 90g) Japanese curry roux50g grated mozzarella50g grated medium or mild cheddar50g grated Emmental1 small handfulflat-leaf parsley,finely choppedSome kind of crunchy onion product,such as cheese and onion crisps, onion rings, or fried shallots (Ihighlyrecommend the brand Wild Rice), to garnishRub a medium baking dish (around 23cm square,) with butter. Pack the cooked rice into the bottom of the dish in an even layer, using a bit of force so it’s relatively dense – if it has too many air gaps, the curry sauce will flow into it, and the gratin will become more stodgy than saucy.Then, prepare the mushrooms. Oyster mushrooms,shimeji, or ordinary white or chestnut mushrooms can simply be broken into bite-size pieces; smaller mushrooms like buttons and chanterelles can be left whole; shiitake should be de-stemmed; and if you are using any long, tough mushrooms like king oysters orenoki, they should be chopped into roughly 1-inch chunks. Remember to clean any wild mushrooms so they’re free of dirt or grit before cooking.Peel and chop the garlic, sprinkle it with salt, then continue to mince it finely, and drag the side of your knife through it, to smash it into a coarse paste; the salt will help soften the garlic and draw out its pungent oils.In a wide saute pan, melt a generous knob of butter over a medium-high heat, then add the garlic, mushrooms, greens, and a few grinds of pepper. Toss them through the butter, then cook without stirring for four to five minutes, so the mushrooms brown on one side. Remove from the heat, then scrape everything out of the pan and on to the rice in the baking dish. Heat the oven to 220C (200C fan)/425F/gas 7.In the same pan you used to saute the mushrooms, prepare the curry sauce according to packet instructions – but don’t add any additional meat or veg, if it calls for them. Once the sauce is cooked out and smooth, pour this over the mushrooms and rice.Top with the cheeses and bake for about 20 minutes, until browned on top. Serve piping hot, garnished with a little chopped parsley and a scattering of the crunchy onion product of your choosing.Japanese Curry by Tim Anderson is published in October by Quadrille at £14.99. To order a copy for £13.49, visitguardianbookshop.comMaunika Gowardhan’s rajasthanipapad ki sabjiView image in fullscreenAlthough I grew up in Mumbai, I hail from a family with roots in theKonkaniand western coastal region sprawled across the Deccan Plateau in India. Dishes from this region are robust, hearty and we celebrate curries with warmth, aroma, and complex flavours.Travelling across India, the food changes within regions and reflects the ingredients available, the seasons and changes in climate. But this is one of my favourite curries from the state of Rajasthan. Papad ki sabji is a staple in homes across the north-west of India and primarily made with turmeric, coriander and fenugreek in a rich gravy simmered with cooked papad (poppadum). This dish is often served in a Rajasthani thali, which is vibrant and delicious, but it is also served as a weekday curry with plain rice.Yoghurt added to the curry is cooling and lends richness to the gravy. Traditionally, the papad is deep-fried but my recipe uses roast papads, which can be done in the microwave in just a few seconds (follow the packet instructions for cooking the papad). The charred edges on the papad lend a lot of flavour to the curry.Prep10 minCook30 minServes44 garlic cloves,peeled and roughly chopped1inch (2½cm) piece ginger,peeled and roughly chopped1 small bird’s eye green chilli,deseeded if you prefer less heat100gtomatoes,roughly chopped1 tbsp tomato puree3 tbsp vegetable oil or ghee½ tsp cumin seedsA pinch of asafoetida1 tbsp coriander powder1 tsp turmeric powder1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder250gGreek yoghurt,whisked well (make sure there are no lumps; this way it won’t split as it cooks)Salt2 tbspdried fenugreek leaves(kasoori methi)4 roasted papads/poppadumFresh coriander,to garnishPut the garlic, ginger, green chilli and a splash of water in a blender and blend to a smooth, fine paste; set aside.In the same blender, blend the tomato and tomato puree to a paste.Heat the oil in a heavy-based nonstick saucepan over a low heat. Add the cumin seeds and asafoetida, and fry for two seconds. Add the garlic/ginger paste and fry for 20 seconds, then add the blended tomatoes and cook for six minutes, stirring well.As the oil leaves the sides of the pan, add the powdered spices and fry for a minute. Tip in the yoghurt a little at a time, stirring well, then cook and stir on a low heat for three to four minutes.Add 300ml water, season to taste and simmer for six to eight minutes. Add the fenugreek leaves, along with the roasted papad and cook, covered, for two minutes. Garnish with coriander and serve with rice.Curry by Maunika Gowardhan is published by Quadrille at £26. To order a copy for £23.40, visitguardianbookshop.comExplore more on these topicsIndian food and drinkCurryFoodMain courseMalaysian food and drinkJapanese food and drinkChickenfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: From cordon bleu to pasta and pies: the best autumn cookbooks for 2026 – reviewed | Books | The Guardian
description: Felicity Cloake’s must-reads of the season
Author: Felicity Cloake
Headline: Felicity Cloake’s must-reads of the season
Content: You can find this recipe for meringue cake in our autumn star book – Kitchening by Jeremy Lee.Photograph: PR ImageView image in fullscreenYou can find this recipe for meringue cake in our autumn star book – Kitchening by Jeremy Lee.Photograph: PR ImageHobside readingBooksReviewFrom cordon bleu to pasta and pies: the best autumn cookbooks for 2026 – reviewedAn eclectic selection that will take you on a culinary journey – make room on your shelvesFelicity CloakeWed 30 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMy autumn starKitcheningby Jeremy Lee (4th Estate, £30)It’s difficult to say what charms me more about this beautiful book, the second from the Dundee-born chef proprietor of century-old Soho institutionQuo Vadis– the food, or the words, both of which could only have come from Lee.View image in fullscreenThe first chapter, to give you an idea, is entitled “January: the general atmosphere is very Macbeth-ish”, and contains recipes including pickled rhubarb, peppered ox cheek, a warm salad of smoked haddock and brassicas, and a dish of “beans and greens” that, having already tasted it, would have cheered things up in Inverness Castle no end. The photography and design is gorgeous, the prose feels like having this warmest of cooks sitting beside you nattering about what to cook, and there’s also a magnificent lemon and blackcurrant trifle, which can only be described as magnificent. One to hug close – and give to everyone you know for Christmas.Blood, Guts and Black Pudding: Ireland’s dying art of blood as foodby Kate Ryan (Nine Bean Rows, £17.50)View image in fullscreenIf you’re squeamish about blood, this slim Irish history won’t be for you – but if, like me, you appreciate the richly savoury, velvety soft pleasures of an inky slab of black pudding, it’s an utterly fascinating read. As well as delving into why Ireland has had a “uniquely complex cultural and societal connection” with blood as food from ancient times onwards, it explores the ongoing struggle to keep this connection going in the face of a hostile regulatory climate; post-BSE, almost all* black pudding in the UK is made with imported dried blood, and producers in Ireland face many of the same challenges. Folklore, colonisation, rural culture, haute cuisine – it’s all here, but for me, the real treasure lies in the first-person accounts of small-scale farmers and producers, almost lyrical in their celebration of this least lovely, but most vital part of the animal.* the excellent Fruit Pig is the rare exception.The Modern Pie Makerby Calum Franklin (Bloomsbury, £26)View image in fullscreenI frequently bemoan the British reluctance to celebrate our own cuisine in any meaningful sense – if butter pies, the first recipe in pastry wizard Calum Franklin’s new book, were from Pau, rather than Preston, there would certainly be a festival devoted to them, complete with competitions and silly pie-shaped hats. This book, which tackles everything from an 18th-century herb pie to a ploughman’s pork pie from the chef’s own imagination, taking in puddings, pasties,bridies,oggiesand the like en route, is the next best thing. Franklin begins by explaining his belief that “the key to good pie making is … giving equal consideration to what is outside as to what is inside”, followed by a clear explanation of technique, process and equipment that should persuade even the most nervous pastry makers to give his gloriously golden six-meat Yorkshire Christmas pie a go this December: after all, as he points out, “nobody really remembers a roast turkey”.Egyptby Rawah Badrawi and Suzanne Zeidy (Nourish, £30)View image in fullscreenThough Egypt is the most populous country in the Arab world, its rich and varied cuisine is puzzlingly under-represented on my bookcases – but this sweeping survey from writer and restaurateur Suzanne Zeidy and her collaborator, the author and travel writer Rawah Badrawi, is a valuable companion to Zeidy’s previous work: 2013’s Cairo Kitchen. The pair, close friends since their 20s, went on a road trip around their beloved country to write it, amassing stories and recipes from the Mediterranean coast to the edge of the Great Sand Sea: the sourdough baked by the Greek Orthodox monks of Mount Sinai to the pharaonic-era bread that’s still a staple in modern Luxor, and Mohamed Salah’s favourite pitta pockets to the elusive celebrity chickens of Fayoum, the “garden of Egypt”. Egypt’s colourful history is written in the recipe index: Italian biscotti, Greco-Libyan pasta, Sudanese chilli sauce, and a final chapter of treasured family recipes from the capital, all accompanied by evocative location and food photography from Jonathan Gregson. A treasure well worth waiting for.Le Cordon Bleu Culinary Arts Schoolby Le Cordon Bleu (Phaidon, £400)View image in fullscreenThis seven-volume set, produced in collaboration with what is surely the world’s most famous cookery school, is perhaps one to put on your Christmas list – but it would be a serious investment for anyone looking to learn western culinary technique the proper way, fully explained and with accompanying photographs. Though centred, unsurprisingly, around French traditions, the outlook is global; the stocks and sauces volume, for example, which covers the entire classical repertoire, suggests putting it to use in recipes for Vietnamesepho bo, Scottish cock-a-leekie and Turkishkıkırdak, as well as apoule au potorsoup au piston. An astonishing achievement.Modern Masalaby Sanjana Modha (Quadrille, £25)View image in fullscreenA good recipe book invites you to pull up a chair at the author’s table, to share not just a collection of recipes, but a taste of their lives. Modha, a first-generation British-Indian was weaned on a menu of Gujarati classics, and food from elsewhere reimagined with a little Indian spicing, and it’s this latter category of “remixed” cooking that inspired her second book. In its colourful pages, she shares clever family tricks (aubergines stuffed with Weetabix instead of gram flour, fluffy potato curry with instant mash and tomato ketchup), and her own intriguingly bonkers creations, including gnocchi in tomato dal, onion bahjis made with oven chips, and a very tempting “full English”aloo parathabreakfast. Great fun and a very persuasive argument for culinary cross-pollination. It’s also entirely vegetarian.Simple Tooby Yotam Ottolenghi and Verena Lochmuller (Ebury, £30)View image in fullscreenSecond helpings of that Ottolenghi Test Kitchen magic pared down for everyday use – I guarantee you won’t be able to flick through this book without reconsidering your dinner plans, because they really know how to grab the reader by the tastebuds. Recipes, all of which have been designed to fit around the constraints of everyday life, whether time, confidence or energy-related, and many of which embrace a one-pan or baking tray approach, include the seductive likes of butter beans with Urfa chilli butter and sticky orange and harissa pork belly, and ginger peach puffs, plus a whole chapter on condiments that can be repurposed in various dishes throughout the week. Practicalandexciting; it has hit the weekday cooking bullseye.Lozhkaby Alissa Timoshkina (Quadrille, £28)View image in fullscreenLozhka is the Russian word for spoon, the universal utensil “that has always guided us back to the foods that know how to take care of us”. In the aftermath of Putin’s invasion of Ukraine, Timoshkina, has had to become an expert in that department, and writes that cooking has served as therapy and to forge connection in the years that have followed. Eastern European cuisine – and the book includes recipes from the Baltic Sea to the Balkans, as well as from Tatar, Roma and Ashkenazi communities – is rich in dishes that require little more than a spoon and a pot to soothe, from a fruity Crimean borscht with quince dedicated to her great-grandmother to a Persian-spiced Armenian lamb and chickpea stew. Porridges, broths, soups, dumplings and noodles, steamed and set puddings, the book travels thousands of miles in search of comfort, collecting some truly beautiful stories and photography, along the way; this is a book to brighten the dark months to come, but which will earn its place on your shelf all year round.Pasta Tricoloreby Jacob Kenedy (Bloomsbury, £18.99)View image in fullscreenJust when I think I don’t need yet another book devoted to the pleasures of pasta, I realise there’s room for one more, if it changes the way I look at the ingredient that, as Kenedy observes, almost every child in the western world is now weaned on. His theory is that all pasta dishes fall into one of three principal, and patriotically coloured categories: red (tomato), white (fat or meat) and green (pestos and vegetables). Exploring these family trees takes us, in turn, from the simple pleasures of tagliatelle and butter to the cream and radicchio tagliolini gratin that’s been on the winter menu at his restaurantBocca di Luposince it opened (white); from classic pesto Genovese to an unusual combination of green peppers, mussels and linguine he first ate in Sperlonga (green); and from tomato spaghetti to a Roman oxtail rigatoni (red).It is all generously annotated with potential variations. Helpfully, a series of charts at the back of the book allow the reader to see at a glance which dishes can be made with the particular pasta on hand – all in all, a worthy addition to my extensive collection.My seasonal classicThe Dal Cookbookby Krishna Dutta (Grub Street, £16.99)View image in fullscreen“Dal is to India what pasta is to Italy,” according to the cover of this book, which I’ve owned and loved since it came out in 2013 – a bold declaration, but one that gives some clue of the variety and versatility of its contents. Dutta, who began her dal-cooking career in the late 1960s as a student in London desperate for a taste of home, spent decades collecting recipes from all over India. Along with the vivid yellowtadka dalmany Brits might be familiar with from northern Indian restaurant menus, there’s a sinus-clearing gingerrasamshe picked up in Chennai, a creamy Goan prawn and coconut dal and a green mango version from Orissa and many more, plus dal dumplings and fritters, breads and even sweets. If you’re trying to eat more healthy, fibre-rich pulses, this book will make it a pleasure.Explore more on these topicsBooksHobside readingFoodAutumn food and drinkFood and drink booksreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Cullen skink pies, vegetarian haggis and chippy fritters: Ali Stoner’s recipes for twists on Scottish classics | Food | The Guardian
description: Scots have a rich food history that’s been passed down through generations. Here are my modern takes on traditional Celtic staples
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Scots have a rich food history that’s been passed down through generations. Here are my modern takes on traditional Celtic staples
Content: Ali Stoner’s cullen skink bake.Photograph: Ola O Smit/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Lilli Gavin.View image in fullscreenAli Stoner’s cullen skink bake.Photograph: Ola O Smit/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Lilli Gavin.FoodCullen skink pies, vegetarian haggis and chippy fritters: Ali Stoner’s recipes for twists on Scottish classicsScots have a rich food history that’s been passed down through generations. Here are my modern takes on traditional Celtic staplesAli StonerWed 30 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere is a depth and history to Scotland’s food that reaches far beyond deep-fried Mars bars or urban myths about haggis. Kitchens were humble and full of life – recipes passed by word of mouth, scraps of paper shared between friends, generations stitching together simple meals. I’m lucky enough that my mum taught me how a potato, a handful of oatmeal and a bit of salt and butter could make a mealandhold a story, but life changes – new ingredients arrive, we move away, time grows shorter – and, sometimes, those simple, comforting recipes drift out of reach. Today’s dishes began as a keepsake for my children – to save old recipes, to record a feeling of home – but also as an invitation to discover what happens when memory meets invention.Cullen skink bake (pictured top)The starting point for these smoked fish pies is basically a cullen skink soup, which I thicken to make the filling. Traditional cullen skink relies on Scottish smoked haddock for its flavour. There is just nothing else like it, though Shetland smoked cod also works really well here. Finish these wee pies with a grating of sharp cheddar. Delicious.Prep15 minCook1 hr 20 min, plus cooling timeMakes4 pies15gunsalted butter, plus 1 knob extra for fryingOlive oil, for frying100gonions, peeled and finely choppedSalt andblack pepper, to taste250gpotatoes(use a good all-rounder such as maris piper or king edward), peeled and cut into 1cm cubes200mlwhole milk250ggood (ie, undyed) smoked haddock, or smoked cod, cut into bite-sized pieces15g plain flour1 tbsp chopped chives1 tbsp chopped flat-leaf parsley1 tsp dijon mustard1 standard 320g sheet ready-rolled all-butter shortcrust pastry, or puff pastry (27cm × 35cm)Gratedcheddar, to finish1 egg yolk mixed with a little milkMelt the knob of butter and a drizzle of oil in a large saucepan on a medium heat. Add the onions and a pinch of salt, and saute on a low to medium heat for about five minutes, to soften. Add the cubed potatoes, keep the heat low, cover and sweat for 10 or so minutes, until the potatoes start to soften but are still a little hard. Stir in the milk, lay the fish on top of the potatoes, then cover again and simmer for 10 minutes more, until you can easily press the point of a knife into the potato: you want them to retain their shape, rather than be mushy. Using a slotted spoon, carefully lift the fish, potatoes and onion out of the hot milk, then pour the liquid into a jug.Melt the 15g butter in the same pan, then stir in the flour and cook on a low heat for a couple of minutes. Pour in the reserved poaching liquid, stir for about five minutes, until the mixture thickens, then take off the heat and carefully fold in the fish, potatoes and onions. Add the herbs, mustardand black pepper to taste, then leave to cool.Heat the oven to 220C (200C fan)/425F/gas7. Lay out the pastry on a lightly flouredwork surface and cut it into four strips. Pile the filling on one half of each strip, leaving enough of a border to seal around the edges later. Top the filling with a little grated cheddar, then brush some of the beaten egg yolk mixture all around the edges. Fold the empty half of each pastry strip up and over the filling, press all around the edges to seal, then crimp with the back of a fork.With a sharp knife, cut a small steam vent in the top of each pie, then transfer them to a lined baking sheet and brush with the remaining egg yolk mixture. Bake the pastries for 30 minutes, until puffed and golden. I like to serve these with a sharply dressed green salad for a crunchy, vinegary contrast. You will probably have a little filling left over, which is perfect for an omelette or toasted sandwich the next day.Vegetarian haggisView image in fullscreenAli Stoner’s vegetarian haggis.I often make a veggie haggis, mainly for pals who are scared by the real deal, and this one really does replicate the original in flavour, texture and looks. It also makes a brilliant filling for “sausage” rolls. After making so many Scottish dishes over the years, I noticed I was using the same herbs and spices on repeat, so I created a blend that represents the essence of Celtic flavours. It is so adaptable that, if you’re anything like me, you will find yourself using it in so many things, from marinades to roast potatoes and everything in between.Prep25 minSoak15 minCook1 hr 10 minServes6For the Scottish seven-spice blend (makes 1 small jar)25gblack peppercorns15g coriander seeds1tbsp juniper berries1tbsp allspice berries1tbsp dried thyme1tbsp dried rosemary1tbsp ground nutmegFor the haggis15g dried mushrooms(porcini or shiitake), diced2tbsp olive oil25gbutter1 brown onion, peeled and finely chopped2 garlic cloves, peeled and minced4 portobello mushrooms, diced2tsp Scottishseven-spice(see above and method)1 tsp white pepper½ teaspoon ground mace2 sprigs fresh sage, leaves picked and finely chopped1 sprigfresh rosemary, leaves picked and finely chopped2 carrots, very finely diced (I use a food processor)75gblack beluga lentils1tbsp yeast extract(Marmite or Vegemite, say)500ml vegetable stock400gcan white beans, drained and choppedFinely grated zest of 1 unwaxed lemonSalt50g steel-cut or pinhead oatsOnion jam, to serve, ideally spiked with a little whisky and warmed (optional)First, make the Scottish seven-spice blend. Toast the peppercorns, coriander seeds, juniper and allspice berries in a dry pan until fragrant, then blitz to a powder in a spice grinder (alternatively, use a pestle and mortar). Add the thyme and rosemary, blend again, then add the ground nutmeg and blend again. Decant into a jar and use freely and creatively whenever you want to add a bit of Celtic flavour.Now for the haggis. Cover the dried mushrooms in about 100ml boiling water and leave to soak for 15 minutes.Put the oil and butter in a saucepan on a low to medium heat, then add the onion and garlic, and saute gently until they start to soften. Add the fresh mushrooms, followed by the drained rehydrated dried mushrooms (save their soaking liquor) and, after a couple of minutes, when they have softened, add all the spices, herbs, carrots, lentils, yeast extract, reserved mushroom liquor and 400ml of the stock. Simmer, stirring frequently, for about 30 minutes, until the lentils are almost soft.Stir the beans and lemon zest into the mix and add a half teaspoon of salt. Test the lentils for “doneness”: they should still have a little bite and most of the liquid should have been absorbed, so if they need more cooking, add the rest of the stock. Add the oats, cook for five to 10 minutes,until they absorb the remaining liquid, then taste and add more salt, if required.Serve with champit tatties (buttery mash studded with sliced spring onions), mashed neeps (swede) and some warm, whisky-spiked onion jam.Chippy batter potato frittersView image in fullscreenAli Stoner’s chippy batter potato fritters.This simple batter gives the most amazing crunch to fish, fritters and even sausages: no fancy ingredients required. The vinegar reacts with the baking powder to produce a light, airy batter, while the cornflour helps with that all-important crunch. You could serve these with tartare sauce, but the pickled onion mayo, inspired by that big jar on the chip-shop counter, works a treat.Prep15 minCook30 minServes4–6For the fritters2 large unpeeled baking potatoes, cut into 5mm-thick slices (I use a mandoline)Plain flour, for dustingVegetable oil, for deep-fryingSaltFor the chippy batter75g plain flour60gcornflour1tsp baking powder½tsp salt2tsp malt vinegarFor the pickled onion mayo (optional)70gpickled onions, roughly chopped, plus 1–2 tbsp of the onion pickling vinegar20gsmall capers, finely chopped1tbsp finely chopped parsley1tbsp finely chopped chives2tbsp mayonnaise1 pinch saltRinse and drain the potato slices, then put them in a pan of salted cold water – if possible, use a wide saute pan, so the slices aren’t piled on top of each other. Bring to a boil, simmer for five minutes, then lift out with a fish slice or large slotted spoon, transfer to a rack and leave to steam dry. Chill uncovered while you make the batter and pickled onion mayo.For the batter, sift the flours, baking powder and salt into a bowl, then gradually whisk in 150ml cold water until incorporated. Add the vinegar and whisk again to combine.For the pickled onion mayo, simply mix all the ingredients in a bowl.Take the potato slices out of the fridge. Put a bowl filled with flour next to your frying station and season it with salt. Heat enough oil for deep-frying in a deep, heavy-based pan or a deep-fat fryer to 180C (350F) (or until a drizzle of batter sizzles and browns immediately). Working in small batches, dip the potato slices first in the seasoned flour, then in the batter, and deep-fry, turning as needed, for up to five minutes in total, until golden and crisp. When they are cooked, the oil will almost stop bubbling and be nearly still – that’s when you know they’re ready. Lift out with a slotted spoon (remove any bits that fall off into the oil, too) and drain on kitchen paper. Season immediately with salt, then keep warm while you fry the rest of the fritters.Get the fritters into buttered rolls, if you like, or serve them just as they are with some pickled onion mayo, and enjoy the crunch.These recipes are edited extracts from Scran: Modern Scottish Food Inspired by Tradition by Ali Stoner, published by Mitchell Beazley at £27. To order a copy for £24.30, go toguardianbookshop.comThe Guardian aims to publish recipes for sustainable seafood. title: A moment that changed me: My mother fell off a mountain – and my life began again | Life and style | The Guardian
description: A bad breakup had made me afraid I would be mired in anger for ever. But on that family hike, in our fear and horror as we awaited the air ambulance, my old hurts took on a different hue
Author: Louise O'Neill
Headline: A bad breakup had made me afraid I would be mired in anger for ever. But on that family hike, in our fear and horror as we awaited the air ambulance, my old hurts took on a different hue
Content: Louise O’Neill(far right)with Will Alshire, Michelle O’Neill, Michael O’Neill and Marie O’Neill on Carrauntoohil.Photograph: Courtesy of Louise O'NeillView image in fullscreenLouise O’Neill(far right)with Will Alshire, Michelle O’Neill, Michael O’Neill and Marie O’Neill on Carrauntoohil.Photograph: Courtesy of Louise O'NeillA moment that changed meLife and styleA moment that changed me: My mother fell off a mountain – and my life began againA bad breakup had made me afraid I would be mired in anger for ever. But on that family hike, in our fear and horror as we awaited the air ambulance, my old hurts took on a different hueLouise O'NeillWed 30 Sep 2026 01.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTo steal a well-known line, 2023 is not a year on which I shall look back with undiluted pleasure. My annus horribilis began when a long-term relationship broke up in January, only six months after we had bought our first home together. I was about to turn 38 and the future I thought was mine – marriage, children – all fell apart. What followed was blow after blow: my sister announced her engagement, I was told by a fertility doctor that I was “not a suitable candidate” for egg freezing, and I soon began having multiple panic attacks a day.Ordinarily, my work would have been my solace; when I wrote, it was as if time was suspended. But now, my words abandoned me. They would not come, no matter how much I tried. So, in April, I decided to take the rest of the year off to recover. As I was self-employed, this was not a choice I made lightly – but my heart was broken and so too, it seemed, was my brain.As befitting a millennial woman who read Eat Pray Loveat a formative age, I attempted to recover using every kind of therapy imaginable. Unfortunately, even after a five-week trip to Thailand for a yoga and wellness retreat, I didn’t feel “healed”. I still felt resentful and sad, and I became afraid that I would be mired in my anger for the rest of my life.That September, my father turned 63. He didn’t want presents; he wanted the whole family – my parents, me, my sister and her now husband – to climb Carrauntoohil, the highest mountain in Ireland, together.It was a beautiful morning, but I was tired. The insomnia that had plagued me as a teenager had returned, making every day feel like an endurance test. I threw myself into the back seat of my parents’ car, pretending to sleep until we got to County Kerry. I wanted to be left alone with my misery, ruminating on how badly I had been treated, how I was the greatest victim who had ever lived.It was my first time climbing Carrauntoohil. We ascended through the Devil’s Ladder, a steep, rocky gully with loose stones and scree; you couldn’t lose focus, even for a second. At the summit, we ate our sandwiches and took photos atthe wooden crossbefore the descent. I was in a better mood – annoyingly, my parents were right that getting outside would help. We were close to the end, and so close to safety, when I heard a scream. I turned to see my mother falling – 20ft? 30ft? 50ft? I couldn’t tell. Her body picked up speed until she was a blur of limbs and she crashed into a stone boulder with a sickening crack.Well, I thought. My year is about to get a lot worse.I scrambled to reach her, screaming her name, my sister running behind me. My father was trying to get to her, too. His face was pale and I knew he thought the same as me, that she was dead. No one could have survived a fall like that.View image in fullscreen‘I knew it was time to let go of the grief’ … Louise O’Neill.Photograph: Clare KeoghNo one … except my mother. She moaned as she pushed herself up to a sitting position. Once I saw she was conscious, I was relieved to see her teeth were intact; she’d had them straightened for my sister’s wedding, and I knew she would be devastated if they were affected. But she had an ugly gash across her forehead and she was haemorrhaging blood. We waited hours for the helicopter to airlift her off the mountain and they were some of the worst of my life, wondering if every minute that passed was time wasted – time that should have been spent saving her. What if she had a bleed on the brain? What if she lost consciousness and we had to watch her die? Finally, she was taken to hospital and the rest of my family were guided down by volunteers from the Kerry mountain rescue team.I had been so hurt after the breakup and that hurt had seemed very important. The loss, the injustice, the things I had been denied … I carried them with me all year. But on the mountain, for those few terrible minutes in which I thought that my mother had died, something shifted. The things I had been grieving suddenly seemed so small. A house could be sold. A heart could be mended. That which I had thought would break me was, in the end, survivable.All that mattered was that my mother was alive. I could hear her voice again. I could go home and she would be there, waiting for me.That night, as I looked at my reflection in the mirror, I knew it was time to let go of the grief. Not because it was insignificant, but because I was letting it become the most important part of my story. The day on Carrauntoohil gave me perspective. It didn’t fix everything; I still had to deal with the wreckage of my old life. But that was not the same thing as ruin: I was not ruined, I realised. Rather, I had been given a chance to begin again. I just had to take it.A Bigger Life by Louise O’Neill is published by HQ on 24 September (£20).
