title: Stella McCartney makes waves with ‘sea life, not sea food’ theme in zero-wool Paris show | Stella McCartney | The Guardian
description: Designer showcases wool alternatives and ocean-inspired clothes and says ‘kindness requires real work’
Author: Jess Cartner-Morley
Headline: Designer showcases wool alternatives and ocean-inspired clothes and says ‘kindness requires real work’
Content: A model wears a dress inspired by Hokusai waves.Photograph: David Fisher/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenA model wears a dress inspired by Hokusai waves.Photograph: David Fisher/ShutterstockStella McCartneyStella McCartney makes waves with ‘sea life, not sea food’ theme in zero-wool Paris showDesigner showcases wool alternatives and ocean-inspired clothes and says ‘kindness requires real work’Jess Cartner-Morleyin ParisWed 30 Sep 2026 14.47 EDTFirst published on Wed 30 Sep 2026 13.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleStella McCartney has been talking about animal rights at fashion week for 30 years. She is usually a lone voice, but the issue is back in the headlines this season. Outcry over thephysical restraining of a Peta protesterat a catwalk show by Steven Kolb, the president of New York fashion week’s governing body, has put cruelty in wool production – previously considered niche compared to the hot button topic of fur – on the news agenda.“There is no wool on the runway this season, and I’m proud of that,” McCartney said after her show. She has been working on wool alternatives, including Brewed Protein, a fermented alternative to cashmere and wool developed in collaboration with the Japanese biotech firm Spiber, which was first used in her collections a year ago.View image in fullscreenJennifer Lopez, wearing faux fur, and Juliette Binoche on the Stella McCartney front row in Paris.Photograph: Domine Jerome/Abaca/ShutterstockThe issue, she says, is “a tricky one. I’ve got alpacas at home, and I have to shear them. If you can shear a sheep in a kind, humane way, then I don’t, personally, think that’s the end of the world. When we do have wool in our collections it is responsibly sourced. But the way a lot of [wool production] is done today is deeply cruel.“At the end of the day it’s about how kind you are, but monitoring that kindness requires real work. At Stella, we police everything from start to finish at my cost, at my time. If I use wool, I can show you exactly where it’s coming from, and I’m proud of that. But I’m alone in that, and I shouldn’t be.”View image in fullscreenA model wears a sea life-themed sweater on the catwalk.Photograph: David Fisher/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenMiranda Kerr in an ocean-themed dress.Photograph: David Fisher/ShutterstockJonathan Anderson mixes Austen romance with chic streetware in Dior’s Paris showRead moreMcCartney’s remarks on sustainability were interrupted by paparazzi clamouring for a portrait of the designer with the front row guest Jennifer Lopez, wearing a skirt suit with a faux-fur trim and matching stole with a dramatic black net face veil. Tension between fashion week razzmatazz and values-led gravitas is in theStella McCartneyDNA.This season, McCartney’s spotlight is on sea life. “Sea life, not sea food. That’s the point I wanted to make,” she said, after posing with Lopez and dispatching Juliette Binoche with a promise to join her for a glass of champagne shortly. “I’ve never eaten fish, really, but my mum and dad used to point out that one minute people are watching a sea life documentary with David Attenborough and exclaiming about this magical world and the next, they are looking at a seafood menu. It is grotesque.”View image in fullscreenStella McCartney takes to the catwalk.Photograph: David Fisher/ShutterstockThe invitation to the show, held in the vast gardens of the British embassy in Paris, was delivered via a video message from 91-year-old Sylvia Earle, the legendary oceanographer who has spent more than 7,000 hours underwater. Fancy long-sleeved swimsuits walked the catwalk as evening looks; dolphins frolicked on T-shirts. The cursive hems of party dresses looked like Hokusai waves.“We are at war with the oceans, at war with the creatures that live in there,” McCartney said. “For every fish you eat, countless are thrown back dead.”Explore more on these topicsStella McCartneyParis fashion weekFashion weeksFashion industryAnimal welfareAnimalsFrancenewsShareReuse this content

title: Sali Hughes on beauty: a buzzy new brand is aimed at women over 40 – and the industry is taking notice  | Beauty | The Guardian
description: Beauty mogul Sarah Creal decided there was too much emphasis on the teen market – so she designed a range of products for older women. Now others are following suit
Author: Sali Hughes
Headline: Beauty mogul Sarah Creal decided there was too much emphasis on the teen market – so she designed a range of products for older women. Now others are following suit
Content: Sarah Creal felt that her generation was being overlooked by beauty companies. Glasses by Cubitts.Photograph: Kellie French/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSarah Creal felt that her generation was being overlooked by beauty companies. Glasses by Cubitts.Photograph: Kellie French/The GuardianGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Sali Hughes on beautyBeautySali Hughes on beauty: a buzzy new brand is aimed at women over 40 – and the industry is taking noticeBeauty mogul Sarah Creal decided there was too much emphasis on the teen market – so she designed a range of products for older women. Now others are following suitSali HughesWed 30 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s rare that I devote a whole column to one brand, but not as rare as the decision by any beauty company to back women over 40, so I think Sarah Creal is worthy of the inches.Creal, co-creator of Victoria BeckhamBeautyand product developer of countless global companies for more than 30 years, felt that women of her generation (she’s 56) and their specific beauty challenges (hooded eyelids, decreased product wear time and so on) were being overlooked by major brands in favour of teenagers. Wander into any lip-oil slicked, Korean sheet-mask filled, freckle-pen-dotted branch of Sephora and tell me she’s wrong.double quotation markSarah Creal decided to build an entire brand for mature, busy women with a love of luxury and a bathroom cabinet full of products that no longer serve themCreal, a New Yorker who recognised the buying power of what will perhaps be the last generation of consumers to have done better than their parents, decided to build an entire brand for mature, busy women with a love of luxury and a bathroom cabinet full of products that no longer serve them. The buzz around her 2024 US launch had me walking from one Manhattan Sephora to the next, buying whatever scraps I could lay my hands on. But it’s the quality of the products that kept me refilling at each visit.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSali Hughes on beauty: the hero products that kept me cool in the long hot summer of 2026Read moreNow Sarah Creal Beauty is available here, in branches ofSpace NKand viaCreal’s website. So what’s good? A lot.Eyes Up Creamy Kajal Longwear Liners(at £28, a fiver less than the bestselling Victoria Beckham pencils she co-created) outlast any liner I’ve tried. I get no smudging, fading or migrating for 12-plus hours.Moisture Source(£30) is a liquid moisturiser I sandwich underneath my daycream every day. It gives plump, glassy glow without grease. One tiny dot ofFace Flex Correct(£44) under each eye wipes out the signs of perimenopausal insomnia. I’d skip the sunscreen (too pricey in a strong category), eye cream (it pills), and if I had oily skin, the bronzer (I’m dry and love it). But Creal has only just got started – several new launches are brewing.The downside, inevitably, is that Sarah Creal Beauty is expensive. The upside is that her good sense is contagious. US mega brand CoverGirl has formally announced that it will no longer be chasing gen Z, focusing instead on middle-aged consumers. Luxury brands that had once scoffed at the idea of being stocked at M&S are now clamouring for shelf space at what is among gen X’s favourite beauty retailers. In financially precarious times, some basic respect for your customer pays.Explore more on these topicsBeautySali Hughes on beautyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Delays are always welcome’: 10 of the best railway station pubs in England | Bars, pubs and clubs | The Guardian
description: Converted from Victorian buffet bars, ticket offices and waiting rooms, these station pubs offer beautifully restored interiors, real ales and a slice of railway history
Author: Rachel Dixon
Headline: Converted from Victorian buffet bars, ticket offices and waiting rooms, these station pubs offer beautifully restored interiors, real ales and a slice of railway history
Content: The Old Ticket Office in Cambridge has walls painted locomotive green and booths resembling train carriages.View image in fullscreenThe Old Ticket Office in Cambridge has walls painted locomotive green and booths resembling train carriages.Bars, pubs and clubs‘Delays are always welcome’: 10 of the best railway station pubs in EnglandConverted from Victorian buffet bars, ticket offices and waiting rooms, these station pubs offer beautifully restored interiors, real ales and a slice of railway historyRachel DixonWed 30 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 12.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOld Ticket Office, CambridgeNo prizes for guessing what this pub used to be… The Old Ticket Office has high ceilings, walls painted shades of locomotive green and booths resembling train carriages; there are outdoor tables on Station Square. A live train departures board theoretically prevents passengers lingering too long, and a canning machine means any draught beer is also available to take away (the hatch on platform 4 also does takeaway orders). There are five handpulls plus Young’s usual spritz menu and other drinks, plus light bites and pizzas. The pub iscurrently closedfor roof repairs and expected to reopen by the end of October.Tap on the Line, Kew, LondonView image in fullscreenKew Gardens is the only tube station with a pub attached.Photograph: Sunshine/AlamyLondon’s various railway stations have many fine pubs (shout out to theEuston Tap), but Kew Gardens is the only tube station that still has a pub directly attached. When the station opened in 1869, the building was the timber steaming hall, and later become the buffet rooms before becoming a pub. It was bought by Fuller’s in 2012 and reopened the following year after refurbishment. It has high oak beams, picture windows looking on to the platform, an arched glass atrium and a pretty paved outdoor area. It serves two Fuller’s ales and a guest ale, among other drinks, has a full food menu and shows live sport.Stalybridge Buffet Bar, near ManchesterView image in fullscreenStalybridge station has one of the few remaining Victorian buffet bars.Photograph: Anthony Devlin/Getty ImagesThe pub on platform 4 at Stalybridge station, east of Manchester, is one of the few remaining Victorian buffet bars. Built in 1885, it features the original marble bar top, fireplace and fixed seating, plus lots of railway memorabilia. It serves up to 10 changing real ales, plus a cider or perry; bar snacks include hot pork scratchings, with more substantial food in autumn and winter, such as corned beef hash, pies and local black peas. There is a weekly quiz and folk singalong, regular live bands and food pop-ups in the beer garden, and periodic crisp butty pairing events and beer festivals.Camra awards it two starsfor “a pub interior of very special national historic interest”. The buffet bar is now part of the Beerhouses group, which also runs the fantasticWest Riding Reception Roomsat Dewsbury station, and the two pubs are on theTransPennine Real Ale Trail.Sheffield Tap, South YorkshireView image in fullscreenThe Sheffield Tap is in a restored Edwardian first-class refreshment room.For a great night out in Sheffield, visitors don’t even need to leave the train station. The Grade II-listed Sheffield Tap opened in 2009 in the Edwardian former first-class refreshment room. The original 1904 fixtures and fittings have been repaired where possible – including the mahogany bar top, Minton tiles and terrazzo floors – and replicated if not, as with the ornate barrel plaster ceiling. In 2013, the pub expanded into the adjacent tiled and mirrored former first-class dining room, and added a microbrewery. Today it serves 11 cask and 14 keg beers, plus hundreds of bottles and cans; food is limited to locally made pork pies and sausage rolls. The Sheffield Tap hasCamra’s highest ratingof three stars, for “a pub interior of outstanding national importance”. It is now operated by a small group that also runs the excellentYork TapandHarrogate Tapstation pubs.Draughtsman Alehouse, Doncaster, South YorkshireView image in fullscreenThe Draughtsman Alehouse serves local real ale, gin and coffeeDelays are always welcome in Doncaster, for the chance to visit the lovely little alehouse on platform 3b. The former Victorian buffet bar had been empty for 18 years when the pub opened in 2017. It is a family business, named after engineering draughtsman grandfather Barry and run by his son Russ and grandson Luke. The decor features original wall tiles, old photographs and draughtsman’s drawings of steam locomotives; Camra hasdesignated itan “outstanding conversion and restoration”. The Draughtsman serves real ale from Yorkshire breweries, gin distilled in Harrogate and coffee roasted in Sheffield.Scott & Brassey, Carlisle, CumbriaView image in fullscreenCarlisle station’s Grade I listed former waiting room is now home to Scott & Brassey.Photograph: Yasmin Platt/Lancaster BreweryThose lamenting the loss of the 301 Miles From London pub at Carlisle station, which closed in 2023, had reason to celebrate in February, when Scott & Brassey opened on the same site. This Grade II-listed former first-class waiting room dates from 1848, and became the station buffet in the 1950s. Now it has had a slick makeover, but still retains the original wooden entrance lobby on platform 4, the hammerbeam roof and Tudor-style stone fireplaces. There is a mahogany bar, a feature wall full of clocks (no excuse for missing your train) and some platform-side seating. As well as eight handpumps, it serves a host of keg beer, wine, spirits and soft drinks.The Centurion, Newcastle upon TyneView image in fullscreenThe opulent, Grade I listed Centurion bar inside Newcastle station.Photograph: Graeme Peacock/AlamyThe Grade I-listed Centurion has a colourful history. It was designed by the architect John Dobson and opened in 1893 as a particularly luxurious first-class waiting lounge. By the 1960s, it had been turned into prison cells used by the British Transport Police. It then became a storage facility, but thankfully was restored and reopened as a pub in 2002. It has incredible tiling by Burmantofts Pottery said to be worth £3.8m. Columns, a marble fireplace and a high ceiling with a huge tiled skylight add to the air of opulence. The pub serves everything from real ale to cocktails, has an all-day food menu, shows sport on a gigantic screen and has live music every Friday.The King’s Headand theHead of Steam, Huddersfield, West YorkshireView image in fullscreenThe Head of Steam outside Huddersfield railway station.Photograph: Gary Calton/The ObserverLucky passengers at Huddersfield have a choice of two great pubs, both accessible from platform 1, sitting on either side of the station’s grand neoclassical entrance (opened 1847). The independent King’s Head, in the former waiting room, has a mosaic floor, wood panelling and wood-burning stoves, and serves about a dozen cask ales. There is live music on Sunday afternoons. The Camerons brewery-owned Head of Steam, in the former ticket office, is now a four-room pub: a bar, a lounge, a family room and a buffet room. It serves up to 14 cask ales and Pieminister pies. Both pubs appear in Camra’sGood Beer Guide.Steamworks, Seaford, East SussexView image in fullscreenThe Steamworks pub is in the former waiting room of Seaford stationThis micropub opened in Seaford station’s former waiting room (built 1864) in 2017. Passengers can go straight from platform 2 (now the only platform!) into the pub, where there are Sussex real ales on rotation, ciders, sandwiches and other snacks, plus regular live music. After it proved a hit, the husband-and-wife owners opened asecond Steamworksat nearby Glynde, where the station is even older (1846). They are just two of the micropubs that have opened in old station buildings in the past decade, including theTrack & Sleeperin Knaresborough, North Yorkshire; theLittle R’Alehousein Wellingborough, Northamptonshire; theWaiting Roomin Durham; and theHexham Station Platform Barin Northumberland.Codsall station, StaffordshireView image in fullscreenCodsall station’s bar occupies the old waiting room, offices and stationmaster’s houseCodsall is a village on the Shrewsbury to Wolverhampton line. In 1997, the station’s Grade II-listed waiting room, offices and stationmaster’s house were converted into a pub. It has a bar, lounge, conservatory and snug with a fireplace, and steps leading up to a patio area overlooking the platforms. The pub serves three regular beers and two changing ones from Dudley’s Holden’s brewery, while food comprises cobs and pork pies. There are occasional pizza pop-ups and live music, and Cask Club Tuesdays with beer at bargain prices. It is aCamra outstanding conversions and restorations pub.Explore more on these topicsBars, pubs and clubsFood and drinkRestaurantsRail travelPubsBeerfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Country diary: The land here is scarred from a year of hard weather – now what will winter hold? | Extreme weather | The Guardian
description: Camborne, Cornwall: There will be more storms like Goretti and more fires next summer, but we can make the landscape more resilient
Author: Alexandra Pearce-Broomhead
Headline: Camborne, Cornwall: There will be more storms like Goretti and more fires next summer, but we can make the landscape more resilient
Content: Western gorse still charred from fire in the summer.Photograph: Alexandra Pearce-BroomheadView image in fullscreenWestern gorse still charred from fire in the summer.Photograph: Alexandra Pearce-BroomheadCountry diaryExtreme weatherCountry diary: The land here is scarred from a year of hard weather – now what will winter hold?Camborne, Cornwall:There will be more storms like Goretti and more fires next summer, but we can make the landscape more resilientAlexandra Pearce-BroomheadWed 30 Sep 2026 00.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAgrey wagtail flits at the stream’s edge, its flaxen underbelly matching the woodland’s autumn swatch. A few months ago, this bird may have struggled to catch a midge or water snail here, after the streambed nearly ran dry. Sitting by the water now, it’s easy to forget the damage this area suffered this year. But the land remembers.Many months on fromStorm Goretti, the entrance to these woods is still a battlefield of fallen trees, Scots pines and ageing oaks torn ungainly from the ground. Just over a mile away, a gorse break is still scarred from a late-summer wildfire that blackened the coastline. I stopped by the other day; the western gorse should have been blooming, delicate coconut notes luring in late pollinators. Instead, their petrified remains jutted lifelessly out towards the sea.The common denominator in all this is the climate crisis, and yet, in our severely nature-depleted country, the natural world itself can help minimise the damage, if we give it half a chance.View image in fullscreenA stream recovering from drought, Camborne, Cornwall.Photograph: Alexandra Pearce-BroomheadJust over the border in Devon, theDartmoor Headwaters Projecthas shown how native woodland increases water infiltration compared with nearby grazed pasture, and how restoring peatland can improve water storage; both have helped to slow runoff during heavy rainfall. AtWoodland Valley Farm, near Truro, the introduction of beavers has also helped with water storage and absorption into the floodplain.Farther north, in Tywi Forest, up in the Cambrian mountains, rewetted peatlands haveproved resilient to fires, thanks in part to sphagnum moss. And the mix of hazel and sweet chestnut canopies rustling above me, in high heat, will offer just the sort of cover that cools the air, provided we preserve and plant them.All this just scratches the surface of what can be done. Looking at this stream now, I wonder what the future holds. One intense winter storm could bring yet more damage, and next summer the threat of wildfires will arrive once more. We know it’s coming, but while we cannot control the weather, we can influence how the land copes with it.The grey wagtail disappears, leaving the stream to purl steadily on.Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now atguardianbookshop.comExplore more on these topicsExtreme weatherCountry diaryClimate crisisRural affairsDevonCornwallfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Inside the Ukrainian military unit training fighters from China | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Despite the risks, a number of soldiers from the country seen as Russia’s biggest backer have found their way to Ukraine
Author: Yu-chen Li
Headline: Despite the risks, a number of soldiers from the country seen as Russia’s biggest backer have found their way to Ukraine
Content: All of the volunteers agreed that scrutiny from the Chinese authorities would make it difficult to return home. Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The GuardianDespite the risks, a number of soldiers from the country seen as Russia’s biggest backer have found their way to UkraineByAmy Hawkinsin Kharkiv, photographs byJulia KochetovaWed 30 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 11.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn the makeshift workbench in the cramped front room of a cottage near the frontlines of the Russia-Ukraine war, there are all the accoutrements of adrone workshop. The walls are lined with pliers and rolls of duct tape; the table is cluttered with screwdrivers and piles of wire. Propped up against the wall are two kamikaze drones. Only one item looks out of place in this Ukrainian village house: a pot of Chineselongjingtea, the leaves wilted from repeated top-ups.Good tea is one of the many things that Tim misses about his life in China. His parents post monthly supplies toUkraine. “I think about all of it,” the 44-year-old said, of his home country. “It brings back memories and emotions.”View image in fullscreenTim’s teapot at the drone workshopTim, who asked to be referred to by his English name, is the lead volunteer in a Ukrainian military unit that this year launched an unusual project: to recruit soldiers from the country seen as Russia’s biggest backer,China.Many Ukrainian military units have their own brands and public presences as they compete with each other for funding and new recruits. But in this case, the commander of the unit, which focuses on reconnaissance, asked that its identity be withheld because of the sensitivity of theChinese volunteersproject.“It’s for their sake first and foremost,” said the commander, known by the call sign Muse. “For their own safety and that of their families.”Muse said five Chinese men who had joined his unit had returned to China after completing their training because of pressure from the Chinese authorities. “We’d put our heart and soul into them,” he lamented. He is fearful that more Chinese soldiers – there are about a dozen so far in the unit – could quit if their identity is revealed. He asked that none of his soldiers’ faces be shown in photographs.Ukraine’s military is facing an acutemanpower shortage. Most of those willing to volunteer to fight have done so, and are fatigued, while some civilian men have gone into hiding to avoid being mobilised. That has turned attention to another pool of potential recruits:foreigners.View image in fullscreenMemorial to Peng Chenliang, a Chinese soldier killed in action, fighting for UkraineView image in fullscreenPart of the memorial for fallen soldiers, dedicated to Chinese volunteersThere are about 16,000 foreign fighters in Ukraine, making up less than 3% of the armed forces. Before being sacked as defence minister in July,Mykhailo Fedorovpassed several reforms designed to make foreign recruitment easier. He predicted that 50% of frontline service members or assault troops could be foreign citizens.But Chinese volunteers present a unique challenge.On the one hand, they are uniquely vulnerable to pressure from their own government. The Chinese authorities keep close tabs on their citizens. Chinese law does not specifically forbid citizens from joining foreign armies, but several Chinese volunteers in Ukraine said security services had questioned them or their relatives about their work.A spokesperson for China’s foreign ministry said it had issued multiple security alerts “to ask Chinese nationals to stay away from areas of armed conflict … and, in particular, avoid participation in any party’s military operations”.On the other hand, the Chinese soldiers hail from a country that has provided overwhelming support for Russia during the war in Ukraine. Although China claims to be neutral, Beijing hasincreased trade links with Moscowto record levels since 2022 and provideddiplomatic supporton numerous occasions. There have also been reports, denied by China, of high-level military cooperation between the two countries.View image in fullscreenRoads covered with anti-drone nets in Sumy regionSome people worry that the Chinese soldiers in Ukraine could provide useful military intelligence to Beijing. An officer from another brigade said he would “think twice” before taking someone from China.Muse, however, is unbothered. “In this situation, for us commanders, for the Ukrainian people, anyone will do. Because there aren’t enough people,” he said.View image in fullscreenTim, one of the Chinese volunteers, at his drone workshopView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenPlus, he added, the Chinese work hard. Tim’s main job in the unit is repairing drones. In one week he repaired about 10 Mavics and 15 first-person view (FPV) drones. Impressed, Muse joked that “it is better to have one Chinese person than 10 Ukrainians”.Chinese volunteers find their way to Muse’s unit through social media and word of mouth. Although there are cursory background checks done by central authorities in Kyiv, Muse entrusts Tim to do the main screening, through a series of interviews.Tim said the main qualities he looked for were a commitment to Ukraine’s democracy and sovereignty and an ability to communicate well. He added: “I am firmly against accepting someone who is driven simply by hatred for his own country.” He said he had already rejected more than 30 Chinese applicants since joining the unit himself in January, and that he attempted to screen out people with criminal records as well.But in the murky world of foreign fighters, where people come with stories and claims that are often impossible to verify, dissatisfaction with one’s own country is often a factor.View image in fullscreenVanya, one of Chinese volunteer soldiersVanya, a 36-year-old from central China’s Hubei province, joined the unit over the summer.Sitting under a trellis of grapevines outside a cottage near the frontlines, stalked by Russian FPV drones, he said life in China had become “suffocating”.Using a VPN to jump over China’s firewall of internet censorship, he had read about the war in Ukraine, and become familiar with “ideas about democracy and freedom”. That awakening coincided with China’s owneconomic downturn. His own income, working in home renovations, fell by as much as 50% in some months.He had long been interested in the military, but was too old to enlist in China. The decision to come to Ukraine “didn’t come out of the blue”, Vanya said. “It was the result of a lot of things building up over time: my weariness of my previous life, my longing for democracy and freedom, as well as my views on Ukraine.”View image in fullscreenNero, one of the Chinese volunteer soldiersOther members of the unit claim a more fervent ideology. Nero, a 37-year-old from Fujian province, spent years posting online in support of Ukraine, becoming a well-known influencer. Several of his accounts were deleted; Nero thinks this was in response to his pro-Ukraine views.He said the blowback he got from suspected Russian spam accounts for his support for Ukraine propelled him towards volunteering.“I thought: the world shouldn’t be like this. Why should I suffer or go through all this just for speaking the truth?”His move, which he publicised on social media, led to more harassment. As he arrived in Ukraine, a Russian-language “wanted” poster, which included his real name, date of birth, and picture, appeared online. The poster, which appeared to be faked, accused him of “participating in an armed conflict as a mercenary” and “illegally crossing the state border of the Russian federation”. Nero suspected it was produced by a Chinese propaganda agency working on behalf of Russia, and denied making it himself, saying that revealing his identity endangered him.Until recently a project manager earning a decent salary in China, Nero is now training to be an FPV drone pilot. “I want people to know that not all Chinese people support Russia’s aggression. Many Chinese people, like me, are kind and want to help Ukraine,” Nero said.View image in fullscreenL to R: Vasco, Nero, Jinmu, Chinese volunteer soldiersAll of the volunteers agreed that scrutiny from the Chinese authorities would make it difficult to return home. “If I go back now, it would be hard to leave again,” said Jinmu, a welder by trade, now working as an electrical engineer, specialising in explosives and batteries.Whatever contribution they may ultimately make towards peace, or to war, as Chinese nationals their decision is likely to have consequences that last beyond the conflict that they are now a part of. On 23 September, one of their Chinese comrades in the unit was killed in a Russian attack. Upon hearing the news, one volunteer, a doctor, decided to leave. The rest, said Nero, insisted on staying.Additional research by Illia Dyadik, Yu-chen Li and Artem MazhulinExplore more on these topicsUkraineChinaEuropefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: All of a flutter: how butterflies avoid being a predator’s lunch | Animal behaviour | The Guardian
description: Their whirring wings and bright patterns help keep them safe from birds, British study finds
Author: Steven Morris
Headline: Their whirring wings and bright patterns help keep them safe from birds, British study finds
Content: A European swallowtail butterfly and its motion trail, which is thought to confuse predators.Photograph:  George HancockView image in fullscreenA European swallowtail butterfly and its motion trail, which is thought to confuse predators.Photograph:  George HancockAnimal behaviourAll of a flutter: how butterflies avoid being a predator’s lunchTheir whirring wings and bright patterns help keep them safe from birds, British study findsSteven MorrisWed 30 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 14.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNaturalists have long wondered how brightly coloured butterflies manage to evade the attention of birds that make a meal of other insects.New research from British ecologists suggests it is not simply a matter of good luck but instead a visual illusion created by their fluttering wings.The study by researchers from the universities of Exeter and Essex concluded that the spots and stripes found on many butterfly wings – combined with their dancing flight – scramble a predator’s sense of the insects’ speed and direction.George Hancock, of the University of Exeter’sCentre for Ecology and Conservationin Cornwall, said very few European butterflies were toxic or unpalatable and they were relatively easy to spot in flight, so they needed something special to stay out of harm’s way.“The illusions interfere with the predator’s most basic visual targeting system and disrupt the final ballistic attack,” Hancock said. “As a result, birds and other predators often miss.”View image in fullscreenGeorge Hancock of Exeter University says swallowtails deploy illusions to scramble a predator’s sense of their speed and direction.Photograph:  George HancockJolyon Troscianko, also of the University of Exeter, said: “Butterfly wings deform as they fly, clapping together on the upstroke and peeling apart on the downstroke, so their stripes shift angle and point in different directions as they flap.“Combined with their unpredictable flight paths, this patterning creates misleading motion illusions, causing a predator to miss entirely or to strike a less vulnerable part of the wing, such as the hindwing or tail.”The experts compared the mechanism to the “barber pole illusion” – the red and white stripes appear to travel upwards even though the pole is only spinning in place.The breakthrough came when Troscianko put a slow-motion video of a butterfly flying upwards through a “bird-vision” computer model. It seemed to indicate – wrongly – that the butterfly was moving downwards.Troscianko said: “First I checked this wasn’t a coding error, that I’d swapped up and down somehow, but then it dawned on me that this would be a perfect way to confuse attacking predators.”The team looked at hundreds of types of European butterflies and found different patterns created different effects.Swallowtail butterflies were found to be among the best at using motion confusion. Troscianko said: “They are also thought to be closest to the ancestral butterflies, suggesting motion confusion might have been around right at the point when butterflies evolved away from night-flying moths.“Swallowtails have little tails trailing from their hindwings that help increase their levels of motion confusion. They are frequently found with their tails missing and beak-shaped holes cut from their wing edges by failed bird attacks. This fits with our modelling that shows how the wing markings should deflect attacks sideways and behind the butterfly’s vital body and inner wing sections.”The team used a high-speed camera to film butterflies taking off to capture how their patterns behave in flight. To test how patterns might affect attacks, 100 human volunteers acted as “predators”, trying to catch virtual butterflies on a touchscreen. They struggled.The study found that largely white butterflies also managed to dodge predators. The researchers believe that when in flight they appear to move more quickly than they actually do because of the stark contrast they make with their background – which may put out the timing of strikes from predators.Troscianko said the discovery could be used to begin to explain how other animals used motion confusion. “We think it is likely to be far more widespread in nature than previously realised, from the flapping wings of birds to the flicking tails of lizards and fish. It opens up an exciting new research avenue.”The study – Butterfly wing patterns in flight create powerful illusory motion cues – is published inthe journal Nature.Explore more on these topicsAnimal behaviourButterfliesnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I just saw this furry brown bottom disappear!’ In search of Samba – the fearless fugitive capybara | Zoos | The Guardian
description: Six months ago, Samba made a brave, unprecedented escape from Marwell zoo. Her life on the lam continues today. We join the team hunting desperately to find her in the Hampshire countryside
Author: Chris Godfrey
Headline: Six months ago, Samba made a brave, unprecedented escape from Marwell zoo. Her life on the lam continues today. We join the team hunting desperately to find her in the Hampshire countryside
Content: ‘They’re designed to be quite stealthy’Composite: Guardian Design; Dgwildlife/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘They’re designed to be quite stealthy’Composite: Guardian Design; Dgwildlife/Getty ImagesZoos‘I just saw this furry brown bottom disappear!’ In search of Samba – the fearless fugitive capybaraSix months ago, Samba made a brave, unprecedented escape from Marwell zoo. Her life on the lam continues today. We join the team hunting desperately to find her in the Hampshire countrysideChris GodfreyWed 30 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 03.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSamba the capybara is still at large. Along with her older sister, Tango, the intrepid rodent made her escape from Marwell zoo in Winchester in March. Tango all but gave herself up on day two; Samba broke for the marshy wetlands of the River Itchen. Word spread and within days the fugitive was an international social media star. But despite an intense search, the denseHampshirecountryside has afforded her a haven. Six months on, Samba remains elusive.Marwell’s staff still aren’t sure how the capybaras escaped, although they have their suspicions. Tango and Samba were born on Jimmy’s Farm andWildlifePark in Suffolk in the summer of 2025. They arrived at Marwell zoo on Monday 16 March, to great excitement. “They were a little bit shy when they got here, as you would expect,” says Laura Read, the chief executive of Marwell Wildlife. “But they were fine.” They were immediately placed in a quarantined habitat, as is standard procedure for new arrivals. The plan was to keep them there for 30 days.The next day, the vet and zookeepers did their morning checks and everything was fine. But when they returned that afternoon, Samba and Tango had vanished. “There was no sign of them digging out – they don’t dig – and there was no sign of them chewing their way out,” says Darren Ives, a senior zookeeper who has been at Marwell for 15 years. He’s a member of the hoofstock team, who are responsible for “horses, equids, that kind of stuff … basically anything that’s big and shits a lot”. That includes capybaras – which are native to most of South America – although rather than hooves they have partly webbed toes.A potential footprint found in June.“We think they really squeezed under a tiny gap in a gate,” says Read. “That’s the only explanation we have.” After 30 minutes of searching the enclosure, the alarm was raised. “In a situation like this, we are really well versed and have set drills that we practise regularly around animal escape.”When an animal escapes at Marwell, a call identifying the species and type of emergency is sent out over the zoo’s radio network. Staff then send out searchers, contact the relevant authorities (Natural England, Winchester city council, the police) and mobilise drone support (provided by the University of Southampton, which Marwell already works with on population mapping conservation projects). Every species has its own emergency procedure, which includes determining whether a firearm response is required. Despite being the world’s largest rodents, capybaras do not demand a firearm response.The search was initially confined to Marwell zoo’s 57 hectares (140 acres). By the evening, staff had located two warm bodies inside a dense section of tree and bush clippings used for composting. Neither was reachable. As dusk turned to night, staff did their best to secure the perimeter, laid out some food and left. The next morning, Tango left the compost pile and was captured with throwing nets (“without trying to stress her out too much,” says Read). Samba, however, had vanished.Later that day, Marwell heard that Samba, who is about the size of a spaniel, had been spotted near the Ship Inn pub in Owslebury, nearly 2 miles away. A convoy of Land Rovers set off with transport crates and nets, while farmers were contacted to ask for permission to cross their land. Or, as Ives puts it: “In about five minutes, someone in Marwell uniform will be walking across – don’t shoot them.”Read convened a crisis meeting, which looked at the threats to Samba’s wellbeing. “It was cars,” she says. “She’s got no natural predators here. She’s too big. We knew she’d probably seek out water as well, and they’re fantastic swimmers. Water would be her sanctuary.”The decision was made to go public. Was there any hesitation? “That was the quickest way to find her and secure her welfare, so no. Our PR, you know, in terms of: ‘We’ve lost an animal,’ came second.”Local people poured out to look for Samba, including a woman with a trained search dog. “But, in hindsight, did all that activity drive her further away from our direct locality?” Read wonders.View image in fullscreen‘Without a doubt, that’s our girl’ … Samba is spotted in the wild.Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianBy Friday, the local press was taking an interest, then social media, with waves of AI capybara memes appearing. Soon, the story was being reported as far away asthe USand Australia.Glenn Moores also joined the search after seeing the hunt on social media. “I had a bunch of drones and a skill set that could help.” He runs Digital Fauna, a company that conducts wildlife surveys with drones, mostly counting deer (“there’s far more deer than anyone even estimated,” he says).Moores’ involvement has been pivotal, says Ives. “It meant that he could search areas and go: ‘Don’t bother looking there.’” Staff would have to respond to every credible sighting, but “until we had him, we were literally just on foot … walking like a police search when they’re looking for a lost person.” Such was the quality of Moore’s thermal imaging that he was able to detect rats. “We were going out at six in the morning, we were going out at night, we were walking the fields around the river,” says Moores. “It’s amazing that nobody saw Samba in that time.”Is he surprised how hard it has been to find her? “I’m used to counting deer at night, so we’re not strangers to finding animals about the size of a capybara with thermal imaging. That’s what we do. But finding one specific animal in an entire landscape is very different.” How long has he spent hunting for Samba? “My goodness. Days, days and days. Probably about three weeks’ worth of evenings.” His selflessness is not lost on the Marwell team. “All of his time has been given for free!” says Read, appreciatively. (Moores says he wants a free pass to the zoo.)Video shows capybara sunbathing on the riverbank in TwyfordOn Sunday morning, five days after Samba vanished from her enclosure, a member of the public was walking along the bank of the Itchen in Twyford when she spotted a capybara sunning herself. Then her dog, Growler, chased Samba into the river. The video she took of the incidentfound its way to Marwell and the focus of the search shifted: staff donned waders and mounted paddleboards. On land, they looked for tracks, droppings, a body. They flushed out barn owls, deer, a pheasant, but no capybara. Read is convinced she caught a flash of her. “I just saw this brown furry bottom disappear into the river.”For the next week, the search was constant: at least six people a day, mornings and nights. “Everything went really quiet,” says Read. “We just couldn’t find any trace of her.”Six months later, my own trip to Marwell begins with a capybara hunt. Peering into their enclosure – a mixed wetland habitat they share with two swamp-dwelling antelopes called sitatungas – I can’t spot Tango or her new companion, Ripple, a seven-year-old male. “They’re in there, definitely. Don’t worry,” says Read, who has just come from proofreading a press release about a monkey vasectomy performed at the zoo. It’s easy to see how Samba has evaded capture: “Try that in acres and acres and acres of an SSSI [site of special scientific interest] along the Itchen.”Ten minutes later, Tango and Ripple waddle out to the grazing area. Ripple was brought in from a zoo in Blackpool a few months after the escape – partly to breed with Tango, but mostly to keep her company. Capybaras are sociable animals, Ives says, used to living in packs of between 10 and 20. Ripple is calmer and much bigger than Tango – the size of a small sheep, he weighs about 40kg. Capybaras can start breeding once they are about a year old and Tango has already started showing signs that she is in the mood to do so. “When you put the two of them together, they seem to complement each other,” says Ives.View image in fullscreen‘We were going out at six in the morning, we were going out at night’ … Glenn Moores.So, how has Samba evaded capture for so long? For one, her biology. Capybaras are quick. “The things that would hunt these guys [in their native habitat] are jaguars. They need to be able to outrun them,” says Ives. Capybaras are quite angular, he says, making them streamlined when running – it’s an explosive speed, rather than one sustained over long distances. When chased, they head towards water and dive, barely breaking the water’s surface as they do so. Submerged, they canhold their breath for up to five minutes, or furtively breach the surface revealing just their eyes, ears and nose. “They’re designed to be quite stealthy. They’re very good at hiding in the undergrowth.”Is Samba a danger to the public? “They’ve got a cracking set of teeth,” says Ives. “If she were to bite you, she’d probably take your finger off. But also if you get that close – I mean you’re doing better than us! – she would just run away. She would see you, smell you, hear you way before you see her.” As Read says, capybaras have “a reputation, shall we say, for being quite slippery customers in the zoo world”.Also in Samba’s favour is her likeness to local wildlife, particularly muntjac deer. Marwell set up a hotline for sightings. “We had everything from: ‘We’ve seen her dead on the side of the M3,’ to: ‘She’s in my back garden,’” says Read. “We had one man who was absolutely adamant that she was in his back garden and was behaving weirdly. And we were like: ‘Right!’ We went down there … and it was a hedgehog.”Some calls came from as far away as Stonehenge, about 40 miles away. More frustrating were the prank calls from drunk people in the middle of the night. “You very quickly got the gist of who was serious,” Read says. (If you think you have seen Samba, take a picture, record your exact location and send it to the zoo.)In August, Marwell received an image of a rodent-like creature from a camera trap used to spot poachers. The zoo set up its own cameras and a week later received unmistakable proof of life. The first image: a hairy, rotund animal bottom. The second: Samba. “Without a doubt, that’s our girl looking fat and healthy,” says Read.View image in fullscreen‘Capybaras inspire people’ ... Laura Read, chief executive of Marwell Wildlife.Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianShe was two to three miles away from the zoo, near where she had been chased by Growler. “It’s an ideal location for her to stay and disappear,” says Ives. The plan now is to make Samba feel comfortable in that area, allowing the keepers to narrow their search. They want to tempt her back to the same spot repeatedly with food (sweet potato and honeydew melons, apparently). They have laid more camera traps and put down bedding used by Tango and Ripple to see if she is enticed by their scent.Read and her team insist they are doing everything they can, but interest in Samba has brought with it criticism of the zoo. “It’s been really upsetting for me and for the team, because we know how hard we’re working,still,on bringing Samba back,” says Read. “A lot of what we’re doing isn’t necessarily publicly visible, because it is things like drone flights at 6am, it’s camera traps, it’s someone sitting at a desk reviewing camera-trap footage hour after hour. It’s scientifically grid-mapping where we’re camera-trapping. We know that loads of boots on the ground will just drive her further away.”She dismisses accusations of carelessness. “We’ve been here for 50 years. Our record speaks for itself. We’re award-winning for our animal welfare. No one did this because of carelessness. No one did this because they couldn’t be bothered or didn’t do their job properly. This happened because an animal did something that we could not have foreseen it doing.”View image in fullscreen‘They seem to complement each other’ ... Ripple and Tango at Marwell zoo.Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianAs for whether Marwell should have capybaras in the first place: “Just because the capybara itself is not an endangered species doesn’t mean that the ecosystems and the habitats that they occupy aren’t under threat,” says Read. The Amazon and Pantanal – the capybaras’ native habitats –areunder threat and Read believes capybaras could be used to tell that story, not least because they are trendy and draw a crowd. “With the caveat that their welfare needs to be exceptionally well met,” says Read. “Yes, they’re here for conservation, for breeding programmes, for insurance and all the rest of it, but also they’re here to tell a story and to inspire people.”Samba’s story will help with that, she hopes. “We are a conservation charity first and foremost,” says Read. “We are hands-on with our conservation work. We don’t just make donations to NGOs. We have teams in the field doing the work. We want to be really famous for the great work that we do and if Samba is one way of us doing that, then great. We’d like to shine a light on that as well as ‘we’ve lost a capybara’.” She pauses. “Although we did. We own that.”Winter could prove crucial: with less vegetation, Samba may be easier to spot, but capybaras are not built for harsh weather. Is it a race against time? “If we got a really cold snap, we’d all be pretty worried,” says Read. If, on the other hand, it’s just “wet and windy, she’ll be fine with that. It’s more that we have no control over her welfare out in the world, whereas here we can give her everything she needs, including socialisation.”Are they confident they’ll find her? “Well, technically, we’ve already found her!” says Ives. “We’ve seen her on the camera-trap footage. She’s very chunky. She’s very healthy.” If they do catch her, a reunion with her sister beckons. “But when –when,notif– we get her back, it’s going to be a very slow process to mix them, because she’s now a wild animal.”How much longer she stays that way remains to be seen. For Samba, the net is closing in.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
