title: Trump administration diverts human rights funds to push far-right agenda abroad | US foreign policy | The Guardian
description: Support such as for white Afrikaners and anti-communism reveals how US is redefining what qualifies as human rights
Author: Andrew Roth
Headline: Support such as for white Afrikaners and anti-communism reveals how US is redefining what qualifies as human rights
Content: Afrikaner refugees from South Africa hold American flags as they arrive at Dulles airport in Washington last May.Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/APView image in fullscreenAfrikaner refugees from South Africa hold American flags as they arrive at Dulles airport in Washington last May.Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/APUS foreign policyTrump administration diverts human rights funds to push far-right agenda abroadSupport such as for white Afrikaners and anti-communism reveals how US is redefining what qualifies as human rightsAndrew RothandJoseph Gedeonin WashingtonWed 30 Sep 2026 15.51 EDTFirst published on Wed 30 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWith hours left before the funding expires, theTrump administrationis pushing to direct more than $175m of the state department’s flagship human rights fund to a slate of awards that includes a huge $40m grant for an anti-communism fund, support for a group advancing white Afrikaner rights in South Africa, a campaign against Brazil’s supreme court and programs that would reward ideological allies in Europe who protect “western civilizational norms”.On Wednesday, the state department obligated the funds to the grantees hours before the deadline despite congressional concerns and requests not to do so, according to a source familiar with the negotiations. The state department declined to comment on questions from the Guardian specifically on whether it had obligated the funds and had “blown” holds from Congress due to concerns about the money’s use.Critics have focused on 43 awards of a combined $176.9m that will bolster rightwing and conservative causes around the world while probably angering US allies over interference in internal politics. The Guardian has seen a sample of the controversial grants, which make up most of the $205m in funding that Congress has appropriated for the entire Human Rights and Democracy Fund (HRDF).Sources with knowledge of the grant process have told the Guardian that the awards were personally lobbied for by members of the Trump administration, and reflect interests that include JD Vance’s warnings of the collapse of traditional western values in Europe and Stephen Miller’s push against immigration and to support white minorities in countries likeSouth Africa.“The story for me is the high-level – including White House-directed – attention on these programs,” said a person familiar with the discussions over the democracy awards. “These awards have been briefed at the highest levels of the department and have buy-in from the White House.”The proposed awards represent a significant shift in US support for dissidents, human rights defenders and civil society groups under authoritarian governments. The new slate includes projects in wealthy nations, and those focused on opposition to regulation, Brexit, immigration, anti-communism, Christian protection and opposition to “gender ideology”, offering a window into how the Trump administration is redefining what qualifies as human rights and merits tens of millions of dollars in US foreign assistance.“Congress appropriated money for the democracy fund on a bipartisan basis to support defenders of human rights, to assist victims of human rights violations and to instead promote the growth of democracy abroad,” said Jeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the US Senate committee on foreign relations.“The Trump administration’s proposals would use taxpayer funds to promote far-right organizations and programs in established democracies. This is a waste of resources and undermines United States values and relations with democratic partners, including allies in Europe.”A Democratic congressional aide said Shaheen had maintained 10 holds on $22m of awards focusing onBrazil, South Africa, Nigeria, and the promotion of a rightwing ideology in the United Kingdom and in Europe. According to the aide, secretary of state Marco Rubio had personally signed a memo to disregard the holds and obligate the funds.The largest award, of $40m, was directed to a consortium led by the Victims of Communism Memorial Foundation (VOC), an anti-communist non-profit that has received far smaller grants in the past. A state department vetting document seen by the Guardian records $96,997 in previous contracts in the last five years between the foundation and the department, all in the 2022 fiscal year, and notes that it had been vetted in 2019 in connection with tickets to the foundation’s gala. The vetting document also identifies Andrew Bremberg, a former Trump White House domestic policy adviser and US ambassador to the UN European office, as a “senior leader” of the foundation.In July, ProPublica reported that Samuel Samson, a 27-year-old deputy assistant secretary overseeing the new grants, was linked to senior members of VOC through his studies at the Christian conservative Hillsdale College graduate program. (A state department official then told the outlet that the relationship had nothing to do with the grant).Samson has described the US and Europe as partners in a shared civilizational struggle. SamsontouredAustria, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia last December – all countries that were floated to receive a $2m grant to counter migration weaponized by Russia and Belarus – and criticized NGOs that previous administrations had worked with for promoting what he called radical concepts, including gender theory and DEI.The state department did not comment on individual grants but said the programs were still in “active deliberation”, that awardees would meet guidelines for federal grants, and that all programming would undergo a “standard and rigorous vetting process by grant professionals”.“Our programming in Europe aims to support our European allies in defending those rights and principles, along with their civilizational self-confidence and sovereignty from those who seek to undermine them,” a state department official said. “The national security strategy highlights our priorities in Europe, which includes advancing political liberty, promoting free speech, and collaborating with European partners to jointly support European revitalization and civilizational self-confidence.”Under the legislation authorizing the fund, the money must be assigned by 30 September, the end of the fiscal year, when unobligated funds typically lapse.The Guardianfirst reportedthat Trump officials had drawn up no-bid grants aimed at rightwing and anti-immigration causes in Europe. ProPublicasimilarly reportedthat there were at least a dozen no-bid grants earmarked for rightwing projects.The document now shows how much of the fund the plan takes up, and which awards have since been dropped.A $1m award titled “Countering Lawfare and Censorship in Brazil” would fund civil society groups opposing what it calls judicial overreach and censorship by Brazil’s supreme court. The Trump administration sanctioned the Brazilian justice Alexandre de Moraes last year after lobbying by Eduardo Bolsonaro, son of the former president.A program titled “Promoting Western Civilization Allies” would be limited to implementers who do not subscribe to “ideologically weaponized accounts of human rights, such as gender ideology”, according to the document, and will receive $2m. It names possible recipients in Poland, Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Hungary, and the Balkans with “anti-communist” and “natural rights” approaches.One award was allocated to document “democratic backsliding” in Europe tied to “mass and illegal migration” and legislation by “supra-national entities”, while a $1m journalism consortium would push back against designations of “trusted” media outlets. The list also includes $2m for early-warning networks protecting Christians in Nigeria.And a $3m no-bid award would go to the Jobs Foundation, a UK group run by Matthew Elliott, who led the Vote Leave campaign. The grant, titled “Countering Overregulation to Advance American Investment”, would promote a “common good capitalism index” and pro-business policy, including how the foundation promoted Brexit as a chance to cut the UK’s climate regulations.The document also shows that a proposed $5m no-bid grant to the Free Speech Union, the British group founded by Toby Young, has been marked “withdrawn”. When the award was first reported in July, Young said the group had never applied for or received US government money (though Trump officials had reportedly met with the group during a European tour late last year).The grant would have paid the group to campaign against online safety and hate speech laws, including Britain’s Online Safety Act, a law passed under the Conservatives in 2023. Meant to protect children from harmful content and enforced by Ofcom, it has age-verification rules – which took effect last year – that have drawnconstant criticism from the Trump administration, which cast them as censorship.The Free Speech Union is the second British group to drop off the list. A $7m no-bid award to 878, a thinktank whose stated missions include restoring Judeo-Christian culture and “ending mass migration and deporting illegal immigrants”,was abandoned in Julyafter pushback from Congress. It was founded by Jacob Rees-Mogg, who served as Brexit opportunities minister and business secretary before losing his seat at the 2024 election, and now presents on GB News.The British awards would have sent $15m in US taxpayer money to groups run by two sitting Conservative peers and a former cabinet minister, regarding issues including online safety law to immigration.Explore more on these topicsUS foreign policySouth AfricaAfricaTrump administrationUS politicsBrazilAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: South African leader urges men to speak up on gender-based violence after series of killings | South Africa | The Guardian
description: President announces measures amid anger at authorities over recent murders of women
Author: Rachel Savage
Headline: President announces measures amid anger at authorities over recent murders of women
Content: South Africa has been gripped with grief and fury after the discovery of 11 women’s bodies dumped across Ekurhuleni, a city adjoining Johannesburg, since 15 July.Photograph: Esa Alexander/ReutersView image in fullscreenSouth Africa has been gripped with grief and fury after the discovery of 11 women’s bodies dumped across Ekurhuleni, a city adjoining Johannesburg, since 15 July.Photograph: Esa Alexander/ReutersSouth AfricaSouth African leader urges men to speak up on gender-based violence after series of killingsPresident announces measures amid anger at authorities over recent murders of womenRachel Savagein JohannesburgWed 30 Sep 2026 10.16 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 16.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSouth Africa’s president has called on men to take more responsibility for violence against women as he announced measures to tackle the problem, amid anger at authorities over a recent wave of murders.Cyril Ramaphosa acknowledged that not enough had been done to protect women. He said police would be reviewing unsolved murders, attempted murders and serious sexual offences against women and children, as well as producing a funded plan to reduce the forensic backlog for such cases, both within 60 days.In atelevised speechon Tuesday night, the president said local governments would have five months to address issues that compromised women’s safety, from broken streetlights to overgrown public spaces and abandoned buildings. He added that he had tasked five ministers to come up with a plan within 60 days to reduce alcohol-fuelled violence.View image in fullscreenCyril Ramaphosa acknowledged that not enough had been done to protect women.Photograph: Jairus Mmutle/South African Communications and Information Services/AP“Alcohol does not cause gender-based violence and it can never excuse it. Responsibility always lies with the perpetrator,” Ramaphosa said. “But harmful alcohol use is a significant aggravating factor in interpersonal violence and it must be addressed as part of our wider prevention effort.“Women should not have to live in fear because government has failed to repair a light, clear a public space, process evidence or enforce a law.”South Africa has beengripped by grief and furyafter the discovery of 11 women’s bodies dumped across Ekurhuleni, the municipality adjoining Johannesburg to the east, since 15 July. Eight of the women were found in the last three weeks, including Elizabeth “Tsontso” Moselakgomo, who was discovered on 12 September after she went missing when she went for a run after work.View image in fullscreenPeople take part in a memorial run in honour of Elizabeth ‘Tsontso’ Moselakgomo.Photograph: Alet Pretorius/ReutersRamaphosa said suspects had been arrested in connection with three of the killings and that the other cases would not be left to go cold. He added that police had not found evidence that a serial killer was responsible for all 11 killings, but that all possibilities were still being investigated.He directly addressed South African men, urging them to challenge relatives, friends and colleagues who harassed, humiliated or abused women. “It is time for good men to stop being silent men,” he said.“For too long, gender-based violence has been treated as a woman’s problem to solve. Women march, the women of our country organise, they speak out, they protest, they confront and they comfort survivors,” Ramaphosa said.“Women change their routes home. Avoid going out at night and warn one another about dangerous places and dangerous men. We have placed the burden of male violence on women. That must change.”View image in fullscreenStudents gather at the University of Cape Town during a vigil for victims of gender-based violence and femicide, while calling for stronger action against violence against women.Photograph: Esa Alexander/ReutersActivists expressed their frustration that solid policy actions had not been taken years ago and scepticism that the measures Ramaphosa had announced would work.Shenilla Mohamed, the executive director of Amnesty International South Africa, said: “These are not new issues and as a country we have been talking about ways to tackle the high numbers of [gender-based violence and femicide], especially since 2019 when women took to the streets to protest, and yet here we are again in the face of continued attacks against women.“Amnesty International South Africa also notes the timelines put in place by the president, but this will only mean something if it results in action, and if there are consequences for inaction.”Mpiwa Mangwiro-Tsanga and Bafana Khumalo, of Sonke Gender Justice, an NGO, said: “Our concern … is that the response remains heavily weighted towards what happens after violence has already occurred.”They added: “Investigating unresolved cases, processing forensic evidence and repairing unsafe public spaces are necessary, but they do not constitute a comprehensive prevention strategy. It is concerning that the president is asking municipalities to do what is actually their mandate and yet they do not deliver on these.”Explore more on these topicsSouth AfricaCyril RamaphosaViolence against women and girlsFemicideAfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Burundi agrees to receive ‘third-country’ migrant deportees from US | Trump administration | The Guardian
description: Burundi joins several other African nations in accepting people deported under Trump’s hardline policy
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Burundi joins several other African nations in accepting people deported under Trump’s hardline policy
Content: An Eastern Airlines plane carrying Venezuelan migrants from Phoenix, Arizona, landing at Maiquetía, Venezuela, on 3 December 2025.Photograph: Miguel Gutiérrez/EPAView image in fullscreenAn Eastern Airlines plane carrying Venezuelan migrants from Phoenix, Arizona, landing at Maiquetía, Venezuela, on 3 December 2025.Photograph: Miguel Gutiérrez/EPATrump administrationBurundi agrees to receive ‘third-country’ migrant deportees from USBurundi joins several other African nations in accepting people deported under Trump’s hardline policyReutersWed 30 Sep 2026 08.47 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 12.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBurundihas agreed to join a clutch of ⁠other African nations inreceiving migrantsfrom other countries deported from the US under ⁠Donald Trump’s hardline ⁠immigration ​policy.However,Burundiwill only accept those not accused of crime or terrorism links, said ⁠Nancy Ninette Mutoni, a spokesperson for the country’s president, Évariste Ndayishimiye. Tuesday’s announcement gave no details of numbers, timing or financial ⁠details.Washingtonhas sentso-called “third-country deportees” to about half ​a dozen African nations ‌as well as many other countries,often wherethey have no ties, have never been and find themselves detained indefinitely, under opaque deals ‌that Senate Democrats sayhave costtens of millions of ‌dollars.Banished to alien lands: Trump’s secret deportation dealsRead moreIn many cases, deportees had secured legal protections from immigration courts in the US against repatriation. Butrights groupssay the third-country deals allow the US to circumvent those protections.Mutoni said preparations were under way to arrange accommodation, ‌living conditions and integration into local communities inBurundi. “Receiving them requires serious planning – where they will stay, what they ​will eat and how they will live alongside the local population,” she said.“If they choose to join Burundian citizens and make a valuable contribution to national development, the law ⁠will be respected,” she said, regarding potential citizenship.Burundi aimed ​to both ​strengthen diplomatic relations and provide ​hospitality to people in need, the spokesperson ​added.The US ‌state department ​did not ​immediately respond to requests for comment while a spokesperson for the Burundi foreign ministry said details of the agreement were not yet available.Explore more on these topicsTrump administrationBurundiUS immigrationUS politicsAfricaDonald TrumpMigrationnewsShareReuse this content

title: MI5 China alert will send chill through UK’s cash-strapped universities | Universities | The Guardian
description: Institutions have for years turned to China for funding opportunities but national security concerns are mounting
Author: Amy Hawkins
Headline: Institutions have for years turned to China for funding opportunities but national security concerns are mounting
Content: The headquarters of MI5, which has warned researchers to cease work with the China Academy of General Technology.Photograph: Peter Nicholls/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe headquarters of MI5, which has warned researchers to cease work with the China Academy of General Technology.Photograph: Peter Nicholls/ReutersUniversitiesAnalysisMI5 China alert will send chill through UK’s cash-strapped universitiesAmy HawkinsSenior China correspondentInstitutions have for years turned to China for funding opportunities but national security concerns are mountingMI5 issues spy alert to UK universities over Chinese front company stealing researchWed 30 Sep 2026 09.36 EDTFirst published on Wed 30 Sep 2026 09.07 EDTShareThe security alert issued by MI5 regarding a Chinese state-owned conglomerate accused of conducting espionage in the UK reveals the extent to which British intelligence remains concerned about Beijing’s influence, and risks casting a shadow over UK-China cooperation at a time when the bilateral relationship is enjoying a revival.The UK’s domestic security serviceon Wednesday warnedresearchers and academics to cease work with the China Academy of General Technology (CAGT), an organisation MI5 described as a “significant threat”.The CAGT, which is also known as the China General TechnologyResearchInstitute, is accused of paying UK academics working in sensitive fields such as artificial intelligence and cybersecurity for “research that directly improves MSS technical capability for espionage”. The MSS is China’s Ministry of State Security, its intelligence agency.MI5 issues spy alert to UK universities over Chinese front company stealing researchRead moreChina’s approach to intelligence gathering involves hoovering up vast amounts of data, often from unsuspecting individuals who believe they are participating in normal research or consultancy work.This year the UK’s National Cyber Security Centrewarnedbusinesses about Beijing-backed attempts to hack into everyday devices such as wifi routers.Last year, MI5 issued anotherChina-related security alert, warning parliamentarians about approaches from two LinkedIn profiles thought to be linked to Chinese intelligence.Wednesday’s alert said academic institutions or researchers should be aware of the2023 National Security Act, which makes it an offence to engage in conduct that is likely to materially assist a foreign intelligence agency. The warning is likely to send a chill through the UK’s cash-strapped higher education institutions, which have for years turned to China for funding and collaboration opportunities.The UK is one of the leading countries to partner with China’s higher education sector. In May, China’s education ministry announced 219 new transnational education partnerships, with more than a fifth of the approvals being with British universities. That puts the UK at the top of the list of partner countries, ahead of Russia, France and Italy.Chinese students are also the largest group of non-EU international students in the UK, generating about £600m a year for the higher education sector.There has been growing concern in the UK that partnerships with China pose a risk to national security. The 2023 Intelligence and Security Committeereporton China said UK academic institutions “provide a rich feeding ground for China to achieve both political influence and economic advantage” and flagged the risk of China “directing or stealing UK academic research”.In this case, MI5 said that more than 100 academics linked to the UK had contributed to projects funded by the MSS via the front company. The areas of interest were AI, cybersecurity andsteganography, the embedding of hidden data in pictures online.Sam Goodman, the senior policy director at the China Strategic Risks Institute, said UK academics were “between a rock and a hard place” when trying to navigate areas of advanced interest that could be of interest to Chinese intelligence. “There is a lack of a coherent steer from government on something like AI. It isn’t particularly clear on AI at this juncture what levels of collaboration we can have with the Chinese,” Goodman said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnalysts say the UK should do more to highlight which areas are of potentially dual-use interest to Chinese intelligence and provide more guidance to universities and academics.“It’s all very well issuing these warnings,” says Charles Parton, a senior fellow at the Royal United Services Institute. “Actually far more important, surely, is a consideration of which technologies can be cooperated with China, and which can’t.” He said naming specific Chinese companies as a risk would not help UK researchers to do due diligence on every potential partnership. “The Chinese are not stupid. If they want to hide the origin of someone, they’ll do it,” Parton said.Meia Nouwens, a senior fellow at the International Institute for Strategic Studies, said more clarity was needed on the UK side to help guide researchers working in sensitive fields.Nouwens said: “A problem has been that in the past there hasn’t been a great deal of discussion of what areas of research constitute a national security risk. Without understanding the limits are of what the UK seeks to protect, it is impossible to have a conversation about managing risk.”TheMI5alert specifically accused the CAGT of being a front for China’s intelligence. But any research institution in China is ultimately controlled by the Chinese Communist party. “Research institutes that are conducting research on areas of strategic interest for China such as technology will have oversight from the party-state,” Nouwens notes.That does not mean any collaboration with Chinese educational institutions is inherently dangerous, but it does mean UK academics working in sensitive fields will feel increasingly uneasy about working with a country that has financially underpinned the UK’s higher education sector for decades.Explore more on these topicsUniversitiesUK security and counter-terrorismChinaHigher educationAsia PacificMI5EspionageanalysisShareReuse this content

title: MI5 warns UK universities over ‘theft of tech secrets by Chinese front company’ | UK security and counter-terrorism | The Guardian
description: Security service says academics should stop working with and taking grants from firm backed by Chinese intelligence
Author: Vikram Dodd
Headline: Security service says academics should stop working with and taking grants from firm backed by Chinese intelligence
Content: The alert warns of ‘potential criminal consequences’.Photograph: Richard Baker/In Pictures/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe alert warns of ‘potential criminal consequences’.Photograph: Richard Baker/In Pictures/Getty ImagesUK security and counter-terrorismMI5 warns UK universities over ‘theft of tech secrets by Chinese front company’Security service says academics should stop working with and taking grants from firm backed by Chinese intelligenceMI5 China alert will send chill through UK’s cash-strapped universitiesVikram Dodd,Sally Weale,Simon GoodleyandRichard AdamsWed 30 Sep 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMI5 has issued a rare public warning to UK universities that China’s intelligence service is using a front company to pay for research by UK academics and steal the secrets of hi-tech projects.Britain’s domestic security service said researchers and academics should cease work with the China General TechnologyResearchInstitute (CGTRI), sometimes also known as the China Academy of General Technology (CAGT).MI5 believes the body poses a “significant threat” and is now prepared to say publicly that the CGTRI is a front for Chinese intelligence, namely the Chinese ministry of state security (MSS). It said continued collaboration by UK academics could be prosecuted under the National Security Act 2023.The Chinese organisation has funded 100 or more academics at a string of universities across the UK, in return for access to the research, which it is alleged found its way back to China’s intelligence service.On Wednesday, the Chinese embassy in London issued a strongly worded rebuttal, describing the accusations as “imaginary and purely fabricated”. A spokesperson said: “We firmly oppose such baseless allegations and have lodged solemn representations with the UK side.“Exchanges and collaboration between UK universities and China have always been conducted on a voluntary basis and in compliance with laws and regulations. Such exchanges and collaboration are mutually beneficial.”The MI5 warning sent a shock wave through the UK university sector, with staff reviewing the implications for existing or future partnerships with China, and experts raising concerns about the rigour of the vetting process in sensitive research collaborations.Areas of research targeted include AI, cybersecurity, covert communications and steganography – the embedding of secret data in seemingly innocuous files. MI5 believes it has clear evidence of sensitive information being passed back to Chinese intelligence, and the Guardian understands that some British-based academics were given honours and awards by the Chinese as well as research money.View image in fullscreenThe security minister, Dan Jarvis, has written to all UK universities demanding they cut any ties with CGTRI.Photograph: Leon Neal/PASuccessive British governments have courted Chinese investment and encouraged academic cooperation. Sam Dunning, the director of the UK-China Transparency group, said: “It is reasonably obvious from the internet that CGTRI was focused on areas of high interest to the military and intelligence services.“Granted, CGTRI used various aliases and have certainly obscured some funding streams, but as for the UK universities or academics who knew they were dealing with CGTRI, open-source research made clear that CGTRI had military or intelligence links.”Vice-chancellors who spoke to the Guardian said they were not aware of receiving any funding from the Chinese institute, but warned that individual academics working on joint projects with other universities or third parties may not know the original sources of funding.Prof Peter Mathieson, vice-chancellor of the University of Edinburgh and the lead for international security forUniversitiesUK, which represents 142 institutions across the UK, said MI5’s warning meant that future collaborations with the CGTRI would be illegal.“They are saying that anyone who has a link to this institute up until now has not committed any kind of offence, because it’s not previously been said this was a high-risk activity.“Now that they have said it, we have to sit up and take notice. It’s very much a forward-looking directive.He added: “I can’t speak for MI5, but I think what they are attempting to say is that people may not realise that the institute they are working with is connected to the security services of the Beijing government. And there’s no reason why anyone should have realised that, because it’s a new piece of information that MI5 has discovered.”In the alert issued on Wednesday, the Security Service said: “MI5 has identified that the primary purpose of CGTRI is to fund academic research that directly improves MSS technical capability for espionage.”It said that CGTRI had “very strong ties to the … MSS, China’s civilian intelligence and security service”.The alert continued: “Many academic institutions and individuals will to date have engaged with CGTRI in good faith given CGTRI’s obfuscated links to MSS.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“UK academic institutions are strongly advised to immediately review any ongoing or planned collaboration with CGTRI. This is to ensure MSS derives no further benefit from UK universities or research institutions. Further, academics are advised to establish the ultimate funding source when conducting any research collaboration with Chinese institutions, to ensure CGTRI is not involved.”That MI5 has decided on a public alert as a deterrence strategy, rather than trying to pursue every single case, demonstrates the scale of Chinese state espionage targeting the UK. It hopes universities will heed the warning and immediately cease their work with CGTRI.The Guardian understands that cutting-edge British research on scraping social media (gathering large amounts of information from social sites and apps) is among the data to which MI5 believes Chinese intelligence gained access.The security minister, Dan Jarvis, demanded universities end ties to the CGTRI. He said: “This alert exposes attempts by Chinese intelligence to covertly benefit from the expertise and research of our academics, undermining our national security and that of our allies.“I have written to all university vice-chancellors to ensure they support their staff to end all arrangements with this company, preventing further benefit to the Chinese intelligence services and ensuring compliance with the National Security Act.”Responding to the MI5 alert, Vivienne Stern, the chief executive of Universities UK, said universities took their responsibilities around research security and national security extremely seriously.“The sector has made significant investments in recent years to strengthen due diligence, risk assessment and research security processes, while continuing to support the international collaboration that is essential to world-leading research and innovation,” she said.Chinese government filings suggest that CAGT is connected to the China General Technology Group, a major state-owned conglomerate administered directly by the government of China that isalso known as Genertec.The Genertec brand has a UK presence, with a company called Genertec (UK) Ltd, appearing to be owned by the Chinese state.The British company, which has been registered in the UK for a decade and is based in a shared office address on Southwark Bridge Road, had £5.6m in the bank according to accounts to the end of 2024 – cash that seems to have come exclusively from a single property transaction.Additional reporting by Helena HortonExplore more on these topicsUK security and counter-terrorismMI5EspionageResearchUniversitiesHigher educationChinanewsShareReuse this content

title: AI tool that copied actor’s ‘lustrous’ voice violated his rights, Tokyo court rules | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Kenjiro Tsuda wins case against TikTok account in landmark Japanese verdict to protect publicity rights
Author: Justin McCurry
Headline: Kenjiro Tsuda wins case against TikTok account in landmark Japanese verdict to protect publicity rights
Content: Tsuda Kenjiro’s legal team argued that the content posted by the anonymous TikTok account was ‘sordid’.Photograph: Dick Thomas JohnsonView image in fullscreenTsuda Kenjiro’s legal team argued that the content posted by the anonymous TikTok account was ‘sordid’.Photograph: Dick Thomas JohnsonAI (artificial intelligence)AI tool that copied actor’s ‘lustrous’ voice violated his rights, Tokyo court rulesKenjiro Tsuda wins case against TikTok account in landmark Japanese verdict to protect publicity rightsJustin McCurryin TokyoWed 30 Sep 2026 07.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA court inJapanhas ruled that the human voice has legal protection after a landmark case involving a well-known actor and a TikTok account that he claimed had cloned his “lustrous” baritone voice in its AI-generated videos.Tokyo district court said on Wednesday that voices should enjoy the same protection as publicity rights, at the end of a closely watched legal action brought againstTikTokby Kenjiro Tsuda – best known for voicing the character Kento Nanami in the anime Jujutsu Kaisen.But the court dismissed Tsuda’s request that the operator ofTikTokremove the videos, noting that the user had deleted them soon after the suit was filed last November. “The unauthorised use of a performer’s voice … can be considered an infringement on publicity rights,” said the presiding judge, Aya Takahashi.The lawsuit is believed to be the first in Japan seeking to defend an individual’s vocal identity against AI-generated copies. Japan’s voice actors, many of whom achieve star status through their “appearances” inanime, are increasingly worried that AI mimicry is threatening their livelihoods and the industry as a whole.An actor’s voice “is the result of years of rigorous training and apprenticeship”, Yuko Sasaki, executive director of theJapanActors Union said ahead of the ruling.Tsuda, 55, claimed that the 188 TikTok videos uploaded on an anonymous account between July 2024 and September last year had been narrated by a “deep” and “lustrous” voice that could only be his. In response, the platform argued that the videos contained a “generic male voice” and that any perceived similarities to Tsuda’s voice were highly subjective.The verdict is the first in which a Japanese court has declared that the human voice is protected under publicity rights, a reference to the ability to control and profit from aspects of an individual’s identity, in Tsuda’s case his distinctive voice.The protection applies “if the purpose of using the voice is exclusively to take advantage of its commercial appeal”, Takahashi said, describing a voice to be “as symbolic of one’s personality as portraits are”.The TikTok account, whose picture resembled Tsuda’sJujutsu Kaisencharacter, combined images and AI-generated speech about urban legends, the occult and conspiracy theories.At one point, the account had more than 200,000 subscribers and, according to the legal complaint, the clips would have earned its owner between ¥500,000 (£2,395) and ¥75,000 in monthly revenue, the Kyodo news agency said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWe need ‘right to intervene’ in AI amid growing threat, says Bank of England bossRead moreDescribing the content as “sordid”, Tsuda’s legal team claimed the account had only attracted attention because it had cloned the “attractive voice of a popular actor”.TikTok said in a statement it would “respect the court’s judgment while considering what steps to take after scrutinising [the ruling’s] details”. It added: “We will continue to sincerely work on the balance between technology development and rights protection.”In 2024, actors in Japan launched a campaign called “No More” to oppose the unauthorised use of their faces and voices in AI-generated content.With reporting by Agence France-PresseExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)JapanAsia PacificIntellectual propertyTikToknewsShareReuse this content

title: South Korea calls for apology from North Korea after mine injures three soldiers | South Korea | The Guardian
description: Blast during search operation near border fuels political tensions amid attempts to revive diplomatic channels
Author: Raphael Rashid
Headline: Blast during search operation near border fuels political tensions amid attempts to revive diplomatic channels
Content: A North Korean military guard post, top, and a South Korean post near the border between the two countries.Photograph: Ahn young-joon/APView image in fullscreenA North Korean military guard post, top, and a South Korean post near the border between the two countries.Photograph: Ahn young-joon/APSouth KoreaSouth Korea calls for apology from North Korea after mine injures three soldiersBlast during search operation near border fuels political tensions amid attempts to revive diplomatic channelsRaphael Rashidin SeoulWed 30 Sep 2026 03.53 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 04.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSouth Korea has demanded an apology fromNorth Koreaover a landmine blast that injured three soldiers, saying they were hurt by North Korean mines on the southern side of the border.Kang Hyun-woo, the director of operations at South Korea’s joint chiefs of staff, demanded an apology and “responsible measures” from Pyongyang over the blast, which occurred on 21 September during a search operation south of the border.He also called for an immediate halt to North Korea’s mine-laying and border fortification, which he said violated the armistice and the spirit of inter-Korean agreements. North Korea would bear “all responsibility” for any future developments, he said.Why is South Korea so angry with Ukraine over two North Korean prisoners of war?Read moreThe incident echoesa 2015 mine blastin the demilitarised zone between the countries that seriously injured two South Korean soldiers and prompted Seoul to resume propaganda broadcasts over loudspeakers. North Korea responded to the move with artillery fire across the border beforeexpressing regret during high-level talks.The US-led UN command (UNC), which oversees the 1953 armistice that halted but did not end the Korean war, said on Wednesday that a joint investigation with South Korea’s military had identified a live North Korean anti-personnel mine on the southern side of the military demarcation line (MDL), the de facto border.The UNC said an armistice violation had occurred and that it was addressing the issue through “established armistice mechanisms”.The explosions occurred about 10 metres south of the MDL on the western front, as troops searched an area where North Korea was suspected of laying mines.Two blasts went off about a minute apart, seriously injuring a battalion commander, whose foot was reportedly severed at the ankle, and an engineer. A third officer was present and has minor injuries from the explosion.On Monday, South Korea’s military said interim findings showed the blasts were “highly likely” to have been caused by North Korean minesNorth Korea has denied involvement. In a statement carried by state media on Wednesday, Kim Yo-jong, thesister of leader Kim Jong-un, called the incident “an obvious self-staged farce”.“Our soldiers have never once crossed the border,” she said, warning that if South Korean troops fired directly at North Korean soldiers, border units would carry out “immediate and merciless retaliation”.View image in fullscreenKim Yo-jong, seen here in 2022, has denied any North Korean involvement in the incident.Photograph: 朝鮮通信社/APChris Green, a senior consultant at the International Crisis Group, said the investigation findings would not settle the matter politically because the North would always have “guaranteed plausible deniability”.There are no working communication channels between the two Koreas. Pyongyang severed ties in 2024,declared South Korea a hostile stateand has since laid mines and built fortifications along the border. “Accidental escalation on the Korean peninsula is always just a few steps away and it’s fewer steps now than it was in 2015,” Green said.The blast presents a challenge for South Korea’s president,Lee Jae Myung, who has sought to revive diplomacy with Pyongyang. Last week, he told the UN general assembly that Seoul would be a “pacemaker” for peace, and urged Washington to ease sanctions in exchange for a freeze on North Korea’s weapons programmes.The incident has also fuelled political tensions at home. Opposition politicians questioned whether the investigation had been delayed to avoid overshadowing Lee’s UN speech, a suggestion the presidential office denied.The conservative People Power party has also called for the return of the propaganda loudspeakers, which wereswitched off and dismantledunder Lee last year.The mine blast adds to other diplomatic difficulties facing Lee. On Monday, Seouldemanded an apologyfrom Ukraine after its president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, disclosed the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea.Seoul said the two sides had agreed to keep the transfer secret, citing the men’s safety and diplomatic and security considerations. Some critics said the secrecy was about not upsetting Pyongyang.Explore more on these topicsSouth KoreaAsia PacificNorth KoreaLee Jae MyungKim Jong-unnewsShareReuse this content

title: Property prices are plunging in almost every capital city across Australia – see how your suburb rates | Housing | The Guardian
description: Cotality data shows median house prices fell in September as interest rates hit borrowing capacity
Author: Luca Ittimani
Headline: Cotality data shows median house prices fell in September as interest rates hit borrowing capacity
Content: House prices in Australia are at the same point they were a year ago, the latest Cotality data shows.Photograph: Hollie Adams/ReutersView image in fullscreenHouse prices in Australia are at the same point they were a year ago, the latest Cotality data shows.Photograph: Hollie Adams/ReutersHousingProperty prices are plunging in almost every capital city across Australia – see how your suburb ratesCotality data shows median house prices fell in September as interest rates hit borrowing capacityFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastLuca IttimaniWed 30 Sep 2026 16.53 EDTFirst published on Wed 30 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHousing prices are falling in almost every suburb in Australia’s biggest cities, with values dropping faster in Brisbane than Sydney as the slowdown intensifies.Prices nationally have fallen 5.2% from their peak in March to where they were a year ago, Cotality data released on Thursday shows.Economists say prices are on track to fall at least 10% after the Reserve Banklifted rates for the fourth timethis year on Tuesday, pushing more buyers out of the market.Brisbane’s home prices – including houses and apartments – dropped 1.5% in September, with every suburb in the city recording lower prices compared with June.‘Small price to pay’: the young homeowners welcoming falling house prices even as it hurts themRead moreThe median Brisbane home was worth $1.05m, down by $59,000 since May. The Queensland capital had seen prices surge 18% over the preceding 12 months.Darwin was the only city where prices have continued to rise, up 0.4% in September.Sydney median values dropped 1.4% in the month and were down 8.6% from their record high in March, the equivalent of a $112,000 drop. Just four Sydney suburbs held steady in recent months.TableMelbourne prices were down0.7% in September and down 6.4%, or $53,000 for the median home, since March.While a handful of suburbs have seen prices continue to rise, Joe Trucchio, a buyer’s agent at Property Home Base, said the downturn had swept the city.“We’re fully into the spring buying carnival, and we haven’t seen it pick up the way that it had in previous years,” Trucchio said.“It just takes some time and it takes some good news and right now we’ve had a sequence of bad news.”Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailInterest rates have become “the biggest conversation” among hesitant buyers, Trucchio said. Comparison website Canstar has estimated this year’s four hikes have cut $47,400 from the borrowing capacity of someone earning an average annual full-time wage of $108,650.Housing prices would have to fall roughly 10% to offset a 1 percentage point increase in interest rates and no suburbs have reached that threshold.However, Trucchio said dwellings on thecheaper end of the markethad garnered more interest as first home buyers regained confidence.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAustralian house prices are falling but are still almost double what they were a decade agoRead moreStrong-entry level demand has been observed in the 5% deposit scheme, which underwrites almost half of all first home loans.The Albanese government on Thursday reported over 102,000 people had been supported with first home loans under the 5% deposit scheme in the year since it was expanded.The scheme has supported over 8,400 new first home buyers a month since June on average, relatively stable compared to the 8,600 a month average from October to May.The RBA governor, Michele Bullock, said on Tuesday the central bank considered leaving rates on hold amid an unexpectedly weak housing market but ultimately decided to lift.She said falling prices would probably worsen housing supply by making new construction unprofitable.Economists expect Australia’s shortage of housing will force home prices back up in future, though the receding chance of interest rates cuts has made a longer downturn more likely.AMP chief economist, Shane Oliver, said the Cotality data supported forecasts of prices falling at least 10% nationally.“Rate hikes, tax hikes and poor confidence are the big drags but rising distressed listings with rate hikes and rising unemployment do risk a deeper fall of around 15%,’” Oliver said.This story was amended on 1 October 2026 to clarify Melbourne property prices were down 0.7% in the month of September rather than since March.Explore more on these topicsHousingEconomicsBusinessAustralian economynewsShareReuse title: Australia’s cheapest mayonnaise is also the best tasting, Choice test finds  | Australian food and drink | The Guardian
description: Two supermarket home brands claim equal first while the worst-ranked condiment has double the sugar content of almost all the other products
Author: Yvonne C Lam
Headline: Two supermarket home brands claim equal first while the worst-ranked condiment has double the sugar content of almost all the other products
Content: Fair shake of the sauce bottle: some of the 29 store-bought mayonnaises blind-tested by Choice’s judges .Photograph: ChoiceView image in fullscreenFair shake of the sauce bottle: some of the 29 store-bought mayonnaises blind-tested by Choice’s judges .Photograph: ChoiceAustralian food and drinkAustralia’s cheapest mayonnaise is also the best tasting, Choice test findsTwo supermarket home brands claim equal first while the worst-ranked condiment has double the sugar content of almost all the other productsFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastYvonne C LamWed 30 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 19.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA condiment worthy of compliments, or one that gets a dressing down? Consumer advocacy group Choice has taste tested 29 store-bought mayonnaises, and found the cheapest product is also the best.Aldi’s Colway Real Mayonnaise placed equal first with a score of 80%. A jar costs $2.79, or 61c per 100g – the lowest price per unit of the product spread. Judges relished its “mild” and “pleasant” aroma and “traditional mayonnaise appearance”, while noting its “creamy, smooth texture with balanced citrus acidity, subtle sweetness, mustard and whole-egg flavour”.Woolworths Whole Egg Mayonnaise also received a score of 80% for its “good shape retention” and “balanced flavour with pleasant vinegar acidity, sweetness, oil and mustard”. It costs slightly more than its equal-first counterpart, with a price tag of $2.80per bottle or 64c per 100g.Bog standards: Australia’s best toilet paper is also the most expensive in Choice testRead moreThe silver medal went to Aldi’s Colway Authentic Mayonnaise, which scored 77% and costs 78c per 100g. Judges remarked on its “homogeneous texture with a balanced flavour of mustard, vinegar and fat” – although, judge and food consultant Brigid Treloar told Guardian Australia, she noted its slightly orange appearance, like it has “been under the sunlamps”.Sign up for a weekly email featuring our best readsTreloar, one of three judges including chef Serkan Tamcelik and food technologist Petra Sugiarto, said the products were assessed for their appearance (“Does it dollop?”), smell (“I don’t think mayo should have a strong aroma”), and whether its flavour was creamy, smooth and balanced.She also considered whether the mayonnaises were properly emulsified. “In some of them, it was like … here’s a little bit of salt, here’s a little bit of sugar, here’s a little bit of oil, but it didn’t come together.”View image in fullscreen‘I don’t think mayo should have a strong aroma’ … Choice’s mayonnaise taste-testing judges, (L-R) Serkan Tamcelik, Brigid Treloar and Petra Sugiarto.Photograph: ChoiceOne mayonnaise simply didn’t cut the mustard. According to Choice the worst-ranked product was Coles 97% Fat Free Mayonnaise at a score of 47%, with judges giving it the wooden spoon for its “translucent, pale appearance” and “thick, gummy, glue-like consistency”.“It was so sweet,” Treloar said. The mayonnaise has a sugar content of 18.9g per 100g, at least double the sugar content of almost all the other tested products. Praise 99% Fat Free Traditional Mayo had the highest sugar content overall, with 20.9g per 100g, but still scored 63%.The Choice taste test revealed that 27 of the 29 mayonnaises contained sugar, which is not traditionally found in French-style mayonnaise.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFive Great ReadsEach week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSpeaking generally, Treloar sad due to cost, some mayonnaise manufacturers might use thickening or emulsifying agents to achieve a desired texture and mouthfeel. French mayonnaise typically comprises of egg yolks and a neutral-tasting oil, as well as lemon or vinegar, and dijon mustard.Kewpie – which Treloar acknowledged has a “diehard” fanbase – was given a middle-of-the-pack score of 67%. Treloar said compared with the other products, Kewpie was more “savoury”, with a more prominent soya bean oil flavour. Comprising 9.5% egg yolk, Kewpie had the highest egg content of the tested mayonnaises.Some products, meanwhile, didn’t contain egg at all and are therefore suitable for vegans. The best vegan mayonnaise was Hellmann’s Plant Based Mayo, which attracted a score of 77% and an overall equal-third ranking. Judges said it had a “thick and glossy appearance”, although it was “slightly gummy” on the palate.Treloar said the taste test was one of the “most gruelling” she has done. “Certainly doing 29 mayonnaises, I was pacing myself, because it can make you feel quite sick.”Explore more on these topicsAustralian food and drinkSauces and graviesSupermarketsFoodConsumer affairsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Colleges warned ‘do not try to game’ student visas after last-minute enrolments for cancelled diploma soar | Australian immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: Julian Hill says educational providers are being closely watched by government after course attracted non-genuine students
Author: Krishani Dhanji
Headline: Julian Hill says educational providers are being closely watched by government after course attracted non-genuine students
Content: Julian Hill says students should be wary of anyone pressuring them to start another course while they are still completing their existing studies.Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAPView image in fullscreenJulian Hill says students should be wary of anyone pressuring them to start another course while they are still completing their existing studies.Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAPAustralian immigration and asylumColleges warned ‘do not try to game’ student visas after last-minute enrolments for cancelled diploma soarJulian Hill says educational providers are being closely watched by government after course attracted non-genuine studentsFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ournew political email,free appordaily news podcastKrishani DhanjiWed 30 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 19.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePrivate colleges have issued nearly 3,000 last-minute enrolments to a diploma course that is being cancelled after allegedly being “misused” by non-genuine students, as Labor threatens to suspend providers that are manipulating new rules.Guardian Australia revealed last month thatprivate colleges were offering discounts to rush studentsinto the graduate diploma of management (learning) ahead of its deregistration on 5 October, which the government says was being used by some non-genuine students to remain in the country. The assistant minister for international education, Julian Hill, said at the time the system had been “misused”.The regulator says since the ban was announced on 4 September, more than 1,300 new enrolments had been issued and more than 1,500 students have had their future enrolments brought forward.Private colleges around Australia offering last-minute discounts for diploma allegedly ‘misused by shonks’Read moreSome immigration education agents have offered promotions for the month of September, including in WhatsApp messages and texts, encouraging students to join the course or those who have a future enrolment to study now. Several ads promote discounted course fees or a free certificate of enrolment to join immediately.The Department of Home Affairs has issued letters of concern to several providers asking them to explain their behaviour and practices.Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter hereHill said he was prepared to use powers not previously exercised on colleges that have breached the rules, preventing them from being able to recruit new students.“The message to providers, agents and students is simple: do not try to game this measure,” Hill told Guardian Australia.“A paper enrolment, a rushed orientation or token activity is not a licence to evade the intent of the action and curious patterns are now being actively examined.“Providers should expect any attempt to circumvent the intent of these measures to attract close regulatory scrutiny, looking at the substance of what occurred, not simply the paperwork.”The course is taught by close to 450 institutions, has more than 15,000 current students and has more than 40,000 future students registered. More than 1,500 of those students have brought their enrolment forward. Any student who begins the course before 5 October will be allowed to complete it “where no integrity breaches are identified”.One private college has sent immigration agents a promotion offering “attractive” commissions with same-day offer letters and confirmation of enrolment for students, with two “special intakes” on 21 September and 2 October – just three days before the course is cancelled.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toPolitics, reallyOur political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAs part of the rule changes, students who have “packaged” a lower-level vocational course with the graduate diploma will need to enrol on to a higher-level course to meet their visa requirements. By fast-tracking the start date of the graduate diploma, that could mean studying two courses at the same time.Hill said regulators were monitoring students whose study arrangements appeared not to be genuine, such as those studying two full-time courses at once.He warned students in “non-genuine” arrangements could put their student visa or any future visas at risk.“Students should be very wary of anyone pressuring them to start another course immediately, particularly while they are still completing their existing studies,” Hill said.“Genuine students deserve clear advice and quality education – not arrangements created for someone else’s commercial benefit.”Explore more on these topicsAustralian immigration and asylumAustralian educationAustralian politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Stella McCartney makes waves with ‘sea life, not sea food’ theme in zero-wool Paris show | Stella McCartney | The Guardian
description: Designer showcases wool alternatives and ocean-inspired clothes and says ‘kindness requires real work’
Author: Jess Cartner-Morley
Headline: Designer showcases wool alternatives and ocean-inspired clothes and says ‘kindness requires real work’
Content: A model wears a dress inspired by Hokusai waves.Photograph: David Fisher/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenA model wears a dress inspired by Hokusai waves.Photograph: David Fisher/ShutterstockStella McCartneyStella McCartney makes waves with ‘sea life, not sea food’ theme in zero-wool Paris showDesigner showcases wool alternatives and ocean-inspired clothes and says ‘kindness requires real work’Jess Cartner-Morleyin ParisWed 30 Sep 2026 14.47 EDTFirst published on Wed 30 Sep 2026 13.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleStella McCartney has been talking about animal rights at fashion week for 30 years. She is usually a lone voice, but the issue is back in the headlines this season. Outcry over thephysical restraining of a Peta protesterat a catwalk show by Steven Kolb, the president of New York fashion week’s governing body, has put cruelty in wool production – previously considered niche compared to the hot button topic of fur – on the news agenda.“There is no wool on the runway this season, and I’m proud of that,” McCartney said after her show. She has been working on wool alternatives, including Brewed Protein, a fermented alternative to cashmere and wool developed in collaboration with the Japanese biotech firm Spiber, which was first used in her collections a year ago.View image in fullscreenJennifer Lopez, wearing faux fur, and Juliette Binoche on the Stella McCartney front row in Paris.Photograph: Domine Jerome/Abaca/ShutterstockThe issue, she says, is “a tricky one. I’ve got alpacas at home, and I have to shear them. If you can shear a sheep in a kind, humane way, then I don’t, personally, think that’s the end of the world. When we do have wool in our collections it is responsibly sourced. But the way a lot of [wool production] is done today is deeply cruel.“At the end of the day it’s about how kind you are, but monitoring that kindness requires real work. At Stella, we police everything from start to finish at my cost, at my time. If I use wool, I can show you exactly where it’s coming from, and I’m proud of that. But I’m alone in that, and I shouldn’t be.”View image in fullscreenA model wears a sea life-themed sweater on the catwalk.Photograph: David Fisher/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenMiranda Kerr in an ocean-themed dress.Photograph: David Fisher/ShutterstockJonathan Anderson mixes Austen romance with chic streetware in Dior’s Paris showRead moreMcCartney’s remarks on sustainability were interrupted by paparazzi clamouring for a portrait of the designer with the front row guest Jennifer Lopez, wearing a skirt suit with a faux-fur trim and matching stole with a dramatic black net face veil. Tension between fashion week razzmatazz and values-led gravitas is in theStella McCartneyDNA.This season, McCartney’s spotlight is on sea life. “Sea life, not sea food. That’s the point I wanted to make,” she said, after posing with Lopez and dispatching Juliette Binoche with a promise to join her for a glass of champagne shortly. “I’ve never eaten fish, really, but my mum and dad used to point out that one minute people are watching a sea life documentary with David Attenborough and exclaiming about this magical world and the next, they are looking at a seafood menu. It is grotesque.”View image in fullscreenStella McCartney takes to the catwalk.Photograph: David Fisher/ShutterstockThe invitation to the show, held in the vast gardens of the British embassy in Paris, was delivered via a video message from 91-year-old Sylvia Earle, the legendary oceanographer who has spent more than 7,000 hours underwater. Fancy long-sleeved swimsuits walked the catwalk as evening looks; dolphins frolicked on T-shirts. The cursive hems of party dresses looked like Hokusai waves.“We are at war with the oceans, at war with the creatures that live in there,” McCartney said. “For every fish you eat, countless are thrown back dead.”Explore more on these topicsStella McCartneyParis fashion weekFashion weeksFashion industryAnimal welfareAnimalsFrancenewsShareReuse this content

title: No 10 gathering evidence on public support for UK rejoining EU | Brexit | The Guardian
description: Senior Downing Street officials reach out to thinktanks and pollsters as they look to test backing for reversing Brexit
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: Senior Downing Street officials reach out to thinktanks and pollsters as they look to test backing for reversing Brexit
Content: Andy Burnham said he would lay out ‘the different options for Britain’s long-term relationship with our European partners’.Photograph: Susannah Ireland/ReutersView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham said he would lay out ‘the different options for Britain’s long-term relationship with our European partners’.Photograph: Susannah Ireland/ReutersBrexitNo 10 gathering evidence on public support for UK rejoining EUSenior Downing Street officials reach out to thinktanks and pollsters as they look to test backing for reversing BrexitKiran StaceyandLisa O’CarrollWed 30 Sep 2026 14.33 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSenior Downing Street officials have been reaching out to thinktanks and pollsters as they look to test public support for the UK rejoining the EU.Aides toAndy Burnhamhave been talking to EU experts in a range of organisations about how the public would view a promise to rejoin, as momentum builds behind including such a pledge in the next Labour manifesto.Some in No 10 are keen to promise thatLabourwould at least negotiate over re-entry to the bloc, something Burnham has previously said he wants to see happen “in his lifetime”. Others are nervous, however, that making such a promise could revive the flagging political fortunes of Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader.Burnham used hisfirst Labour conference speechas leader to announce a review ofthe optionsfor Britain’s relationship with Europe, and added on Wednesday that these options should include rejoining entirely.The prime minister told delegates on Tuesday: “Brexit has done more harm than good. So I will take the opportunity around the [UK-EU] summit to lay out to you, to lay out to the country, what I believe are the different options for Britain’s long-term relationship with our European partners.”View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham announced a review of the options for Britain’s relationship with Europe in his speech at the Labour party conference.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianOn Wednesday he clarified that this wouldinclude an optionto rejoin – something ruled out by his predecessor Keir Starmer.Burnham told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme: “We could stay as we are. That’s definitely an option, if people think this is the right place to stay. We could look at what [the former Conservative chancellor] George Osbornehas said about a customs union, we could look at what the Liberal Democratssaid at their conferenceabout the single market, or we couldgo all the way.”Andy Burnham wants to review the UK’s relationship with the EU. What are the options?Read moreBurnham’s comments sparked joy among pro-EU campaigners, who argue that rejoining is the best way to boost UK growth rates – and outrage from political opponents.Alex Burghart, the Conservative deputy leader, said: “Labour cannot blame a democratic vote from over a decade ago for the consequences of their own economic decisions.”The Guardian has learned that Burnham’s comments are part of a wider effort by No 10 to test consensus over rejoining, with a view to possibly including such a promise in the next manifesto.Officials have been in talks with several prominent thinktanks and pollsters, who have been working on projects to flesh out arguments over rejoining and test public opinion.Last week, the Tony Blair Institutereleased a paperarguing that Burnham should seek talks with Brussels over becoming a member once more but should only do so if Europe relaxed its regulations in sectors including energy and technology.On the same day, the pro-EU campaign group Best for Britain released a megapoll conducted by YouGov suggesting Labour could more than double its seat total if it went into the next election promising to rejoin.Over the coming weeks, the influential Institute for Public Policy Research will release a paper calling for the country to rejoin, while Think Labour has also been looking into how difficult it would be to do so.Some in Downing Street are buoyed up by polling which shows that promising to re-enter the bloc does little to boost support for Reform. They also point out that Farage attacked the prime minister’s speech for the promise to change the pensions triple lock, rather than his comments about Europe.View image in fullscreenPro-EU campaigners argue that rejoining is the best way to boost UK growth rates.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/Zuma Press/ShutterstockThe Guardian has been told that some at the top of government wanted the prime minister to use this week’s speech to promise to begin work on rejoining after the next election, rather than carrying out a review.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn the end, such an option was ruled out because the party was already bracing itself for a fight over pensions and did not want to give succour to Farage while he faces accusations about millions of pounds’ worth of donations to his party.No 10 said the prime minister did not ever consider making such a promise in the speech and that it was not included in any draft of it.Some believe it would be difficult to persuade Brussels, which has engaged in multiple rounds of talks about Britain’s relationship with the EU, to embark on negotiations over re-accession.But in a major boost to supporters of rejoining, Emmanuel Macron on Wednesdaywelcomed Burnham’s comments. “Welcome back,” the French president said in English at a press conference in Madrid on Wednesday.He continued in French: “If the British want to come back and if the prime minister is moving in that direction, I think that is very good news, both for his country and for the Europeans.”An EU spokesperson said: “The UK is a close and valued partner of theEuropean Union. It is for the UK government to set out how it wishes to develop its relationship with the EU going forward. We remain open to engaging on the options it may put forward.”Burnham’s willingness to look at all options seems to have been accompanied by fresh engagement on the EU’s Made in Europe legislation, which threatens to lock UK goodsout of certain supply chainson the continent.No 10 has sought to have British manufacturers classified as European for the purposes of that legislation, with officials threatening to delay an EU-UK summit until London receives signals that there could be an accommodation.Since Burnham’s speech, however, there is now talk of holding the summit on 20 November.One EU diplomat said it was necessary to get Starmer’s old reset agenda concluded before talks of “a real reset” could begin, confirming support for a UK-EU summit as early as possible.A second diplomat said there was “a good feeling” that Burnham was now looking at all options and seeking a consensus, “something Brussels has wanted to see”.Explore more on these topicsBrexitForeign policyAndy BurnhamLabourEuropean UnionEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Macron says ‘welcome back’ to Burnham suggestion UK could rejoin EU | European Union | The Guardian
description: French president, speaking alongside Spanish counterpart Pedro Sánchez, says EU bid would be good news for UK and Europeans
Author: Jennifer Rankin
Headline: French president, speaking alongside Spanish counterpart Pedro Sánchez, says EU bid would be good news for UK and Europeans
Content: France's Macron says UK could rejoin the EUEuropean UnionMacron says ‘welcome back’ to Burnham suggestion UK could rejoin EUFrench president, speaking alongside Spanish counterpart Pedro Sánchez, says EU bid would be good news for UK and EuropeansUK politics live – latest updatesJennifer Rankinin BrusselsWed 30 Sep 2026 12.40 EDTFirst published on Wed 30 Sep 2026 12.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe French president,Emmanuel Macron, has reacted warmly to Andy Burnham’s suggestion that the UK could rejoin the EU.“Welcome back,” the French leader said in English with a smile at a news conference in Madrid on Wednesday. Macron continued in French: “If the British want to come back and if the prime minister is moving in that direction, I think that is very good news, both for his country and for the Europeans.”Spain’s prime minister,Pedro Sánchez, said his country would open its arms to any bid from the UK to rejoin the EU.The two leaders were responding to the British prime minister’sspeech at the Labour party conferencein which Burnham said Britain would not have a clear path “until we decide on a long-term relationship with what is still our largest market” and that Brexit had “done more harm than good”.In a series of interviews on Wednesday, Burnham said the government could maintain the status quo, seek a customs union, return to the single market or“go all the way”for full EU membership.Macron said the British had “always been useful in helping us simplify things” when the UK was part of the EU and were “demanding partners”. Burnham “is right to have this boldness”, he added.View image in fullscreenPedro Sánchez, right, speaking alongside Macron, said Spain would open its arms to any bid from the UK to rejoin the EU.Photograph: David Niviere/Sipa/ShutterstockEarlier, Macron, who hasfrequently accused the proponents of Brexit of misleading the public, said Brexit had been “the biggest lie of the last 30 years”, pointing to shortfalls in promised economic growth and trade opportunities.Sandro Gozi, an Italian Social Democrat, told the Guardian: “Burnham has finally swept away the so-called red lines that have constrained the debate on Britain’s relationship with Europe. That is a welcome and important step.”The MEP, who co-chairs the EU-UK parliamentary partnership assembly, added: “Europe should respond with the same openness. We should be ready to turn the page and build a new EU-UK partnership, removing unnecessary barriers and restoring much closer economic and political cooperation.”EU officials welcomed the change in tone but said it was up to the UK to define what it wanted from the future relationship. They have told their British counterparts that the UK is welcome to join the customs union orsingle market via membership of the European Economic Area.In recent weeks Brussels has again mooted British membership of the customs union as an answer to thebloc’s Made in Europe policy, which could exclude British clean technology and electric vehicles from valuable European subsidy programmes and public contracts.But EU officials also stress that joining the customs union would require full alignment with EU trade policy and tariffs. Single market membership means accepting free movement of people, alongside free movement of goods, services and capital.More than 10 years after the Brexit vote, the EU remains attached to its red lines. A recent proposal from the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, thatCanada should become the EU’s first-ever associate member, is not seen as a serious option for the UK (or even Canada). The idea is widely regarded by EU insiders as anill-defined symbolic gesturewith no legal basis.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe EU and UK are due to hold a summit in Brussels, with a date in the second half of November expected to be announced in the coming days. The annual gathering was postponed after the resignation of Keir Starmer.Andy Burnham: UK could ‘go all the way’ by rejoining EURead moreThe Burnham government has made resolving Britain’s exclusion from Made in Europe a top priority, but several EU sources say the issue will not be settled at the summit as the EU is yet to agree its internal position on key legislative texts.France is thestaunchest opponent of opening Made in Europeto countries outside the EU, including the UK.Macron pointed to the limits of the UK seeking close ties with the EU while remaining outside. “You cannot choose between the freedoms of the union, nor can you decide to take what suits you and leave the rest,” he said. “So, come back.”A European Commission spokesperson said: “The UK is a close and valued partner of theEuropean Union. It is for the UK government to set out how it wishes to develop its relationship with the EU going forward. We remain open to engaging on the options it may put forward.”Explore more on these topicsEuropean UnionBrexitEmmanuel MacronFrancePedro SánchezSpainEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: French court jails six men for manslaughter over mass drowning in Channel | France | The Guardian
description: Seven others found guilty of lesser charges in connection to incident in 2021 when inflatable dinghy sank killing at least 27 people with four more still missing
Author: Angelique Chrisafis
Headline: Seven others found guilty of lesser charges in connection to incident in 2021 when inflatable dinghy sank killing at least 27 people with four more still missing
Content: French police patrol the Slack dunes the day after 27 people died attempting to cross the Channel.Photograph: Pascal Rossignol/ReutersView image in fullscreenFrench police patrol the Slack dunes the day after 27 people died attempting to cross the Channel.Photograph: Pascal Rossignol/ReutersFranceFrench court jails six men for manslaughter over mass drowning in ChannelSeven others found guilty of lesser charges in connection to incident in 2021 when inflatable dinghy sank killing at least 27 people with four more still missingAngelique Chrisafisin ParisWed 30 Sep 2026 11.58 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 16.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA Paris court has jailed six ⁠men for manslaughter over the deaths of at least 27 people in theworst mass drowningon record from a small-boat crossing in the Channel.Seven other men were ⁠found guilty of lesser smuggling charges with varying degrees of seriousness, including facilitating illegal immigration as part of ⁠an organised gang and criminal conspiracy.Five years on, another four people are still missing.The court heard that the sinking of an inflatable dinghy in November 2021 was caused by “individuals driven by greed, with utter disregard for human life”.Prosecutors said the convicted men helped launch a “substandard small boat, uncertified, unfit for navigation on the open sea, overcrowded and lacking appropriate lifejackets”.Emmanuel Daoud, a lawyer for one victim’s family, called the proceedings a “trial of greed, cynicism and inhumanity”.Twenty-seven peoplewere confirmed dead when theirinflatable dinghy sankin the early hours of 24 November 2021. Four people remain unaccounted for.View image in fullscreenLawyers and relatives of victims arrive at court in Paris for the trial of the alleged smugglers.Photograph: Simon Wohlfahrt/AFP/Getty ImagesThe victims were mostly Iraqi Kurds, but also included people who were Afghan, Ethiopian, Iranian, Somali, Vietnamese and Egyptian. The youngest known victim was a seven-year-old girl. The confirmed dead included 15 men, seven women and two teenagers.Sentences for the six men found guilty of manslaughter ranged ‌from six to 10 years in prison. For others, sentences ranged from six months suspended to four ​years in prison. The court heard that the men were linked to Afghan and Iraqi-Kurdish smuggling networks ⁠that organised the migrants’ passage to Britain from camps near Grande-Synthe and Calais in northernFrance.
