One man was found innocent.According to testimony from the two survivors, the flimsy boat, which had attempted to cross one of the world’s busiest shipping lanes between the northern French coast and Kent in southern England began to deflate and take on water after several hours at sea.Passengers fell overboard and drowned one after another, despite making about a dozen desperate calls for help to French and British rescue services. Only two men survived.For the people onboard the sinking boat, despite several distress calls, it was nearly 12 hours after the first pleas for help before the dinghy was finally found by a French fishing vessel.A separate investigation is continuing in France into seven French military personnel – five members at a maritime rescue coordination centre, and two sailors onboard a patrol vessel. They have been under investigation since 2023 for failing to help a person in danger. They deny the allegations.Zana Mahmand Mohammed travelled from Erbil in Iraqi Kurdistan to address the court about his younger brother, Twana, 18, who drowned in the disaster but whose body has never been found.He said: “We’ve been waiting for our brother’s body for five years. I live with the uncertainty of ever finding out what happened. We lost a member of our family. He had a project for another future to live … ”The family had tried to dissuade Twana from leaving home, but he had wanted to find a job and develop his sporting success as a black belt in taekwondo and escape the violence and insecurity of his region.Mohammed said every time he read in the media about other small boats in difficulty, he relived the tragedy. “Destruction is being repeated,” he said.Explore more on these topicsFranceRefugeesImmigration and asylumMigrationEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Sweden must apologise for harm done to Sami people, says state-backed report | Sweden | The Guardian
description: Truth commission accuses country of failing Indigenous people, amid rising tensions over land rights
Author: Miranda Bryant
Headline: Truth commission accuses country of failing Indigenous people, amid rising tensions over land rights
Content: Sami children campaigning with the climate activist Greta Thunberg in Jokkmokk, Sweden, in 2020.Photograph: Naina Helen Jama/EPAView image in fullscreenSami children campaigning with the climate activist Greta Thunberg in Jokkmokk, Sweden, in 2020.Photograph: Naina Helen Jama/EPASwedenSweden must apologise for harm done to Sami people, says state-backed reportIndependent commission accuses country of failing Indigenous people, amid rising tensions over land rightsMiranda BryantNordic correspondentWed 30 Sep 2026 11.40 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn independent commission set up by the Swedish state has called on the country’s government to apologise for the “harm and injustice inflicted upon the Sami people” and to start a national process for “redress and reconciliation”.The Truth Commission for the Sami People also called for a special apology to be issued urgently to elderly Sami people who were forced as children to attendsegregated so-called “nomad school”and other boarding schools where they were “subjected to violations or abuse”.‘The same struggles as 100 years ago’: exhibition highlights lives of Sami people in SwedenRead moreThe commission’s report, published on Wednesday, is the outcome of a four-year investigation and hundreds of interviews with Sami people across Sweden. It was due to be presented to a government representative at a ceremony featuring readings from the text, but with no government yet in place after theelection earlier this month, it went instead to Parisa Liljestrand, the last government’s culture minister.The commission’s chair, Lena Nyberg, told her: “We hand over a big responsibility.” Liljestrand thanked the members of the commission and those who were interviewed for the report, saying it had been a “historic process”.There have been similar truth commissions into the treatment of Sami people – Europe’s only recognised Indigenous people – in Norway and Finland. Norway hasissued an official apologyand discussions in Finland are ongoing.The new report accusesSwedenof failing to meet its domestic and international human rights obligations and says that as a “direct consequence” of mistreatment, the Sami people today face “major challenges” in preserving and developing their culture.View image in fullscreenPlans to expand mining operations in Kiruna, Sweden, threaten traditional grazing lands used by Sami reindeer herders.Photograph: Johan Ylitalo/The GuardianIt coincides with rising anti-Sami rhetoric in Sweden, including from political leaders, amidclashes over landused for grazing by Sami reindeer herders for hundreds of years, which the state wants to mine for rare-earth minerals.The report says issues with the handling of Sami land rights in Sweden have been “reinforced and aggravated” by an ideology that Sami people are “an inferior people and therefore neither deserving of nor capable of exercising the same rights and responsibilities as other citizens”.It adds that the Swedish state has failed to implement theUnited Nations declaration on the rights of Indigenous peoples.The commission’s71-point call to actionrecommends an official apology for the harm and injustice inflicted upon the Sami people, as well as financial compensation and completing the process of ratifying the International Labour Organization’sconvention on Indigenous and tribal peoples.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt calls for the establishment of a national centre for redress and reconciliation, and for authorities to recognise that the Swedish nation was founded on lands belonging to two peoples – the Sámi and the Swedes – and that parts of the land have Sami names and are part of Sami cultural heritage.It also urges recognition that Sápmi, the region traditionally inhabited by the Sami people, extends across present national borders; an end to racial discrimination against Sami people; and better provision for children to learn Sami languages. It adds that the Swedish government must uphold the Sami people’s right to practise reindeer husbandry and other cultural practices on their traditional lands.The report concludes that the state, including the Swedish parliament, government and public authorities, and in some cases the Church of Sweden, must “bear responsibility” for policies and decisions that led to the violation of Sami rights.It says: “Accepting responsibility also requires the state to work towards providing redress for the harm inflicted on the Sami people and individual Sami, while pursuing policies that do not repeat these historical injustices.”Explore more on these topicsSwedenIndigenous peoplesEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Pilot who stabbed co-pilot on Israel-bound plane may have tried to crash it, says Netanyahu | Israel | The Guardian
description: Accused pilot being questioned in Saudi Arabia as Israeli officials investigate if incident was attempted terror attack
Author: William Christou
Headline: Accused pilot being questioned in Saudi Arabia as Israeli officials investigate if incident was attempted terror attack
Content: Passengers disembarking from the plane in Saudi Arabia.Photograph: X.comView image in fullscreenPassengers disembarking from the plane in Saudi Arabia.Photograph: X.comIsraelPilot who stabbed co-pilot on Israel-bound plane may have tried to crash it, says NetanyahuAccused pilot being questioned in Saudi Arabia as Israeli officials investigate if incident was attempted terror attackWilliam Christouin Beirut andAndrew Rothin WashingtonWed 30 Sep 2026 18.30 EDTFirst published on Wed 30 Sep 2026 05.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne of the pilots of a plane flying from the United Arab Emirates toIsraelstabbed his co-pilot and appeared to tryto crash the aircraft, the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has said, as Israeli officials said they were investigating whether the incident was an attempted terror attack on Israelis.Eyewitnesses reported chaos onboard the flydubai flight, as the attacker tried to barricade himself and the wounded co-pilot in the cockpit, and then attempted to disable the controls, forcing the plane to descend 17,000 feet in just two minutes.Passenger Yaniv Hayoun later recounted how he and other passengers heard screaming and felt pressure as the plane dived before forcing their way into the cockpit and finding the attacker at the instrument panel.“I grabbed the attacker, put him in a chokehold, and dragged him out first,” Hayoun said during a meeting with Netanyahu after the plane had landed safely and the passengers were flown to Israel. “He was trying to destroy the instruments to disable the plane.”MapAs others wrestled with the attacker, Hayoun said he grabbed the controls and pulled them the way he had seen on television. Then other crew members took over.Another passenger, Miryam Shira Ohayon, told reporters via her mother’s phone at Tel Aviv airport that a pilot had attempted to “basically carry out a suicide attack on the plane”, saying: “It was really on the way to crashing.” She added that a doctor onboard had treated the wounded pilot.The stabbed pilot was identified as Indian national Captain Smit Machchhar, who was said to have made the emergency call and opened the door to the cockpit, allowing others to rush in and subdue the attacker.“Despite being stabbed and seriously injured, he fought back, resisted, opened the cockpit door, and enabled passengers and crew to overpower the attacker – preventing a catastrophic mid-air disaster,” Netanyahu said, crediting him with saving 174 people onboard.View image in fullscreenSmit Machchhar, the Indian captain of flydubai Flight 1073, fought back after being stabbed in the cockpit.Photograph: Israel Foreign Ministry @IsraelMFAThe plane was forced to make an emergency landing inSaudi Arabia, with the two pilots wounded but other passengers safe, according to a statement from Prince Sultan bin Abdulaziz international airport, more commonly known as Tabuk airport.The pilot accused of carrying out the stabbing was being questioned by Saudi authorities, Netanyahu said. Israel’s transport ministry said it would carry out a joint investigation with the defence establishment.It was not immediately clear what motivated the apparent attack.The Israeli defence minister, Israel Katz, described the incident as an “attempted jihadist attack”. The foreign ministry later briefed Israeli diplomats around the world that the incident was an “attempted terrorist attack against Israelis, the United Arab Emirates, and the Abraham Accords,” referring to the deal that normalised relations between the two countries in 2020.Donald Trump said he spoke to Netanyahu on Wednesday, but suggested that the motive behind the incident remained unclear.“I did speak to Bibi Netanyahu at length about this event, and it seems as though the co-pilot was perhaps a terrorist or perhaps a whack-job, and he stabbed the pilot,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office.The passengers of the diverted flight landed in Israel on Wednesday evening on a replacement aircraft, eight hours after their emergency landing. Netanyahu praised the bravery of the crew members and passengers who subdued the attacker and landed the plane safely.“They saved many lives. They prevented a heavy disaster,” he said.Israeli officials, speaking on condition of anonymity to reporters, said the attacker was an Omani national and that Israel’s current assessment of the incident was that it was a terror attack. There was no comment from Oman or the UAE.Two and a half hours after flight FZ 1073 took off from Dubai, the plane sent out an emergency signal – squawk code 7700, indicating a general emergency – before sending out another – code 7500, indicating a potential hijacking attempt. Passengers heard screams from the front of the plane, and the wounded pilot managed to open the latch on the cockpit door, leaving it ajar.Graph illustrating rapid descent of the planeThe plane also began toabruptly descend, falling about 17,000ft in two minutes. As the plane began to dive, passengers and a crew member pushed their way into the cockpit, subduing the attacker. Other crew members then stabilised the descent of the plane and began to land it safely in north-western Saudi Arabia.Among those who intervened was an off-duty British pilot, according to a passenger, Almog Itali, who said the plane was carrying a pair of relief pilots who were meant to fly the next flight.“The relief pilots are European, one of them British, who entered [the cockpit] and pulled the aircraft up, pulled the yoke, stabilised the plane and landed us in Saudi Arabia,” Itali said in a clip posted by the BBC.Also among those who stopped the apparent attack were Israeli security forces and air marshals, the Associated Press reported, citing sources close to the Saudi investigation into the incident.Chaos onboard flydubai flight to Tel Aviv after pilots altercationVideos of the incident showed passengers screaming as the plane descended, as well as a blood-covered man who appeared to be the pilot injured and on the floor.Yasmin Abu Kaiss, whose daughter was on the flight, told Reuters her daughter said she had heard screaming and a man with a knife had put a pilot on the floor, and that there was blood everywhere.Passenger on the plane appeals for helpIsraeli officials initially scrambled fighter jets after the emergency signals were sent out, fearing an attack on Israel or that the plane would be diverted to a third country. A spokesperson for the Israeli prime minister’s office then said the incident was not a hijacking, as media reports circulated of a fight between the two pilots.As more information emerged about the violent nature of the attack, Israeli and international media began to report officials anonymously saying an investigation had been opened into whether this was an attack on Israelis.On Wednesday evening flydubai announced it was suspending flights to and from Israel while an investigation into the incident continued.View image in fullscreenA photograph taken on the plane that appears to show a man with blood on his T-shirt.Photograph: Amit SegalView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Amit SegalThe head of the Israeli military, Lt Gen Eyal Zamir, has postponed a visit to the US over the incident, where he was meant to have a meeting with US joint chiefs of staff and the head of US Central Command.The incident came just days after Netanyahu had warned there were indications an attack would be carried out during Israel’s October elections. Israel’s military, quoted by Israeli media, said it had no intelligence that an attack was being planned.7:37Mid-air panic as pilot attacked on Israel-bound flight - The LatestYair Lapid, the opposition figure and former prime minister, cast doubt on the connection between the alleged attack and Netanyahu’s warning, saying a security briefing on Tuesday night gave no information about any potential incident similar to what happened on Wednesday.Israel experienced a series of hijackings and attacks on planes by Palestinian militants in the 1960s and 1970s, but has not experienced anything similar in decades. The country maintains some of the strictest airport security procedures in the world, including security checks before passengers board Israel-bound flights.Flights between Dubai and Israel started after the countries normalised ties in 2020. Israel does not have diplomatic relations with Saudi Arabia, but in 2025 landed a plane in Riyadh because of a medical emergency.Flydubai confirmed that flight FZ 1073 en route to Ben Gurion airport experienced an incident and landed safely in Tabuk on Wednesday. “Our teams are working closely with the relevant authorities,” the carrier said. “Further updates will be issued as additional confirmed details become available.”Israeli media reported that a later flydubai flight heading to Tel Aviv turned around in mid-air and headed back towards Dubai after the incident.Explore more on these topicsIsraelAir transportSaudi ArabiaMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Israeli forces overwhelmed by violent settlers in ‘terrorist attack’ on Palestinian family | West Bank | The Guardian
description: Settler violence in West Bank makes everyday life ‘untenable’ for Palestinians, says ICRC after assault on family trying to return home in Jalud
Author: Emma Graham-Harrison
Headline: Settler violence in West Bank makes everyday life ‘untenable’ for Palestinians, says ICRC after assault on family trying to return home in Jalud
Content: Israeli settlers attacked the West Bank village of Jalud, south of Nablus, early on Tuesday.Photograph: Atef Safadi/EPAView image in fullscreenIsraeli settlers attacked the West Bank village of Jalud, south of Nablus, early on Tuesday.Photograph: Atef Safadi/EPAWest BankIsraeli forces overwhelmed by violent settlers in ‘terrorist attack’ on Palestinian familySettler violence in West Bank makes everyday life ‘untenable’ for Palestinians, says ICRC after assault on family trying to return home in JaludEmma Graham-Harrisonin JerusalemWed 30 Sep 2026 15.01 EDTFirst published on Wed 30 Sep 2026 10.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) has said Israeli settler violence in the West Bank has made everyday life for Palestinians “untenable”, as a mob attack on Palestinians trying to return home prompted one of Benjamin Netanyahu’s main rivals to warn of a campaign of settler terror.More than 100 militant settlers overwhelmed Israeli security forces early on Tuesday to attack a Palestinian family as they attempted to reclaim their homes which had been seized by settlers in theWest Bankvillage of Jalud. Three Israeli security officials were injured and houses were set on fire.The impotence of the Israeli military, the scale of the assault and the injuries inflicted on Israeli security officers by settlers prompted unusually harsh condemnation from Israeli politicians and commenters.Israel is facing unprecedented international pressure over surging violence in the occupied West Bank, where settler militants backed by cabinet ministers have accelerated acampaign of ethnic cleansingahead of Israel’s elections next month.Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, condemned the attacks in Jalud as a “moral stain”. Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief andNetanyahu’s leading challengerin the upcoming elections, called for action to halt a “campaign of terror and violence”.Deadlier attacks by Israeli settlers, including ones targeting Palestinian children, have drawn less attention inside Israel.“Palestinian rights or safety are not the concern, even for people who are in the opposition,” said Mairav Zonszein, a senior analyst on Israel-Palestine with International Crisis Group. “The settler violence is an issue [for them] because it’s making Israel look bad, and also the idea that the military is losing control.”View image in fullscreenA Palestinian family were attacked as they attempted to reclaim their homes which had been seized by settlers in Jalud.Photograph: Atef Safadi/EPAThe ICRC said attacks, settlement expansion and severe restrictions on movement were making everyday life untenable for Palestinian civilians, who Israel has a responsibility to protect under international law. .“The frequent and severe violence must be brought to an end,” said Julien Lerisson, the head of the ICRC’s delegation for Israel and Palestine. “What international humanitarian law says on the protection of private and public property, and on the population’s access to essential services, must be respected.”A graphic showing number of Palestinians killed in the West Bank by settlers or Israeli civiliansA bar on imports of settlement goods came into force in the Netherlands last week, the UK has announced plans foreven broader controlson trade and financing of settlements, and a similar bill will be introduced in the US legislature on Thursday.‘The settlers brought the violence’: the ethnic cleansing of a West Bank villageRead moreOn Tuesday, a Senate bill demanding a human rights report on Israel’s occupation of the West Bank wasnarrowly defeatedafter winning backing from all but one Democrat.“Tonight a disaster was averted, but the barrier has been broken,” the Israeli analyst Roy Sharon wrote on social media after the vote, warning that “anarchy in the West Bank” may cost Israel military aid from the US and its international legitimacy.A cartoon in Israel’s largest-circulation newspaper, Yedioth Ahronoth, on Wednesday showed two soldiers watching an arson attack on a Palestinian home. “They’re going to ruin my trip to Amsterdam,” one says to the other.More than 60 Palestinian communities in the occupied West Bank have been wiped off the map since October 2023 and 18 others have been partly displaced, according to the Israeli rights group B’Tselem. Nearly 5,000 people have been forced from their homes, almost half of them children.View image in fullscreenMahmod Tubasi, 60, and his wife, Aedah, 51, and their family had been forced out of their homes this summer by settler militants.Photograph: Ammar Awad/ReutersThe Tubasi family, whose homes were burned in Jalud, had been forced out this summer after a weeks-long siege by settler militants. Last week they secured a high court ruling ordering the Israeli state to evict settlers and secure their return.Late on Monday the Israeli military told the family that about 15 military police officers would escort them home immediately, Israel’s Haaretz newspaper reported. That was a small number given that Israel is celebrating the Sukkot holiday. The number of violent extremists in illegal settlements usually rises during festivals, and the force was outnumbered by a violent crowd within minutes of arriving.“To carry out an operation such as this, and during the holiday of Sukkot when the [settler] outposts are packed, is madness,” a security source said. The military had not informed national police and the Shin Bet domestic intelligence service of their plans, so they had no security backup.Settlers attacked a house when the Tubasi family arrived, forcing them to the roof, before the military decided to evacuate them in armoured military vehicles. The crowd then set the homes on fire, blocked roads and threw stones at Israeli security forces, injuring three personnel.The two houses “were damaged beyond description”, said Wael ​Tubasi. “They damaged everything – the doors, the tiles were removed, the stairs were removed. They smashed the bathrooms, doors and windows. They left nothing, everything was broken,” he told Reuters.View image in fullscreenThe Tubasi family’s homes were ‘damaged beyond description’, said Wael Tubasi. ‘Everything was broken.’Photograph: Ammar Awad/ReutersEarlier this year the former prime minister Ehud Olmertcalled forthe international criminal court to intervene to stop settler violence because the state had failed.Netanyahu condemned the “violent riots” and called for prosecution of the attackers, but defended the illegal settler movement. “The handful of rioters are not representative of the law-abiding settler public in Judea and Samaria,” the prime minister said, using an Israeli term for the occupied West Bank.A landmark 2024 ruling from the UN’s international court of justice found that the occupation violated international law, a position the British government has endorsed.An Israeli military spokesperson said two suspects had been detained, and called for action to tackle settler militants who targeted Israeli security forces.“The violence directed at soldiers while they were carrying out their duties crosses a clear red line and is unacceptable,” the spokesperson said. “There is no place for such incidents in the state of Israel, and they must not be allowed to become the norm. Such phenomena must be addressed at their root.”On Wednesday, some in Israel questioned whether the army and the state had the capacity to do that. “We have to look reality squarely in the eye: this was a terrorist attack and a failure by the Israeli defence establishment in its entirety,” Avi Ashkenazi wrote in the Maariv newspaper. “It is clear at this point that the real sovereign in Judea and Samaria are the extreme rightwing terrorist activists.”Explore more on these topicsWest BankPalestineIsraelInternational Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC)Middle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Pentagon says it has formally completed withdrawal of US troops from Iraq | US military | The Guardian
description: Twelve years after US mission against IS began, Trump hails ‘great day for America’ and calls Iraq war ‘a quagmire’
Author: Alba Asenjo Domínguez
Headline: Twelve years after US mission against IS began, Trump hails ‘great day for America’ and calls Iraq war ‘a quagmire’
Content: Iraqi security forces parade during celebrations marking the withdrawal of US and coalition forces, in Baghdad on Wednesday.Photograph: Murtadha Al-Sudani/Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIraqi security forces parade during celebrations marking the withdrawal of US and coalition forces, in Baghdad on Wednesday.Photograph: Murtadha Al-Sudani/Anadolu/Getty ImagesUS militaryPentagon says it has formally completed withdrawal of US troops from IraqTwelve years after US mission against IS began, Trump hails ‘great day for America’ and calls Iraq war ‘a quagmire’Alba Asenjo Domínguezin WashingtonWed 30 Sep 2026 14.40 EDTFirst published on Wed 30 Sep 2026 10.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Pentagon has announced it has formally completed its withdrawal of US troops from Iraq, two years after the withdrawal was agreed to and 12 years since the US mission to fight theIslamic Statestarted.After the announcement, Iran and its allies celebrated the departure as a victory, while Iraqi security experts worry that the withdrawal could give IS and others a chance to recover.“Today, the United States and our coalition partners formally concluded Operation Inherent Resolve in Iraq,” the Pentagon said in a statement, adding that the departure of its forces “marks the successful conclusion of the military mission that defeated Isis in Iraq”.The Pentagon said it would continue to provide training and intelligence support to Iraq “to ensure Isis can never reconstitute from Iraqi territory.“The primary responsibility for addressing Iraq’s remaining security challenges, including Isis remnants and Iran-aligned militias that undermine Iraqi sovereignty and regional stability, now rests with the government of Iraq.”Speaking on Wednesday about the withdrawal at a White House event for Hispanic Heritage Month, Donald Trump cast it as a win, calling the Iraq war a “quagmire” that grew out of “very bad decision-making”. He said: “This is a great day for America.”He also described it as a victory for both countries, saying it was “a victory for Iraq, and a decisive victory over Isis”.Trump claimed credit for defeating IS, saying: “I decimated them and took them out in my first administration.” He said his administration “refused to let a temporary presence become a permanent one”, adding that he “felt, without question, it was time for America to go home”.Trump contrasted the exit with Afghanistan, where he said equipment was left behind, insisting that this time US forces took everything. “I want every screw taken,” he said. “We came to fight a caliphate, and there is no longer a caliphate, so we are going home indeed.”He also praised Iraq’s new prime minister, whom he said he endorsed during the Iraqi election campaign, saying he hoped he would “do a fantastic job”.The US invaded Iraq in 2003 to oust its dictator, Saddam Hussein, who ruled the country for nearly 24 years.Theinvasion led to hundreds of thousands of civilian deaths, civil war and sectarian violence in Iraq, as well as the rise of the IS militant group.In 2011,Barack Obama declared an end to the Iraq warand announced that all US troops would be withdrawn from the country by year’s end. At that moment, the US military presence in Iraq stood at under 40,000, and 4,400 US military members had been killed.But in 2014, Obama sent troops back to Iraq after IS militants seized large swaths of territory, including Mosul. A coalition of more than 80 countries led by the US was formed to fight IS, which subjugated millions during a cruel war before losing its hold in Iraq in 2017 and in Syria in 2019.In 2024, during Joe Biden’s presidency, the US and Iraq agreed to wind down the US-led coalition operations.Some analysts fear that Iraqi security forces remain unprepared to ensure the country’s stability. Jassim al-Bahadli, who also serves as an adviser to the security forces, told Reuters that security vacuums can be extremely dangerous. Mohammed al-Juburi, a retired Iraqi army general, also told Reuters that the most important question is whether Iraq has prepared a plan for this new phase.Explore more on these topicsUS militaryIraqMiddle East and north AfricaIslamic StateUS foreign policyUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Whoever is hearing me, we need help’: how flight 1073 survived its 17,000ft plunge | Israel | The Guardian
description: On morning service from Dubai to Tel Aviv, 150 passengers witnessed a horrific cockpit assault and a daring rescue
Author: Oliver Holmes
Headline: On morning service from Dubai to Tel Aviv, 150 passengers witnessed a horrific cockpit assault and a daring rescue
Content: Passengers arrive at Ben Gurion airport in Israel via a second flight from Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, where their original flight FZ 1073 was forced to make an emergency landing.Photograph: Ariel Schalit/APView image in fullscreenPassengers arrive at Ben Gurion airport in Israel via a second flight from Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, where their original flight FZ 1073 was forced to make an emergency landing.Photograph: Ariel Schalit/APIsrael‘Whoever is hearing me, we need help’: how flight 1073 survived its 17,000ft plungeOn morning service from Dubai to Tel Aviv, 150 passengers witnessed a horrific cockpit assault and a daring rescuePilot who stabbed co-pilot on Israel-bound plane may have tried to crash it, says NetanyahuOliver HolmesWed 30 Sep 2026 13.47 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 16.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs flight FZ 1073 soared west over the waters of the Gulf towardsIsrael, its passengers may have bemoaned a 20-minute delay at takeoff. For a low-cost airline route, flydubai’s daily service to Tel Aviv is usually convenient and reliable. The nonstop flight takes about three and a half hours and departs early enough from Dubai that it usually lands at Ben Gurion airport at about 9am local time.That was not the case for Wednesday’s catastrophic flight. The passenger jet never made it to its scheduled destination. Instead, it dropped thousands of feet in seconds before limping down to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia – perhaps miraculously, since photos suggested a large part of the tail of the aircraft was missing.Flight path mapPassengers evacuated, some covered in blood, with stories to share of a pilot-on-pilot stabbing, and footage posted online from inside the fuselage showed the aftermath of violence.In one video, two men lie on the floor with breathing masks on their faces as passengers stand over them in the cramped gangway. One wears a white shirt soaked red with blood, and the distinctive pilot stripes on his shoulders. He appears almost unresponsive. The other man blinks slowly, with blood smeared on the wall next to him. A person off camera appears to encourage the injured man to remain conscious: “No sleep,” he says.7:37Mid-air panic as pilot attacked on Israel-bound flight - The LatestMore footage, apparently from a seat further back, shows passengers screaming and weeping in distress as the Boeing 737 Max shakes. Israeli media reported that the plane was carrying about 150 Israeli passengers.Accounts from the airline, passenger testimony, flight trackers and Israeli officials describe a series of horrific events starting about two and a half hours after takeoff.The flight tracking website Flightradar24 recorded the aircraft abruptly descending from its cruising altitude of about 34,000ft to 17,000ft in less than two minutes. Investigators will look at whether such a sudden and ferocious movement was the reason for damage to the aircraft’s rudder.Flight altitude graphicMinutes later, the plane sent out a series of emergency transponder signals in the form of “squawk codes”. These four-digit codes are normally used by pilots to broadcast their position but can be used in an emergency situation, even if pilots are in radio contact with air traffic control.Aircraft trackers at Flightradar24 said the flydubai plane transmitted emergency and hijack signals. The aircraft made an erratic circle close to the Jordanian border before turning around and heading south.In one video, a passenger with blood dripping from an open wound on his head pleads for assistance and says the jet is descending into Saudi Arabia. “Whoever is hearing me, we need help,” the man says in Hebrew. “We are in the Tabuk area of Saudi Arabia, which we don’t know. All the passengers are OK except for the pilot. We need help.”Passenger on the plane appeals for helpWhat was happening during these critical minutes is still being investigated, but early unconfirmed reports pointed to a cockpit fight, followed by passengers storming up the aisle, and then either one or more pilots who were travelling as passengers wresting control of the plane to avert a disaster.The Israeli newspaper Haaretz cited a passenger as saying that the plane lost control and began to dive.Dalia Shpigel was quoted as saying that “suddenly there were terrible screams throughout the plane” before “three to five guys burst into the cockpit” and subdued the alleged assailant and began treating an injured pilot.“We realised that the situation was stabilising and continued the flight. Gradually, information began to emerge about what had happened in the cockpit,” Shpigel told Haaretz.Chaos onboard flydubai flight to Tel Aviv after pilots altercationHer fellow passenger Miryam Shira Ohayon said the “co-pilot tried to murder the pilot and basically carry out a suicide attack on the plane”.Speaking to reporters via speakerphone held up by her mother, who was waiting at Ben Gurion airport, she said the plane “was really on the way to crashing, and it was simply the resourcefulness of many people who took control of the co-pilot and neutralised him”.“There was also a doctor who gave first aid, and people who treated both of them … but the bigger fear was really a crash, which is exactly what he was trying to do,” she said.The Emirati carrier, in a statement later on Wednesday, said the aircraft was “successfully secured by on-duty flydubai crew travelling on the flight”, who diverted and landed the aircraft safely at Tabuk airport. Airlines often move pilots around different airports as passengers, and it is possible it was these pilots who sent the emergency codes.One passenger, Almog Itali, was quoted by the BBC as saying that one of the pilots onboard who stabilised the plane was British. “There were two spare pilots who were supposed to operate the next flight,” he said. “The relief pilots are European, one of them British, who entered [the cockpit] and pulled the aircraft up, pulled the yoke, stabilised the plane and landed us in Saudi Arabia.”1:19Mother of passenger on Israel-bound flight describes incident – videoStanislav Bukhman, the head of risk at Osprey Flight Solutions, an aviation security firm based in the UK, said investigators were likely to focus on a few key areas, including how pilots were vetted, and crew screening at the departure airport.On how the flight deck might have been accessed, he said cabin crew could request entry to the cockpit using an emergency access code. “This exists for situations where the pilots are incapacitated. There is a safeguard built in, though. If the pilots are conscious and operating normally, they can deny that request and keep the door locked. This is designed to protect the flight deck in a hijacking or hostage situation,” he said.What we know so far about alleged stabbing of pilot by co-pilot on flight to IsraelRead more“At this stage there isn’t enough information to say how the flight deck on FZ 1073 was accessed. The door may have been opened by the captain, who reportedly resisted the co-pilot’s attempt to take control, or by cabin crew using the emergency procedure.”The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, announced that one of the pilots had planned to crash and kill its mostly Israeli passengers, who stopped a “major disaster” with their actions. The alleged assailant was arrested after the plane landed, Netanyahu ‌said.“During the flight, as they approached the country, one of the pilots stabbed the other pilot and apparently tried to crash the plane with everyone onboard,” Netanyahu said in a video message, calling the passengers “heroes”. All the passengers were accounted for and safe.Flydubai, however, said an “altercation” occurred in the flight deck of flight FZ 1073, and it warned against drawing conclusions about the motive.“At this early stage, the underlying reasons and motives behind this event are unknown and remain subject to a formal investigation,” a flydubai spokesperson said in a statement. “We urge all parties to refrain from premature speculation while authorities gather the facts.”Agence France-Presse contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsIsraelAir transportMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Netanyahu says pilot arrested after stabbing fellow pilot and apparently trying to crash Israel-bound plane – as it happened | Air transport | The Guardian
description: Israeli PM issues statement on flydubai incident, which saw plane plummet mid-air before emergency landing in Saudi Arabia
Author: Tom Ambrose
Headline: Israeli PM issues statement on flydubai incident, which saw plane plummet mid-air before emergency landing in Saudi Arabia
Content: 10.23 EDTWhat we know so farA commercial plane travelling from Dubai in the United Arab Emirates to Israel has been forced to make an emergency landing inSaudi Arabia, after an apparent brawl between its pilots prompted distress signals that briefly raised fears of an attempted hijacking.The flydubai flight was over Jordan when it diverted to Saudi Arabia, transmitting three emergency signals, one of which indicated a possible unlawful interference.The plane dipped dramatically during the reported fight, descending about 16,000ft in just two minutes.Israeli officials scrambled fighter jets, fearful of a possible hijacking attempt on a plane containing dozens of Israelis, and the plane landed at Tabuk airport in north-western Saudi Arabia.Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu said one of the flydubai pilots stabbed his fellow pilot and intended to crash the plane.He added that one of the passengers on the flight managed to break into the cockpit with one of the crew members, and together they “neutralised” the attacking pilot.Netanyahu described it as “an extremely severe security incident”. Other officials, including defence minister Israel Katz, have called it an attempted terrorist attack.Netanyahu thanked the passengers and crew who helped to stop the attack, saying they “showed exceptional resourcefulness and courage”.An Israeli official has identified the attacker as an Omani national, Reuters is reporting.The co-pilot of a flight fromDubaito Tel Aviv is believed to have stabbed the captain in a possible attempted “terror attack”.The Boeing 737 plane, which Israeli officials said had between 160 and 180 passengers on board, transmitted a general emergency signal about two and a half hours after departing from Dubai, according to flight-tracking website Flightradar24.Passenger Miryam Shira Ohayon said the plane was “pretty much out of control” when the alleged stabbing took place over Jordan on the flight’s path fromDubaito Tel Aviv.“The co-pilot tried to murder the pilot and basically carry out a suicide attack on the plane,” she told reporters by speakerphone held up by her mother who was waiting at Ben Gurion Airport near Tel Aviv.The plane again transmitted the initial general emergency signal before later landing at Saudi Arabia’s Tabuk airport.Tabuk airport said the plane landed at 9.45am local time and that both pilots were taken to hospital after sustaining injuries.A second flydubai flight fromDubaito Tel Aviv landed safely at its destination after the tracking data website Flightradar24 initially showed the plane diverting back towards the UAE.Flight FZ1081 was later shown to be on its way toIsrael, where it landed in Tel Aviv this afternoon.ShareUpdated at10.44 EDT

title: ‘We want justice’: series of rapes trigger mass protests at Indian universities | Delhi | The Guardian
description: Women say nothing has changed since Delhi’s infamous Nirbhaya bus rape case 14 years ago
Author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen
Headline: Women say nothing has changed since Delhi’s infamous Nirbhaya bus rape case 14 years ago
Content: Student activists protest against alleged gang rapes.Photograph: Rajat Gupta/EPAView image in fullscreenStudent activists protest against alleged gang rapes.Photograph: Rajat Gupta/EPADelhi‘We want justice’: series of rapes trigger mass protests at Indian universitiesWomen say nothing has changed since Delhi’s infamous Nirbhaya bus rape case 14 years agoHannah Ellis-PetersenandAakash Hassanin DelhiWed 30 Sep 2026 11.56 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 16.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe posters, just like the women holding them, were taking no prisoners. “Girls don’t need curfews, rapists need consequences,” read one. “Lock your dicks rather than your women at home,” read another.As hundreds of women walked from the gates of their university campus into the streets ofDelhi– where sexual harassment, assault, catcalling and molestation are a constant, daily threat – they shouted together in a chorus of rage and defiance: “We want justice.”The fury that has erupted on India’s university campuses over the past week has been double-edged. The trigger was a series ofbrutal rapesthat have taken place in Delhi in recent weeks, including the alleged gang-rape of a 17-year-old in a public park close to Delhi University by three men who posed as police officers.From Jamui to Delhi, the burden of safety from sexual assault cannot fall on womenRead moreJust a week earlier, another 17-year-old was gang-raped and murdered in Delhi’s Swaroop Nagar neighbourhood after she went to meet friends. The accused allegedly raped her, stabbed her to death and dumped her body in a field, where it was discovered days later half eaten by dogs.Rapes of an 11-year-old and a six-year-old were reported in the same month. Last month, a 16-year-old was allegedly raped by a bus driver and conductor after she boarded a sleeper bus in Delhi.Women who have taken part in protests on Delhi university campuses have condemned these alleged violent rapes on minors as disgusting and unforgivable – but they have also been at pains to emphasise that they are not out of the ordinary.Fourteen years have passed since Delhi’s infamous Nirbhaya rape case, when a woman was gang-raped on a bus and died from her injuries. But while it provoked international outrage and a slew of legislation and government promises, women say nothing has changed; for them, India’s streets, particularly in Delhi, remain as unsafe as ever. According to statistics, a women is raped inIndiaevery 20 minutes – though the real scale is believed to be far worse due to chronic under-reporting.This week, the supreme court said the five successive rape cases “starkly underlined a systematic failure” and it could not help but “draw painful parallels to the Nirbhaya incident of 2012”.Vaishnavi Dhruw, 21, a history student at Delhi University, was among the female protesters at the “smash the patriarchy” protest march on Wednesday afternoon. “I don’t know a single woman who lives in this city and feels safe,” she said.View image in fullscreenStudents’ Federation of India (SFI) members protest over the alleged rape of a 17-year-old girl.Photograph: Rajat Gupta/EPAWhile some of the key demands of the protest have been better lighting and policing, Dhruw emphasised that for anything to change, the country required a deep societal shift where men no longer felt they had ownership over women’s bodies.“We are not marching for safety, we are here to protest for our freedom, for the most basic right to walk in our own streets,” she said. “Again and again, women are told to stay indoors, to not go out at night, to cover ourselves, to protect ourselves. When will society tell men in our country not to rape?”Much of the anger driving the protests has also been prompted by the response by the authorities to the rapes, which women say once again has only been to police their freedoms. Women in Delhi were told to stay out of parks at night, and classes were temporarily halted at one of Delhi’s most prestigious female colleges. Many hostels where female students stay impose strict curfews preventing them from going out at night.“Instead of going after criminals, you’re going to tell women to sit at home,” said Aranya Rathore, 25, a student at Delhi University. “A demand for more surveillance is not a solution. In fact, it’s going to curtail our freedom more.”Female students say a lot of their time is taken up by safety logistics – from wearing modest clothes to reorganising their days to ensure they do not travel alone or at night and always having a trackable live location on their phones. There is widespread awareness that should anything happen, the onus of blame – both within the family home and more widely in society – tends to fall on women. As one poster at Wednesday’s march pointed out, “no one ever asks what the rapist was wearing”.Yet despite their best efforts, many women said it was almost impossible to avoid harassment. Ananya Wig, a 26-year-old graduate of Delhi University and the founder of Her Huq, a gender equality initiative, said she had experienced harassment both around university campuses and in public spaces.She recounted an incident where a driver rolled down his car window and began masturbating as she and female friends got off a rickshaw and walked through the college gates. “This wasn’t at night, it was in the middle of the day,” she said. “I’ve always lived in Delhi and the city has not changed.”‘If you saw her body, you will never sleep again’: despair as India rape crisis growsRead moreThe protests have brought into focus a dilemma faced by many Indian women, who are being educated in greater numbers than any time in the country’s history and have better job opportunities than ever before, but still have to navigate the constant debilitating threats to their safety and the conservative pressures from their families.“I know so many girls, not just 10 years ago but even today, who end up choosing educational institutions and jobs and other employment opportunities depending on how close they are from their home,” said Wig. “Not on the basis of their marks, not on the basis of their aspirations, but simply, ‘OK, the shorter the distance is, the more likely it is that I will be safe’.”Many of the Delhi University students who took part in the marches said that sexual harassment had become prevalent on campus, and have demanded better accountability mechanisms for reporting assault. The university has not responded.Devyani Sarkar, 24, who is studying for a master’s in English, said: “Delhi University is one of the most prestigious universities in India right now but there are various cases of women being assaulted by professors, sometimes unfortunately also for grades. It’s despicable, but it’s also a living truth.”Many on the marches said it was no coincidence that they were taking place in the aftermath ofIndia’s “cockroach” movement, in which hundreds of thousands of young Gen Z Indians took to the streets over education reform.“My generation is not afraid to stand up and protest. We know that society has to change,” said 17-year-old Subhani. “The days of women being silent is over.”Explore more on these topicsDelhiIndiaRape and sexual assaultViolence against women and girlsProtestSouth and central AsianewsShareReuse this content

title: Floating scarecrows: how Cornish fishers are stopping seabirds drowning in their nets | Fishing | The Guardian
description: Simple deterrents can slash the number of razorbills and guillemots being trapped underwater, two-year study shows
Author: Patrick Barkham
Headline: Simple deterrents can slash the number of razorbills and guillemots being trapped underwater, two-year study shows
Content: Cornish fishing vessels were used to test the deterrent effect of the towed ‘scarecrow’ buoy.Photograph: Nina Constable MediaView image in fullscreenCornish fishing vessels were used to test the deterrent effect of the towed ‘scarecrow’ buoy.Photograph: Nina Constable MediaFishingFloating scarecrows: how Cornish fishers are stopping seabirds drowning in their netsSimple deterrents can slash the number of razorbills and guillemots being trapped underwater, two-year study showsPatrick BarkhamWed 30 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 19.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBird-shaped kites and a floating scarecrow are being tested to try to stop endangered seabirds drowning in fishing nets.Every year an estimated 95,000 diving birds, including razorbills and guillemots, are accidentally caught in nets off European coasts.But simple deterrents tested by Cornish fishers and devised by scientists and the RSPB have been shown to reduce the toll by about two-thirds.The scarecrow – or more properly a looming-eyes buoy – has a spinning head with two large eyes that scare diving birds away from gillnets, walls of netting which hang vertically beneath the surface.The LEB was tested alongside a commercially availablescarybird kite.View image in fullscreenThe buoy cut the chance of seabirds being caught in gillnets by 59%. Kites achieved a 71% figure.Photograph: Nina Constable MediaTen Cornish fishers andFishtek Marine, which created the LEB, fitted cameras to boats to monitor the effect of the devices on seabird behaviour.The results of the two-year trial, which was analysed by scientists from the University of Exeter and published in the journalConservation Letters, showed that the chance of seabirds being caught in gillnets fell by 59% using LEBs and by 71% using kites.The research revealed that inCornwallmost seabirds were caught in winter, which will help target the use of the devices by season.Tom Horton, lead author of the University of Exeter research, said: “This study provides some of the strongest evidence to date that simple, practical deterrents can substantially reduce seabird bycatch in gillnet fisheries.“By also identifying when and where bycatch risk is highest, we now have a clear opportunity to target mitigation measures where they can deliver the greatest conservation benefit for vulnerable seabird populations and encourage sustainable fishing practices.”Yann Rouxel, bycatch programme manager at the RSPB, said: “After over a decade of research into gillnet bycatch and its solutions, it’s great to see this work moving towards real-world implementation.“The performance of the LEB and kite, as evidenced in this study, is a major milestone in the effort to reduce seabird bycatch without impeding gillnet fishers while at sea.”Explore more on these topicsFishingFishing industryBirdsCornwallMarine lifeWildlifenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Hugely exciting’ finds on tiny Scottish island shed light on spread of Christianity | Archaeology | The Guardian
description: Community-funded archaeological excavations of ‘really important’ sixth-century monastery also rewrite story of Lismore
Author: Esther Addley
Headline: Community-funded archaeological excavations of ‘really important’ sixth-century monastery also rewrite story of Lismore
Content: Islanders and volunteers have been digging in the early medieval cemetery, where they have discovered the earlier buildings, burial grounds and other finds.Photograph: Robert HayView image in fullscreenIslanders and volunteers have been digging in the early medieval cemetery, where they have discovered the earlier buildings, burial grounds and other finds.Photograph: Robert HayArchaeology‘Hugely exciting’ finds on tiny Scottish island shed light on spread of ChristianityCommunity-funded archaeological excavations of ‘really important’ sixth-century monastery also rewrite story of LismoreEsther AddleyWed 30 Sep 2026 19.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTo the residents of the Scottish island of Lismore, population 190, history is never very far away. The tiny island near Oban in Argyll has no row of shops or even a pub – if islanders want to meet for a coffee, the only place to do so is in the livelyGaelic heritage centrethat records the many centuries of community life on the island.This quiet place, documentary evidence records, was home to a monastic settlement in the sixth century AD, when missionaries from Ireland were first moving into northern Britain to spreadChristianity. But apart from a few fragments of an early carved cross, there was almost nothing to see from this period of history.A group of local people from the island’s historical society were determined to look a bit harder, however. After scraping together funding from grants, donations and legacies of locals and a crowdfunding campaign, they commissioned a professional archaeologist, Dr Clare Ellis of ArgyllArchaeology, to lead a group of islanders and other volunteers in an excavation on the site of a much later medieval cathedral.View image in fullscreenThe site contains extensive burial grounds, decorated stonework and early buildings.Photograph: Robert HayTheir “hugely exciting” findings have not only rewritten the story of the island but cast new light on the spread of Christianity in the period, according to archaeologists. What the islanders discovered were extensive burial grounds, decorated stonework and early buildings – all the features belonging to a major sixth-century monastery, comparable to the much better known site of Iona a little to the south-west.In addition, the excavations uncovered rare evidence of slightly later high-status craftworking, including huge numbers of crucibles which had been used to cast gold and silver. The finds have shown that rather than being a small island church in an overlooked backwater, the monastery of Lios Mór, founded bySaint Mo Luóc or Moluag, was a high-ranking site of international importance, experts say.To Robert Hay, a retired plant scientist who moved to the island in 2001 and who coordinated the fundraising and volunteer efforts, the experience was thrilling. “We were [excavating] in this really unfavourable, boggy area. To be digging out the best small crucibles ever found inScotland– it’s extraordinary,” he said.View image in fullscreenA crucible freshly out of the soil.Photograph: Robert Hay“The most exciting moment for me was when they were doing the post-excavation analysis and they found that they had been melting gold, copper, silver, and they were making jewellery on our little island in the seventh century.”While plenty of islanders have an idle interest in its history, a “dynamic minority” of mostly older people had mustered the volunteers and funds to carry out the digs, said Hay. Raising the low five-figure sum needed to pay for it all had been “just a business of getting down to it and organising and so on”, he said. “It was actually a lot easier than what my previous job used to be.”Gordon Noble, a professor of archaeology at the University of Aberdeen, said the finds were highly significant. “We know about sites like Iona having these very famous monastic sites from this early medieval world. But apart from the association with Moluag and a piece of sculpture from this site, we knew practically nothing really about Lismore. So it was hugely exciting to see the results emerging through the local group’s work with Clare [Ellis] … This was clearly a really important early Christian establishment.”View image in fullscreenNewly identified early-medieval sculpture fragments from Lios Mòr.Photograph: Gordon NobleWhile professional archaeologists often worked with local people, Noble said, “it’s not always the community themselves coming up with the ideas. Here, it was very much a bottom-up approach of the heritage society coming up with a plan, working with professionals – and lo and behold, what a great series of discoveries they’ve made at the site.”Hay said he hoped the finds would go some way to restoring the reputation of Moluag, who has long been overshadowed by the more celebrated Saint Columba, the founder of Iona and the subject of an influential ninth-century biography. “Unfortunately, Moluag never had a hagiographer, so his contribution to the evangelisation of Scotland has been very much underestimated,” he said. “So finding his monastic site and [the evidence of metalworking] – it’s all about recalibrating the situation. I think Moluag had a very big impact on the evangelising of Scotland, but unfortunately, he didn’t get his PR right.”The results of the community excavations will bepublished in the forthcoming edition of Antiquity.Explore more on these topicsArchaeologyScotlandHeritageChristianityReligionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Grenfell police hand files on 20 organisations and 54 people to CPS | Grenfell Tower fire | The Guardian
description: Met calls move ‘milestone’ moment that paves way for ‘very best possible evidence for charging decisions’
Author: Ben Quinn
Headline: Met calls move ‘milestone’ moment that paves way for ‘very best possible evidence for charging decisions’
Content: The fire on 14 June 2017 led to the deaths of 72 people and was found by a public inquiry to have been avoidable.Photograph: Ben Bauer/PAView image in fullscreenThe fire on 14 June 2017 led to the deaths of 72 people and was found by a public inquiry to have been avoidable.Photograph: Ben Bauer/PAGrenfell Tower fireGrenfell police hand files on 20 organisations and 54 people to CPSMet calls move ‘milestone’ moment that paves way for ‘very best possible evidence for charging decisions’Ben QuinnandPeter WalkerWed 30 Sep 2026 13.33 EDTFirst published on Wed 30 Sep 2026 09.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePolice investigating theGrenfell Tower firehave asked prosecutors to consider charges including manslaughter and fraud against a range of companies and individuals.TheMetropolitan policeannounced they had given prosecutors evidence relating to 20 companies and organisations and 54 individuals ahead of charging decisions, in what the force described as a “milestone moment”.Andy Burnham joined survivors’ groups in saying it had “taken too long”, but he pledged to support Grenfell families “to ensure they get the justice and accountability that they deserve”.Potential charges include corporate manslaughter, gross negligence manslaughter, health and safety offences, fraud and fraud-related offences and misconduct in public office.The housing secretary, Angela Rayner, said on Wednesday that the files passed to prosecutors by police included one relating to her department. The Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) would review whether the department, which police began investigating in 2023, had potentially breached the Health and Safety at Work Act.“I recognise the significance and gravity of this development, and we will respond with the appropriate and necessary diligence and care,” she said.The Guardian has learned that a leading prosecutor has been appointed to head any possible court cases.The fire in North Kensington, westLondon, on 14 June 2017, led to the deaths of 72 people and was found by a public inquiry to have been avoidable.It was the result of “decades of failure” by central government to stop the spread of combustible cladding, combined with the “systematic dishonesty” of multimillion-pound companies whose products spread the fire, a public inquiry found in 2024.The CPS has said charging decisions will be made before the 10th anniversary of the disaster, which falls on 14 June 2027.Kevin Southworth, a deputy assistant commissioner at the Met, said: “This is a milestone moment in the police investigation into this devastating tragedy which took the lives of 72 people.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDirector who oversaw Grenfell cost-cutting given senior council housing roleRead more“We appreciate, of course, it has taken nine years to get to this point. As we have said before, this is one of the most complex investigations ever undertaken by any UK law enforcement agency – the scale is truly enormous.“While we know this has had a significant impact on those waiting for answers, it has necessarily taken this long to ensure our investigation is meticulous and presents the very best possible evidence to the CPS for charging decisions.”Investigators have looked at the role of more than 15,000 people and 700 organisations as part of the inquiry, and have submitted 12,600 pages of evidence to the CPS.A total of 14,700 statements have been taken and more than 27,000 exhibits, including cladding, insulation, doors, windows and other parts of the building – down to screws, nuts and bolts – are stored in a secure warehouse.Scale replica parts of the tower are being built at a cost of £2m in anticipation of potential court proceedings.Grenfell United, which represents some bereaved families and survivors, said: “We expect the Met and the CPS to do everything in their power to make sure this case moves forward without further unnecessary delay. Our families have waited long enough.“We want those responsible to face justice. If people are found guilty of crimes that cost our loved ones their lives, we want to see them behind bars. Only then will people see that there are real consequences for what happened at Grenfell.”Burnham told Channel 5 News: “It has taken too long, but at least [the evidence] has been submitted. To be fair to the Metropolitan police, it has been a complex and wide-ranging investigation and they’ve had to do it in a forensic way, dealing with multiple, multiple organisations.”He cited the role of the Hillsborough law, which he was involved in campaigning for, and which imposes a duty of candour on public authorities to prevent cover-ups.“It’s intended to speed up situations like this so we can get the truth and justice much more quickly. And accountability, that’s the piece that’s often lacking. There must be accountability for Grenfell,” he said.Frank Ferguson, the head of the CPS’s special crime and counter-terrorism division, said the service remained confident that it would complete the process and make charging decisions before the 10th anniversary of the fire next year.Explore more on these topicsGrenfell Tower fireMetropolitan policeLondonEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Scottish screen sector boom brings questions over jobs and overtourism | Scotland | The Guardian
description: The Traitors and big film shoots help boost economy but some highlight lack of opportunities for local talent
Author: Eve Livingston
Headline: The Traitors and big film shoots help boost economy but some highlight lack of opportunities for local talent
Content: The Traitors has had added £21.8m to the Scottish economy since 2022, according to the BBC.Photograph: BBC/PAView image in fullscreenThe Traitors has had added £21.8m to the Scottish economy since 2022, according to the BBC.Photograph: BBC/PAScotlandScottish screen sector boom brings questions over jobs and overtourismThe Traitors and big film shoots help boost economy but some highlight lack of opportunities for local talentEve LivingstonWed 30 Sep 2026 12.53 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 16.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleScotland’s striking Ardross Castle, the oldest star of The Celebrity Traitors, which kicks off on Thursday night, is just one of the stops on the Scottish tourist board’s “screen tourism” trail. From Outlander and The Odyssey filming in the Highlands and islands, to Glasgow city centre standing in for New York and Gotham City in the latest instalments of Indiana Jones and Batman respectively, film and TV is increasingly big business inScotland.The country’s screen sector,growing year on year, is projected to be worth £1bn to the economy by 2030. But while some have celebrated the upsides of a booming production sector, others highlight a lack of opportunities for Scottish talent and the challenges of excessive tourism in areas featured on screen.After last year’s Celebrity Traitors finale, theBBC announcedthat the show had added £21.8m to the Scottish economy since 2022 through employment, supply chain spend and screen tourism, where visitors travel specifically to see on-screen sites in real life.Butresearch last yearby Peter Strachan, a documentary film-maker and academic who set up the campaign group Standing Up For Scotland’s Screen Talent, found that only about 6% of production staff on series three of The Traitors were Scottish, despite the production counting towards Ofcom quotas stating that the BBC must use 8% of network hours and expenditure in Scotland.“This is the tip of the iceberg,” Strachan wrote at the time. “We have found many other supposedly Scottish productions are failing to create jobs for broadcast freelancers in Scotland.”The BBC reiterated thatThe Traitorswas a Scottish production, and Studio Lambert, which makes the show, said Scottish representation was increasing behind the scenes each year.View image in fullscreenSet dressers transforming a street in Glasgow into Gotham City for the Batgirl film shoot.Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PAEarlier this month, Strachanalso calledfor Sony Pictures to release a breakdown of the local crew hired in Glasgow for Spider-Man: Brand New Day, which filmed in the city in 2025.“Local hiring is not necessarily the same thing as employing Scotland’s established screen-sector workforce,” he said. “Someone can be locally hired to work on a film without normally working in film and television – a Glasgow carpenter brought in for a few weeks of set construction, for example.”David Smith, the interim executive director of Screen Scotland, the national body for the country’s film and TV industry, said Scotland had benefited from its growing screen sector, but that there had been a “consistent decline” in the number of shows commissioned by public service broadcasters from Scottish production companies.“We think this needs to change,” Smith said. “Ultimately, we want to see a sustainable mix of film and TV projects made across genres, broadcasts and platforms.”Even for those not directly involved in the industry, its effects are still being felt. Glenfinnan, in Lochaber in the Highlands, is home to only about 150 people – as well as a majestic viaduct made world-famous when it doubled as the Hogwarts Express railway bridge in the Harry Potter films. In the years since, the tiny hamlet has become so overrun with film tourists that Police Scotland last monthissued a warning to visitorsover dangerous parking and antisocial behaviour.View image in fullscreenGlenfinnan viaduct doubled as the Hogwarts Express railway bridge in the Harry Potter films.Photograph: JP Offord/Rex/ShutterstockGillian Shields, 54, lives in Inverness, close to the village of Culloden where the Clan Fraser stone has become a major tourist attraction for fans of historical fantasy series Outlander. In 2023, the site was temporarily closed after deterioration caused by excessive visitor numbers.“People here are welcoming, and most of the visitors are lovely and respectful,” she said. “We’re not trying to turn anyone away, it’s just we see more and more every single year and it’s a worry whether our beautiful area can keep up with it.”Culloden battlefield, which features heavily in Outlander, saw a43% increase in visitor numberslast year, according to data from Glasgow Caledonian University and the Association of Scottish Visitor Attractions.‘Scots are the kindest people on earth!’ Meet the Americans moving to ScotlandRead moreJenni Steele, the film and creative industries manager at VisitScotland, said the benefits of film tourism “are worth millions to the economy, bringing jobs and opportunities, and are felt long after the film or TV series is released”.But she said: “We know that success can bring with it challenges in certain locations. Film and TV fans will be drawn to them regardless. That’s why we work with partners and local bodies to understand the challenges so we can educate and inform visitors of where and when they should visit and encourage them to act responsibly and explore beyond the on-screen locations.”Many Scots, though, are in full support of the country’s booming screen sector. Matthew, 42, lives in Glasgow city centre and has watched on in recent years as the streets around his home have been transformed into everything from 1960s New York (Indiana Jones and the Dial of Destiny) to dystopian America (The Running Man) and Soviet-era Moscow (Tetris).“Some people moan about road closures and parking, but it’s great to see the city buzzing with excitement when a new show comes to town,” he said, noting that local residents he knew had been employed as extras, and nearby restaurants as on-set catering suppliers. “The city needs those jobs and that money – and, to be frank, a bit of fun and glamour never hurt a Glaswegian either.”Explore more on these topicsScotlandTelevision industryThe TraitorsOvertourismnewsShareReuse this content

title: Kristi Noem, former Trump homeland security chief, files for divorce | Kristi Noem | The Guardian
description: Noem cites irreconcilable differences in filing that comes after husband Bryon Noem involved in tabloid scandal
Author: Robert Tait
Headline: Noem cites irreconcilable differences in filing that comes after husband Bryon Noem involved in tabloid scandal
Content: Kristi Noem with her husband Bryon Noem, right, at a Senate judiciary committee hearing in Washington in March.Photograph: J Scott Applewhite/APView image in fullscreenKristi Noem with her husband Bryon Noem, right, at a Senate judiciary committee hearing in Washington in March.Photograph: J Scott Applewhite/APKristi NoemKristi Noem, former Trump homeland security chief, files for divorceNoem cites irreconcilable differences in filing that comes after husband Bryon Noem involved in tabloid scandalRobert Taitin WashingtonWed 30 Sep 2026 19.58 EDTFirst published on Wed 30 Sep 2026 16.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKristi Noem, who was fired by Donald Trump after a rumbustious stint as homeland security secretary, is divorcing her husband, Bryon Noem, after 34 years of marriage, citing “irreconcilable differences”.The divorce claim “for settlement purposes only” was disclosed in court records filed in Hamlin county,South Dakota, the state of which Noem was previously governor.The document was signed by Noem’s lawyer, Michael Sabers, on 6 April – just over a week afterthe Daily Mail published picturesof her husband wearing inflated fake breasts under a spandex shirt.At the time, Noem issued a statement saying she was “devastated” by the images, adding that “the family have been blindsided by this”.The papers were only filed in court this week, according tothe New York Times.Sabers confirmed Kristi Noem had filed for divorce and said she would reserve further comments for the legal process.Tim Bottum, Bryon Noem’s attorney, said his client was “saddened that the marriage is ending” and would welcome the opportunity to share his perspective if court proceedings were necessary.“Bryon’s priority is to protect the family and move forward as loving parents and grandparents,” Bottum said in a statement.The revelations came weeks after Noem had lost her job at the department of homeland security.The state of her marriage had already been subject of speculation amid rumors that she was in a relationship with her aide at the department, Corey Lewandowski.In a Capitol Hill on 4 March, a Democratic member of Congress asked her openly whether she had sexual relations with Lewandowski.Answering under oath, Noem – who was accompanied to the hearing by her husband – dismissed the question as “tabloid garbage” but did not say no.She was fired the following day after Trump was reportedly angered by her answers to questions about a taxpayer-funded publicity campaign that promoted Noem’s image. Noem told the committee that Trump had signed off on the spending.Noem was replaced by Markwayne Mullin as homeland security secretary after a controversial period that had included the shooting deaths of protesters Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis during an immigration enforcement surge. Noem came under intense criticism after calling Good and Pretti “domestic terrorists”.Noem, 54, married Bryon Noem, 56, in 1992. They have three adult children.Explore more on these topicsKristi NoemUS politicsSouth DakotaRepublicansnewsShareReuse this content

title: Federal Reserve watchdog finds no criminal violations for building renovation cost overruns | Federal Reserve | The Guardian
description: Trump criticized $2.4bn rehab amid attempts to pressure then Fed chair Jerome Powell into lowering interest rates
Author: Lauren Aratani
Headline: Trump criticized $2.4bn rehab amid attempts to pressure then Fed chair Jerome Powell into lowering interest rates
Content: Donald Trump and Jerome Powell visit the Federal Reserve building on 24 July 2025 in Washington DC.Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/APView image in fullscreenDonald Trump and Jerome Powell visit the Federal Reserve building on 24 July 2025 in Washington DC.Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/APFederal ReserveFederal Reserve watchdog finds no criminal violations for building renovation cost overrunsTrump criticized $2.4bn rehab amid attempts to pressure then Fed chair Jerome Powell into lowering interest ratesLauren Arataniin New YorkWed 30 Sep 2026 13.49 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 15.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn internal watchdog said theFederal Reservemismanaged costs associated with a $2.4bn renovation of its Washington DC headquarters, but noted that no criminal violations occurred, according to a report released on Wednesday.For over a year,Donald Trumphas centered his attacks against the Fed and former chairJerome Powellaround the renovations, including a months-long Department of Justice criminal investigation that wasdroppedin April.The report said that the Fed’s board of governors “has not effectively managed” the construction project and “repeatedly deviated from its cost-management provisions”, but noted that the mismanagement was not criminal and that it did not find any administrative misconduct in its evaluation.“At no point during our evaluation did we find reasonable grounds to believe that a violation of federal criminal law had occurred,” the report said.Over the course of renovations, construction costs have gone from an initially budgeted $921m in February 2020 to $2.018bn by December 2024. Construction was supposed to be completed in mid-2024 but is not slated to go until December 2027.The renovations have been a key part of the tension between the White House and the Fed, which by law is supposed to be non-partisan and independent. Trump has long been trying to pressure the Fed into lowering interest rates, to no avail.‘The weaker he gets, the more dangerous he gets’: Trump lashes out as his power wanesRead moreTrump latched on to the Fed’s ongoing renovations as an attack point against Powell in June 2025, suggesting that it amounted to corruption. He suggested that renovations included elaborate features including a VIP dining room and a garden terrace.In response, the Fed posted a video tour of the ongoing construction, noting that two buildings have not undergone renovations since the 1930s.Trump visited the Fed’s headquarters to highlight the expenses that July. Donning hardhats in the bowels of the construction site, Trump and Powell had a spat over budget figures.“It looks like it’s about $3.1bn,” Trump said at the time. “It went up a little bit or a lot.”The typically reserved Powell became visibly annoyed. “I am not aware of that,” he said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSoon after, Trump turned his Fed fight toward Fed governor Lisa Cook, whom hetriedtofireover mortgage fraud. The supreme courtruledearlier this summer that the firing was unconstitutional because the White House did not follow proper procedure.In January, Powell released a stunningvideo statementannouncing that the Department of Justice was investigating the renovations as part of a criminal investigation, noting that the investigation was “pretext” for the Fed not lowering interest rates.“This is about whether the Fed will be able to continue to set interest rates based on evidence and economic conditions – or whether instead monetary policy will be directed by political pressure or intimidation,” Powell said at the time.The justice department investigation would end up stalling theconfirmationof current Fed chairKevin Warsh, after a key Republican senator said he would be a holdout until the department ended its investigation. In April, the justice departmentclosedthe investigation.Trump and his economic advisers have continued to call for the Fed to lower interest rates, though the Fed most recentlyhiked rates, citing high inflation.Explore more on these topicsFederal ReserveDonald TrumpJerome PowellTrump administrationUS economyUS politicsWashington DCnewsShareReuse this content

title: Good news in US inflation report boosts chances Fed won’t hike rates | US economy | The Guardian
description: Traders see about a 35% chance of an October rate hike, down from ​about 45% following White House pressure
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Traders see about a 35% chance of an October rate hike, down from ​about 45% following White House pressure
