title: Andy Burnham admits to ‘concern’ if Manchester City lose their owners after guilty verdicts | Manchester City | The Guardian
description: The primer minister said: ‘City have been a huge partner in building modern Manchester,’ while the Independent Football Regulator said it is monitoring the case
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: The primer minister said: ‘City have been a huge partner in building modern Manchester,’ while the Independent Football Regulator said it is monitoring the case
Content: Andy Burnham has thanked the City Football Group for investment in Manchester.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham has thanked the City Football Group for investment in Manchester.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianManchester CityAndy Burnham admits to ‘concern’ if Manchester City lose their owners after guilty verdictsClub ‘a huge partner in building modern Manchester’Independent Football Regulator monitoring caseMatt HughesWed 30 Sep 2026 14.31 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham has said he would be “really concerned” to lose Manchester City’s owners as a result of the club being found guilty of more than 100 breaches of Premier League rules.On the day that the Independent Football Regulator confirmed it has powers to investigate the suitability of the Abu Dhabi United Group to own an English club afterthe damning judgment of an independent commissionregarding £900m of sham contracts, the prime minister praised City’s owners for their investment of billions of pounds into Manchester.Manchester City could be forced to pay Premier League up to £50m in legal costsRead more“I would be really concerned to lose them,” Burnham said. “They’ve been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester, and the building of Manchester City into the global force that it is.“I do actually thank the City Football Group and the wider ownership for the money that they didn’t just put into the Etihad [Stadium] and the campus around it but also into the city.”Burnham insisted he would not get involved in the Premier League’s disciplinary process, despite the potential impact that punishing City could have on the UK-Abu Dhabi trading relationship, which is worth around £30bn a year.Despite this, Burnham appeared to express some sympathy for City’s plight by referring to his previous involvement in campaigning on behalf of Everton, who in 2023were docked six pointsby the Premier League for breaching profitability and sustainability rules.“I can’t intervene more in the process,” he said. “It would be wrong for me to do that. It would be wrong, I think, to jump to a conclusion before having really studied all of the detail. But obviously it’s ongoing, and because it’s still contested by Manchester City then I think it’s right that I don’t say much more.“Everton was in this position a few years ago and you might remember that I fought for Everton in that situation. I still hold the view very firmly that they weren’t fairly treated in that process. I remember people proclaiming Everton guilty at the time and, with hindsight, I think more people would say that wasn’t fair the way that was handled.”In a statement released earlier on Wednesday the IFR chief executive, David Kogan, confirmed the regulator is monitoring the City case and could take action. “The independent commission’s decision raises serious issues,” Kogan said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“The IFR has powers to assess the suitability of owners, directors and executives and we will use these powers where appropriate, in the interests of protecting the sustainability, honesty and integrity of English football where there is clear evidence of wrongdoing by individuals.“This includes taking account of findings made by the leagues. However, as the proceedings remain ongoing between Manchester City and the Premier League we will await further developments.”Explore more on these topicsManchester CityAndy BurnhamPremier LeagueFinancesBusinessnewsShareReuse this content

title: Swiss FA ‘cannot justify’ its support for Infantino’s re-election as Fifa president | Gianni Infantino | The Guardian
description: The Swiss Football Association has withdrawn its support for Gianni ⁠Infantino’s bid for another term as Fifa president
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The Swiss Football Association has withdrawn its support for Gianni ⁠Infantino’s bid for another term as Fifa president
Content: Gianni Infantino was born in Brig, an Alpine town in southern Switzerland.Photograph: Denis Balibouse/ReutersView image in fullscreenGianni Infantino was born in Brig, an Alpine town in southern Switzerland.Photograph: Denis Balibouse/ReutersGianni InfantinoSwiss FA ‘cannot justify’ its support for Infantino’s re-election as Fifa presidentSFV withdraws support after endorsing candidacy in JuneSwiss-born Infantino has faced calls for his resignationReutersWed 30 Sep 2026 13.19 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Swiss Football Association (SFV) has withdrawn its support for Gianni Infantino’s bid for another term as Fifa president, the organisation confirmed on Wednesday.The executive committee reversed its support for Infantino, who was born in Brig,an Alpine town in Valais canton in southern Switzerland, in a meeting this week after endorsing his candidacy in June.‘The emperor is naked’: Uefa president Ceferin takes new swipe at InfantinoRead more“The decision follows a comprehensive reassessment of developments over the past few months,” the SFV said in a statement. “From the SFV’s perspective, various incidents raise fundamental questions regarding leadership, governance, transparency and ‌decision-making processes withinFifa.”Infantino is seeking re-election in March but has faced growing opposition since his plans to sell a stake in Fifa tournaments, including the World Cup,were revealed in July. The subsequent outcry led to themswiftly being abandoned.The withdrawal is the latest blow to Infantino, with football associations in England, Wales, France, Serbia ‌and other European countries having already pulled their endorsements before the election. Uefa has pledged to present a rival candidate before the November deadline.Infantino, who has been Fifa president since 2016, has faced calls for his resignation amid widespread pleas for reform in the governing body. The 56-year-old wrote this month in a letter to member associations thathe was open to talks over reform, but the SFV said key questions regarding Fifa’s ‌responsibilities and decision‑making process had been left unanswered.“As these have not been convincingly clarified, we cannot justify continuing to support Gianni Infantino’s candidacy,” the SFV said.Explore more on these topicsGianni InfantinoFifaFootball politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘We don’t need boos’: Astros players frustrated as own fans turn on them in playoffs | Houston Astros | The Guardian
description: Large sections of Daikin Park sat empty as Houston opened the postseason with a 6-3 loss – and Astros players were frustrated by boos from the home crowd
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Large sections of Daikin Park sat empty as Houston opened the postseason with a 6-3 loss – and Astros players were frustrated by boos from the home crowd
Content: Fans sit among empty seats at Daikin Park during Game 1 of the American League wildcard series between the Houston Astros and Chicago White Sox on Tuesday in Houston.Photograph: Karen Warren/APView image in fullscreenFans sit among empty seats at Daikin Park during Game 1 of the American League wildcard series between the Houston Astros and Chicago White Sox on Tuesday in Houston.Photograph: Karen Warren/APHouston Astros‘We don’t need boos’: Astros players frustrated as own fans turn on them in playoffsHouston announce crowd of 34,011 for playoff openerPlayers criticize boos during 6-3 defeat by White SoxAstros are first division winner with .500 or worse markAgenciesWed 30 Sep 2026 12.46 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 17.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe crowd at Daikin Park was surprisingly sparse as the Houston Astros – baseball’s first division winner with a .500 or worse record – opened their AL wildcard series with a 6-3 loss to theChicago White Soxon Tuesday.MLB playoff predictions: are the Dodgers heading for an inevitable fall?Read moreLarge swaths of seats, especially in the upper deck, sat empty while right-hander AJ Blumbaugh delivered the game’s first pitch at 4.10pm. The bottom two levels were much fuller than the upper deck, but many seats in the lower two decks were also empty.The announced attendance was 34,011, in a park with a capacity of 40,963.All those empty seats are a rare sight in a stadium that is normally packed for the postseason. And some of the fans that did show up weren’t too happy with the performance of the home team with boos raining down on the Astros in the first and second innings as they fell behind 3-0.“It’s extremely frustrating as a home player,” first baseman Christian Walker told the Athletic. “We’re here, playing at home; we need cheers. We need energy. We don’t need boos. What purpose does that serve in that moment? Whatever fans are feeling, we’re feeling it tenfold. We’re the ones out there. We’re the ones in the fight. We worked our butts off this whole season to put ourselves in this spot, and for guys to get booed, it’s frustrating.”Reliever Bennett Sousa was subjected to some boos after spiking two breaking pitches in the seventh inning.“This team has laid a lot on the line to be in this position to give the fans a playoff game – a playoff series,” Sousa told the Athletic. “We want their support.”Astros manager Joe Espada attempted to play down any tensions on Wednesday, before Game 2 of the series.“I understand both sides,” Espada said. “There’s frustration. Our players and the fans have the right to ... show their emotions, and I get it. But one thing I do know is that our players love our fans. We respect our fans. We need our fans. We need the energy from our fans. We feed off that.”Major LeagueBaseballhas previously had trouble filling stadiums for some afternoon games in the wildcard round. When Cleveland hosted Detroit last year, the series opener started at 1.08pm with 26,186 in attendance. All three games in that series were played in front of fewer than 30,000 fans. The Tampa Bay Rays drew just 19,704 for an ALWCS opener against Texas in 2023 that started at 3.08pm, the lowest attendance for a non-Covid MLB postseason game since the 1919 World Series.Houston returned to the playoffs after missing out last year despite finishing 81-81. It’s the first time a team made the postseason without a winning record in a non-shortened season.The Astros averaged 30,519 fans per game during the regular season, which ranked 14th in the majors.Houston fought through an injury-plagued season to reach the playoffs for the ninth time in 10 years. The Astros reached the American League Championship Series seven straight times from 2017-23 and advanced to the World Series four times, winning championships in 2017 and 2022.Explore more on these topicsHouston AstrosMLBChicago White SoxBaseballUS sportsShareReuse this content

title: We need ‘right to intervene’ in AI amid growing threat, says Bank of England boss | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Andrew Bailey’s comments come as fears grow that rogue models could take financial system hostage
Author: Kalyeena Makortoff
Headline: Andrew Bailey’s comments come as fears grow that rogue models could take financial system hostage
Content: A number of frontier AI models have gone rogue in recent months.Photograph: ReutersView image in fullscreenA number of frontier AI models have gone rogue in recent months.Photograph: ReutersAI (artificial intelligence)We need ‘right to intervene’ in AI amid growing threat, says Bank of England bossAndrew Bailey’s comments come as fears grow that rogue models could take financial system hostageBusiness live – latest updatesKalyeena MakortoffBanking correspondentWed 30 Sep 2026 11.22 EDTFirst published on Wed 30 Sep 2026 06.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe governor of theBank of Englandhas called for the “right to intervene” in the AI industry amid growing fears that rogue models could take the financial system hostage.Andrew Bailey said the risks posed by frontier AI models – a number of which havegone rogue in recent months– were “real and increasingly significant”. Meanwhile, it was becoming harder for the public to have proper oversight of powerful AI models that were “functioning within a self-reinforcing loop”.That is putting financial stability at risk, with the new technology having increased the “scale and sophistication of cyber threats to the financial system”, he said. The governor warned it could threaten daily card payments, bank transactions, and stock and bond trading across financial markets.View image in fullscreenAndrew Bailey said the risks posed by the rapid advancement of frontier AI models were ‘real and increasingly significant’.Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianThe comments came as the Bank’s financial policy committee (FPC) said thegrowing mountain of AI debtwas increasing financial stability risks.The potential benefits of AI “are immense”, Bailey said but he added that authorities needed to be ready to step in.In an opinion piece penned for the Bank of England’s Insight series, he said: “If we are to realise those benefits safely, we must answer one critical question. Should society retain the ability to intervene, to establish the boundaries within which these systems operate and to revise those boundaries as the technology evolves? To my mind, the answer is unequivocally yes.”But Bailey said authorities needed to figure out why they might be forced to step in. He said a “sensible starting point” would be rigorous testing of new AI models to understand how they behave and identify “credible points” where authorities could intervene.“In time, that understanding could be codified into a set of standards which will help to ensure consistency in approach across the financial system, and perhaps more broadly across the economy,” he said.However, the governor stopped short of calling for a regulatory clampdown, saying it was “not, in my view, the right place to start. In the excitement surrounding AI development, there is a risk that we move too quickly to debates about regulatory architecture before establishing where the failure exists in the first place.”A growing number of lawmakers, AI researchers and even some AI companies have called for more government oversight of artificial intelligence in recent weeks. However, hopes for international cooperation faded after Donald Trump broadly rejected calls for more regulation of AI technology – most of which is being developed in the US – warning it could hurt efforts to compete with China and threaten economic growth.But Bailey said a set of standards could help safeguard the financial system from harmful AI, which may end up operating outside well-established “shared norms, obligations and responsibilities”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Central banks have a responsibility to safeguard the stability of the system as a whole,” Bailey said. “We cannot stand aside and assume that technological progress will resolve these questions on its own. The public interest requires that we engage with them now, before the risks become more difficult to contain.”Warning of the ballooning AI debt pile, the FPC said large players in the sector had taken on $450bn (£339bn) worth of debt between January and September this year, already overtaking the $333bn worth of gilts due to be issued by the UK government for the whole of 2026.That has tied investors – including hedge funds, asset managers and private credit firms – to the fortunes of AI companies at a time when those tech businesses have yet to turn a profit.“The rapid increase in artificial intelligence-related debt issuance broadens the exposure of capital markets to development in AI,” minutes of the recent FPC meeting on 25 September said.“The committee underscores the importance of timely and careful management of these intensifying, interconnected risks.”Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)Bank of EnglandAndrew BaileyTechnology sectornewsShareReuse this content

title: Reanimated AI Greta Garbo stars again … in a ball-bearing advert | Greta Garbo | The Guardian
description: Relatives of Hollywood legend say her doppelganger could now be used for more glamorous roles
Author: Robert Booth
Headline: Relatives of Hollywood legend say her doppelganger could now be used for more glamorous roles
Content: Greta Garbo in Anna Christie from 1930. Her likeness was created using AI imaging technology, including Google’s Nano Banana Pro.Photograph: MGM/Sportsphoto/AllstarView image in fullscreenGreta Garbo in Anna Christie from 1930. Her likeness was created using AI imaging technology, including Google’s Nano Banana Pro.Photograph: MGM/Sportsphoto/AllstarGreta GarboReanimated AI Greta Garbo stars again … in a ball-bearing advertRelatives of Hollywood legend say her doppelganger could now be used for more glamorous rolesRobert BoothUK technology editorWed 30 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 02.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleShe shimmered in Hollywood’s silent movie era and lit up the first talkies – nowGreta Garbomay be about to star in cinema’s new AI age.More than a century after her screen debut and decades after her ashes were laid to rest in a Swedish woodland cemetery, the Hollywood superstar’s descendants are ready to consider an AI version of her taking a 21st-century film role.Her likeness has already been reanimated for an advert for a Swedish industrial company, using AI generation technology. The practice some critics call “ghostploitation” has also been used in the case of the actorVal Kilmer, who died last year.SKF advert review – let’s hope this dull AI Greta Garbo is not the futureRead moreAsked if the AI Garbo could be cast in other roles, Craig Reisfield, one of three relatives who manage her legacy, told the Guardian: “I won’t say no, especially having seen what I’ve seen. It’s pretty incredible and lifelike. So what’s to say that you can’t bring Greta Garbo back in some kind of fashion in a film role?”Reisfield said he was “flabbergasted” when he saw the AI version of his great-aunt created for publicity for the ball-bearings giant SKF. The connection comes because Garbo’s second-ever screen role was in a 1921 promotional film involving the Gothenburg-based company.While Garbo was the definition of glamour in Hollywood’s golden age, appearing as a famous ballerina in Grand Hotel (1932) and as a doomed courtesan in Camille (1936),the 99-second AI performance for SKF is intercut with shots of ball-bearings.However, the quality of the AI production has prompted the possibility, at least, of a greater digital comeback.“I was totally impressed: the mannerisms that they could capture and manipulate, her dress, facial images and even her voice,” said Reisfield, a Swedish-American who used to drive for Garbo and saw her often for family occasions when she lived in New York.“It was startling what they could do and very impactful. And it was touching, from my perspective having known her.”View image in fullscreenGreta Garbo and John Barrymore in Grand Hotel. Her famous line ‘I want to be alone’ comes from the 1932 MGM film.Photograph: PictureLux/The Hollywood Archive/AlamyA far cry from the hand-cranked cameras that captured Garbo’s early work, the SKF performance was conjured by humans prompting AI models including China’s Seedream and Google’s Nano Banana Pro.Unusually for AI film-making, the creators did not feed moving or still images of Garbo into the AI because the material was protected by copyright. Instead, they used text prompts to create her likeness, including her ice-blue eyes and wavy blond bob. A human actor then played her role with her AI-generated appearance overlaid. Her voice was recreated from a recording from an early film.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekSign up toFilm WeeklyTake a front seat at the cinema with our weekly email filled with all the latest news and all the movie action that mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe resulting version of Garbo appears to have gone beyond the “uncanny valley” – the problem for AI film-makers in which the closer to an actual likeness an AI rendering becomes, the more strangely implausible it seems.AI Garbo’s lines, however, are not perhaps quite up to the standards of those given to her by MGM studio writers. At one point, she sounds likeLiz Truss complaining about the “disgrace” of Britain’s cheese imports, when she says “around 20% of all global energy is lost to friction: a terrible waste”.Several big film studios are investing in AI startups or collaborating with new AI studios. Veteran directors including Ron Howard and Paul Schrader are working on AI-enabled films, while a new generation ofAI-native film-makerssuch as Kavan the Kid andGossip Goblinare using AI to build huge audiences outside the conventional studio system.Asked whether the real Garbo would have wanted to continue performing as an AI-enabled actor, Reisfield said: “She was at the forefront of cinema in the silent film era. She made the transition to ‘talkies’ and dominated box office receipts.“So to imagine her as an AI-enabled actor given her track record and ability to captivate and connect with audiences of both men and women isn’t inconceivable.”Reisfield said the custodians of the rights to Garbo’s voice, name, image and publicity aimed to “preserve, protect, and enhance” her legacy and were “very discerning” on partnerships. Her likeness has been posthumously used by the fashion houses Ferragamo, Gucci and Louis Vuitton but the AI performance for SKF is her first in moving images.Whatever the future holds for AI Garbo, it kept to the true spirit of the actor by signing off the ball-bearing advert with her immortal line from Grand Hotel: “I want to be alone.”Explore more on these topicsGreta GarboAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingVal KilmerSwedenEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Nandy says children’s social media ban only ‘staging post’ in online safety drive | Internet safety | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Culture secretary says UK will crack down further and be ‘pioneer of tech as a force for good’
Author: Alexandra Topping
Headline: Exclusive: Culture secretary says UK will crack down further and be ‘pioneer of tech as a force for good’
Content: Lisa Nandy, pictured in Downing Street in July, said: ‘We shouldn’t accept that this is the end.’Photograph: Victoria Jones/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenLisa Nandy, pictured in Downing Street in July, said: ‘We shouldn’t accept that this is the end.’Photograph: Victoria Jones/ShutterstockInternet safetyNandy says children’s social media ban only ‘staging post’ in online safety driveExclusive: Culture secretary says UK will crack down further and be ‘pioneer of tech as a force for good’Alexandra ToppingPolitical correspondentWed 30 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 09.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLisa Nandy has warned technology firms that the government’s online safety crackdown is not finished, saying that banning under-16s from social media platforms is only a “staging post”.Earlier this year the government announced thatteenagers under the age of 16 would be bannedfrom accessing “high-risk” social media apps, while safer platforms would be subjected to restrictions.The social media ban will come into effect by March, with further measurestargeted at 16- and 17-year-olds– including restrictions on websites that allow infinite scrolling and algorithms promoting harmful content as well as tighter age-verification checks – to follow.Nandy has now vowed to go further. “We shouldn’t accept that this is the end,” the culture secretary said before her speech at theLabourparty conference, which will be introduced by Georgia Harrison, a campaigner against image-based sexual abuse. “This is a staging post to what must be a very active interventionist state, policing and regulating the online space so that people are safe.”View image in fullscreenLisa Nandy at the Labour party conference in Liverpool on Tuesday.Photograph: Jon Super/APShe said the UK would be “pioneers of tech as a force for good” and would promote online spaces that were “genuinely safe, inclusive and empowering”.She praised the former prime minister Keir Starmer and the former technology secretary Liz Kendall for announcing the ban in June. But she felt there had been a “step change” in the government’s approach since Andy Burnham became prime minister in July and handed her the online safety brief.Comparing social media to real-world civic spaces, she said: “If we were in a situation where we were saying our town centres are now so unsafe that we’ve decided that every child is going to have to stay in their bedrooms, people would rightly be up in arms.“How have we got to a point where we’re saying these social media sites are so harmful and dangerous that we cannot conceive of any way of protecting our children except to remove them altogether? This ends now.”A consultation on the ban, which will apply to apps such as TikTok, Snapchat, YouTube and Instagram, attracted more than 116,000 responses, with 85% of parents thinking the risk of social media outweighed any benefit.Nandy said she had told families bereaved as a result of teenagers experiencing online harm: “I want you to understand that that era ends today, and we start a new chapter where we have an active and empowering state that shapes those civic spaces so that they work for us.”The MP for Wigan said the government had already shown a willingness to take on the big tech companies – and risk disapproval from US authorities – withplans to hand established broadcasters and media companies greater prominenceon digital platforms such as YouTube and TikTok. “That is a difference of opinion with the US administration, but we do reserve the right to take a different approach,” she said.While new technologies had always “upended society”, the internet was the only one to have been “entirely outsourced to the private sector” with no role for the state, Nandy said. “It’s not acceptable to outsource this to [the X owner, Elon] Musk or anybody else,” she said.In one of her first moves on online safety, Nandy ordered technology companies to her office, and she said she was “not surprised, but appalled” that representatives from X failed to attend.She acknowledged “there really is a problem” with Ofcom’s ability to enforce regulations and make firms adhere to the Online Safety Act. “Laws are only as good as the ability to enforce them,” she said.Nandy has welcomed a suggestion from the BBC director general, Matt Brittin, that a“public service algorithm”could compete with big tech, which she felt fitted “with [Burnham’s] vision about the UK being a world leader in tech as a force for good”.“In order to do that, you’ve got to be in the game, investing [and] shaping the technology,” she added. “But I think to win the permission of the public to do that, they’ve got to hear from us loud and clear that we will take action to protect people, particularly children, right now.”This article was amended on 30 September 2026. An earlier version said the UK’s upcoming social media ban would include “restrictions for 16- and 17-year-olds on websites that allow infinite scrolling and algorithmic content”; in fact, these restrictions are planned but do not yet have a determined date.Explore more on these topicsInternet safetyLisa NandyLabour conference 2026LabourSocial media banSocial mediaTechnology sectornewsShareReuse this content

title: US trade regulator opens investigation into AI giants including Anthropic and OpenAI | Trump administration | The Guardian
description: FTC move is first official US enforcement ⁠action on rogue AI agents, following surge in incidents first reported in July
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: FTC move is first official US enforcement ⁠action on rogue AI agents, following surge in incidents first reported in July
Content: Dario Amodei, Anthropic CEO, at the White House in Washington DC on Tuesday.Photograph: Shawn Thew/EPAView image in fullscreenDario Amodei, Anthropic CEO, at the White House in Washington DC on Tuesday.Photograph: Shawn Thew/EPATrump administrationUS trade regulator opens investigation into AI giants including Anthropic and OpenAIFTC move is first official US enforcement ⁠action on rogue AI agents, following surge in incidents first reported in JulyReutersWed 30 Sep 2026 14.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US’s main trade regulator is conducting an industry-wide investigation ⁠intoAnthropic, OpenAI and other ⁠AI labs ​to uncover the potential dangers their technology poses to consumers.The investigation by the Federal Trade Commission is the first official US enforcement ⁠action that delves into rogue AI agents, following a surge in incidents first reported in July that have stoked fears among the public that uncontrolled AI could one day ⁠harm humans.The FTC plans to issue formal demands for information and compel testimony from executives at top ​AI developers, including Anthropic, OpenAI and the research ‌group Metr, according tomultiplereports.Anthropic and ‌OpenAI have used Metr to conduct independent investigations into security incidents involving their agentic AI technology.Anthropic, OpenAI and ‌Metr did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The New York Post first reported the news.Andrew Ferguson, the FTC chair, had concerns about the companies before AI agents developed by OpenAI hacked the open-source platform Hugging Face. The incident, in which OpenAI agents probed the AI coding hub for vulnerabilities before carrying out a large-scale attack, sparked global discussion of the issue.Ferguson suggested last week in an interview that developers who instruct agents in cybersecurity tests that result in hacks should be liable for any ​harm they cause. The US should look to existing laws before seeking to pass new ones regulating AI, Ferguson said at an event in Austin.The FTC has broad authority to sue companies over unfair or deceptive practices, and has used that authority in the past to take action against companies for failing to ⁠take reasonable measures to secure consumers’ data.Donald Trump met with top ​AI executives on Tuesday, where the ​companies agreed to establish voluntary standards.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTrump AI deal rebrands ‘artificial intelligence’ as ‘superintelligence’Read moreTrump has ​repeatedly called fears about AI a hoax as he seeks to prioritize US dominance ​in the technology over regulation. ‌At the same ​time, he has ​also said the government can use existing laws against AI companies for any harm they may cause.Explore more on these topicsTrump administrationOpenAIAnthropicAI (artificial intelligence)US politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Senate Democrats block datacenter energy bill, saying ‘toothless’ legislation ‘misses the mark’ | US Senate | The Guardian
description: Republicans supported legislation although Democrats said it wouldn’t effectively address energy consumption
Author: Chris Stein
Headline: Republicans supported legislation although Democrats said it wouldn’t effectively address energy consumption
Content: Detroit residents protest against DTE Energy's plan to provide power for a proposed $7bn datacenter in rural Michigan, on 3 December 2025.Photograph: UCG/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDetroit residents protest against DTE Energy's plan to provide power for a proposed $7bn datacenter in rural Michigan, on 3 December 2025.Photograph: UCG/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesUS SenateSenate Democrats block datacenter energy bill, saying ‘toothless’ legislation ‘misses the mark’Republicans supported legislation although Democrats said it wouldn’t effectively address energy consumptionChris Steinin WashingtonWed 30 Sep 2026 13.48 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 15.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSenateDemocratson Wednesday blocked legislation intended to offset the impact ofdatacenterson consumer electricity bills, calling it a “toothless” attempt to address a top voter concern ahead ofNovember’s midterm elections.The Ratepayer Protection Act failed by a 57-to-43 vote, falling just shy of the 60 votes necessary to advance through the Republican-controlled chamber. Four Democrats – Maggie Hassan of New Hampshire, Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota and both Georgia senators, Jon Ossoff and Raphael Warnock – joinedRepublicansin support of the measure.“Americans are calling for real solutions, real guardrails, real solutions on AI. Republicans’ toothless datacenter bill completely misses the mark,” the Senate Democratic leader, Chuck Schumer, said in a floor speech before the vote. Schumer assailed Trump for a meeting with top tech executives on Tuesday that the president saidyieldeda “morally binding” agreement to put controls on artificial intelligence.“Relying on ‘self-regulation’ is how we got into this mess,” Schumer added.Earlier this month, theHouse of Representativeshad approved the bill by an almost unanimous vote.Datacenter construction and electricity consumption has grown in recent years amid advances in AI and other technologies, and with it has comeincreasing anxietyamong voters about the facilities’ impacts on their energy bills.Datacenter developers accused of skirting key US pollution rulesRead moreThe bipartisan legislation is an attempt by Congress to address those anxieties, and would have required electric utilities to consider adopting new standards so that datacenters pick up the costs of any necessary upgrades to transmission, generation and distribution, which can otherwise be transferred to households and businesses.It was proposed ahead of the 3 November midterm elections in which Democrats are campaigning on lowering the cost of living in their bid to regain control of the Senate and House. Its sponsor in the lower chamber was Gabe Evans, a Colorado Republican who isa top targetof Democrats, while the Ohio Republican Jon Husted championed the bill through the Senate.“It’s clear that big tech should be paying their own way, not passing the cost on to local communities and states – and this bill does that,” Husted said in a floor speech on Wednesday, urgingDemocratsto back the bill that the president had indicated he would sign.Though Ohio voted for Trump by an 11-point margin two years ago,recent pollshave shown Husted trailing his opponent, the Democratic former senator Sherrod Brown, who has accused the incumbent of bowing to the demands of the datacenter industry.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhile the proposal was seen as an attempt by Republicans Senate leaders to bolster Husted’s re-election chances, it also presented a quandary for the chamber’s Democrats, since voting it down could be seen as running counter to their pledges of lowering electricity bills.Nonetheless, the party’s leaders opted to oppose the measure, saying it would have been ineffective at actually addressing datacenters’ electricity consumption.The vote was one of the last the Senate is expected to take before the midterms. The chamber is scheduled to conclude its work on Friday, after which senators will return to their states to campaign.Explore more on these topicsUS SenateDatacenters – USEnergyAI (artificial intelligence)DemocratsRepublicansHouse of RepresentativesnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘President of the Unites States’: White House’s AI accord includes spelling error | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: Donald Trump and six tech executives voluntarily signed the document, which included a misspelling, committing to safely developing AI
Author: Ariana Baio
Headline: Donald Trump and six tech executives voluntarily signed the document, which included a misspelling, committing to safely developing AI
Content: Donald Trump speaks during a meeting with technology executives about artificial intelligence at the White House in Washington DC on Tuesday.Photograph: Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDonald Trump speaks during a meeting with technology executives about artificial intelligence at the White House in Washington DC on Tuesday.Photograph: Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty ImagesDonald Trump‘President of the Unites States’: White House’s AI accord includes spelling errorDonald Trump and six tech executives voluntarily signed the document, which included a misspelling, committing to safely developing AIAriana BaioWed 30 Sep 2026 12.11 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 12.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe White House misspelled “United States” under the signature ofDonald Trumpon an accord he signed with AI executives on Tuesday.At the bottom of the accord on “Super Intelligence”, the term Trump has used to rebrand artificial intelligence, the president’s signature appeared as “President of the Unites States”.It is unclear how the misspelling occurred or whether it will appear in the Federal Register, the database that contains official presidential actions and other government documents.Trump and six tech executives signed the document voluntarily committing to safely developing AI to address widespread concerns, sparked by industry leaders who warned the technology is evolving too rapidly to control.Trump has largely brushed aside concerns about AI harming humans and called for companies to continue developing the technology so the US can become the global leader in AI. Even while signing the accord on safety, the US president praised the business executives for growth.Trump posted the document containing the misspelling on Truth Social, and the White House Communications Team emailed it out shortly after it was signed.The Bloomberg News correspondentDavid Gura appeared to be the firstto notice the spelling error.The Guardian has asked the White House for commentThe accord on artificial intelligence outlined four layers of “controls and audits” that companies will implement to ensure AI capabilities operate as intended. That includes “robust” internal controls and partnering with an “independent external auditor or evaluator”.Potential internal controls could include empowering a team to monitor and detect that AI is operating correctly and creating monitors to ensure AI technologies will not hack or access technical systems in cybersecurity, biosecurity and chemical threats.External monitors would also check to make sure the AI is operating as intended and companies could designate a committee of the board of directors to oversee reports from teams operating the controls of the AI.The accord is the first step in addressing concerns, raised by industry experts in mid-September.Americans have become increasingly skeptical of AI.A recent New York Times/Siena College pollfound that 61% of voters opposed the construction of datacenters, while anSSRS/CNN pollfound that 71% of Americans believed the government wasn’t doing enough to regulate the growth and development of AI.While Tuesday’s document is only an accord, it left open the possibility of codifying the framework into formal regulations or laws – something Trump has repeatedly rejected.“I think I’m seeing tremendous self-policing,” Trump told reporters outside the White House on Tuesday. “And they understand that they have to self-police.”The six executives who signed the accord are Dario Amodei from Anthropic; Elon Musk from SpaceXAI; Greg Brockman from OpenAI; Jensen Huang from Nvidia; Mark Zuckerberg from Meta; and Sundar Pichai from Google.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpAI (artificial intelligence)Trump administrationUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: The best dehumidifiers: 14 favourites to beat damp and cut bills, tested | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Fed up with condensation, mould and musty smells? A dehumidifier could help – plus, they’re a cheaper way to dry laundry compared with tumble dryers
Author: Caramel Quin
Headline: Fed up with condensation, mould and musty smells? A dehumidifier could help – plus, they’re a cheaper way to dry laundry compared with tumble dryers
Content: View image in fullscreenGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterLife and styleReviewThe best dehumidifiers: 14 favourites to beat damp and cut bills, testedFed up with condensation, mould and musty smells? A dehumidifier could help – plus, they’re a cheaper way to dry laundry compared with tumble dryersThe best electric blankets and heated throws, tested by our expertCaramel QuinWed 30 Sep 2026 10.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou don’t have to live in the American deep south to feel the effects of humidity. At home, just breathing makes the air more humid, let alone cooking or showering.And when it gets too humid, it’s bad for our health as well as our homes. In fact, the two are connected: humidity lets mould and dust mites flourish – and they, in turn, can trigger asthma and allergies.Dehumidifiers can make your indoor environment more comfortable by reducing the amount of moisture in the air. Because of this, they’re also a great laundry-drying hack. I use mine to dry clothes fast, and for a fraction of the cost of tumble drying.Not sure if you need one? You can buy a hygrometer cheaply –the one I used for testing cost less than £10– to check your home’s relative humidity and make an informed decision. Should you opt to buy one, do your research at reputable sources (like, hint, the Filter). Researching this piece, I was shocked to learn thatcustomers had been dupedinto buying very basic dehumidifiers for well over the odds.At a glanceBest dehumidifier overallEbac4650e£309.99 at EbacBest budget dehumidifierVonHausSmart dehumidifier with laundry mode£144.99 at AmazonBest combined dehumidifier and air purifierDevolaPlatinum hybrid DVHA20L£161.99 at DevolaBest dehumidifier for drying laundryDuuxBora Smart£279.99 at DuuxBest quiet dehumidifierMeacoDryArete Two£299 at John LewisBest compact dehumidifierDevolaDVH12L£135.99 at DevolaWhy you should trust meI’m an award-winning consumer technology journalist with decades of experience testing electrical appliances; I’ve been reviewing gadgets for almost 30 years. I live in a terrace house with a lovely number of children and far too many pets, so there’s lots of laundry: I use a dehumidifier to dry clothes. I’ve also been known to use one for speedy DIY, drying plaster and paint faster.How I testedView image in fullscreenEach dehumidifier’s performance, energy consumption and noise levels were recorded.Photograph: Caramel Quin/The GuardianI selected 14 dehumidifiers from leading brands to test, then set them up and used them, each for several days. I used a power meter to measure how much electricity (and therefore money and carbon) they use. Using the Sound Meter app, I measured the noise from 1m away in decibels (dB) on multiple occasions – the figures featured here are all the ones that I measured at home, in consistent conditions, so they often differ from manufacturers’ official figures, which are measured in lab conditions but in inconsistent ways. More subjectively, I paid attention to the quality of the sound – was it annoying, gurgly, hard to ignore, easy to fall asleep to? And I measured each dehumidifier’s size.To measure the room’s humidity while testing, I used a digital hygrometer held 1m away (though humidity would be roughly the same elsewhere in the room), and a thermometer to check the temperature. Like its big sibling, the MeacoDry Arete Two (above), it purifies the air thanks to an included medical-grade H13 Hepa filter and dust filter. For only a little more, you can buy the larger Devola DVHA20L, which features a built-in PM2.5 air quality monitor. I also didn’t like the looks, finding the green and white a bit clinical.Dimensions:32 x 24 x 49cm (WDH);dailyextraction rate:12l;tank capacity:2.5l;peak power use on test:200W;average noise level on top setting:20dB;target humidity range:30-80%;laundry setting?Yes;running costs:5p/hourMeaco12 LEfrom£154.97£154.97 at Aircon Centre£189.99 at MeacoWhat we loveCompact, and you can add a Hepa filter for air purificationWhat we don’t loveI prefer models that measure air quality tooBlyss Madden WDH-316DBBlyssMadden WDH-316DB£120£120 at B&QWhat we loveIt’s easy to carry around the houseWhat we don’t loveIt’s a smaller model with no sleep functionView image in fullscreen£120 at B&QBest for:easy carryingThis has a daily extraction rate of 16 litres, which isn’t the weediest but is one of the smaller models on test. It has a simple handle across the full width that’s well balanced. If you find it difficult to carry heavy items up and down stairs, choose a smaller model like this.I liked the display, with relative humidity and temperature shown inside a cartoon house. And there’s a fan swing function that helps with drying laundry.It didn’t make the final cut because …there’s no sleep function, although it’s fairly quiet.Dimensions:30 x 19 x 47cm (WDH);dailyextraction rate:16l;tank capacity:2.4l;peak power use on test:230W;average noise level on top setting:20dB;target humidity range:50-70%;laundry setting?Yes;running costs:6p/hourBlyssMadden WDH-316DB£120£120 at B&QWhat we loveIt’s easy to carry around the houseWhat we don’t loveIt’s a smaller model with no sleep functionBlack+Decker BXEH60014GBBlack+DeckerBXEH60014GBfrom£174£174 at AO£186 at AmazonWhat we loveIt displays the precise humidity, and it has app controlWhat we don’t loveHigher running costs and loud at times£174 at AO£186 at AmazonBest for:smart controlsI liked the Black+Decker’s design, from the coloured light at the top that indicates humidity (red for high, green for good, blue for low) to the large, white digits on its front that tell you the precise relative humidity.These quick-glance displays work well when it’s paired with the app, so you can control it from afar. You can even add Google Home and Amazon Alexa voice controls. I could use my phone as a remote control from anywhere in the home to check on progress – rare for a dehumidifier at this price.It didn’t make the final cut because …the machine was loud at times (although the sleep setting averaged 17dB).Dimensions:34 x 24 x 57cm (WDH);dailyextraction rate:20l;tank capacity:6.5l;peak power use on test:395W;average noise level on top setting:20dB;target humidity range:30-80%;laundry setting?Yes;running costs:10p/hourBlack+DeckerBXEH60014GBfrom£174£174 at AO£186 at AmazonWhat we loveIt displays the precise humidity, and it has app controlWhat we don’t loveHigher running costs and loud at timesWhat you need to knowWhat is relative humidity?Relative humidity is the percentage of water vapour in the air compared with the maximum that the air can hold.Warm air can hold more water vapour than cold air. So if the amount of water in the air stays the same but the temperature drops, relative humidity increases.When relative humidity hits 100%, the air is fully saturated, and water condenses on surfaces, like how dew condenses on cool morning grass.What humidity should I aim for?All the dehumidifiers tested here measure the relative humidity (a percentage) and let you set a target.If the air is too humid, it feels muggy, and it’s hard for sweat to cool you on a hot day. If the air is too dry, it can lead to problems such as dry eyes and throats.For your health and your home, the ideal relative humidity is 40-60% in summer and 30-50% in winter.Do I need a dehumidifier?You may benefit from a dehumidifier if you have damp and mould problems. Humidity helps mould and dust mites flourish – and they, in turn, can trigger asthma and allergies.Another benefit is drying laundry fast. Use a dehumidifier to pull moisture out of the air, then clothes in the room dry much faster and without causing damp problems such as condensation on windows or walls.Dehumidifiers are also good for specific uses, such as drying paint or plaster faster, or helping a room dry out after flooding.If in doubt, usea cheap hygrometerto check your home’s relative humidity and make an informed decision.What are the different types of dehumidifier?Most of the dehumidifiers tested here arecompressor dehumidifiers, so they work a bit like a fridge, compressing and then expanding a refrigerant to cool a metal coil. Water from the air then condenses on the coil and drains off into a water tank. These are usually the best style of dehumidifier for the home.Don’t throw away the plastic tube if you find one in the box. Some models come with a drain hose – so you can constantly dry rather than stopping when the tank is full. Other models let you add a hose if you need it (but most people don’t use them, which is why they’re not always included).I tested onedesiccant dehumidifier. These excel in cold environments, such as garages, cellars and outbuildings. This is because they work by using moisture-absorbing materials that don’t rely on temperature to remove humidity. However, they use more electricity to do so. They don’t require refills (none of the units featured here needs refills for dehumidification – the only ongoing cost apart from electricity is that some have Hepa air filters that need replacing every three to six months).Peltier dehumidifiersare small and quiet, but they’re not very effective, and they use more energy, so we haven’t featured any in this roundup.What size dehumidifier do I need?The larger (20l a day) models tested here are good for larger homes and open-plan spaces. You can put them somewhere central to tackle humidity in the whole home.The smaller (12l a day) models are very popular and better for smaller homes or single tasks, such as drying laundry. However, if you have persistent damp problems, then it could be worth sizing up.You can add a hose to most dehumidifiers if you want to keep them in constant use without having to empty the tank.How much does a dehumidifier cost to run?I measured each dehumidifier’s power use on the top setting, in watts (W). Electricity costs are in kilowatt hours (kWh). For example, if you’re running a 200W dehumidifier for four hours, it would use 800Wh or 0.8kWh.The energy price cap for 1 October to 31 December 2026 is 26.32p a kWh. Multiply this by the last figure, and you’ll discover it costs about 21p to run the dehumidifier for four hours.This compares favourably with a tumble dryer.One load in a traditional model uses about 4.5kWh (£1.18), although an energy-saving heat pump model uses half that. Either way, it’s much cheaper to run a dehumidifier than either type of tumble dryer.What’s a laundry mode?Many dehumidifiers have a laundry mode that aims for a low relative humidity of 35%, with a timer that turns off automatically, typically aftersix hours.To dry laundry effectively, hang it in a room, turn on the dehumidifier and close the doors. That way, it’s drying the air (and speeding the laundry drying) without having to dry moist air that comes in from the outside world.How to clean your dehumidifierEmpty the water tank after each use, or when it’s full. Regular cleaning mainly involves dusting the unit and cleaning the air filters. Dust filters can usually be vacuumed and washed, while paper Hepa filters need replacing. How often depends on use: about three months for continuous use, six months for average use, or annually if you only run it occasionally. Smart models should track usage and alert you when the filter needs changing.If you use your dehumidifier mainly in the winter, then give it a thorough clean before storing it away.Start by running the unit on fan-only mode to dry the interior; if it doesn’t have one, set it to its highest humidity setting. Clean the unit and filters, then wash and disinfect the tank with a 50/50 mix of white vinegar and water to help prevent mould. Finally, leave everything to air-dry for at least 24 hours, ensuring it’s completely dry before reassembling and packing it away for the summer.How often should you empty your dehumidifier?A dehumidifier will stop working when its water tank is full, usually signalled by a flashing light, beep or app alert. But it’s good practice to empty the tank regularly rather than wait for this to happen.I mainly use a dehumidifier to dry laundry, which takes two to three hours and costs far less than tumble drying (see “How much does a dehumidifier cost to run?”).I simply turn it off when the clothes feel dry and empty the tank, or set the timer if I’m going out. Some models also have a dedicated laundry mode that switches off automatically.If you run a dehumidifier continuously, don’t aim for the driest air possible. Ideally, indoor relative humidity should be 40-60% in summer and 30-50% in winter. How often you need to empty the tank depends on the humidity, how much you use it, and tank capacity. A larger tank means you’ll have to empty it less often.Can dehumidifiers also cool rooms down?No. If anything, a dehumidifier makes a room a little bit warmer while it’s running. However, humid air makes sweat evaporate less effectively, so reducing humidity can help youfeelcooler on a warm day.This isn’t the case on a cold day, when high humidity can make you feel colder. That is because water vapour conducts heat away from the skin more efficiently than dry air. So getting the relative humidity right year-round improves comfort.For more, read the Filter’s guides:The best heated airers, testedThe best electric heatersThe best electric blankets to keep you toasty for lessCaramel Quin is a journalist specialising in consumer technology. She prides herself on real-world testing and plain language. Her pet hates are jargon, pointless products and overcomplicated instruction manuals. Caramel is an engineering graduate who has won awards for communicating hi-tech subjects to normal people.
