title: Who’s your Uber driver on the phone to? Welcome to the long, long diaspora phone call | Life and style | The Guardian
description: For those employed in arduous solitary work such as cab driving, a marathon phone call is the perfect place to navigate the dislocations of immigrant life
Author: Nesrine Malik
Headline: For those employed in arduous solitary work such as cab driving, a marathon phone call is the perfect place to navigate the dislocations of immigrant life
Content: ‘Shooting the breeze’ … long distance conversations aid decompression.Illustration: Joe Plimmer/Guardian Pictures/Getty/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘Shooting the breeze’ … long distance conversations aid decompression.Illustration: Joe Plimmer/Guardian Pictures/Getty/ShutterstockThe Long WaveLife and styleWho’s your Uber driver on the phone to? Welcome to the long, long diaspora phone callFor those employed in arduous solitary work such as cab driving, a marathon phone call is the perfect place to navigate the dislocations of immigrant lifeDon’t get The Long Wave delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereNesrine MalikWed 30 Sep 2026 09.19 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 09.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe question of the week is: “who are Uber drivers always talking to on the phone?” It’s one that regularly surfaces on Reddit threads and social media and even, on a couple of occasions, in the office. It’s not my question (I know who they are talking to), but I think the fact that many people are so baffled by it tells us a lot about the separate worlds we occupy.View image in fullscreenLong distance … seemingly aimless phone calls can mean so much to loved ones across continents.Photograph: Maskot/AlamyWhen you get a cab on a ride-hailing app, the chances that your driver will be on the phone is high. The conversation is almost always quiet, containing pauses so long that it often seems they are actually no longer on a call. But then comes a rejoinder, a laugh, an interjection, and the marathon continues.For anyone of an immigrant background, the question of who they are talking to is absolutely no mystery. They are talking to us; their siblings, parents, cousins and friends. Sometimes the person on the end of the line is back home, other times they are in a western city also navigating the dislocations of immigrant life. The long phone call is a regular feature of diaspora lives, and even more so for those employed in long, solitary work such as cab driving. These conversations are about nothing and everything.What are they talking about?View image in fullscreenKeeping close … the conversations that help the diaspora stay close to family, and home.Photograph: 10’000 Hours/Getty ImagesThis is not an exhaustive list, but based on the calls I constantly field from friends and family, the content I receive in a follow-up call, and familiar themes from chats with drivers in Arabic (which I sometimes get drawn into), the subjects are remarkably consistent. The range includes family gossip, wedding updates, complaints about the cost of living in the west, advice on navigating complex immigration systems, extremely detailed health updates, and political analysis of whatever crisis is unfolding. These conversations can broadly be sorted into one of two categories: “serious technical resolution of a problem” or “shooting the breeze”.In my experience, these beast mode long phone calls are between someone on a long shift, commute or drive, and a mother cooking in the kitchen. There is a languorous quality to the call. Time and conversational convention shift to accommodate long silences without explanation, as one person or the other breaks away to get on with something – dismount or park or blitz something in the food processor. Because the point is not the actual chat. It is a broadly phatic – that is to say language used for bonding – form of communication, an exercise in yearning and homesickness. It helps us bridge a gap between long distances and absences, and simulate a proximity that is so deeply longed for.Why talk all through the working day?View image in fullscreenLong distance … when physical socialisation is impossible, the phone does the work.Photograph: Sergey Strelkov/Getty ImagesThe interminable phone call is an immigrant’s lifeline, now made cheap and stable by voice over IP (the ability to make calls on an internet connection). But it is also a feature of broader cultural and economic patterns. Western time is personal, individual, literally “me time”, something that is violated if demanded without permission. This time is parcelled out necessarily for decompression, for work, for leisure. In other cultures, time is social and public.In Sudan, for example, there is no such thing as calling ahead before a visit. Your home is a drop-in destination from about 11am onwards. A neighbour will pop in for a chat, a relative will be driving home and swing by, and if there are children in the household, their own social lives mean you just never know how many people you are cooking for. The corner shop is a lifeline of last minute provision as numbers swell unexpectedly. If you are an introvert, good luck.When that physical socialisation is impossible, the phone does the work. Certain conditions make the visit and the call possible. Homes where there is often a homemaker to receive, or work that does not require strict, in-office professional deportment and execution. Highly structured working environments and fast-paced modern lives mean that entire societies are firmly post-casual-phone-call. In these contexts, I find myself so wary of ambushing or alarming people with a call that I send a clear warning beforehand. No, there is nothing to worry about, and are you sure this is a good time to speak? Absolutely no worries if not.But it is also a mindset, which you can lose over time. I find myself becoming increasingly post-phone call outside work, constantly thinking to myself that I will ring a relative back when I have the time. Generally, I prefer to message or voice note, conscious that when I return the call, it absolutely will not be a quick and efficient catch up. But, in truth, I do have the time, I have just assimilated the same rigid notions of downtime and non-urgent phone calls as an incursion. Fundamentally, this is an extremely capitalist notion of time as purely a function of work, where even if you are not working, you are “re-charging” in anticipation of more work.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe Long WaveNesrine Malik, Micha Frazer-Carroll and the team guide you through the biggest Black stories from around the worldEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionReclaiming the lost art of the ambling phone callView image in fullscreenA lost art … the case for bringing back the long, meandering phone call.Photograph: Maskot/Getty ImagesThe fact that the long driver call is such a bewildering anomaly is a meeting of those two worlds. In one, a passenger cannot fathom that you might have so much to say to someone over the phone, because everyone you love or want to see is generally within your immediate social reach, and because it is unfathomable to dedicate so much of your precious bandwidth to seemingly aimless conversation. In another, loved ones are in a different country or sprawl all over the world, and without their constant companionship life is just alienation and monotonous work.But I suspect there is more to the lost art of the phone call in certain societies than just the pressures of modernity. In contemporary life, there are so many ways to feel like you are in touch and in conversation when you are not. So many ways to feel part of some slipstream of humanity, when in fact we are scrolling, meme-ing, seeing news from friends and strangers alike via story updates, while not exchanging anything meaningful or even uttering a single word. Those in exile are acutely aware of alienation, and reach out to remedy it. But for those in their home countries, loneliness still lurks in ways harder to recognise. A phone call is honestly less time consuming and more replenishing than anything else we use our devices for.Tap inDo you have long, aimless phone calls? How do you think your preferred mode of communication connects to your culture? Share your thoughts by replying to this, or emailing us atthelongwave@theguardian.comand we may include your response in a future issue.Diaspora discussesLast week, we explored Britain’s fraught relationship with its historical role in enslavement. You shared your thoughts on the publication of theRegister of British Slave Tradersand therecords of enslaved people, and mounting calls for recognition and reparations.double quotation markI started to search online for my enslaved ancestors for the first time and discovered that decades of British secrecy means I have no written records of my ancestors to start with. No names no approximate births or death dates. This legacy means I have a family left not literate enough to document their history. Ancient family members that don’t speak English. People who make up their new own names because their family names derived from the slavers. It’s great that we have this info but I wish there was more help in finding the people we want to know about.Michelle B, based in Stroud, UKdouble quotation markThe stories that a country tells itself make a huge difference. Kudos to Germany for making sure that the blot on their journey is never forgotten among their own. Former colonial powers would do well to teach history accurately – otherwise they risk forgetting the past rather than learning from it, and helping to correct the damage that was done while they enriched themselves for generations.David P.A. Mullings, based in the US and Jamaica• To receive the complete version of The Long Wave in your inbox every Wednesday,please subscribe here.Explore more on these topicsLife and styleThe Long WaveAfricaCaribbeanRemittancesFamilyMobile phonesnewslettersShareReuse this content

title: How Zach Cregger’s Resident Evil stands out from all other game adaptations | Games | The Guardian
description: There’s no Leon, Claire or Ada Wong in Cregger’s adaptation. Instead, it re-creates something more fundamental – the strange, terrifying experience of actually playing the game
Author: Keith Stuart
Headline: There’s no Leon, Claire or Ada Wong in Cregger’s adaptation. Instead, it re-creates something more fundamental – the strange, terrifying experience of actually playing the game
Content: Director Zach Cregger (right) with actor Austin Abrams on the set the new Resident Evil film.Photograph: Dušan Martinček/CTMGView image in fullscreenDirector Zach Cregger (right) with actor Austin Abrams on the set the new Resident Evil film.Photograph: Dušan Martinček/CTMGPushing Buttons newsletterGamesHow Zach Cregger’s Resident Evil stands out from all other game adaptationsThere’s no Leon, Claire or Ada Wong in Cregger’s adaptation. Instead, it re-creates something more fundamental – the strange, terrifying experience of actually playing the gameDon’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereKeith StuartWed 30 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 10.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’ve been surprised by the number ofResident Evilfans complaining on social media about Zach Cregger’s cinematic adaptation of the survival horror series. “It’s not arealResident Evil movie,” they’ve claimed. Were we watching the same film? Certainly, it doesn’t feature any of the familiar heroes – there’s no Leon, no Claire, no Ada Wong – and there’s a distinct lack of recognisable antagonists and well-known locations. Despite all of this, Cregger’s interpretation is one of the most accurate and interesting video game films ever made.On the surface, it’s about a zombifying virus that gets accidentally released in Raccoon City by the Umbrella Corporation. These are, of course, the foundations of the Resi mythos. More interestingly, Cregger seeks to replicate and explore the structural and narrative conventions of the series. In the film, the player character, hapless courier Bryan Hodukavich, is thrust into a viral outbreak, with no weapons and no idea what’s going on. He is then submerged into an uncanny shadow world of escalating peril and body horror. The film takes us through a series of locations dragged straight from the games – an abandoned farmhouse, a road tunnel crammed with abandoned cars, a hospital andthe obligatory sewer level. As he progresses, Bryan finds increasingly powerful weapons, from a handgun to an assault rifle – but he is always short on ammo. And there are typewriters in at least two scenes!Bryan’s understanding of the world is shaped, as in any Resident Evil game, through found footage (voice recordings, emails etc) and via short, enigmatic interchanges with non-player characters. There’s a sequence in the road tunnel where a recently infected young girl says to Bryan: “My mom bit me, I don’t know where she went.” This is a classic Resident Evil exchange: in one terse sentence she gives us narrative informationandan implied threat – the mother could be lurking anywhere nearby, waiting to pounce …Aware perhaps of online discourse, Creggerreleased a videoexplaining his vision for the movie, and how he has sought to reflect not just the fictitious universe of the games, but also the experience of playing them – that sense of quickly moving through a world of endlessly evolving horror. It’s also been interesting to see theories emerge about Bryan’s role as a sort of NPC precursor to a true lead character, leaving the hints, tips and ammo behind for someone capable to pick up.View image in fullscreenOmnipresent merchant … Resident Evil.Photograph: CapcomI always thought thatthe subsidiary non-playable characters in the early Resident Evil titles had the most interesting stories: affable old Barry Burton from the first game, cowardly helicopter pilot Brad Vickers fromResi 3,Resident Evil 4’s omnipresent merchant. “I’m interested in vulnerable characters, in normal human beings,” series creator Shinji Mikamionce told me. “The horror experience is most scary when the player really isn’t sure whether their character is going to live or die – death and survival need to be on a constant see-saw. If there’s a situation where you’re not 100% sure that you can avoid or defeat the enemies, if you feel maybe there’s a chance you’ll make it – that’s where horror lies.” Bryan Hodukavich lives in that space for the whole film.Cregger’s Resident Evil should perhaps be put alongside Kane Parsons’sBackroomsand Genki Kawamura’sExit 8as a movie that is as much an exploration of video game mechanics as it is any sort of translation. These movies make us feel like players, trapped in an unfamiliar nightmare world with its own rules, characters and temporal conventions, which we have to gradually unpeel. Cinema has always deconstructed other media, whether that’s the theatre (Les Enfants du Paradis, The Producers) or superhero comics (Unbreakable, Logan), and it’s fascinating to see video games having the same sort of scrutiny. This is, after all, the most self-reflexive medium – the audience is spectator and participant, the world is naturalistic yet necessarily artificial, with its yellow-painted walls (see:Keza’s newsletter just last week), and its indestructible barriers (to stop a player wandering out of the rendered environment).So yes, this is definitely a Resident Evil movie – it’s just that the camera pans away from Claire as she blasts another zombie, or Leon as he makes a daft wisecrack. Instead, it takes us just around the corner, to where the huddling masses of Raccoon City await their destiny, with maybe three bullets, two lines of dialogue and a voice recorder.What to playView image in fullscreenRagdoll-physics gore-fest … Happy Wheels is now available on Steam.Photograph: Jim Bonacci/Fancy ForceFirst appearing as a browser-based game back in 2010, the ragdoll-physics gore-festHappy Wheelsis now on Steam – and it’s just as ridiculous as ever. Your aim is to make it across an obstacle-laden landscape in whatever vehicle you’re given without falling into a chasm or being chainsawed in half, or stabbed or eaten. There are dozens of levels but you can also design your own and share them with the community. I’m not surprised the Steam version has been wishlisted by 750,000 players. This kind of hilarious, awkward, experimental game thrived in the Flash era of the noughties and it’s lovely to see a classic example return in all its blood-drenched, clipart-esque glory.Available on:PCEstimated playtime:Several laughable hoursWhat to readView image in fullscreenMicrosoft and Sony have filed for ad and monetisation patents, respectively.Photograph: Lucy Nicholson/ReutersIt’s been weird to watch Microsoft and Sony seemingly trying to find yet more ways to antagonise gamers after concerns over mass redundancies and the death of physical media. Two weeks ago, the gaming site Respawn FirstdiscoveredaMicrosoft patentto serve ads to Xbox players during down times in games, perhaps while loading a level or after a boss battle. Not to be outdone, Sony hasfiled a US patentfor technology allowing players to tap their phone or credit card on a PlayStation controller to pay for digital goods. Call me cynical, but perhaps more convenient advertising and monetisation models are not the best way to win back hearts and minds.Naughty Dog studio head Neil Druckmannhas revealedthat there are twoLast of Usprojects on the go, expanding on the canon of the first two games. Both are in the very early stages of development, and it’s not even known if they are games – they could include a new TV series, movie or graphic novel.Looking for somewhere nice to visit?Minecraftis getting itsfirst new dimension in 15 years,a particularly lush world named The Sift, filled with pastel-hued meadows, multicolour lakes and bunny-like mobs. It arrives in Minecraft Dungeons II this month, and will be in the main editions of the game next year.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat to clickAce Combat 8: Wings of Theve – brilliant aerial combat game fulfils the Top Gun fantasy | ★★★★★Playing video games with my 22-year-old son has brought me to tearsMeet the real-life Pokémon professors, the unsung heroes of competitive monster-battling‘Mum, where did my Robux go?’ :The Roblox scam targeting childrenQuestion BlockView image in fullscreenExtremely relaxing … Unpacking, a relaxing tidying game.Photograph: Witch BeamA cosy question fromSimon, via email:“Last year I ended up spending a lot of time supporting mydad during a roughpatch with this health, and this led to me playing a lot of Animal Crossing: Pocket Camp Complete on my iPhone. I havefound it really soothing during a challenging year but I’ve pretty much exhausted it.[Someone] recommended [playing] Stardew Valley but it doesn’t feel especially suited to playing on a relatively small mobile, nor my limited free time. Any suggestions? Hopefully nothing involving micro transactions?”Smartphone games can be an amazing tonic during tough times – I’m glad they helped you through them. If you’ve not playedUnpackingyet, it’s an extremely relaxing narrative tidying game with lots of subtle emotional touches. I also like the gentle platforming adventureSpiritfarerabout shepherding spirits to the afterlife. If you’re looking for more of an Animal Crossing vibe, there’sWilderness: Meadowfell, a lush exploration game set in a procedurally generated landscape, or try one of the classics from Japanese developer, Kairosoft, such as theGame Dev StoryorJumbo Airport Story. If you can stomach a couple of suggestions with very noninvasive in-app purchases My Leisure Time and Animal Restaurant, have been recommended to me as great life sims with bags of character.If you have a question for Question Block – or anything else to say about the newsletter – hit reply or email us atpushingbuttons@theguardian.com.Explore more on these topicsGamesPushing Buttons newsletterResident EvilAction gamesFilm adaptationsHorror filmsZombiesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Ken Paxton’s Christian identity politics obscure a history of scandal | Sidney Blumenthal | The Guardian
description: The Texas Senate candidate rose to power as a culture warrior. His record is a marriage of hypocrisy and cynicism
Author: Sidney Blumenthal
Headline: The Texas Senate candidate rose to power as a culture warrior. His record is a marriage of hypocrisy and cynicism
Content: ‘The more unnerved Paxton becomes, the deeper he descends to smears to incite a sexual panic.’Photograph: Jessica Koscielniak/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘The more unnerved Paxton becomes, the deeper he descends to smears to incite a sexual panic.’Photograph: Jessica Koscielniak/ReutersOpinionUS politicsKen Paxton’s Christian identity politics obscure a history of scandalSidney BlumenthalThe Texas Senate candidate rose to power as a culture warrior. His record is a marriage of hypocrisy and cynicismWed 30 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 06.01 EDTShareKen Paxton’s political career, more than that of any other Republican candidate campaigning in this cycle, charts the arc of the religious right. The most influential of its activists and donors engineered his rise as a culture warrior at each of its phases from his creation through every disgrace. His race for the Senate, the culmination of his ambition, has become not only his last stand, but also the Alamo for Christian nationalists inTexas.Paxton’s rap sheet explains his Christian identity politics as a shield to distract from the liability of his own record of financial and sexual scandals scrolling back decades. The20 articles of impeachmentagainst Paxton, adopted by the Republican-controlled Texas house of representatives in May 2023, were double the Ten Commandments that Paxtoninsistsshould be displayed in every Texas classroom.Paxton hadallegedly engaged in briberywhen a campaign contributor, Nate Paul,secured a jobfor Paxton’s alleged mistress, aformer senate aide, at World Class Holdings, a real estate firm owned by Paul. Paul allegedly created afake Uber accountfor Paxton to travel secretly for liaisons with his mistress andpaid forrenovations at Paxton’s house. In exchange, Paxton allegedlyinterferedwith a federal inquiry into accusations of financial fraud against Paul involving$172m in loansby passing on sealed FBI documents, installing a special prosecutor in his office as the state’s attorney general to target and harass the federal agents and judges investigating Paul’s crimes, and halting foreclosures on Paul’s properties. In April 2025, Paul took aplea dealoffour monthsof home confinement, five years of supervised release, and a $1m fine.Trump-backed Ken Paxton unveils ‘Texas first’ datacenter plan aimed at ‘negative impact’Read moreThe Republican-dominated Texas senate by a 16-to-14 voteacquittedPaxton in his impeachment trial in September 2023. After Paxton’s federal indictment in 2015 on felony counts of financial securities fraud, he avoided trial by copping apleaunder which he would perform 100 hours of community service,take 15 hoursof legal ethics courses, and pay $271,000 in restitution to the fleeced investors.Paxton’s wife, the state senator Angela Paxton, attended the impeachment trial, but wasbarred from voting. She had beeninstrumentalin advancing his career, a political force in her own right, a crucial conduit to Christian nationalist leaders and funders. They had met as students at Baylor University, had four children, and she presented their “sacred covenant” as a faith-based partisan calling. “I’m a pistol-packing mama, and my husband sues Obama,” shetoldcheering crowds. He financed her election with a $2m loan from his campaign fund, and once in office shefiled billsto increase his office and salary.In July 2025, Angela Paxtonfiled for divorceon “biblical grounds”. This July, Paxton wasphotographedon a trip to Iceland and London with the Christian influencer Tracy Duhon.The religious right that raised up Paxton has cared little about his transgressions so long as they could prop him up to wield power. The alliance has been a perfect marriage of hypocrisy and cynicism in the name of traditional values.The origin story begins at New Orleans’ legendary Café du Monde in 1967, wherePaul Presslerand Paige Patterson forged a pact to take over the Southern Baptist Convention to transform it into a political machine for a “Conservative Resurgence” and to purge moderates. Both had been duly anointed for their holy task.Pressler’s grandfather and hero, EE Townes, an oil industry lawyer, was a leader of the Texas Regulars movement in favor of “white supremacy”, as Townesexplained, and the lifting of wartime price controls on oil and gas. The Regulars sought to defeat President Franklin D Roosevelt’s re-election in 1944. Four years later, the Regularsfolded intothe segregationist Dixiecrat party. Townes leveraged the election of his grandson, young Pressler, to the Texas house, where he sponsored pro-segregationist legislation.Pressler sought out Paige Patterson, an apostle of WA Criswell, fundamentalist pastor of the mammoth First Baptist Church of Dallas, who denounced civil rights activists as “infidels” and John F Kennedy’s candidacy for president in 1960 on thebasisthat he was a stalking horse for the pope. Criswell would appointPattersonthe head of his Criswell Center for Biblical Studies, a power base of 14 churches.In 1979, Pressler, by then appointed a Texas state judge, and Patterson applied their clout within the SBC to elect its president. “It was like Gettysburg,”saidPressler. “But this time the right side won.” Moderates were systematically fired from Southern Baptist seminaries and bureaucracy. “We are going for the jugular,” Presslersaid.Pressler and Patterson begat Kelly Shackelford, who in 1997 founded the First Liberty Institute, a Christian conservative legal organization, around which he created a powerful political machine, raising tens of millions from a handful of billionaire oilmen, mobilizing evangelicals and electing rightwingRepublicans. In effect, the vision of the Texas Regulars was realized.Republican says Trump’s support of Ken Paxton in Texas primary was ‘colossal mistake’Read moreShackelfordbegatGreg Abbott, elected Texas attorney general in 2002, meshing their operations on religious right cases. At the same time, Shackelford begat Ken Paxton, the force behind his run for the Texas house. Shackelford, Paxton and his wife Angela had all attended Baylor together. Then, when Abbott ran for governor in 2014, Shackelford backed Paxton to replace him as attorney general. Pressler served on Paxton’s advisory committee.Paxton hired more than half a dozen of Shackelford’s staff lawyers, including his general counsel, Jeff Mateer, who became the assistant attorney general, and threw the full weight of his office behind Shackelford’s culture war litigation. In 2020,Mateerhad a crisis of conscience and reported Paxton to the FBI for alleged bribery, but Shackelford stood by Paxton, keeping the Christian right in line and providing money for his legal defense.Shackelford had been busy begetting a slew of rightwing politicians to take over the Texas Republican party: SenatorTed Cruz, the lieutenant governor,Dan Patrick, and a host of Texas legislators. The Texas state senate that refused to remove Paxton after he was impeached by the house had been packed. The Defend Texas Liberty Pac, funded by Shackelford’s oilmen, threatened the political future of any Republican who voted to convict Paxton. Dan Patrick, who presided over the trial as judge,received$3m in loans and contributions.Shackelford also begat Mike Johnson, long before he became speaker of the House, originally a litigator at First Liberty, selected in 2010 to become the foundingdeanof the new Paul Pressler School of Law in Louisiana, which collapsed in 2012 due to lack of funding and failure to achieve accreditation.Since the early 1980s, there were more than rumors about Pressler’s predations as a pedophile. Moderate Baptists were closely documenting his observable pattern of sexual abuse of boys and young men. In 2004, the First Baptist Church of Houston where Pressler was a deacon investigated a complaint that Presslermolested a young man. Church leaderssent Presslera private warning letter saying the conduct was “morally and spiritually inappropriate” and could “distort your testimony” if it came to light. That letter remained private for more than a decade. In a separate incident that year, Pressler privately settled a suit for $450,000 with Duane Rollins, who alleged that as a 14-year-old he had been repeatedly raped by Pressler.Jared Woodfill, Pressler’s law partner who helped fundraise for Paxton, was informed of the allegations. For years afterwards, Woodfill maintained Pressler as a law partner, though he performed no work, compensating him by sending him a string of young men to serve as assistants,three of whomhave accused Pressler of sexual misconduct. (Pressler, whodied in 2024, denied the allegations against him and wasnever criminally charged. Woodfill hasdenied wrongdoing.)Duane Rollins filed a new lawsuit in 2017, this time naming the SBC and multiple Baptist entities, not just Pressler, and alleging the SBC leadership covered up the abuse. After the news of his suit broke in the Texas Tribune, other young men stepped forward with similar allegations. In 2019, the Houston Chronicle reporter Robert Downen wroteinvestigative reportsdocumenting widespread sexual abuse across Southern Baptist churches broadly, of which Pressler was only one example.Downen’s reporting sparked the SBC to commission aninvestigationthat unearthed allegations against 263 church leaders in 30 states and an extensive pattern of cover-up. After its publication, the SBCstonewalledfurther inquiry and its officialsdenouncedit all as a “reckless hoax”.Pressler died in 2024. Paige Patterson was disgraced when he was accused of advising women who endured marital abuse to pray for their husbands while he was president of the Southwestern Baptist Theological Seminary. He wasousted in 2018.Patterson and the Southwestern Baptist Theological Seminary were dismissedfrom Rollins’s lawsuit against Pressler in 2023. The school had immortalized Pressler and Patterson as virtual saints withstained glass windowsin its chapel, but after their fall from grace the windows were quietly removed.If Democrats are to win Texas, James Talarico must win blue-collar voters | Dustin GuastellaRead moreOn a political precipice, Paxton projects himself as a specimen of hypermasculinity to feminize his opponent – his actual opposite in other respects – a Presbyterian seminarian animated by social justice, James Talarico. “Low-T Talarico Too Weak For Texas,” ran oneTV ad. Paxton has mocked him with a blizzard of nicknames: “Tofu Talarico”, “Six-gender Jimmy” and “James Tala-freako”. Stephen Miller, the White House deputy chief of staff, haschimed in, falsely, on X: “The Democrats made history in Texas by nominating their first transgender senate candidate.” A conservative group produced an AI generatedadwith a phoney Talarico in a dress singing a song from The Sound of Music about “changing the gender of all your offspring”. Paxton then posted an AI-generatedadof a fake Talarico drawing in crayon on a “Talarico King James Bible”, delivering a sermon of false and distorted statements about religion and sex: “wrong for Texas”. A rightwing Pac supported Paxton with a $10m buy of a deepfakeAI addepicting Talarico as a surgeon apparently performing a sex reassignment operation on a girl. In fact, Talarico isopposed to transgender surgery for minorsandtrans athletes’ participationin women’s sports.The more unnerved Paxton becomes, the deeper he descends to smears to incite a sexual panic. Through his calumnies, he positions himself as defender of the faith. He evangelizes for restoring “Judeo-Christian values” and protecting them from the threat of Talarico, “a Christian who hates Christianity”,he says.Paxton is indeed a throwback to a venerable tradition. His archetype appeared in Sinclair Lewis’s novel, Elmer Gantry, published in 1927, about a licentious preacher and political conman. “He had, in fact,” wrote Lewis, “got everything from the church and Sunday School, except, perhaps, any longing whatever for decency and kindness and reason.”Sidney Blumenthal, former senior adviser to President Bill Clinton and Hillary Clinton, has published three books of a projected five-volume political life of Abraham Lincoln:A Self-Made Man,Wrestling With His AngelandAll the Powers of Earth. He is a Guardian US columnist and co-host of theCourt of History podcastExplore more on these topicsUS politicsOpinionRepublicansChristianityTexasReligioncommentShareReuse this content

title: If turbocharged petrol prices are driving up inflation, then why are Australia’s unemployed on the line? | Greg Jericho | The Guardian
description: Avoiding a rise in unemployment is important for the RBA – but apparently not a dealbreaker
Author: Greg Jericho
Headline: Avoiding a rise in unemployment is important for the RBA – but apparently not a dealbreaker
Content: ‘Without the increase in petrol prices driven by the war on Iran, inflation in August would have fallen,’ Greg Jericho writes.Photograph: George Chan/AAPView image in fullscreen‘Without the increase in petrol prices driven by the war on Iran, inflation in August would have fallen,’ Greg Jericho writes.Photograph: George Chan/AAPGrogonomicsAustralian economyIf turbocharged petrol prices are driving up inflation, then why are Australia’s unemployed on the line?Greg JerichoAvoiding a rise in unemployment is important for the RBA – but apparently not a dealbreakerFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ournew political email,free appordaily news podcastWed 30 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 18.58 EDTShareAnd here we are again. Hello darkness my old friend.Interest ratesup again and talk of a recession if needed.The Reserve Bank’s enacting legislation gives it a dual mandate – “price stability [ie stable inflation] and the maintenance of full employment in Australia”. But in reality the RBA seems to ignore the “full employment” aspect overall and we now need to worry about a recession.It’s not just me who noticed this. After the RBA governor, Michele Bullock, held a press conference where she announced that the cash rate was being raised to 4.6%, the ABC’s Alan Kohler (enjoyyour retirement, Alan!) told Afternoon Briefing: “She defines ‘full employment’ in terms of inflation. There’s really only one mandate that means – the mandate is inflation. That’s it.”The market also understands this.After the RBA’s July meeting, the markets predicted no rate rise this month and maybe no more to come. Now a rise to 4.85% is priced in before March next year:If the graph does not display click hereThey predict this even though without the increase in petrol prices driven by the war on Iran,inflation in Augustwould have fallen (which is why core inflation remained steady at 3.6%):If the graph does not display click hereWhen thinking about petrol prices, recall thatAmpol’s interim profit this year rose 376%, and its share price has risen so much since the war on Iran began that Woodside and Santos seem like the poor cousins:If the graph does not display click hereApparently, companies are not to blame for raising prices.Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter hereNever mind thathousehold spending in Augustfell once you took away the increase due to petrol prices:If the graph does not display click hereNo, forget all that, the RBA is devoted to getting inflation under 3% regardless of what is causing that inflation.Bullock said the RBA was not failing to deliver full employment because “the full employment target is the unemployment rate, if you like, or the level of employment which is consistent with low and stable inflation. And what we’re saying at the moment is that the rate of unemployment or the employment, is actually a bit tight, and it’s not consistent, we don’t think, with low and stable inflation.”TrulyHumpty Dumpty language territory.If you are not angry now, you should be.But just wait.With inflation at 4.0% mainly driven by petrol prices due to a war in Iran and a massive boom in datacentres (which are not delivering any productivity benefits yet), the RBA is worried we might think this clearly abnormal period is normal and that inflation will always be above 3%.God spare us.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toPolitics, reallyOur political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe governor was askedif she could see a situation “where you do actually need to put the economy into recession in order to get what you desperately hope for which is basically the mid-point of 2.5%? Can you see a scenario where that would be needed?”Now for me that is a pretty easy question to answer; something along the lines of “No! Are you crazy? There is no way lowering core inflation from 3.6% to under 3% would justify a recession.”Instead, Bullock replied: “Well, I hope it’s not needed. Are there scenarios in which it might have to happen that way? I guess possibly. And the scenario that I’m thinking of there is if inflation expectations get away from us.If inflation expectations start – if people start saying, ‘You know what,three point something is fine or four is fine,’ and you do hear some of that, if that gets away, then that is a circumstance in which I think you might need to have quite a dramatic slowdown in the economyto – and that’s our worry.” [My italics]Just think on that – the central bank thinking if people would start considering that inflation between 3% and 4% is OK, then a recession could be on the table, even if it wasn’t their “central base case at this moment”.Single, couple or family: not all Australian middle-income earners are equal | Greg JerichoRead moreBullock once again on Tuesday told journalists that rising unemployment “doesn’t mean job losses. What it often means is that people might be taking longer to find a job.”She’s technically right but for her to say that “we’ll do what we have to do to get inflation down because we need to”, shows the skewed priorities. Sure, she went on to say, “but if we can avoid massive job losses and a massive increase in the unemployment rate, that is a really important thing to be able to try and do”. Avoiding massive increases in unemployment is important but, for the RBA, apparently not a dealbreaker.Recessions are horrible things and many a central bank has come a gutser thinking they can just lower rates and get things going again.During Covid the percentage of adults with a job fell by as much as during the 1990s recession but it was due to lockdowns, not economic conditions, so the recovery was very quick. The GFC was almost a recession but the percentage of adults with a job fell much less than in the 1990s recession.In the 1990s recession, not only was there a massive loss of jobs, it took a decade to recover:If the graph does not display click hereRecessions over the past 55 years have seen the level of men in full-time work fall and never recover. Never:If the graph does not display click hereBut that, it seems, might be the price we have to pay to lower inflationary expectations from 3.5% to 2.5%.Greg Jericho is a Guardian columnist and chief economist at the Australia InstituteExplore more on these topicsAustralian economyGrogonomicsReserve Bank of AustraliaInterest ratesHousingUnemploymentInflationUS-Israel war on IrancommentShareReuse this content

title: Electoral reform could be a gamble too far for Burnham – but so far he’s on a winning streak | Zoe Williams | The Guardian
description: Though proportional representation poses risks for Labour, it’s a change that feels necessary for today’s volatile politics, says Guardian columnist Zoe Williams
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: Though proportional representation poses risks for Labour, it’s a change that feels necessary for today’s volatile politics, says Guardian columnist Zoe Williams
Content: Andy Burnham at the Labour party conference in Liverpool on 30 September 2026.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPAView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham at the Labour party conference in Liverpool on 30 September 2026.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPAOpinionElectoral reformElectoral reform could be a gamble too far for Burnham – but so far he’s on a winning streakZoe WilliamsThough proportional representation poses risks for Labour, it’s a change that feels necessary for today’s volatile politicsWed 30 Sep 2026 10.55 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 13.13 EDTShareAnumber of people have admitted to tears during Andy Burnham’s Labour partyconference speech, and most of them mean when he talked about his father, who died very recently. But then there were a few (not me) who welled up when he announced a commission onelectoral reform. It was just the sheer shock of it: that we may finally have a prime minister who will follow through on his own long-held beliefs and remain loyal to his long-term support base, even if it makes him avoidable enemies and, medium-term, destroys Labour’s only-trodden path to victory. It felt a bit like slipping through time, and I couldn’t even tell you to when (definitely not the 1990s).Burnham’s support for proportional representation has always been extremely unusual for a Labour politician. To this day, he ascribes that to his experience of winning an election as mayor of Greater Manchester on a supplementary votes system, where people get to choose a first- and second-preference candidate. He said thatcampaigning under that system“finally aligned the conversation on the door with what people want from politics, which is about problem-solving first and foremost, not about point-scoring”. He went a bit further this morning, asking Nick Robinson on the Today programme: “Can we really watch a party with less than 30% walk into Downing Street?”Plainly, he was talking about the spectre of a Reform government, and it’s that very context that makes this already difficult constitutional conversation even more vexed. Back in May, the all-party parliamentary group for fair elections held a meeting to discuss theaftermath of the local elections. It feels like a long time ago, and furthermore, so different in atmosphere as to be irrelevant to the prime minister, but 2020s politics are defined by their switchblade turns. In the matter of constitutional reform, the overriding priority has to be to build a system that’s fair across a range of imaginable scenarios, not just the one in front of you.The locals delivered great results for Reform, and satisfactory ones for the Liberal Democrats, which reflected the realities of a first-past-the-post (FPTP) system – first, it rewards the winner, and second, it rewards geographical concentration. Labour walked away from the 2024 general election with 63% of the seats on 34% of the votes, thelargest overrepresentation ever. The Greens have spent years commanding the fervent support of a geographically diffuse but not insignificant minority, with almost nothing to show for it in parliamentary terms.The distortions of FPTP have been well-known for years, but historically they were only ever discussed in terms of the barrier to entry they presented to insurgent parties, and the democratic deficit they constituted to any voter who didn’t live in a marginal seat, which is to say the majority of voters. So the counter-arguments were that, for all its flaws, by keeping out insurgents, the traditional voting system kept out extremists: and who wouldn’t sacrifice a little bit (or a huge amount) of democracy, for the sake of steadiness?Stability was the first myth to fall, when it transpired, over the past 10 years, that you can keep on returning one of two main parties as reliably as you like, and they will have no problem confecting so much intra-party turmoil that you might as well have voted for the Monster Raving Loony party. The efficacy of FPTP in keeping out extremists, meanwhile, was – like a stock market bubble – true until it wasn’t. Once politics has fragmented, the system rewards short bursts of popularity with potentially very long periods of power. That has a toxic effect on the supposedly sober heads of the political centre who, once they see extreme, often bigoted, positions pay off in the polls, steer straight towards them. The best prophylactic against extremism is not a gamified voting system but some political backbone. Undoubtedly in response to all that, public attitudes to proportional representation have changed enormously, hitting an all-time high of60% support last year. In 2011 it was27%.To return to that meeting in May, there was one more finding from the local elections: once you start to lose, under FPTP, you lose calamitously. So the obvious solution, to a room full of already fully committed constitutional reformer MPs, was for the next prime minister to change the system, right? Psephologists John Curtice and Prof Tim Bale sounded the warning: you can’t change the rules just because you’re losing. The point was so self-evident, from such trusted sources, that all the air seemed to leave the room. But four months on,Labouris ahead in the polls, Reform’s support is tailing off and seems to have further to fall. Far more importantly, this week Burnham showed himself prepared to have a thorny, inconvenient debate that wouldn’t necessarily even serve his political interests, and even if it did, would certainly disperse his power, because he believes in his cause and does so persuasively. So he doesn’t look like he’s losing.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionZoe Williams is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsElectoral reformOpinionAndy BurnhamLabourFirst past the postProportional representationLabour conference 2026Constitutional reformcommentShareReuse this content

title: Things are changing behind the scenes, so you must decide: do you want human civil servants or AI bots? | The civil servant | The Guardian
description: Rapidly expanding AI use within the government is numbing departments to its profound threats. And try arguing with a faceless digital bureaucrat, warns a British civil servant
Author: The civil servant
Headline: Rapidly expanding AI use within the government is numbing departments to its profound threats. And try arguing with a faceless digital bureaucrat, warns a British civil servant
Content: Protesters on Whitehall demand the government pause its AI use, London, 16 September 2026.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenProtesters on Whitehall demand the government pause its AI use, London, 16 September 2026.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesOpinionUK newsThings are changing behind the scenes, so you must decide: do you want human civil servants or AI bots?The civil servantRapidly expanding AI use within the government is numbing departments to its profound threats. And try arguing with a faceless digital bureaucratWed 30 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 12.27 EDTShareAnother day, another apocalyptic warning about the likelihood that rampantly uncontrollable artificial intelligence will solve all of our problems, including the problem of being alive.Hot on the heels of disgruntled Anthropic researchersannouncing the end of civilisationby 2030, we’ve now had the portentously namedHugging Face incident, as well as the Australian government’s grim discovery of a rogue AI’sattackon its Medicare website. Swarms of experts are nowfalling over each otherto warn us that much, much worse is on the way.Thank God, then, that PM Uncle Andy has thrust Britain on to the bleeding edge of the fight against the rise of the self-improving machines. Except he hasn’t. Not really.Yes, Burnham went to the United Nations and riskedenraging the Orange Onewith talk of Britain’s prospects of leading the drawing-up of international rules for AI. Slightly awkwardly, however, one of Burnham’s first acts after sweeping into office wasto abolishthe Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT), the very department that had been leading work on AI safety. It’s a move that the Institute for Government warns will cause “real harm” and which former government AI adviser Matt Clifford has said “wastes time and energy that’s desperately needed for the actual substance”.Isn’t there something gloriously British about all this? Having failed thus far to regulate the technology effectively at home, we are going to world-beatingly coordinate its regulation everywhere else. Whatever it is, it doesn’t quite feel like the response of a state gripped by existential urgency.But perhaps that is because all of us – government ministers included – have already become desensitised to the risk of AImageddon. You can get used to anything. Sure, if one industry insider inadvertently leaks the news that scientists building a new technology believe it might kill everyone, a spot of existential panic is to be expected. But if you ram these tidings down our collective throat every couple of weeks, eventually the prospect of mass extinction acquires the urgency of that bowel cancer screening kit you’ve been meaning to send back to the doctor.Civil servants understand this aspect of human nature only too well. Like the prospect of the galloping climate crisis, we too are simultaneously terrified by AI and utterly bored by it. The extraordinary becomes familiar; the familiar becomes an item on a civil service risk register, after which the real fear is that someone will arrange a Teams call to talk about it.AI could kill all humans in next decade, warn experts: but how seriously should we take them?Read moreThemedian age of civil servants, remember, is 43 years, so many have already witnessed enough technological revolutions to choke a chatbot. Which means that, like me, there’s a large faction of the workforce that remembers the replacement of fax machines by email, and their first introduction toClippy, that damnably moronic AI ancestor office assistant whose principal stab at sentience was appearing uninvited to chirp: “It looks like you’re writing a letter. Would you like help?”So it’s entirely possible that civil servants of my vintage might not yet have been compassionately euthanised by the time government departments such as the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) or HMRC contain more AI agents than carbon-based officials.It may sound melodramatic, but that’s where we are headed. Ministers – convinced that harnessing AI will help keep Reform at bay by offering the tantalising possibility of slashing civil service jobs – have calmly and robotically emoted their concerns about the machines jumping their guardrails, while enthusiastically searching for things to give them. That’s amid civil service union concerns that the government is moving too quickly, citing theFabian Society’s research findingthat only 29% of those surveyed said they had been consulted about AI tools in their workplace.They’re right to be worried. Before DSIT was deleted, its permanent secretary, Emran Mian,reportedly had plansfor AI to eventually replace almost every departing civil servant in his department rather than replacing them with humans. Elsewhere, the DWP has beenbusily experimenting with AIacross the welfare state, directing its machine-learning systems to identify supposedly high-risk universal credit claims. And in response to “serious concerns” about transparency and the handling of personal data, the DWP has been careful to insist that humans retain the final decision and that AI does not determine entitlement.Is this just practical common sense, or the kind of world-beating complacency thatsome have pointed outis an echo of the government’s response to the climate emergency? Either way, the reassurances given by AI minister Kanishka Narayan to theparliamentary business and trade committeesound increasingly hollow after the spate of recent AI rampages.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCivil servants – especially those in public-facing government departments – are acutely aware that saying “a human remains in the loop” is not the same thing as saying “a human remains in charge”.This really, truly, matters, because the commodity on which every government ultimately runs is not data, or productivity, or even money. It is trust, including the trust that – while below theOECD average– the British public still has in the civil service, and which, according to thepublic accounts committee, is being jeopardised by inadequate transparency and weak standards on AI.We already have a national catchphrase for what happens when human discretion – and the accountability that comes with it – disappears. Little Britain’s “computer says no” still resonates – thanks in part to the haunting legacy of the Post Office’sHorizon scandal. Everyone recognises the terror of the human being behind the desk surrendering responsibility to a system whose conclusion can’t be questioned because nobody in the room understands how the hell it got there.And that may be the real warning from Whitehall. Not that killer robots are about to lock the doors and announce the abolition of humanity. But that long before then, governments might quietly surrender thousands of small human judgments to a swarm of digital bureaucrats because doing so is cheaper, quicker and can be passed off in a ministerial speech as “transformation”. It will not feel like that to the public.The author works for the UK civil serviceExplore more on these topicsUK newsOpinionCivil serviceAI (artificial intelligence)Technology policycommentShareReuse this content

title: Prosecco pratfalls and coffee catastrophes: Neets are missing out on formative first-job experiences | Isabel Brooks | The Guardian
description: Work in the hospitality industry made me who I am. Without it, young people are denied not only an income and a step on the career ladder, but important life skills, says freelance writer Isabel Brooks
Author: Isabel Brooks
Headline: Work in the hospitality industry made me who I am. Without it, young people are denied not only an income and a step on the career ladder, but important life skills, says freelance writer Isabel Brooks
Content: A young woman working behind the bar of a pub.Photograph: Keith Morris/AlamyView image in fullscreenA young woman working behind the bar of a pub.Photograph: Keith Morris/AlamyOpinionYouth unemploymentProsecco pratfalls and coffee catastrophes: Neets are missing out on formative first-job experiencesIsabel BrooksWork in the hospitality industry made me who I am. Without it, young people are denied not only an income and a step on the career ladder, but important life skillsWed 30 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 12.22 EDTShareEveryone remembers their first job. More often than not, it’s in the service industry. I started at 14, pouring drinks, serving food and standing with an ice-cream tray. This is where I learned how to handle mistakes,such as dropping an entire tray of prosecco glasses, or spraying hot coffee all over a bridesmaid because I plunged the cafetiere with too much gusto. I learned how to talk to angry strangers, and what it means to have a bad manager. I learned that the customer is always right, except when you’re talking to chefs, who will throw ham at your head if you tell them that. All in all, I did 10 years of restaurant, bar, pub and cafe work, from the age of 14 to 24, and I largely attribute the formation of my character to that decade of work.But this kind of character-building experience is under threat. Job postings for temporary work in hospitality in the UK weredown by 25% year-on-yearbetween 2024 and 2025, with 22,369 fewer unique postings. Hospitality leaders haveblamedrising wage and tax costs for their inability to hire new starters, and young people are bearing the brunt: nearly1 million young peopleare not in education, employment or training (Neet), despite84% of theseseeking work. The Recruitment and Employment Confederation hasexplicitly warnedthat the industry relies heavily on 16- to 24-year-olds, so the impact will be on teenagers seeking their first job. In Manchester, Nell’s Pizza advertised 10 part-time roles for people between the ages of 14 and 18, and receivedabout 2,000 applications.But it’s not just the career prospects and the financial setbacks that are at stake here – young people will miss out on a more fundamental process of maturing. For many British teenagers, myself included, those summer jobs pulling pints are an apprenticeship in adulthood.Working in hospitality as a teenager was how I grew up. If I hadn’t managed to get these jobs, I would never have had to apologise to an irate customer for the large snail that was crawling on the rim of their bowl (“our salad is just really fresh, sorry”), nor peel paralytic pensioners off the floor and deposit them into taxis. These may not immediately seem like transferable skills, but learning how to conduct myself in difficult encounters with people,in person, regardless of how random the specific instance, is a skill I am grateful to have – especially when people only a little younger than me are being served social, life and job opportunities that are increasingly remote and online.I also think I would have less character, whatever “character” is, without this experience. In fact, the word comes from the Greek verb to scratch, cut or engrave, only becoming the term for “a sum of qualities that define a person” in the 1600s. Both still apply; the scratches we get along the way define us, or, in the words of Friedrich Nietzsche and Kelly Clarkson: what doesn’t kill you makes you stronger.Could Britain’s Neet problem partly be one of young people losing access to the kind of first jobs that used to get them on to the career ladder? Of today’s 24-year-old Neets, 45% havenever had a job, which suggests the salient issue is getting a foot in the door. The Neet crisis should be renamed the “teenagers can’t get bar work” crisis, because which 16-year-old or university student is getting a job that isn’t in hospitality?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPlans are under way to finally help Britain’s unemployed young people – will Labour pull it off? | Polly ToynbeeRead moreIt’s a mistake not to prioritise this industry, which, given the encroachment of AI, holds Britain’s future job prospects – more so than manufacturing or high-productivity service sectors. We need to stop seeing these jobs as merely stepping stones to better-paying, more prestigious jobs, but instead as a crucial part of the economy and, importantly, our lives. I am struck by how the rhetoric around Neets relies heavily on the word “cost”: the “cost” to that person later in life “will be up to £300,000” in lost earnings. The “cost” to the economy and the taxpayer is £125bn every year – “more than we spend on education”. What a bleak way to talk and think about people.And what will happen to all these young people who miss out? There is strong evidence that a part-time job while at school leads tohigher self-efficacyandgreater confidence. So, without this training ground to experiment in adulthood, the scratches formed when young people finally join the workforce may be more painful. This forecasted damage has been given a name: “long-term scarring”.As a young graduate, I was very lucky to get a job in a busy London restaurant. It was during the summer of 2020, prime pandemic time, and I had applied for 100 other jobs without hearing back. But employers since have never been interested in this part of my CV. How ironic, because that was the hardest job I’ve ever had, and it set the bar for the type of employee, colleague, friend and overall person I am now.Isabel Brooks is a freelance writerExplore more on these topicsYouth unemploymentOpinionYoung peopleUnemploymentHospitality industrycommentShareReuse this content

title: I heard one thing loud and clear in Andy Burnham’s landmark speech: the left has won the arguments | Owen Jones | The Guardian
description: The PM’s stated trajectory is a rebuke to past Tory and Labour governments. The challenge now is to make his project progressive in word and deed, says Guardian columnist Owen Jones
Author: Owen Jones
Headline: The PM’s stated trajectory is a rebuke to past Tory and Labour governments. The challenge now is to make his project progressive in word and deed, says Guardian columnist Owen Jones
Content: Andy Burnham at the Labour party conference in Liverpool, 29 September 2026.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham at the Labour party conference in Liverpool, 29 September 2026.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesOpinionAndy BurnhamI heard one thing loud and clear in Andy Burnham’s landmark speech: the left has won the argumentsOwen JonesThe PM’s stated trajectory is a rebuke to past Tory and Labour governments. The challenge now is to make his project progressive in word and deedWed 30 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 08.18 EDTShareAs Andy Burnham delivered hisconference speechto the Labour faithful yesterday, it was hard not to recall Jeremy Corbyn’s words after the party’s shattering 2019 election defeat. “I am proud that on austerity, on corporate power, on inequality and the climate emergency,” hewrotefor this publication, “we have won the arguments and rewritten the terms of political debate.” Given Boris Johnson’s 80-seat majority, widespread mockery ensued.But when it comes to rhetoric, who can now deny that the left has won the argument? ALabourprime minister has declared that “Britain has been on the wrong path for a long time”, listing five villains: “Deindustrialisation, deregulation, privatisation, austerity, Brexit.” His speech was infused with class politics, as he condemned a society “run for vested interests, not in the public interest, with power held in too few hands”.When he committed to break with the “flawed thinking of the last 40 years”, he lumped together Conservative and Labour governments. He has already repeatedly labelled the culprit:neoliberalism. This has long been the received wisdom of the left: that as Clement Attlee’s postwar government established a social-democratic consensus that the Tories upheld for a generation, so Margaret Thatcher bequeathed a settlement that New Labour maintained.These beliefs were condemned to the fringes of Labour, even though Tony Blair himselfeventually confessed: “I always thought my job was to build on some of the things she had done rather than reverse them.” Any mention of neoliberalism was a sure way of provoking an eye-roll from a mainstream politician or commentator. We were denied any debate about an economic system based on extraction rather than investment; an economy based on financialisation rather than making things. Corbynism was an insurgency against all of this – until it crashed on the shores of Brexit.Add to this the new foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, telling those who opposed Israel’s genocide and were infuriated by Labour’s position on Gaza: “You were right.” We should add, too, the disastrous past wars backed by Labour: Iraq, Afghanistan and Libya.The left should feel vindicated by the political shift taking place. We were right – at home and abroad. We were mocked, demonised and marginalised for making these arguments. Now most of the left’s worldview is embraced by the Labour top brass. This happened after Keir Starmer’s faction based their entire project on defining themselves against the left. As the Labour activistAli Milani– who was part of Burnham’s team – told me, that strategy nearly brought about the party’s destruction.Burnham only became prime minister because Labour’s leftwing voters rebelled – by defecting en masse to Zack Polanski’s Green party in the Gorton and Denton byelection, then in local elections in England, Scotland and Wales. That is clearly understood by Burnham’s team, or they would not be so confidently doubling down on their new strategy.But winning the argument on a rhetorical level is not the same as substance. Burnham is clearly shifting towards state intervention. That’s taking the form ofGreat British Grid, a new publicly owned network body, and he condemned privatised water as “a symbol of what has gone wrong with Britain”.The shift in this direction actually began under the last Conservative government. Did Liz Truss not commit to asubsidy for energy billsworth tens of billions of pounds? What of Rishi Sunakbeing forcedto bring railways into public ownership? Starmerism expanded the semi-nationalisation of the railway and foundedGreat British Energy. Neoliberalism has exhausted itself and governments are being forced to abandon its tenets, whether they want to or not.But full public ownership of water seems far off, with “public control” acting as a rather flexible label. Burnham has committed to a large-scale building of new council homes and preventing them from being flogged off through right to buy. Yet he hasalready backtrackedon a pledge to spend the government’s entire £39bn affordable homes programme on council and social housing.Crucially, he remains committed to the suffocating fiscal rules that block the investment Britain’s crumbling infrastructure and starved services need, especially given there remains no promise to hike taxes on the well-to-do.While committing to a national care service is extremely welcome, scrapping the triple lock on pensions is not. Britain still spends significantly less on pensions than other major European countries such as Germany, France and Spain, and about two million pensioners languish in poverty.Burnham has a battle plan, with social care the flagship. Risks lie ahead, but Labour now travels in hope | Polly ToynbeeRead moreConsider, too, that the Labour parliamentary benches were stuffed with candidates deemed loyal to the Starmer project. The rightwing factionalists who ran the party may currently be sulking on the fringes, but do not underestimate their capacity to inflict damage.A key difference between Burnhamism and what came before may well be expressed by what Miliband told activists attending a Labour fringe event organised by the soft-left pressure group Mainstream. “Too often in the past, we thought that kicking some of our supporters would do us political credit,” he said, “and we were absolutely wrong.” Offending people “in the progressive community”, he admitted, was sometimes done “deliberately”.Because of pressure from the streets and the ballot box, Labour has shifted its rhetoric. The substance is a bit more complicated. Where Starmerism defined itself against the left, could this new government be pushed in a more progressive direction? That question has not yet been answered. But the left should indeed feel emboldened. The winds are shifting in our direction.Owen Jones is a Guardian columnist. His latest book, The Fall of the West: How They Really Lost It, is published on 1 October. title: It shouldn’t take the eviction of an 87-year-old to get Spain’s housing crisis fixed | María Ramírez | The Guardian
description: Pédro Sanchez is an admirer of Zohran Mamdani. It’s time Spanish politicians emulated the New York mayor’s relentless focus on affordable homes, says María Ramírez, deputy managing editor of Spanish news outlet elDiario.es
Author: María Ramírez
Headline: Pédro Sanchez is an admirer of Zohran Mamdani. It’s time Spanish politicians emulated the New York mayor’s relentless focus on affordable homes, says María Ramírez, deputy managing editor of Spanish news outlet elDiario.es
Content: A protester holds up a picture of Maricarmen Abascal in Barcelona, 28 September 2026.Photograph: Matteo Secci/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenA protester holds up a picture of Maricarmen Abascal in Barcelona, 28 September 2026.Photograph: Matteo Secci/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockOpinionSpainIt shouldn’t take the eviction of an 87-year-old to get Spain’s housing crisis fixedMaría RamírezPédro Sanchez is an admirer of Zohran Mamdani. It’s time Spanish politicians emulated the New York mayor’s relentless focus on affordable homesWed 30 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 10.44 EDTShareMaricarmen Abascal is a determined woman who uses a wheelchair to get around. She has needed her determination over the years she has spent fighting the real estate company that forced her out of her Madrid apartment last week. She had lived in the flat for more than 70 of her 87 years.Police forced their way into her apartment after a judge approvedAbascal’s eviction. By then, protesters had gathered around the building, including the actor Carlos Bardem, Javier’s brother.Teargas was usedagainst them. Abascal was taken to a Madrid hospital, suffering from anxiety and extreme exhaustion, while her supporters chanted: “You are not alone.”Demonstrations of solidarity with her and “all the other Maricarmens” have since erupted across Spain, with protest encampments springing up atPuerta del Solsquare in Madrid as well as inBilbaoand Málaga.Thousands of people are evicted from their homes in Spain every year. In the first quarter of 2026 alone there were, on average,44 eviction ordersa day, mostly for disputes about rent. Behind those figures, cases involvingsingle mothersandelderly tenantsoften come to light. But no eviction has sparked such a public outcry, a national protest movement and a call for urgent political action like the tale of Abascal.Evictions are actually in decline in Spain and are now about a third of what they were in the aftermath of the financial crisis. In 2014, there weremore than 68,000 evictionscompared with about 24,000 in 2025. Spain is one of the fastest-growing economies in the west. Employment and consumer data continue to defy the odds despite global economic uncertainty. But many young people and poorer older people surviving on pensions struggle to pay rent or buy a home, especially in the most prosperous cities.In Abascal’s case, the real estate companyUrbagestiónbought her apartment in 2018, ending her rent-controlled arrangement.Her rentwas initially increased from €500 a month to €2,650, way beyond what her pension could cover.The Spanish supreme court upheld Urbagestión’s claim that the tenancy was invalid as it had been transferred twice, first to Maricarmen’s mother and later to her. But the original 1956 contract was signed by her father under Franco’sdiscriminatory laws against women.As Abascal lay in hospital, the company and her representativesreached an agreement, mediated by Madrid city council, for her to return home. The monthly rent will be similar to the amount she has paid for years,about €500. This is a victory for the activism and solidarity of ordinary citizens who mobilised for a neighbour in need.But her case reflects how property companies, banks and hedge funds profit from vulnerable tenants and their once-affordable homes. It is also a reminder of the failure of politicians to protect the right to “decent and adequate” housing that has been enshrined in the Spanish constitution since 1978.View image in fullscreenMaricarmen Abascal, 87, is transported on a stretcher to an ambulance after being evicted from her apartment in Spain, 23 September 2026.Photograph: Susana Vera/ReutersThe centre-left governing coalition has failed to change the law to protect the most vulnerable tenants from eviction, and to push through comprehensive housing reforms.On Tuesday, Pedro Sánchez’s minority coalition finallyintroduced a new housing billthat would ban evictions of vulnerable tenants until 2030, limit rent hikes for two years and ban investment funds purchasing houses for two years. Now the bill needs to be approved by parliament within a month.But Sánchez’s reliance on the support of a range of parties since 2023 has limited his room for manoeuvre.The socialist PM’s leftwing coalition partner, Sumar, had pushed for reforms to prevent cases such as Abascal’s. But Sánchez had shelved the proposals until now, fearing rejection in parliament. The latest uproar is forcing his hand, even if it meansincluding tax breakssought by Junts, a rightwing nationalist Catalan party.Madrid’s regional and municipal governments, in the hands of the conservatives, were slow to offer alternatives to Abascal until she was evicted, using the case instead to attack the national government. For the past three years, the Madrid regional government, led by the conservative Isabel Díaz Ayuso,has refusedeven to apply the existing national law to limit rent increases.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSpain’s highly decentralised system, with power divided at a local, regional and national level, is once again the perfect cover for politicians to do the minimum and blame each other while individuals suffer.Spaniardsrepeatedly identify housingas the country’s biggest problem, but the issue has not earned the intense political attention it deserves.A few days ago, Sánchez visited Zohran Mamdani, who is becoming a point of reference for the left in Spain and acrossEurope. Instead of trying to imitate the mayor of New York’s videos or his charm, fellow progressives could emulate his relentless focus on housing.Mamdani supports solutions across the ideological spectrum, from pushing for the construction of new apartment buildings to taxing real estate investment funds. He is supporting public housing and protections for tenants in rent-controlled apartments, but also working with private developers, even exchanging pleasantries with Donald Trump to advance aproposal for a large urban developmentproject over Sunnyside Yard in Queens, New York.There are no magic bullets on housing. Fixing it will require hard work, smart planning, laser focus and an open mind. Winning progressive politicians have only now started treating this problem with the urgency it deserves.Will Abascal’s eviction prompt a new era in housing policy in Spain? If it happens, change will have come at a high price. It should not take the forcible eviction of an 87-year-old woman who just wants to remain in her home for the corrosive effects of unaffordable housing to be taken seriously.María Ramírez is a journalist and deputy managing editor of elDiario.es, a news outlet in SpainExplore more on these topicsSpainOpinionHousingRenting propertyPedro SánchezEuropeProtestOlder peoplecommentShareReuse this content

title: Forget the inflation blame game – politicians should let the RBA get on with its job | Saul Eslake | The Guardian
description: The war in the Middle East and ‘excessive’ levels of government spending have contributed to the rebound in inflation and interest rates in Australia
Author: Saul Eslake
Headline: The war in the Middle East and ‘excessive’ levels of government spending have contributed to the rebound in inflation and interest rates in Australia
Content: ‘The Reserve Bank itself has to accept some of the blame for the rebound in inflation, and hence in interest rates,’ Saul Eslake writes after the cash rate in Australia was hiked to 4.6%.Photograph: Nikki Short/AAPView image in fullscreen‘The Reserve Bank itself has to accept some of the blame for the rebound in inflation, and hence in interest rates,’ Saul Eslake writes after the cash rate in Australia was hiked to 4.6%.Photograph: Nikki Short/AAPOpinionReserve Bank of AustraliaForget the inflation blame game – politicians should let the RBA get on with its jobSaul EslakeThe war in the Middle East and ‘excessive’ levels of government spending have contributed to the rebound in inflation and interest rates in AustraliaFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastTue 29 Sep 2026 20.45 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 03.31 EDTShareAs universally expected by economists and financial markets, the Reserve Bank of Australia’s monetary policy board on Tuesday lifted its cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.6%, the highest level since October 2011 (at the peak of the mining investment boom).The treasurer,Jim Chalmers, has attributed this week’s decision – and the inflation concerns underpinning it – to the war in the Middle East. Others, including the shadow treasurer,Tim Wilson, andsome economists, blame it on “excessive” levels of, and growth in, government spending.In truth both of these factors, and others besides, have contributed to the rebound in inflation and interest rates that Australia has experienced this year.Danger zone: why war in the Middle East has landed the RBA’s inflation fight in tricky territoryRead moreOil prices have rebounded from just over US$70 a barrel in late June, when it briefly appeared that the Middle East conflict might be over, to more than US$100 a barrel in recent weeks, now that there seems little prospect of an imminent end to that conflict.Less well recognised, but no less important, the “crack spreads” between crude oil prices and prices of refined petroleum products such as gasoline and diesel, have remained at elevated levels since the conflict began, and seem unlikely to come down given the damage that has been done to refining capacity in the Middle East and in Russia.Additionally, the US (the world’s biggest oil producer) and China (the world’s biggest oil importer) appear to have run down their reserves as far as they deem prudent, and so are now exporting less and importing more oil, respectively, than they had been doing in the early months of the conflict.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailThese influences have been evident in other “advanced” economies which have lifted their interest rates in recent weeks in response to higher inflation – including the US, Japan, South Korea, the Euro area and New Zealand.But the rebound in Australian inflation began well before Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu started the conflict in the Middle East.The RBA’s preferred measure of “underlying” inflation bottomed out at 2.8% over the year to June 2025, and had already risen to 3.3% by February this year, before the outbreak of the conflict.
