Since then, this measure of underlying inflation has risen to 3.6% over the year to July.So most of the increase in inflation which prompted the Reserve Bank to raise interest rates three times between February and May this year cannot be attributed to the conflict in the Middle East.double quotation markThe rebound in Australian inflation began well before Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu started the conflict in the Middle EastRather, it reflects the persistent imbalance between “aggregate demand” – the sum total of spending on goods and services by Australian households, businesses and governments – and “aggregate supply” – the sum total of what is produced by businesses and governments, less what is exported to foreign countries, plus what is imported from abroad.The growth of aggregate supply has been held down by ourabysmal productivity performanceduring this decade, which effectively sets a “speed limit” on how fast our economy can grow, once we’ve attained “full employment” (which we have done since 2022), without generating inflationary pressure.Growth in aggregate demand has been driven by both public and private spending.Growth in public spending as measured in the GDP statistics hasslowed – from more than 4% a year in real terms in 2023-24 and 2024-25 to 2% in 2025-26. But the national accounts measures of public spending only include directspending by governments and government-owned enterprises on goods and services. They don’t include other forms of government spending – in particular, cash payments to households and cost-of-living relief measures which the federal government and, of no less importance, state and territory governments have handed out in recent years.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThus thefinal budget outcomedocument released on Monday showed that total expenses by the federal government rose by 5.1% in real terms in 2025-26, only marginally less than the 5.6% figure for 2024-25, and that both of those figures were higher than in all but five of the past 25 years.And although most of the states and territories are yet to publish their equivalent documents, based on the estimates presented in their 2026-27 budgets it is likely that spending by state and territory governments and their instrumentalities rose by about 6% in real terms in 2025-26 – the largest increase since 2019-20.Most of the cost-of-living relief given by the federal and state and territory governments, whether by way of cash handouts or tax cuts (such as the temporary halving of fuel excise), has been untargeted – that is, it has been given to households which might notneed it as well as those which undoubtedly do. And most households appear to have spent it. That shows up in the national accounts as private sector spending – but it has really been facilitated by government policy.The RBA has hiked interest rates. Use our loan calculator to check how it affects youRead moreIn circumstances where inflation is running persistently above the Reserve Bank’s target because aggregate demand is running persistently in excess of aggregate supply, what governments give by way of cost-of-living relief or tax cuts, the Reserve Bank takes away in the form of higher interest rates. Except that the burden of higher interest rates falls primarily on a smaller group of households – those with big mortgages – than those who received the cost-of-living relief and tax cuts.The Reserve Bank itself has to accept some of the blame for the rebound in inflation, and hence in interest rates. That’s because – with the benefit of hindsight – it cut interest rates prematurely last year. Its belief that inflation hadsustainablyreturned to the 2% to 3% target band turned out to be wrong.The RBA was of course under considerable pressure from the government to cut rates – recall, for example, Chalmers’ unjustified assertion in August 2024 that the Reserve Bank had“smashed the economy”(if it had, inflation wouldn’t have rebounded in the way that it subsequently did). But – again, with the benefit of hindsight – the RBA should have resisted that pressure.In many ways this “blame game” is beside the point. As the RBA governor,Michele Bullock, reiteratedthis week, “high inflation hurts all Australians, especially the most vulnerable” and “it’s critical that we stop high inflation from becoming embedded in price-setting decisions across the economy or the problem will only get worse”.Politicians should avoid doing, or advocating, things that will “make the problem worse”, and let the Reserve Bank get on with its job.Saul Eslake is a vice-chancellor’s fellow at the University of Tasmania and an independent consulting economistExplore more on these topicsReserve Bank of AustraliaOpinionInterest ratesAustralian economyCost-of-living crisiscommentShareReuse this content

title: The political battle over Australian immigration is really a story of what kind of nation we want to be | Peter Lewis | The Guardian
description: One Nation may have changed the outlines of the debate, but a majority of Australians still support immigration
Author: Peter Lewis
Headline: One Nation may have changed the outlines of the debate, but a majority of Australians still support immigration
Content: One method of investing in a ‘working-class liberalism’, as advocated by the economist Daron Acemoglu, is by helping immigrants become citizens instead of being treated as short-term guest workers.Photograph: Tracey Nearmy/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenOne method of investing in a ‘working-class liberalism’, as advocated by the economist Daron Acemoglu, is by helping immigrants become citizens instead of being treated as short-term guest workers.Photograph: Tracey Nearmy/Getty ImagesOpinionEssential pollThe political battle over Australian immigration is really a story of what kind of nation we want to bePeter LewisOne Nation may have changed the outlines of the debate, but a majority of Australians still support immigrationFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ournew political email,free appordaily news podcastTue 29 Sep 2026 20.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 02.12 EDTShareAnyone who thinks the current immigration debate is simply about the number of foreigners being granted legal passage to Australia each year is only seeing half the picture.Beyond the crude numerical projections (that a growing number of Australians believe have way too many zeros) is a more basic contest that is both economic and cultural and is being played out around the globe.The (spin) doctor is in: the Albanese government is in good health, but that could all vanish in an instant | Peter LewisRead moreThis is whatDaron Acemoglu, a 2024 Nobel prize-winning economist,casts as liberal democracy’s post-industrial crisis – a project that he argues has ceased to deliver on its core promise of sharing economic prosperity by vesting power in the people.He places immigration at the fulcrum of this reckoning because it brings to the surface a disparate set of cultural questions of shared values, identity and belonging which, if not resolved, drive people into populist waves of illiberalism.Through the Guardian Essential report, we have benchmarks on Australians’ attitude to immigration charted over more than a decade now. They show that even as the immigration debate has raged over recent months, general support for immigration remains.Chart graphing responses to the question: Do you think immigration to Australia is generally positive or generally negative for the country?What has changed is the contours of this political debate with the rise ofOne Nation. Where those opposing immigration were once a minority inside two major parties that broadly supported an expansive program, now they have a political home base.One Nation’s blunt call to reduce immigration numbers resonates with voters concerned about their jobs, their access to housing, the safety of their community and the availability of services. Immigration becomes a simple explanation for a series of complex problems.But it is more than that: the major parties have both pushed the expansion of short-term visas to paper over failures in workforce planning and skills development, and then been too quick to dismiss those who raise questions as playing the politics of division – or worse, race.To Acemoglu, this is the toxic sludge that has poisoned liberal democracy: the tendency of economic elites to impose first their business models, then of the cultural elites to dismiss their concerns.In times when an economy is expanding and benefits are shared this might be a sustainable ruse; but when prices are rising, the property market is distorted and technology is upending entire industries, political blowback is hardly surprising.A second question suggests Australia is at an inflection point where a majority now say they want to reduce immigration, with even 30% of those who say they support immigration in principle wanting to slow things down.Chart of responses to the question: To what extent would you like to see Australia’s yearly immigration intake increase, decrease or stay about the same?The most significant part of immigration minister Tony Burke’s intervention a fortnight ago was his explicit concession that reducing immigration was, indeed, now government policy.Burke named the specific areas where the scheme operates and showed how these would be administered: constraints around student visas, ballots for working holidays, less flexibility on family reunion. This week’s poll shows that there is strong support for all these measures.Stuck between Labor’s technocratic management and One Nation’s nihilist populism, the Coalition is attempting to contain the issue as some sort of algorithmic trade-off between housing and immigration. Its problem is that a separate question shows that the vast majority of those who think immigration is too high say that an increase in housing would do nothing to change their opinion.Now that the parties have staked out their positions, the real battle will commence, not one of numbers, but a story of nation. A final question shows where the respective camps are starting from.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionResponses to a question asking the respondent to select the option that best matches their viewpoint on immigration. The choices are: Immigration is good for Australia and we should keep welcoming people (13%), Immigration overall benefits Australia, but the numbers should be gradually brought down (23%), Immigration is far too high. More people should be leaving Australia than arriving (19%), None of these reflects my view (5%) and Unsure (5%)We can see each party has a sweet spot: Labor voters are a somewhat qualified pro-immigration, Coalition voters are between a slowdown and a crackdown, One Nation firmly on the depopulation train and Greens more likely to embrace the positives of immigration.So how to break what seems like a destructive and divisive zero-sum culture war? By recognising the majority lie in a more moderate middle, where they seek control over the pace and scale – not the existence – of immigration.Acemoglu advocates what he calls a “working-class liberalism” that would recognise the inherent value in vesting authority in community, the constant testing of ideas and the bias towards freedom of thought and expression.First, the government would do more to vest the economic benefits of immigration in local communities. It’s been revealing how rural communities with connections to local families have been such staunch defenders of theirneighbours and workmates.Second, he argues liberal society owes an obligation to new arrivals to afford them not just the rights of the society but the responsibilities. Ensuring those welcomed into communities reflect cultural norms should not be considered nativist or extreme, asLabor frontbencher Julian Hillpointed out in a speech earlier this year: respect for women and tolerance of free thought should be the price of admission.Third, pathways to citizenship should be central to immigration. Simply seeing individuals as short-term guest workers in a financial transaction does nothing to deepen community ties. The proportion of non-citizens has almost doubled this century, from 11% in 2001 to18% in 2022,with another increase expected in this year’s census. Can we really be one nation when one in five are not Australian citizens?Finally, Acemoglu argues that immigration must be negotiated within a broader liberal democratic framework: good jobs, decent services, fair distribution of national wealth, mutual respect that starts to look like some sort of control on those who accumulated the power.As the world seeks refuge in the nation-state, the challenge is not to convince people who want to slow down immigration that they are wrong, but to give them a real say in the nation we are building.Peter Lewis is non-executive chair of Essential, a progressive strategic communications and research company that undertook qualitative research for Labor in the last federal election. He is the host of the weekly podcastBurning Platforms. His columns are accreditedProudly HumanExplore more on these topicsEssential pollOpinionAustralian immigration and asylumAustralian politicsOne NationLiberal partyLabor partyAustralian GreenscommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on Lula v the Bolsonaros: the decision of Brazilian voters will affect us all | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Sunday’s general election is too close to call, with the incumbent president facing the son of the man who attempted a coup against him
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Sunday’s general election is too close to call, with the incumbent president facing the son of the man who attempted a coup against him
Content: Flávio Bolsonaro campaigning in São Paulo on 28 Sepptember 2026.Photograph: Allison Sales/APView image in fullscreenFlávio Bolsonaro campaigning in São Paulo on 28 Sepptember 2026.Photograph: Allison Sales/APOpinionBrazilThe Guardian view on Lula v the Bolsonaros: the decision of Brazilian voters will affect us allEditorialSunday’s general election is too close to call, with the incumbent president facing the son of the man who attempted a coup against himWed 30 Sep 2026 13.37 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 18.41 EDTShareSunday’s election in Brazil could hardly be a clearer-cut choice – nor a closer call. President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, known as Lula, isneck and neckin the polls with Flávio Bolsonaro, the son and champion of the jailed far-right former president Jair. Mr Bolsonaro senior is serving a 27-year sentence forplotting a coupto “annihilate” democracy after losing the last election.Brazil is Latin America’s largest democracy, but military dictatorship is in its recent past. Mr Bolsonaro wants to free his father and those who rioted in his support in 2023. The senator has campaigned as a less crass and temperamental version of his father, but he is no less extreme. For many on both sides, this is a vote against a man they detest more than an endorsement of their own candidate. Most votersdisapprove of bothmen.Initially, pundits predicted victory for the leftwing incumbent. Some feel that at 80 he is too old to begin a fourth term, though he remains energetic. His social programmes are extensive, but frustration at Brazil’s enduring failure to match its economic record to its potential may hobble him, especially with growth slowing. Violent crime remains a top issue.View image in fullscreenPresident Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.Photograph: Adriano Machado/ReutersThen came the Banco Master financial scandal, which has snowballed into a corruption case spanning Brazilian politics and the judiciary. First, Flávio Bolsonarowas caught on tapeasking the failed bank’s playboy owner, Daniel Vorcaro, for almost $27m to make a film about his father. He denies wrongdoing.Then compromising messages between Mr Vorcaro and the supreme court judge who led the prosecution of the ex-presidentwere revealed. The allegations fed the perception that politicians are all dirty, and bolstered the unfounded far-right claim that Mr Bolsonaro Sr was stitched up. His son has also papered over a damaging public rift with his stepmother Michelle – an influential figure, key to the evangelical support he needs.Mr Bolsonaro Jr has said he will abide by the election’s result. But the Bolsonaros have spent years working toundermine trustin internationally respected Brazil’s electronic voting system. A narrow first-round victory for Lula would probably be contested. With other candidates on the right, Mr Bolsonaro Jr would also have an advantage in a second-round vote. He has talked up theprospect of privatisationand cuts to public spending and taxes if he wins. He has pledged to pack the supreme court with anti‑abortion conservative judges, who would also be critical to future election disputes. He has vowed to introduce the kind of aggressive anti-crime drive that has trampled human rights elsewhere.President Donald Trump and Marco Rubio, his secretary of state, will be further emboldened in their “Donroe doctrine” of aggressive intervention in the western hemisphere if Mr Bolsonaro Jr is victorious.US meddlingin this election has often backfired – high tariffs on Brazil have allowed Lula to run as the patriot defending the country against foreign interference. But it is no less disturbing.Mr Trump’s more ruthless and reckless second term also offers an alarming vision of how another Bolsonaro presidency might look. The first showed historic levels of deforestation in the Amazon as well as a surge in illegal resource extraction and the invasion of Indigenous people’s lands. Those fell sharply once Lulareturned to power. A Bolsonaro presidency would be bad for women, the poor and minorities. Democracy would probably be its first, local victim. But the climate would surely be another – with consequences for us all.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsBrazilOpinionLuiz Inácio Lula da SilvaJair BolsonaroAmericaseditorialsShareReuse this content

title: Esther Rantzen, TV presenter and Childline founder, dies aged 86 | Esther Rantzen | The Guardian
description: Rantzen announced lung cancer diagnosis in 2023 and became a vocal assisted-dying campaigner
Author: Alexi Duggins
Headline: Rantzen announced lung cancer diagnosis in 2023 and became a vocal assisted-dying campaigner
Content: Esther Rantzen at home in Wiltshire in 2021.Photograph: Millie Pilkington/The GuardianView image in fullscreenEsther Rantzen at home in Wiltshire in 2021.Photograph: Millie Pilkington/The GuardianEsther RantzenEsther Rantzen, TV presenter and Childline founder, dies aged 86Rantzen announced lung cancer diagnosis in 2023 and became a vocal assisted-dying campaignerFrom Childline to changing TV for ever: Esther Rantzen’s revolutionary lifeEsther Rantzen: from That’s Life! to Childline – in picturesAlexi DugginsandPriya BharadiaWed 30 Sep 2026 14.55 EDTFirst published on Wed 30 Sep 2026 14.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEsther Rantzen, the Bafta-winning TV presenter and founder of Childline, has died aged 86.In a statement, her family paid tribute to “the most wonderful mother” and “cherished grandmother”, whose “legacy of compassion and understanding will live on in her charities Childline and the Silverline, and through those of us who were lucky enough to love and be loved by her”.From Childline to changing TV for ever: Esther Rantzen’s revolutionary lifeRead more“We are grateful she is finally at rest with her beloved husband, Desmond Wilcox, but we will miss her immeasurably. She was our sunshine. We will always remember her endless capacity for joy, her ability to comfort every heartache, her beautiful way with words and her expert guidance in all things,” said her three children.Rantzen announced a diagnosis of stage four lung cancer in 2023, and becamea vocal campaigner to change the law around assisted dying. In September 2026, she announced she had to abandon plans to end her life in Swiss clinic Dignitas,due to being too physically frail.“Unfortunately, when I was strong enough to make the flight and go to Dignitas, my life was not unbearably painful; indeed, I was able to relax in my beloved cottage in the New Forest,” she said in a statement. “And by the time life did become unbearable, I was too physically fragile to make the journey and go through the Dignitas process.”“So even though I had spent the money and made the plans, I was not ready to end my life back then, and did not realise that would be my last chance.”The prime minister, Andy Burnham, said: “Very sad to hear that Dame Esther Rantzen has died. Through her decades of campaigning, including founding Childline and The Silver Line, she changed countless lives and gave a voice to people who often went unheard.“And I will always admire the characteristic courage and openness with which she spoke about her illness, making us all think about the difficult questions we face at the end of life. My thoughts are with her family and all who loved her.”Kim Leadbeater, the Labour MP who introduced a bill to legalise assisted dying, said: “Esther was a strong, warm and compassionate woman and a fighter to the end.“Her positivity and determination never to give in gave me strength, but more importantly helped all those others like her who were confronting a terminal illness to keep going in the knowledge that they were not alone.”Rantzen was born in Berkhamsted, Hertfordshire, in 1940 and began her career in 1963 as a BBC radio studio manager. Having moved into television as a researcher, she became a presenter in 1968, as part of the consumer affairs show Braden’s Week, before being appointed as the main host of its replacement programme, That’s Life!, in 1973.View image in fullscreenRantzen with the cast of That’s Life in 1987.Photograph: BBCPart magazine, part consumer show, with hard-hitting investigations and jokes, That’s Life! drew more than 20 million viewers at its peak – and ran for 21 years with Rantzen as anchor. After she successfully pitched an episode about child abuse to the then BBC controller Michael Grade, a set of phone lines was opened for 48 hours, which enabled children to call in and speak to social workers. The volume of responses led her to turn the service into a permanent fixture, launching the children’s charity Childline in 1986.Esther Rantzen: from That’s Life! to Childline – in picturesRead moreIn 1988, Rantzen created Hearts of Gold, a series focusing on people responsible for outstanding acts of kindness, and hosted her own BBC Two chatshow, Esther, from 1994, when That’s Life! came to an end, until 2002. Further TV projects included the consumer affairs show Old Dogs New Tricks, as well as competing in Strictly Come Dancing’s second series and the 2008 edition of the ITV reality show I’m a Celebrity … Get Me Out of Here! She received an OBE for services to broadcasting, Bafta’s Richard Dimbleby award for factual programming anda lifetime achievement prize at the Women in Film and Television awards.View image in fullscreenEsther Rantzen on the campaign trail in 2010 as a candidate for Luton South.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianHer wide-ranging charity work saw her act as a patron or vice-president of numerous organisations. In 2010, she launched the Silver Line – a free confidential helpline for older people, which led to her being made a dame for services to children and older people.In 2010, she stood as an independent candidate for Luton South in that year’s general election,coming fourth after winning 4.4% of the vote. She wrote numerous books, including a murder-mystery novel. In later years, she was a regular contributor to the One Show andhosted a podcast with her former That’s Life! colleague Adrian Mills.On Instagram, the television presenter Anna Williamson described Rantzen as “somebody truly iconic, who really cared, and who has left behind one hell of a legacy”.Fellow presenter Lorraine Kelly also paid tribute to Rantzen on social media for being a “pioneer and a force of nature – [who] helped so many people – funny, forthright and fabulous”.One of Rantzen’s former co-hosts of That’s Life!, Howard Leader, said: “Over the time that I was with her, through her fantastic generosity, she taught me how to be a journalist.“I think Esther’s skill was that she really understood how to use the platform she had to create an effect for, we hope ... the improvement of people in our country.”Her husband, Desmond Wilcox, whom she married in 1977, died in 2000. Rantzen is survived by their three children, Miriam, Rebecca and Joshua – as well as five grandchildren.Explore more on these topicsEsther RantzenTelevisionAssisted dyingnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘The Savage Skulls were the most dangerous gang in the Bronx’: Jean-Pierre Laffont’s best photograph | Art and design | The Guardian
description: ‘I’d read stories about gangs killing drug-pushers who targeted young people. Police would find their bodies at the bottom of five-storey buildings. I didn’t want to go looking for them alone’
Author: Chris Broughton
Headline: ‘I’d read stories about gangs killing drug-pushers who targeted young people. Police would find their bodies at the bottom of five-storey buildings. I didn’t want to go looking for them alone’
Content: ‘If you want just to look at our life, you’re welcome’ … New York street gang Savage Skulls by Jean-Pierre Laffont, 1972.Photograph: Jean-Pierre LaffontView image in fullscreen‘If you want just to look at our life, you’re welcome’ … New York street gang Savage Skulls by Jean-Pierre Laffont, 1972.Photograph: Jean-Pierre LaffontMy best shotArt and design‘The Savage Skulls were the most dangerous gang in the Bronx’: Jean-Pierre Laffont’s best photograph‘I’d read stories about gangs killing drug-pushers who targeted young people. Police would find their bodies at the bottom of five-storey buildings. I didn’t want to go looking for them alone’Interview byChris BroughtonWed 30 Sep 2026 10.41 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 16.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe late 1960s and most of the 1970s were a difficult time forNew York. I’d moved there from France in 1965 with a reporter friend and a plan to start a little agency, but soon found myself working alone. It could be a dangerous city, especially at night, but I enjoyed taking pictures of everyday life around me. In 1969, I became the first foreign correspondent for the Paris-based Gamma Agency, but always insisted on working on personal projects rather than assignments.Reading the New York Times in 1972, I would see stories about gangs in the Bronx that were killing drug-pushers who targeted young people in the area. The police would find their bodies on the kerb at the bottom of five-storey buildings they’d been thrown off. The gangs included the Savage Nomads and the Dirty Dozen, but the one I was most interested in was the most dangerous: the Savage Skulls.I didn’t want to go looking for them alone, so I drove with a French cameraman friend to Fox Street in the Hunts Point neighbourhood. As soon as we spotted members of the gang on the sidewalk, we stopped and wound down the window and they immediately came over wanting to know who we were. When they realised we were French and didn’t want to interview them, they said: “If you want just to look at our life, you’re welcome.” We spent that afternoon with them, then I came back alone the following day.double quotation markI didn’t meet their chief because he was in hospital having taken a bullet to the abdomenThe gang showed me their territory: the basement where they had their club, played music and kept a lot of their weapons, and the sidewalks where Savage Skulls tags appeared on walls, doors and trash cans. They also spent a lot of time on a nearby basketball court. They didn’t actually play basketball – they just fought all the time, play-fighting, like little cats.While on the court with them, I said: “OK, I’ll take a picture of you.” They immediately went over to the fence and got into the formation you see in the picture. I didn’t ask them to do that: it was completely spontaneous. They were keen to show off the sleeveless denim vests they wore, with a skull and crossbones painted on the back. You can see here how young they were. I think the youngest member I photographed was 13 and none of them were much older than 20. The photograph reminds me of a scene from West Side Story, but I don’t think members of the Savage Skulls ever left the Bronx.When I told the police about my project, they warned me they couldn’t offer any protection, but while I was with the gang one time they stopped a patrol car and I took a picture of them having a friendly chat with the officers inside. The members were mostly Puerto Rican and spoke Spanish to one another, so we communicated in broken English. I hardly spoke English then, so I think they considered me a fellow outsider. We had an easy connection and they seemed very relaxed, even exchanging guns in front of me. I didn’t meet their chief during the few days I spent with them because he was in hospital at the time, having taken a bullet to the abdomen.Last year, a woman called to ask if I remembered a photograph I’d taken of some of the gang members walking down the street, side by side, and if I recalled one of the people in it being a woman. When I told her I remembered the picture and the woman very well, she said: “That was my mother, and she died yesterday.” She asked for a copy, saying this was the only picture of her mother that she knew.As it happened, her mother appeared in a few more of my pictures from the time, including this one, where you can see her in front of the fence. I sent some big prints for the funeral. It was a very moving moment for me, because it made me realise that life goes on. Those kids I photographed in 1972 weren’t kids any more.Jean-Pierre Laffont: Rebels with a Causeis published by Damiani.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sam MatamorosJean-Pierre Laffont’s CVBorn:French Algeria, 1935.High point:Being made a Knight of the Order of the Legion of Honour for 60 years at the service of photojournalism in 2023.Top tip:My way of working is over, and the profession of photojournalist is being rewritten; it is up to young photojournalists to rewrite it. Yet there are essential things that define the profession and I have a few pieces of advice: go to museums, look at the work of the great photographers who inspire you, research the stories you want to cover, be observant, humble and curious – and don’t forget that you are doing the most beautiful job in the world. This profession is more important than ever and still makes people dream.Explore more on these topicsArt and designMy best shotGangsPhotographyYoung peopleSocial historyNew YorkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How Zach Cregger’s Resident Evil stands out from all other game adaptations | Games | The Guardian
description: There’s no Leon, Claire or Ada Wong in Cregger’s adaptation. Instead, it re-creates something more fundamental – the strange, terrifying experience of actually playing the game
Author: Keith Stuart
Headline: There’s no Leon, Claire or Ada Wong in Cregger’s adaptation. Instead, it re-creates something more fundamental – the strange, terrifying experience of actually playing the game
Content: Director Zach Cregger (right) with actor Austin Abrams on the set the new Resident Evil film.Photograph: Dušan Martinček/CTMGView image in fullscreenDirector Zach Cregger (right) with actor Austin Abrams on the set the new Resident Evil film.Photograph: Dušan Martinček/CTMGPushing Buttons newsletterGamesHow Zach Cregger’s Resident Evil stands out from all other game adaptationsThere’s no Leon, Claire or Ada Wong in Cregger’s adaptation. Instead, it re-creates something more fundamental – the strange, terrifying experience of actually playing the gameDon’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereKeith StuartWed 30 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 10.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’ve been surprised by the number ofResident Evilfans complaining on social media about Zach Cregger’s cinematic adaptation of the survival horror series. “It’s not arealResident Evil movie,” they’ve claimed. Were we watching the same film? Certainly, it doesn’t feature any of the familiar heroes – there’s no Leon, no Claire, no Ada Wong – and there’s a distinct lack of recognisable antagonists and well-known locations. Despite all of this, Cregger’s interpretation is one of the most accurate and interesting video game films ever made.On the surface, it’s about a zombifying virus that gets accidentally released in Raccoon City by the Umbrella Corporation. These are, of course, the foundations of the Resi mythos. More interestingly, Cregger seeks to replicate and explore the structural and narrative conventions of the series. In the film, the player character, hapless courier Bryan Hodukavich, is thrust into a viral outbreak, with no weapons and no idea what’s going on. He is then submerged into an uncanny shadow world of escalating peril and body horror. The film takes us through a series of locations dragged straight from the games – an abandoned farmhouse, a road tunnel crammed with abandoned cars, a hospital andthe obligatory sewer level. As he progresses, Bryan finds increasingly powerful weapons, from a handgun to an assault rifle – but he is always short on ammo. And there are typewriters in at least two scenes!Bryan’s understanding of the world is shaped, as in any Resident Evil game, through found footage (voice recordings, emails etc) and via short, enigmatic interchanges with non-player characters. There’s a sequence in the road tunnel where a recently infected young girl says to Bryan: “My mom bit me, I don’t know where she went.” This is a classic Resident Evil exchange: in one terse sentence she gives us narrative informationandan implied threat – the mother could be lurking anywhere nearby, waiting to pounce …Aware perhaps of online discourse, Creggerreleased a videoexplaining his vision for the movie, and how he has sought to reflect not just the fictitious universe of the games, but also the experience of playing them – that sense of quickly moving through a world of endlessly evolving horror. It’s also been interesting to see theories emerge about Bryan’s role as a sort of NPC precursor to a true lead character, leaving the hints, tips and ammo behind for someone capable to pick up.View image in fullscreenOmnipresent merchant … Resident Evil.Photograph: CapcomI always thought thatthe subsidiary non-playable characters in the early Resident Evil titles had the most interesting stories: affable old Barry Burton from the first game, cowardly helicopter pilot Brad Vickers fromResi 3,Resident Evil 4’s omnipresent merchant. “I’m interested in vulnerable characters, in normal human beings,” series creator Shinji Mikamionce told me. “The horror experience is most scary when the player really isn’t sure whether their character is going to live or die – death and survival need to be on a constant see-saw. If there’s a situation where you’re not 100% sure that you can avoid or defeat the enemies, if you feel maybe there’s a chance you’ll make it – that’s where horror lies.” Bryan Hodukavich lives in that space for the whole film.Cregger’s Resident Evil should perhaps be put alongside Kane Parsons’sBackroomsand Genki Kawamura’sExit 8as a movie that is as much an exploration of video game mechanics as it is any sort of translation. These movies make us feel like players, trapped in an unfamiliar nightmare world with its own rules, characters and temporal conventions, which we have to gradually unpeel. Cinema has always deconstructed other media, whether that’s the theatre (Les Enfants du Paradis, The Producers) or superhero comics (Unbreakable, Logan), and it’s fascinating to see video games having the same sort of scrutiny. This is, after all, the most self-reflexive medium – the audience is spectator and participant, the world is naturalistic yet necessarily artificial, with its yellow-painted walls (see:Keza’s newsletter just last week), and its indestructible barriers (to stop a player wandering out of the rendered environment).So yes, this is definitely a Resident Evil movie – it’s just that the camera pans away from Claire as she blasts another zombie, or Leon as he makes a daft wisecrack. Instead, it takes us just around the corner, to where the huddling masses of Raccoon City await their destiny, with maybe three bullets, two lines of dialogue and a voice recorder.What to playView image in fullscreenRagdoll-physics gore-fest … Happy Wheels is now available on Steam.Photograph: Jim Bonacci/Fancy ForceFirst appearing as a browser-based game back in 2010, the ragdoll-physics gore-festHappy Wheelsis now on Steam – and it’s just as ridiculous as ever. Your aim is to make it across an obstacle-laden landscape in whatever vehicle you’re given without falling into a chasm or being chainsawed in half, or stabbed or eaten. There are dozens of levels but you can also design your own and share them with the community. I’m not surprised the Steam version has been wishlisted by 750,000 players. This kind of hilarious, awkward, experimental game thrived in the Flash era of the noughties and it’s lovely to see a classic example return in all its blood-drenched, clipart-esque glory.Available on:PCEstimated playtime:Several laughable hoursWhat to readView image in fullscreenMicrosoft and Sony have filed for ad and monetisation patents, respectively.Photograph: Lucy Nicholson/ReutersIt’s been weird to watch Microsoft and Sony seemingly trying to find yet more ways to antagonise gamers after concerns over mass redundancies and the death of physical media. Two weeks ago, the gaming site Respawn FirstdiscoveredaMicrosoft patentto serve ads to Xbox players during down times in games, perhaps while loading a level or after a boss battle. Not to be outdone, Sony hasfiled a US patentfor technology allowing players to tap their phone or credit card on a PlayStation controller to pay for digital goods. Call me cynical, but perhaps more convenient advertising and monetisation models are not the best way to win back hearts and minds.Naughty Dog studio head Neil Druckmannhas revealedthat there are twoLast of Usprojects on the go, expanding on the canon of the first two games. Both are in the very early stages of development, and it’s not even known if they are games – they could include a new TV series, movie or graphic novel.Looking for somewhere nice to visit?Minecraftis getting itsfirst new dimension in 15 years,a particularly lush world named The Sift, filled with pastel-hued meadows, multicolour lakes and bunny-like mobs. It arrives in Minecraft Dungeons II this month, and will be in the main editions of the game next year.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat to clickAce Combat 8: Wings of Theve – brilliant aerial combat game fulfils the Top Gun fantasy | ★★★★★Playing video games with my 22-year-old son has brought me to tearsMeet the real-life Pokémon professors, the unsung heroes of competitive monster-battling‘Mum, where did my Robux go?’ :The Roblox scam targeting childrenQuestion BlockView image in fullscreenExtremely relaxing … Unpacking, a relaxing tidying game.Photograph: Witch BeamA cosy question fromSimon, via email:“Last year I ended up spending a lot of time supporting mydad during a roughpatch with this health, and this led to me playing a lot of Animal Crossing: Pocket Camp Complete on my iPhone. I havefound it really soothing during a challenging year but I’ve pretty much exhausted it.[Someone] recommended [playing] Stardew Valley but it doesn’t feel especially suited to playing on a relatively small mobile, nor my limited free time. Any suggestions? Hopefully nothing involving micro transactions?”Smartphone games can be an amazing tonic during tough times – I’m glad they helped you through them. If you’ve not playedUnpackingyet, it’s an extremely relaxing narrative tidying game with lots of subtle emotional touches. I also like the gentle platforming adventureSpiritfarerabout shepherding spirits to the afterlife. If you’re looking for more of an Animal Crossing vibe, there’sWilderness: Meadowfell, a lush exploration game set in a procedurally generated landscape, or try one of the classics from Japanese developer, Kairosoft, such as theGame Dev StoryorJumbo Airport Story. If you can stomach a couple of suggestions with very noninvasive in-app purchases My Leisure Time and Animal Restaurant, have been recommended to me as great life sims with bags of character.If you have a question for Question Block – or anything else to say about the newsletter – hit reply or email us atpushingbuttons@theguardian.com.Explore more on these topicsGamesPushing Buttons newsletterResident EvilAction gamesFilm adaptationsHorror filmsZombiesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Explosions of colour, cold war paranoia and hyper-erotic intimacy: five free shows to see | Art and design | The Guardian
description: In a new series, we review the best art exhibitions currently showing in commercial galleries, where entrance is free
Author: Eddy Frankel
Headline: In a new series, we review the best art exhibitions currently showing in commercial galleries, where entrance is free
Content: A bit of a squeeze … La DS (Cornaline) by Gabriel Orozco showing  at White Cube Bermondsey.Photograph: Matthew Chattle/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenA bit of a squeeze … La DS (Cornaline) by Gabriel Orozco showing  at White Cube Bermondsey.Photograph: Matthew Chattle/ShutterstockEddy Frankel's gallery crawlArt and designExplosions of colour, cold war paranoia and hyper-erotic intimacy: five free shows to seeIn a new series, we review the best art exhibitions currently showing in commercial galleries, where entrance is freeEddy FrankelWed 30 Sep 2026 10.29 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 11.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGabriel Orozco: Chronotopic★★★☆☆Walking into Gabriel Orozco’s show is like waking up with a headache and trying to piece together whatever the hell you did last night. Everything in the Mexican conceptualist’s exhibition is splintered, disjointed, a history you can’t make sense of.There’s a round of applause as you walk in, but the ovation morphs into the sound of rain. There are recognisable things here – cars, a football, cigarettes – but they don’t make sense. They’re suspended mid-air, broken into pieces, flipped upside down. An old Citroën has been split in half and glued back together too small, too narrow. There are kids’ toys and games, ceiling fans twirling with rolls of toilet paper attached to their blades, tree branches that have sprouted cigarette butts.So many artists deal with the idea of memory and the passing of time, but few manage to capture the slipperiness of it all like Gabriel Orozco. The whole show feels as if it’s about history, but stripped of its big names and important dates, leaving behind a bunch of fragmented memories instead.It’s all a bit too ephemeral, dense and self-satisfied, as if he can’t stop patting himself on the back for being so clever. But that doesn’t mean it isn’t good, it’s just odd, discomfiting art that makes you feel you’re about to forget your pin number.White Cube Bermondsey, London, until 8 NovemberMary Ramsden: The Feeling of What Happens★★★★★View image in fullscreenInstallation view of Mary Ramsden: The Feeling of What Happens.Photograph: Photo by Ben Westoby / Fine Art Documentation. Courtesy the artist and Pilar Corrias, LondonI like colour as much as the next guy, unless the next guy is Mary Ramsden, and then I might be beat. What you see first in the Yorkshire-based artist’s huge new abstracts is big washy swathes of colour, one canvas all neon pink and green lost in a haze of deep purple, another all mauve and lilac in a vastness of blue. They’re explosive bursts of hue and tone, totally mesmerising, abstraction at its abstractest.But look more, look longer, are those flower petals? Shafts of daylight through slats in a window? Everything is being constantly pulled between abstraction and reality, each work vacillating between still life and colourfield experimentation.Years ago Ramsden was painting love hearts over and over, as if she was abstracting her teenage diaries. Then she did the same thing to interior scenes of living rooms and furniture. Now nature has crept its way in. She says these works are all about the limits of consciousness and perception. Yeah, maybe, but what makes this show so good is its total, obsessive, overwhelming dedication to colour.Pilar Corrias, London, until 7 NovemberMartine Syms: Knot Eye★★★☆☆View image in fullscreenStill from RW-LO, 2026 by Martine Syms .Photograph: © Martine Syms. Courtesy the Artist, Sadie Coles HQ, Hoffman Donahue and Sprüth MagersI asked the ether – AKA people who follow me on social media – if anyone could explain what the hell Martine Syms’ show at Sadie Coles HQ is about, and someone replied “it’s about Martine Syms”. Which is as good an answer as any. The LA-based artist’s work is about brand Syms – literally, there’s a concept store of Syms merch, books and candles on the ground floor. But it’s about that idea in a wider societal sense too, about how we’re all brands: personalities constructed for display, amalgams of fiction, memory, capitalism and pop culture.There are two films upstairs. In the newest piece, three people at an afterparty talk about DMT and interdimensional travel, one starts tripping while the others fall asleep. Reality and fantasy crash together and never really get pulled apart.The other film follows a teenager who’s obsessed with an early 2000s reality star, an obsession that makes it impossible to distinguish a real person from the character they portray.None of it is brilliantly acted or scripted, but somehow it still sends you out into the street with a head full of questions. Syms lives in a world where the lines between who we are, who society wants us to be, and who we present to the world, are all being constantly blurred.Sadie Coles HQ, London, until 7 NovemberColin Self: Unseen★★★☆☆View image in fullscreenDetail from 365: A journey in that direction, 2000–2026  by Colin Self.Photograph: Courtesy the artist and Frith Street Gallery, London All works © the artist, DACS 2026If you had a penny for every exhibition that rediscovers some long-lost pop art innovator 60 years after they first nicked imagery from ads or cartoons, you’d have a ton of pennies. But Colin Self is worth adding to the purse.What sets Self apart from the other pop artists of his generation is an overwhelming atmosphere of paranoia and dread. While the rest of them were tackling ideas of consumerism and fame, Self was dealing with the aftermath of the second world war, the looming threat of nuclear annihilation in the cold war, and shivering with fear.A grinning face hangs by a thread as a Nazi bomb flies past in one work; a dog bares its teeth in front of a battery of missiles in another; he sculpts a war plane out of nails and fake leopard fur, he creates a portrait of a man made up of saws, knives, springs and tools. It’s atomic terror in a newly mechanised society that’s perpetually on the verge of self-annihilation. These early works are brilliant, pop art with all the fun and colour replaced by abject horror.Self is still at it, still making work at 85. Newer landscape paintings show his native East Anglia as a bleak old place filled with broken caravans and bomb craters. None of the more recent stuff here is brilliant, but it’s all still marked by that terror and dread.Frith Street Gallery, London, until 7 NovemberSomaya Critchlow: Pastels★★★★☆View image in fullscreenFigure in Front of Window, 2026, by Somaya Critchlow.Photograph: Courtesy of the artist and Maximillian William, LondonCritchlow’s erotic portraits have always been marked by a palpable sense of threat. The young English painter’s coquettish, 70s soft-focus nudes locked eyes with the viewer aggressively, confrontationally, as if they were on the verge of punching your lights out or throttling you with their negligees. But in this exhibition – her first since showing atDulwich Picture Gallerylast year – you don’t have to fear for your life.Instead, in these tiny, ultra-intimate pastels, Critchlow is luxuriating in form. These are unabashed celebrations of sensuality, nudity and eroticism. They’re still confident and confrontational figures, but you feel as if Critchlow is enjoying herself a bit more, letting things be sensual for their own sake, without being weighed down by anger and revenge. I miss the implication of violence, but they’re still really good, hyper-erotic, intimate images. They could also just be lulling you into a sense of false security – so watch your back.Maximillian William, London, until 14 NovemberExplore more on these topicsArt and designEddy Frankel's gallery crawlPaintingInstallationArtDulwich Picture GalleryfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Post your questions for Michael Winterbottom | Movies | The Guardian
description: With us to mark the 24th anniversary of 24 Hour Party People, the director’s work includes everything from Cracker to A Cock and Bull Story, Wonderland to Welcome to Sarajevo. And, of course, The Trip
Author: Rich Pelley
Headline: With us to mark the 24th anniversary of 24 Hour Party People, the director’s work includes everything from Cracker to A Cock and Bull Story, Wonderland to Welcome to Sarajevo. And, of course, The Trip
Content: Trip adviser … director Michael Winterbottom.Photograph: Marc Piasecki/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTrip adviser … director Michael Winterbottom.Photograph: Marc Piasecki/Getty ImagesFilm & Music reader interviewMoviesPost your questions for Michael WinterbottomWith us to mark the 24th anniversary of 24 Hour Party People, the director’s work includes everything from Cracker to A Cock and Bull Story, Wonderland to Welcome to Sarajevo. And, of course, The TripRich PelleyWed 30 Sep 2026 10.17 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 10.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOf course, the 90s couldn’t be any more in vogue at the minute – but the 90s couldn’t have happened without the 80s. And that’s where 24 Hour Party People comes in, Michael Winterbottom’s riotous 2002 film that charts Manchester’s music scene from the Sex Pistols’ legendary 1976 Lesser Free Trade Hall gig through Factory Records, Joy Division, New Order and into the Madchester era of Happy Mondays and the Haçienda. It’s the story of Manchester music before Oasis swaggered in and took over the world, and it stars Paddy Considine, Shirley Henderson, Andy Serkis and John Simm – plus Steve Coogan as the late broadcaster and Factory Records boss Tony Wilson.After studying English at Oxford, Winterbottom started out in television in the late 1980s, directing everything from documentaries about Ingmar Bergman to episodes of Boon and Cracker, before making his feature debut, 1995’s Butterfly Kiss – a dark road movie about a serial killer and her lover travelling across northern England. His subsequent films included 1996’s Jude, 1997 Bosnian war drama Welcome to Sarajevo, 1999 London ensemble piece Wonderland and 2000 western The Claim. Since then we’ve seen the sexually explicit 9 Songs in 2004, literary comedy A Cock and Bull Story (adapted from Tristram Shandy) with Coogan and Rob Brydon, political docudrama The Road to Guantánamo and 2010 noir thriller The Killer Inside Me.He has also regularly reunited with Coogan, most famously for 2010’sThe Tripand its sequels, in which Coogan and Brydon travelled, ate and attempted increasingly competitive celebrity impressions – including a Michael Caine-off that became almost as famous as the films themselves. The trio are now making a fifth instalment, The Trip to the Northern Lights, which sees Coogan and Brydon eating, bickering and impersonating their way through Scandinavia and the Nordic countries.And with 24 Hour Party People back in cinemas 24 years after its original release, Winterbottom is joining us for a chat. Please get your questions in by 6pm on Sunday 4 October and we’ll print his answers as part of reader interview section. Rave on!24 Hour Party People is in UK cinemas from 9 October and on 4K UHD Disc from 26 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmFilm & Music reader interviewMichael WinterbottomJoy DivisionTony WilsonHappy MondaysThe TripSteve CoogancalloutShareReuse this content

title: Verity review – Dakota Johnson leaves teethmarks as she goes back to Fifty Shades erotic thriller territory | Movies | The Guardian
description: Anne Hathaway and Josh Hartnett co-star in this unconvincing mystery about a struggling writer who is asked to ghostwrite for a bestselling author
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Anne Hathaway and Josh Hartnett co-star in this unconvincing mystery about a struggling writer who is asked to ghostwrite for a bestselling author
Content: Power couple … Anne Hathaway (Verity Crawford) and Josh Hartnett (Jeremy Crawford) in Verity.Photograph: Amazon Content Services LLC/PAView image in fullscreenPower couple … Anne Hathaway (Verity Crawford) and Josh Hartnett (Jeremy Crawford) in Verity.Photograph: Amazon Content Services LLC/PAMoviesReviewVerity review – Dakota Johnson leaves teethmarks as she goes back to Fifty Shades erotic thriller territoryAnne Hathaway and Josh Hartnett co-star in this unconvincing mystery about a struggling writer who is asked to ghostwrite for a bestselling authorPeter BradshawWed 30 Sep 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 09.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe nation is crying out for a really enjoyable erotic mystery-thriller, a taste potentially at least as strong as the cosy-crime fetish currently dominating our every waking moment. The success of Paul Feig’s naughty-but-not-nice movie The Housemaid proves it. We are thirsting for a sexy encounter with a dishy yet maybe problematic nice-guy husband; we are pining for a damaged and dangerous beautiful wife; we are longing to identify with a vulnerable yet gutsy young person who finds herself in the middle of their creepy scenario and we are yearning to spend some time in a secluded luxury lakeside villa of gigantic modernist proportions down whose night-time corridors we can tremblingly tiptoe. So here is a drama, adapted by screenwriter Nick Antosca from the novel by Colleen Hoover, in which someone has such excitingly transgressive sex that they leave teeth marks on the headboard. During this film, audiences may be leaving teeth marks in the seatback in front of them. Or the back of someone’s head. But not in a good way.Dakota Johnson goes back into “Fifty Shades” ingenue-cute territory as Lowen, a struggling writer mysteriously approached by a legal team working for Verity Crawford, played by Anne Hathaway, a mega-bestselling author whose recent indisposition means that she is unable to finish her hugely lucrative novel series. Crawford’s people ask Lowen if she might be willing, in exchange for several shedloads of money, secretly to ghostwrite the rest of Crawford’s darkly saucy page-turners. Lowen agrees, largely because she is strangely drawn to Verity’s handsome, sensitive husband Jeremy, played by Josh Hartnett. She has to go and stay in their gorgeous Vermont home where she is upset to find that Verity is now immobile, using a wheelchair, and cannot speak. And she is even more upset to discover a certain manuscript by Verity which hints at a terrifying situation of which the world has no clue.So far, so silly and so entertaining, surely? There are cheeky hints of Daphne du Maurier and Brian De Palma that promise a good time. But we are entitled to wonder why Lowen doesn’t ask someone, anyone, how exactly Verity came to be in this unhappy situation. Perhaps she might be tempted to ask the sinister nurse (Irina Dvorovenko) but this character soon simply and bafflingly disappears. After a sensational opening sequence, the film gradually unwinds, and the entirety of the third act disintegrates into a shower of small substandard plot points that don’t convince. The narrative structure seems to rest on Lowen finding not one but two manuscripts, and we are finally asked to accept a lamely unresolved situation as something fascinatingly ambiguous. This needed a new draft.Verity is out on 1 October in Australia and on 2 October in the UK and USExplore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsSexDakota JohnsonAnne HathawayFilm adaptationsCrime filmsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: How do you cope when your sacred land becomes Times Square? The art of the first Native New Yorkers | Native Americans | The Guardian
description: A new exhibit of Lenape paintings, traditional dress and music proves their modern-day culture is vibrant and alive
Author: Alaina Demopoulos
Headline: A new exhibit of Lenape paintings, traditional dress and music proves their modern-day culture is vibrant and alive
Content: Jessie Gould, Kaylin Williams, 2023.Photograph: Museum of the City New YorkView image in fullscreenJessie Gould, Kaylin Williams, 2023.Photograph: Museum of the City New YorkNative AmericansHow do you cope when your sacred land becomes Times Square? The art of the first Native New YorkersA new exhibit of Lenape paintings, traditional dress and music proves their modern-day culture is vibrant and aliveAlaina DemopoulosWed 30 Sep 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 14.02 EDTShareDuring the 19th century, the US government funded more than 500 “Indian boarding schools” aimed at forcibly assimilating Native American children into western culture. Students weretakenfrom their families, frequently by force, and forced to cut their hair. They were stripped of their original names, and taught to feel shame regarding their heritage and customs. Run like military academies, these institutions required children to wear uniforms andsubjectedthem to severe physical punishment, such as solitary confinement and flogging. Richard Henry Pratt, who established the first of these schools, declared that their explicitpurposewas to “kill the Indian, save the man”.These assimilation practices persisted for decades, during which numerous children endured physical and sexual abuse. At least 1,000 childrenlost their lives, though the actual casualty count is believed to be significantly higher. The US government issued no formal apology for these atrocities until 2024, when former president Joe Bidendescribedthe boarding school system as “one of the most horrific chapters in American history”.Some of the children at these schools were Lenape people, an Indigenous group that live on the north-eastern coast of the US. In 1874, a Toronto missionary society published a hymnal that translated Christian worship songs into Munsee, one of the languages spoken by the Lenape. The hymnal was part of the state’s attempt to assimilate Indigenous children; they were expected to learn Christian worship songs instead of their own culture’s prayers.View image in fullscreenBoarding school class, unknown creator.Photograph: Courtesy of Peyton PowellToday, the hymnal hangs in a new exhibit at the Museum of the City ofNew Yorkcalled Halumii Ktapihna: Lenape Legacies and Futures. More than 150 years after its publication, the book now serves as the opposite function it was intended for. Rather than forcing Lenape children to learn English, it has become a primary source for Lenape people who are now revitalizing a language that was nearly lost due to systemic racism and genocide. The hymnal, once a symbol of erasure, teaches vocabulary and grammatical structures to a new generation.Halumii Ktapihna contains visual art created by Lenape people, along with traditional dress, samples of music, and efforts to revitalize Lenape words and phrases. “We lost a lot of the culture and language, but yet [some] has remained,” said Brent Stonefish, a founding member of the Éenda-Lŭnaapeewáhkiing Collective and curatorial adviser on the project. Next to the hymnal hangs a bolo tie made in 2024 that reads: “We matter.” “Between those two [pieces], there’s a whole history there,” Stonefish added.If most people know anything about the Lenape, it’s their role in New York’s apocryphal origin story: that Manhattan was sold to the Dutch for $24 worth of trinkets. The story goes that Dutch settler Peter Minuitswindledthe island’s Native inhabitants, the Lenape people, out of what would eventually become one of the most expensive places on Earth, in effect displacing them from the island they called home and named. Manhattan comes from Manhatta, which means “a place for gathering wood to make bows” in Lenape.View image in fullscreenUntitled, June Lee Van Dunk, 2023.Illustration: Museum of the City of New YorkView image in fullscreenMy Lenape Grandmother, Elizabeth Doxtater, 2026.Illustration: Courtesy of the artistView image in fullscreenNot Enough, Said the Imposters, Zoe Hundley, 2025.Illustration: Courtesy of the artistView image in fullscreenPlace Where the Hickories Will Grow, Myles Jackson Lynch, 2022.Photograph: Courtesy of the artistView image in fullscreenComfort, Keitha Keeshig-Tolbias Bizindam 2023.Photograph: Courtesy of Keitha Keeshig-Tolbias BizindamView image in fullscreenSelf-portrait, Jack ‘Crying Raven’ Anderson, 2015.Illustration: Courtesy of Cynthia AndersonThis story isnot true: there’s no paper record of the trade, and the Lenape peopledid not believethat land could be owned or sold. Most scholars agree that what we now know as New York sits on stolen, unceded Lenape territory. There are now land acknowledgments posted around the city’s cultural institutions, such as a plaque outside an entrance to the Metropolitan Museum of Art. This gives the impression that the Lenape people’s story ended hundreds of years ago – but the new exhibit aims to correct that assumption, presenting the tribe’s modern-day culture as still very much alive.double quotation mark[The Lenape] found a way of dealing and engaging with those historical wounds in ways that are not uglyAngel ‘Monxo’ LópezBy the Revolutionary war, most of the Lenape people had been killed or pushed west by settlers. The US government’s ensuing genocide and forced displacement of Native Americans further decimated the Lenape population. But there are still state and federally recognized tribes in the US and Canada dedicated to preserving their heritage and language. Some of these groups have sovereign tribal governments and have receivedgrantsto buy back ancestral land.Modern-day art in the exhibit highlights the Lenape’s original homeland of New York; one piece by Ramapough Munsee artist June Lee Van Dunk explicitly juxtaposes the silhouette of an Indigenous figure clad in traditional dress with the scene of a bustling, New York block with the Empire State Building in the background.View image in fullscreenUntitled, June Lee Van Dunk, 2023.Illustration: Museum of the City of New YorkAngel “Monxo” López, the museum’s curator of community histories, worked on the exhibit. López is not Lenape; he hails from Puerto Rico and now lives in the Bronx. Going into the project “I was originally expecting a lot of resentment, sadness, grievances, name-calling against the occupiers of their land,” López said. “But when you walk into the gallery, there is not a single moment that speaks about that. They found a way of dealing and engaging with those historical wounds in ways that are not ugly, nasty, or resent-driven. I’m like, ‘Oh shit, I wouldn’t be so polite.’”The exhibit also features a protest banner made in 2019 by Georgetown professor Ashton Pemapanik Dunkley. The image of the Earth and an Indigenous woman in red is spray-painted over canvas alongside the words: “Mother Earth and her Indigenous daughters are under attack.” This banner connects the disastrous impacts of the climate crisis with the issue of missing and murdered Indigenous women, who face a high rate of assault, abduction and murder. (More than 1.5 million Indigenous women have experienced some sort of violence in their lifetime; red dresses have come to represent these women.)View image in fullscreenMother Earth and Her Indigenous Daughters are Under Attack, Ashton Pemapanik Dunkley, 2019.Photograph: Courtesy of Denise Bright Dove Ashton-DunkleyStonefish attended the opening of the exhibit with his daughter Emma, who is coordinating an upcoming Lenape/Lunáapeew Nations Pow Wow in Brooklyn’s Prospect Park, a tradition which started back up last year after a 53-year break. When speaking about his family, Stonefish referenced the Indigenous concept of “seven generations” – a rule that every community decision should be made with seven generations in mind, to promote a sustainable future.‘People often say – you don’t look Native’: indigenous life in America – in picturesRead more“My kids used to ask me, ‘What generation am I?’” Stonefish said. “I would tell them, you’re the seventh, and you’re the first. You’re tied to those who are behind you, but you’re also creating the foundation for the next set. You’re all of them.”Halumii Ktapihna: Lenape Legacies and Futuresis on display at the Museum of the City of New York through 17 April 2027

title: Start spreading the news… New York’s opera giveaway shows UK politicians how to be brave | Opera | The Guardian
description: New York’s mayor Mamdani is putting his political capital behind one of our greatest art forms with his pledge of Opera for All – and 70,000 free tickets to prove it
Author: Tom Service
Headline: New York’s mayor Mamdani is putting his political capital behind one of our greatest art forms with his pledge of Opera for All – and 70,000 free tickets to prove it
Content: Giveaway … Isabel Leonard as Frida Kahlo in Gabriela Lena Frank's El Ultimo Sueno de Frida y Diego (The Last Dream of Frida and Diego) at the Metropolitan Opera House in New York earlier this year.Photograph: Timothy A Clary/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGiveaway … Isabel Leonard as Frida Kahlo in Gabriela Lena Frank's El Ultimo Sueno de Frida y Diego (The Last Dream of Frida and Diego) at the Metropolitan Opera House in New York earlier this year.Photograph: Timothy A Clary/AFP/Getty ImagesTom Service on musicOperaStart spreading the news… New York’s opera giveaway shows UK politicians how to be braveTom ServiceNew York’s mayor Mamdani is putting his political capital behind one of our greatest art forms with his pledge of Opera for All – and 70,000 free tickets to prove itWed 30 Sep 2026 07.27 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 13.34 EDTShareOpera for All. It’s the credo of every opera house in the world, and each has its own ways and means of attracting new – and, crucially, younger – audiences. But it’s rare that one gives away thousands of tickets to anyone who applies. In New York last week, mayor Mamdani took to the stage of the Metropolitan Opera to tell his city that previouslyopera-shy citizensshould apply for one of the70,000 free ticketsthat he and the opera house are giving away this and every season. That means a staggering 10,000 free tickets a month. Not just for the under-25s, not just for the productions that they can’t shift tickets for on Mondays and matinees.New Yorkers simply enter the lotterythe day before and if successful, will get a pair of tickets to the next day’s show.Mamdani’s announcement coincides with the Met’s general manager, Peter Gelb,going on a fundraising drivehoping for $1.5bn to secure the opera house’s future. Generous as the offer seems, the Met can surely spare the tickets, given how few of their shows actually sell out the 4,000-seat hall – the Met averaged only72% capacity the last season.But what’s different about the Met scheme to that of, say, English National Opera’sfree tickets for under-21s, or the heavily discounted ticket schemes on offer elsewhere is that it’s the mayor who’s doing the talking, putting his political capital and small-p populist appeal behind the art form. And that’s where there’s no comparison between Mamdani and British politicians in terms of cultural bravery. Whatever party they belong to, no UK politician for several decades past has wanted to get too close to opera for fear of being contaminated by its associations of elitism, out-of-touchedness, unaffordable posho luxury, and cultural irrelevance. Angela Rayner was branded achampagne socialistfor daring to enjoy opera at Glyndebourne (her ticket cost her £62); politicians who are known opera-lovers, including George Osborne and Michael Gove, saw no benefit in being associated with Opera North or Covent Garden during their time in office, and didn’t really want their shameful opera-loving secret getting out.View image in fullscreenOne of the greatest art forms we have … L’Orfeo by Monteverdi in William Kentridge’s 2026 staging for Glyndebourne.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianWhich is where Mamdani’s essential message is so refreshing: that the best of what humanity has done in music and theatre, in opera as in all forms, belongs to everyone. That sounds like the most straightforward proposition there could possibly be when it comes to arts policy, but it has never been as powerfully articulated by any British politician in recent memory as Mamdani has just done. “Opera is one of the greatest art forms we have … and every New Yorker should have the opportunity to see it, no matter how much money is in their pocket,” he said.Mamdani referenced a previous incumbent in his announcement: Fiorello La Guardia, who was mayor from 1934-45, and his creation of “the people’s opera”, theNew York City Opera Company, in 1943.La Guardia said: “I want justice on the broadest scale … justice that gives to everyone some chance for the beauty and the better things of life”. Mamdani is taking on that mantle. Will any British politician have the courage to do the same, and bet their political fortune on a belief in the socially transformative power of culture in general, and opera in particular?Mind you, if you do get lucky in the Met’s lottery, your first opera could be Macbeth, it could be La Bohème – or it could be Parsifal. Wagner’s last opera – all four to five hours of it – is as divisive now as it was in 1882. Seeing the piece for the first time at ENO in the 1990s changed my life – I just couldn’t believe an orchestra was capable of that time-warping, pain-racked sensuality in the transformation scene in the first act, the place where “time becomes space” as theold knight Gurnemanz sings to Parsifal– that’s the alchemy that Wagner’s orchestration literally makes happen.View image in fullscreenGateway drug … Andreas Schager as Parsifal and Claudia Mahnke as Kundry in Parsifal in Hamburg State Opera’s 2017 staging of Wagner’s opera.Photograph: Dpa Picture Alliance/AlamyI think Parsifal would be an incredible gateway drug to the whole art-form, but ifyou’re allergic to Wagner’s language, you’ll quite probably disagree. A new production opens tomorrow at Covent Garden conducted byJakub Hrůša. Tickets aren’t free – youneed at least £27– but get there if you can, and be converted, or repelled, but either way you will be moved.This week Tom has been listening to:Bruckner’s String Quintet. Listen to the third movement, the Adagio, and prepare to have your preconceptions about Bruckner overturned. The intimacy of the soundworld, the volatility of how the melodies melt into different keys, the lines of lyricism that spread over this movement, and the whole piece – it’s magical.
