title: Gaza documentary NAZA beats Avengers Endgame: Encore to top Italian box office | NAZA | The Guardian
description: Award-winning, Guardian-produced film focused on Israel’s mass killing of civilians extends run after sold-out screenings
Author: Catherine Shoard
Headline: Award-winning, Guardian-produced film focused on Israel’s mass killing of civilians extends run after sold-out screenings
Content: Extended run … A scene from NAZA, directed by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor.Photograph: The GuardianView image in fullscreenExtended run … A scene from NAZA, directed by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor.Photograph: The GuardianNAZAGaza documentary NAZA beats Avengers Endgame: Encore to top Italian box officeAward-winning, Guardian-produced film focused on Israel’s mass killing of civilians extends run after sold-out screeningsCatherine ShoardandAngela GiuffridaWed 30 Sep 2026 13.11 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNAZA, the award-winning documentary about Israel’s systemic mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza, has opened at No 1 at the Italian box office, beating rival titles including Avengers Endgame: Encore, which came in at No 2.The 80-minute film was booked for a three-day run in Italy, but after sold-out auditoriums and positive audience reaction, its release window will be extended. On its opening day on Monday, the documentary took a total of €451,872, with a per site average of €1,153.By the end of Tuesday, this rose to about €1.1m. Avengers Endgame: Encore – a rerelease of the 2019 blockbuster featuring a new introduction and post-credits scene – made €356,000 over the same period.Appetite in Italy was particularly primed for the film, which was directed by Oscar-winning film-makers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor and produced by the Guardian, and won the Special Jury Prize at the Venice film festival earlier this month. Its premiere a few days before was met with a 25-minute ovation – a festival record.In packed cinemas across Italy some people in the audience held the Palestinian flag and there was applause at the end of the film. But at the Tibur, a small cinema in the San Lorenzo area of Rome where NAZA is being screened in both of its auditoriums, the audience watched in complete silence. “In general, the public was in shock as they watched,” said Marco, a member of staff at the cinema. “There was silence throughout the whole film. Even at the end, nobody spoke.” The film’s run at the Tibur has been extended for at least another week, he added.More than 150 other cinemas in Italy have extended programming and the number is expected to grow. “As long as theatres want to show it, NAZA will continue to be screened,” Andrea Romeo, founder of I Wonder Pictures, the film’s distributor in Italy, toldLa Repubblica.Simone Gialdini, president of Anec, a trade association representing cinema owners, said that while the massive turnout can partly be explained by the film’s political nature and a strong desire among activists “to send a strong signal about a terrible situation that has been dragging on for years”, it has drawn a diverse audience of all ages that might not ordinarily be associated with this kind of film. “It is an audience that knows what it is going to see and is aware of the tragedy we are living through,” he told La Repubblica.The film, which will be released in more than 50 territories over the next month before being made freely available on theguardian.com in mid November, features the testimony of 24 anonymised Israeli soldiers and intelligence officers, who describe the AI-powered surveillancesystemsused to select their targets.View image in fullscreenAward winners … NAZA directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor receive the Special Jury Award at Venice film festival.Photograph: Yara Nardi/ReutersThe project takes its name from an acronym used euphemistically by Israeli intelligence to indicatehow many civilians it expects to die in an airstrike.Filmed in secret on rooftops in Tel Aviv, NAZA builds on reporting published from 2023 to 2025 in the Guardian; +972 Magazine, an Israeli-Palestinian publication; and Hebrew-language outlet Local Call.The documentary opens in New York on Wednesday, before a wider release rolls out across the US from 9 October. Speaking at its North American premiere on Saturday, Abraham and Szor addressed the escalatingthreatsby Israeli officials to strip them of their citizenship for making the film.“Our country is doing so much to hide these systems,” Szor told the audience at the post-screening Q&A. “It’s not a world that is open even to the Israeli public.”Added Abraham: “These crimes that you saw are ongoing. They’re ongoing because it’s what our country is doing, and because of what your country is supporting and funding.”Explore more on these topicsNAZADocumentary filmsIsrael-Gaza warFilm industryShareReuse this content

title: Iranian singer’s 74 lashes for performing without a hijab ‘a form of torture’, say rights groups | Global development | The Guardian
description: Iranian court upholds sentence against 29-year-old star Parastoo Ahmadi and other musicians in crackdown on women flouting hijab law
Author: Deepa Parent
Headline: Iranian court upholds sentence against 29-year-old star Parastoo Ahmadi and other musicians in crackdown on women flouting hijab law
Content: Parastoo Ahmadi singing live in 2024. The singer was sentenced after a concert streamed online went viral and had millions of views.Photograph: Parastoo Ahmadi/YoutubeView image in fullscreenParastoo Ahmadi singing live in 2024. The singer was sentenced after a concert streamed online went viral and had millions of views.Photograph: Parastoo Ahmadi/YoutubeRights and freedomGlobal developmentIranian singer’s 74 lashes for performing without a hijab ‘a form of torture’, say rights groupsIranian court upholds sentence against 29-year-old star Parastoo Ahmadi and other musicians in crackdown on women flouting hijab lawSupported byAbout this contentDeepa ParentWed 30 Sep 2026 07.09 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 07.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn Iranian court’s decision to uphold a sentence of 74 lashes against the popular singer Parastoo Ahmadi for performing without a hijab has sparked outrage among rights groups, who described it as “a form of torture”.In June, Ahmadi, 29, and eight members of her production team, including musicians, weresentenced by a courtin the city of Qom over a concert that was streamed online in 2024, which went viral and racked up millions of views. The court said the group had violated the country’s “legal and cultural norms” and called the performance “obscene and vulgar”.Under Iran’s“hijab and chastity” law– passed in 2024 but not yet officially implemented – women caught “promoting nudity, indecency, unveiling or improper dressing” face severe penalties, including fines, flogging and prison sentences ranging from five to 15 years for repeat offenders.Lawyers say the verdict, announced last week, was not a surprise as the head of the Iranian judiciary had recently said the regime should not be afraid of the resulting “uproar” from a harsher crackdown on those not wearing the hijab. Ahmadi and her production crew are expected to be punished with lashings within the next three months.Roya Boroumand, co-founder of the Abdorrahman Boroumand Center for Human Rights, said: “This concert is treated as an act of defiance not only because a woman is singing unveiled, but because she is singing old pre-revolutionary popular songs.”View image in fullscreenThe singer Hiwa Seyfizade, who was sentenced last month to four years in prison over a performance.Photograph: CreativeMorningsMoein Khazaeli, a human rights lawyer at Dadban, a legal counselling centre for Iranian activists based outside Iran, said: “The verdict is against humanity. It is a form of torture under the [United Nations] convention against torture. Unfortunately, in the Islamic republic’s judicial system, applying torture is effectively legal. It’s against human rights – a crime against humanity.”The harsh sentence of lashes imposed on Ahmadi has alarmed the musical community in Iran. Leili, 36, a singer in Tehran, told the Guardian that she felt like a “coward” for “helplessly” watching fellow musicians pay the price for expressing themselves and doing what they loved.According to Hengaw, a Norway-based group that covers human rights in Kurdistan and Iran, another singer,Hiwa Seyfizade, was also reportedly sentenced last month to four years in prison over a performance on charges of “promoting corruption and prostitution”.Despite years of arrests and prosecutions aimed at enforcing the law on mandatory hijabs, women continue to appear without headscarves in public. Some Iranians attribute this change not to a relaxation of the regime’s policy, but to women continuing to defy the restrictions.Leili said: “What you are seeing on social media about women freely walking around is true, and I see fewer and fewer women wearing the hijab. But the regime has no contribution here; it’s us women who continue to push. We aren’t scared to go protest [against] this.”In what appears to be a renewed wave of protests against mandatory dress codes and worsening economic conditions, students at Allameh Tabataba’i University in Tehran demonstrated this week. Protesters chanted: “Exploitation, unemployment, compulsory hijab for women” and “Top academic rankings, but crumbling dormitories”.Calling for the sentences against Ahmadi and other musicians to be overturned, Skylar Thompson, the deputy director at the US-based organisation Human Rights Activists in Iran, said flogging was “an archaic and deliberate act of violence against a person’s body and dignity” and was being used on Ahmadi to “frighten other women into compliance”.Explore more on these topicsGlobal developmentRights and freedomIranMiddle East and north AfricaCensorshipIslamic veilCorporal punishmentTorturenewsShareReuse this content

title: Van Gogh goes on display before sale of ‘almost mythical’ private collection | Vincent van Gogh | The Guardian
description: Châtaigniers en fleurs, valued at $180m, to be auctioned along with 11 other works by likes of Cézanne and Monet
Author: Kim Willsher
Headline: Châtaigniers en fleurs, valued at $180m, to be auctioned along with 11 other works by likes of Cézanne and Monet
Content: Châtaigniers en fleurs was painted in May 1890 shortly after Van Gogh arrived in Auvers-sur-Oise. It and the other works have not been seen in public in decades.Photograph: Sotheby's New York/Blaquier-Arrieta collectionView image in fullscreenChâtaigniers en fleurs was painted in May 1890 shortly after Van Gogh arrived in Auvers-sur-Oise. It and the other works have not been seen in public in decades.Photograph: Sotheby's New York/Blaquier-Arrieta collectionVincent van GoghVan Gogh goes on display before sale of ‘almost mythical’ private collectionChâtaigniers en fleurs, valued at $180m, to be auctioned along with 11 other works by likes of Cézanne and MonetKim Willsherin ParisWed 30 Sep 2026 06.11 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 16.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor more than 50 years it was held in a private art collection with an “almost mythical status” that was likened to a miniature version of Paris’s Musée d’Orsay.But on Wednesday a painting byVincent van Goghcreated during the last two months of his life has gone on display before it is put up for auction with a value of $180m (£136m).Châtaigniers en fleurs (Chestnut Trees in Flower) was painted in May 1890 shortly after Van Gogh arrived in the French village of Auvers-sur-Oise. He died just weeks later.Most Van Gogh works from this period now hang in the world’s leading museums – but Châtaigniers en fleurs is one of 12 impressionist and modern masterpieces from the collection of the Argentinian collector Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier, who died in 2020.View image in fullscreenFleurs dans une coupe by Paul Gauguin is among the 12 works up for sale.Photograph: Sotheby’s New York/Blaquier-Arrieta collectionPhilip Hook, a former director of impressionist and modern art at the auction house Sotheby’s and a regular expert on BBC One’s Antiques Roadshow, said the opening of the collection to buyers was a “historic moment”.“For decades the Blaquier-Arrieta collection has been the stuff of legend: whispered about, kept from public view, it has attained an almost mythical status in the art world,” he said.“One of the last great private collections of impressionist and post-impressionist art, it was formed when major examples by the great names were still within reach.”View image in fullscreenPaul Cézanne’s Arlequin is valued at $150m.Photograph: Sotheby’s New York/Blaquier-Arrieta collectionThe Sotheby’s auction will also include Paul Cézanne’s Harlequin, painted in the late 19th century and valued at $150m.They will be sold along with 10 other significant works by Camille Pissarro, Pierre-Auguste Renoir, Edgar Degas, Claude Monet, Paul Gauguin, Alfred Sisley, André Derain, Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec and Maurice de Vlaminck.All 12 paintings, which are expected to fetch more than $450m in total, have gone on display at Sotheby’s in London on Wednesday for two days before being flown to Taipei, then Hong Kong and Paris before the auction on 18 November in New York.View image in fullscreenClaude Monet’s Le Jardin des Tuileries.Photograph: Sotheby’s New York/Blaquier-Arrieta collectionVan Gogh painted at least four major works featuring chestnut trees in Auvers-sur-Oise during a period of optimism and energy after his discharge from a psychiatric hospital at Saint-Rémy-de-Provence. After his death in July 1890, Châtaigniers en fleurs passed to his brother, Theo. A subsequent owner was George Gard “Buddy” DeSylva, the US songwriter and film producer who co-founded Capitol Records.It is one of only eight paintings Van Gogh produced in Auvers that are in private hands.View image in fullscreenAndré Derain’s Bâteaux au port de Collioure was painted in 1905.Photograph: Sotheby’s New York/Blaquier-Arrieta collectionSimon Shaw, a senior art adviser at Sotheby’s, said the collection felt “like a small museum – a miniature Musée d’Orsay, now opening its doors for the very first time”.Explore more on these topicsVincent van GoghPaintingArtnewsShareReuse this content

title: Missouri Williams and China Miéville among writers on ‘adventurous’ Goldsmiths shortlist | Goldsmiths prize | The Guardian
description: Six writers are in contention for the £10,000 books prize, which celebrates fiction that ‘breaks the mould or extends the possibilities of the novel form’
Author: Emma Loffhagen
Headline: Six writers are in contention for the £10,000 books prize, which celebrates fiction that ‘breaks the mould or extends the possibilities of the novel form’
Content: On the shortlist … top to bottom: Dooneen by Keith Ridgway, Attention-Seeking Behaviour by Aea Varfis-Van Warmelo, The Vivisectors by Missouri Williams, Said the Dead by Doireann Ní Ghríofa and The Rouse by China Miéville, Goldsmiths prize 2026.View image in fullscreenOn the shortlist … top to bottom: Dooneen by Keith Ridgway, Attention-Seeking Behaviour by Aea Varfis-Van Warmelo, The Vivisectors by Missouri Williams, Said the Dead by Doireann Ní Ghríofa and The Rouse by China Miéville, Goldsmiths prize 2026.Goldsmiths prizeMissouri Williams and China Miéville among writers on ‘adventurous’ Goldsmiths shortlistSix writers are in contention for the £10,000 books prize, which celebrates fiction that ‘breaks the mould or extends the possibilities of the novel form’Emma LoffhagenWed 30 Sep 2026 04.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMissouri Williams, China Miéville and Polly Barton are among the writers shortlisted for this year’sGoldsmiths prize.The £10,000 award recognises fiction that “breaks the mould or extends the possibilities of the novel form”.Judging chair Francis Spufford, novelist and professor of creative writing at Goldsmiths, University of London, said the judges had found “newness of many different kinds” in this year’s submissions, adding: “We enjoyed ourselves, and we enjoyed being challenged.”Williams was shortlisted for her Booker-longlisted novel The Vivisectors, set in an unnamed university town where academics and a group of gardeners are locked in a power struggle. In aGuardian review,Ian Maleney wrote: “Williams writes with a singular brand of Ballardian ferocity – she revels in the wretched and the craven.”Miéville’s The Rouse, an epic 1,200-page paranormal novel 20 years in the making, was described inStuart Kelly’s Guardian reviewas “affecting, intelligent and, in more than one place, very, very frightening”.The shortlist features two debuts, including the first novel from translator and nonfiction author Barton. What Am I, a Deer? follows a young woman who moves to Frankfurt to work for a video game company and becomes fixated on a man she encounters on her commute. It was described ina Guardian reviewas “a piercing study of yearning, and of the modern condition of feeling perpetually on the verge of one’s own life”.Also on the shortlist is Said the Dead by Doireann Ní Ghríofa, one of two Irish authors on the shortlist and the author ofA Ghost in the Throat. The book explores the history of women incarcerated in a Cork asylum, and was described byBrian Dillon in his Guardian reviewas a work of “extraordinary formal and ethical force”.Another Irish author, Keith Ridgway, is shortlisted for Dooneen, which paints a picture of social unrest in Dublin. It is an “appealingly labyrinthine novel” featuring “wonderfully absorbing and offbeat comedy”, according toMichael Donkor’s Guardian review.Completing the shortlist is another debut, Aea Varfis-Van Warmelo’s Attention-Seeking Behaviour, which is narrated by a compulsive liar and combines fiction with memoir and essay. Judge David Sexton said the book brings “brio worthy of a Muriel Spark heroine to telling us what she thinks we should know about her promiscuous, deceitful life in London now”.“The Goldsmiths prize exists to remind us that the novel, as the name suggests, is new,” Spufford said. “It may be 300 years old, but in adventurous hands, it still has limitless possibilities as a form.”The judging panel also includes writer and translator Kate Briggs, novelist Hari Kunzru and journalist and former Evening Standard literary editor David Sexton.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTanjil Rashid, culture editor at the New Statesman said: “A spirit of experimentation and freedom has been central to the novel and its enduring appeal; all of these books have that.”The winner will be announced at a ceremony at Foyles on Charing Cross Road in London on 4 November.Last year’s prizewas won by CD Rosefor We Live Here Now. Previous winners of the prize, which was launched in 2013 in association with the New Statesman and is now in its 14th year, include Rachel Cusk, Eimear McBride, Ali Smith, Isabel Waidner and Benjamin Myers.Explore the shortlist for this year’s Goldsmiths prize atguardianbookshop.comExplore more on these topicsGoldsmiths prizeAwards and prizesFictionChina MiévillenewsShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: a new mismatched detective duo for crime drama fans | Television | The Guardian
description: Richard Armitage’s smug scientist and Annabel Scholey’s frosty cop team up to solve a murder. Plus Martin Compston’s raucous cocktail sesh in Las Vegas. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Phil Harrison
Headline: Richard Armitage’s smug scientist and Annabel Scholey’s frosty cop team up to solve a murder. Plus Martin Compston’s raucous cocktail sesh in Las Vegas. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Body of evidence … Dr Ethan Winter (Richard Armitage) and DI Lauren Bell (Anna Scholey) in Winter.Photograph: Eagle Eye DramaView image in fullscreenBody of evidence … Dr Ethan Winter (Richard Armitage) and DI Lauren Bell (Anna Scholey) in Winter.Photograph: Eagle Eye DramaTV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: a new mismatched detective duo for crime drama fansRichard Armitage’s smug scientist and Annabel Scholey’s frosty cop team up to solve a murder. Plus Martin Compston’s raucous cocktail sesh in Las Vegas. Here’s what to watch this eveningPhil Harrison,Priya Elan,Jack SealeandGraeme VirtueWed 30 Sep 2026 01.20 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 05.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWinter9pm, ITV1If you have room for one more mismatched detective duo in your life, this new drama introduces Dr Ethan Winter (Richard Armitage), an unbearably smug forensic pathologist who can “read a body like a book”, and DI Lauren Bell (Annabel Scholey), a diligent, frosty cop. The pair are on a collision course as the murder of a young woman lands in their in trays. But when an explosive postmortem raises the stakes, they are forced to tolerate each other.Phil HarrisonThe Shaman’s Grave8pm, BBC FourThe capacity of archaeology to open a window into human belief systems is at the heart of this documentary exploring a very cold case from Germany. What do the bodies of a stone age woman and child – and the other items in their shared grave – tell us about the era’s spiritual practices?PHCause of Death9pm, Channel 5Nineteen-year-oldJay Slaterwas holidaying in Tenerife when he tripped and fell to his death at the bottom of a ravine. Now, pathologist Dr Richard Shepherd returns to the scene of the tragedy with Jay’s mum, Debbie, recreating his last walk in order to work out what killed him: deyhdration, a lack of sleep or something else?Priya ElanYuja9pm, Sky ArtsThisintriguing portraitof the prodigious Chinese-American pianist Yuja Wang does a good job of telling her life story while leaving some of her essential mystery intact. She’s a charming but abstracted interviewee: reclining, as if in therapy, and struggling to fully explain her brilliance.PHNot Going Out9.30pm, BBC OneView image in fullscreenEverybody needs good neighbours … Toby (Hugh Dennis), Anna (Abigail Cruttenden) and Lee (Lee Mack) in Not Going Out.Photograph: Pete Dadds/BBC/AvalonThere are shades of the Fawlty Towers anniversary episode as Lee (Lee Mack) desperately tries to deflect withering house guests Anna and Toby (Abigail Cruttenden and Hugh Dennis) away from the discovery that Lucy (Sally Bretton) is hiding from them upstairs. The cat doesn’t help.Jack SealeMartin Compston: Living Las Vegas10pm, Channel 4“Now I know why John Wayne walked like that …” Affable tour guide Compston saddles up for an authentic cowboy adventure in the second instalment of his Sin City travelogue. Other highlights include a raucous cocktail sesh with Scottish drag star Lawrence Chaney and a belated trip to the Grand Canyon.Graeme VirtueExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The secret lives of men who read romance books: ‘My life is full of love, so I’m drawn to them’ | Romance books | The Guardian
description: It’s often assumed straight men are not interested in romantic fiction – but many are sharing their passion in forums online
Author: Amandas Ong
Headline: It’s often assumed straight men are not interested in romantic fiction – but many are sharing their passion in forums online
Content: The bromantasy boom: why are so many men secretly obsessed with romance novels?Illustration: Laurie Avon/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe bromantasy boom: why are so many men secretly obsessed with romance novels?Illustration: Laurie Avon/The GuardianRomance booksThe secret lives of men who read romance books: ‘My life is full of love, so I’m drawn to them’It’s often assumed straight men are not interested in romantic fiction – but many are sharing their passion in forums onlineAmandas OngWed 30 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter a tiring day as a school maintenance worker, 28-year-old Paul loves nothing more than unwinding with a good romance novel – ideally one with a fantasy or horror element to it. He reads five or six a month – most recently Love Bytes, about an 8ft-tall werewolf woman who runs an extremely successful AI company and falls in love with a handsome ballroom instructor.Paul got into romance fiction via what he calls its “more traditional” side – such as the Regency romance series Bridgerton. He is partially sighted, so he mostly reads on his Kindle, where he can adjust the font size. In the first Bridgerton novel, “Simon, the main character, has a speech impediment that he has to work through,” says Paul. “I’m more attached to that one. Typically, I don’t come across disabled protagonists that much.”He doesn’t talk to anyone about his love of romance novels, communicating only with other users of a Discord channel called Romance for Men. “I was on a separate Reddit thread for book recommendations and someone asked if there’s romance out there for men,” he says. “And half of the comments were just, ‘Oh, you mean porn?’”View image in fullscreenThe Bridgerton TV series is based on the Regency romance novels.Photograph: NetflixStraight men like Paul who read and write romance are largely invisible to the wider world. Women are the genre’s main audience, followed by queer romance, which is a well documented success. The fifth volume of Alice Oseman’s Heartstopper – about the friendship between two teenage boys blossoming into love – is the UK’s fastest-selling graphic novel and a hit Netflix show, while novelists such as Alexis Hall are widely read and critically acclaimed. But in this corner of publishing, straight men are rarely seen and usually stigmatised.At Mills & Boon, the best known publisher of romantic fiction, men account for only 4% of sales, according to an editorial director, whileless than 2%of the UK’s Romantic Novelists’ Association is male. Almost nothing is known about how many men read romantic fiction, and why.For those I spoke to, however, reading romance is more than just entertainment. It offers a kind of liberation, allowing them to feel deeply, imagine being desired, and accept parts of themselves that conventional masculinity has little room for. Many would only speak anonymously, worried about being misunderstood or mocked.Before books, Paul’s path into romance began with role-playing video games in his teens: “You have some non-playable characters who are your companions, and you can build romantic relationships with them as you go along.” He gravitated towards playing aggressive male characters rallying different factions to war, realising later that the diplomatic approach worked better. The appeal of these characters was that they were so different from him. “I’m downright afraid of conflicts, and if there’s an argument, I just want to hide,” he says.In 2015, Paul learned that Stephenie Meyer, author of the vampire romance Twilight, had released a gender-flipped version of the book. “As a teenager, it was so cool to just hate on Twilight. But I read it anyway, and there’s a moment where Edythe, the vampire, tells the male protagonist that she is tired of trying to stay away from him. That’s when it hit. There’s a fantasy aspect in being wanted that badly.” Today, he seeks out novels known to fans as romance for men (RFM), such as Charlotte’s Reject by KR Treadway, which features a female character who’s “kind of scary”. “With women’s romance, it’s always the man being the aggressor,” he says. “Reading men’s romance is often the opposite, and it made me realise I’m fine being the way I am. I’m able to accept myself more, because I’ve seen that this is a possible dynamic in romantic relationships.”View image in fullscreenMen account for only 4% of sales of Mills & Boon books.Photograph: AlamyAndrew’s entry into romance was a deliberate experiment. The 31-year-old, who works in tech, is a huge lover of sci-fi and fantasy who considers himself “on the feminist side of the world”. He couldn’t look past the reality that the bulk of the dialogue in his favourite books was written by men and between men. “I just got really bored,” he says.Wandering around a bookshop three years ago, he made it his mission to pick up a book by a female author, and found Rebecca Yarros’ Fourth Wing, about the dragon-riding, lightning-wielding Violet Sorrengail. “I had very little context and just bought it. I didn’t know what romance or romantasy was,” he says. “It was refreshing to see things from the perspective of a female protagonist. I’d also never read a fantasy book that had so much in it about romance and sex.”Since then, Andrew has sought out other romantasy writers, from Penn Cole to Carissa Broadbent and Sarah J Maas. And he has introduced his wife to the genre. “She has a women’s book club, and they were all very sceptical in general, and then they all got hooked on it,” he says.Romantasy is not “grim” in the way that pornography is, Andrew says, but he would still blush at publicly buying books that are “substantially about sex”. “I like the anonymity of reading it on my phone or on Kindle, as opposed to a physical book on the tube,” he says. Still, he wonders if the genre’s constant idealisation of sex comes with a cost. “Every time they do it, it’s the best thing that’s ever happened to them. I can imagine there being some subtle toxic element to it, because real-life sex could be a bit of a letdown.”View image in fullscreenIt is not known how many men read romantic fiction.Photograph: Kosijerphotography/Getty ImagesAli, 54, a former investment banker, had his “first dedicated exposure to romance” 40-odd years ago. His younger sister had a subscription to the now defunct teen magazine Jackie, and as a teenager he used to read its romance photo-strips. “They were all boy-meets-girl stories,” he remembers. Another publication that stuck with him was Judy Blume’s Forever, a book so candid in its treatment of teenage sex that it has been targeted by censors since it was published in 1975. Later, as a student journalist at Oxford, Ali had the chance to interview Barbara Cartland, the undisputed queen of paperback romances. “It’s not a momentous event that changed my life,” he says, “but it’s quite funny to think about now.”A voracious reader, from contemporary historical romance writers such as Tessa Dare and Evie Dunmore to Jane Austen and Daphne du Maurier, Ali is not bothered by criticism that the genre is formulaic. Even Shakespeare, he points out, tells you upfront if a play you’ll be watching is a tragedy or comedy; the latter “will end with a wedding, probably more than one”. “Formulas are a blessing and a curse. The curse is when it’s done badly, and everyone yawns,” he says. “But when done right, there are huge payoffs – the dark moments, the happy endings.”Although Ali is happy to talk about romance “all day long”, he observes that other readers – male and female – might feel the need to lie about what they read to look good. He points to a market research phenomenon: “Everyone says they listen to Radio 3 or 4, but actually they all listen to Radio 2, right? And I think this insecurity is a genuine problem.”After studying creative writing at Kingston University in his 40s, Ali is now in two writers’ groups, where he’s notably the only person writing romance. He’s since written a series of three historical romance novels, all set in Mayfair in the late Victorian era. The first will be published soon, under the pen name Ali Murphy – combining his name and his wife’s birth name. “I chose it as a gender-neutral name,” he says. “I’m not trying to mislead people. But I don’t want anyone to pick up the book and say, oh God, it’s a bloke writing romance.”While Ali and Andrew prefer more mainstream romance, Paul and many other men are fans of a lesser-known strand of the genre. RFM is mostly self-published and sold digitally. It has a significant following: more than 10,000 weekly visitors to its dedicated Reddit, and a thriving Discord community where book recommendations are exchanged and discussed.Fans caution against any single definition of what RFM is, but agree that some patterns recur. It is typically written from the perspective of an ordinary man whose love interest is an unusually powerful woman – a straightforward inversion of narrative conventions in mainstream romance, where the heroine is expected to be relatable and the hero mythologised. Many readers indicate that the central crisis in RFM is often external to the couple’s relationship, such as a war or a shared enemy, rather than emerging from misunderstandings or jealousy between the two leads. There’s also a long-running argument about “harem” fiction, where one man is paired with several women. Some consider it the genre’s biggest success, while others don’t think it’s romance at all.Thirty-three-year-old Jonny Rogers works in finance. He reads copiously, has finished 90 books this year, and loves everything from Dostoevsky to the popular RFM series Would You Love a Monster Girl?, which he finished in six days. Two-thirds of what he reads is romance, most of it RFM.“I watched Titanic when I was about 11 and it really moved me,” he says. “I know it’s a little corny, but I just loved the idea of meeting someone and falling in love the way Jack and Rose did.” Wanting more of that feeling on the page, Jonny stumbled upon The Rosie Project, Graeme Simsion’s novel about an awkward, probably autistic man’s search for love. “I think there may have been some kinship there,” he says, explaining that he suspects he’s on the spectrum himself but is undiagnosed. Years later, a friend recommended Sarah J Maas’s A Court of Thorns and Roses. He read it in a week, then found his way to the RFM Reddit.View image in fullscreen‘I just loved the idea of falling in love the way Jack and Rose did.’Photograph: Photo Credit: Merie Weismiller Wallace/20th Century Fox/AllstarWhat keeps him riveted isn’t the fantastical trappings – spaceship battles, magic-wielding warrior women – so much as what’s underneath. “I just love following along with two people who fall in love with each other,” he says. “It’s the most human thing in the world, and it’s really magical.” He’s drawn to books with strongly written female leads, and insists a well written romance can be enjoyed by anyone.His girlfriend encouraged him to expand a short writing experiment into something longer. This became Daniel’s Dilemma, a novel about a young man falling for his best friend’s mother, warmly received by the RFM community. He chose the pen name Jonny Rogers not out of shame, he says, but caution: the book contains some explicit content, and “I don’t want my grandma or parents to buy my book and know I wrote that scene”. When he read his girlfriend a date scene between the two leads, she asked him: “That’s so romantic. How come you’re never that romantic with me?”Jonny’s close male friends know about his foray into writing. “None of them have actually bought it,” he says with a laugh. “I think when I told them, they were picturing erotica.” Although he’s never been bullied or insulted for enjoying romance, it’s not information that he volunteers outside his inner circle.One of RFM’s often-recommended authors is DH Willison, 58. He’s known for his Tales of Arvia series, set in a fantasy world where dragons and other creatures are central characters rather than obstacles for humans to conquer, and where unconventional pairings, such as a harpy and an incompetent adventurer, are ubiquitous.Willison feels he’s found more resistance among fellow writers than readers. At one writers’ group, someone mentioned finding an old pulp romance novel and gleefully picking it apart line by line as proof of the poor quality of romance stories, he recalls. In another writing group, he was told that a “real” romance requires the male and female leads to conform to certain rigid roles, down to genre conventions such as the “age gap” trope, which is assumed by default to mean an older man. The opposite is known as a “reverse age gap”. Willison thinks the distinction is “kind of silly”. This sort of gendered thinking, he adds, is self-fulfilling when extended to marketing: “I think romance is for everyone, but if you’re writing and selling with only women in mind, then you end up appealing only to women.”The other, more upmarket end of the romance spectrum mostly leaves sex off the page, together with the more obvious conventions. Mike Gayle and Bobby Palmer write at this more literary end, and publish under their own names.Gayle, 55, has been writing about love and relationships since his 1998 debut My Legendary Girlfriend, about a young man struggling to recover from heartbreak. He won the Romantic Novelists’ Association’s outstanding achievement award in2021, becoming the first man to do so, joining names including Jilly Cooper and Joanna Trollope. “I know of female readers who find it a breath of fresh air to read about love from a man’s perspective,” he says. “The more we’re exposed to different perspectives, the more we see we can both be right.”View image in fullscreen‘True romance is about staying together and making it work’ … Mike Gayle.Photograph: Hodder & StoughtonOver the years, Gayle has become more interested in writing about what happens after couples get together, rather than the lead-up – which is what most romances focus on. “It’s much sexier to write about the getting together,” he says. “But true romance is about staying together and making it work.” His writing has evolved in line with his personal life. “I was in my 20s, and kind of obsessed with finding ‘the one’. Now that I’ve seen relationships go by the wayside and taken for granted, I wanted to write about something deeper and more substantial.”Gayle’s next novel, Not Quite Myself, will be published in 2027. It’s co-written with his wife, Claire, and explores the lives of a couple who find themselves body-swapped after their youngest son goes to university. “It’s interesting to look at that stage of life where the only thing really keeping the couple together as a unit is the fact that they’ve got kids in the house,” he says. “How do you begin seeing your partner as a separate person again, from a fresh perspective?”Where Gayle now writes about what happens after the happy ending, Palmer, 33, is upending expectations around how romantic stories are told with his recently published third novel, Main Characters. It’s narrated entirely by the people around the central couple – but not the couple themselves – so that their relationship stays, as he puts it, “this kind of beautiful, private thing”, where readers never learn directly what the leads think or feel about each other.It’s also – in a departure from his previous books – being marketed as romance in the UK, with a bright pink cover. He’s noticed already that fewer men are getting in touch about it than with his other work.It’s their loss, of course, though not every man needs romantic fiction to teach them anything. Jonny, for his part, doesn’t think it has shaped him. “I’ve had a life filled with love,” he says. “Rather than romantic novels shaping my life, it’s actually that my life has been so full of love that I’m drawn to them.”Some names have been changedDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Dèy by Edwidge Danticat review – motherhood and trauma in Miami  | Books | The Guardian
description: The first novel in over a decade from the acclaimed Haitian-American author lacks the power of earlier works
Author: Sukhdev Sandhu
Headline: The first novel in over a decade from the acclaimed Haitian-American author lacks the power of earlier works
Content: Edwidge Danticat.Photograph: Slaven Vlašić/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenEdwidge Danticat.Photograph: Slaven Vlašić/Getty ImagesBooksReviewDèy by Edwidge Danticat review – motherhood and trauma in MiamiThe first novel in over a decade from the acclaimed Haitian-American author lacks the power of earlier worksSukhdev SandhuWed 30 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDèy, Edwidge Danticat’s first novel in over a decade, begins with a bang. Magnolia, the daughter of Haitian parents now shopping for a birthday present for her own daughter, hears gunfire, maybe bombs, in a Miami mall. A killer is on the loose – a young man high on hate, the author of online screeds about how “our country is under attack”, obsessed by cane toads who’ve been coming in from the Amazon basin. As she scrambles to the floor of a restaurant called Oasis, surrounded by dozens of diners playing dead, a man asks, “Is this a mass grave?”Things have always been tough for Magnolia. Her mother chases pigeons by day, sleepwalks at night, is on and off lithium. Her father worked for many years as a bus driver in Brooklyn, saving every cent so he could buy a nice retirement home back in Haiti. She was brought up by an “aunt” whose family had been killed by goons employed by Haiti’s dictator-in-chief Papa Doc Duvalier. Later she gets to college, where “school was my refuge”.Magnolia makes it out of the mall alive but finds herself rattled. Why can’t she tell the father of her child about what she witnessed? She doesn’t confide in her work colleagues either. At a pool party she almost has a seizure when a friend playfully sprays her with a water gun. Is this trauma? She has often felt brittle – finding a photo of herself in her early 20s, when she was a new mother, she says her eyes “look like headlights in a staring contest with a deer” – but now the ground beneath her feet feels especially shaky.Her anxieties – about her daughter’s future, her parents’ health – keep mounting.double quotation markDanticat, a sometime travel writer, is at her most appealing in her commemorations of Miami’s Little HaitiViolence in Dèy isn’t confined to the mall. It runs through the news stories about Ramallah and Yemen and Congo that Magnolia follows. The reports she hears of daily life in Haiti, where gangs abduct young girls, torch homes, storm schools and even churches, prompt fears for the home her father has worked so hard to build. Then, both in the background and in everyone’s face, there is the US president himself, with his poisonous thought-blurts about Haitians eating dogs and coming from a “shithole” country.Danticat, a sometime travel writer, is at her most appealing in her commemorations of Miami’s Little Haiti, a weathered world full of bakeries and barbershops, churches and religious stores, beauticians whose clientele watch Nollywood movies and read old copies of Ebony. But these hubs are being priced out by fusion restaurants and pilates studios. Magnolia works in property and is an agent of the displacements she and her colleagues bemoan.Magnolia’s job attunes her not just to the economics but to the poetics of place. Her ears prick up when someone describes Haiti as “down there” or, in the case of her boss, “‘over there’, as though she were looking at its distant shores from the upper deck of a cruise ship”. A short but powerful chapter is devoted to the backstory of a Haitian security guard who was killed at the mall: after the 2010 earthquake he moved to Brazil to build stadiums for the 2016 Olympics, then on to Chile and Colombia, before braving swamps and mountains to get to the US/ Mexico border and low-paid jobs loading trucks, allowing him to send money to his siblings back home.These peripheral characters are more vivid than Magnolia herself, who remains a wan, disassociated narrator throughout. Her language is sometimes academic (she describes her own daughter as “a liminal creature”), sometimes straight from a lifestyle magazine (“flaxen-tressed Black woman”). Motifs are spelled out for hard-of-hearing readers (“houses have always fascinated me, not only as physical structures, but as ideas, stories”) or in the manner of reading-group prompts (“We don’t always choose where we call home. Sometimes it’s others who decide”). The churn in her head – the violence that terrifies her – emerges in the tamest, most gentrified prose imaginable.In the end, Dèy, which is set in 2018, reads like a tribute to 1990s postcolonial fiction. There are nods to the spectral (“I was sure my mother was a ghost”), riffs on “sympathetic pain” and “somatic knowledge” (“My period came for the first time on another September 11”), too much dining-table diplomacy. “Visual clutter bothers me,” admits Magnolia at one point; this novel – so tasteful, so scented – could do with more noise, smears, life.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. title: On the Equality of All Things by Carlo Rovelli review – a physicist’s guide to life, the universe and everything | Science and nature books | The Guardian
description: Near-mystical musings from a scientist who believes we are on the brink of a revolution in understanding ourselves
Author: Farrah Jarral
Headline: Near-mystical musings from a scientist who believes we are on the brink of a revolution in understanding ourselves
Content: The Milky Way above the Grand Canyon of Thailand.Photograph: Suchart Kuathan/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Milky Way above the Grand Canyon of Thailand.Photograph: Suchart Kuathan/Getty ImagesBook of the dayScience and nature booksReviewOn the Equality of All Things by Carlo Rovelli review – a physicist’s guide to life, the universe and everythingNear-mystical musings from a scientist who believes we are on the brink of a revolution in understanding ourselvesFarrah JarralWed 30 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 12.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUnder the letter “B” in the index at the back of Carlo Rovelli’s latest book you will find Francis Bacon, bats, behaviourism, Henri Bergson, and the big bang. This intriguing little miscellany reflects the sweeping ambition of what is perhaps Rovelli’s most overtly philosophical work to date.Rovelli, who directs a quantum gravity research group in Marseille, has written several books on physics for the general reader, including the global bestseller Seven Brief Lessons on Physics.His latest is an attempt to integrate principles and theories from the discipline into a broaderWeltanschauung: one of the essential unity of all things, and the profoundly relational and perspectival nature of the universe. “Electrons and minds, stones and laws, judgments and galaxies do not essentially differ in nature from one another,” he writes. “They are notions that illuminate each other.”If this sounds familiar, that’s because it is. Rovelli echoes concepts that have been around for millennia in ancient thought, including Hinduism and Buddhism, from whose sacred texts he quotes. But what sets him apart from the countless other modern writers, dreamers and thinkers who preach the oneness of it all is that he grounds his ideas in scientific theory rather than theology or new age conjecture.double quotation markIt’s enough to give you vertigo, and Rovelli admits itOn the Equality of All Things is a slender volume holding an extraordinary density of ideas. Translator Simon Carnell, himself a poet, maintains the clarity and concision we have come to expect from Rovelli’s writing. In six chapters, or “lessons”, Rovelli lays out the philosophical significance of what he believes is a major scientific revolution, happening right now. The first lesson refers to his theory of relational quantum mechanics to ask us to abandon the notion that the world is made up of things with fixed properties. Rather, physical systems have propertiesrelativeto other physical systems. Also, everything’s moving, all the time, and there’s no fixed point around which we are in motion.The second lesson takes aim at the idea of linearity. Rovelli urges us to accept circularity and question the need to identify the ultimate foundation of things, when in fact, it’s turtles all the way down. The lessons continue. The world is not made up of things at all, butprocesses.“Even a stone is a process”, and so are we. Time itself is mutable and passes at different speeds in different places. Our knowledge of anything can only ever be partial.It’s enough to give you vertigo, and Rovelli admits it. “The resulting image of reality is haunting. Every fact is only a fact relative to something else, and even the fact that a fact is relative to something else is itself relative. There is no ground floor.” Yet, in contrast to the bleakness that can shroud such unflinching scientific accounts of the universe, Rovelli’s telling validates our messy, subjective human experiences. “None of this prevents us from describing the world from one perspective. Ours.” But the physics tells us that our perspectives are just that, and that there may be others.On the Equality of All Things takes its place as part of a blossoming movement that asks us to see the world as a set of interconnected relationships. As such, it sits alongside the work of mycologist Merlin Sheldrake, botanist Robin Wall Kimmerer, physiologist Denis Noble and nature writer Robert Macfarlane. Rovelli’s emphasis on perspective and relationality in physics echoes similar intellectual turns in social anthropology, ecology and biology that invite us to stop thinking about the world as something we stand without, and instead take our rightful placewithinit. Distancing himself from the more hubristic elements of the Enlightenment – an emphasis on certainty, linearity, and overconfidence in the imperfect instrument that is Reason – Rovelli asks us to embrace “the nimble lightness of circularity, complexity, ambiguity, metaphors, emotions, the acceptance of uncertainty and change”.His refusal to denigrate human culture as being inferior to or incompatible with hard science is refreshing. He observes wryly that the term “consciousness” has superseded the word “soul” because it is perceived to be more scientific, even though it is just as nebulous. Provided we understand that physical processes underlie everything, Rovelli sees no reason why we may not “calmly speak of the soul and emotions just as we speak of tables even if tables are collections of atoms”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFor all Rovelli is a gifted communicator, some of the science in this book required a level of intellectual scaffolding that, alas, my rusty physics A-level did not provide. At his explanation of loop quantum gravity, my brain started to creak and let off steam. Yet, even if you don’t have the foggiest idea what the granularity of spacetime means, engaging with this book as an internally coherent work of philosophy and literature is rewarding enough. And Rovelli’s conclusion is powerful: we are physical systems dancing among other physical systems, and the world “is our blood brother”. We’re at home, among family. Perhaps it’s time we honoured that kinship.On the Equality of All Things: Physics and Philosophy by Carlo Rovelli is published by Allen Lane (£20).
