title: The Swan contestants on the ‘sadistic’ pageant reality show: ‘Ultimately, we were just a job’ | Documentary films | The Guardian
description: In a new documentary, film-maker Erin Lee Carr lifts the lid on the 2000s TV series that shocked America
Author: Adrian Horton
Headline: In a new documentary, film-maker Erin Lee Carr lifts the lid on the 2000s TV series that shocked America
Content: A publicity image for the 2004 TV show The Swan.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyView image in fullscreenA publicity image for the 2004 TV show The Swan.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyDocumentary filmsThe Swan contestants on the ‘sadistic’ pageant reality show: ‘Ultimately, we were just a job’In a new documentary, film-maker Erin Lee Carr lifts the lid on the 2000s TV series that shocked AmericaAdrian HortonWed 30 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 11.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was in 2003, while listening to country radio, that Kelly first heard the casting call: “Have you dreamed about plastic surgery but never thought you could afford it?” She immediately turned up the volume. The pitch sounded too good to be true: free cosmetic procedures, a nutritionist, self-esteem work – one “life-changing opportunity” that “could transform everything”. Kristy, Cindy, Tawnya and Beth heard the call, too: the chance to overhaul oneself from the outside in, fulfilling the implicit but omnipresent promise that if you just lost a little weight and just tweaked your face a bit, your whole life would open up. You, too, could be an ugly duckling transfigured into a swan.The catch? It would all be filmed for television, of course, for a short-lived show that some have called one of the most sadistic of all time: The Swan. The Fox reality program, which ran for two seasons in 2004, brought the spectacle of intensive plastic surgery – the endurance of extreme pain and humiliation in pursuit of a narrow beauty ideal – to US living rooms with shocking bluntness: bandages and bruises, surgical cannulas pounding into flesh, curt assessments of lumps and bumps and “masculine” teeth that must be corrected in pursuit of a better you. Even among similarly thin-obsessed programs from the infamously ruthless wild west of early reality television –America’s Next Top ModelandThe Biggest Loser, to name a few – The Swan stands out as especially cruel, at once hopelessly bought into punitive beauty standards on-screen and shamelessly manipulative off it.‘Our job was not to attack’: how do you make a documentary about America’s culture wars?Read moreIt’s the “XXL version” of the many issues endemic to reality television, said Erin Lee Carr, the director ofThe Swan: Behind the Mirror, a new Hulu retrospective on the infamous series. “Unconscious people, secret pageants, sunk-cost principle, people having to leave, teeth coming out even if you might not need it” – if there were ever a reality series deserving of a second critical look, it would be The Swan.The show, developed by former Telemundo executive and “life coach” Nely Galán, was in some ways a natural, if extreme, outgrowth of growing fascination with, and exposure to, celebrities under a tightening microscope. Carr, the director of 2021 Netflix filmBritney vs Spears, is somewhat of an expert on the aughts’ relentless pressure on women to stay tight, taut and sexual. An early montage rips through a horrifying array of the period’s worst impulses:Lindsay Lohan’s figure analyzed on the evening news, celebrities hospitalized for “exhaustion”,Anna Nicole Smithbragging about diet pills on a late-show couch.But the 100-minute film is less an examination of the extreme diet culture that begat something like The Swan – for many, we know it all too well – than a more truthful accounting of what the 32 women who went on the show endured. As numerous contestants and a handful of producers reveal, very little of what was shown on TV in 2004 was accurate or truthful, beyond the physical pain and discomfort of its contestants. (Galán, the show’s creator, on-screen judge and off-screen “mentor”, declined to participate.) As several attest, the initial appeal of the series was, yes, possibly some “free boobs”, but also a genuine chance to improve their self-esteem through fitness, therapy and scarce personal time. “I was juggling it all, taking care of my family financially,” says Beth, a first season participant, in the film. “I was dealing with a lot of emotional baggage at the time, and I needed a change.”View image in fullscreenDr Terry Dubrow prepares a contestant for plastic surgery in a 2004 episode of The Swan.Photograph: Robert Voets/FoxThe reality was, of course, more complicated and less altruistic. While “the original concept of The Swan, as it was told to me, was transforming women’s lives”, a producer named Julee recalls, the entertainment dictates of reality TV (as another producer put it: “we’re gonna take ugly chicks and make them hot”) demanded otherwise. Contestants were isolated from friends, family and themselves – there were no mirrors present for the duration of filming – lest they gain any outside perspective. Nurses or other caretakers were so infrequent the women resorted to changing each other’s bandages, preparing each other’s liquid foods or helping to clean up when, say, one’s lipo continuously leaked on the bed.‘The face doesn’t move’: Hollywood’s obsession with cosmetic surgeries has led to stiffer looks – and performancesRead moreThe women maintained their own scrapbooks and calendars, and agreed to a series of rules familiar to any diet culture survivor’s delusional plan for total metamorphosis: “I am solely responsible for ensuring my time here is a success; I will not see my family or friends; I will follow the plan provided by the swan team of experts; I will go to therapy once a week; I will stick to a strict diet; I will work out six days a week sometimes twice a day; I will work with the swan coach to stay motivated; and I will not see myself in a mirror so I can focus on my internal transformation.”The women were given little choice in what procedures they had done – everything from rhinoplasties to breast augmentation to veneers, as many as six surgeries in 10 hours of anesthesia. Cameras rolled as they woke up from surgery, still groggy from anesthesia, swollen and heavily bandaged. (That is, if they woke up – one second-season contestant whose oxygen levels plummeted after surgery, ending filming, says she still does not know if she underwent chest compressions to survive.) Such grotesque footage, which Carr used judiciously, “hurt my heart, on a human level”, she said. “I don’t think anybody that is coming off of anesthesia who barely knows that they’re conscious could consent to being filmed.”There was virtually no recovery time; within days, the women were required to be in the gym, berated as their post-procedure faces burned, on a strict diet of no more than 1,200 calories a day; by the second season, that allowance was halved, putting the participants in a dangerous and unsustainable calorie deficit. “I think they had to dehumanize us because, ultimately, we were just a job,” says Beth, next to old footage of her giving a thumbs up while completely obscured by medical bandages.View image in fullscreenFormer contestant Kristy Garza in The Swan: Behind the Mirror.Photograph: Courtesy of HuluPerhaps most egregiously – at least, according to the participants – the women were not informed until post-surgery that there would be a pageant, including a lingerie portion and swimsuit competition, that would pit the women against each other. Or, as the show more bluntly put it to viewers, “two average-looking women” face off to survive another week as The Swan.“I don’t think the pageant was ever a part of the original format. I think it was a discussion at Fox that was: ‘What’s the craziest thing we could cook up?’” Carr said, reflecting on the shift from “life transformation” show to post-surgery onstage parade. “It felt like everybody was flinging things at the wall to see how they could get people to react.” As Dr Randal Haworth, one of the show’s designated plastic surgeons, put it when selecting the best candidates for the most intensive surgeries: “you want to see drama”.‘A very paternalistic attitude’: why is female desire still not taken seriously?Read moreEven in an era saturated with fatphobia, fad diets and laxatives, The Swan engendered intense backlash as a new low for reality TV. Its staying power was limited – while the first season premiered to 10 million people, making it America’s self-proclaimed “No 1 makeover show” – viewership fell off precipitously in the second season, which killed the show before it could even see 2005. But it lives on as “a harbinger of what’s to come for our future – in terms of thinness, mental health and basically trying to evaporate”, said Carr. Much of what was said on the show – that physical beauty is power worth sacrificing for, that a few nips and tucks will change your life, that plastic surgery is a form of psychiatry practiced by “interior designers” of the body – has been recycled into ourpresent plastic surgery nightmareof procedures ever more invisible, insidious and extreme, though in sleeker, more humanist-sounding terms. What is the assertion from many an influencer that being thinner just ups your quality of life, if not “nothing tastes as good as skinny feels” by another name? Now, as then, “everyone is quite sadistic when it comes to other people’s looks,” said Carr. “And everybody forgets that the other person is a human being.”Given all that, it is perhaps surprising that almost all of the women say they do not regret participating in The Swan – if only to meet each other. The film ends with “the flock” gathering for a long-overdue reunion that Carr called “one of the greatest days of my life”.“The healing and the joy that comes from a group of women understanding each other is profound,” she said. “You don’t have to change the way you look for somebody else to think you’re beautiful.”The Swan: Behind The Mirror is streaming now on Hulu in the US and on Disney+ in the UK and AustraliaExplore more on these topicsDocumentary filmsReality TVTelevisionUS televisionPlastic surgeryWomenfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: SKF advert review – let’s hope this dull AI Greta Garbo is not the future | Greta Garbo | The Guardian
description: Swedish-American actor exhumed for bizarre, humourless 99 seconds that give us another reason to resent AI
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Swedish-American actor exhumed for bizarre, humourless 99 seconds that give us another reason to resent AI
Content: ‘This Garbo is a bizarre soignée figure, a Stepford robo-star, a Hallmark-greeting-card parody.’Illustration: SKFView image in fullscreen‘This Garbo is a bizarre soignée figure, a Stepford robo-star, a Hallmark-greeting-card parody.’Illustration: SKFGreta GarboReviewSKF advert review – let’s hope this dull AI Greta Garbo is not the futureSwedish-American actor exhumed for bizarre, humourless 99 seconds that give us another reason to resent AIPeter BradshawWed 30 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 02.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePoorGreta Garbo.Perhaps, in life, she thought her final indignity would be the Peter Cook and Dudley Moore TV sketch from 1970, showing Pete as the legendary recluse standing on the back of a flatbed truck as it rumbles through the crowded city streets, shouting at everyone through a megaphone: “I vant to be alone!”Reanimated AI Greta Garbo stars again … in a ball-bearing advertRead moreBut now, 36 years after her death in 1990, there is something worse. As if to give us yet another reason to fear and resent AI, this technology has exhumed Garbo and brought her to a state of bland, mediocre undeadness for a bizarre 99-second TV ad from the Swedish ball-bearings company Svenska Kullagerfabriken (SKF), in which the screen legend, dressed in a silk blouse and stylish slacks, key-lit like a movie star, at first in dreamy profile-silhouette and then standing by a stool and prefacing her script by saying movie-type things like “Are we rolling?”, drones out her appreciation for this very boring industrial product. At the end, we get an odd, stilted sort of joke about her well-known yearning for solitude.There is a reason for it. In 1921, the 15-year-old future screen icon, then known as Greta Gustafsson, really did briefly appear in a promotional film for SKF. (This appears to have been an offshoot for the women’s clothing commercials she was doing at the time for Stockholm’s PUB department store, which got her into the movies.)The AI Greta Garbo is a bizarre soignée figure, a Stepford robo-star, a Hallmark-greeting-card parody of the icy hauteur, distraite sensuality and deadpan comedy that Garbo projected in life. The AI Garbo is like the classiest ever presenter of a TV shopping channel, purring her way through a dull and humourless script that seeks to create a brand synergy between the frictionless ball-bearings manufactured by SKF and what the company imagines to be Garbo’s own all-important smoothness. But Garbo’s impact rested on something other than smoothness. “One of my first films was for SKF and now I’m back for my last,” AI Greta remarks.Her last? Well, this film is supposedly derived not from any of Garbo’s own movie appearances, but reportedly from images and pictures that exist elsewhere. This perhaps means that SKF need not negotiate with any of the corporate movie studios – who might be rather chary of people making free with Garbo’s image, which is part of their copyright-protected IP – but only with Garbo’s distant relatives, who might well be more amenable. And they say that they are not averse to the idea of licensing the AI Greta Garbo for other movies. We need Mrs Merton to ask what first attracted them to that idea. Perhaps Humphrey Bogart, Gary Cooper and Rita Hayworth also have distant great-great-great nephews and nieces who can be induced to greenlight similar projects.Let’s hope this dull AI Garbo is not the way of the future. Guardrails were never more badly needed.Explore more on these topicsGreta GarboAI (artificial intelligence)SwedenTelevisionreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Cotton Queen review – mystery, matriarchs and magic in pioneering Sudanese debut | Movies | The Guardian
description: Suzannah Mirghani’s first feature contains a powerful performance by Rabha Mohamed Mahmoud as a village’s elder woman and tackles the long shadow of British imperialism and women’s rights
Author: Cath Clarke
Headline: Suzannah Mirghani’s first feature contains a powerful performance by Rabha Mohamed Mahmoud as a village’s elder woman and tackles the long shadow of British imperialism and women’s rights
Content: Can she shape her own future? … Rabha Mohamed Mahmoud as Al-Sit and Mihad Murtada as Nafisa in Cotton Queen.Photograph: Frida MarzoukView image in fullscreenCan she shape her own future? … Rabha Mohamed Mahmoud as Al-Sit and Mihad Murtada as Nafisa in Cotton Queen.Photograph: Frida MarzoukMoviesReviewCotton Queen review – mystery, matriarchs and magic in pioneering Sudanese debutSuzannah Mirghani’s first feature contains a powerful performance by Rabha Mohamed Mahmoud as a village’s elder woman and tackles the long shadow of British imperialism and women’s rightsCath ClarkeWed 30 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 06.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Idecide my past,” says a village matriarch in this intriguingly political and poetic drama from Suzannah Mirghani, making her feature debut – and with it becoming the first Sudanese woman to direct a feature. (She was forced to cancel the original shoot in Sudan whenwar broke out in 2023, moving production to Egypt.) It’s a film with things to say about the long shadow of the British empire, neocolonialism, women’s rights and female genital mutilation. But it mostly says it all without undermining its sense of mystery and shivers of magic realism.We’re in present daySudan, where village elder Al-Sit (Rabha Mohamed Mahmoud) is an iron-willed woman not to be messed with. Everyone knows the story of how as a young girl she ran the British out of town; small children in the village gleefully tell the story of how she slaughtered every single last one of them. Can it possibly be true? The trauma of her past is at the centre of the film, and Mahmoud’s witchy performance, fierce and powerful, is utterly compelling.Al-Sit is arranging the marriage of her beloved 15-year-old granddaughter Nafisa (Mihad Murtada). But Nafisa’s mother has another husband in mind – businessman Nadir (Hassan Kasala), who is of Sudanese heritage, but grew up abroad. He arrives in the village to flog farmers genetically modified cotton seeds manufactured by a multinational – and there is perhaps a sense here of history repeating itself, international interests trying to control local resources.Poetry-writing Nafisa is appalled by both husband options. She has a teenage crush on a sweet kid who grows onions. But while fault lines are set for a showdown, the film is not really about who she should marry, but her ability to shape her own future. It’s not perfect, and its tonal shifts don’t always work, but you’re unlikely to see another film like it this year.Cotton Queen is in UK and Irish cinemas from 2 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsSudanColonialismAfricaMiddle East and north AfricaWomen's rights and gender equalityreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Rapture review – cult Spanish horror is a deeply strange cheese dream of cinemania | Movies | The Guardian
description: Pedro Almodóvar provides a vocal cameo and his style can be traced back to this influential film
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Pedro Almodóvar provides a vocal cameo and his style can be traced back to this influential film
Content: Unnerving … Rapture.Photograph: Courtesy of MUBIView image in fullscreenUnnerving … Rapture.Photograph: Courtesy of MUBIMoviesReviewRapture review – cult Spanish horror is a deeply strange cheese dream of cinemaniaPedro Almodóvar provides a vocal cameo and his style can be traced back to this influential filmPeter BradshawWed 30 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis cult supernatural mystery from 1979 is a deeply strange cheese dream of a film fromSpain, in which almost the entire opening 10 minutes unfolds in a jittery quiet. There are some longueurs and some pop-eyed silent-movie acting from one of its leads, yes, but also a deeply unnerving, enveloping atmosphere of dread.At least some of its fascination stems from the marginal involvement of the youngPedro Almodóvar, who did voice-overdubbing for one female character. Director Iván Zulueta was to maintain his connection with Almodóvar from then on and much of Almodóvar’s procedure can be traced back to this influential film: the rapture for movies (what a character here calls “cinemania”), the double-stranded narrative, the queer euphoria and the importance of extended flashbacks.Rapture, or Arrebato, is, without acknowledging it, a kind of vampire film and a film about addiction (it bears comparison, incidentally, with Abel Ferrara’s The Addiction). Eusebio Poncela plays José, a failing horror movie director with a heroin addiction, trying and failing to get a new film off the ground called Wolf Man or The Curse of the Wolf Man, and living in co-dependent squalor with Ana, played by Cecilia Roth – who was later, of course, to become a totemic repertory player for Almodóvar. José needs a country house to film in and his garrulous ex Marta (Marta Fernández Muro) offers to take him to a handsome property owned by her Aunt Carmen (Carmen Giralt) to scout the location. It is there that they come across her eccentric cousin Pedro (Will More), whose drug addiction is quite as bad as José’s.Pedro spends all day stalking around the grounds wearing a heavy overcoat in the sultry heat, talking to himself and shooting his interminable Super 8 home movies. Having declared José to be a kindred spirit, Pedro fatefully gets in contact with him after their acquaintanceship has been established (which we see in flashback), trying to convey his own obsessive passion for film which has been triggered by a kind of creative breakthrough. He has attached a timer to his cine-camera, enabling him to take eerie time-lapse movies of his home life and his night-time roaming, particularly in the big city after he moved to Madrid. But most weirdly of all he has taken to shooting Warholian films of himself asleep during which his time-lapse camera seems to have developed a mind of its own, adding strange single red frames. Pedro is convinced that the act of filming is causing in him a rapture which cancels the agony of addiction, and his generalweltschmerz.Rapture is not precisely a scary movie: most of its conventional scariness is saved for the final five minutes, although the moment in which a red-eyed Betty Boop doll appears to make a TV show speed up is disturbing. It is more about the sublime yet unwholesome and uncanny experience of movie immersion, of never seeing daylight, like a vampire. In a bizarre way, Pedro’s film obsession redeems José’s bleary professional disillusion; the washed-up director had before this been said to have a “magnetic halo” around him, created by his growing hatred of making films, although only a true believer would have any sort of halo at all. There are some very startling images: the shot of a penis becoming erect is juxtaposed with a cigarette’s long curling ash as it burns out, in a horribly inspired pairing.The last time I saw Poncela on screen was inJuan Carlos Fresnadillo’s mysterious chiller Intact from 2001; there he played a man working for Max von Sydow’s casino owner, employed to use his mysterious gift for ill fortune to drain good luck away from gamblers enjoying winning streaks. He has the same haughty, doomy aura here.Rapture is on Mubi from 1 October.Explore more on these topicsFilmHorror filmsSpainPedro AlmodóvarEuropereviewsShareReuse this content

title: How Deep Is Your Love review – under the sea at Earth’s last frontier with the Psychedelic Elvis Worm  | Movies | The Guardian
description: Film-maker Eleanor Mortimer accompanies a scientific expedition to the deep Pacific, where new creatures are abundant yet threatened by sea mining
Author: Cath Clarke
Headline: Film-maker Eleanor Mortimer accompanies a scientific expedition to the deep Pacific, where new creatures are abundant yet threatened by sea mining
Content: Wait – isn’t that a Headless Chicken Monster? … still from How Deep Is Your Love.Photograph: Luna Films, Ngauruhoe Films.View image in fullscreenWait – isn’t that a Headless Chicken Monster? … still from How Deep Is Your Love.Photograph: Luna Films, Ngauruhoe Films.MoviesReviewHow Deep Is Your Love review – under the sea at Earth’s last frontier with the Psychedelic Elvis WormFilm-maker Eleanor Mortimer accompanies a scientific expedition to the deep Pacific, where new creatures are abundant yet threatened by sea miningCath ClarkeWed 30 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor the marine biologists in this whimsical eco-documentary, the answer is about 5000 metres down. In the lab, we watch them observing, describing, and classifying the bonkers-looking creatures that survive in the freezing-cold waters of the deep sea: blobby little sea pigs and alien glow-in-the-dark sea cucumbers. It seems 90% of life in the deep sea has yet to be named, explains film-maker Eleanor Mortimer in her quirky voiceover. It is the last frontier of exploration on Earth.Mortimer accompanies a team of scientists on an expedition to the eastern Pacific. It takes the ship’s robot four hours to descend the four kilometres to the ocean floor where it trundles along, grabber claw at the ready. A biologist explains that 80% of what they bring up to the surface is new to science. And one of the film’s pleasures is watching the wonderstruck awe on their faces as they clap eyes on never-before-seen creatures. The process of acquiring a Latin name for a new discovery can take years, so in the meantime scientists give them excellent temporary names like the Headless Chicken Monster and the Psychedelic Elvis Worm.In truth, it’s a niche-feeling film, gentle and playfully curious, but an environmental story lurks beneath: deep sea mining. The ocean floor is covered in nodules – lumps the size of baked potatoes – that are rich in metals and minerals. They take millions of years to form, and significantly less time to mine. We listen in to a frustrating debate at the International Seabed Authority about whether mining should be permitted. How high this new eco-worry should rank on the spreadsheet of doom and gloom is as yet unknown. The environmental impact of mining is not yet established. But add it to the list.How Deep Is Your Love is in UK and Irish cinemas from 2 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsMarine lifeConservationMiningWildlifereviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘They’ll never bring us dowwwwwwwn!’ Wicked’s stars pick their favourite songs from the smash hit | Stage | The Guardian
description: The musical powerhouse has spawned huge hits, but which do its troupers love to belt out – even for the 1,700th time? From Broadway legend Idina Menzel to composer Stephen Schwartz, they reveal all
Author: Miriam Gillinson
Headline: The musical powerhouse has spawned huge hits, but which do its troupers love to belt out – even for the 1,700th time? From Broadway legend Idina Menzel to composer Stephen Schwartz, they reveal all
Content: ‘I asked if I could take it up an octave since the whole song is soaring’ … Idina Menzel as ElphabaPhotograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘I asked if I could take it up an octave since the whole song is soaring’ … Idina Menzel as ElphabaPhotograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianStage‘They’ll never bring us dowwwwwwwn!’ Wicked’s stars pick their favourite songs from the smash hitThe musical powerhouse has spawned huge hits, but which do its troupers love to belt out – even for the 1,700th time? From Broadway legend Idina Menzel to composer Stephen Schwartz, they reveal allInterviews byMiriam GillinsonWed 30 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 01.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDefying GravityIdina Menzeloriginated the role of Elphaba, the witch of the west who turns out not to be so wicked (but still very green). Shewon a Tonyon Broadway, starred in the West End run and made a cheeky cameo in the recent film versionI’ll never forget the exhilaration I felt the first time I sang Defying Gravity in dress rehearsal. All the lights were as they should be. The smoke machine was blowing. The orchestra was playing. I was locked into my safety belt and I started to rise up over the theatre. To have that incredible moment and to see how the audience leapt to their feet – I felt so proud but I also just wanted to cry.I was part of the developmental process of writing Wicked for four years and stood at a piano with [composer and lyricist]Stephen Schwartzmany a time, being introduced to new ideas and songs – often written just the night before. He came to really understand my voice. Not just how high I could hit a note but where it sat emotionally. Originally, Defying Gravity didn’t go up an octave at the end. It stayed in this low place. So I asked Stephen if I could take it up an octave – the whole song is soaring, I said, and I have it in me to go up there: “Looook to the western skiiiiiiy!” I do take credit for that change.double quotation markI botched it in my audition. I said: ‘I’m going to do that again.’ Then I nailed itThe final note is actually easy for me. It’s like a release. There are other notes I find much harder. Singing notes on an “E” vowel is not easy: “Bring meeeee down”, that’s really tricky. I actually botched that note in my call-back audition. But instead of falling to pieces, I looked at the accompanist and said: “I’m going to do that again.” And then I just took all this angst and frustration at not being perfect and nailed it. Joe Mantello [director of Wicked on Broadway] always told me that’s how he knew I was going to be their witch – because I had this power and ferocity about me. That’s why, to this day, whenever young people ask me for advice, I always tell them not to fear their mistakes. Embrace those moments.Thank GoodnessZizi Strallenplays Glinda the Good in the currentWest Endcast. She’s used to stepping into the shoes of iconic roles – and hinting at cracks that lie beneath a pristine surface – after a breakout performance as Mary PoppinsView image in fullscreen‘I channel my mistakes when I sing Thank Goodness’ … Zizi Strallen as Glinda the Good.Photograph: Matt CrockettWhatever you’re going through in your life, Wicked somehow manages to hit a nerve. Everyone can relate to not feeling accepted for who they truly are or trying to figure out different parts of their personality. I’ve definitely gone through phases where I’ve made mistakes or said the wrong thing – so I channel all of that when I sing.Thank Goodness shows the journey Glinda goes on throughout the whole show. It tells the audience that’s she’s struggling with the prospect of fame and recognition – and all the things that come with being Glinda the Good – but also wanting to stand up for her friend Elphaba and for what’s right. She’s getting everything she ever dreamed of but at what cost? That’s a beautiful arc for any actor to play: to start a song at one point and finish at an entirely different emotional one.It’s wonderful to perform but very difficult to learn. The rhythms are really different to how you think they’re going to be. Stephen wrote it so that it’s sung exactly the way you would speak it, with little gaps here and there: “There’s a kind of a sort of – cost.” It’s similar to the way that Sondheim writes. It only really made sense to me when I sang it with the full orchestra and their rhythms accompanying me.Dancing Through LifeJordan LitzplayedFiyero, the student who gets romantically entangled with Glinda and Elphaba, more than 1,700 times in the US. He makes his West End debut in the roleView image in fullscreen‘More swagger! More confidence!’ … Jordan Litz as Fiyero.Photograph: Matt CrockettDancing Through Life wasn’t always in the show. It was originally a song called Which Way Is the Party? The lyrics were a little sleazy: “Which way is the next keg of winkie beer?” It was all very frat boy and didn’t have nearly the same carefree attitude. You can hear they kept some stuff from the original number – the intro and the bridge – but the rest of the song is much more light and easy.This was initially the hardest song for me to do because it’s the one that’s least like me. Growing up, I wasn’t the super-cool popular kid. I was 5ft 4in in my freshman year, singing soprano in my high-school choir and wearing oversized trainers. Finding the confidence to play Fiyero didn’t come naturally. It was always the song I got the most notes on during rehearsals for the Broadway run. More swagger! More confidence!For the first year, performing it was a constant battle – trying to find that carefree confidence. And that struggle would show up in my dancing. My moves weren’t big enough or sharp enough. You’re surrounded by these incredible dancers and it’s very easy to shrink into yourself and not commit. It took a lot of support from people around me, convincing me that I have it inside myself. I was fighting against the person I envisioned myself to be, growing up, and who I actually am today. That’s probably why it’s become my favourite number: it feels like the song that I’ve learned the most from.The Wizard and IMusical supervisorStephen Oremusconducted and helped to craft the Broadway premiere of WickedView image in fullscreen‘It’s an amazingly simple song but brilliantly written and executed’ … Wicked musical supervisor Stephen Oremus.Photograph: Bruce Glikas/WireImageThe Wizard and I was Stephen’s third try at a song in that spot in the show and it unlocked Elphaba’s journey. The first try felt very earnest and wide-eyed. It was a beautiful and heartfelt song called Making Good, about this young green girl who just wanted to do good things. But it wasn’t quite multi-layered enough. The second attempt was written after Idina was cast. It was a little bit more soaring and it suited Idina’s voice and personality more: it was the next step towards giving the number more of a sweeping grand gesture. Then in the third version, Stephen just hit it. He was able to combine everything good from the other takes and make it work. It’s an amazingly simple song but brilliantly written and executed.The way we built the orchestrations, you can feel the excitement and anticipation of the character. The colours and flow of the song are relatively simple as Elphaba’s working out her thoughts and then it all shifts when she gets to that “unlimited” bridge. The orchestration gets dreamy and really expansive musically. Elphaba throws her arm out and allows herself to really feel for the first time. You’re seeing this very cerebral and intense girl start to get excited about the possibility of it all. It’s overwhelmingly beautiful to me.For GoodThe offers from Hollywood came flooding in afterGregory Maguirewrote his novel Wicked, a spin on L Frank Baum’s The Wizard of Oz. But it wasn’t until composer and lyricistStephen Schwartzsuggested setting it to song that an adaptation felt possible – and Wicked’s musical journey beganView image in fullscreen‘Stop right there – you just gave me the song’s title’ … Schwartz.Photograph: Charles Sykes/Invision/APThe final song between Elphaba and Glinda was one that I approached very cautiously. I knew it was going to be the heart of the show. If we got it right, we had our emotional ending. If we didn’t, it could undercut everything that had come before. So I phoned my collaborator, Winnie Holzman, and talked to her about this final meeting. What kind of things would they say to one another? At one point Winnie said: “They’ve had such an enormous impact on each other – they’ve changed each other for good.” “Stop right there,” I said. “You’ve just given me the title.”‘They changed my ending, I felt aghast’: how we made WickedRead moreI always knew what the song was going to feel like. I wanted something that was heartfelt and uncovered. Completely vulnerable. A lot of Glinda’s songs are about presenting a specific version of herself to the public. But I wanted this song to feel like a true expression from the heart. Then I started to think about the lyrics. My daughter Jessica was visiting at the time. She’d always had a deep friendship with a woman, Sarah, whom she first met when they were six or seven. So I sat down with Jess and I said: “Imagine you’re only going to see Sarah one last time. What would you say?” Jess started to talk about people coming into each other’s lives for a reason, about helping and hurting each other and about forgiveness. I wrote it all down and that was pretty much the entire first verse of For Good. I think that’s one of the reasons the song has such an impact – because people intuitively feel the truth of it.Wickedis playing in London, New York, on a North American tour, and in Japan and KoreaExplore more on these topicsStageMusicalsTheatreWest EndIdina MenzelStephen SchwartzBroadwayfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: All at Sea review – faked death of ‘canoe man’ inspires waves of intrigue | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Fictionalising the true story of John Darwin, Alison Carr’s gripping two-hander follows the unexpected consequences of its antihero’s bid to escape debts
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: Fictionalising the true story of John Darwin, Alison Carr’s gripping two-hander follows the unexpected consequences of its antihero’s bid to escape debts
Content: Fleurs du mal … Phil Corbitt in All at Sea at Live theatre, Newcastle.Photograph: Von Fox PromotionsView image in fullscreenFleurs du mal … Phil Corbitt in All at Sea at Live theatre, Newcastle.Photograph: Von Fox PromotionsTheatreReviewAll at Sea review – faked death of ‘canoe man’ inspires waves of intrigueLive theatre, NewcastleFictionalising the true story of John Darwin, Alison Carr’s gripping two-hander follows the unexpected consequences of its antihero’s bid to escape debtsMark FisherWed 30 Sep 2026 08.53 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 08.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt sounds like a good plan. With credit cards maxed out, Colin Wilson will set off in his canoe and never come back. Once he is presumed dead, his wife, Deborah, will claim the life insurance. Pension and mortgage payouts will follow. Meanwhile, Colin will go into hiding until they can make a fresh start.View image in fullscreenA marriage capsized … Sarah Belcher and Phil Corbitt in All at Sea.Photograph: Von Fox PromotionsInspired by the true story of“canoe man” John Darwin, Alison Carr’s two-hander looks as though it will head into the sitcom territory ofCan You Keep a Secret?Like that BBC comedy, in which Mark Heap does a bad job at hiding, All at Sea considers the hurdles of staying out of sight. Where to go if someone comes around? What if the phone rings and you accidentally answer? How to stay sane?But unlike that show, Carr plays it for drama, not laughs. The further we go into Maria Crocker’s production, the more the challenges are not just practical but psychological. At first, this is primarily to do with Colin’s life in limbo. Played by Phil Corbitt, he is the captain relegated to the subs bench, at once controlling and ineffectual. It drives him to distraction.But the real intrigue is what happens to Deborah. Played by Sarah Belcher, she remains engaged with the world. Having gone through the motions of grieving, she finds herself living an emotionally independent life. It is as if Colin really were dead.While nothing changes in the prison of their home – in a functional if too literal design by Hannah Sibai – things continue to evolve for Deborah: the people she meets, the clothes she wears, the self-worth she feels. Slowly, subtly, the man she loved looks ever more patronising, jealously keeping her in check.Corbitt and Belcher are excellent at the push-pull of contradictory emotions, their troubling chemistry making the play’s grisly conclusion feel necessary.AtLive theatre, Newcastle, until 10 October and atStephen Joseph theatre, Scarborough, 16–31 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTheatreStephen Joseph theatreJohn Darwin canoe disappearancereviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Pussycat Dolls review – Nicole Scherzinger’s star power dominates fraught reunion | Music | The Guardian
description: First announced in 2019 and now launching with just three of the original lineup, the Dolls whip up a whirlwind of hair-flipping and put on a decent spectacle
Author: Alim Kheraj
Headline: First announced in 2019 and now launching with just three of the original lineup, the Dolls whip up a whirlwind of hair-flipping and put on a decent spectacle
Content: Back in formation … the Pussycat Dolls perform at Utilita Arena, Birmingham.Photograph: Jason Sheldon/Junction10/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenBack in formation … the Pussycat Dolls perform at Utilita Arena, Birmingham.Photograph: Jason Sheldon/Junction10/ShutterstockMusicReviewThe Pussycat Dolls review – Nicole Scherzinger’s star power dominates fraught reunionUtilita Arena, BirminghamFirst announced in 2019 and now launching with just three of the original lineup, the Dolls whip up a whirlwind of hair-flipping and put on a decent spectacleAlim KherajWed 30 Sep 2026 08.08 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 13.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe road to the Pussycat Dolls’ comeback tour has been fraught. Originally announced in 2019 with all but one of the group’s original members on board, the pandemic and then a legal dispute, led to its cancellation. After a few years of silence, three members –Nicole Scherzinger, Ashley Roberts and Kimberly Wyatt – shared plans for a 53-date world tour as a trio. Poor ticket sales nixed the US leg, though, while Maga-supporting former member Jessica Sutta alleged she was left out of the reunion because she was viewed as “a liability” (the group did not comment).Does a girlband ostensibly created as a dance troupe work as a trio? While Scherzinger’s voice pushed them into pop stardom – they scored six UK Top 3 hits in their initial 2005-09 run – their appeal was largely the fierce group choreography. On stage in Birmingham, they give it their best go. The nearly two-hour show is a whirlwind of hair-flipping, booty-shaking and synchronised strutting. Throughout When I Grow Up, Beep and I Don’t Need a Man, Scherzinger is still on lead vocals, predictably so after her recent Tony award-winning run on Broadway in Sunset Blvd. Roberts and Wyatt are given some time to shine, though: their solos amid the clacking pots-and-pans percussion of Wait a Minute feel pointed, as if to say that, yes, their mics are on.View image in fullscreenEntertaining, uneven … the Pussycat Dolls.Photograph: Jason Sheldon/Junction10/ShutterstockEach member also gets their own solo section to varying degrees of success. Wyatt’s involves a DJ set, while Roberts, showing off her dancing skills, is more restrained. Scherzinger gets the most airtime, beginning with a vocally impressive version of Sunset Blvd’s As If We Never Said Goodbye complete with X Factor-style cascading pyrotechnics, before her white gown is unwound like toilet paper for a breathless joyride through her solo material. Thundering Eurodance ballad Don’t Hold Your Breath and the cacophonous EDM of Wet are particular highlights.Pussycat dolls star Ashley Roberts looks back: ‘We had to be resilient – if your toe breaks, you still do the show’Read moreIt’s all very entertaining, but uneven, with Roberts and Wyatt struggling against Scherzinger’s imperious star power. With more members, this inequality may not have mattered, and in the final act – especially during honking 2020 single React and the slinky Buttons, which features a dance break by students from Wyatt’s dance academy – the scales seem to just about level out. Whether this imbalance is sustainable remains unknown, but it works for tonight’s spectacle, at least.ThePussycat Dollsplay Leeds First Direct Bank Arena, 2 October; then touring UK until 13 OctoberThis article was amended on 30 September 2026. Owing to a misunderstanding, an earlier version referred to Kimberly Wyatt playing a “faux DJ set”; to clarify, this was a live performance and not a recording.Explore more on these topicsMusicNicole ScherzingerPussycat DollsPop and rocklive music reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Renoir and Love review – the happiest exhibition of the year? Pourquoi pas! | Pierre-Auguste Renoir | The Guardian
description: Grab your straw boater – and revel in these light-as-souffle masterpieces that celebrate life’s pleasures, from picnics to dances to frolics in the bushes
Author: Jonathan Jones
Headline: Grab your straw boater – and revel in these light-as-souffle masterpieces that celebrate life’s pleasures, from picnics to dances to frolics in the bushes
Content: A flickering fragile wonder … Dance at the Moulin de la Galette, 1876, by Pierre-Auguste Renoir.Photograph: © Musée d'Orsay, Dist. RMN-Grand Palais / Patrice SchmidtView image in fullscreenA flickering fragile wonder … Dance at the Moulin de la Galette, 1876, by Pierre-Auguste Renoir.Photograph: © Musée d'Orsay, Dist. RMN-Grand Palais / Patrice SchmidtPierre-Auguste RenoirReviewRenoir and Love review – the happiest exhibition of the year? Pourquoi pas!National Gallery, LondonGrab your straw boater – and revel in these light-as-souffle masterpieces that celebrate life’s pleasures, from picnics to dances to frolics in the bushesJonathan JonesWed 30 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 13.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘They knew how to enjoy themselves,” David Hockney once told me, gleefully pointing out the cigarette and cigar butts littering the ground under Renoir’s dancers. There are broken clay-pipes too beneath the swirling pink skirts and blue trousers of the couple in his tall, narrow 1883 canvas Dance at Bougival as they bring their faces close, placing their arms around each other and pirouetting in the soft, airy space Renoir makes you feel as well as see. It’s an outdoor afternoon dance enclosed by fluffy, lime-coloured trees. A couple sitting at a table get friendlier with each swig of beer.And oh, the lunches! Renoir seems to have invented the slow French lunch, relaxed and liquid, that launched a thousand bistro daydreams. In After the Luncheon, another one to delight Hockney, we see a white-clothed, open air table neatly arranged with porcelain coffee cups, carafes and glasses – and a woman sipping a liqueur while the bearded man she’s lunching with lights up, savouring the moment as his cigarette end glows fire-red against the pale blues, whites and silvers. The Lunch at the Restaurant Fournaise (The Rowers’ Lunch) lingers on the same climactic moment, one man lounging back in tobacco reverie while the lovers or about-to-be-lovers on the other side of the table chat soulfully.View image in fullscreenLove is everywhere you look … Dance at Bougival, 1883, by Pierre-Auguste Renoir.Photograph: © Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, Picture FundPierre-Auguste Renoir, who was born in 1841 and lived until 1919, saw the height and fall of the French bourgeois civilisation whose pleasures he so infectiously celebrates. His son, the film director Jean Renoir, revisits his father’s world with the sadness of hindsight in his screen recreation of an impressionist picnic,Partie de Campagne: there you know the happiness is fragile. But in Pierre-Auguste’s paintings, there’s no punishment. Nobody gets syphilis or drinks themselves to death, or drowns in the Seine. This is the happiest art exhibition of the year.Et pourquoi pas? Renoir, this perfect exhibition lays bare, is the most radical of the impressionists, which will come as a shock to anyone who sees him as the soppiest and most kitsch. Impressionism started as a pejorative label chucked at a loose group of artists in 1870s France who tried to capture modern life in motion. It is Renoir who most enthusiastically embraces this as a philosophy of life itself. He doesn’t just paint the changing light of the passing moment. He urges us to live in it.This ideal of enjoying life as it comes makes his masterpiece Dance at the Moulin de la Galette, lent by the Musée d’Orsay, as grand as a history painting and as light as a souffle. As hosts of people take pleasure in each other’s company in this open air hangout in Montmartre, their flirtations, longings and consolations are caught in a dappled, mobile dance of golden light and cool shadow. The light is so ethereally pervasive it turns the crowded canvas into a flickering fragile wonder, a brief moment of revelation that you might have, sitting in this crowd silently for a second and seeing a blue-and-white dress, a straw boater, a woman’s sensitive face as she puts an arm around her friend, a young man’s open admiration as he looks at her.The exhibition is called Renoir and Love, and love is everywhere you look. On a rainy street under the canopy of umbrellas, a man looks dotingly on a woman who appears lost in her own daydream. In what seems at first a simple painting of a boatyard by the Seine, View of Bougival, we actually get to spy on a lovers’ tryst: the woman lowers her parasol, letting her dog play in the sun, as she converses deeply with her beloved.View image in fullscreenPerhaps she’s married … The Promenade, 1870, by Pierre-Auguste Renoir.Photograph: The J. Paul Getty Museum, Los Angeles, CaliforniaIt’s not all heterosexuality either. The curators cite a story by Maupassant to suggest that The Skiff, in which one woman rows another on the glittering, hallucinogenic, light-kissed water, may be a lesbian scene. Who knows? But there is no question that Renoir, like Maupassant and Zola, sees women as autonomous characters. In Place Clichy he focuses so exclusively on the flushed face of a woman in a furry coat and hat about to cross the road that the crowd behind her become blurred. It’s a cinematic close up from before the age of film – no wonder his son went into the movies.Renoir paints the moment but he is also a storyteller. Almost every lunch, rowing party and stroll in the park feels like a languid set-up for what will follow. Couples, or solitary women, in theatre boxes as the show is about to start fascinate him. Parks too are stages. The Promenade was painted in 1876 but recreates the 18th-century love scenes of Watteau as a man leads a well-dressed woman by the hand into the bushes. She looks uncertain. Perhaps she’s married. Or perhaps here is the menace Renoir usually doesn’t see.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toArt WeeklyYour weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitionsEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRenoir can strike some as a soft touch, especially when you compare him with the tough, ironic realism of Manet. He also went off later in his career. The National Gallery acknowledges this by including his anti-impressionist, nude indulgenceThe Great Bathers. The work’s fun in its way – but it’s the early Renoir who shines here as a truly great modern artist. Let’s remember the good times. Be happy, be in love,mes amis.AtNational Gallery, London, from 3 OctoberExplore more on these topicsPierre-Auguste RenoirArtPaintingExhibitionsNational GalleryreviewsShareReuse this content

title: How to turn gherkin brine into a savoury ice-cream – recipe | Food | The Guardian
description: This sweet-and-sour combo is possibly one of the quirkiest flavours out there – epic served with waffles and bacon, it’s one for true pickle fanatics
Author: Tom Hunt
Headline: This sweet-and-sour combo is possibly one of the quirkiest flavours out there – epic served with waffles and bacon, it’s one for true pickle fanatics
Content: Tom Hunt's pickled cucumber and vodka ice-cream.Photograph: Tom Hunt/The GuardianView image in fullscreenTom Hunt's pickled cucumber and vodka ice-cream.Photograph: Tom Hunt/The GuardianWaste notFoodHow to turn gherkin brine into a savoury ice-cream – recipeThis sweet-and-sour combo is possibly one of the quirkiest flavours out there – epic served with waffles and bacon, it’s one for true pickle fanaticsTom HuntWed 30 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhile researching gherkins for aFood Filter columnlast year, I came acrossKühne’s recipe for pickled cucumber ice-creamand couldn’t resist. Niche, I know, but I’ll bet there are a lot of gherkin fanatics out there who’d be willing to give it a go. If not, the cocktail I’ve used as inspiration might well suffice. The pickleback is made with pickle juice and a spirit such as whisky, tequila or, my favourite, vodka, and that same punchy, sweet-and-sour combination comes together to make possibly the quirkiest ice-cream flavour you ever come across. Delicious in a cone and topped with a gherkin, and out of this world when served with waffles, bacon and maple syrup.Pickled cucumber and vodka ice-creamThis is one for the true gherkin fanatic, with a wild and funky flavour that tricks the mind with a rollercoaster of unexpected tastes. It’s sweet and dilly, but also tart and sour, with a lingering complexity from all the spices used to make the pickles. Fortified with a classic, creamy custard base, it’s best served with savoury waffles.1 egg70g sugar100ml milk250ml double cream10g dill, finely chopped10ml pickle juice20ml vodka(or rum, tequila or whisky)4 ice-cream cones, to serve4 pickles, to serveIn a bowl, whisk the egg, sugar, milk and cream until well combined, then pour into a thick saucepan and cook, stirring continuously, over a very low heat until the custard thickens enough to coat the back of the spoon. (Take care not to let it catch on the bottom, but, if it does, don’t fret: simply pour the custard through a fine sieve without scraping the bottom of the pan.) Take off the heat, stir in the dill and pickle juice, then stir in the vodka.Blend smooth, then churn in an ice-cream machine or transfer to an airtight container and freeze for at least five hours, stirring every 30 minutes to break up any ice crystals. Serve at once, or, if serving the next day or thereafter, pop the ice-cream in the fridge for 30-45 minutes (or leave it out at room temperature for 15 minutes) to soften. Serve in cones and topped with a gherkin.Explore more on these topicsFoodWaste notFood wasteIce-cream and sorbetSpiritsPickling, fermenting and preservingVegetablesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Cullen skink pies, vegetarian haggis and chippy fritters: Ali Stoner’s recipes for twists on Scottish classics | Food | The Guardian
description: Scots have a rich food history that’s been passed down through generations. Here are my modern takes on traditional Celtic staples
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Scots have a rich food history that’s been passed down through generations. Here are my modern takes on traditional Celtic staples
Content: Ali Stoner’s cullen skink bake.Photograph: Ola O Smit/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Lilli Gavin.View image in fullscreenAli Stoner’s cullen skink bake.Photograph: Ola O Smit/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Lilli Gavin.FoodCullen skink pies, vegetarian haggis and chippy fritters: Ali Stoner’s recipes for twists on Scottish classicsScots have a rich food history that’s been passed down through generations. Here are my modern takes on traditional Celtic staplesAli StonerWed 30 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere is a depth and history to Scotland’s food that reaches far beyond deep-fried Mars bars or urban myths about haggis. Kitchens were humble and full of life – recipes passed by word of mouth, scraps of paper shared between friends, generations stitching together simple meals. I’m lucky enough that my mum taught me how a potato, a handful of oatmeal and a bit of salt and butter could make a mealandhold a story, but life changes – new ingredients arrive, we move away, time grows shorter – and, sometimes, those simple, comforting recipes drift out of reach. Today’s dishes began as a keepsake for my children – to save old recipes, to record a feeling of home – but also as an invitation to discover what happens when memory meets invention.Cullen skink bake (pictured top)The starting point for these smoked fish pies is basically a cullen skink soup, which I thicken to make the filling. Traditional cullen skink relies on Scottish smoked haddock for its flavour. There is just nothing else like it, though Shetland smoked cod also works really well here. Finish these wee pies with a grating of sharp cheddar. Delicious.Prep15 minCook1 hr 20 min, plus cooling timeMakes4 pies15gunsalted butter, plus 1 knob extra for fryingOlive oil, for frying100gonions, peeled and finely choppedSalt andblack pepper, to taste250gpotatoes(use a good all-rounder such as maris piper or king edward), peeled and cut into 1cm cubes200mlwhole milk250ggood (ie, undyed) smoked haddock, or smoked cod, cut into bite-sized pieces15g plain flour1 tbsp chopped chives1 tbsp chopped flat-leaf parsley1 tsp dijon mustard1 standard 320g sheet ready-rolled all-butter shortcrust pastry, or puff pastry (27cm × 35cm)Gratedcheddar, to finish1 egg yolk mixed with a little milkMelt the knob of butter and a drizzle of oil in a large saucepan on a medium heat. Add the onions and a pinch of salt, and saute on a low to medium heat for about five minutes, to soften. Add the cubed potatoes, keep the heat low, cover and sweat for 10 or so minutes, until the potatoes start to soften but are still a little hard. Stir in the milk, lay the fish on top of the potatoes, then cover again and simmer for 10 minutes more, until you can easily press the point of a knife into the potato: you want them to retain their shape, rather than be mushy. Using a slotted spoon, carefully lift the fish, potatoes and onion out of the hot milk, then pour the liquid into a jug.Melt the 15g butter in the same pan, then stir in the flour and cook on a low heat for a couple of minutes. Pour in the reserved poaching liquid, stir for about five minutes, until the mixture thickens, then take off the heat and carefully fold in the fish, potatoes and onions. Add the herbs, mustardand black pepper to taste, then leave to cool.Heat the oven to 220C (200C fan)/425F/gas7. Lay out the pastry on a lightly flouredwork surface and cut it into four strips. Pile the filling on one half of each strip, leaving enough of a border to seal around the edges later. Top the filling with a little grated cheddar, then brush some of the beaten egg yolk mixture all around the edges. Fold the empty half of each pastry strip up and over the filling, press all around the edges to seal, then crimp with the back of a fork.With a sharp knife, cut a small steam vent in the top of each pie, then transfer them to a lined baking sheet and brush with the remaining egg yolk mixture. Bake the pastries for 30 minutes, until puffed and golden. I like to serve these with a sharply dressed green salad for a crunchy, vinegary contrast. You will probably have a little filling left over, which is perfect for an omelette or toasted sandwich the next day.Vegetarian haggisView image in fullscreenAli Stoner’s vegetarian haggis.I often make a veggie haggis, mainly for pals who are scared by the real deal, and this one really does replicate the original in flavour, texture and looks. It also makes a brilliant filling for “sausage” rolls. After making so many Scottish dishes over the years, I noticed I was using the same herbs and spices on repeat, so I created a blend that represents the essence of Celtic flavours. It is so adaptable that, if you’re anything like me, you will find yourself using it in so many things, from marinades to roast potatoes and everything in between.Prep25 minSoak15 minCook1 hr 10 minServes6For the Scottish seven-spice blend (makes 1 small jar)25gblack peppercorns15g coriander seeds1tbsp juniper berries1tbsp allspice berries1tbsp dried thyme1tbsp dried rosemary1tbsp ground nutmegFor the haggis15g dried mushrooms(porcini or shiitake), diced2tbsp olive oil25gbutter1 brown onion, peeled and finely chopped2 garlic cloves, peeled and minced4 portobello mushrooms, diced2tsp Scottishseven-spice(see above and method)1 tsp white pepper½ teaspoon ground mace2 sprigs fresh sage, leaves picked and finely chopped1 sprigfresh rosemary, leaves picked and finely chopped2 carrots, very finely diced (I use a food processor)75gblack beluga lentils1tbsp yeast extract(Marmite or Vegemite, say)500ml vegetable stock400gcan white beans, drained and choppedFinely grated zest of 1 unwaxed lemonSalt50g steel-cut or pinhead oatsOnion jam, to serve, ideally spiked with a little whisky and warmed (optional)First, make the Scottish seven-spice blend. Toast the peppercorns, coriander seeds, juniper and allspice berries in a dry pan until fragrant, then blitz to a powder in a spice grinder (alternatively, use a pestle and mortar). Add the thyme and rosemary, blend again, then add the ground nutmeg and blend again. Decant into a jar and use freely and creatively whenever you want to add a bit of Celtic flavour.Now for the haggis. Cover the dried mushrooms in about 100ml boiling water and leave to soak for 15 minutes.Put the oil and butter in a saucepan on a low to medium heat, then add the onion and garlic, and saute gently until they start to soften. Add the fresh mushrooms, followed by the drained rehydrated dried mushrooms (save their soaking liquor) and, after a couple of minutes, when they have softened, add all the spices, herbs, carrots, lentils, yeast extract, reserved mushroom liquor and 400ml of the stock. Simmer, stirring frequently, for about 30 minutes, until the lentils are almost soft.Stir the beans and lemon zest into the mix and add a half teaspoon of salt. Test the lentils for “doneness”: they should still have a little bite and most of the liquid should have been absorbed, so if they need more cooking, add the rest of the stock. Add the oats, cook for five to 10 minutes,until they absorb the remaining liquid, then taste and add more salt, if required.Serve with champit tatties (buttery mash studded with sliced spring onions), mashed neeps (swede) and some warm, whisky-spiked onion jam.Chippy batter potato frittersView image in fullscreenAli Stoner’s chippy batter potato fritters.This simple batter gives the most amazing crunch to fish, fritters and even sausages: no fancy ingredients required. The vinegar reacts with the baking powder to produce a light, airy batter, while the cornflour helps with that all-important crunch. You could serve these with tartare sauce, but the pickled onion mayo, inspired by that big jar on the chip-shop counter, works a treat.Prep15 minCook30 minServes4–6For the fritters2 large unpeeled baking potatoes, cut into 5mm-thick slices (I use a mandoline)Plain flour, for dustingVegetable oil, for deep-fryingSaltFor the chippy batter75g plain flour60gcornflour1tsp baking powder½tsp salt2tsp malt vinegarFor the pickled onion mayo (optional)70gpickled onions, roughly chopped, plus 1–2 tbsp of the onion pickling vinegar20gsmall capers, finely chopped1tbsp finely chopped parsley1tbsp finely chopped chives2tbsp mayonnaise1 pinch saltRinse and drain the potato slices, then put them in a pan of salted cold water – if possible, use a wide saute pan, so the slices aren’t piled on top of each other. Bring to a boil, simmer for five minutes, then lift out with a fish slice or large slotted spoon, transfer to a rack and leave to steam dry. Chill uncovered while you make the batter and pickled onion mayo.For the batter, sift the flours, baking powder and salt into a bowl, then gradually whisk in 150ml cold water until incorporated. Add the vinegar and whisk again to combine.For the pickled onion mayo, simply mix all the ingredients in a bowl.Take the potato slices out of the fridge. Put a bowl filled with flour next to your frying station and season it with salt. Heat enough oil for deep-frying in a deep, heavy-based pan or a deep-fat fryer to 180C (350F) (or until a drizzle of batter sizzles and browns immediately). Working in small batches, dip the potato slices first in the seasoned flour, then in the batter, and deep-fry, turning as needed, for up to five minutes in total, until golden and crisp. When they are cooked, the oil will almost stop bubbling and be nearly still – that’s when you know they’re ready. Lift out with a slotted spoon (remove any bits that fall off into the oil, too) and drain on kitchen paper. Season immediately with salt, then keep warm while you fry the rest of the fritters.Get the fritters into buttered rolls, if you like, or serve them just as they are with some pickled onion mayo, and enjoy the crunch.These recipes are edited extracts from Scran: Modern Scottish Food Inspired by Tradition by Ali Stoner, published by Mitchell Beazley at £27. To order a copy for £24.30, go toguardianbookshop.comThe Guardian aims to publish recipes for sustainable seafood. title: From Malaysian chicken to Caribbean crab: four global curry recipes  | Indian food and drink | The Guardian
description: A Japanese fusion-fuelled garlic mushroom doria, an aromatic Malay chicken and squash curry, a rich Rajasthani papad ki sabji, and a Caribbean curry crab with roasted corn and dumplings
Author: Tim Anderson
Headline: A Japanese fusion-fuelled garlic mushroom doria, an aromatic Malay chicken and squash curry, a rich Rajasthani papad ki sabji, and a Caribbean curry crab with roasted corn and dumplings
Content: Mandy Yin’s chicken and squash curry.Photograph: Photography: Laura Edwards/The Guardian. Food styling: Joss Herd. Prop styling: Tabitha Hawkins.Indian food and drinkFrom Malaysian chicken to Caribbean crab: four global curry recipesA Japanese fusion-fuelled garlic mushroomdoria,an aromatic Malay chicken and squash curry, a rich Rajasthanipapad ki sabji,and a Caribbean curry crab with roasted corn and dumplingsTim Anderson,Maunika Gowardhan,.Mandy Yin, Keshia SakarahWed 30 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 30 Sep 2026 08.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMandy Yin’s chicken and squash curry (pictured top)Curry runs through Malaysia’s veins; it’s in every kitchen and at every food stall, whether run by Malays, Chinese or Indians. We tend to cook curries using either a wet spice paste (rempah) straight from the morning market, or a good curry powder – every household keeps a pack ofAdabiorBaba’sin the cupboard as a fallback; we have no shame in this at all. Only when you’ve got time on your hands, or you’re cooking to impress, do you build arempahfrom scratch.My favourite curries come from the Mamak Tamil Muslim cooks behind Malaysia’s all-nightkopitiams, who make the bestroti canaigoing. Go for the roti and the meat curries alongside, washed down withteh tarik– strong black tea sweetened with condensed milk, pulled until it froths.In my cookbook Simply Malaysian, I included my take on Dad’s Mamak lamb and potato curry. He starts with a whole leg, which he bones and trims himself, a heavy hand of curry powder, then the aromatics Malaysians callempat sekawan(the four friends): star anise, cassia, cloves, cardamom. Here, I’ve swapped the lamb for chicken thighs on the bone – they’re cheaper, quicker and what most of us reach for on a weeknight – and the potatoes for butternut squash. Pumpkins and gourds are a staple of Malay cooking, and are most at home in a coconut gravy, though they rarely share a pot with meat. So, squash takes the potatoes’ place and earns its keep, holding its shape and drinking up the sauce.A word on the meat. In Malaysia we cook it in the curry it’s going to be served in – not seared or simmered separately and folded in at the end – so the two season each other the whole way. And we cook it on the bone, always: bone-in gives a richer, glossier sauce than any fillet will. Like all curries, this eats even better the next day, once the flavours have settled. If you’re not eating it straight away, reduce the cooking time in the penultimate step to 10 minutes (to allow the squash to finish cooking when reheating it). Any leftover sauce eaten with rice and a fried egg or two is one of life’s simple pleasures.Prep15 minCook45 minServes4-61 medium onion,peeled and roughly chopped4 garlic cloves,peeled1 inch (2½cm) piece ginger,peeled and roughly chopped5 tbsp vegetable or peanut oil¾ tbsp table salt4 tbsp Adabi meat curry powder –alternatively, combine 1 tbsp chilli powder, 1 tbsp ground coriander, 1 tbsp ground turmeric, 1 tsp finely ground black pepper and 2 tsp ground cumin½ tsp chilli powder1 star anise4 cloves1 stick cassia bark,or ½ cinnamon stick2 green cardamom pods,lightly bashed with a pestle to crack the skin1kg skinless, bone-in chicken thighs200gtinned chopped tomatoes,or fresh tomatoes, roughly chopped1butternut squash,or part of a pumpkin, peeled, deseeded and cut into 3cm x 2cm chunks (approximately 800-850g)200ml coconut milk30g bunchcoriander,finely chopped stalks and all (optional)Emiko Davies’ Japanese curry rice (kare raisu) – recipeRead moreFinely chop the onion, garlic and ginger in a food processor. Heat the oil in a large, non-stick wok/saucepan or a deep casserole dish over a medium heat, then add the onion-garlic mix and salt, and stir-fry for five minutes, until softened.Turn the heat down to medium-low, then add the curry powder, chilli powder, star anise, cloves, cassia and cardamom, and stir-fry for two minutes. Add a splash of water if the spices start to catch on the bottom of the pan.Add the chicken thighs and turn them through the paste, until every piece is coated. Pour in 200ml water and the tomatoes, stir, then bring up to a boil. Lower the heat to medium-low, cover and simmer for 15 minutes, turning the thighs and stirring every five minutes.Add the squash/pumpkin and coconut milk, then cover and bring back to a boil over a medium heat. Check in every few minutes to see whether it has come up to a boil, and give it a stir. Take your time, as the chicken and squash slowly release their juices into the sauce, so you end up with enough liquid to keep almost everything submerged.Once boiling, lower the heat to medium-low and cook, uncovered, for 15 minutes, stirring every few minutes and nudging the squash carefully back under the sauce. Turn the heat off, stir through the coriander and serve with plenty of rice.Simply Malaysian by Mandy Yin is published by Quadrille at £27. To order a copy for £24.30, visitguardianbookshop.comKeshia Sakarah’s curry crab, roasted corn and cassava dumplingsView image in fullscreenWhen most people think of curry, they probably don’t think of the Caribbean, yet many of our dishes incorporate spices in a variety of ways. While they aren’t native or indigenous ingredients, they are now very much part of daily life.They were introduced to the region by the indentured labourers from the Indian subcontinent. Their use of spices in this new part of the world transformed the cuisine in many ways, using ground spices to flavour slow-cooked meat and fish, or toasting whole ones in oil to finish vegetables, and brought about a brand-new cooking style.I’ve eaten curry throughout my life, and thinking of my love for it unearths many fond memories: when I’m at Notting Hill carnival, I have to support my favourite food stands off Kensal Road. And then there are my many visits to the Caribbean. Experiencing curry on different islands, in a variety of ways, always piques my curiosity; it speaks to the cultural layers of the region and how the Caribbean really is a microcosm of the many communities that make up the world. In Guadeloupe, I triedcolombo– a classic French Caribbean curry (usually chicken or fish), which incorporates toasted, ground rice into the spices and lots of lime juice into the sauce. Unlike the curries of the anglophone islands (Jamaica, Antigua, Grenada, for example), it is more acidic and paler in complexion, yet still served with rice and beans. In Trinidad, home to one of the largest Indo-Caribbean communities, curry is a staple, originally found mostly in homes, but now also in roti shops across the island. Some of the best are in central Trinidad, where generations of Indian communities have settled for generations.Prep10 minRest30 minCook55 minServes4For the cassava dumplings125g cassava flour125g plain flour1⅛tsp fine sea salt,plus extra for cooking the dumplings½tsp baking powder1 tbsp olive pomace or rapeseed oil, plus extra for cooking the dumplings180ml cold waterFor the green seasoning2 spring onions6 garlic cloves,peeled5cm piece ginger15g flat-leaf parsley,leaves and stalks30g coriander,leaves and stalks75ml cold water1 lime,juiced2tbsp rapeseed oilFor the curry base2 fresh corn cobs3tbsp ghee or rapeseed oil2tbsp curry powder2tsp ground turmeric4tsp garam masala oramchar masala1 scotch bonnet,pierced600ml good-quality coconut milk290gwhite crab meatCombine all the ingredients for the cassava dumplings in a bowl, then knead to form a soft dough; set aside to rest for 30 minutes.Blend all the green seasoning ingredients apart from the oil in a blender until almost smooth, then transfer to a jar and stir in the oil.Roast the corn cobs over an open flame or under a hot grill, turning occasionally, until charred all over; set aside to cool. Once cool enough to handle, slice off the kernels and set aside, discarding the husks.For the curry base, heat the ghee/oil in a pan set over a medium heat. Add the spices and toast lightly for 30 seconds to a minute. Add 200ml cold water and gently boil for three to four minutes, then add two tablespoons of the green seasoning, the scotch bonnet and half the grilled corn, and mix well.Tip in the coconut milk, increase the heat until lightly boiling, then reduce to a simmer and cook for 10-12 minutes, until the sauce looks smooth and emulsified.Meanwhile, divide the dumpling dough into 32 equal pieces, then roll into balls. Place them spaced out on a tray, dusting with a little extra flour if they’re sticky. Cover with a tea towel and set aside.Bring a pan of water to the boil, then add a teaspoon of salt and a teaspoon of oil. Once boiling, cook the dumplings in batches for eight to 10 minutes, or until they float. Remove from the pan with a slotted spoon to a bowl of cold water (they will cook further in the curry later).To finish the curry, give the pan another stir – it should have reduced and thickened slightly. Remove the scotch bonnet and discard, then pour the curry into a blender and blitz smooth. Pass through a sieve, then return the liquid to the pan.Put over a medium-high heat, add the cooked dumplings, then reduce to a low simmer and cook foreight to 10 minutes, until the dumplings are soft and have absorbed some of the colour from the curry. Remove from the heat and gently fold in the crab meat, ensuring it doesn’t break up. Finish with the remaining grilled corn and a few more drops of the green seasoning, then serve.Caribe by Keshia Sakarah is published by Hardie Grant at £30. To order a copy for £27, visitguardianbookshop.comTim Anderson’s garlic mushroom currydoria(Japanese rice gratin)View image in fullscreenTim Anderson’s garlic mushroom curry doria (Japanese rice gratin).Japan’s currydoria– also known as yaki-curry, or baked curry – is one of my all-time favourite blank-slate meal formats. It is essentially a rice gratin, containing plump grains of Japanese short-grain rice smothered in smooth Japanese curry sauce, all tucked under a luxurious duvet of molten cheese. In other words, a masterclass in comfort cookery.Because its core elements are so amenably mellow in terms of flavour, the curry doria format works with just about any veg or protein you like, or whatever’s in season. But I like to lean into its heartiness with rich, meaty ingredients, such as the mushrooms and greens I’ve used here, along with a liberal dose of garlic and butter, inspired by old-school baked mushroom starters.Prep10 minCook45 minServes4Butter,as needed4 portions cooked Japanese rice (300g uncooked)400g mushrooms –I love oyster mushrooms, but use any you like4 garlic clovesSalt and black pepper100g mustard greens or chard,coarsely chopped1 pack (around 90g) Japanese curry roux50g grated mozzarella50g grated medium or mild cheddar50g grated Emmental1 small handfulflat-leaf parsley,finely choppedSome kind of crunchy onion product,such as cheese and onion crisps, onion rings, or fried shallots (Ihighlyrecommend the brand Wild Rice), to garnishRub a medium baking dish (around 23cm square,) with butter. Pack the cooked rice into the bottom of the dish in an even layer, using a bit of force so it’s relatively dense – if it has too many air gaps, the curry sauce will flow into it, and the gratin will become more stodgy than saucy.Then, prepare the mushrooms. Oyster mushrooms,shimeji, or ordinary white or chestnut mushrooms can simply be broken into bite-size pieces; smaller mushrooms like buttons and chanterelles can be left whole; shiitake should be de-stemmed; and if you are using any long, tough mushrooms like king oysters orenoki, they should be chopped into roughly 1-inch chunks. Remember to clean any wild mushrooms so they’re free of dirt or grit before cooking.Peel and chop the garlic, sprinkle it with salt, then continue to mince it finely, and drag the side of your knife through it, to smash it into a coarse paste; the salt will help soften the garlic and draw out its pungent oils.In a wide saute pan, melt a generous knob of butter over a medium-high heat, then add the garlic, mushrooms, greens, and a few grinds of pepper. Toss them through the butter, then cook without stirring for four to five minutes, so the mushrooms brown on one side. Remove from the heat, then scrape everything out of the pan and on to the rice in the baking dish. Heat the oven to 220C (200C fan)/425F/gas 7.In the same pan you used to saute the mushrooms, prepare the curry sauce according to packet instructions – but don’t add any additional meat or veg, if it calls for them. Once the sauce is cooked out and smooth, pour this over the mushrooms and rice.Top with the cheeses and bake for about 20 minutes, until browned on top. Serve piping hot, garnished with a little chopped parsley and a scattering of the crunchy onion product of your choosing.Japanese Curry by Tim Anderson is published in October by Quadrille at £14.99. To order a copy for £13.49, visitguardianbookshop.comMaunika Gowardhan’s rajasthanipapad ki sabjiView image in fullscreenAlthough I grew up in Mumbai, I hail from a family with roots in theKonkaniand western coastal region sprawled across the Deccan Plateau in India. Dishes from this region are robust, hearty and we celebrate curries with warmth, aroma, and complex flavours.Travelling across India, the food changes within regions and reflects the ingredients available, the seasons and changes in climate. But this is one of my favourite curries from the state of Rajasthan. Papad ki sabji is a staple in homes across the north-west of India and primarily made with turmeric, coriander and fenugreek in a rich gravy simmered with cooked papad (poppadum). This dish is often served in a Rajasthani thali, which is vibrant and delicious, but it is also served as a weekday curry with plain rice.Yoghurt added to the curry is cooling and lends richness to the gravy. Traditionally, the papad is deep-fried but my recipe uses roast papads, which can be done in the microwave in just a few seconds (follow the packet instructions for cooking the papad). The charred edges on the papad lend a lot of flavour to the curry.Prep10 minCook30 minServes44 garlic cloves,peeled and roughly chopped1inch (2½cm) piece ginger,peeled and roughly chopped1 small bird’s eye green chilli,deseeded if you prefer less heat100gtomatoes,roughly chopped1 tbsp tomato puree3 tbsp vegetable oil or ghee½ tsp cumin seedsA pinch of asafoetida1 tbsp coriander powder1 tsp turmeric powder1 tsp Kashmiri chilli powder250gGreek yoghurt,whisked well (make sure there are no lumps; this way it won’t split as it cooks)Salt2 tbspdried fenugreek leaves(kasoori methi)4 roasted papads/poppadumFresh coriander,to garnishPut the garlic, ginger, green chilli and a splash of water in a blender and blend to a smooth, fine paste; set aside.In the same blender, blend the tomato and tomato puree to a paste.Heat the oil in a heavy-based nonstick saucepan over a low heat. Add the cumin seeds and asafoetida, and fry for two seconds. Add the garlic/ginger paste and fry for 20 seconds, then add the blended tomatoes and cook for six minutes, stirring well.As the oil leaves the sides of the pan, add the powdered spices and fry for a minute. Tip in the yoghurt a little at a time, stirring well, then cook and stir on a low heat for three to four minutes.Add 300ml water, season to taste and simmer for six to eight minutes. Add the fenugreek leaves, along with the roasted papad and cook, covered, for two minutes. Garnish with coriander and serve with rice.Curry by Maunika Gowardhan is published by Quadrille at £26.
